units: the inner circulation of the tree starts up again at the end of the cold season
the nourishing liquid climbs from the root system toward the top of the tree
the pressure gap between waterlogged ground and dry air drives that climb
a very thin living tissue under the protective layer of the trunk carries this liquid
the growth organs open and release a folded blade
during the warm season the foliage makes sugary reserves
the tree stores these reserves in its trunk and its roots
in the season of falling leaves the foliage loses its green coloring
through the cold season the tree keeps a faint breathing
the cycle repeats only if the base of the trunk stays healthy and water keeps coming
text: When the cold finally loosens its grip, a tree sets to work where nobody can see it. Sap climbs out of the roots and up toward the highest branches, driven by the gap in pressure between soaked ground and the dry air above. Just under the bark, a thin sleeve of living cells carries that sweet flow upward. One by one the buds swell, split open, and let out a leaf folded tight like a fan. Through the warm months those leaves manufacture sugars, and the tree banks them away in its trunk and its roots. Come the season of falling leaves, the green drains out of them and they let go. Winter looks like sleep, yet the tree still breathes, faintly, living off what it put by. The whole round begins again as long as the base of the trunk stays sound and the roots find water deep enough down.

units: someone the narrator knows told him about an incident in his hedge
he had seen a round opening dug under a shrub
he closed that opening with a slab of rock to drive off a small mammal
the leaves of the shrub yellowed about two weeks after it was blocked
the underground tunnel was in fact draining rain water away
closing it turned the base of the hedge into a hollow where water stood
the roots, cut off from air, wasted away
he took the slab off and dug a channel to carry the water out
the shrub got its vigor back the following season
text: An acquaintance of mine described what went wrong in his hedge, and the story has stayed with me ever since. He had found a neat round hole dug under one of the shrubs, so he laid a flat slab of rock over it to drive off the small animal he blamed for it. About two weeks later, the leaves on that shrub yellowed and curled. The tunnel, it turned out, had been draining the place: rainwater vanished down into it. Once the mouth was plugged, the ground under the hedge became a shallow basin, water stagnated there, and the roots suffocated for want of air. He removed the slab again and excavated a channel to carry the water away. By the next growing season the shrub had all its strength back. He regards holes differently now, wondering what the animal had worked out about that soil long before he did.

units: a sharp drop in temperature at the end of the cold season can destroy an orchard crop in one night
ice crystals damage the open blossom and the new shoots
watching the sky in the evening is advised, to judge the danger
no cloud and no wind are signs of high risk
watering the ground moderately before the temperature falls helps it hold heat
wrapping the vulnerable trunks in a breathable cloth, without tightening it, is recommended
no cutting at all should be done on the branches at this time
any cut makes a wound that the cold makes worse
at sunrise the frosted branches should be sprayed with lukewarm water, little by little
writing the episode down is advised, to keep the memory of the seasons
text: A hard freeze late in the cold season can wipe out an orchard crop overnight, since the ice burns the open blossom and the shoots that have just come out. Here is how to hold the damage down. Look at the sky first, in the evening: no cloud and no wind, and the danger is high. Water the ground lightly before the temperature falls, because damp earth takes heat in and gives it back through the night. Wrap the trunks that are most at risk in a cloth that breathes, loosely, so the air can still move around them. Cut nothing at all in this stretch of the year, since every cut leaves behind a wound that the cold will make worse. At sunrise, spray the frosted branches with lukewarm water, little by little. Then write the whole episode down, so the memory of the seasons is not lost.

units: one side of the valley is covered with dense forest growth
there you find a bed of rotting plant matter and a smell of organic soil
the opposite side still carries the marks of felling done long ago
on that bare side the stone shows and water cuts grooves in it
the thin grassy cover there does not hold the nourishing layer
a member of staff in charge of the sector takes visitors from one side to the other
she explains that under the trees water sinks into the ground instead of running off the surface
the water point at the bottom of the valley is still flowing at the end of the hot season
gradual planting has been started on the stripped side, with species whose roots spread wide
the result will not be visible for several decades
text: On one side of the valley the forest has closed over everything: close-packed trunks, a deep bed of rotting leaves, a smell of damp earth that clings to your fingers. The far slope still carries the scars of the felling carried out there long ago. Bare stone shows through, rainfall gouges grooves down it, and the thin grass cannot keep the fertile layer in place. A warden who looks after the sector escorts visitors from the one side across to the other. Under the trees, she says, water sinks straight in instead of running off, and the spring at the foot of the valley is still flowing at the end of the hot season. On the stripped slope, replanting has begun, shrub by shrub, with species chosen for roots that spread wide. What comes of it will not show for several decades yet.

units: the outermost layer is thin and greasy and limits water loss
the middle layer holds lime salts and provides the strength
the inner layer, more pliable, serves as an anchor for the muscles
plates set across the back keep the organs out of harm
the jointed segments of the rear part allow the animal to curl up
the joints of the limbs bend in one direction only
sensing hairs lodged in fine pits pick up movement in the water around it
the drawback of this casing is that it cannot get any bigger
the animal must leave its casing from time to time and wait for the new one to harden
through this fragile period it hides under a stone
text: A crustacean's shell reads like a suit of armor put together piece by piece. Its outermost layer is thin and waxy, and it keeps the water inside from escaping. Underneath lies a stiffer layer, saturated with lime salts, which gives the whole casing its strength. A third layer, more pliable, lines the inside and gives the muscles something to pull against. Plates across the back shield the organs. The jointed rings of the tail let the animal curl in on itself. The legs bend on hinges that work one way only. Fine sensory hairs, set in minute pits, pick up every stir in the water around it. All of this carries one flaw: it cannot grow. Every so often the animal has to climb out of its own casing and wait for the replacement to harden. While it is still soft, it hides itself away beneath a stone.

units: the writer finds the lack of response to the retreat of pollinating insects unacceptable
the first warnings sat in field observations that were ignored some thirty years ago
successive counts then established a steady fall in numbers
fruit growers saw that the fertilizing grains were spreading badly
orchards had to fall back on artificial fertilization, costly and unreliable
the writer holds that the burden of proof should change hands
he demands that harmful practice prove it does no damage
strips of flowers along the edge of a plot are named as a cheap remedy
keeping hedges and mowing less often are among the solutions put forward
text: Nothing excuses how little has been done about the retreat of the insects that carry pollen. The first warnings sat there in field notes taken a generation ago, and nobody judged them worth reading. Then came the counts, one after another, each of them showing fewer insects than the one before. Then the fruit growers saw that pollen was no longer traveling as it should, and that their orchards had to be pollinated by hand, an expensive procedure, and an unreliable one. We have reached the point where the burden of proof should change hands. It is not for naturalists to prove the danger, it is for harmful practice to prove that it does no harm. A strip of flowers along the edge of a plot costs next to nothing. Nor does leaving a hedge standing, or mowing the grass less often.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman who runs a place producing young trees had no plans for that trade
she was studying the chemical make-up of soils
a disease striking the young plants of her area changed her path
the seedlings were dying with no visible cause
her examination of the roots turned up a parasitic organism tied to too much watering
she urged watering less often, even at the cost of losing the weakest stock
the growers doubted her at first, then applied her advice
the death rate among the young plants dropped by fifty percent
she was given a nursery to run and set up full tracking of every batch there
she now passes her experience on to beginners
text: The woman who runs a nursery for forest trees had never intended to end up in that trade at all. She was studying the chemistry of soils when a disease swept through the young trees of her district, and that turned her whole path around. Seedlings were dying with nothing visible to account for it, so she dug up the roots and identified a fungus that flourished wherever the watering ran too generous. Her recommendation was blunt: water less often, and accept the loss of the weakest stock. The growers doubted her at first, then did as she said, and mortality among the young trees fell by half. That success earned her a nursery of her own to manage, where she set up a record for every batch, from the seed to the planting out. These days she passes on what she knows to beginners.

units: the narrator was let down by her first visit to an observation trail
the signs gave nothing but scientific names, without saying what to look at
a remarkable pond was hidden by tall growth and was not signposted
she came back after the trail had been overhauled
half the signs have been replaced by questions
an opening has been cleared toward the pond
a low seat has been put in for watching the young water insects
the trail now teaches you to spot the traces animals leave
what is missing is a shortened route suited to families with a stroller
text: My first walk along that observation trail was a genuine disappointment. The signs listed scientific names one after another and never once told you where to put your eyes. A fine pond lay a few steps off the path, hidden away behind a curtain of tall reeds, and nothing pointed to it. I went back once the whole trail had been rebuilt. Half the signs are gone, replaced by questions. An opening has been cleared through toward the pond. A low bench has been installed there, so that you can watch the young insects dart about under the surface. And the trail teaches you at last to read what the animals leave behind, the tuft caught on a thorn, the flattened grass, the bark scraped raw. What it still lacks is a shorter loop, with no steps and no loose gravel, for families pushing a stroller.

units: the writer of the letter writes from her garden to a friend
she compares two planted areas she had already spoken about
the area higher up gets sun from dawn to dusk
the soil there dries out fast and the stems are short and thick
the flowers in the upper area open early and wilt within seven days
the lower area is sheltered by a wall and gets no sun before midday
the plants in the lower area are taller and flower twice as long
the gap comes mainly from how much water the soil holds, since watering and feeding are the same
a rose bush moved from the dry area to the damp one doubled in size in one season
she invites her friend to come before the cold arrives
text: Dear friend, I am writing from the far end of the garden to describe those two beds I mentioned to you. The upper one takes the sun from first light until it goes down again. The soil there dries out quickly, the stems come up short and thickset, and the flowers open early but wither within a week. The lower bed sits against a wall and sees no sun at all before midday. Everything there grows taller and more tender, and the flowering there lasts roughly twice as long. The difference comes down to how much water the ground holds, since I water the two beds in exactly the same way and feed them with the same compost. I moved a rose bush from the dry bed over to the damp one, and it doubled in size within a single season. Come and see the difference for yourself before the cold weather arrives.

units: the renewal of the body covering is presented as a rebuild and not a simple abandonment
in the snake the old casing comes away in a single piece
the snake's eyes go cloudy before this change
the snake rubs against a rough surface to start the tear
in birds the replacement goes part by part, so that the power of flight is kept
the light new plumage grows under the old one and pushes it out
in insects the young stage breaks down almost entirely to form a winged adult
a damaged casing no longer offers protection
an old casing does not adjust to a gain in size
worn plumage gives poor shelter from the cold
text: What is going on when an animal leaves its old skin behind? Molting is not a costume dropped on the floor, it is a rebuild from the ground up. A snake sheds its covering in a single piece. Its eyes cloud over first, and then it rubs itself against something rough to start the tear. A bird renews its covering one feather at a time, so that the power of flight is never lost, and the fresh down grows in underneath until the old feather drops away. In an insect the change goes further still, the young stage breaking down almost entirely and putting itself back together as a winged adult. Why go to such trouble? Because a damaged casing no longer protects, because an old one will not stretch to fit a body that keeps on growing, and because worn feathers hold in hardly any warmth at all.

units: the person leading the group states that the moisture does not fall from the sky
during the dark hours the ground surface loses its heat by radiation
that surface ends up colder than the air touching it
the moisture in the air turns into fine drops on the chilled plants
a woman in the group reports that she saw no such deposit the day before
the stirring of the air by the wind had prevented the cooling
a cover of cloud sends the heat back down
the whitish veil at the bottom of the valley comes from the same mechanism
text: The guide stops at the edge of the trail and asks her group to look down at the flattened grass. Dew never falls out of the sky, she tells them, contrary to what most walkers imagine. Throughout the darkness the ground radiates the heat it holds toward an open sky, and its surface ends up colder than the air resting against it. The moisture suspended in that air condenses into tiny beads along the chilled blades. One woman interrupts: she observed nothing of the kind the previous morning. Wind, the guide answers: it kept stirring the air, so nothing had the opportunity to cool. Cloud behaves identically, she adds, reflecting the heat back down toward the ground. And when a pale veil lingers in the hollow of the valley, that is the very same process again, spread through an entire layer of air.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the growers of older generations could do nothing against the rising water
the rising water destroyed the young plants and the pens
storage buildings were sometimes carried away
people noticed that the harvests were better once the water had pulled back
the muddy deposit fed the worked ground better than animal manure
the aim became keeping the fertility without taking the destruction
feeder channels steered the flood toward shallow basins
banks were raised along the shores
adjustable openings let the water in at the chosen moment
farm production stopped being left to chance
text: You are probably wondering what the growers of older generations did when the river swelled and came over. Not much. They took it. The flood tore out the seedlings, drowned the pens, and now and then carried off a whole storehouse. Then somebody noticed an odd thing: wherever the water had pulled back, the next harvest came in richer than before. The mud left lying there fed the worked ground better than any animal manure. So the trick was to keep hold of the fertility and skip the wreckage. The answer arrived piece by piece. They dug channels that steered the flood into shallow basins. They raised packed banks of clay along the shores. They cut gates that two men could open at the hour they chose. The water came in, dropped its load, and drained away on its own. Farming stopped being left to chance.

units: two agents shape the stones of a valley in different ways
running water knocks the blocks together and wears them down by friction
the stones carried by the water become rounded and smooth
running water sorts its deposits by size along its course
ice carries its load without rolling it
the fragments left behind by ice keep their cutting edges
deposits from ice mix huge pieces with very fine material
a specialist recognizes where a deposit came from by its look
this distinction makes it possible to rebuild the past of a slope with no clue left
text: Two agents shape the stones of a valley, and they do not go about the work in the same way. Running water rolls its blocks along the bed, knocks them into one another, and wears them down by steady friction; what comes out of it is round, smooth, and sorted by size all the way down the course. Ice rolls nothing at all. It carries its load like a slow belt and drops it just as it was, so the fragments keep their cutting edges and lie jumbled together, a huge piece sitting beside a smear of clay dust. A specialist tells the two deposits apart at a single glance. Where water did the work, the grains match one another and settle into clean layers. Where ice passed over, the sediment stays chaotic. That contrast lets you rebuild the past of a slope when nothing visible is left of it.

units: a child regularly brought back finds picked up in a wood
she arranged her feathers by shade, from the darkest to the palest
the shells she brought home were fragile enough to break in her hand
she smelled the pieces of bark after rubbing them
a violent gust had brought down a tree during the cold season
since that tree came down she also picked up splinters of pale wood
her collection of stones held three distinct kinds of rock
her elder did not keep these objects herself
that woman provided her with a container and listened to her descriptions
text: The child came back from the wood with her pockets sagging, and nobody ever knew what she would pull out of them. Feathers came first, laid out in a row by shade, from the darkest to the palest. Then the empty shells, so thin that they cracked open in her palm. Then strips of bark, which she rubbed and held under her nose for the smell of resin and rain. A hard gust had brought down a beech in the cold season, and ever since she carried home splinters of pale wood torn from the split trunk. Last of all, right at the bottom, lay the stones: a streaked pebble, a lump of milky quartz, a piece of shale that peeled apart between her fingers. Her grandmother kept none of it herself. She lent out a box, listened to the account of every piece, and waited for the next haul to come in.

units: the test plot must be marked out on an even, uncovered slope
a stiff border driven in along three sides stands slightly above the ground
the side that lies downhill is fitted with a tilted channel
the water collected ends up in a buried container carrying graduations
the amount caught is read off as soon as a shower ends
a sample is taken after the contents have been stirred
the suspended matter is left to settle before being dried and weighed
the slope and the look of the surface are written down
repeating the measurement gives the solid matter carried off by the surface flow
putting in a plant cover brings that value down
text: Begin on an even slope with no dense cover growing on it, and mark off a square plot with stakes. Drive a metal border into the ground along three of its sides, so that it stands a hand's height above the surface. On the downhill side, fit a tilted trough that carries the water into a marked jug set down in a pit. Now wait for a shower. The moment it stops, record the volume collected, stir the contents thoroughly, then draw a sample into a clean bottle. Let the mud settle overnight, pour off the clear water, dry the residue and weigh it. Write down the slope of the plot and the condition of its surface. Repeat this measurement after every shower and you will have the solid load the runoff carries away, and you will watch that figure drop as soon as plant cover takes hold.

units: a crack several paces long has appeared at the edge of a farmed plateau
the administration has closed the way that runs across this plateau
specialists put the opening down to a run of downpours out of the ordinary
the water working its way in has soaked a clay bed lying under the fields
that soaked bed has lost its ability to hold what it carries
the mass lying above it has begun to move down toward the slope
the failure of a poorly drained retaining structure sped up the sliding
the farmers fear the loss of the water point meant for their livestock
the crack diverts part of the underground movement of the water
measuring instruments will be put in before the rainy period
text: A crack several paces long opened this week along the flank of a farmed plateau, forcing the authorities to close the track that runs across it. The geologists sent out to survey the site attribute the opening to a succession of downpours well out of the ordinary. Water working its way underground has soaked a bed of clay buried beneath the fields; once saturated, that bed lost its grip on the load above, and the ground began to creep toward the bank. The movement, at first too slow to notice, picked up speed when a poorly drained retaining wall gave way. The farmers now fear for the spring that waters their livestock, since the fissure is turning aside part of the underground flow. Measuring instruments will be put in place before the wet season to follow how far the break advances.

units: past a low bridge the river meets a shoulder of rock and changes direction
a standing whirlpool digs itself in at that spot
the inner side of the bend piles up fine sand
the outer side loses about the width of a hand every rainy period
the roots of the trees on the bank end up hanging in open air
one rise in the water is enough to bring down a tree left bare
the people living along the river ruled out the use of concrete
living stakes were driven in at an angle and then linked by a weave of branches
the wood taking hold and rooting slows the water and holds the bank
text: Past a low bridge the river runs into a shoulder of rock and swings sharply aside. A standing whirlpool has dug itself in there, dark at the center, ringed with brown foam. On the inside of the bend fine sand keeps building up, while the outer bank gives back about the width of a hand every rainy season. The alder roots end up hanging in open air, and once a rise in the water strips them, the tree goes over. The people living along the river ruled out pouring concrete on the bank. They drove living willow stakes in at a slant where the water bites hardest, then wove supple branches between them. The wood takes hold, the roots stitch the soil together, and the current loses its force among the drowned leaves. The whirlpool remains, but it now digs the bed instead of eating the bank.

units: the writer invites the reader to set two ways of handling a river side by side
the first approach boxes the river in with a straightened bed and hardened banks
that approach means raising the protective works at every warning
when that arrangement gives way, the body of water goes faster and higher than in its natural state
the second approach hands back to the river surfaces that can flood
it means pulling the buildings back and accepting that uninhabited fields go under
the spreading slows the water and drops the fertile matter in a useful place
the writer grants that the second option calls for giving up land that is owned
he judges that the first option forces endless spending and costs at the worst moment
text: Honestly, we would do well to set two ways of handling a river side by side before picking ours. The first boxes it in: straighten the bed, harden the banks, raise the levees another notch at every warning. That works, right up to the moment it stops working, and then the water goes all at once, faster and higher than it ever would have without us. The second way looks far less impressive. You hand the river back its floodable meadows, pull the works back, and accept that fields with nobody on them will go under. The water spreads, slows, and drops its silt where it enriches instead of wrecking. I know the second choice means giving up land you own, and giving up has never pleased anyone. But the first commits us to raising the stakes forever, and its bill lands at the worst possible moment.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: this water specialist comes from a family of river boatmen
those in charge of water retention works call on her
her working life falls into three parts
she long drew loaded water from a cradle slung above the current
those samples served to measure the matter the river carries off
she worked out a low-cost way of separating grains
poorly equipped teams took up that method
she trains beginners by sending them into the field before the theory
those around her describe her as rough but always there in an emergency
text: Nothing marked out a boatman's daughter to become the hydrologist that the keepers of dams now call on for advice. Her working life falls into three distinct parts. There is the field first: she spent whole seasons scooping muddy water out of the middle of the current, slung in a cradle suspended above it, to weigh what the river was carrying off. Then the laboratory, where she worked out a way of sorting grains so inexpensive that far-off teams with no money for equipment took it up. Last comes the passing on: every season she takes in beginners and sends them wading through the silt long before she opens a manual for them. Those close to her describe a blunt woman, sparing with her praise, and quite unable to turn down a call in the night when a bank threatens to give way.

units: the visit begins in a room with almost no lighting
the sound of a hard wind surrounds the visitor while cloud shadows slide across the floor
the next room shows upright cores of deposits in cases
the pale and dark bands of those cores render the alternation of the seasons
the writer judges the explanatory gallery to be the weakest part
he faults the panels for restating what the objects already show
the last room displays a wet clay surface that dries out during the visit
the cracking of that surface makes a sound that can be heard in the quiet
the writer holds that a still image could not have rendered this ageing of matter
text: The exhibition opens in a room with almost no light, and the choice makes sense from the doorway onward, because you listen before you see. A gale turns around you while the shadows of clouds slide across the floor. The second room lights its cases at last: cores of sediment standing upright like columns, layered in pale and dark bands that tell of dry seasons and wet ones. After that comes a more instructive gallery, the weakest stretch by far, where too many panels repeat what the objects had already said better. The last room makes up for everything. A wall of wet clay, lit from the side, dries as you watch and splits open during the visit; the cracking carries in the quiet. You come out feeling you have seen matter grow old, which no photograph could ever have given you.

units: the writer is writing to a friend from a shared garden
the young plants were no longer coming up out of the seed
the surface of the ground had hardened into a tight crust
water slid off toward a drainage ditch instead of soaking down to the roots
a grower from a nearby plot suggested a tried remedy
the soil material was sifted to take out the stones
an organic amendment was mixed in to keep water available
the surface is broken up after every watering
the plants came up after about three weeks
text: Dear friend, I am writing from the shared garden I told you about back in the spring. For weeks nothing came up. The seed stayed shut and none of us could figure out what was holding it. Then we looked closer. The top of the bed had baked into a hard crust, and every drop we poured ran sideways into the drainage ditch instead of sinking down to the roots. A grower from the plot next door told us what he does. We put the soil through a sieve and picked out the stones, then worked in well rotted compost, which holds moisture without smothering anything small. Now we scratch the surface open after every watering. About three weeks later the first leaves broke through, thick and green. I will send you a picture of the row once it fills in. Write back and tell me whether your balcony has finally given you anything.

units: an insect specialist compares two kinds of pollinators
kept colonies hold a very large number of workers
kept foragers travel long distances
wild species nest on their own in hollow stems or sandy banks
wild species range over a small radius
wild species work flowers the others pass over
the specialist will not name one kind as better
an orchard leaning on hives alone gives an uneven crop
ground with few flowers defeats both kinds
text: So are wild bees worth as much as kept bees when it comes to pollination? The question comes up again and again, and an insect specialist I put it to answered me with a comparison. Hive bees go out in huge numbers, thousands of workers to a colony, and they will fly a long way for a crop. Their strength is sheer weight of bodies. Wild bees do the opposite. Each one nests alone in a hollow stem or a sandy bank, stays close to home, and works the flowers the others pass over. Their strength is precision. So which one do you pick? Neither, she said, laughing. An orchard leaning on hives alone brings in an uneven crop, since a share of the blossom opens on cold days, when the hive stays shut. Then she put a limit on all of it. On ground with no wild flowers left, she said, neither kind will hold out.

units: the head of a laboratory presents her monitoring beside a body of water
she lists the signs used to judge a stream
insect larvae living under the stones are the first sign
the loss of those larvae points to pollution
algae spreading over the bottom betrays fertilizer coming off farmland
a bright floating object serves to gauge the speed of the current
the state of the banks is among the signs people overlook
a bank without plants gives way at the first rise in water
bankside shrubs hold the soil and shelter birds
a proper reading calls for repeated visits
text: The head of the laboratory meets us at the edge of a shallow pond with a hand lens ready. She runs through the signs her team looks for when it judges whether a stream is healthy. Start with the insects clinging under the stones, she says. Their larvae cannot cope with fouled water, so a bare stone bed points to pollution. Next comes the algae coating the bottom. Once that coat thickens, fertilizer has leached in from the fields upslope. Third is the speed of the current, which a bright float will gauge well enough. Then she names a sign that hardly anyone bothers with, the bank itself. A bare edge slumps away with the first rise in the water, while a bank held by shrubs keeps its soil and shelters the birds that nest close to the surface. None of this, she finishes, shows up in a single visit.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: a glass worker notices the magnifying effect of a curved piece of glass
clear stones were shaped and rubbed smooth to read fine writing
wooden frames were made to hold the gap between the eye and the lens
those frames left the hands free
a lens maker set two glasses one above the other inside a tube
that stacking raised the magnification further
tiny living things were seen in standing water
living beings inside a single drop astonished the learned
color faults along the rim were corrected as the craft improved
the instrument ended up making the basic unit of life visible
text: Long before anyone thought to call it science, a glass worker noticed that a swollen chip of glass thickened the threads of the cloth beneath it. Curiosity did the rest. Clear stones were ground and rubbed smooth so that cramped writing could be read at last. Wooden frames followed, holding the glass a fixed distance from the eye and leaving both hands free. Then a lens maker set two glasses one above the other inside a tube, and the image swelled further still. A patient watcher turned such a tube on stale water and found tiny creatures twitching in it. That a whole living thing could fit inside one drop shook the learned men of the day. Later hands polished better and cleared away the colored fringes that blurred the rim, until the glass gave up the cell itself. What the naked eye withheld, the glass granted.

units: a dried seed puts its biological activity on hold
that state lets it survive extreme conditions
taking up water swells the tissues and splits the protective coat
the arrival of water wakes enzymes
those enzymes turn the stored starch into usable sugars
the root heads downward under gravity
the shoot grows in the opposite direction
mild warmth speeds the work of the enzymes
excessive heat wrecks the enzymes and halts emergence
waterlogged ground drives out the oxygen and rots the seedling
text: A dry seed does nothing at all. Its chemistry is on hold, and in that state it comes through cold and drought that would kill a growing plant outright. Let moisture through the coat and the tissues swell until the pressure splits the shell. The water also wakes a set of enzymes, and these break the stored starch down into sugars the embryo can burn. Growth follows. A root pushes down, pulled that way by gravity, while a shoot climbs the other way. Warmth speeds the whole business up, since enzymes work faster in a mild bed. Push the heat too high, though, and they fall apart, and the seedling never reaches the surface. Too much water does comparable harm. It drives the air out of the ground, starves the tissues of oxygen and rots the young stem before a leaf ever opens.

units: a seed conservation station rewrote its procedure after a technical fault
the smallest seeds clung to the metal surfaces of the sorting machine
that clinging built up into lumps
the weight readings came out wrong
the worker felt an electric shock near the feed hopper
seeds rubbing against dry metal were producing static electricity
replacing the equipment lay beyond what the site could pay
an engineer advised running a conductor from the metal parts down to the ground
she also advised keeping damp in the air of the room
the fault was gone by the following harvest
text: At a station where seed is kept and sorted, a small mishap ended in a whole procedure being rewritten. The worker running the sorter found that the finest seed was sticking to the metal walls of the machine and gathering there in lumps, so that not one of the weighings came out right. Reaching toward the feed hopper, he took a sharp shock, and a pale spark jumped across to the panel. Static, raised by dry husks rubbing on dry steel, accounted for the whole fault. Management thought first of replacing the line, an outlay far beyond what the station could carry. An engineer put forward two much plainer measures. Run a copper wire from every metal part down to the ground, she said, and hold a moderate damp in the air of the room with a fine mist. The lumps were gone by the following harvest, and the weights could be trusted once more.

units: the kit takes in a clear jar, a mesh sieve, a funnel, a pair of tweezers and a magnifying glass
two separate methods serve to pull the living things out of a soil sample
the two methods answer different aims
the dry method means shaking the crumbled earth on the sieve over a pale surface
the mineral grit drops through the mesh
the crawling animals stay held above
the tweezers serve to move the animals under the glass without harming them
the wet method means thinning the sample in water and letting the particles settle
the roots and the eggs ride up while the sand sinks
the first method suits looking at whole insects and the second suits gauging how much sand there is
text: You will need a clear jar, a fine sieve, a funnel, a soft pair of tweezers and a magnifying glass. There are two ways to pull the living things out of a soil sample, and they answer different questions. The dry way is to crumble the clod onto the sieve and shake it gently over a pale sheet. Grit and mineral bits drop straight through the mesh, while the crawling animals stay held on top, and the tweezers will carry them under the glass one at a time without hurting them. The wet way is to fill the jar with water, stir the clod into it, then let the mix stand until the particles settle out. Roots and eggs ride up to the top, and the sand goes to the bottom. Take the first way when you are after whole insects to look at, and the second when you want to gauge how much of the sample is sand.

units: a group of about twenty volunteers goes out once the sun is down
their aim is to count the amphibians around a pond
two volunteers help the toads across a road
another post means netting the animals so they can be named
the netted animals go straight back into the water
every sighting is written down with the time and the water temperature
the coordinator says that readings piled up over several seasons bring out trends
one night on its own cannot bring out those trends
the coordinator grants that the conditions are hard and sometimes yield nothing
text: There are about twenty of them, boots on and lamps strapped to their heads, heading down to the pond as soon as the light goes. They are volunteers, and the job of the night is to count amphibians. First station, the road, where two of them pick up the toads crossing it and carry them over to the far side. Second station, the water, where someone dips a net, names the species and puts the animal straight back. Third station, the notebook, where every sighting goes down with the time and the water temperature. Add those figures up season after season, the coordinator says, and trends appear that no single night could ever show. She admits the thankless side too, the cold, the mud, the evenings that turn up nothing. Then a call rises from the ditch and the whole group stops to listen.

units: the calm look of the surface hides the activity underneath
at the end of the cold season the mud on the bottom lets go of bubbles
a greenish film spreads along the edges
jelly-like clumps cling to the plants under water
the embryos come out of their eggs at last
dark larvae gather in swarms near the warmed edge
the larvae feed on the algae coating the stones
the hind limbs form while the tail wastes away
the falling level crowds the last larvae into a small patch of water
the changed animals leave the water for the plants
text: Nothing on the surface of the pond gives away what is going on beneath it. As the cold season loosens its hold, the mud on the bottom lets go of its bubbles and a green film creeps along the edges. Jelly-like clumps show up among the stems, stuck to the reeds under water. They pale, they fill with dark commas, and at last the eggs hatch. Black tadpoles swarm in the warm shallows by the bank, grazing the algae that furs the stones. The shape shifts quietly, with no sign of effort. Back legs push out, the tail wastes away, the skin darkens. Once the heat turns heavy the level drops, the mud cracks open and the last tadpoles crowd together into one narrow puddle. Those that have changed slip off into the tall grass. Next season the clear water will keep no record of any of it.

units: hedgerows are taken out faster than new ones go in
taking those hedgerows out makes room for farm machinery
the wind sweeps the opened ground with nothing in its way
the layer of soil that feeds the crop is carried off into the ditches
rainwater runs down the slopes and cuts channels there
the streams take in more silt
the birds that settled in that brush have grown scarce
fewer such hunters means more spraying against crop insects
replanting is money spent with nothing to show at once
text: Hedgerows are coming out faster than anyone puts them back, and the fields are already showing the bill. Yes, every line of brush removed makes a plot easier to work with machinery. But the wind, which used to break against something living, now sweeps the opened ground and carries the fertile layer off into the ditches. Storm water behaves the same way. It runs straight down the slope, cuts channels as it goes, and loads the streams with silt. The birds that nested deep in the branches have grown scarce, and with them the hunters that kept crop insects in check, so more spraying is needed. A saving in labor is paid back in lost soil, in chemicals and in ditches to clear. Replanting costs money and returns nothing for several seasons. That is exactly why it should start now.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: one of the two scientists watches the water that moves below the ground surface
the other scientist follows the watercourses that run in the open
both women study the same resource
water underground cleans itself as it passes through permeable material
surface water carries sediment and plant debris along with it
surface water has to settle before it can be analyzed
the buried reserve sustains the stream when the water runs low
spells of strong flow recharge the buried reserve
text: One of them spends half her working life under the rock, headlamp on, notebook damp in her pocket, tracking water where nobody can see it move. Her colleague works in the open air, boots in the current, walking the channels that lie out in daylight. Both women measure the same water, yet they never meet it in the same state. Below the stone it threads through porous ground and clears itself as it crosses bed after bed of sand. Out in the light it drags silt, leaves and insects along, so a sample has to stand and settle before anyone can test it. The first reads a hidden reserve by how slowly it moves. The second reads a stream by how hard it pushes. Set their records side by side and one thing shows up twice: the buried water feeds the open channel when the level drops, and every strong flow sends water back down to fill the reserve again.

units: the visitor did not expect to enjoy the visit
a first section shows what sand does when the air drives it
a wall crumbles in front of the public behind a glass screen
a second section shows what cold does to water that has seeped in
the rock breaks apart when water freezes inside a crack
a third section deals with chemical attack by plants
two pebbles side by side compare an intact surface with a hollowed one
the fourth section disappoints because it carries too much written text
a rebuilt coastal wall closes the visit
text: Honestly, the show about stone wearing away knocked me sideways, and I had expected nothing from it. First room, the wind one: sand is thrown at a soft slab, and the slab crumbles while you watch, safe behind a pane of glass. Second room, the cold one: water works into a crack, stiffens, swells, and the rock cracks open like a shell. Third room, my favorite, the acid one: quiet mosses gnaw at limestone, and two pebbles lying together make the case, one still smooth, the other bitten full of hollows. Fourth room, the weak one: too much wall text, too little to look at, and you drift off fast. The ending pulls it all back, with a model cliff that the water eats away in front of you, again and again. I walked out thinking nothing hard stays hard, and I went back that same evening, on my own.

units: the writer is writing from a shelter put up beside a basin
the spring stopped flowing with no warning sign
the crew first blamed the measuring instrument
a probe brought up an obstruction made of small stones
workmen pulled the obstruction out by hand
the water came back hard before it settled down
the rock around here breaks up easily under pressure
the blockage happens again with every turn of the season
a metal guard will be fitted upstream
text: I am writing from the hut we put up at the edge of the basin, with the ink half stiff in the pen. Yesterday at first light the spring stopped, no warning of any kind, and the crew blamed the gauge before anything else. Around midday the engineer lowered a probe into the pipe and brought back the answer: gravel, packed tight. Early in the afternoon two workmen cleared the passage by hand, stone after stone, taking their time over it. The flow came back all at once. Water shot up over the rim, then eased into a steady thread. In the evening we pulled the readings together and laid the week out as a curve. The conclusion fits on one line. The rock up here is brittle, it gives way under pressure, and it plugs the pipe every season. A metal grate goes in upstream. I come home once the report is signed.

units: water works into cavities too fine to be seen
freezing makes the water take up more room
that gain in volume widens the crack
the crack stays open once the mild weather returns
mineral deposits and roots move into the opening
the push of growing plants completes the break
the broken rock travels down the slope and is ground into particles
those particles feed the making of a soil
the bare slope and the grassland below share one origin
moving air carries the finest fragments down to the low country
text: What becomes of a stone once water settles in its veins? It learns patience, and then it gives way. The water works into pores so fine that no eye picks them out. Cold arrives, the water stiffens and takes up more room than it should, and the crack widens by a line nobody will ever notice. Mild weather comes back, the water withdraws, and the crack stays open. What follows? Mineral dust drifts in, roots find room to sit, and the push of growing things finishes the work. Should we say the rock dies? No, it scatters. Every splinter goes down the slope, grinds against its own kind, and ends as grains that feed a young soil. The bare ground above and the grassland below are one matter, parted by a long fall. What is finest of all rides the moving air out to the flat country.

units: the filtering unit was clogging far sooner than expected
the readings showed that most of the particles were clay
those particles turn sticky as soon as they meet moisture
the blockage forms in the lower part of the unit
the supervisor proposed a coarse screen set at the inlet
she also proposed a settling tank ahead of the unit
the technician feared a loss of flow at peak demand
two tanks used in turn solved the flow problem
the time between two blockages grew much longer
text: The technician at the basin told the supervisor that the inlet filter was choking up in two weeks instead of six. She asked him whether the load of particles had gone up. He answered that the readings pointed at fine clay, which turns sticky the moment it takes on any moisture and seals the mesh from the bottom. The supervisor put forward a coarse bar screen on the raw water, and then a tank where the water could stand and settle before it reached the filter. The technician pushed back, since a tank of that kind would drag the flow down when demand peaked. She suggested two tanks in parallel, with a switch from one to the other. The trial ran a whole season. The filter now holds eight weeks, and the crew cleans out the tanks instead of buying mesh, which works out a good deal cheaper.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the study of rock once rested on the senses of the researcher
the observer judged weight hardness and the sound of a knock
descriptions depended on the memory of whoever had looked
two researchers far apart gave different names to the same material
cutting rock into a transparent slice changed the discipline
that technique makes the crystals and their arrangement visible
the older approach was quick but confused materials that looked alike
the newer approach calls for equipment and patience
the two ways of working are still combined in the field
text: Before optical instruments grew fine enough to be trusted, rock was studied by hand and by eye. The observer weighed a block in the palm, scratched it with a fingernail, listened to the note it gave when struck. A description was worth what the memory of the describer was worth, and two scholars far apart would file the same stone under different names. The thin slice overturned all that. Cut down until the rock lets light through, a sample gives up its crystals, their outlines and the way they sit together, and matter can be named without being touched. The older method read the surface, the newer one questions the structure. One moved fast and was fooled by stones that felt alike. The other asks for a workshop, for patience and for a steady cutting flow. They still work as a pair: on the slope, the hand picks what the slice will confirm.

units: three kinds of soil sit together on one slope
the soil where sand dominates lets water drain away at once
its grains never stick together between the fingers
clay soil holds water and turns sticky in the rain
as it dries clay hardens and splits open
the middle soil keeps the moisture that is useful and drains the surplus
a dark surface layer holds the remains of plants
that layer feeds whatever grows in it
shaping a lump by hand tells you which kind dominates
text: Three kinds of soil share one and the same slope, and the hand tells them apart. Sandy soil lets water drain almost as fast as it arrives. It is open and light, and the grains roll between the fingers without ever clinging. Clay soil does the reverse. It holds on to water, turns sticky under rain, then hardens as it dries until it splits into plates. Loam lies between the two. It keeps back enough moisture for the roots and lets the surplus run off downhill. Above these three sits a dark layer at the surface, thick with the remains of plants, and it feeds everything that grows there. A gardener finds out which soil he has by rolling a damp lump in the palm. It falls apart into dust where sand rules, and it draws out into a smooth rope where clay has the upper hand instead.

units: the group set out before sunrise to watch a spring that flows in bursts
the narrator complained about the cold on the way there
a former herder acted as guide for the group
the walk in took nearly an hour along a muddy track
on arrival the site looked like nothing at all
the guide asked the group to wait without making a sound
a deep noise came before the pool drained away
the water rose higher than the tops of the trees
it was over quickly and the visitors were soaked
the guide wrote down the gap between two bursts
text: We set off before sunrise to watch a spring that spills over in bursts, and I grumbled the whole way there, because the cold was already biting my fingers. Our guide, a herder before he gave it up, walked us a solid hour along a track thick with mud. Then we arrived and there was nothing to see: a steaming hole, a warm pool, two birds that could not have cared less. He told us to stand still and make no sound. After a while a low rumble came up out of the ground, the pool drained in one gulp, and the water leapt higher than the tops of the trees, in a warm cloud that soaked us to the socks. It was over fast, and the quiet came back as if nothing had happened. The guide, meanwhile, wrote down the gap between one burst and the last. We walked off wet, laughing, delighted, and I stopped grumbling.

units: take the sample at the depth where the roots grow
leave out the surface layer because it holds debris
dry the sample away from heat so that its structure holds
take out the coarse pieces by passing the material over a screen
keeping them would throw the result off by their weight
then put the material into a jar of water
the particles settle in order from the heaviest down
read the thickness of the layers from the bottom upward
note the color once when wet and once when dry
text: Start by lifting a handful of soil at the depth where the roots run, never from the top, because the upper layer is loaded with debris and will throw your reading off. Spread the sample on paper and let it dry in the shade, since fierce heat bursts the crumbs apart and alters the texture. Sieve the dry material next so the gravel comes out, or its weight will crush the fine fraction in the count. Tip what is left into a jar of clear water, shake it, then put it down and leave it alone. The heavy grains land first and the fine ones after, so the bands can be read through the glass. Measure each band from the bottom upward, because the order of settling tells you what the soil is made of. Write down the color last, wet and dry, since drying turns it into another color altogether.

units: the current has cut into the raised edge down to the roots of the plants
the path that ran along the watercourse is collapsing in sections
people living nearby see the edge give ground at every rise of the water
the loose nature of the ground makes it easy to tear away
the current speeds up in the bend and makes the problem worse
the material torn away travels downstream
a built wall was ruled out for its cost and its effect on the far edge
the answer chosen brings together planting and bundles of branches
a hollow dug upstream slows the water as it arrives
the path will be moved further from the watercourse
text: On the low side the water has gnawed into the raised edge, right down to the roots of the bushes, and the path that ran along the channel is dropping away in whole sections. The people who live there put it plainly: every rise takes another step off the edge. The ground is loose here, sand mixed with silt, and the current lifts it without effort as it gathers speed in the bend, then carries what it has torn off downstream. The team that looks after the basin ruled out a built wall, costly and blunt, which would only have thrown the force of the water at the far side. They chose to plant the slope with bushes that root and creep, to lay bundles of branches at its foot, and to dig a hollow upstream so the water arrives slower. One season held the toe. The path moves higher, out of reach.

units: a damp place high up gathers several natural settings within a small stretch
a plant carpet soaked with water rims the pool
organisms clinging to stone withstand the lack of water
hollow stems serve as shelter for young insects
the water looks clear but carries plant debris
small almost see-through animals move in short bursts
seeds buried in the bottom wait for a favorable spell
each level depends on the others and losing one makes the whole poorer
text: A mountain bog crowds several very different settings into one small patch of ground. Right at the water's edge lies a carpet of moss, soaked through and spongy, which gives way under a boot and closes over again at once. Above it the bare rock wears a coat of gray lichen, rough under the thumb, able to ride out one drought after another. In between stand tall grasses whose hollow stems shelter tiny larvae. The water counts as a setting of its own. It looks clear on top, yet stir it and a cloud of shredded plant matter comes up. See-through insects dart through it in short jerky bursts, almost impossible to spot. Deeper down, under the silt, seeds lie asleep and wait for a kinder season to sprout. Every layer leans on the others, and take one out and the whole place grows poorer.

units: artificial lighting was aimed first at the safety of public ways
it then spread to buildings and parking areas
commercial signs shine at night over empty walkways
only the strongest bodies in the sky stay visible
an orange glow hides the depth of the sky
birds on migration circle lit-up buildings
insects active after sundown die near the lamps
some communities have already switched the lighting off in the middle of the night without complaint
text: Let us be honest about it: we lost the sky without ever noticing. Street lighting came first, for safety, and that much holds up. Then it spread to building fronts, parking lots, storefronts and crossings, and everyone found that normal. Shop signs took to burning all night over sidewalks with nobody on them. What is left overhead? A scatter of the brightest bodies in the sky, and behind them an orange wash where the depth used to be. Migrating birds steer by starlight, so they circle lit towers instead. Night-flying insects wear themselves out against the lamps and die at the foot of the posts. We could switch off after midnight and nothing would fall apart. Whole communities have tried it, and not one voice was raised against it. It would be a pity to wait until the dark is a memory before missing it.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman leading the team explores a network of galleries not yet mapped
a fall into a crack during her childhood set off her calling
she discovered then a chamber crossed by falling water
her parents worked a dry sloping plot
she understood that the water missing at the surface was moving lower down
she trained in a field devoted to the study of water
her measurements show the deep reserves refilling faster than expected
the neighboring communities changed their water intakes after these results
text: The researcher who runs the team spends her weeks under rock, in a maze of galleries no survey had ever put on paper. Her calling began with a fall. As a child she slipped into a narrow crack in the family pasture and landed in front of a chamber where water came down in a sheet. Her parents worked a dry slope, so she grasped early that whatever went missing at the surface was moving along just beneath it. She went off to study water itself, then came back to measure what she had glimpsed. Her readings showed the deep reserves refilling far faster than anyone had assumed, and the settlements nearby rewrote their intake plans because of it. The map she keeps updating now serves as an argument for farmers and officials alike, and her quiet manner no longer keeps people from listening.

units: the exhibition deals with the deep sea
the first room shows animals kept in a liquid
this display conveys neither the pressure nor the darkness of the depths
the end of the route makes up for that flaw
a dark passage forces the visitor to move forward blind
projected images show jelly-like animals overhead
a trembling of the floor goes with that scene
the writer regrets that this choice was not applied from the start
text: You come out of this deep-sea show feeling you have brushed against something vast and been poorly served. The weakness hits you in the opening room. Case after case lines up pale specimens set in alcohol, with nothing to suggest the pressure or the darkness they came from. Under a hard lamp, a glowing fish is nothing more than one more jar. The closing stretch of the route makes up for the blunder. Here the designers dug out a dark corridor where you feel your way forward while projections send drifting jellyfish high across the ceiling. The floor trembles faintly underfoot. At last you get the effect they were after, a crushing body of water with rare creatures adrift in it. Had that choice been made at the door, the whole thing would have won over even the most distracted visitor.

units: the sender reports on two methods for tracking freshwater animals
the first method uses catching devices sunk in the water
the second consists in laying boards on the ground
the underside of the boards holds the moisture
the sunken devices take more grown individuals
they call for regular visits and sometimes injure the animals' limbs
the boards give fewer catches but steadier records
a grainy material spread under the boards favors the young ones
the sender suggests splitting the two methods over two separate sectors
text: Dear colleague, I owe you an account of the two protocols we settled on for tracking the pond amphibians. The first relies on smooth-walled traps sunk in the water. The second uses boards laid flat on the ground, whose rough underside keeps a film of moisture. Traps take more adults, but somebody has to walk the line every other evening, and the animals often come out with damaged legs. Boards go down once and draw only whatever is looking for cover, so the yield drops while the data comes out cleaner. One more thing is worth passing on. The grainy layer we spread under the boards seems to suit the young ones and to bother the grown ones. If you agree, let us keep the boards on the upper sector and the traps on the lower one, then set the catches side by side once the season closes.

units: a handful of forest soil shelters a great many living things
the combined work of those beings produces fertility
threads coming from fungi extend the reach of the roots
these threads take in water and dissolved minerals
they receive in exchange sugary compounds made by the foliage
the tearing of that network lets the rain carry off the surface layer
bringing a damaged soil back takes tens of years
the measures named include covering with plant waste and cutting down machine traffic
dark springy crumbs show that the soil is recovering
text: What lives in a handful of forest soil? Fungal threads, bacteria, mites and worms by the thousand, and it is their combined work that builds the fertility of the place. What do those threads do? They stretch the reach of tree roots, draw in water and dissolved salts, then trade them for the sugars the leaves have made. What happens when that web tears? The ground loses its grip, rain carries off the top layer, and whatever grows back comes up thin. Can a damaged plot be brought back? Yes, provided you are willing to accept a scale of several decades. Cover the surface with plant waste, keep the heavy machines off it, bring in deep-rooted plants that open channels again. What tells you the effort has worked? Dark springy crumbs that come apart between the fingers without crumbling into dust.

units: the forest keeper advises coming before the female returns
the group sets out in the dark without a light
the assistant notices that the nest hole sits higher than the year before
the keeper climbs with a ladder
he draws out of the hole a young bird covered in soft feathers
the bird cannot stand up yet
three other chicks fill the hollow
the visitors measure the feathers and look at the shade of the beak
the female comes back to the nest shortly after the group leaves
text: The forest keeper had warned us the day before: “Come before the mother takes up her rounds again,” so we set out ahead of dawn with no lamp, finding the path by the sound of our own steps on it. At the foot of the beech his assistant whispered that the hole opened higher up than the year before. The keeper hauled the ladder into place, climbed it, slid a hand inside and drew out a chick still in soft down, not yet able to hold itself up on its feet. “Three more behind it,” he said, and settled the bird back at the bottom of the nest. We took the length of the feathers and the shade of the beak, and moved nothing else. On the way down he boiled his trade down to watching, counting and going away again. The mother was back soon after we left, as though nothing had happened.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: quarry workers found remains of shellfish in a stone lying high up
these shapes were put down at first to a whim of the rock
cutters observed that the remains stacked up in a steady order
that stacking recalled the floor of calm water
the same order showed up in different valleys
the explanation by chance became hard to believe
observers put forward that the stone had taken shape under water
this idea assumed a lifting of the ground
the idea was accepted because its forecasts held up in the field
text: Picture the quarry workers who split a slab far above the sea and found shells running right through the stone. For generations the marks were put down to a whim of the rock, which people said could mimic living things. Then some of the more curious cutters noticed that the shells sat in layers, in a steady order, much the way they settle on the floor of a quiet bay. Since the same order turned up in one valley after another, chance grew hard to believe in. A few observers came out with an unwelcome account. The rock had taken shape under water, and the ground had risen afterwards. The idea took decades to get through, because it meant admitting that the land itself moves. It won in the end because its forecasts held: where it promised sea layers, sea layers were found.

units: a watercourse boxed in between straight walls sheds its water too fast
the water reaches the lower ground all at once during heavy rain
the low parts of the built-up areas are flooded
the bed dries out with the first spell of strong heat
the straight line had been dug to win farming ground
that line did away with the bends that slowed the water and let it soak in
putting things right means handing back to the watercourse part of the room it once had
the work includes tearing out the built banks and planting trees again
the overflows turn less violent and a flow stays on through the dry spell
text: A river running straight between two concrete walls sheds its water faster than it should. Hydrologists say the same thing after every flood. The flow reaches the lower ground all at once, swamps the low-lying blocks, then drains away, and the bed dries out with the first heat wave. That straight cut was dug to win farming ground, and it did away with the bends where the water used to slow down and soak in. The fix now being tried is to hand the river back part of the room it once had. Crews break up the built banks, reopen old side channels, and plant trees whose roots hold the edges together. The water winds again, spreads across meadows made to flood, and works its way down to the water table. Floods lose their punch, and a thread of water stays in the bed through the dry months.

units: the walkers climb a steep face and come down by the other
the face they climb is dry and rocky
only short grasses grow in the cracks of the rock
the walkers' water supplies empty fast during the climb
the change of face happens within a few steps at the top
the other face is covered with thick growth
very cold water runs from the wall
a group of farm animals rests in the shade on that side
the narrator concludes that a height is made of faces exposed in different ways
text: We had decided to climb the steep face and come down by the other, with no notion of how far the two faces would contradict each other. The way up was dry and stony, all hot slabs and tufts of short grass wedged into the cracks, with the rasp of insects for company. Nothing up there held water, and our bottles emptied while we watched. The switch took about three steps. Past the ridge the slope opened out thick and green, carpeted with ferns, the air smelling of wet moss. Threads of water seeped from the wall, cold enough to numb a hand. We came upon a herd grazing in the shade while behind us the other pitch went on baking. One mountain, cut by a single crest, kept two climates and two sets of tenants. Since that walk I no longer look at high ground as a single solid mass.

units: a charger in use turns warm
current runs through a copper winding inside the device
every conducting material pushes back against the current
that opposition turns part of the energy into heat
a higher power draw raises the share that is wasted
makers provide openings, metal contact parts and sometimes a cooling propeller
a device that runs too hot slows its own pace
a soft object placed under a computer blocks the air openings
text: Touch a charger that has been sitting plugged in all afternoon. It feels warm, and there is nothing mysterious about that. Inside the casing, current travels through slender wires and a copper winding. No conductor carries electricity for free. The material pushes back, and that resistance converts part of the energy into heat. Demand more power from the thing and the wasted portion climbs. Manufacturers understand this perfectly, so they cut ventilation slots into the shell, press metal tabs against the hottest components, and sometimes tuck a miniature fan inside. When the heat cannot escape, the circuits throttle themselves back for their own protection, and the whole machine turns sluggish. That is also why a cushion underneath a laptop suffocates it. The openings are covered, the air stagnates, the temperature climbs. Unplug it, give it room to breathe, and everything settles.

units: dead tablets were piling up in a repair workshop
the devices showed no sign of working at all
the explanation on offer blamed the fault on the battery
the head of the workshop doubted that diagnosis
a teardown revealed a cracked metal joint under the charging connector
a light knock was enough to break that joint
the team built a holder that clamps the board while the joint is rebuilt
the repair became cheap to carry out
the workshop puts its repair notes on public display
text: At a repair counter tucked into the back of a shopping arcade, dead tablets had been stacking up for weeks. The explanation was always the same. Black screen, no response, and a battery blamed for everything. The lead technician never accepted that convenient answer. He opened one unit, then a second, and found a hairline crack in the solder underneath the charging connector, too fine to detect without a magnifier. A knock against a table edge was enough to split it. Rather than swap whole boards, the team built a small jig that clamps the board flat while a hot iron rebuilds the joint. The work now costs almost nothing, and owners walk out with a machine that wakes up again. The shop pins its repair notes to a board beside the door, so people stop discarding a device that a bead of solder can revive.

units: two distinct ways exist for taking apart an old playback device
the first means backing out the screws one at a time
the first calls for marking where each part sat on a sketch
the second means forcing the shell open with a flat tool
the second usually wrecks a clip
the careful way needs a lamp that swivels and a bench swept clear
the bundles of wiring make the gap between the two ways obvious
the text advises taking the careful way
putting it back together runs in the opposite order to taking it apart
text: Before you loosen a single screw, settle on your road, because an old player opens in two different ways. The first belongs to patience. You back out every screw, drop it into a saucer, and mark on a sketch exactly where it lived. The second belongs to nerve. You slide a flat blade beneath the shell, save yourself a minute, and snap a retaining clip. Patience wants a lamp on a bending arm and a workbench swept clear. Nerve wants nothing but a firm wrist. Yet the moment the wiring reveals itself, a pale ribbon glued along the floor of the chassis, the difference opens wide. The patient hand knows where every strand returns. The hasty one tugs at random and tears. Take the first road, then build the machine back together the other way round, and let the tray spring seat itself before the lid comes down.

units: the sorting line described holds three machines that work together
light sensors read the reflection to work out what the packaging is made of
jets of pressurised air push the unwanted pieces aside
that ejection happens without anything touching the objects
belts running at uneven speeds spread the stream and stop pieces from riding on each other
the manager holds that upkeep counts for more than the software
a dirty nozzle bends the path of the ejected pieces
a slack belt upsets the timing of the line
a dusty sensor reads glass as clear plastic
a worker walks the line at intervals to clean it
text: The shed hums on one long note, and the guided tour opens in front of the first sorting line. Three machines operate together there. A row of optical sensors reads the light bouncing off each package and deduces what material it is made of. A rail of compressed air nozzles fires next, knocking unwanted pieces aside within a thousandth of a second, without anything ever touching them. Behind it, belts driven at uneven speeds thin the stream out so that no piece rides on top of another. The plant manager keeps pressing a point that visitors tend to overlook. Reliability rests on maintenance far more than on the software. A clogged nozzle throws the puff off course. A slackened belt drags the timing. A dusty sensor mistakes glass for clear plastic. So an operator walks the line at regular intervals, cloth in hand.

units: the assembly described follows a fixed run of steps
a cut sheet of metal takes its final shape under a press
a coated metal wire laps around a central core
the ends of that winding are stripped of their coating
a magnetic part drops into the ring and is then locked by a collar
the shaft is oiled before it goes in
the turning of the shaft is checked with no load on it
the wires of the winding are held by solder on conducting pads
the shell closes with a seal that keeps dust out
the finished object faces a test under load in a booth
text: Watch an assembly line and a strict order reveals itself, from the opening movement to the last. A cut steel blank arrives on a turntable, and a press stamps the housing shape into it. The winding comes next. Lacquered copper wire feeds off a spool and laps evenly around a core, and its two ends are afterwards stripped bare. A permanent magnet then drops into the outer ring, and a collar locks it into position. The shaft is offered up, oiled, pressed home, and its rotation is checked with no load upon it. Once that reading satisfies, the ends of the winding meet two conducting pads, where a machine deposits a bead of solder. The casing closes last of all, with a supple seal that keeps the dust away. The finished unit travels onward to a testing booth, where a measured load proves that it holds.

units: putting a household appliance back in order has grown hard
shells are now held together with glue rather than screws
the screw heads in use are not sold in ordinary shops
spare parts stop being sold soon after a model reaches the market
the buyer drops the repair and picks up a replacement
objects that half an hour would mend are thrown out
independent workshops close for want of custom
technical skill fades as those workshops shut
some makers show that a cover made to come off adds no bulk
the text calls for standard screws, wiring plans anyone can get and parts kept in stock
text: Mending a household appliance used to be ordinary work. It now takes something close to a feat, and the reasons are not hidden. Makers glue the shells together rather than screw them. They pick screw heads that no ordinary supplier keeps. They stop selling spare parts a short while after a model reaches the shelves. Each choice has a plain result. The owner gives up, buys a replacement, and something half an hour would have mended goes out with the rubbish. Independent workshops close for want of custom, and the skill they carried fades along with them. The old defence about slimness and sealing no longer holds, since some makers show that a cover made to come off adds no bulk at all. Asking for common screws, a wiring plan anyone can get and parts kept in stock is no fond dream. It is what long use costs.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman at the centre of the story knew none of the words for machine parts at the start
she taught herself by taking broken toys apart
she runs a small shop wedged between two other businesses
her first trouble came from how awkward her customers felt
the customers were afraid of getting the description of their trouble wrong
she changed the way she takes people in
she opens the device in front of its owner and points at each part while naming it
customers come back having worked out the fault by themselves
the shop is no longer short of custom
text: She says that at the beginning she could not tell a cog from a pulley, and that she taught herself by taking broken toys apart. The neighborhood fixer now runs a narrow shop wedged between a laundry and a florist. Her first difficulty was never the machinery. It was how awkward her customers felt. People would not describe a fault out loud, for fear of saying something foolish. So she changed the way she takes them in. She sets the device on the counter, opens it while its owner watches, and names each component aloud. Here is the catch that sticks. Here is the power socket. Here is the gear that slips. Customers walk out understanding what went wrong. Plenty of them come back later with a fault they have identified themselves, and the shop is never short of customers any more.

units: the two devices compared follow opposite designs
the first puts suction power and toughness first
the first does well on thick woven floor coverings
the first makes a noise that drives the household out
the first leaves dirt in the corners
the second stands out for how well it finds its way about
the second pulls with less force and takes longer to finish the floor
the second steers clear of obstacles and slips under low furniture
the choice hangs on the kind of floor and how crowded the home is
both devices open and empty without a tool
text: Set side by side on a single shelf, two robot vacuums argue for opposite ideas. The first bets on muscle. An eager motor, a broad brush, a roomy bin, and a shell that shrugs off knocks. It shines on deep carpet, but the racket it makes empties the room of its occupants, and its side arm leaves little crescents of grit in the corners. The second bets on judgment. It reads a room accurately, keeps track of its own position, and finds its base without dithering. It pulls less air and needs longer to cover the floor, yet it collides with nothing and slips beneath low furniture. The verdict follows the household. Hard floors and crowded rooms favor the second, thick rugs and open space give the first the advantage. On one count they tie. The bin empties in a second, and the lid lifts without tools.

units: the writer reports on the restoring of a radio set found under the roof
the work splits into three separate jobs
