the cabinet was sanded, glued back at one corner and waxed
the inside was covered in a thick deposit
two wires had lost their insulation
the connections were made again wire by wire
the needle on the display no longer follows the turning knob
the writer supposes that a springy part has worn out
the writer promises to write again once the set works
text: You asked how the radio from under the roof was coming along, and I finally owe you a proper account. Three separate pieces of work have kept me occupied. The cabinet came first. I sanded the lifted veneer, glued a corner that had sprung open, and rubbed in a wax that woke the grain of the wood again. The inside came second, and that is where my patience wore thin. Dust lay like grey felt across every valve, and two wires had shed their sleeving entirely. I made the connections again, strand by strand, with fresh wire and a clean joint. The third undertaking holds me still. The needle on the dial refuses to follow the knob, and I suspect a tired spring behind it. When the whole thing is ready, I will stand the set beside the window and write to tell you what the first voice says.

units: a specialist describes the updating of the program held inside a device
the device first checks that the file it received is genuine
the procedure stops if that check fails
the new data is written into an area of memory apart from the one in use
that separation guards the device if the power is cut
the earlier version stays in place until the restart
a counter of attempts sends the start-up back to the old area if the writing fails
the user then notices nothing but a slower start
the prints of the two areas are compared once the switch has happened
the room held by the stale version is won back only after a session with nothing amiss
text: What happens exactly when a machine updates the software held inside it? The engineer we asked walks through the steps in order. First the device checks the signature on the file it received. If the signature fails to match, the process halts on the spot. Next the image is written into a second block of memory, never over the one that is running, so a power cut harms nothing. And the version already there? It stays whole until the machine restarts. What if the writing fails? A retry counter sends the start-up back to the older block, and the user notices nothing but a heavier start. Once the switch has happened, a last check compares the prints of both blocks. The machine frees the room held by the stale version only after one full session with nothing amiss. That caution explains why the job seems to drag.

units: a neighbor reports that his printing machine was damaging the paper
the user had tried rough handling without getting any result
a local repairman blames the fault on a worn drive belt
the belt had lost its grip from turning with no load
the repairman advises reaching the back part of the device
a round part must be turned one notch to tighten the belt again
the device pulls the paper properly after the operation
the owner had thought of throwing out a machine that could be fixed
he decides to keep the instructions within reach
text: A neighbor across the street told me his printer kept pulling sheets in crooked and creasing every one of them. He had shaken it, thumped it, yanked at the tray, and all he ever got was another jam. Then a repairman down the street set him straight: the drive belt had gone smooth from spinning with nothing to grip, so it slipped instead of pulling. Open the back panel, the man said, find the little wheel sitting on the side, and turn it one notch to take up the slack. My neighbor grumbled the whole time, but he called me the next morning sounding almost cheerful, because the paper was finally feeding in straight. He laughed about it later. He had nearly thrown out a working machine over a stretched piece of rubber, and from now on the manual stays in the drawer where he can reach it.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: two ways of sending messages far off existed side by side for a long period
the first method used tall towers carrying movable arms
one worker set the arms and another read the shape through a telescope
the second method sent a current through an insulated metal wire
this wire was buried along the roads or hung from posts
mist and darkness cut off the working of the arm device
the wire worked without depending on the weather
the chain of towers took a large staff to run
the electric line kept only one worker busy at each of its ends
the price of the cable held back the spread of the second method
text: For a long stretch of years, two ways of throwing a message across country ran side by side. The older one built tall towers up on the ridges, each crowned with jointed wooden arms that an operator swung into shape on command, while a second man at the next tower read that shape through a telescope and passed it on down the chain. The other pushed a current along a metal wire sheathed in insulation, buried beside the roads or strung up from posts. The towers went blind the moment the mist rose or the daylight failed. The wire, for its part, never cared in the least what the sky happened to be doing. Keeping the chain alive took whole crews of watchful operators, while the electric line needed one man at each end and nobody at all in between. What held the wire back was the price of the cable, which slowed its spread for a long while yet.

units: the machine described builds an object by stacking layers of matter
its bulk is close to that of a piece of luggage
a spool carries a plastic thread that unwinds toward the machine
a heated tip softens this thread and lays it down in thin ribbons
a moving support drops a little at every pass of the tip
the object is therefore built from the bottom upward
a blower cools the fresh matter to keep it from sagging
an electronic board rules the movements of the whole assembly
the device is light enough to stand on a household table
text: A machine that lays matter down layer by layer fits inside a box hardly wider than a suitcase. Look first at the spool, where a translucent plastic thread lies coiled like patient rope and feeds inward slowly, without hurry. Next comes the nozzle, a heated point that softens the thread and sets it down again in thin ribbons, still faintly warm to the touch. Beneath it the bed slides along and drops by a hair with every pass, so that the object grows upward as it takes shape. A small fan breathes on the fresh ribbon and sets it firm before it has time to slump. Last of all, tucked away under the frame, an electronic board counts the pulses and rules every movement. None of it weighs much at all. The whole thing stands on an ordinary kitchen table and hums away like a diligent insect.

units: a crew raised a mast on the roof of a technical building
the part put up is a hollow cylinder made of a light metal
it took the place of a device that vibration had cracked
the fitters bolted the base down onto a thick metal plate
they checked that it stood upright before the final tightening
a rising wind set the mast humming on a steady note
the supervisor stopped the work and measured the frequency
the structure was resonating with the gusts
fitting two diagonal stays moved the natural frequency
the closing readings confirmed the performance expected
text: Work started well before first light, when the crew hauled the mast sections onto the flat roof of the technical building. The antenna itself was a hollow cylinder of light alloy, brought in to replace an older one that vibration had cracked. The fitters bolted the base down flat onto a thick steel plate, then checked it against a plumb line before they took the nuts up tight. By midday the wind had picked up and the mast began to hum on a low, steady, unsettling note. The supervisor called a halt, measured the frequency, and saw that the structure was resonating with the gusts. Two extra stays went on at an angle, which shifted the natural frequency well clear of the danger band. The cable was landed at dusk, and the closing readings confirmed the gain that everyone had been promised.

units: the power must be cut and the machine left to cool before any work
a hot liquid swells and may spurt out when the fitting is opened
a container has to be set under the lower coupling
the draining is done by the weight of the liquid alone
the valve must be opened by a quarter turn and no more
opening too fast draws in air and the flow stops
the bleed control at the top lets air enter from above
the refill is done through the upper port once the valve is shut
filling little by little keeps bubbles from forming
a circuit without bubbles carries heat at a steady rate
text: Before you touch the cooling circuit at all, unplug the machine and let it cool down. Hot water swells, and the pressure it builds up in the flexible hose will send the liquid spitting out the moment a fitting comes loose. Set a pan under the lower coupling next, since the draining is done by weight alone and nothing else. Open the valve a quarter turn and no more. Cracked open too quickly, it draws air in, the flow stalls, and the whole job comes to nothing. Now drop the bleed lever at the top of the circuit, so that air enters from above and drives the liquid downward. Once the pan stops filling, shut the valve, wipe the coupling dry, and top the circuit up through the upper port. Fill little by little to keep bubbles out, and a circuit without bubbles carries heat at a steady rate.

units: a volunteer group takes in broken devices every week
the place used is a covered hall lent by the neighborhood
most of the objects have a fault of small scale
the faults named are a soldered battery a corroded contact or a glued shell
the makers explain these joins by sealing and slimness
the repairers read them as a deliberate cut in how long a product lasts
the workshop records every opening in a logbook and in pictures
the sheets produced are handed out freely
a partner supplier sends over batches of standard contacts
most of the devices brought in leave again in working order
text: Under a covered hall lent by the neighborhood, a volunteer group takes in broken machines and discouraged owners week after week. What the volunteers keep finding is small: a battery soldered into place, a corroded contact, a shell glued shut that no ordinary tool opens without cracking it apart. Manufacturers point to sealing and slimness to explain these permanent joins, while the repairers read them instead as a way of cutting short how long a product lasts. So the workshop has answered with a method of its own. It keeps a logbook of every model it has opened, photographs each step, and hands the resulting sheets out for anyone at all to use. A parts supplier has joined in with them and now sends over batches of standard contacts. Since this season, two machines in three walk back out working.

units: two speakers are looked at side by side
the first is a cube of very light plastic
its grille copies the look of metal
the second has a shell of folded metal and weighs more
a stretched cloth covers the front of the second one
the cube lacks strength in the low sounds
the heavier one holds the low notes without shaking
the cube travels easily and takes knocks
the second one needs a wall socket and a steady surface
the choice comes down to what the speaker will be used for
text: Stand the two speakers next to each other and you see the difference before anything is plugged in. The first is a molded plastic cube, light as an empty box, with a printed grille that pretends to be metal. The second has weight in the hand: folded sheet metal, edges turned over, and a stretched cloth across the front that hints at a real cone behind it. Listen, and the cube snaps in the treble but runs out of breath as soon as the bass drops. Its heavier neighbor holds the note, fills the whole room, and barely shivers on the shelf. The other side of the ledger counts for something too. The cube slips into a bag, charges overnight, and shrugs off knocks, while the big one wants a wall socket and a steady corner. Each has its own ground, and what you plan to do with it settles the argument.

units: the writer argues against the praise given to thin devices
the first complaint bears on the battery held down with adhesive
a glued battery dooms the object as soon as the charge fades
the second complaint targets screws with an exclusive head
these screws keep independent shops away from repair work
the third complaint concerns software that turns away an unpaired part
the three obstacles strengthen one another
the writer grants that shrinking a case forces trade-offs
he asks that the buyer be told before the purchase
text: We ought to stop praising a thin device as though slimness were a moral achievement. The case against it comes in three parts. Take the glue first: bonding a battery to the frame does the owner no good at all, and it dooms the whole object the day the charge starts to fade. Then the odd screw, cut with a head that no common driver will grip, whose only job is to keep the independent shop out of the work. Then the software, which turns away a spare part identical in every respect because the factory never paired it to the machine. The three locks feed one another. The glue makes opening risky, the screw makes it awkward, the software makes it pointless. Yes, shrinking a case forces trade-offs, and that much is true. The buyer should hear about them at the counter, not the day after the breakdown.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: as a child she took apart the clocks in her house
she rarely put them back together in full
her training took place in a mechanics workshop
that workshop repaired lifting machinery
her first job was greasing the grooved wheels
she watched how metal tires and how a groove wears away
once she became a technician she went down into the pit alone
she carried a hand crank for emergencies at her belt
she was later handed the diagnoses her colleagues had given up on
she now passes her trade on to apprentices
text: As a child she pulled apart every clock in the house to see what was ticking inside, and rarely got one whole again. As a teenager she took an apprenticeship in a mechanics workshop that repaired hoists. Her first job was a thankless one: greasing pulleys, one after another, until the cable ran without a squeal. What she learned there was how matter tires, how an alloy grows weary and a groove wears away. Once she made technician she earned the right to go down into the pit alone, a hand crank for emergencies hooked to her belt. Later they handed her the hard diagnoses, the ones her colleagues had given up on. She listens first, palm flat on the frame, and names the guilty part before the housing is even open. Now she trains apprentices, and tells them the ear comes before the tool.

units: the laptop under review weakens as soon as the load runs on
the fault comes from the shape of the device
a powerful processor sits under a very thin lid
the heat pipe has only a small cross section
the heat piles up against the electronic board
the controller pulls the clock down to keep the chip safe
the fan grows loud and the compute speed drops
the keyboard turns warm and long stretches of typing suffer
a perforated stand improves the airflow without removing the cause
a thicker case would give better output for the same money
text: This ultrathin laptop falls apart as soon as the load runs longer than a handful of seconds, and the reason sits entirely in its shape. The maker dropped a generous processor under a lid pared down past sense, which leaves the heat pipe a laughable cross section. With nowhere to go, the heat piles up against the board, and the controller pulls the clock down at once to keep the silicon safe. You hear the result as clearly as you measure it: the fan climbs into a whine, compute speed sheds a third, then wanders without settling. The keyboard turns warm under the fingers, which spoils any long stretch of typing. Set the thing on a perforated stand and you buy some airflow and push the drop back, though the cause stays where it was. For the same money, a thicker case delivers more.

units: the writer addresses an acquaintance who had left a device with him
he pulls the older device out of storage and looks it over
he has just bought a recent model of the same kind
the older device weighs twice what the recent one weighs
its metal shell warms up while it is being used
the screen of the recent model renders colors better
the older device opens up so its battery can be replaced
the recent model is glued together and will not open
the writer asks his correspondent for a reply
text: Do you remember that old tablet you left with me before you moved out? I dug it out of the closet last night and set it down next to the one I just bought. The gap between the two made me laugh. The old one weighs twice as much, the thick metal shell warms up the second you open two windows, and the charger is the size of a brick. The newer one slips into a coat pocket, charges while you forget about it, and shows colors the older screen never managed. Still, I will say one honest thing for the old one: it can be fixed. I have already unscrewed the back to swap the battery, while the newer one is glued together and cracks if you try to pry it open. One wins on lightness, the other on being willing. Guess which one stays on my desk? Write back and tell me what you think before you get home.

units: excess heat is what wears laptops down most
built-up dust clogs the ventilation openings
the blockage keeps the fan from cooling the machine
the device throttles its own performance to protect itself
a steady or crackling sound announces the fault
the keyboard turns warm to the touch
the computer slows down for no visible reason
power has to be cut before the case is opened
replacing the fan costs little and takes one visit
text: What wears a laptop down fastest? Heat, says the repair shop that takes us in. And where does the heat come from? From dust, which mats the vents, jams the fan, and forces the machine to throttle itself. What warns you before it quits? Three signs keep coming back. Sound first: a steady rush of air, then a crackle once the fan starts rubbing against its housing. Then the keyboard itself, gone warm under your fingers. And then the slowdown, settling in for no reason you can see. So what do you do? Unplug the machine, back the screws out of the bottom plate, blow the dust outward, close it up. And if the noise stays? The fan has to go, a cheap swap the shop handles in a single visit. Should you open it yourself? The technician hesitates for a moment, then says a careful hand beats a smothered machine.

units: a repairwoman announces that she has found the fault
the person in charge of the place questions her about her diagnosis
a blinking colored light pointed her in the right direction
she cleaned a corroded deposit off the board
she soldered back a wire that had come loose
she warns that the machine must be kept away from the wall
otherwise hot air builds up behind the device
the person in charge promises to move it the next day
the device comes back on once it is reassembled and plugged in
text: The technician set her bag on the bench and said she had the fault. The manager asked what she had found. She told him that an orange light was already blinking when she opened the case, and that it had put her on the trail. Then she explained how she had pulled the board, scraped a greenish crust off one track, and soldered a dangling wire back in place. The manager wanted a guarantee. She answered that the joint would hold as long as the shop stopped pressing the machine flat against the wall, since otherwise the hot air would sit behind it. He promised to move it the next morning. She closed the cover, drove the four screws back in the order she had laid them out, and plugged the thing in while he watched. The screen lit up a pale blue. The manager smiled and said he would never have guessed one loose wire could cost a week.

units: early calculating machines ran on toothed wheels
every added wheel raised the mechanical resistance
that resistance bent the transmission shafts
the number of columns therefore stayed limited
manufacturers set out to do away with moving parts
the electromechanical relay avoided gears but wore out
it also made a sharp noise with every calculation
the vacuum tube was fast but gave off a great deal of heat
that thermal limit led to the solid-state component
text: Before electricity, adding by machine meant toothed wheels linked by pawls. Every wheel added friction; friction called for a firmer push on the crank; and the push ended up bending the shafts. That set the ceiling for such machines: past ten columns or so, the gearing seized. Builders therefore went looking for a way to get rid of the moving part. The electromechanical relay offered a first way out, since it switched with no gears at all, but its contacts wore down and its clack gave away every operation. The vacuum tube came next. It ran faster and quieter, and so hot that each cabinet needed a blower of its own and a steady supply of glass to replace what burned through. That heat, as much as the bill, pushed the workshops toward the solid-state part: cold, tiny, and with nothing inside that moves.

units: a battery that runs down early is not necessarily worn out
three habits account for the quick drain
a display held at full brightness draws the most power
software reaches the network without being used
heat permanently reduces the capacity of the cell
lowering the brightness and setting it to adjust itself is advised
updating for unused software has to be turned off
leaving the device on the charger all night damages the battery
these steps put off the battery swap without restoring it
text: A battery that runs flat before evening worries its owner, though wear rarely explains it. Three habits account for most of the loss. The first is a screen held at full brightness, when the panel draws more power than the processor does. The second is the long list of programs that reach out to the network in the background. The third is heat, since a warm cell gives up capacity for good. The answer comes in three moves. Lower the brightness first, and let the device adjust it on its own. Next, shut off updating for the programs you almost never open. Last, keep the thing out of direct sun, and unplug it rather than leaving it on the charger all night, because a charge pinned at the top tires the cell. None of this brings a battery back to what it was, but it puts off the day you replace it.

units: two employees of one department each receive an unmanned flying machine
these machines are used to examine the roofs of buildings
one of the models is heavy and can be repaired on the spot
the other model is compact and easy to carry
any breakage of the compact model means sending it back to the maker
a gust of wind comes up during the first outing
the compact machine drifts off and strikes a water gutter
one of its blades snaps
its user waits two weeks for the spare part
the two machines are now used according to how exposed the site is
text: Two coworkers in one maintenance crew were handed flying machines the same week, both meant for inspecting roofs. The first picked a sturdy model on a thick fiber frame, the kind whose rotors you swap by hand in seconds. The second went for a light one that folds into a jacket pocket, quicker to get airborne, but where a single broken part means shipping the whole thing back to the maker. The wind came up during their first inspection. The heavy machine held its place over the rafters while the light one drifted and clipped a gutter. A blade snapped clean off. Its owner waited two weeks for a part his coworker carried in the trunk of his car. Since then the heavy one goes out to open sites and the light one to sheltered yards, and neither of them argues about which is better.

units: the power has to be cut before anything is handled
this precaution is presented as one that cannot be undone
a working surface has to be laid out beforehand
the tools include a fine screwdriver and flat pliers
a container serves to hold the screws
the corner screws come out before the edge ones
the screws are of different lengths and their places must be noted
a conductive ribbon ties the cover to the board
a dark charging light indicts the connector more often than the battery
text: Kill the power and pull the charger before you touch anything: that is the one step you cannot take back. Then set up your corner of the table. You want a fine screwdriver, flat pliers, a dry rag, and a small dish for the screws, or they roll onto the floor and you end up crawling after them. Start on the back of the case: take the corners out first, then the edges, and note where each screw came from, because they are not all the same length. Lift the cover slowly, never with a jerk, since a soft ribbon usually still ties it to the board. Now find the charging light: if it stays dark, the trouble is far more often the connector than the battery. Clean it, put it back together, drive the screws in without forcing them, plug it in, and watch the screen before you pack up.

units: a sound fault in a station is reported before sunrise
the departure display then went dark altogether
maintenance workers reach the equipment room shortly afterward
a backup power unit had gone into protection
its red light stayed on without blinking
a stalled fan had heated the cabinet past its limit
the workers replaced the fan and cleaned the filters
the display was brought back gradually, platform by platform
management now requires the cabinets to be checked every quarter
some travelers missed a train change for want of information
text: The call reached the control desk just before dawn: a crackle in the loudspeakers of a station, then the departure board going dark all at once. A maintenance crew got down to the equipment room half an hour later. They found first that a backup power unit had tripped into protection, its red light steady rather than blinking. By midday the cause was plain. A stalled fan had let the cabinet climb past the temperature at which it shuts itself down. The crew swapped the fan, cleared the filters, and brought the supply back in the early afternoon. The board came alive platform by platform, in the reverse order it had died. That evening management announced that the cabinets would be checked every three months instead of once a year. No train ran late, but travelers missed connections with nothing to tell them.

units: an adjustable lamp is aimed at the working surface
printed boards are stacked up waiting to be repaired
a pencil mark shows the burned area on each board
the soldering tool sits in its holder and is still giving off smoke
the smell of resin has soaked into the walls of the room
the craftsman has practiced this trade since the shop opened
runs of melted metal have marked the floor
the seat has left four pale round marks
having no window forces air to be drawn out at all times
the noise stopping signals a break in the power supply
text: Over the repairman's bench, a jointed lamp leans down toward an orderly mess. Green boards wait their turn in a stack, each one marked with a pencil stroke where the circuit went black. On the right the iron rests in its holder, its fine tip still smoking with the smell of resin. That smell has soaked into the walls, because the man has been soldering here since the shop first opened. The floor keeps a record of the trade as well: drops of solder melted into the covering, and four pale rings worn in by the stool. Since the room has no window, an extractor fan turns above the door without stopping, and its steady drone ends up passing for silence. When it cuts out, he lifts his head sharply, because that hole in the sound means the power has gone and a joint has just been ruined.

units: putting something back in order often costs more than buying it new
the writer blames this imbalance on how products are designed
a battery held on with adhesive makes taking it apart harder
screws with an unusual head call for tools kept for them alone
a soldered link instead of a plugged one draws the job out
makers justify these choices by keeping water out
a compressed gasket and ordinary screws would hold just as well
the writer proposes that board schematics be published
he asks that parts be sold at what the components cost
the obstacle is commercial and not technical
text: Fixing a thing ought to cost less than replacing it, and it seldom does. The fault lies not in the labor but in the design. A battery glued to the frame, screws with heads that nothing standard will turn, a ribbon soldered where a plug would do: each of those choices adds half an hour to the job and turns a cell swap into a full teardown. The defense offered is keeping water out, yet a compressed gasket and ordinary screws hold it out just as well for almost nothing. Three measures would be enough: require common fasteners, publish the board schematics, and sell spare parts at what the components cost. None of them calls for a technical breakthrough; all of them run into a trade that lives on replacement. As long as a sealed device costs less to build than one that opens, the bench will keep unscrewing sealed shells.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the main figure works as a repairer of technical objects
she starts with the energy cells
she can tell in advance which cells will run too hot
she is also drawn to very small drive motors
she opens sealed housings without harming the gasket
her workroom is cramped and poorly lit
she keeps her screws sorted by size
she greets and informs curious passers-by
she refuses to discard an object she has not examined
she machines the parts she cannot find
text: Walk past her door and you would never guess her occupation in the back room. She fixes broken gear for a living, and among everything reaching her bench, batteries come first. She opens them, coaxes a charge back into them, and knows which ones will overheat before ever connecting them. Tiny motors hold her next, the sort demanding fine pliers to release a bent shaft. Then come the housings, above all the sealed ones you have to crack open without ruining the gasket. Her workroom is one dim space: a bench, a swing-arm lamp, drawers of screws sorted by size. She likes explaining the trade to anyone curious enough to push the door open, and she will not throw out a device she has not opened yet. When a part cannot be had, she cuts it herself, filing a blank of metal all evening long if that is what the job takes.

units: the maker promised a week of use with no charging
the unboxing gives a flattering first impression
the device is described as very light
the display stays readable under strong light
the machine makes no noise during demanding work
after long use the shell warms up near the hinge
battery life drops once the radio link is switched on
a software fix has not removed the typing lag
the reviewer finds the price too high for what is offered
text: A week away from an outlet with nothing to plug into: that was the maker's claim for this small handheld reader. Unpacked, the promise looks believable: a matte shell, a hinge that clicks firmly under the thumb, a body almost weightless in the hand. The first sessions do nothing to spoil that. The screen stays readable in hard sun, and the thing never makes a sound, not even while it grinds through a heavy file. A week on, the mood cools. The shell grows warm near the hinge, and the battery life on the box melts away the moment the wireless link goes on. An update has since gone out and fixed part of that, yet the keys still lag behind the fingers. Call it a pleasant machine, roughly finished, and asking far more of the wallet than it hands back. The next one may be worth the wait.

units: the writer is writing from his workroom
an old sound receiver sits beside him
the reader had predicted that the device was beyond saving
a damaged electrical wire cut the sound at the slightest knock
the writer mended the link by soldering it again
damp had made the wooden case swell
the top no longer fitted into its housing
sanding restored the sliding of the lid
the device now keeps the writer company in the evenings
the writer invites his correspondent to come and see the result
text: I am writing to you from the workroom, the window open onto the yard, the old radio beside me on the bench. You told me it would never work again, and you were nearly right: a wire had frayed inside it, so the sound dropped out whenever anyone brushed the table. I stripped the cable back, soldered the two strands together again, and the crackle went away all at once. Damp had worked its way into the case as well. The wood swelled, the lid no longer dropped into its groove, so I sanded it patiently until it slid as before. Now the voices fill the room once night falls, and I drift off with them still going, never touching the volume. You see, it took almost nothing at all in the end. Come by whenever you can and hear for yourself how it sings, now that it breathes freely again.

units: the readings of a heat sensor become inaccurate
the sensing element is usually not to blame
a deposit of particles on the wall disturbs the flow of heat
replacing the whole unit is not necessary
cleaning followed by adjustment on two fixed marks is enough
checking means comparing the values with those of a control instrument
a steady offset can be taken up by the software
an erratic swing reveals a loss of sealing in the housing
the gasket must be renewed before readings start again
text: What is going on when a heat sensor stops giving readings you can trust? The probe itself is seldom to blame. Dust settles on the membrane and gets in the way of the heat exchange, and the drift begins right there. Does the whole unit need swapping out? Hardly ever. Clean the membrane, then set the instrument against two steady reference marks, and the trouble usually ends. How can you tell the work took? Leave the sensor beside a known-good instrument for a good stretch and compare what each one gives. A constant offset points to a leftover shift, and the software can take care of that. And when the gap wanders with no pattern behind it? The housing has most likely lost its seal, letting damp reach the contacts. Fit a fresh gasket before you begin another round of readings.

units: a technical manager asks a skilled worker about the choice of a machine
two devices are weighed against each other
the older device runs without any electrical supply
it is started by a foot control
the newer device is markedly faster
the newer device stops by itself when something jams
the newer device calls for regular upkeep
the older one is mended with basic tools
the two speakers decide to keep both machines
a second look at the choice is planned after a season of use
text: The engineer asked the technician which of the two systems he would rather have standing on the workshop floor. He spoke up for the older one: purely mechanical, worked by a pedal under the foot, and tied to no electrical supply at all. She pushed back. The newer machine runs far quicker, she said, and it halts on its own the instant a part jams. He granted her that much, then reminded her what the newer one wants in return, steady upkeep week after week, while the old one can be put right with a wrench and some patience. Her proposal was to keep both machines and to bring the powered model in only for the long runs. He agreed, but on one condition: the crew must learn to handle the old one properly first. They settled on taking up the question again once a full season of work has gone by.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: keeping sounds meant finding a way to write them down
the first method cut a groove with a vibrating point
this method made it possible to bring a voice back later
the second method rested on magnetizing a ribbon coated with grains
magnetizing allowed the content to be wiped and written again
the third method turned the signal into a run of separate values
each method changed practices as much as devices
recordings became in turn portable, copyable without loss, then freed from any object
this change is presented as a series of trade-offs between quality, sturdiness and ease of copying
text: Before sound could be carried anywhere, someone had to work out how to hold it still. The first answer was mechanical. A needle tied to a membrane cut a groove into soft material, so that a voice could be carved down and brought back long afterward. The second answer was magnetic. A ribbon coated in fine grains held the pull of a field, which meant a recording could be wiped and written over. The third answer counted instead: the smooth signal was chopped into a string of separate values, stored, and put back together on playback. Every one of these steps reshaped what people did as much as what they owned. Recordings turned portable, then copyable with nothing lost, then loose from any object at all. Read from end to end, the story amounts to a run of bargains struck among quality, sturdiness and ease of copying.

units: sending a message sets off its cutting into very short pieces
each piece carries a mark showing the address it is bound for
the pieces first travel through the air to the nearest relay
walls and structures are not enough to stop that relay from hearing them
the pieces then run on through buried or underwater cables
their route changes at every node according to congestion
the receiving device puts the pieces back in the right order
the whole trip takes an extremely short time
a lost piece is asked for again automatically without the user noticing
text: Consider what becomes of your message the second you tap send. Your handset chops it into tiny pieces and pins a label on every one of them, saying where it has to end up. Off they go through the air to the nearest tower, which manages to hear your handset through however many walls happen to stand in the way. From there they run along cables, mostly buried beneath streets or laid across the seabed, and at every junction they pick a fresh route depending on how crowded the last one is. They come down at the far end, where the receiving handset sorts them back into order and rebuilds the sentence you wrote. The whole trip is over faster than a blink, however far it had to go. And if a piece goes astray on the way, your handset quietly asks for it again, and you never notice a thing.

units: the night crew took no notice of a stopped fan in a technical cabinet
the coolness of the room discouraged any immediate action
the heat sensor had been shifted the day before because of wiring work
it was reading the temperature of a nearby corridor instead of the trapped hot air
no alarm went off despite the building heat
two storage units failed toward the end of the night
the incident cut off mail service for a very large public
the inquiry blames the failure on the unrecorded shifting of the sensor
a written procedure now covers any change in the position of a sensor
text: The whole thing started with a detail that the night crew shrugged off at first: the fan on one of the computer cabinets had gone quiet. The room itself felt cool, so nobody saw any reason to go and look into it before morning. But the heat probe had been shifted the day before to make room for cabling work, and it was now reading the air of the corridor next door instead of the stale air trapped behind the machines. So the heat built up behind them and no alarm ever sounded. Toward dawn two of the drives gave out, and mail service went down for many thousands of users. The internal report put the failure not on the hardware but on a probe that had been moved without anyone writing the move down anywhere. Ever since, shifting a sensor anywhere calls for a written note and a check the following day.

units: a hand-cranked torch stops working when its generator seizes
it is advised to lay the object on a light-colored cloth
this precaution keeps the screws from being lost
the four fasteners in the base come out before the two half-shells are parted
the parting must be gentle so as to spare the catches
the coil of wire turns out to be fouled with a greasy deposit
cleaning is done dry before the shaft bearing is oiled
a lingering squeak comes from the return spring, which has to be tightened
putting it back together means not driving the screws home at once
the light comes back little by little after long cranking
text: A hand-cranked flashlight usually ends up dead at the back of a drawer, the reason nearly always being a seized dynamo. Here is how to bring it back to life. Lay it on a pale cloth first, so that no screw can vanish against the surface. Take out the four screws in the base, then ease the two shells apart slowly, without straining the catches. Inside sits a gray coil furred with greasy dust matting the windings together. Brush it clean while it is dry, work the shaft free, and put one drop of light oil on the bearing. If the crank squeaks even then, the return spring is the culprit: unhook it and pull it back to tension. Close the shells, start the screws without driving them home, and turn the crank for a good long while. The beam will come back, faint at first, then full and steady.

units: the managers of a water supply have weighed two monitoring systems
the two systems are fitted to comparable pipes
the first uses pressure sensors wired to the mains supply
these sensors talk over a shielded wired link
the first gives very frequent readings and flags a water loss quickly
the second rests on standalone sensors closed inside a watertight case
the second sends its data over a radio link that draws little power
the second offers less precision but spares any digging work
the study recommends the wired one on sensitive stretches and the standalone one on distant branches
both systems depend on a water-flow model kept up to date by operators
text: The people running a water network have just weighed two monitoring setups fitted to twin mains. The first works from pressure sensors drawing power from the grid, wired back to a central controller over shielded cable. It reports at very short intervals and catches a leak long before the next round of readings. The second uses standalone probes sealed inside a watertight case, sending what they measure over a radio link that sips power. Its resolution is coarser, but putting it in place calls for no trench at all. The report lands on a split answer: keep the wired build on the stretches that matter most, where a leak costs dearly, and hand the far-flung branches to the standalone probes. Both share one weakness, a reliance on a water-flow model that someone has to update by hand.

units: the object described is a listening accessory set down on a piece of furniture
a colored signal crosses the surface before the charge ends
a short sound announces that the cell is full
the shell shows marks of use along its edges
the hinged joint bends without breaking
the cord stows away in a side compartment
an opening pushes the heat produced toward the rear
the stand can be tilted in successive steps
the whole thing folds small enough to fit at the bottom of a bag
text: Set the earpiece down on the table and watch what comes next. The shell warms up under your fingers first. Then a pale blue band slides across the top, and a soft click says the rechargeable cell has filled. The case is small enough to disappear inside one palm. Its edges have gone dull from handling, and the supple hinge bends over and over without cracking. The wired cord coils beside it and tucks into a pocket along one side. Later, once the shell runs hot, a thin grille pushes the warm air out the back. The adjustable stand lifts one notch, then another, until the angle finally sits right. When the session is over, everything folds away. The base drops into its sleeve, the cord follows, and the whole thing goes flat enough to vanish at the bottom of a bag. Nothing bulky, nothing brittle, nothing to take apart.

units: the text questions the early wearing out of electronic equipment
glued assembly prevents the replacement of a single component
repair shops observe this pattern
whole objects are thrown away although only one joint has failed
manufacturers shorten the period of software support
hardware in good condition becomes unusable without a patch
the buyer bears a double cost
local repairers lose their trade
the author calls for a demountable assembly and available diagrams
the author asks that the cell be replaceable on its own
text: Should we worry that our machines wear out before their time? Repair shops have known the first cause for a long time. Once a case is glued shut instead of screwed, one failed part kills the whole device. You can read the effect in the sorting bins, piled with hulls that lost nothing but a single joint. A second cause piles onto the first one and deepens it. Makers cut short the years of software support, so a perfectly healthy unit turns useless for want of a patch. The buyer pays twice, once for a machine and once for the machine that follows it, and the shop down the street loses the trade that fed it. None of this has to hold, and the whole thing can be turned around. Screws instead of glue, open diagrams, and a rechargeable cell you can swap on its own would hand the repairer back everything the adhesive took.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the main figure is designated by her trade as a repairer
the smell of melted metal stays on her hands after closing time
she began with old dusty sound receivers
those devices came from a woman living nearby
at first she could not identify the failed part
she replaced parts at random and spent her money on it
she took up the habit of writing down every fault
her notebook records the symptom and the part at fault
she now recognizes recurring families of faults
she repairs almost without ever accepting money
text: Her hands hold the smell of melted solder long after the shop closes. The repairwoman started out on dusty radio sets handed down by a woman next door, opening them with no diagram and closing them with no certainty. Her trouble came down to one thing. She could not tell which part had failed, so she swapped components at random and burned through her savings doing it. What rescued her, in the end, was a notebook. In it she sets down every fault, the symptom, the guilty part, the reading she took. The notebook has grown thick and stained, limp from years of thumbing. Now she reads whole families of faults in it, and she guesses before the case is even open. Neighbors from the surrounding streets bring her dead lamps and wired keyboards. She brings them back one at a time, and mostly she turns down the money.

units: two soldering devices are compared
one reaches the wanted heat far faster than the other
this gap weighs on the pace of the workshop
the slower device offers fine adjustment of the heat
the fast device gives only a small number of settings
the massive base of one gives better stability
the other moves as soon as its cord is pulled
the softened lead of one of them absorbs jolts
the other lead stiffens when the weather is cold
one of the two requires costly branded tips
text: Two soldering stations fight over one bench, and the ruling between them comes down to differences you can measure. The first one brings its tip up to the set temperature almost the instant you switch it on. The second dawdles, and that gap drags on the pace of the shop. The slow one, though, dials the heat in by the degree, while the quick one gives you three fixed settings and nothing between them. One base is heavy and eats up a good deal of bench room, yet it never shifts. The other skates the moment you tug on its cord. The lead on the first wears a supple silicone jacket. The second stiffens in the cold and sends every jolt straight to the point. Last of all, one takes ordinary spare tips, and the other demands a costly house brand. For a repair shop, the slow heavy machine wins, waiting and all.

units: the writer addresses the woman in charge of a workshop
the message concerns equipment lent to a group
the embroidery machine now takes the designs sent by the club
its arm sags when facing thick fabric
the jointed support of the lamp no longer holds a high position
the tablet works only once plugged into the mains
its cell no longer lasts a whole session
the rolling cabinet blocks movement in the room
two input devices are missing from the storage cupboard
the writer asks that these remarks be passed to the technical staff
text: To the workshop director, I am writing about the equipment on loan to the assisted sewing group. First, the embroidery machine now takes the patterns the club sends over, but its arm begins to sag as soon as the cloth gets thick. Second, the jointed lamp still gives good light, though its adjustable neck will no longer hold a high position. Third, the tablet lent to the students still works, provided it stays plugged in. Its rechargeable cell no longer covers half a session. Fourth, the rolling cabinet takes up far too much room for this space and blocks the way through it. Last of all, two wired keyboards have gone missing from the dusty cupboard at the back of the room. I would be grateful if you passed these notes along to the technical staff, and I am glad to walk anyone through them.

units: a visitor asks a workshop how an electronic board is made
the layout is first designed on a screen
the pattern is carried onto a metal coated sheet by exposure
the surplus metal is removed in a chemical bath
a guided rotating tool drills the passages meant for the connections
solder paste is laid down before the parts are set in place
the whole is brought to high heat to fix the joints
a camera inspects each board looking for a flaw
this check comes before final assembly
text: A visitor to the workshop starts by asking how a printed board comes into being. The answer runs through the work in the order it is done. It begins as a drawing on a screen, then moves onto a copper clad sheet by exposure to light. What becomes of the copper nobody wants, the visitor asks next. A bath of acid eats it away, and the sheet comes out of it with clean, fine tracks running across it. Then comes the drilling, where a guided cutter opens the holes the pins will sit in. Is the sheet ready to use now? Not yet, because solder paste still has to go down, the parts have to be set in place, and the whole thing has to ride through an oven whose hot air locks every joint. One last question covers the checking. A camera looks over each board and catches the bad track before final assembly.

units: a man from the floor above complains about the running time of his drilling tool
his neighbor blames the fault on the way the device is recharged
the power pack stayed permanently on its charger
the casing of the pack had swollen
a measuring device was used to test the cells one by one
two cells no longer delivered any current
this explains the loss of force while drilling
he is advised to store the pack half charged in a cool place
he must take it off the charger as soon as the green light shows
text: The neighbor from upstairs came down with his drill tucked under one arm, saying over and over that the battery held nothing anymore. My sister told him that the tool itself was innocent, and that the fault lay in his habit of leaving the pack sitting on its hot cradle around the clock. He argued for a while, and then he admitted that the casing had swollen out of shape. So she pulled a wired meter out of the dusty drawer and took a reading on each cell on its own. Two of them were dead, which explained why the power fell away the moment the bit bit into the wood. She told him to store the pack half charged somewhere cool, and to lift it off the charger as soon as the green light comes on. He went back upstairs pleased with himself, with a drill that ran again and a fresh bit thrown in.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the first mechanical looms raised a repeated blockage
changing the pattern required taking the mechanism apart
the threads had to be set again one by one
production stopped for several weeks
customers turned to weavers working by hand
the solution was to put the pattern information outside the machine
a craftsman devised a series of pierced boards linked together
the presence or absence of a hole decided whether the thread rose
changing the design came down to replacing the band
this principle was later taken up by calculating machines
text: In the earliest mechanized weaving shops, one obstacle kept coming back. Every change of pattern meant taking the mechanism apart and threading the yarns again one by one, and output stopped for weeks at a stretch. Orders drifted off to weavers working by hand, slower but far more willing. The way out came from outside the cloth trade, and it was to put the pattern into something that lives apart from the machine. A craftsman thought up small pierced boards, chained into a supple band that the loom read as it went by. Where a needle met a hole, the thread rose. Everywhere else it stayed down. Changing the design now meant changing the band, nothing more. The idea outgrew weaving fast, and that split between the order and the part that carries it out still runs through calculating machines.

units: the antenna is compared to a string that vibrates when a wave passes
the antenna produces no energy by itself
the loudspeaker follows the opposite path
a current sets the cone of the loudspeaker in motion
this motion makes the nearby air vibrate
in one case the energy arrives from outside and becomes electrical
in the other the energy leaves the conductor and becomes sound
both devices cope badly with too harsh a setting
an attracting metal mass bends the signal
text: An antenna is less like an ear than like a taut string stretched at the edge of a river you cannot see. The string makes nothing of its own. It shivers when a wave goes by, and it falls quiet when the wave moves off. A loudspeaker runs that path backwards. Send it a current, its supple cone stirs, and the air around it starts to shake. One listens, one speaks, and both live off the same family of motion. What separates them is the direction of the trade. In the antenna, energy arrives from outside and turns into a faint current. In the speaker, energy leaves the wire and turns into audible breath. One more thing ties them together, and it is that both hate hard matter around them. A stiff mount kills the motion, a magnetized mass bends the signal, and ear and mouth alike go deaf.

units: a failure occurs at night on a backup server
the team examines three subsystems in turn
the power supply shows an abnormal variation of voltage
a damaged capacitor is the origin of this fault
a fan no longer turns steadily
its clogged bearing lets the temperature pass the allowed limit
two storage units contain unreadable areas
no notification had reported these areas
the faulty parts are replaced and the data rebuilt
the lesson drawn is that a silent fault costs more
text: The failure hit in the middle of a maintenance night, on a backup server that the team had always taken for indestructible. They worked their way through three areas, one after another. On the power side, the readings showed odd ripple on the main rail, the mark of a worn, bulging capacitor. On the cooling side, a failing fan turned in fits and starts, and its dusty bearing let the board run well past the allowed limit. On the storage side, two drives reported sectors they could not read, and no warning had ever gone out about them. The repair went down that same list in order. Capacitor replaced, fan swapped for a fluid bearing model, drives rebuilt across the array. The team came away from that night with a lesson that stuck. A silent warning costs far more than a breakdown that makes noise.

units: sitting still for a long stretch loads the spine
the deep back muscles stiffen for want of movement
the pain comes and goes at first, then settles in for good
care providers see this trouble in adults who are younger and younger
the trouble also reaches people who have never lifted anything heavy
the cause is a slumped back rather than an injury
straightening up and moving often releases the muscular tension
adjusting the seat height keeps the thighs level with the floor
the discomfort fades within a season for those who apply these measures
text: Sitting still for hours puts far more strain on the spine than most people suspect. The deep back muscles, starved of movement, stiffen bit by bit and drag on the lower vertebrae. A dull ache sets in, coming and going at first, then settling in for good. Care providers see this complaint in adults who are younger and younger, including people who have never lifted anything heavy. The cause is rarely an injury. It lies in a slumped back, shoulders rolled forward, hips tipped backward. Putting that right costs almost nothing. Straightening up often, walking a little, stretching the muscles down the back of the legs already releases the tension that has piled up. Raising or lowering the seat so the thighs stay level with the floor finishes the job. Those who hold to this see the discomfort fade within a season.

units: the woman breaks her ankle a second time as an adult
in childhood she had worn a splint without suffering over it
as a child she kept running and laughed at her uneven walk
the adult fall happens on a slippery step
as an adult she finds her walking aid heavy and trips across the house exhausting
she understands that being still wears her out more than activity does
what made her laugh as a child shames her as an adult
a fine mark stays on her skin once the bone has knit
she takes up walking again, watching every step she places
text: The second break was nothing like the first, and that was what surprised her. As a child she had worn a light splint for a whole season without losing any of her spark: she almost ran, she hopped down hallways, she laughed at her own lopsided walk. Grown, the same joint gave way on a wet step, and the thing took on quite another color. The crutch felt heavy, the staircase hostile, the trip to the kitchen endless. She discovered that stillness wears you down more than effort ever does. What had amused her once now shamed her, not out of vanity, but because she could measure what she had stopped taking for granted. When the bone had knit, a fine scar marked the skin, a quiet trace of an ordinary fall. She learned to walk again, watching every step she placed, wary as anyone still mending.

units: the care kit is divided into three compartments
the first compartment holds the material that covers a wound
the pads must be sterile and wrapped one by one
the second compartment gathers the products spread on the skin
a soothing ointment is provided for minor burns
a gel treats bites that bring on an itch
the third compartment carries what holds or supports a limb
the expiry dates must be checked whenever the season turns
the container must be hard and kept away from heat
text: A well-built care kit sorts into three separate compartments. The first takes in whatever covers a wound: sterile pads, each one wrapped in its own sachet, adhesive dressings in several widths, a roll of tape and a pair of round-tipped scissors. The second gathers what goes onto the skin: an alcohol-free antiseptic solution, a soothing ointment for light burns, a gel for the sort of bite that brings on an itch. The third carries the holding gear: an elastic bandage, a sling, a soft splint to keep a finger or a wrist from moving at all. Check the expiry dates whenever the season turns, and throw out without hesitation anything that has already been opened. Keep the whole lot in a hard container, well away from heat and out of the reach of children, then write on the lid whatever is running low.

units: a rehabilitation center was to go up in a district that had none
the work reused a disused warehouse and kept its metal frame
the first patients taken in were coming out of major surgery
those patients often moved with a support or a device holding a limb still
a heated pool opened in the cold season that followed
the heated water serves joints that cannot bear weight on the ground
a workshop on holding the back and on preventing falls came next
that workshop is meant for older people of the area
local officials find the capacity too small and ask for an extension
text: The word went out just as the mild season opened: a rehabilitation center would go up in a working district that had never had anything of the kind before. Work began without delay inside a disused warehouse whose metal frame was left standing where it was. By autumn the first rooms were taking in patients coming out of heavy surgery, many of them leaning on a crutch or strapped into a brace. The winter that followed brought a heated pool into service, which made it possible to treat joints far too sore to bear any weight at all on the ground. Management then announced a workshop on holding the back and on preventing falls, open to the older people of the area. Local officials now hold that demand outruns the capacity that had been planned, and they are asking for the building to be made larger.

units: the heel turns red and grows slightly warm at the start
the rubbing of the shoe parts the top layers of skin
clear fluid fills the space thus opened and forms a blister
the tension of the pouch changes the way of walking
shifting the weight onto the other foot brings on a sore hip
the skin laid bare after a burst risks an infection
the area is covered with a clean pad and not opened on purpose
a thick ointment spread before walking lowers the rubbing
a final thickening of the skin makes the trouble disappear
text: The heel turns faintly red at first, a shade warmer than the skin around it. The shoe rubs it over and over, the top layers of skin part company, and clear fluid seeps into the gap that opens: a blister. Its taut roof makes standing on that foot unpleasant and alters the walk, which throws the weight onto the other foot and brings on, some time later, a sore hip. Should the pouch burst, the raw patch turns tender and lies wide open to infection. That is why it gets covered with a clean pad rather than opened on purpose. A thick ointment worked in before a long walk cuts down the rubbing that starts the whole thing off. Thin socks with no bulky seam hold the heat down as well. Once the skin thickens over that spot, it stands up better and the trouble goes away on its own.

units: the writer holds that lack of sleep is treated as ordinary
drowsiness and short temper are blamed on the load of work
sleep loss is never held responsible
evening screens push the hour of going to bed back
the stimulating drink of the next day delays the following bedtime further
the writer advises cutting the screens before entering the bedroom
the bedroom must be kept cool and dark
he recommends a steady bedtime, the end of the week included
the effects are felt after a handful of nights
sleep is presented as a repair owed and not as a privilege
text: Let us own up to it: we sleep badly, and we make our peace with that far too readily. The yawn cutting through a meeting, the heavy eyelid at mid-afternoon, the temper souring over nothing, we blame the workload for all of it, never the nights we keep cutting short. Come evening, the screen wins: one video, then another, and bedtime arrives long past the hour we had settled on. The next morning, coffee makes up the difference, pushing the following bedtime later still. Escaping that spiral involves no particular mystery. Shut the screens off before entering the bedroom, keep the room cool and dark, choose one steady bedtime, weekend included. Austere, perhaps, yet noticeable after a handful of nights. Sleep is no treat you grant yourself. It is a repair you owe yourself.

units: the physical therapist meets her patients standing, with no desk between them
she started out in a hospital ward with injured athletes
there she treated sprains, tears and painful muscle contractions
the sessions there were short and the results measurable
she now practises with elderly patients in a residential district
her aim is no longer to bring a joint back to top-level sport
she teaches how to get up alone and climb a staircase without fear
she works on standing steadiness in order to prevent falls
she says she enjoys this slower rhythm
her patients are after a confidence that is built one session at a time
text: The physical therapist meets each patient on her feet, at the door of her room, never from behind a desk. She started out in a hospital ward where the work was mostly injured athletes: sprains, torn muscle, a stubborn contraction after an effort nobody had prepared for. The pace ran quick there, the sessions short, the outcome easy to measure. She practises now in a residential district with elderly patients, and the trade has changed in kind. Her aim is no longer to bring a joint back to top-level sport, but to teach someone to get up off the floor alone, to climb a staircase without fear, to stand steady enough to keep from falling. She says she enjoys the slower pace of it. Where the athlete wanted a date, her patients are after confidence, and confidence gets built one session at a time.

units: the reviewer praises three aspects of the work and disputes only one
the first quality is the sharpness with which the movements are described
every handling is broken down into elementary movements with no obscure vocabulary
the second quality is the restraint of the writing
the author points out the limits of care given at home
the author states when a doctor's opinion becomes indispensable
the third success lies in the hand-drawn illustrations
the reviewer finds these drawings warmer than medical photographs
the passage on muscle pain is handled too briefly
the reader closes the book pleased but slightly let down
text: This handbook of home care earns praise on three counts and objection on one. Its first strength is the sharpness of the movements it lays out: putting on a dressing, changing a pad, spotting a wound that has turned. Each handling is taken apart into elementary movements, with no murky vocabulary. Its second quality is restraint. The author marks out, without wearying of it, the limits of care given at home and the moment a doctor's opinion becomes indispensable. Its third success is a matter of beauty: the hand-drawn plates lend the volume a warmth that clinical photographs never reach. Now the objection. The chapter on muscle pain dispatches soreness and cramp in a single page, as though troubles that common deserved no study. You close the book pleased, and slightly let down.

units: the sender recounts what followed his operation at the reader's request
the procedure took place under a local anaesthetic late last week
the surgeon removed a piece of bone that was jamming the joint
the dressing was renewed the next day by a nurse
a rigid device must be kept on until the follow-up visit
the pain went away in the course of the week that followed
an itch around the stitching signals healing according to the care team
a plain ointment must be spread on without rubbing
the sender now puts his foot on the ground with a single support
rehabilitation will begin once the stitches are taken out
text: I am writing to tell you what followed the operation, since you asked for the detail. It was done late last week under a local anaesthetic, and the surgeon took out the piece of bone that was jamming the joint. The next day a nurse renewed the dressing and fitted a rigid brace that I have to keep on until the follow-up visit. Over the week that followed the pain went away, though an itch came up around the stitching, the usual sign of healing according to the care team. They told me to use a plain ointment and spread it on without rubbing. Since the day before yesterday I put the foot on the ground with a single crutch, and I take the stairs leading with the sound leg. Rehabilitation will begin once the stitches are taken out. Write and tell me what your doctor makes of that schedule.

units: the night-time contraction strikes a muscle already worked in the evening
a shortage of water and mineral salts locks the muscle fibres
the episode is harmless in most cases
the attack clears in very little time
stretching the muscle by pulling the toes back stops the signal
a warm compress laid on afterwards loosens the fibre
that warmth limits the muscle soreness of the next day
drinking enough in the evening and avoiding late effort prevent a return
certain medicines that flush out water must be watched
frequent attacks that cut through sleep warrant a consultation
text: What sets off a contraction at night? The muscle seizes when it has already been worked through the evening and runs short of water and mineral salts, so the fibres lock and will not let go. Is there an illness to fear? In most cases, no: the cause stays harmless and the episode clears in a handful of moments. What can be done during the attack? Stretching the muscle gently, pulling the toes back toward the shin, stops the signal that keeps the contraction alive. A warm compress laid on afterwards loosens the fibre and limits the muscle soreness of the next day. Can a return be avoided? Drink enough in the evening, keep away from late hard effort, watch any medicine that flushes out water. When is a consultation warranted? If attacks cut through sleep and repeat without letup, an examination is in order.

units: a rehabilitation professional describes two opposite attitudes among the people she treats
the first attitude consists in locking the injured joint and no longer using it
the second attitude consists in wanting to stretch the muscle at the very first appointment
the specialist judges that neither of these two behaviors is good
the absence of movement ends up weakening the joint and stiffening the muscle attachments
an effort that is too violent prolongs the irritation of the tissue
a colleague points out that the same uncertainty appears with hand injuries
both practitioners recommend moderate and frequent movement, stopped in case of sharp pain
they recall that recovery is judged over several weeks and not over a single appointment
text: A physical therapist says that her patients walk through the door holding two opposite ideas about what healing should feel like. One group wants a sore ankle locked into a rigid brace and left alone until it settles down on its own. The other group asks for a deep stretch at the very first session, sure that soreness must be the sign of progress. Neither approach works, she tells them. A joint that stops moving grows weak, and the tendons harden around it. A joint pushed too hard keeps the inflammation burning. A colleague of hers adds that people who hurt a wrist get stuck on exactly the same question. What helps, both of them say, is small movement repeated often, and stopped the moment the pain turns sharp. They finish with the part patients skip past: recovery is measured in weeks, not in a single appointment.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: healers of the past relied on an oral inheritance for lack of reliable instruments
this know-how was limited to a small number of practices
plant drinks were used against fever and against throat irritation
fragrant ointments were spread on swollen areas
warm plasters were laid on at bedtime and removed on rising
the drawing of blood was both feared and demanded
the healer's speech weighed as much as his preparations
giving the illness a name already brought relief
science kept few of these treatments but drew from them a lesson about waiting and trust
text: Long before medicine had any instrument it could trust, healers leaned on a memory passed along by word of mouth, and that memory came down to a handful of practices. Boiled plants came first: a bitter drink for fever, a sweetened one to quiet a throat rubbed raw. Then came the ointments, spread thick over swollen skin, whose scent alone was enough to persuade the sufferer. Warm poultices had their place too, laid on at bedtime and lifted again at dawn. Drawing blood stood apart from the rest, feared one week and begged for the next. And the healer's voice weighed as much as anything he mixed: he gave the illness a name, and the naming eased it. Out of that tangled inheritance, research has kept few remedies, though it took from it a lasting lesson about waiting and about trust.

units: the medicine in shell form first travels down the tube leading to the stomach
muscle contractions carry it down
the acidity of the stomach dissolves the shell and frees its contents
the folded wall of the thin intestine takes up the active matter
the blood then carries the matter to the organ that transforms it
this transformation lowers the strength of the remedy
the remaining share attaches to precise targets in the tissue concerned
the action rises to a peak then decreases as elimination goes on
a liquid preparation acts sooner because its active matter is already in solution
text: A swallowed capsule has a long way to go before it does anything at all. It travels down the food pipe, pushed along by steady waves of muscle. Acid in the stomach eats through the shell and frees the powder packed inside it. The drug then reaches the small intestine, whose deeply folded wall offers an enormous surface for taking it up. From there it crosses into the blood, which carries it along to the liver, and the liver breaks down part of the molecule, so that less of it stays active. Whatever survives moves out to the target tissue and locks onto specific receptors there. The effect builds, peaks, and then fades as the kidneys and the liver clear the drug away. A syrup follows much the same route, but it starts working sooner, since the drug in it has already been dissolved.

units: a string player sought advice for headaches that were cutting his playing sessions short
no disorder was found on the side of the eyes or the ears
the clinician spotted a clenching of the jaws during the difficult passages
this repeated clenching wore out the muscles between the skull and the neck
the strain spread toward the sides of the forehead and brought on the pain
the dread of the attacks increased the contraction and kept the trouble going
the clinician taught the player a short release between two pieces played
she added a deep breathing exercise to it
the headaches became rarer after one season
the player put his trouble down to the fear of failing rather than to his instrument
text: A string player sought advice about the headaches that were cutting his practice short. Nothing turned up in his eyes or in his ears. What the clinician did notice was the way he clenched his jaw whenever a hard passage came up. Held through session after session, that clenching wore out the muscles running from the base of the skull down into the neck, and the strain spread forward to the temples, where the ache began. Dread of the next attack only tightened him further, and the whole thing fed itself. So she taught him a short release to run through between pieces, along with a slow breathing drill. Within a season the headaches came less often. He decided in the end that his trouble grew less out of the instrument in his hands than out of fearing a failure in front of it.

units: an unpleasant mouth odor on waking rarely comes from the stomach
it is caused mainly by micro-organisms that multiply on the tongue and near the gums during sleep
the method offered holds five actions that call for no costly equipment
the teeth must be cleaned on waking and before sleeping, with the brush aimed toward the flesh of the gum
floss must pass between the teeth because the brush cannot reach those gaps
the tongue must be scraped gently to remove the pale film that settles on it
drinking water helps because a dry mouth sharpens the odor while saliva cleans
an appointment with the dental practitioner is needed if the trouble goes on
an inflamed gum or a damaged tooth can keep the trouble going without being visible
text: Bad breath in the morning worries a lot of people, though the stomach is almost never behind it. It comes mostly from the bacteria that build up overnight on the tongue and along the gum line. Five habits will handle it, and not one of them calls for costly gear. Brush when you get up and again before bed, angling the bristles toward the gum rather than scrubbing away at the enamel alone. Run floss between every tooth, since bristles cannot reach into those narrow gaps. Scrape the surface of the tongue gently, where a pale film settles overnight. Keep drinking water through the day: a dry mouth sharpens the smell, while saliva rinses it away. If the trouble holds on despite all this, see a dentist, because an inflamed gum or a damaged tooth can keep it going without ever showing.

units: two opposite opinions circulate in a neighborhood gym
one group defends sessions in a very hot cabin
these followers claim that their muscles loosen after sweating heavily
the other group prefers immersion in very cold water
the latter maintain that the pain switches off abruptly
the trainer of the place refuses to side with either camp
he explains that heat softens tissue and speeds up the flow of blood
he explains that cold numbs and calms the irritation of the tissue
according to him the two methods suit different moments
he judges that sleeping enough and drinking enough counts for more than these practices
text: At a neighborhood gym you can hear two camps arguing it out, and neither one of them gives an inch. The heat crowd books session after session in an overheated cabin, walks back out soaked through, and swears that their muscles have loosened right up. The cold crowd drops into an icy pool instead and claims the ache just switches off. The trainer of the place grins and refuses to hand either side the win. Heat softens tissue and gets the blood moving, he says, while cold numbs and settles the inflammation, so both of them are useful, though not at one and the same moment. What he really notices is that the regulars keep missing the plain part of it: sleeping enough and drinking enough. No cabin anywhere, he laughs, ever made up for short nights and for meals eaten standing up.

units: the care room sits on the floor above a food shop
it holds two rooms with little furniture
the waiting room holds only seats, a plant and worn magazines
the second room is used for consultations and holds a table covered in paper, a weighing device and an instrument for measuring pressure
the boxes of medicine are stored up high and sorted by ailment
the clean supplies are kept in a drawer, every injection instrument in a sealed wrapper
the tap of the sink opens with the arm to limit the passing on of germs
the caregiver takes people without an appointment three half days a week
she treats wounds, changes dressings and listens to the fears of those who come
the place is very quiet, only the cold storage device makes any noise
