text: The clinic sits above a grocery store and takes up two rooms, with nothing extra in either of them. The waiting room holds a row of chairs, one leafy plant, and a stack of dog-eared magazines. Next door is where people are examined: a narrow table covered in paper, an old scale, a pressure cuff hanging on the wall. Boxes of tablets line the top shelf, sorted by ailment. A drawer keeps the sterile supplies, every needle still sealed inside its packet. By the window stands a sink whose tap you work with your elbow, which keeps germs from traveling around. The nurse who runs the place takes walk-ins three afternoons a week, dressing wounds, changing bandages, listening to whatever frightens the people who come. It is very quiet in there, apart from the hum of the refrigerator.

units: night rest was first looked down on before being reconsidered
it was held at the start as a hollow gap that had to be cut short
active minds believed themselves bound to sleep less
a later phase prized long waking hours as a mark of courage
exhaustion was then displayed as a distinction
studies run at night then showed intense activity in the sleeping brain
this activity covers sorting, the fixing of memories and repair
of late people count their nights and worry about a result judged poor
the writer holds that this measured watching is a mistake
he maintains that rest calls for steadiness, darkness and a calm mind
text: Sleep spent a long time in disgrace before anyone thought to speak up for it, and the path it took is worth a look. It counted at first as an empty gap, a stretch of time torn out of living, which hardworking minds owed it to themselves to cut short. Then came the age of the guilty sleeper: staying up late proved your drive, and exhaustion was worn like a badge. Research opened the night laboratories after that, and what turned up there was a busy brain, sorting, fixing memories in place, repairing. Lately the swing has gone the other way. We count our nights, we score them, and we fret over a poor result. That strikes me as a mistake. Sleep asks for no heroics and no watching over. It asks for steadiness, for darkness, for a quiet mind. Wanting it badly is enough to drive it off.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the head of a workshop of healing plants had not meant to take up this work
a lasting allergic reaction, poorly calmed, pushed her to look into what plant drinks were made of
this interest led her to study plants and then to work in a place of analysis
she saw that the richness of plants changes with the nature of the ground and the moment of the picking
she therefore made a check of each batch compulsory before it dries
this rule slowed her rate of making
impatient buyers left her because of these delays
the sellers of medicine trust her and take the greater part of what she makes
she refuses to announce cures and recalls that a plant drink soothes without treating an infection
her coworkers put the long life of the business down to this restraint
text: The woman who runs the medicinal plant workshop had never planned on the work. A stubborn allergy that ordinary treatments barely touched pushed her to look into what was actually in the herbal drinks people kept recommending to her. That question carried her into botany, and from botany into an analysis lab. Since she could see that the strength of a plant shifts with the soil and with the timing of the picking, she made testing every batch compulsory before drying. The rule slowed her output and cost her the customers who were in a hurry. It also won over the pharmacists, who now buy the greater part of what she makes. She still refuses to promise cures: an infusion soothes, it does not clear an infection. That restraint, her staff will tell you, is why the workshop has lasted.

units: a prevention scheme meant for the staff of a company draws a divided appraisal
the opening analysis is judged accurate
stillness in front of a screen stiffens the neck and dulls the shoulders
it also brings on pain at the joint of the hand that remedies do not erase for long
the answer chosen is a sound signal that cuts off the work and suggests a short loosening exercise
the first reactions report less discomfort at the end of the week
the carrying out is criticized for its lack of flexibility
the signal goes off without regard for the attention under way
many employees switch the scheme off after a week
the writer suggests letting each person set their own break times and taking up a discreet visual reminder
text: The prevention program offered to the staff at this company deserves a divided verdict. Its starting point is sound enough: frozen postures in front of a screen stiffen the neck, leave the shoulders dull and heavy, and bring on the kind of wrist pain that no medicine clears away for long. The answer it proposes is an audible alert that breaks off the task and suggests a short loosening exercise. The idea appeals, and the early feedback reports less discomfort by the end of the week. Where the thing falls down is rigidity. The alert fires with no regard at all for what anyone happens to be concentrating on, and plenty of employees switch it off after a week. A fix looks within reach: let each person set their own break windows, then trade the sound for a quiet reminder on the screen.

units: the writer answers a complaint from the reader about poor sleep
the writer has asked a caregiver at a care center
the recommendations are sorted into three separate groups
the first group covers what one eats in the evening
a lack of iron is presented as a source of lasting weariness
the second group deals with physical activity and loosening exercises
the third group describes the conditions of the bedroom
the caregiver advises seeking help if the spells come back
the writer asks for a reply about the measures tried
text: You wrote that your evenings are restless and that sleep keeps slipping away from you. I put the question to a nurse at the care center I go to, and she arranges her advice under three separate headings. The first is about what you eat late in the day: no heavy meals before bed, and she reminded me that a shortage of iron feeds a stubborn, lingering tiredness. The second is about moving: walk every afternoon, loosen the shoulders once evening arrives, avoid violent exertion as night approaches. The third heading is the bedroom itself, which she wants cool, dark, quiet, with no screen glowing anywhere. One remark of hers has stayed with me since. If the dizzy spells or the chills return, don't wait them out, seek attention quickly. Write and tell me what you have attempted, and I will say whether it matches her description.

units: a patient being interviewed describes the stages of her recovery
the first sensation mentioned is a heaviness in the limbs
a state of turned stomach then arrives in waves
the first week felt endless to her
the second week went by almost unnoticed
quiet and dim light helped her get better
a caregiver kneaded the back of her neck at the end of the day
a slow-healing wound on her arm worried her more than her diagnosis
she advises asking nothing of oneself
text: What comes first? The patient we spoke with describes a dull heaviness, as though her arms and legs had doubled in weight. And after that? Nausea, she says, a wave that rises and pulls back without warning. Does that stage last? She hesitates, then answers that the first week felt endless, while the second slipped by almost without a trace. What eased it? Quiet, dim light, and the hand of a nurse's aide who came at dusk to knead the back of her neck. And the nights? Sleep returned in pieces, never in one whole stretch. Was she afraid she would not recover? She admits that a wound on her arm was slow to close, and that this small thing worried her more than the whole diagnosis. What does she advise in the end? Ask nothing of yourself, and take slowness as an ally rather than an enemy.

units: a sports doctor explains a chain of causes to his patient
an unprepared muscle stays cold and short on suppleness
a cold fiber tears more easily during a sudden lengthening
the tear brings on a local inflammatory reaction
the inflammation draws in blood and sets off the pain
the patient asks about the swelling of his knee
the swelling follows from the same chain
cold applied to the area eases the phenomenon
loading the joint too soon delays the healing
text: The sports doctor walks his patient through the chain of events. Skipping the warm-up, he explains, leaves the muscle fibers cold and short on stretch. The patient wants to know what that changes in practice. A cold fiber handles a sudden lengthening badly, the doctor answers, and tears without much resistance. The tear then sets off inflammation right at that spot, and the inflammation pulls blood in, which is where the pain comes from. The patient is puzzled by the swelling that has come up around his knee. Same mechanism, the doctor tells him, and a cold pack held against the area will settle it down. A muscle that has been properly prepared takes those jolts without giving way. He finishes with a warning: load the joint too soon and the healing drags on and on. Build the training back up step by step.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: in the past minor wounds killed patients with no other illness
practitioners saw fever and discharge without understanding the source
infection was then judged unavoidable
observers noticed a difference between the treatment rooms
the rooms where hands went unwashed lost more patients
the measure adopted was the cleaning of hands and instruments
this measure was poorly received at first by the caregivers
the death records ended up convincing them
this rule remains a foundation of care
text: There was a time when minor wounds carried off patients who had nothing else wrong with them. Doctors watched the fever climb, the chills set in, the wound run, and could not name what tied these things together. The trouble lay in a belief: infection was taken as unavoidable, almost part of the natural order. Patient observers eventually caught a pattern across the wards, since the rooms where hands went unwashed lost more of the sick than the rest. The remedy was severe in its plainness. Wash the hands, scrub the instruments clean, before every single procedure. Resistance ran high, because such a demand pointed a finger at the caregivers themselves. The death counts won the argument in the end, and the losses began to fall. That modest rule still holds as one of the foundations of care.

units: two close sensations are often confused with each other
one gives the illusion that the room is turning
the other feels like an inner collapse without turning
the first has its origin in the inner ear
the inner ear tells the brain how the head is tilted
the second comes from a short drop in blood supply to the brain
faced with the first one should sit down and stare at a fixed point
faced with the second one should lie down and raise the legs
a repeat of these episodes calls for a medical examination
text: Two neighboring sensations get mixed up all the time: vertigo and faintness. With vertigo the whole room seems to spin around you, while faintness feels more like an inner collapse, with no spinning at all. Vertigo most often starts in the inner ear, the part that reports to the brain on how the head is tilted. Faintness, for its part, comes from a brief drop in the blood supply reaching the brain. The useful response differs in each case, and bystanders who confuse the two delay the appropriate reaction. When vertigo strikes, sit down, lock your eyes on something motionless, and hold the neck still. When faintness comes on, lie down and raise the legs so that blood flows back toward the head. One isolated episode is hardly alarming, but repeated recurrences deserve a full medical examination.

units: the narrator recounts a stay at a treatment center
the treatments included bubbling baths and clay wraps
a therapist kneaded his back with vigor
he describes the other guests he met there
a teenager had been sent there by his lung doctor
the food lacked taste but was served with solemnity
he slept better than he had in a very long time
he left lighter and convinced that rest is something one learns
text: Alright, let me tell you about my week at the treatment center, because it was worth the trip. The treatments first: bubbling baths, clay wraps, and a therapist who worked my back over until I laughed from the pain. Then the other guests: a former swimmer who talked nonstop, a retired woman who knew every hallway, a teenager sent there by his lung doctor and sulking about it. Then the meals: bland, honestly, though served with a seriousness that made the blandness almost ceremonial. And then the nights: I slept the way I hadn't slept in ages, no sudden jolting awake, none of that knot sitting in the throat. The thick quiet of the corridors surely had something to do with it. I came home lighter, a bit ridiculous in a bathrobe that was far too short, and convinced that rest is something you learn.

units: the first check concerns the state of the shoes
a worn sole upsets the footing and strains the knees
a warm-up of wide movements comes before the run
the calves and the thighs are loosened without forcing
the start is at a pace that allows talking
the speed rises only past the first third of the route
the stop must be gradual and followed by walking
a lukewarm shower relaxes the muscles on getting home
a sharp pain in a knee means giving up the next session
text: Start with your shoes: a worn sole throws the stride off balance and wears the knees out over time. Then devote a dozen or so wide swinging movements to the warm-up, enough to raise the heart rate gradually rather than abruptly. Stretch the calves and the thighs, and never force a joint that feels stiff. Set off at an easy pace, one you could sustain while talking out loud. Pick the speed up only past the first third of the route. At the finish, don't stop dead: keep walking, let the breathing settle, drink in small spaced sips. Tell someone your intended route if you head out alone as evening falls. Once home, a lukewarm shower is enough to soothe the muscles. Drink again half an hour afterward. If a sharp pain shows up in a knee, skip the following session and have it examined.

units: seats are short in the waiting room of a clinic
the closing of a nearby practice moved its clientele to this place
the wait before an appointment has grown longer
the visits have become shorter
unanswered questions bring the patients back one more time
a caregiver says she recognizes the same faces too often
mild disorders worsen for want of steady follow-up
management announces two more practitioners in the warm season
text: Seats have been short in the clinic waiting room since autumn. The practice down the street shut its doors and pushed a whole clientele in here, and the effect spread outward from there. Appointments drift further off, so visits get shorter; shorter visits leave questions hanging, so patients come back again. A mother who came in for her son leaves with one question out of three answered. A nurse's aide talks about faces she recognizes far too often. Without steady follow-up, mild problems worsen quietly: a deficiency left untreated, a wound that refuses to close, a blood pressure climbing with no alarm. Management says two more doctors will arrive when the warm season comes. Until then, care goes to whoever needs it most, and everyone senses that the backlog will be paid for later.

units: a first-aid kit fits in a hard case closed with a strap
the main difficulty comes from the mess and not from the contents
one searches inside it at a moment when the hands are shaking
the solution is to split the supplies into labeled compartments
the first compartment holds what is needed to clean a wound
the second gathers dressings wraps and round-tipped scissors
the third holds gloves an emergency blanket and a medical book
the book lists the current treatments and the allergies
the kit is placed near the entrance so a visitor can find it
text: A well-planned first-aid kit fits inside a hard case that closes with a strap. The usual trouble is not what goes into it but the mess that builds up inside, since you end up digging through it exactly when your hands are shaking. The remedy is to distribute the supplies among clearly labeled compartments. The first one holds sterile pads and the saline for cleaning out a wound. The second keeps dressings in several sizes, elastic wraps, and a pair of round-tipped scissors. The third stores disposable gloves, a folded emergency blanket, and a small book that lists the treatments being taken along with any known allergies. A recent prescription can be slipped in alongside it. Kept near the front door, the case stays within reach even for a visitor who does not know the place.

units: two directions of care are set against each other
the first acts once the illness has declared itself
its effectiveness is easily observed
the second steps in before the disorder appears
its results stay invisible because they consist of illnesses avoided
this difference in visibility explains the gap in funding
the writer holds that preventing costs less and spares suffering
the writer asks that both directions be funded equally
text: We are too quick to set the medicine that repairs against the medicine that prevents, as if one had to hand its resources over to the other. The first steps in once the illness has declared itself: it operates, prescribes, relieves, and its results are easy to measure. The second works before any disorder appears, and what it achieves stays out of sight, since it consists of illnesses that never happened. That imbalance in visibility explains the imbalance in the budgets. Repair can be seen, prevention cannot. Still, it deserves saying plainly that prevention costs less and spares whole stretches of suffering, whereas repair tends to arrive late in the day. Our health institutions ought to fund both paths with the same steadiness, instead of treating the second as an optional add-on.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the main figure first held a junior job in a care facility
an experienced colleague pushed her to get trained
she studied in the evenings for three years before earning her diploma
she won the creation of a room set aside for expectant mothers to move about
her superiors resisted the request at first
she passed her experience on to caregivers who came from distant regions
she still runs a training session after the end of her working life
she holds that listening works as well as a drug treatment
text: The midwife at the valley clinic started out as a nursing aide. She stripped beds, wheeled carts down long corridors, and listened to women describe pains that no one took seriously. An older nurse pushed her to go back to school. She sat through evening classes and earned her certificate after three years of it. Once she joined the ward, she asked for a room where expectant mothers could walk, breathe, and doze between contractions. Her supervisors said no, then gave way. Later she trained colleagues who traveled in from far-off districts, showing them small movements no textbook had ever bothered to describe. She retired not long ago, yet she still runs a workshop where young caregivers practice listening before they reach for a prescription pad. Patience, she says, soothes as well as any carefully measured drug.

units: the most striking feature of the place is how quiet it is
an absorbing surface swallows the noise of people moving about
visitors lower their voices without being asked
the writer holds that noise breeds fatigue
fatigue sours the mood and gets in the way of falling asleep
cutting out the source of noise breaks that sequence
the writer finds the shared rooms and the kitchen dull
after two nights the muscle tension eases
text: What stays with you after a week at this rest center is not the pale architecture but the quiet it manufactures. The corridors run wide, lined with thick felt, and the material swallows footsteps so thoroughly that the ear finally lets go. The effect catches people off guard: visitors who arrive wound tight begin lowering their voices, though nobody asks them to. The reason behind it is plain, almost mechanical. Noise wears you down, weariness sours the mood, and a soured mood keeps sleep at bay. Cut the first link and the whole chain falls apart. You could fault the shared rooms for their blandness and the kitchen for playing it far too safe. Such complaints weigh little against the result: after two nights the shoulders drop, the jaw unclenches, and you catch yourself dozing in an armchair without a shred of guilt.

units: the writer blames the night cough on the state of the bedroom
the air in the room is too dry and never renewed
dryness irritates the lining of the throat and sets off a cough
he advises opening the window before going to bed
he explains that cold air, once warmed, brings moisture in
he recommends turning the heating down
he suggests setting a bowl of water near the heat source
he proposes drinking enough through the evening
he asks for a nightly note on how the symptom changes
he urges seeing a doctor if the attempt fails
text: Writing because that night cough is keeping you awake, and my hunch is that the trouble sits in your bedroom rather than in your chest. The air in there never moves: the window stays shut, the radiator runs all night, and the moisture drops below anything comfortable. A dried-out throat lining gets irritated, then answers with a hacking cough that shows up the moment you lie flat. Worth a week of trying: open the window a quarter of an hour before bed, even when it is bitter out — outside air, once it warms up indoors, carries more vapor than the stale kind. Turn the heat down a notch after that, and set a bowl of water beside it. Drink enough through the evening too, without overdoing it. Write down each night whether the cough came back. If nothing shifts, see a doctor and let me come along.

units: the question raised weighs the value of running against that of brisk walking
running puts a heavier demand on the heart within a short session
walking calls for a longer session to reach a comparable result
each running stride crushes the joints under a load greater than the person's own weight
follow-up surveys show that the gentler practice is given up less often
walking or exercise in a pool suits a damaged joint better
the writer concludes that running gives more per session and walking more across a year
text: Do you have to run to keep the heart in shape, or is brisk walking enough? It depends on what you are after. Running leans harder on the heart muscle and burns more within a short session, while a fast walk calls for a longer outing to reach the same place. The pounding, though, is another matter. Every running stride crushes the joints under a load well above the walker's own weight, and the gentler pace spares them that. Which raises a second question: which of the two do people actually keep up? Follow-up surveys point the same way every time, since the less demanding habit gets dropped less often. And what about a sore knee, or a hip that makes you limp? Caution leans toward walking, or better yet toward exercise held up by water. Per session running wins; across a year the walker does.

units: the pharmacist asks the customer when the fever began
the customer reports chills that came on the evening before
she lists a sore throat, a runny nose, sneezing and aching muscles
she admits to restless sleep and night sweats
the pharmacist marks out three priorities in what should be done
he states that an ordinary medicine is enough against a bothersome fever
he puts making up the loss of water first
he sets difficulty breathing as the signal to see a doctor
he advises rest for as long as the muscles stay tender
text: The pharmacist asked the customer how long she had been running a fever. She said the shivering had come on the evening before, out of nowhere. He wanted to know what else she felt. She listed a raw throat, a streaming nose, a constant urge to sneeze, and calves that ached. He put a question about her sleep as well; she admitted she slept badly and woke up soaked. The pharmacist then marked out three priorities. First the fever itself, which an ordinary medicine will settle whenever it bothers her. Next came fluids, which he called the urgent part, since sweating drains the reserves. Last, watchfulness: should her breathing turn difficult, a visit to a doctor becomes necessary. The customer asked whether she ought to stop moving around. He advised rest for as long as the muscles stayed tender.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: surgeons once operated without cleaning their hands
a dirty operating garment was a point of pride back then
a stubborn doctor compared the death rate of two delivery wards
deaths fell where hands were disinfected
his fellow doctors mocked him and he lost his post
research on micro-organisms brought his idea acceptance
sterilizing instruments and airing the rooms then spread
infections following operations dropped sharply
text: Picture a hospital where surgeons moved from one bed to the next without rinsing their hands, proud of the grime caked onto their aprons. That was the standard back then, and nobody saw a fault in it. Then a stubborn doctor compared two delivery wards and noticed that deaths collapsed in the one where staff scrubbed their fingers with a biting solution. His fellow doctors laughed at him, and he ended up pushed out of his post. Only the work on micro-organisms, years later, got his idea taken seriously. After that the whole thing turned over fast: instruments boiled, gowns swapped, wards aired between operations. You know the rest. Infections following surgery dropped hard, and washing your hands became the cheapest and most rewarding thing a doctor could do. Quite a reversal, wouldn't you say?

units: sitting for a long stretch makes the feet swell
the calf muscles push blood upward by squeezing the veins
staying still halts that pumping action
fluid gathers in the tissue and presses on the nerves
the pressure on the nerves accounts for the prickling feeling
heat widens the vessels and makes the whole thing worse
going short on water thickens the blood and hampers the flow
in a healthy adult the trouble normally clears after a night
staying still for a long time raises the risk of a clot forming
doctors advise standing up, tightening the calves, drinking, and keeping away from tight clothes
text: Sit still through a long trip and your feet swell while the toes go numb. The mechanism behind it is well understood. Blood climbs from the legs back toward the heart because the calf muscles squeeze the veins with every step. Stay motionless and that pump simply quits. Fluid then gathers in the tissue, the foot puffs up, and the pinched nerves send back a prickling feeling. Heat makes matters worse, since it widens the vessels. So does going short on water, because thicker blood moves less easily. In a healthy adult the whole thing stays harmless and clears after a night. The risk climbs, though, once the stillness drags on and a clot begins to take shape. Which is why doctors tell you to stand up often, tighten the calves, drink water, and keep away from clothes that grip the waist.

units: a bookbinder stayed bent over her bench through long stretches of work
a dull ache took over her forearm and then her fingers
she dropped her tool in the middle of a session
she ignored the symptom at first, taking it for something passing
the doctor she saw measured the height of the cutting surface instead of prescribing a remedy
the bench sat two hand-widths too low
the workshop was rearranged with a raised, tilted top and an adjustable seat
short breaks were brought in every half hour
the pain went away within three weeks
text: The bindery smelled of warm glue and damp paper. The binder stayed hunched over her bench through long stretches of work, wrist bent, jaw locked with concentration. A dull ache took over her forearm, then spread into her fingers, until one afternoon the folding tool slipped out of her hand mid-session. She put it down to a passing weakness and gritted her teeth. The trouble grew. A sports doctor, consulted without much hope, prescribed neither ointment nor a long rest: he measured the height of her workbench. Two hand-widths too low. They raised the top, tilted the surface, added an adjustable stool, and built in a short break every half hour. The pain went away within three weeks. She tells the story to her apprentices and laughs about it, since her ache never lived in her hands but in her furniture.

units: the choice between a cold and a warm application depends on the nature of the injury
cold suits a recent injury that comes with swelling
the ice pack must be kept off the skin by a cloth
the cold application alternates spells of a quarter of an hour
heat suits an old stiffness with no swelling
a warm water bottle is left on for half an hour
the duration must be timed with a watch and stopped if the skin turns deeply red
cold soothes and tightens while heat loosens and widens
when in doubt, cold carries fewer drawbacks
text: Before reaching for a compress, decide between cold and heat, because the two of them serve altogether different purposes. For a fresh injury, a joint that is swelling, or a knock taken the day before, go with cold. Wrap the pack in a thin cloth, hold it on for a quarter of an hour, take it off just as long, then begin the cycle over again. Never lay ice straight against the skin. For an old stiffness, a knotted neck, or a sore muscle with no swelling, heat is the better choice. A warm water bottle, left on for half an hour, loosens the fibers and frees up the movement. Either way, time it with a watch and stop once the skin turns deeply red. Keep the difference in mind: cold soothes and tightens, heat loosens and widens. When you are unsure, pick cold, which carries considerably fewer drawbacks.

units: a health survey run in a rural area picks out three areas of fragility
the diet of the adults questioned rests on soft, sugary products
too little chewing goes with damaged teeth from middle age onward
nights are short and broken by waking
the lack of sleep tells on alertness at the wheel and on mood
motorized trips have taken over from walking even across short distances
distance from care facilities stands out as a shared factor
appointments get put off until the situation turns into an emergency
the report calls for travelling clinics, dental screening among children, and marked footpaths
the health authorities will look at these proposals before the year is out
text: A health survey run across a rural area picks out three pockets of fragility. The first is diet: the adults questioned eat soft, sugary products, chew little, and show damaged teeth from middle age onward. The second concerns sleep. Nights there run short and broken by waking, which tells on alertness at the wheel and on mood. The third touches physical activity, where motorized trips have taken over from walking even across short distances. The authors point out one factor shared by all three, namely distance from care. An appointment means a long journey, one that many put off until the situation turns into an emergency. The report calls for travelling clinics, dental screening among children, and marked footpaths around the towns. The health authorities will look at these proposals before the year is out.

units: a fitness coach notices that beginners are out of breath after a single flight of stairs
a seated life weakens the breath without drawing attention
the heart muscle gets used to reduced effort
the vessels become less elastic
nightly rest deteriorates in bodies that are rarely worked
the coach advises brisk walks repeated during the week
those walks include moderate climbs
late-afternoon weariness lessens once this habit is kept
text: At a neighborhood gym, a trainer watches the door. Newcomers come in winded, and all they have done is climb one flight of stairs. He knows the pattern well. A seated life wears down the machinery of breathing quietly, never announcing itself. Sit still for months and the heart muscle settles for very little work, while the vessels stiffen and lose their spring, so that any short run turns punishing. There is a quieter cost too. Sleep frays, because a body that asks nothing of itself never earns deep repair. His remedy is a modest one: brisk walks, several times a week, with a few moderate climbs worked into the route. The change shows up fast. Breathing stretches out, the late-afternoon slump loosens its grip, and the mood clears. Nothing dramatic here, only an ordinary cause, an ordinary correction, a chain that runs backward.

units: evenings are taken over by bright screens
falling asleep is pushed later and later
the writer refuses to blame the devices themselves
the writer blames the lack of a limit set in advance
he recommends choosing a stopping hour before the evening
he advises leaving the device outside the bedroom
he suggests replacing that habit with quiet reading
he claims that a gentle rule is what makes it last
text: Our evenings have filled with bright screens until they overflow. After dark the eye catches on a cold glow, thought thins out inside it, and sleep slides back half an hour, then half an hour more. I distrust the easy accusation. The harm does not live in the device. It lives in the missing boundary, the one nobody drew before tiredness stripped away our judgment. A blunt ban would fail, the way severe diets fail. What I defend is a calmer arrangement, negotiated with oneself. Pick the stopping hour at midday, while the mind is still clear. Leave the device outside the bedroom, so that reaching for it costs something. Put a slow book, a low conversation, a long stretch where the electric vigil used to sit. Sleep is never rescued by heroic denial, only by a mild rule you keep without thinking about it.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a rehabilitation therapist has worked with back patients since the start of his career
he contrasts two profiles among the people he sees
the first profile carries heavy loads and has tight musculature
the second profile stays seated and lacks muscle tone
both profiles complain of a comparable discomfort
he treats the first with stretching and heat
he treats the second with gradual strengthening
he refuses to apply the same protocol to both cases
text: The therapist in this practice has spent his whole working life on backs, and he sorts every patient into one of two groups before examining anyone. The first hauls weight for a good part of the week. The muscles come in tight, the shoulders locked, the neck hard under the palm. The second sits at a screen all day. The tissue is slack, the posture caves inward, the belly wall holds nothing up any more. Both describe the same ache low in the spine, which is why people assume one treatment would serve them equally. He says the opposite. For the first he orders slow stretching, heat, and release guided by the breath, until a clenched back moves freely again. For the second he sets out gradual strengthening, and without it no relief lasts. One symptom, he says, hiding two opposite machines.

units: a cookery book meant for people recovering from illness is examined
the reviewer approves of the plainness of the preparations
the recipes limit fats and long cooking
the book offers combinations rich in protein
the portions are suited to a weakened appetite
the explanations about chewing are judged useful
the review faults the absence of any guidance on keeping food
the closing lines recommend the book to family kitchens all the same
text: This collection of dishes written for people recovering from illness deserves close attention, since its choices cut against nearly everything the genre produces. Restraint comes first. The author drops the endless braises and the heavy fats in favor of plates a weakened stomach accepts without protest. Then come the pairings, each one built around a protein source, so that a meal sustains rather than crushes. The servings, too, are cut back to what a faded appetite can honestly face. And the pages on chewing are worth more than several longer treatises. One reservation remains. Nothing is said about keeping dishes that were made ahead of time, a regrettable gap for readers with little strength to spare. Even so, the book belongs in any household kitchen where somebody is getting well again.

units: the writer of the message sends news to someone close
a chill came on at the end of the week
a consultation took place the following day
the nurse ruled out any complication
an extended rest of three nights was prescribed
a hot drink and a light soup made up the whole diet
the fever dropped before the treatment was over
the writer promises a visit as soon as he is well
text: I am writing to you from bed, and there is nothing here that should worry you. It all began at the end of the week. A chill caught me while I was tidying the kitchen, and I went down feverish, incapable of finishing my own sentence. The following day the nurse at the clinic nearby examined me thoroughly. She ruled out any complication and prescribed three nights of strict rest, which I accepted without argument. The first two dragged. Nothing went down except warm tea and a thin soup, and I fell asleep the moment the light went out. Then the fever broke abruptly, before the course was even finished, and my hunger returned like a friend who had walked off in a temper. I can cross the hallway now without leaning on the wall. I will visit as soon as this tiredness releases me.

units: the person being asked explains night sweating
an overheated bedroom prevents the inner temperature from falling
that fall is what allows proper sleep to begin
the body makes up for it by producing sweat
wakings multiply because of that discomfort
the next day's tiredness follows from those interruptions
the woman answering advises turning down the heat in the bedroom
she recommends natural fabrics rather than synthetic ones
text: You want to know why your pillow is drenched every night although you have exerted yourself in no way. Short answer: your bedroom is overheated. Here is what happens. To drop off properly, your body must let its own temperature fall by a fraction of a degree, and if the surrounding air prevents that, it brings out the heavy machinery and makes you perspire. So what? So you surface clammy, shove the blanket off, drag it back, and that whole performance chops your night into useless fragments. That is where the heavy morning comes from, although you never stayed up late. What should you actually do? Turn the heating down well before bed and let the room cool by itself. Swap the bedding too. Natural fabrics let the damp escape, synthetics trap it against your skin. Give it a week and see.

units: an intake nurse describes the crowding in an emergency department
most of the arrivals involve complaints of no seriousness
seriously ill patients wait longer because of that crowding
a senior doctor points to ignorance about the options available
a telephone line for guidance has been set up
walk-in appointments open in the evening
average waiting time has fallen since these measures
the nurse holds that informing the public must go on
text: The nurse on intake describes a waiting room that is full before the doors have properly opened. Most of the people in it, she says, have come with something inconsequential, a mild sprain, a cough that refuses to clear, a shallow burn, and those files push the genuinely threatened patients back down the queue. The senior doctor agrees, with a qualification. People rarely know what exists outside the hospital, he explains, so they head for the building they can name. Two measures followed. A telephone line now sorts callers before anyone sets off, and walk-in evening clinics have opened around the district. Average waiting time has already fallen, he notes. The nurse remains more guarded about it. The room empties for good only once everyone knows where to turn, and not a day sooner.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the healers of the past put illness down to tainted air
they advised airing rooms out and keeping away from unhealthy places
that explanation rested on observation without proof
the discovery of micro-organisms changed that view
handwashing was brought into the care wards
deaths after childbirth fell afterwards
both approaches shared the same distrust of dirt
the older approach knew nothing of the true source of contagion
text: Before anyone could look at the invisible, healers laid the blame on the air. A thick smell rising off a marsh, an alley with no draft, a shut room: that, people believed, was where contagion came from. So they opened windows, burned herbs, and kept away from the low quarters. The instinct was not foolish. It was simply blind to its own reason. Then curved glass revealed a minute population swarming across the fingers, and the whole picture turned over. An unremarkable instruction, wash your hands between one ward and the next, brought down deaths among women who had just given birth as no smoke ever had. Set the two doctrines honestly side by side. Each mistrusted filth, and each prescribed much the same gestures. But the older one aimed at a shadow, while the newer could finally name what it was fighting.

units: the text describes what happens when the body is plunged into cold water
the skin reacts by tightening the vessels near the surface
the blood pulls back toward the organs at the core
breathing speeds up sharply on contact
controlling the breath limits that reaction
stimulating substances are released after coming out
heart trouble is a reason not to take it up
a short spell is advised for beginners
text: Going into cold water works on three separate levels, and each one is worth taking apart on its own. Circulation comes first. On contact the vessels just under the skin clamp down, the blood pulls back toward the organs at the core, and pressure climbs for a short while. Breathing follows. A reflex gasp arrives the instant you go under, fast and outside your control, and steadying the out-breath softens that panic and makes the whole thing workable. Last comes the chemical answer. Once you climb out, the body releases stimulating messengers, which is what regular swimmers mean when they call it bracing. Two limits frame all of it. Any known heart trouble rules the practice out without medical advice, and a beginner keeps the immersion very short, never alone, never on a full stomach.

units: a librarian suffered from pain in her wrists
she first put that pain down to her age
a colleague pointed out the unsuitable height of her work surface
an ergonomist examined her workstation
the chair and the screen were raised
regular breaks were brought into her day
the pain went away after several weeks
she then urged the same approach on her colleagues
text: The head of the town library endured a dull ache in both wrists for the better part of two seasons, and she put it down to her age and to ordinary wear. She went on shelving, carrying, typing out references, until a younger colleague remarked on the odd height of the sorting counter she worked at. An ergonomist was called in. He measured the station, watched how her forearms sat, and gave his verdict without softening it: the chair was too low, the screen too far back, and the neck was paying for the whole imbalance. Both were raised. Short breaks were written into the day at fixed intervals. Some weeks later the ache had gone, and not one tablet had been swallowed. From then on she preached the same procedure to her staff, with a stubbornness nobody could talk her out of.

units: two neighboring workshops run on opposite principles
the joiner takes material away with his cutting tool
the wood lifts off as a curled ribbon
the smith reshapes the heated metal without losing any of it
the bar changes shape under the blows
both craftsmen show the same kind of patience
each material warns the worker about its resistance
missing that warning ends in a broken piece
text: Stand between two workshops that share a single wall and you meet two opposite ideas of what making means. In the first, the plane rides forward and the board gives way: a thin ribbon of wood lifts, curls over, and drops to the floor, and the surface grows smoother with every pass. Matter leaves the piece and never returns. In the second, nothing leaves at all. The smith brings his hammer down on hot iron and the bar stretches, thickens, bends, yet weighs exactly what it weighed before. One workman subtracts, the other merely displaces. Still, the two of them wait alike. Every material speaks first and says where it will yield and where it will hold. Wood warns through its grain, iron through its color. Whoever misses that warning splits the piece, and the whole workshop answers him with an embarrassed hush.

units: a beginner recounts his first months in a locksmith shop
the clamping tool holds the piece without marking it
the teeth of the file clog when it is worked at a wrong angle
the shop supervisor cuts a checking template out of sheet metal
an overtightened screw snapped inside its hole
polishing before flattening forces the work to be started again
the upkeep habits include greasing the jaws
classroom theory meant nothing to him before the work of his hands
text: A first-year locksmith sorts his opening months into three sets of memories. The tools come first. The vise grips hard enough to hold a piece and gently enough to leave no mark. The file loads up with metal the moment he attacks a surface at a careless angle. The shop supervisor cuts a template out of sheet steel so that every corner can be checked against something fixed. Mistakes come next: a notch driven too deep, a screw forced until it snapped off inside its hole, a face polished before it was ever brought flat, which sent the whole job back to where it began. The habits of upkeep close the list. Clear the file with a wire card, grease the jaws, shelve the templates by family of profile. He admits that the classroom meant nothing to him until he had felt the metal push back against the blade in his own hand.

units: the piece must be held still before any work begins
the marks are scribed with a metal point
the cavity is chopped first with a chisel, in short bites
the bottom of the cavity is finished with a hollow blade
a slack fit ruins the strength of the joint
the male part is sawn outside the scribed line
a dry trial checks that the entry takes moderate pressure
glue is spread only once that trial has succeeded
text: Work on a mortise and tenon joint properly begins only once the bench is clear and the stock sits perfectly still under the holdfast. Lay the joint out first of all, scribing both parts with a steel point rather than a pencil, the gauge held flat against the edge. Chop the mortise next with a chisel, taking short bites and working from the middle outward toward each end. Pare the bottom of the housing with a gouge and leave the cheeks alone, because a slack fit robs the joint of the strength it was cut for. Only then saw the tenon, keeping the blade outside the scribed line, and bring it down to size with fine paring cuts. Bring the two parts together dry: if steady palm pressure alone seats the tenon, the fit is right. Glue follows that trial and nothing else, and the clamps go on immediately afterward.

units: the last tannery in the valley is about to stop working
the price of energy has climbed steeply
the vats of the works are worn out
the expected buyer dropped the plan for want of money
the leather workshops nearby will have to buy from far away
waiting times on supplies are going to stretch
the closing works took in two trainees a year
a cooperative takeover is being talked about locally
text: The last tannery still working in the valley is closing, and the leather workshops around it are uneasy. The chain of causes behind the decision is short. Energy bills climbed steeply, the vats reached the end of their service life, and the buyer everyone expected walked away once his funding fell through. The first effect is already plain. Shops that used to fetch their hides a few steps from their own door will order them from far off instead, waiting longer for each delivery and judging the quality of the skins at a distance. A second effect touches training. The tannery took on two apprentices every year, the only place within reach where vegetable tanning could be learned by hand. Officials in the valley speak of a cooperative buyout. The craftsmen fear the order book will fold before it arrives.

units: wood dust has taken over the whole workshop
it works its way into the joints of the machines
it sets the man at the saw coughing
opening the windows only walks the cloud around
every machine has been hooked up to a soft hose
a collector box has been set up outside
a cloth filter holds back the finest particles
the dust that is caught goes into a neighbor's animal bedding
text: Push the workshop door open and you spot the trouble straight off: sawdust. It coats the floor, settles along the beams, creeps into the hinges of every machine, and has had the fellow at the saw coughing since the beginning of the week. The windows stay wide open, but the draft only walks the gray cloud from one end of the room to the other. What the joiner finally came up with is nothing clever. He ran a soft hose from each machine out to a collector box parked under a tin roof behind the wall. A cloth sleeve holds the finest stuff back, and a sack underneath takes the rest. He still sweeps, of course, but he no longer breathes his own shop. And the dust, instead of going on the fire, goes down the road to a neighbor who spreads it as bedding for his animals. The air, he swears, smells of cut wood again.

units: the writer weighs learning at a screen against learning at a bench
a filmed movement can be stopped and pulled apart
teaching in a classroom wastes no material
the workshop costs money and wears the machines down
every failed attempt turns wood into scrap
only the workshop passes on what the tool feels like
an aching forearm tells the learner the pressure is wrong
the writer holds that what the classroom saves will be paid back later
text: Should a trade be learned at a screen or at a bench? Training centers are split on the question, and the comparison deserves an honest, unflattering hearing. The classroom has a real edge. A filmed movement can be halted, run again, pulled apart step by step, and a poor posture corrected without spoiling a single board. The workshop, for its part, eats money, wears the machines down, and turns wood into scrap every time a beginner misses. What it gives back is what no screen will ever hand over: the tool trembling in the palm, the smell of glue that is setting badly, the ache in the forearm that says the pressure is wrong. Drop that side of the training and you turn out graduates who can describe a joint they would never manage to cut. The arithmetic is false. The bench collects later what the classroom kept.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the villagers name her by her trade and nothing else
her hands carry old scars
she no longer tells where those cuts came from
her tools are ranked by width on her bench
the handle of her mallet has been worn smooth by use
a grinding wheel brings the edges back
she holds that a block is chosen before it is shaped
she will not show unfinished work to anyone
some ten pupils have come through her shop
she started as a laborer before a cutting tool was put in her hand
text: In the village she is the stonecutter, and the word does for a name. Her hands come first: broad, dry, crossed with old cuts whose stories she has long since stopped telling. Then her tools, laid out on the bench with something close to tenderness, the mallet worn smooth at the grip, the chisels ranked by width, the wheel that brings each edge back and fills the shed with a bright hiss. Then her road into the trade: she came in as a laborer and pushed a barrow for a whole year before anyone put a chisel in her hand. Then her rules: a block is chosen before it is cut, a flaw is worked around rather than hidden, and unfinished work is shown to nobody. Some ten pupils have come through her shop, three of them still cutting stone in the valley. They will carve truly, she says, once they stop counting their blows.

units: a panel judges a chest in the order it was built
the timber that was chosen shows an even color
the joint marks were not carried over from one template
a gap shows up at the corner set at the back
the cuts that were made run true and close tight
the finishing stage lets the judges down
abrasive marks remain beside the metal fittings
the wax went onto a surface that still carried dust
the piece is called sturdy despite a rushed last stage
text: The chest presented to the panel is best judged in the order it was built. The timber comes off well: cut through the quarter, quiet grain, an even color running from board to board. The layout that follows already wavers, because the dovetail marks were never carried over from one master template, and the drift shows at the corner at the back. The execution wins a good part of that ground back. The saw cuts run true, the sockets are clean, and the joints close tight without being forced. The finishing stage is where the work slips. Sanding was rushed, grinder marks still catch the light beside the hinges, and wax laid over a surface that had not been wiped has frozen a haze of fine scratches into the wood. What the panel will finally remember is a sturdy piece whose last hour gave the maker away.

units: the craftsman announces a delay of two weeks on an order
the wood he had planned on was soaked under a torn cover
its moisture runs higher than his shop will accept
using that wood would shrink the panels once they were assembled
the drawers would bind as soon as the heating season came
the boards have been stacked in the drying kiln
the work starts again on an older batch
the new shade is darker than was foreseen
photographs will be sent at the dry assembly
text: I am writing about the chest of drawers you entrusted to me, which will now reach you two weeks later than agreed. The wood itself is the reason. The batch I had set aside spent a long spell under a canvas cover that had split open, and it carries far more moisture than my shop will accept. Worked as it stands, the panels would shrink once assembled, and the drawers would bind as soon as the heating season came round. I have stacked those boards in the drying kiln, then, and started again from an older batch, which pushes the whole job further back. One agreeable thing comes out of the delay: the older wood runs to a deeper shade, and I will suggest a pale wax that brings it forward. I will send photographs as soon as the piece stands dry, so you can settle the choice before any glue is spread.

units: a restorer is blamed for how slowly she prices a job
every piece of furniture hides repairs made earlier
an assessment made too fast leads to costs nobody saw coming
she takes part of the object apart before naming a price
this inspection is charged to the owner
half of her clients refuse to pay for it
she now offers a pair of estimates
the survey fee is credited back if the work is hers to do
quarrels with clients have almost stopped
text: What does a furniture restorer say when clients grumble that her pricing takes too long? She names the problem plainly: every piece hides a history of earlier repairs, and a rushed reading of it ends in bills nobody saw coming. Asked how she goes about the job, she describes taking part of the piece apart, testing the glue joints, looking behind the backboards, and only then naming a price she means to hold. Asked what that care costs, she grants that she charges for it and that one owner in two turns it down. Her answer is a pair of estimates: a survey fee, credited back if the restoration is hers to do, and a wide figure for anyone who wants an answer on the spot. Quarrels have almost stopped since. One difficulty stays, which is persuading a hurried owner that patience costs less than doing the work twice.

units: the metalworker describes his place of work as a living body
he gives the device that pushes air the role of a lung
he explains that without that air the burning weakens
he likens the block he strikes on to a shoulder
he presents the gripping tools as fearless fingers
he says those tools seize the glowing metal without flinching
he compares the hearth itself to an organ that beats
his student asks him which part she stands for in that body
he answers that she will be the memory of the gestures
text: The blacksmith spoke about his workshop as though it were a sleeping animal, and he would name its limbs one by one. The bellows, he said, stood in for the lungs: let that patient breathing stop, and the coals sank down, the bar of iron went cold. The anvil played the shoulder, since it received the whole violence of the hammer without a single flinch. The tongs, he added with a laugh, were fingers a great deal braver than his own, for they closed on glowing metal and never once trembled. As for the hearth, he called it a heart beating dully at the back of the room. His apprentice listened and never cut in, and afterwards she would ask which part of that body she stood for. She would be the memory, he answered, the one who kept the gestures once the old man's hands had given up.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: weaving started out as an entirely handmade operation
the earliest devices held the threads taut upright
lumps of clay served to keep those threads under tension
the worker put the crosswise thread in row by row
a treadle device then parted the threads to open a gap
the tool carrying the crosswise thread crossed the width in one move
a cord and a mallet then threw that tool mechanically
the pace doubled without calling for a second worker
punched cards later governed the lifting of each thread
the pattern moved from human memory onto a coded support
text: Weaving began in the fingers and only later ended up in machinery. The earliest frames held the threads upright, weighted at the foot with lumps of baked clay, and the worker pushed the crosswise thread through by hand, one row after another. Then came the treadle: press it down, and a whole group of threads lifted together to open a clean gap, so the shuttle could cross the entire width in a single throw. Someone soon tied that shuttle to a cord and a mallet, which flung it across on its own and doubled the pace without calling for a second worker. Later still, punched cards took over the lifting of each separate thread, and the pattern moved out of a weaver's memory onto a coded strip. Every stage took away a movement of the hand. Not one of them took away the eye that watches the tension.

units: the glassy layer is not paint laid on the surface
heat turns a mineral deposit into glass
the maker spreads a mix of powders on before firing
those powders melt and then spread into one continuous layer
cooling sets the material with no crystal structure
that lack of crystals explains the clearness obtained
sealing the pores keeps the liquid from seeping out
the hardness of the layer guards the wall against scratches
uneven shrinking between the two materials brings on a web of fine cracks
text: A glaze is not a coat of paint brushed onto a pot. It is glass, and the heat of the kiln makes it right on the skin of the clay itself. The potter covers the piece in a slurry of finely ground minerals and then hands it over to the fire. Under that heat the powders melt and spread into one unbroken layer; as they cool they stiffen again without going back to any crystal order, and that is where their clearness comes from. Because the layer seals the pores of the wall, water stops working its way through, so the vessel will hold a liquid. Because the layer is hard, it also guards the surface against scratches. Trouble starts, though, when the two materials shrink by different amounts: if the glass draws in tighter than the clay beneath, it splits into a web of hairline cracks.

units: a storage cabinet reaches the workshop out of true
its doors no longer shut properly
the joiner fears that taking it apart will break the old joints
wetting the panel fails because the curve returns on drying
planing the rebate makes the door gape on the far side
the maker notices that the twist does not run the whole height
he finds that a cracked rail is swinging the side panel
he puts a new rail in place of the split piece
he holds the frame under pressure until the glue sets
the cabinet stands plumb again and its doors work
text: The cupboard came into the workshop barely standing: one of its side panels had twisted badly out of true and the doors would no longer shut. Taking the whole thing apart was tempting, but the ancient joints would likely burst under the strain, so the joiner left them alone. He tried wetting the panel to draw it straight, and the wood curled back to its bend the moment it dried. He planed the rebate instead, and the door promptly gaped along the opposite edge. What solved it in the end was patient looking, nothing more. The panel was not bowed over its whole height; it swung around a single cracked rail. He cut a fresh rail, fitted it in place of the split one, clamped the frame until the glue had set hard, and hung the hinges again. The side stood plumb, and both doors swung true.

units: the text compares two ways of finishing the edge of a cloth
the hand method means folding the edge over twice
the iron serves to set each fold before the sewing
the hand stitches catch only one thread on the visible side
the hand finish calls for patience and moves along slowly
sewing done by hand ends up invisible on the right side
the machine method uses the same double fold
close pins hold the cloth before it goes under the needle
the machine finish stands up better to repeated washing
the machine stitching leaves a visible line on the outer face
text: Want a hem that hangs perfectly straight, with no ripples and no lumps? Look at both ways of doing it before you sew a single stitch. By hand, you fold the raw edge over, set the crease with the iron, fold it over a second time, and work blind stitches that pick up barely one thread on the right side. It takes patience and it will not be hurried, but the sewing disappears and the cloth keeps every bit of its drape. On the machine, you build the same double fold, pin it close all the way along, and then run it under the needle at a steady speed. It comes out tough, and it survives wash after wash far better than hand work does; in return, a line of stitching shows on the outside. So ask yourself what matters more to you: a hem that lasts for years, or a hem nobody ever notices.

units: a nonprofit teaches the metal trades to adults changing careers
the classes are held under the roof frame of an old market hall
the workshops are grouped by family of gestures
the first workshop teaches laying an even bead without burning through the sheet
the second deals with joining by pieces set in cold
the third takes up the finish obtained by heating and oiling
the last workshop teaches costing a job and buying stock
the woman in charge states that people rarely quit over technique
paperwork often wears the trainees down
text: Under the timber roof frame of an old market hall, a nonprofit teaches metalwork to adults changing careers, and its workshops are grouped by family of gestures. The first is given over to welding, where students learn to lay an even bead without burning through the sheet. The second covers mechanical joining, and every rivet there goes in cold, into a hole reamed carefully to size. The third handles the finish, and much of the talk turns on the patina you get by heating the piece and then oiling it. The last workshop is the surprise, since it deals with costing: pricing a job, buying the stock, promising a date you can actually keep. The woman who runs the place says that trainees rarely quit over technique. Paperwork is what wears them down. The next group starts at the close of the season.

units: the dye workshop smells of wet ash from first light
boards cover the vats while they are still cold
the water in the tubs keeps the color of the day before
the dyer lights a fire under the widest vat
she pulls a mass of undyed yarn out of a basket
steam climbs and the bath takes on the shade of crushed leaves
the wool that goes under takes up the color very fast
the next stage means rinsing the yarn in one tub after another
the yarn hung under the eaves drips and marks the ground
text: From first light onward the dye works smells of wet ash and of damp wool. The vats are still asleep beneath their heavy boards, and the water standing in them keeps the darkened color of the day before. Soon the dyer lights a fire under the widest of them all, then lifts a skein of undyed yarn out of a basket and shakes it out at arm's length to loosen the tangles. Steam climbs, the bath turns the shade of crushed leaves, and the wool goes under all at once, without a moment of hesitation, drinking up the color like a sponge. Rinsing follows: the skeins pass from one tub to the next, paler every time, and heavier between the fingers. By evening they hang in a tight row under the eaves, still streaming, and each one stains the ground below it with the shade that it has taken.

units: the writer disputes the idea that the electronic tool makes the old method useless
the optical device gives a vertical from its own footing
a settling of that footing throws the reading off with no visible warning
the hanging weight answers to a force that never drifts
the apprentice who handles that instrument grasps in his body what he is checking
younger crews no longer question what the screen shows
they do not confirm a reading by a second method
costly rework follows from this on site
the firm puts that rework down to carelessness
the writer holds that passing on the old skill is not nostalgia
text: To claim that an electronic instrument makes the plumb bob no longer worth learning is a failure of reasoning, and the cost of that error shows up on site. An optical device gives you a vertical at once, but it gives it from its own footing; let the tripod settle or the ground shake, and the error spreads with nothing at all to announce it. A hanging weight answers to a force that never drifts, and the apprentice who has held one grasps in his own body what he is checking. That understanding is missing now, and so the younger crews no longer think to doubt the screen, or to confirm a reading by some other means. Costly rework follows from it, which the firm puts down to carelessness when it comes instead of a training cut short. Passing on the older skill, then, is not nostalgia.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the instrument maker took over from her old master
the workshop was losing customers when she took it on
amateur players wanted an instrument that stayed in tune
those players could not pay for a piece shaped entirely by hand
she refused to work with a lesser wood
she split the making into two separate sets
the parts with no bearing on the sound come in batches from a workshop nearby
she shapes the pieces that settle the tone on her own
the price fell by a third with no loss of sound
her old master knew her hand on hearing the instrument
text: The instrument maker discussed here took over the workshop of her old master at the very moment when its customers were thinning out. She soon put her finger on a problem that no catalogue anywhere could solve: amateur players wanted an instrument that stayed in tune, and could not pay for one shaped from end to end by hand. Rather than come down to a lesser wood, she split her work into two distinct halves. The parts that have no bearing at all on the sound, the rough neck and the ribs, now come in batches from a workshop nearby. The parts that settle the tone, the belly and the bass bar, she cuts alone and trims by ear. The price fell by a third, the sound lost nothing, and her old master, who came by the shop to hear a finished order, knew her own hand in the varnish.

units: two runs of chairs are shown in the same room
the first run comes from a workshop attached to traditional joinery
that run uses fitted tenons and a back bent over steam
its sturdiness commands the reviewer's respect
its drawing looks unsure for want of attention paid to the outline
the second run comes from a studio using automated cutting
that second run is made in plywood
its seat meets the back with no cushion added
the object comes apart in a handful of moves
the reviewer holds that neither run clearly wins
text: Two runs of chairs share the same show room, and the pairing teaches you something. The first comes out of a workshop that stands by traditional joinery: tenons pared to fit, a back bent over steam, an oiled finish. Its sturdiness commands respect, and yet the drawing hesitates, as though the maker had spent all his care on the structure and left the outline to fend for itself. The second comes from a studio that makes no apology at all for plywood and automated cutting. The line is clean, the seat meets your back with no cushion added, and the whole thing comes apart in a handful of moves. The edges are dry, though, and no passing hand will ever soften them. Neither run clearly wins the day: one will outlast its owner, the other will charm the eye before it tires at the joints.

units: the writer answers an acquaintance who had asked for news of him
an elderly joiner looking for a beginner took him on
the master handed him a tool and a piece of wood without a word of explanation
his first week went entirely to one cutting motion
success showed as a shaving coming away unbroken
he was then allowed to smooth the surfaces the master had prepared
his first box was called imperfect but honest
he now draws his own designs at home in the evening
he concludes that patience is learned by doing and not by talking
he invites his correspondent to come and see the workshop
text: You wrote asking for news of the workshop, and my answer has been overdue for a while now. An elderly cabinetmaker advertising for a beginner took me on. He set a rough board and a plane before me, without a word of explanation. For a whole week I did one thing only: push that blade along the grain, again and again, until the shaving came away in a single unbroken ribbon. Only afterward would he let me smooth the surfaces he had squared himself. My first small box came out crooked, and he pronounced it clumsy but honest, which I have decided to consider praise. Now I draw my own designs at the kitchen table after nightfall. Whatever I have learned here will not fit into a letter: patience passes through the hands, never through talk. Come and see the workshop, and come soon.

units: bubbles in a casting come from filling the mold too fast
the trapped air leaves hollows that weaken the part
pouring very slowly is not the answer
an alloy that loses its heat too early fails to fill the whole cavity
heating the mold beforehand delays the setting of the metal
that preheating removes the need to pour more slowly
bubbles that persist point to poor escape of the air
the founder cuts narrow channels to release the air as the metal rises
surface flaws trace back either to heat or to the path of the air
text: Why does a casting come out of the mold pitted with bubbles? Begin with the filling. Metal that rushes in imprisons air, and that trapped air leaves hollows which weaken the finished component. Should the founder therefore pour as gently as he possibly can? No. An alloy losing heat on the way in solidifies before it has reached every corner of the cavity, and the resulting shape remains incomplete. What does he rely on instead? He preheats the mold, which postpones the moment the metal sets and spares him any slowing of the filling. And when bubbles appear regardless? Then the air has nowhere to go. He cuts vents, narrow channels that release it steadily ahead of the rising metal. Read a flawed surface closely and it points back either to heat or to the path the air was forced to take.

units: a visitor reports that her old book is losing its leaves
she fears the volume will come apart completely
the specialist blames a broken sewing
the original adhesive has gone brittle and holds nothing
he rejects the idea of giving up on the repair
putting it right means taking the gatherings apart one by one
the old adhesive comes off with moisture
the old outside will be kept and strengthened from within
the time depends on drying under a press, which cannot be hurried
text: The visitor told the binder that her family's old volume was shedding its leaves and that she feared it would soon come apart altogether. The sewing had snapped, he explained, and the glue along the spine had turned to crumbs and held nothing together. She asked whether the book was past saving. Not at all, he said, and laid out the work: take the gatherings apart one by one, soften the old glue with moisture until it lifts away, then sew the sections onto tapes. She wondered how it would look afterward. He would keep the old covering, he said, and line the boards from the inside, so that the repair would remain out of sight. When she asked how long it would take, he answered that a book dries under a press at its own pace and will not be hurried. That candor settled her mind.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: old building sites knew two ways of organizing stonecutting
under the first, one worker carried a block from start to finish
under the second, the stages were shared among specialized crews
the individual arrangement gave very even pieces
it moved at a reduced pace and depended on the skill at hand
the divided arrangement raised output
it made learning easier by isolating a single motion
it demanded strict checking of the fitting
the two methods leave distinct physical clues
those clues inform researchers where no written record survives
text: Old building sites organized stonecutting in two very different ways. Under the first, one man carried a block from start to finish, squaring it, dressing it and cutting it himself. Under the second, every stage belonged to a separate crew that did nothing else. Work done by a single hand came out remarkably even, since one judgment governed all the proportions, but it moved slowly and hung on whatever skill happened to be available. Splitting the stages raised output and let a novice learn by mastering one motion at a time. The price was inspection: unless the fitting was checked severely, the blocks stopped meeting. Each system left its own physical signature, steady tool marks on one side, incised setting marks on the other. Where no written record survives, researchers read those traces instead.

units: a pottery studio holds three categories of tools
the first category serves to shape the form
flat blades bring the wall upright during shaping
the second category serves to take material away
thin metal loops lighten the underside of the pot
the third category gathers the accessories of the last stage
needles serve to decorate or to mark the piece
beginners overrate the part played by the turning machine
a poorly smoothed wall takes the glassy coating badly
success rests on the sequence of stages more than on nimble fingers
text: Walk into a pottery studio and the tools sort themselves into three groups. The first group shapes. The wheel belongs there, and so do ribs, flat blades you hold against the turning wall to bring it upright. The second group takes material away. Trimming loops, thin bands of metal on a handle, shave the excess off the underside of a pot until it stops feeling like a brick. The third group covers whatever happens last: sponges, cloths, soft brushes, and the needles you use to mark or decorate a piece. Beginners imagine that the wheel accomplishes the work. It does not. A wall left rough will drink the glaze unevenly and streak. Each group cleans up whatever the one before it missed, and that order of work, far more than nimble fingers, decides whether a pot is worth keeping.

units: the workshop in the hamlet had closed when the man in charge left
a metalworker bought it two winters later for a small sum
she began by clearing the rubble out of the building
she found the old ventilation device in good order
a former pupil of the place came to explain how the tools were kept
the hearth was back in service at the start of the mild season
she now makes closing hardware to order
she trains two apprentices each season
she finds it harder to convince customers that handwork lasts
text: The forge at the edge of the hamlet had gone cold when its last master departed. Two winters on, a welder from the neighboring valley purchased the building for a derisory sum, half expecting to regret it. She began by hauling out the rubble that filled the hall, and underneath a tarp at the back she found the original bellows, still perfectly sound. Word traveled, and a man who had trained there as a boy came by to show her where the tongs and the swages used to hang. The fire was lit again as the mild season returned. She forges lock and hinge work to order now, and trains two apprentices every season. Beating iron was never the difficult part, she maintains. The hard part is convincing a customer that a fitting shaped by hand outlives anything stamped out by a press in series.

units: the leather must be softened with a greasy product before assembly
a dried hide splits under pressure and cannot be mended
the holes are punched in one stroke with the blade held straight
a crooked hole makes the metal fastening lean
the head of the fastening is struck with short, repeated blows
one single heavy blow deforms the seat of the fastening
the inner lining must form no pucker
a pucker makes the assembly sink under use
the ring around the head is smoothed to erase the tool marks
a sharp edge ends up cutting through the thread that touches it
text: Oil the leather and let it drink to the core before you set a single rivet. Dry hide splits under pressure, and a split never closes again. Punch each of your holes in one clean stroke with the awl held perfectly straight, for an angled hole makes the rivet lean and the collar then bites crooked. Slip the shank through, cap it with its washer, and work the head down with short, repeated taps rather than heavy blows: one hard strike spreads the metal sideways and ruins its seating. Check the inner lining at every stage, because a pucker you let pass now will sink under use and the stitching will part down the middle. Smooth the ring around the head last of all, slowly, until no tool marks remain. A sharp edge left standing will eventually saw through whatever thread rests against it.
