units: glassblowing workshops share one and the same energy constraint
their furnaces have to heat without interruption
a mass of glass left to cool cracks when the heat returns
the workshops keep firing even when orders fall off
that obligation weighs heavily on their spending
several workshops are testing a shared furnace kept fed at all times
the blowers come to draw their material in slots spread through the day
the system calls for movable containers and better insulation
the first readings show lower consumption per object made
the arrangement suits no workshop too far from the shared furnace
text: The glassblowing shops of one narrow valley all live with the same constraint. Their furnaces can never be shut down, because a mass of glass left to cool cracks the moment the heat comes back. So they keep firing even when orders thin out, and the cost of that idle heat sits heavily on every account book. A group of these shops is now testing a shared answer: one furnace, held hot around the clock, serving the blowers nearby in turn, each gathering his glass in a slot agreed in advance. It works only with pots that can be moved, with considerably better insulation, and with the slots respected strictly. The earliest readings show a clear drop in fuel burned per finished piece. Those running the trial admit it does nothing for the isolated shop, too far from the shared fire.

units: two neighboring hammers look alike at first sight
the metal beater's hammer carries a rounded, polished head
that head leaves no mark on the surface it strikes
its handle is short and thick for a quick motion
the decorator's tool has a light and almost flat head
its handle narrows and turns supple toward the grip
the first tool moves material in volume
the second acts on the surface alone
the marks of wear differ sharply from one tool to the other
neither one can stand in for the other
text: Two hammers lie side by side on the bench, and a careless glance would take them for one and the same tool. The first belongs to the coppersmith. Its face is domed and polished, smooth enough to move metal without printing a mark upon it, and its handle is short and thick, made for a quick, close stroke. The second belongs to the chaser. That head is light and nearly flat, and the shaft narrows toward the grip until it flexes under the fingers. One drives the material into shape. The other merely touches its skin. Even the wear tells them apart, for the coppersmith's cheeks are scarred and rounded, while the chaser's edges stay crisp. Set together, they describe two opposite ways of meeting metal. Neither can stand in for the other without betraying the motion it was made for.

units: teaching often ranks manual trades as a fallback route
that ranking ignores how much thinking a skilled motion demands
fine fitting calls for a constant reading of the material
no written work replaces that direct reading
repeating a motion is not the same as acting mechanically
the craftsman alters his settings at every run
a technique that stops being practiced is lost within a generation
such techniques rarely leave anything written behind
objects that can be mended cost less in use than objects thrown away
the writer asks for fair recognition rather than idealization
text: Schools still treat the trades as a landing place for students who fail elsewhere. That ranking deserves to be taken apart point by point. It misses, first, how much thinking a skilled motion carries: fitting a part to a hair's width means reading the material without pause, and no book stands in for that reading. It also confuses repetition with routine, when the craftsman who repeats a movement in fact adjusts every setting inside it. It overlooks how easily the knowledge goes, since a technique that stops being practiced is gone within a generation and leaves nothing written behind. And it rests on a false account of worth, because objects that can be mended cost less over their life than objects meant to be thrown out. Restoring these trades asks not for romance but for an honest reckoning.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the silversmith avoids setting gems at the end of the day because her hands tremble
her mother practiced the same craft in front of her during her childhood
watching her mother decided her choice of trade
the lack of fine tools in the family workshop forced her to improvise
she smoothed her pieces with a hide stretched over a wooden block
that early constraint gave her great patience
her work is known to be sturdy and free of scratches
her refusal of short deadlines lengthens the queue of her customers
she maintains that haste always leaves a mark in the material
text: Her hands shake a little once the light goes, and that is the reason behind a rule the silversmith set for herself early on: she never seats a stone after dusk. As a child she watched her mother tip a blade across warm metal, and that sight settled what she would do with her life. The family workshop held no fine tools, so she learned to bring up a shine with a hide stretched over a block of wood, and the slowness of it built a patience few people carry. Those lean beginnings explain the name she earned later on: her mounts hold fast and her surfaces come away unmarked. She turns down hurried orders, so the line of buyers keeps stretching, and the wait only sharpens what people feel for her work. Metal punishes hurry, she says, and every flaw you can see began in a moment when somebody tried to outrun it.

units: the product is criticized because it sets too early
a dry mark shows up on wide surfaces and can no longer be removed
the thinner evaporates too fast in heated rooms
the maker advises adding an additive that slows the drying
this additive does not weaken the strength of the final coat
he also advises laying it on in thin overlapping bands
tests on hardwood confirm the improvement
the scraping tool has to be sharpened before every coat
the overall judgment is mixed and depends on the willingness to change one's practice
text: The complaint raised most often against this varnish is how early it sets. Spread over a wide panel, it starts to pull while the brush is still traveling, and it leaves a dry edge that nothing will lift out afterward. Bench testing shows why: the thinner flashes off far too fast in a heated room. The maker answers on two fronts. A retarder, stirred in at a low proportion, stretches the working time without weakening the cured coat. The second answer is about the hand rather than the can, since the varnish wants narrow overlapping bands instead of broad sweeps. Trials on hardwood panels bear the gain out, provided the scraper is honed before every coat goes on. So the judgment stays split. Here is a demanding product, dependable for anyone ready to rebuild a habit, and a letdown for anyone who wants a result on the spot.

units: the writer is writing from a workshop recommended by the reader
the rods are sorted before the weaving in this place
the pieces made there keep their shape once dry
the pace was faster in the previous workshop
the pieces from the previous workshop lost their shape quickly
the former teacher merely showed a movement to be copied
the present teacher breaks down every motion and allows mistakes
the writer progresses more slowly but remembers more
the difficult operations are carried out in silence in this new workshop
text: I am writing from the basketry workshop you pointed me to, and I want to set down what marks it off from the last one. Here the rods are sorted before anybody starts weaving, and that one precaution changes the whole result, because the baskets hold their curve once they have dried. In the house I left, the pace ran faster, yet the pieces went out of shape within a week. The teaching parts ways as well. My old master would show a figure once and wait for me to copy it; the master here breaks every motion apart and lets me fail without stepping in. I move ahead more slowly and I hold on to far more. The feel of the room differs too, since the delicate operations are carried out in silence, while the other workshop hummed with talk throughout. Thank you for sending me here. With my respectful regards.

units: three qualities are named as conditions for entering this trade
the folding tool must be handled without stiffening the joint
a tense wrist makes the fold run off true
the shades of the covering materials must agree whatever the surrounding light
the sequence of operations for the rounded spine cannot be altered
workshops state that the training has no set length
a beginner's progress is described as uneven
practitioners name the freedom of the hand among the rewards
mending a damaged object brings a satisfaction the practitioners mention
text: What is asked of anyone who wants a bench in a bookbinding workshop? Three aptitudes come back in the masters' answers. The first belongs to the hand, since the folder is held without locking the wrist, and a tight wrist sends the crease off at a slant. The second belongs to the eye, because the shades of leather and cloth have to agree under a weak lamp as readily as under a bright one. The third is a memory for movement, since a rounded spine grows out of a run of steps whose order will bear no shuffling. And the training, how long does it run? The workshops answer that it has no set end, and that a careful beginner climbs in uneven jumps. What does such a demanding road hand back? Binders name the freedom of the hand, the range of the commissions, and the pleasure of putting a battered volume back into use.

units: the beginner turned up before the agreed hour
he asked for permission to handle the cutting tools
the craftsman refused and gave him a cleaning job
the request came back seven days later
the craftsman then handed him a metal plate and asked for a straight line
the line that came out went off course
the craftsman corrected the position of the tool and of the finger without comment
the next day's line was distinctly better
the craftsman played the success down by mentioning how many lines are needed
he quietly admitted that he had done worse at the same age
text: The apprentice turned up ahead of time and asked the engraver whether he was allowed to touch the burins. The master said no, not yet, and handed him a broom, laughing as he did so. A week later the apprentice put the same question again. That week the engraver laid a copper plate on the bench and told him to try one straight line, nothing beyond that. The line he cut ran off sideways. The master passed no comment at all; he only showed how to tilt the tool and where the thumb belongs. The next day the apprentice cut a line that was nearly clean, and he bragged about it. One line does not add up to a trade, the engraver told him, and he would want thousands of them before he talked that way. Then he added, lower down, that his own line had been the worse of the two at that age.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the spread of trading routes drove orders beyond what the workshops could handle
the craftsmen changed the technique for bending the boards
round hearths replaced heating one piece at a time
several boards were softened at once
the vessels that came out had identical measurements
the traders could work out the size of their loads in advance
disagreements over the quantities carried grew fewer
the rise in demand called for more young people in training
the trade bodies made entry into the craft harder
the fear of the craft weakening produced a codification of the movements
text: Once the trading routes widened, the cooperage workshops watched orders pile up beyond anything they could honor. That pressure pushed the coopers to rethink the way they bent their staves. Rather than heating one piece at a time, they raised round hearths where a dozen boards went supple together. The change carried a result nobody had looked for. Since the casks now came off the bench at matching sizes, traders could reckon their loads before the goods were even carted, and the wrangling over delivered quantities died away. Uniform sizes fed the demand, and the demand called for more apprentices than the trade had ever taken on. The trade bodies tightened their rules of entry, uneasy at the thought of the craft thinning out. From that unease grew the long codification of movement that the workshops held on to afterward.

units: an uneven surface takes up color unevenly
dark patches appear instead of a smooth fade
wood cut across its fibers drinks more of the product
the correction rests on a graded run of abrasives
you begin with a coarse abrasive that removes the ridges left by the tool
no intermediate grit may be skipped
each abrasive removes only the traces of the one before it
the final smoothing follows the direction of the fibers
wetting the wood before the last pass raises the fibers so they can be knocked down for good
text: A rough surface drinks stain unevenly, and the maker who waves that detail away finds dark blotches where he had wanted a soft, even fade. The fault sits in the fiber itself. Cut across, it opens and swallows three or four drops where the flat grain takes only one. The cure is a patient climb through the grits, taken in order. You start with a biting abrasive that shears down the ridges the blade has left. Move on to a middling grit, then a fine one, and skip no stage along the way, since each paper wipes out nothing but the scratches of the paper before it. Polish at the end along the run of the fiber, and damp the wood before the final pass, so the whiskers that stand up are laid down for good. The surface then goes silky under the palm, and the stain settles across it at one even tone.

units: two cutting edges were shown to a doubting beginner
the first edge was ground to a narrow angle
it produced long shavings in a soft wood
it buckled on meeting a hard patch of the wood
the second edge had a wider angle
it damaged the soft fiber and left an uneven bottom
it crossed the hard patches without harm
the conclusion drawn is that a tool can only be judged against its use
the narrow angle is kept for finishing passes
the wide angle suits the fast removal of material
text: Two blades set side by side on the bench did more for the trainee's doubts about angles than any argument would have. The first, a plane iron ground to a narrow bevel, bit into the soft wood and threw off unbroken shavings, yet it buckled the instant it ran into a knotty stretch. The second, ground much blunter, tore the soft fiber and left a ragged floor, while it crossed the same knot without flinching. The shop drew its lesson: a tool is worth nothing away from the job it was made for. So the keen bevel is kept for finishing, where the thickness taken off is counted in slivers, and the stout bevel for hogging off waste, when the bulk to be shifted outweighs the state of the surface. The trainee boiled the rule down his own way: you pick an angle against the material, not against your neighbor.

units: four supplies must be gathered on the working surface
the suppleness of the rods is checked by a bending test
rods that are too stiff must soak for about sixty minutes
the assembly starts with eight rods crossed into a star
the center is held down with the finger during the weaving
each pass must be drawn tight against the one before it without pulling sideways
the upright rods are then raised to form the sides
the evenness is checked by holding the piece at eye level
the top rim is folded inward then held by a stitch
the drying is done flat and away from any heat source
text: Before you begin, lay out on the bench the following supplies: a bundle of softened fibers, a curved needle, a length of waxed thread, and a pair of straight-bladed shears. Bend a strand to make sure it gives without cracking; if it holds stiff, put the bundle under water and leave it for an hour. Move on to the base. Cross eight strands into a star, pin the center under your thumb, then weave, drawing every pass tight against the one before it and never hauling from one side alone. Carry on with the walls. Bring the uprights up one by one and run the weave round in a spiral, checking the evenness at eye level. Close with the rim. Cut the strands on a slant, fold the uprights inward, and stitch the edge with the waxed thread. Dry the piece flat, well clear of any heat source.

units: a demonstration open to the public takes place in a forge of an old district
the craftswoman lit her fire and announced her program to the public
the metal brought to a high temperature was bent with the hammer
the onlookers watched the colors of the piece change
the piece was cooled in a tub
a file served to even out the surface
the craftswoman stressed that sturdiness does not rule out finishing
children were invited to hold the gripping tool
a weekly evening opening was announced
the neighbors will be able to follow the making of a grille
text: A crowd of onlookers presses up against the forge in the old district, where a public demonstration has just got under way. Early in the afternoon the farrier lit her hearth and told the crowd what she meant to turn out. An hour on, the bar came glowing out of the coals and took its curve under measured hammer blows. The watchers saw the piece run from white to brown, then blacken in the quenching tub. The smith next picked up a file and brought the surface smooth, remarking that strength is no excuse for skipping the care. Towards the close of the afternoon she asked the youngest ones to hold the tongs while she struck. The session ended on an announcement: the workshop will open its doors one evening a week, so that the neighborhood can follow the making of a balcony grille.

units: the clay delivered to the workshop loses its moisture far too quickly
paste that is too dry breaks and the walls give way before the kiln
the craftsman wraps every block in a soaked cloth
the blocks are kept away from heat and from drafts
this treatment makes the paste supple again and easy to throw
the dust that settles on damp pieces spoils the glaze
a sheet of cloth has been stretched above the shelves
the floor is wetted before every throwing session
the vessels leave the kiln with a smooth and soft look
the potter credits the result to the care given to what surrounds the work
text: Clay reaches the pottery in dark blocks, and it gives up its moisture far too fast for the work that has to follow. Try to raise a pot from paste that dry and it crumbles: the walls split, they sag, and the piece is lost long before the kiln ever sees it. The potter's answer is a patient one. He wraps every block in a soaked cloth and sets it aside, out of the heat, clear of any draft that crosses the room. The clay softens again, yields under the palm, and climbs easily on the wheel. One trouble stayed. Dust drifts down onto the damp pieces and dulls the glaze, so he stretched a fine sheet above the shelves and wets the floor before he sits down to throw. The bowls now leave the kiln with a smooth, quiet skin. Ask him why that works and he will not talk about his hands. He talks about what surrounds them.

units: the author sets two ways of joining the pieces of a timber frame against each other
the traditional joint spreads the forces through the thickness of the wood
this joint grows tighter as it ages
fixing with bolts piles up stress around the holes
repeated shaking weakens the metal piece
the argument from speed ignores what later repairs cost
strength is measured by the ability to move without breaking
seasoned practitioners set a piece according to the way the tree grew
this judgment cannot be handed over to a machine
the author judges a technique on how long it stays in use
text: Set a pegged timber frame beside a bolted one and a badly framed argument comes into view. Cut joinery hands the load off into the body of the wood, and the years only draw it tighter. Bolts do the reverse. Stress gathers at the drilled holes, and shaking, season after season, leaves the steel brittle. People praise the speed of the bolted method and quietly forget what the patching will cost. A sound frame is not the one that holds best through its first winter. It is the one that can move and still not break. Carpenters trained the old way read the grain, dodge the knots, and lay each piece as the tree grew. No machine makes that call. To defend them is not to pine for anything; it is to say that a method is judged by how long it stays in use, not by how fast it goes up.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman described binds books and is held by her colleagues to be experienced
she learned the trade beside a master who did not speak
that master corrected her way of working through gesture
her equipment includes bone tools, a sewing frame and presses of old wood
she works with leathers, undyed cloth and papers decorated in a bath
she takes on two students every season
she picks them for their stamina rather than for their skill
she holds failure to be more instructive than success
she keeps her own old mistakes at home
her bindings sit in research collections and carry no name
text: The binder in question has worked enough winters at the trade that her peers treat her as a thoroughly seasoned hand. Her life sorts into a few plain headings. Training first: she learned beside a master who never spoke a word to her and who set her hands right by moving them himself. Tools next, bone folders, a sewing frame, wooden presses whose knotted uprights groan at every turn of the screw. Materials after that, soft skins, undyed cloth, marbled papers floated off a bath. Teaching last. Each season she takes on two apprentices, and she picks them for stamina rather than for a deft touch. A binding that failed, she says, teaches more than one that came out right, and she keeps her own early wrecks in a drawer at home. Her books sit in study libraries, none of them signed.

units: the visit follows the order the designers intended
the opening room shows unsharpened blades straight out of the forge
the critic finds this first part clear and bare
the second section brings together tools that have been used
one cutting tool carries a nick left by a flaw in the wood
another tool shows an edge worn down by repeated use
the explanatory texts stay easy to follow without losing precision
the third room mixes the trades together and loses the visitor
the end of the visit shows silent images of hands at work
the verdict is favourable despite a weakening at the middle of the show
text: The show on cutting tools is walked through in the order its makers laid out, and that order is what carries it. The opening room holds unground blades, straight from the forge, still black with scale; the point being made is clear and the staging is bare. Then come the tools that have worked for a living, and the interest rises. A chisel chipped where a hard knot ran through the board. A plane whose dulled iron records thousands of passes. The labels stay plain without ever going vague. The third room is where the thing slips. Cases pile up, trades run together, and the thread you were handed comes loose in your fingers. The closing stretch wins some of that back with footage of hands at work, silent, no music laid over it. You leave persuaded by the whole, even with that dip through the middle.

units: the writer answers a question about whether his workshop is running well
the seat he built would not stand straight
the cause is a joint made on wood that was not dry enough
the wood shrank as it dried and the joint went slack
the writer took the whole thing apart
a craftsman nearby had warned him
he let the wood dry for a full season before starting again
the joints now hold and the finish comes easily
he blames his haste rather than any lack of skill
he asks to borrow a hollowing tool because his own is finished
text: You asked whether the workshop is finally running the way it should, so here it is straight. The stool I put together this winter never sat flat on the floor. I had driven the tenons home into wood that was still green. It shrank as it dried, the joint went slack, and the seat ended up rocking under anyone who sat on it. So I pulled the whole thing apart, every piece of it. The old joiner in the shed next door had warned me, and this time I listened. The boards sat breathing a whole season before I began again. Now the joints hold, and the surface that fought me under the first sanding takes a polish with almost no work. What went wrong was my hurry, not my hands. If you come by, bring your curved gouge. Mine is finished and I dare not hollow a seat without one. Write soon, and tell me whether your kiln is drawing.

units: a guild of weaving craftsmen watches its plantations weaken
the shoots they cut have grown shorter and snap while being worked
worn-out soil is held to blame
cutting too often wears the roots of the plant down
the plots are now worked at wider intervals
organic matter is worked into the soil
older and suppler varieties have been put back into the ground
the crop fell by a third the first season and then climbed again
the spokesman for the group grants that the objects sold cost more
the collective teaches beginners a way of cutting that was nearly given up
text: What becomes of a trade when the raw material it lives on begins to thin out? Put to a guild of basket weavers whose willow beds are failing, the question drew an answer in three parts. The finding first: the rods they cut come up shorter than they used to and snap in the weave. The diagnosis next. Tired soil, and roots cut back far too often, leave the plants with nothing left to push out. Then the fix, two seasons old already, longer rotations between the plots, compost worked into the ground, older and suppler varieties planted again. Their spokesman says the crop dropped by a third that first season before it climbed back. Asked about the price of a basket, he grants that it has gone up and stands by it. The guild now teaches newcomers to cut, a skill almost no workshop was still handing down.

units: a stone craftsman teaches his pupil that every block calls for its own hand
the first stone has a rough texture and hard grains
this stone rings clearly when it is struck
the second stone is softer and takes a smooth finish
the pupil wants to know which of the two is better
the master refuses to compare the materials against each other
he says that only the intended use settles it
the rough stone suits a step because it keeps a foot from slipping
the smooth stone suits a ledge because water runs off it
the master says the pupil will stop asking this one evening
text: The stonecutter kept telling his apprentice that no two blocks ever ask for the same hand. The first one, he said, is coarse, packed with hard grains that catch the point and ring bright under the mallet. The other is softer, takes the rasp kindly, and comes up satin, almost disconcertingly smooth against the palm. The apprentice wanted to know which of the two was the better stone. The question means nothing at all, the cutter answered: you do not weigh one stone against another, you weigh what is being asked of each. A stair tread wants the rough block, the one a boot cannot slide on. A window ledge wants the other, which water washes over and then leaves. Then he wiped the white dust off his forearms and added that the apprentice would know how to choose alone, the evening he stopped asking.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the way metal casting workshops changed is set out theme by theme
burnt wood was given up for a denser fuel
this change raised the heat reached in the vats
the air devices were worked by human strength at first
they were later driven by the force of water
this shift made the rise in heat steady
packed sand took the place of clay for shaping the impressions
this material stands up better to shifts of heat and pulls away without breaking
a measured addition of tin gave a metal that took knocks better
a post for watching the furnace appeared and cut into the founder's authority
text: The history of the casting workshops is best taken one strand at a time. Fuel to begin with: charred wood gave way to denser coals, and the vats ran a good deal hotter for it. Bellows come next. Arms worked them at first, then water turned the wheels that drove them, and the heat rose steadily instead of by fits and starts. Moulds after that, where rammed sand took the place of raw clay, since it stands up far better to sudden shifts of heat and lifts away without cracking. Alloys last of all, where a measured share of tin yielded a metal that rang under a blow without splitting. Each of these developments rearranged the work itself. The founder surrendered part of his authority to the hand watching the furnace, a responsibility that had existed in none of these workshops before.

units: the worker gathers a quantity of molten glass on the end of his rod
this mass is almost running at the moment it is taken up
it is rolled on a metal surface to bring it true and stiffen its skin
blowing air in opens a cavity inside the mass
short reheats alternate with the shaping stages
glass that has gone cold splits at the slightest knock
the opening at the top is widened with a tool that pinches
the piece is then passed to a helper
a last stay in an oven brings the heat down slowly through the night
without this gradual cooling the object would break of its own accord
text: The blower starts by dipping his pipe into the melt and lifting out a thick orange lump that barely holds its own weight as it comes. He rolls it along a steel plate to bring it true and to stiffen the skin of it. Then the first breath: a bubble opens in the heart of the mass and swells out as the air pushes. From there he trades short reheats for shaping, over and over, because glass that has gone cold turns brittle and splits at the slightest knock. Once the belly is right, he spreads the neck open with a pair of jacks, breaks the piece free, and passes it across to a helper. The last stage happens in an annealing oven, where the heat steps down all night long. Without that carefully managed descent, the strain locked inside would in time crack the vessel apart where it stands on the shelf.

units: a damaged drain pipe let water through above a gilding workshop
the store room was reached by the leak
the thin metal leaves kept there are extremely light
the paper sheets between them buckled under the water
the leaves welded to one another and could no longer be used
the want of supplies halted the repair of an old frame
the woman who had ordered the work saw her date pushed back
the accident had consequences for three other trades
the store was moved lower down and shut into a closed cabinet
a notebook now records the state of the lots at every withdrawal
text: A cracked gutter running over the gilding workshop was enough to wreck a whole season of work. Water crept its way into the store room, where beaten gold leaf lay waiting, so thin that a single breath will carry it off. The tissue sheets between them buckled in the wet, the leaves welded into one another, and the whole lot was finished. With nothing left to work from, the gilder had to stop midway through an old frame, which pushed back the woman who had ordered it, and she had a date of her own to keep. The delay ran outward and caught a joiner, a varnisher and a carrier as well. Out of it came a rule she holds to now: the store came down to floor level, into a shut cabinet, and a notebook records the state of every lot each time it is opened. The roof still leaks. The gold stays dry.

units: a mountain route is broken into sections sorted by the ground underfoot
the forest section follows wide switchbacks over soft ground
the gradient there stays moderate and steady
the scree zone comes from the rock face broken apart by frost
these stones shift underfoot and force quick footwork
the ridge section is swept by wind and pinches down in places
the descent leads to a damp gully where water-polished stone turns slick
each section calls for its own equipment
mapmakers flag these ground types with a graphic marking
this information lets a walker weigh the effort before setting out
text: Mapmakers break a mountain route into sections, and what sorts them is the ground underfoot. The first runs through forest: wide switchbacks, soil that gives a little, a climb that never steepens and never eases. Then the scree begins. Frost has been prying the rock face apart for years, and the loose stones it drops shift the moment you weight them, so you learn to step quick and light. Higher up, the route follows a ridge where the wind never lets go and the walking surface pinches down to a narrow lane. The last section drops into a damp gully, where running water has polished the stone until it turns slick. Each stretch asks for its own kit. On their maps the surveyors flag these surfaces with a shading of their own, so a walker can weigh what the day will cost before leaving the door.

units: the party set out from the shelter very early
a veil of mist still lay over the floor of the valley at the start
the guide had warned that the ford might be cut off if the snow melted fast
the descent to the water was made without a stop
the river was running fuller than the day before
the crossing was ordered from the lightest walkers upward
a rope was pulled taut between two boulders to secure the passage
the packs were carried over apart from the heaviest walkers
the party then dried off in an open clearing in the forest
the guide saw the whole maneuver as an ordinary precaution
text: They left the stone shelter before the light came, while mist still lay thick along the floor of the valley. The guide had said it plainly the night before: if the thaw picked up, the ford would be gone by midday. So they went down to the water without stopping once, and reached it as the gray began to lift. The river ran fuller than it had the day before, rolling stones along its bed with a low knock. The guide sent the lightest across first and worked up by weight, a rope pulled taut between two boulders. The packs went over on their own, apart from the heaviest walkers. On the far bank a clearing gave them dry ground, and they wrung out their clothes there. Back home the same walkers told it with a quiet sort of pride. The guide only shrugged. To him it had been an ordinary bit of care.

units: you must read the angle of the slope before committing to a mountain flank
the steepness is what decides the danger
a gentle grade holds its snow in place
a sharp grade lets the snow go the moment you walk on it
a pole serves to test how the snow layers are stacked
a top layer sliding over a hardened layer means you turn back
it is better to travel along a rib of ground than in a hollow of the relief
a chute gathers moving snow and multiplies its force
walkers have to cross one at a time so that they are not swept away together
the sound of water under the snow reveals a void beneath the feet
text: Before you commit to a steep flank, read the angle of the slope. Steepness is what decides the danger. A gentle grade holds its snow in place; a sharp one lets go the moment your boot lands, and what lets go carries the walker down with it. Push a pole into the snowpack and feel how it is stacked. If the top layer slides over a hard crust below, turn back, because that pairing is a break waiting to happen. Pick a line along a rib rather than a hollow, since a hollow funnels everything that moves and multiplies its force. Send the party across one walker at a time, so that a single slip cannot take the whole rope. And listen for water running under your feet: that hollow rush means an empty vault below, and an empty vault gives way under load. If doubt is left, go down. Turning back costs you nothing but the walk.

units: the coast path has been losing ground for two seasons
salt spray and swell hollow out the cliff from underneath
walkers keep using the passage all the same
the warning board keeps disappearing under the greenery
the woman in charge of the paths admits that banning has failed
a new line has been pegged out farther back from the sea in the low heath
that line has cut steps and a timber handrail
walkers take it because it is pleasanter, not out of obedience
the old passage is closing itself under the thorn scrub
the woman in charge holds that a better offer beats a telling off
text: Two seasons now, the coast path has been giving way, chewed at by spray and by swell that hollows the cliff from underneath. Walkers keep on using the path all the same. The view is worth it, the going is easy, and the warning board disappears under greenery about as fast as anyone can clear it. The woman who looks after the paths says so without fuss: banning people did not work, they tried it. So they tried something else. A fallback line was pegged out farther back, through the low heath, with cut steps and a timber handrail. People take it because it is pleasanter, not because they were told to. The threatened stretch is quietly closing itself under thorn scrub. Scolding walkers buys you nothing, she says with a shrug of the shoulders. Giving them something better buys you the path.

units: two valleys on either flank of the same range have almost nothing in common
the eastern valley is broad and flat
its river loops back in slow bends and carries silt
grazing land runs down there to the edge of the water
the western valley is a narrow notch
a fast stream drops through it from pool to pool and throws up foam
its sides carry scattered trees hanging off the rock
the difference comes down to the gradient
ground that barely tilts lets the river wander
the first valley is walked without effort while the second is climbed
text: Two valleys lie on opposite flanks of one range, and they have almost nothing in common. The eastern one opens wide and flat. Its river loops back on itself in slow bends, brown with silt, moving so quietly you hear nothing, and grazing land runs all the way down to the bank. The western one is a narrow notch cut deep into rock. A stream drops through it from pool to pool, white with foam, and thin stands of trees hang off the sides wherever a root can grip. The whole difference comes down to gradient. Where the ground barely tilts, the water takes its time and builds its bends; where it plunges, the water runs straight and digs. Walkers feel that in their legs. The first valley you stroll through. The second you climb like a staircase. Two neighbors, two ways of wearing down the rock.

units: the writer calls up the feeling that comes before a ridge line half hidden in mist
he blames travel as it is sold for running like a checklist
he puts forward three ways of giving up a fixed program
the first is to move very slowly
stopping when the shade settles in belongs to that first way
the second is to walk the same trail at another time of year
that return reveals that the colors, the sounds and the smells have changed
the third is to leave the names of the summits deliberately unlearned
the writer refuses to treat a landscape as something one collects
he sets the walker willing to dawdle against the one who comes to take inventory
text: Stand in front of a ridge half swallowed by mist and something in you goes looking for more than a picture. Everyone has felt it. Travel as it is sold to us runs on lists instead: a lookout, a lake, a photogenic clearing, tick, tick, tick. Let me argue for three ways of losing your route. The first is slowness. Walk at the pace of a grazing herd, and stop wherever the shade settles in. The second is return. Come back to the same trail in the opposite season and find that its colors, its noises and its smells have all changed hands. The third is chosen ignorance. Do not learn the names of the summits beforehand; let them stand there as shapes. A landscape is not a thing to collect. It opens to whoever will lose an afternoon in it, and it shuts against whoever arrives to take inventory.

units: the path repair worker started out hauling stone for the man before him
his first jobs were all muscle
he had to clear away the rubble that came down onto the track
he bedded wooden drainage bars across the slope
he was later handed the setting of the route markers
a marker set wrong can send a walker straight off a drop
he was trained to lay stone without mortar
he raised a first retaining wall under someone else's eye
he now lays out the routes himself, working out the workable gradient and where the water goes
he teaches his apprentices that a well-drained path mends itself
text: The man who keeps the paths in repair learned the work by hauling stone for the fellow who held the job before him. The early years were all muscle: shoveling away the rubble that came down onto the track, bedding wooden drain bars across the slope, scraping out the runnels. Marking the route came later, and it weighed more, because a sign set wrong can walk somebody straight off a drop. He was trained to lay stone without mortar, and he raised his first retaining wall with an older hand watching every course. These days he lays out the lines himself. He works out how much gradient a path can take, angles it so water leaves rather than follows, and picks where the footing goes. He trains apprentices now. His first lesson fits in one line: drain a path properly and it mends itself.

units: the book deals with high mountain paths and it wins the reader over
what it is worth comes from a working method the author owns up to
the author walked every route in it himself
he walked them at different times of the year
the timings he gives can therefore be trusted
first-hand experience brings out dangers that no map carries
the book flags in particular a seeping rock, a ford swollen after rain, and a scree slope that turns loose in a thaw
the reader comes away better equipped and warier
the photographs are faulted for showing nothing but clear sky
that visual choice makes the route look kinder than it is
text: This book about high mountain paths wins you over, and it wins you over because of how it was made. The author walked every route in it himself, and walked them across the seasons rather than once in fine weather. That is why the timings hold up. It is also why the warnings do: no survey on paper tells you where the rock seeps, where the ford swells after a storm, where a scree slope starts shedding as soon as the thaw sets in. The result is a reader who arrives better equipped, and who arrives warier. The pictures are another matter. Every one of them was taken under an open sky, so the mist that governs half of these outings never shows up at all. That weakens the case, since it makes the walking look kinder than it is. The book teaches well. It comforts a little too quickly.

units: the writer doubts that his earlier message ever went out
the letter box in the village looked as though nobody had emptied it
he is writing from an inn down in a valley
his stay has run on longer than he had meant
his boots gave out on the third pass
the vehicle meant to carry him back does not run outside the busy months
he first thought he would have to give up the trip
the innkeeper found him a driver who takes goods over to the next town
a tradesman resoled his boots for next to nothing
he announces that he leaves two stages earlier than planned
text: I hope my last card actually reached you. The box in the village looked as though nobody had emptied it since the spring. I am writing from an inn down in the valley, where I have stayed on far longer than I meant to. Two things went wrong at once: my boots gave out on the third pass, and the little bus that was supposed to carry me back does not run outside the busy months. For a day I thought I would have to give up and find my own way home. Then the innkeeper had an idea. Her brother drives crates over to the next town every week, and he is glad to take me along. Meanwhile a cobbler has resoled my boots for next to nothing at all. So I set off the day after tomorrow, two stages shorter and one story richer. Write to the return address; I will collect the post when I get there.

text: Does the number of visitors change with the season? Hugely, says the forest warden, but not in the way people picture. In the warm months they pour in, she says, and they stay bunched on three or four waymarked routes; they hardly walk at all and they photograph everything. In the cold months almost nobody comes, yet the few who do go wherever they like, paths or no paths. And which of them causes trouble? The second lot, no question. A crowd on a trail packs the soil down, and soil recovers from that. One walker cutting across a clearing puts the nesting birds off, and that does not come back. So what do you do about it? She would rather widen the choice: fresh routes opened in the quiet months, boards that tell you about the nests instead of forbidding you. Does it work? Better than fines, she says, laughing.

text: Before the group started walking, the leader of the outing took them through the route in detail. Top up your bottles at the spring behind the mountain shelter, he said, because the following water comes only beyond the high pass. The opening stretch follows a track cut with ruts deep enough to twist an ankle without warning. One of the hikers asked why anyone should carry a compass on a waymarked trail. Fog wipes the painted blazes off the rock, he answered, and a marker knocked flat by the weather sends you confidently in the wrong direction. He finished by telling them to cinch the pack straps for the steep climb and slacken them on the descent, to spare the shoulders. They set off while dew still lay across the grass, and everyone repeated the gathering point: the last rocky headland.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)

text: Old trading roads followed the shape of the land far more than the shortest line. A pass that climbed too steeply meant hiring extra draft animals, and that added expense was enough to send the convoys down a neighboring corridor, longer but gentler. Whole settlements grew out of that detour. Where the animals had to recover, someone opened a relay house; a smith set up beside it; before long a market was trading in front of the smithy. Then engineers drove a tunnel beneath the ridge, and the whole pattern ran backward. The convoys took the straight line again, the relay houses stood empty, and the town that owed its wealth to the obstacle faded away once that obstacle disappeared. Travelers crossing those valleys now rarely guess that the quiet around them was bought with a slope.

text: A heavily walked trail grows wider with every single year. Walkers step around the puddles, crush the vegetation along the edges, and what began as a footpath becomes a broad bare strip that channels running water. On spongy heathland, or at the margin of a bog, the process accelerates: saturated ground cannot take the trampling and churns into mud. The people who look after such country have two answers. The first is a timber boardwalk, which lifts every step above the peat and confines the traffic to one fixed width. The second is compacted gravel spread over a filter fabric, so the water drains through the layer instead of carrying the surface away. Either way, plants creep back along the margins by the following season, and the trail finally stops eating into the ground around it.

units: the narrator remembered a gentle shore with a broad spread of sand

text: What I had kept in my head was a gentle coastline: a generous beach, low dunes you sank into up to the knee. Returning after years away, I found something entirely different. The sea had eaten into the foot of the cliff, and the wooden stairway down to the sand hung in open air, leading nowhere. A fisherman from the village reckoned two winters of storms had been enough to strip the beach away completely. Where I used to run around as a child, foam was slapping against bare rock. In the end, the surprise outweighed the sadness. The same little bay could pass for a holiday picture one year and a demolition site the next, without a single human hand involved. I left by the upper path, the one running past the cultivated fields, and gave up on a shore that no longer exists anywhere.

units: the text lists the precautions to take before a sea crossing to a nearby island

text: Three things are worth settling before you take a ferry across to a neighboring island. Baggage first: nothing shelters that landing from the wind, and a bag left half open empties itself in seconds, so strap the outside pockets shut and tuck your documents into an inner one. Waiting second: the crossings follow the tide, the departure time posted the day before shifts more often than not, and anyone with sense turns up to board considerably early. Seasickness third: the swell builds the moment you clear the sheltered bay, so stand at the middle of the deck with your eyes fixed on the shoreline instead of sitting inside a closed cabin. Arrival last: count on nothing whatever meeting foot passengers, and expect to walk to the neighboring village with your load on your back.

text: At first light the crews finally cleared the last slide of mud that had blocked the road over the pass. The work had started at snowmelt, when a slab of the embankment tore loose above the hairpin bend. Around the middle of the day a digger climbed the slope to reinforce that embankment, while two teams bolted a steel netting across the cracked rock face. The wind carried the dust out over the moorland, where half wild horses watched the machine and never moved aside. Later in the afternoon an engineer walked the roadway on foot, testing the firmness of the fresh gravel with his heel. The barrier was raised again before nightfall. The first cars took the headland at a crawl, and their headlights drew a trembling line along the ridge, like a vein of fire opened in the rock.

units: a coastal dune builds up in stages you can follow without any instrument

text: Watch a coastal dune closely and you can follow every stage of it without a single instrument. Dry sand, driven by the wind off the water, rolls across the foreshore until it meets something in its way: a scrap of driftwood, a tuft of grass, a stranded plank. The grains pile up in the shelter behind it, a small mound takes shape, and the mound slows the wind in turn, so more sand settles. Roots of creeping grass thread through the fresh layer and bind it, and the hump grows upward instead of scattering. Once the crest stands beyond the reach of the waves, a second dune begins to form seaward of the first, with a damp hollow between them. That hollow carries plants found nowhere else nearby, because fresh water rises close to the surface. Cut a gap through the crest with a boot or a wheel, and the wind pours back in and takes the whole thing apart.

units: the author questions the organized drawing of crowds to places the crowd wears out

the parking areas and the paths were never sized for such flows

he proposes collective transport to clear the lines of vehicles off narrow roads
he proposes honest signposting that sends people toward quiet neighboring valleys
text: Should we keep drawing crowds to wild places that crowds wear out? The question makes local officials uneasy, since their revenue rides on visitors, and it splits the residents, who take the congestion and get nothing back. The pattern is familiar enough. A place praised in pictures moving across screens can double its visitor count in one season, though neither its parking nor its paths were built for anything like that. Closing such places is not the answer; it would be unfair. Spreading the load is. A free booking slot thins the arrivals out across the week. A shuttle clears the lines of vehicles off narrow roads. Honest signposting sends people toward the next valley over, just as fine and left alone. And we might stop selling quiet as though the supply had no limit.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)

text: The lighthouse keeper calls her post a trade of patience, and says it has little in common with the job the man before her did. He lived out on the rock for weeks at a stretch, wound up the wick, greased the mechanism, and wrote the visibility down in a paper log. She watches an automatic lantern from an office on the shore, where screens flag the smallest fault the moment it shows. None of that saddens her. The sea asks for the same watchfulness it always did, she says, and the most reliable gear afloat will quit on the night the swell gets up. As a child she went along with her mother on the runs that resupplied the islands, and she kept a taste for empty horizons. The man before her carried every reef in his head; she finds them by their coordinates, and never trusts that alone.

units: the author recommends a coastal route opened recently in spite of its flaws

text: Honestly, this newly opened coastal route is worth the journey, flaws and all. The line of it first: it hugs the water almost the whole way, swinging between clifftop stretches and drops into coves barely wide enough to stand in, and it keeps you off the long paved sections that ruin so many walks. The waymarking next: clean, steady, no unnecessary forest of signposts, though you do pause and squint on the way into the villages. Then the facilities, and here I will grumble a bit. There is nowhere to sit down, the one water point sits a third of the way along, and the composting toilets the brochure promised exist only in the brochure. What carries it, though, is the feel of the thing: surf working below your boots, birds cutting low across the waves, and nobody ahead of you for an hour.

units: the sender is staying on the upper floor of a wayside lodging

text: I write from the upstairs room of the inn, the route book open in front of me. You asked why we fell behind, so here are the reasons, in order. The track we intended to follow runs along an exposed ridge where the wind never lets up. It chills the skin and burns energy far faster than level ground, so we cut our pace right back. Then there was the previous day's rain. It had soaked the loose rock across the slope, and the stones rolled underfoot. Rather than force the narrow gorge, we worked our way around it. The longer line costs extra distance, but it removes any real danger of a fall. Accumulated tiredness cost us more time still, and we halted for a good while beside a capped spring. So expect us considerably later. The exact hour of our arrival will reach you tomorrow evening.

units: a correspondent asks a question about overcrowding at natural sites

text: A reader writes to ask what can be done about the crowds wearing down the best known natural sites. The difficulty is one of clustering. Most visitors turn up in the same few places, in the same weeks, and the main path breaks apart under the traffic it carries. So what answers are there? The first is to spread walkers across the ground, marking out secondary loops that reach the same plateau from other flanks of the mountain. The second is booking ahead, which staggers arrivals and keeps the high shelters from being swamped. A third approach is to make the quiet months worth choosing, which means keeping the huts open and the shuttle service dependable. The last is a matter of teaching. Tell arriving walkers how thin the plant cover is, and far fewer of them wander off the marked line.

units: a guide judges the southern slope easier
a map specialist disputes his view without losing her temper

this path calls for no particular skill

the northern flank gives continuous shade and water in quantity
the guide points out that the evening wind cools the south
the specialist finds that wind irregular whereas the trees shelter without pause
the lodging is comfortable on one side and basic on the other
the two speakers conclude that the routes are worth the same
text: The guide kept saying the southern valley walks better than the northern one, and the mapmaker kept disagreeing, without once raising her voice. His case was simple. The southern path winds through soft grassland, it climbs at a steady angle, and it asks no skill of anyone. She granted him none of that. The far slope, she said, breaks into stony steps, yet it holds shade all day and water in quantity. He conceded the water, then came back to the heat, which drops as soon as the breeze rises late in the afternoon. A breeze comes and goes, she answered, while a wood shelters you without pause. They moved on to beds, a comfortable inn on one side, a bare hut on the other. In the end he said the choice belongs to the walker, and she agreed the two routes come out even, for opposite reasons.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: before accurate surveys, people traveled on the strength of spoken accounts

a high pass was climbed only if it shortened the road markedly
travelers recorded the places where they could sleep out of the rain

the fear of mist and of unstable slopes also weighed on the routes
these routes look illogical on a survey but obeyed a need for safety
text: Picture the old roads, long before anyone could survey a slope properly. You set out on hearsay and nothing else. Read the travel accounts left from those days and the same three worries come up again and again. Water first. Routes bent toward springs however far it took them, because a stage with nothing to drink cost you dearly. Then the ground itself. A wall of rock was worked around rather than climbed, unless the pass overhead cut whole days off the road. And last, a roof. People wrote down carefully where a traveler could sleep dry, and one lodging with a good name pulled all the traffic into some perfectly ordinary valley. Add the dread of fog, add the loose stone underfoot, and you get routes that look senseless drawn on paper and made plain sense to anyone hoping to stay alive.

units: a build-up of sand starts around a very slight obstacle

the particles climb the exposed face then fall on the other side
this transfer gradually moves the whole landform
the rooting of plants blocks the sand
the landform then stops moving and becomes a fixed rise
text: Where does a dune begin? With almost nothing. A tuft of grass, a pebble, a scrap of driftwood lying on flat sand. Wind carrying grains slows the moment it passes that small block, and what it carries drops out of the air. A bump forms. Every gust adds to it, and season after season the bump takes on a settled shape, sloping gently on the windward side and falling away sharply behind. Grains work their way up the gentle face, cross the crest, and slide down the back. That endless handover is what shifts the whole mass forward, step by patient step. Then plants take hold. Roots reach through the sand and pin it where it lies, and the wandering stops. What used to travel is now a fixed hill, one the breeze no longer redraws and walkers cross without leaving a lasting mark.

units: the boat started taking on water just after leaving the cove

text: The boat began taking on water almost as soon as the cove fell behind them, and the whole journey turned on that. The current stood between the hull and the shore they had left, so they let it carry them, and it grounded them on a shingle beach no chart had bothered to record. Their provisions had swollen and split in the wet, and they abandoned them where they lay. With nothing left to eat, they had no choice but to climb the cliff in search of people. The ascent was long and dry, and it opened onto a level top of heather that the wind crossed as it pleased. From there they made out a pale roof below, and the wreck turned into a lucky detour. The farmer took them in for two nights and dried their belongings. One of them said afterward that a leaking hull had given him the widest view of his life.

units: the text speaks to whoever suffers in the shoulders from the first climb

the heavy items go close to the back, high up

the setting is checked on a short descent

text: Shoulders aching before the first climb is even over? Work through this. Tip the pack out completely onto level ground, then sort the contents into three piles, the indispensable, the useful, and whatever you packed from sheer habit. Discard that last pile without arguing with yourself. Weigh what remains. It should come to no more than a fifth of your own body weight. Pack the heavy items against your back, high, level with the shoulder blades, since weight sitting low drags you backward and ruins your footing on loose rock. Pull the hip belt tight before the shoulder straps, because the hips are meant to carry the bulk of the load. Then test the setting on a short slope you can run down. If a strap bites, let it out one notch and repeat the trial until the pressure feels even.

units: two neighboring valleys chose opposite strategies for receiving visitors

text: Two valleys that share a ridge have taken opposite views of how to receive walkers, and the difference is now written on the ground. The first spent its money on access, a widened road, a parking terrace cut into the hillside, steel footbridges thrown over the torrents. Visitor numbers there have doubled, shops have opened along the street, and residents describe a hum that never quite stops through the busy months. The second closed its road to cars at the last inhabited hamlet, so anyone going higher walks or takes the shuttle. Takings climb more slowly. Yet the riverbanks have stopped crumbling, and quiet has turned into a selling point. Officials from both valleys visit one another often, each watching the outcome he fears most. Neither has yet spoken of turning back.

units: the height described appears in successive levels of different character

this wall once served to guide livestock
the top is open to the wind and carries a smell of stone

the opposite flank drops toward a wooded hollow fitted with a resting place
text: The plateau opens out in steps, and no two of them look alike. At the foot lies grazing land, cut into squares by low hedges, with a path of pale sand threading between the pens and the drinking troughs. Higher up the heath begins. The soil turns dry, the growth stays low, and gray rock breaks through in patches. A wall of dry stone runs the length of the crest, on and on without a scrap of mortar, put there long ago to steer flocks toward the summer pasture. On the top nothing stops the wind, and the air carries a mineral smell, cold and faintly dusty. Two shallow pools hold the rain and draw birds passing through. On the far side a wooded slope falls away into a closed hollow, where a bench, a wooden shelter and a spring capped under a flagstone make a welcome place to halt.

units: the author considers that the way of traveling has gradually gone downhill
at the start, people set off to walk along a watercourse with no set plan

the camera came between the traveler and the scenery
a mountain pass is now looked at through a viewfinder
walkers come down a fine path without looking around them
they hurry toward a viewpoint picked out beforehand
the author does not wish to go back to an idealized time
he asks only for a stop with no purpose, for the pleasure of breathing
text: Honestly, we have let travel slide, and it happened one step at a time. It used to be simple. You went out to walk. You followed a river, slept wherever the day ran out, and came home with aching legs and a couple of blurred pictures. Then the lists arrived, the places you absolutely must see, ranked and scored and ticked off in turn. After that a screen slid in between us and the ground beneath us, and we began looking at the pass through a lens before looking at it at all. Now you pass walkers hurtling down a glorious track with their eyes on their boots, desperate to reach a viewpoint chosen the night before. I want no golden age back, since those old wanderings were badly prepared as often as not. I want the right to halt for nothing whatever, out in the middle of nowhere, and breathe.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a trail-mapping specialist inspects the routes before the busy season

this method cuts down the number of rescue operations

text: Before the walking season opens, the mapper for a trail service goes out and checks every route she keeps. The trouble is a familiar one. Markers hold badly on steep rock faces, and hikers lose the path the moment fog rolls up the valley. She reads the slope with a clinometer, notes what the rock is made of, and picks an anchor that suits it. In hard, close-grained stone she sets a bolt sealed with resin. In crumbling, flaky rock she prefers a weighted post that frost cannot lift out. Then she stakes the route in short runs, placing each marker where a walker can still see the one behind it. That habit cuts down on rescue callouts and keeps people from turning back for no reason. Every position goes into a logbook, and the maintenance crews read it before they head out on their rounds.

units: two viewing platforms overlook the same valley
the upper platform is built on a rocky spur above the gorge

the view from the lower platform is partly hidden by the cliff

the quality of a built feature depends on the fit between a place and its public
text: Two viewing platforms open onto the same valley, and they deserve very different verdicts. The upper one sits on a rocky spur above the gorge, and reaching it is punishing work. The steps rise steeply, the rail is narrow, and the visitor arrives winded in front of a view that pays the effort back. The lower one rests on a grassy shelf, and anyone can stroll to it. What the view loses in sweep it gains in softness, since the cliff hides part of the valley. You might favor the first for its harshness, the second for the mercy it shows families with children. Yet the comparison tilts toward the lower deck as soon as the wind picks up. The high spur turns unpleasant to stand on, while the sheltered one keeps its charm. Good building owes less to height than to the fit between a site and the people it draws.

units: the writer is writing from lodging set on a slope

the drink served tastes bitter

a man minding his beasts gave them water
the writer announces a return worn out and changed
text: I am writing from an inn built into a hillside, where the wind rattles the shutters all night long. Let me hand you this trip in pieces, the way it comes back to me. The lodging first: a bare room, a hard bed, and a huge window that looks out over a dry plateau where nothing moves. The food next: warm flatbread, a goat cheese so salty it stings the tongue, and a bitter brew the keeper pours into chipped bowls. Then the walking. We set out at sunrise on tracks that wind along the slope, and we pass far more sheep and goats than we pass vehicles. One thing more, since it stayed with me. A man minding his animals stopped and handed us water without a word. Nothing here matches what I pictured before leaving. I will come home burned brown, worn out, and probably changed more than a little.

units: the walker set out alone to clear his head

he would do it again with better gear
text: So what got into you, heading out alone onto that plateau? Short answer: I wanted to walk until my head had emptied itself out. Did the start go smoothly? Not even close. I missed the first bus of the day, sat under a metal shelter for half the morning, and ended up crossing the plain in whatever pickup would slow down and stop for me. And where did you sleep? Behind a dike, out of the wind, with a tarp strung between two posts. Rough night? Freezing, yes, though the sky was so clear that I gave up on sleeping and just lay there looking at it. And the way back? That is where it fell apart. A storm turned the track to running mud, and I had to backtrack the whole way to the village. Would you do it over? In a heartbeat, but with a real tent and boots that can hold their grip on loose stone.

units: the keeper of a mountain shelter describes the collapse of a path
the rain fell without a break and the stream swelled
a slope stripped of its trees no longer soaked up the water
the bank slid away after a sound of breaking
a small group of hikers stayed trapped above the break
the rescuers reached them by way of the ridge line
the hikers were guided along a narrow steep ledge
no casualty was reported
the footbridge is destroyed for good
local officials are considering a new route higher up
text: The keeper of a high-valley shelter tells the story of the night the trail gave way. "The rain came down without a break, and the stream doubled in size," he says. The cause is easy enough to trace, and he traces it himself. A slope stripped of its trees held nothing back, so the water ran straight off it and onto the path below. "We heard something crack, and then the whole bank slid off," he goes on. The effect was immediate. A handful of hikers found themselves stuck above the break, with no way down and nowhere else to turn. A rescue team came at them along the ridge and walked them out on a narrow, steep ledge. "Nobody was hurt, but the footbridge is gone for good," he adds. Valley officials are already studying a replacement route, higher up and clear of the channel the water carved.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: crossing a mountain range was once a risky undertaking
trains of pack animals took to snow-filled gorges
even experienced guides lost their bearings
the difficulty came from the lack of visible landmarks
fog wiped out the shapes of the land
the piles of stones were knocked over by the wind
the wooden poles driven in rotted with the damp
people ended up cutting marks into the rock face and whitening them
these notches stayed visible despite fresh snow
today's marking systems descend from that invention
text: Crossing a mountain range was once a gamble with poor odds. Pack trains climbed into gorges where snow wiped out the trail, and even seasoned guides lost their bearings between two slopes that looked alike. Distance was never the real problem. The problem was having nothing fixed to steer by once mist swallowed the shapes of the land. People tried piling up stones at intervals, and the wind knocked the piles flat. They tried driving in wooden poles, and the damp rotted them through. The answer came from a modest idea. Cut a notch into the rock face at shoulder height, whiten it with lime, and it stays visible under fresh snow. Drivers could then move from notch to notch without looking up at a sky that told them nothing. Every marking system we rely on now descends from that humble trick.

units: a valley shaped by ice differs from a valley shaped by a river
the glacial valley has a broad flat floor
the walls of a glacial valley are almost vertical
the mass of ice wears down the base as well as the sides
the river valley forms a narrow deep cut
water erodes mainly the line it runs along
the stones carried by the current wear the rock like an abrasive tool
the side valleys of a former glacier arrive in a raised position
the side valleys of a river join the main course at the same height
text: A valley carved by ice and a valley carved by a river look different at first glance. The glacial one has a broad, flat floor and walls that rise almost straight up, because thick, heavy ice grinds the base and the sides alike. The river valley cuts a narrow, deep notch instead. Water works mainly along the line it follows, and the flanks slump in under their own weight. The mechanics explain the contrast. A glacier moves as one solid mass, slow and unrelenting, while a torrent drags pebbles that saw at the rock like a file. Side valleys tell the same story. Those feeding a former glacier arrive high above the main trough, left hanging, and spill down as waterfalls. Those feeding a river join the main channel at the same height. That one detail often settles the question in unfamiliar country.

units: the narrator reports a crossing he remembers precisely
the landscape was stony and had no tall plants
the swells of the ground threw off the sense of distance
the march counted seven stages begun before sunrise
a halt took place in the shade through the worst of the heat
the water came from built cisterns the guides could find again
the food came down to hard flatbread and a reserve of salt
a strap snapped and one of the party hurt his foot
a train of traders was coming the other way and reported a blocked well
the narrator concludes that bare ground holds many readable signs
text: I ought to set down a crossing I remember clearly, and take its aspects one at a time. The setting: a desert of stone, bare of any tree, rolling in swells that fooled the eye about distance. The march: seven stages, each begun before sunrise and closed at dusk, with a halt in the shade of a boulder through the worst of the heat. The supplies: water drawn from built cisterns that our guides found again without hesitation, hard flatbread, and a reserve of salt. The mishaps: a strap that snapped, a foot hurt on the stones, a night when the wind flattened our shelter. The encounters, last of all: a train of traders working the same track the other way, whose men warned us of a well that had been filled in. What stays with me is that dryness is not emptiness, and bare ground reads like a crowded page.

units: the bag must be packed the day before departure
you first have to lay all the gear out flat to spot what is missing
the heavy items go against the back halfway up
the rain protection is stowed at the top of the bag
the water supplies are filled before leaving the hamlet
the route must be checked on the map before setting out
you have to find the springs and the steep sections
regular stops serve to air out and dry the feet
the sleeping spot is chosen dry and well away from streams
on waking you have to wipe out the traces of the fire
text: Pack your bag the day before you leave, never at the last minute. Start by laying your gear out flat on the floor. You will see right away what is missing and what weighs too much for what it gives you. Load the heavy things against your back, halfway up, so the weight does not pull you backward. Slide the rain layer in at the very top, where you can grab it fast. In the morning, before you leave the hamlet, fill your bottles and trace the route on the map. Find the springs and mark the steep sections. On the way, stop at regular intervals, pull off your boots, and let your feet dry out. Choose your sleeping spot while the light lasts, on dry ground, well away from streambeds. When you wake up, scatter the stones and wipe out every trace of your fire before you shoulder the bag.

units: the traffic on a plateau path rose after it spread online
the village parking area is full very early
the meadows are used as parking space
the fences give way and the livestock escapes
the widening of the path destroyed the plant cover
rain now digs channels into the slope
the town sets up a shared shuttle
the number of spaces available is now limited
the path closes at the start of the week to let the grass grow back
the shopkeepers protest while the herders approve
text: It was supposed to be a quiet season, and it has turned into a headache for the whole valley. Ever since the plateau path started making the rounds online, the number of walkers has shot up, and the parking area overflows before sunrise. So the meadows get used as parking space, the fences give way, and the herders watch their animals wander off. Naming the cause is easy. Living with what follows is less so. The path has widened under all those boots, the plants that held the soil are gone, and rain now digs little channels down the slope. The town has decided to push back. A shuttle takes the place of cars, the number of spaces is capped, and the path closes at the start of the week to let the grass grow back. Shopkeepers grumble, herders breathe easier, and the valley waits for next season.

units: two different routes lead to the same high crossing point
one of them climbs a steep face whose ground is covered with stones
on that steep route the walkers move up in tight switchbacks
the other route loops around a soft rolling landform
the gentle route runs one and a half times longer than the steep one
its unchanging grade lets a walker hold an even pace
workers record the height, the width and the ground type every season
on the steep way they set wooden steps pinned down with stakes
on the gentle way they cut channels to carry the water off
a heavily loaded walker will take the less steep way
text: Two footpaths converge on the same high pass, yet their layouts have nothing in common. One attacks the steep face directly, across ground buried under loose stone, so walkers climb in tight switchbacks, planting each boot squarely on tilted slabs. The other swings wide around a soft, rolling shoulder of the range. It measures half again as long as the steep line, but its gradient never varies, which allows a steady pace from bottom to summit. Maintenance crews survey both paths every season, recording the rise, the usable width, and the composition of the surface. On the steep line they install wooden steps anchored by stakes. On the gentler one they cut shallow channels along the edge to drain the runoff. Anyone carrying a heavy pack chooses the easier gradient; whoever races the mist to the ridge chooses the other.

units: the writer looks at the reasons that push people to go far away
he counts three motives shared by most travelers
the first is the change of setting, which sharpens attention
the second is the exchange with those who live on the spot
the writer holds conversation above mere looking
the third motive consists in piling up places visited
this piling up is criticized because it turns a site into a catch
the writer advises going more slowly and staying on the spot
he suggests giving up any trace brought home from the journey
text: It is worth asking what exactly we are after when we travel into distant country. Three motives recur among the majority of travelers. The first is the break with familiar scenery: the eye confronts a horizon whose rules it does not know, and that ignorance sharpens attention. The second is the exchange with the people who actually live there, since a conversation with a herder, a fisherman or a weaver counts for more than contemplating endless views. The third, harder to admit, is accumulation: one hoards landscapes the way others stack up printed tokens. This last motive deserves severe scrutiny, because it converts a limpid valley into a trophy and the traveler into a bookkeeper of his own exploits. An ethics of movement would mean slowing down, remaining in place, and surrendering any proof that the journey ever happened.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman described leads walkers in the mountains
her father raised cattle

she came back to her valley with a certificate to guide visitors
she can judge a group's exhaustion from the way it walks
she now trains future guides
she says the only thing she misses from her father's work is the smell of fodder
text: Her father raised cattle, and the high-valley guide spent her childhood in a cluster of houses where the road expired at the last meadow.
