As a small girl she drove the animals along waterlogged tracks and learned to read the sky before the other children did. In her teens she left for a training school, where she studied cartography and the techniques of rescue on broken ground. She returned home holding a certificate and offered her services to walkers passing through. Across roughly ten seasons she led parties up to the ridges and learned to gauge a group's exhaustion from its gait alone. Now she teaches: young guides come to her for slopes, for the choice of resting places, and for the art of announcing that a climb is finished. Of her father's trade she misses only the smell of cut hay.

units: the speaker was let down by a walk along the sea
the leaflet announced a shoreline left in its natural state
the path had in fact been widened to let machines through
a railing runs the whole length of the route
that railing hides the drop and removes the sense of danger
the walker ends up watching the ground instead of the landscape
the gravel surface turns dangerous under a fine rain
the final part of the route becomes narrow and wild again
the speaker finds there the interest he expected from the outing
text: Honestly, that coastal walk thoroughly disappointed me, and it took a while to work out exactly why. The leaflet promised a shoreline preserved in its original state. What you actually walk is a track widened for maintenance machinery, bordered by an unbroken railing. Since that railing conceals the drop, you lose the sense of exposure that makes a clifftop worth anything. So you move quickly, you watch your feet, and nothing remains to fear or to admire. On top of that they spread gravel over the surface, which turns slippery the moment a fine rain begins, forcing you to brake without offering a scrap of satisfaction in return. Only the final stretch redeems the outing. There the path narrows again, a heavy sea hammers the rocks, and you finally get what brought you to this coast.

units: the writer of the message is staying at a mountain inn
the local economy depends on walkers coming through
rainfall brought down a long part of the usual path
bookings were cancelled and the lodging emptied out
a solution was found after three evenings of argument
the women of the place suggested a replacement route on the other flank
a woodworker is building a log bridge over a soaked hollow
the postal employee drew the new route on a public map
the walkers came back the following week
text: I am writing to you from a mountain inn, and I will lay the situation out the way a reporter would. The hamlet lives on the walkers who come through, but heavy rainfall brought down a long stretch of the principal path. The bookings evaporated, the rooms emptied, and the innkeeper talks about a season already lost. A way out emerged over three evenings of argument. The women here proposed opening a replacement route along the shaded flank, longer but perfectly walkable. A carpenter is assembling a bridge of logs above the waterlogged gully. The postman, who knows every shortcut in the district, traced the changed route on a map posted at the entrance to the village. The walkers returned the following week. I leave tomorrow by that very path and I will tell you afterwards what it is worth.

units: the question put sets the seashore against the summits
an old walker answers by asking what one wants from walking
he links flat expanses to the dissolving of the self
he explains that flat country wipes out landmarks
he links the summits to physical hardship
effort at altitude brings the walker back to the feel of his skeleton
he is asked which setting leaves the most lasting mark
he picks the emptiest setting, because it offers little to memorize
he sets that emptiness against a rich valley that scatters into small details
he states that one never finds the place as one left it
text: Should one choose the shoreline or the heights? To that question an old walker responded with another: what do you want from walking? If you want to lose yourself, he said, flat country serves better, because it obliterates landmarks and lets the mind drift beneath a hazy sky. If you want an ordeal, the ridge prevails, since every step exacts payment and the effort restores to the walker an awareness of his own bones. He was asked next which of the two scenes lodges longest in the memory. He chose the barest without hesitating. An open expanse with neither tree nor house is retained precisely because it offers almost nothing to retain, whereas a fertile valley crumbles into countless small details. The last question concerned the return. You never come back, he said, smiling, to the place you left.

units: a rock specialist teaches how to examine a slope before climbing it
a rock that splits into sheets lets water work its way in
that kind of ground turns dangerous after rain
a flank under bushes holds better than a flank with no plants
the roots hold the loose part of the ground in place
a side kept from the sun keeps its water longer
flat surfaces on a slope reveal past slides
a member of the group asks the specialist about gullies that look dry
the answer is that a stony bed fills with water during a downpour
the closing advice is to avoid any steep slope whose way out cannot be seen
text: The rock specialist demonstrated to the group how to read a slope before setting foot on it. He began with the stone itself: wherever it splits into flat sheets, water infiltrates, and the ground turns slippery once rain has fallen. He moved on afterwards to vegetation. A slope under scrub holds together better than a bare bank, because the roots grip the loose upper layer. He added that a flank kept out of the sunlight remains damp long after the rest has dried. Last came the shape of the terrain, and he dwelt on the flat shelves, which betray older landslides. Someone in the group asked whether a gully can be trusted when it appears dry. Not at all, he replied: a stony bed fills up in a single downpour. He finished by advising them to skirt any steep passage whose exit they cannot see.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the high crossings first served practical needs
goods carriers opened the first ways
those ways took up the lines worn in by herds
builders then put up works spanning the watercourses
those works cut several weeks off the journeys
travel stayed limited to traders and letter carriers
scholars later climbed the summits out of pure curiosity
their published accounts created a taste for steep country
the earlier generation found that country ugly
the boring of tunnels did away with the hardship of the crossing
text: Crossing the high passes began as a practical necessity, not a pleasure. The earliest routes were opened by carriers hauling salt and wool, who followed the lines of least effort that grazing herds had already worn into the ground. Then came the bridge builders, capable of throwing an arch above a torrent and cutting half a season off a journey. Travel nonetheless remained the business of merchants and letter carriers. Later, scholars undertook to climb the summits from curiosity alone, loaded with measuring instruments and notebooks, and people took them at first for men who had lost their way. Their accounts, printed and circulated, bred a taste for broken country that the preceding generation had considered hideous. At last transport companies bored through the rock, and the pass ceased to be an ordeal.

units: the clearness of a high lake comes from what the water carries
lowland rivers drag along sediment torn from farmed banks
those fine materials hang in the water and hinder sight
up high the area feeding the lake is short and the rock is hard
so the water tears very little material away
the cold limits the spread of microscopic plants
that scarcity of algae raises the clearness of the water further
a walker sees the stones on the bottom and misjudges the depth
the lack of food keeps animal life scarce and fish growth very slow
work upstream can cloud the water for a whole season
text: The water of a mountain lake looks transparent because of what it carries. Lowland rivers drag along silt torn from cultivated banks, and those fine particles remain suspended in the current and blur whatever you try to see. Higher up, the catchment area feeding the lake is short and the rock is hard, so the water strips almost nothing away. The cold restrains the spread of algae, which sharpens the clarity further still. A walker makes out the pebbles on the bottom and mistakes a genuine depth for an insignificant dip. That clarity comes with a price attached. With so little nourishment in the water, animal life remains scarce and fish put on weight at a crawl. A single work site upstream, stirring the mud of some old deposit, is enough to cloud the whole lake for an entire season.

units: two walkers meant to cross a flat wind-exposed expanse without a stop
they had set out with little gear
a thick veil of vapour came down halfway across
the way was marked by small piles of stones
those markers became invisible
one of the two proposed pushing on by guesswork
the narrator refused because of the holes where one can get hurt
they worked out a way of moving where one waits while the other scouts
the one moving ahead calls out as soon as he spots the next marker
the veil lifted near a grassy hollow, close to the shelter
text: We had it in our heads to cross the windswept plateau in a single push, light packs, map folded into a pocket. Bad calculation. Halfway over, the fog dropped without warning and the trail, marked by modest heaps of stones, vanished. My companion wanted to continue by guesswork. I refused, because a plateau like that is pitted with cavities where you snap a bone in your foot. So we devised a method. One of us stayed motionless beside the last visible marker while the other advanced straight ahead to the limit of visibility, shouting continuously. The instant he spotted the next heap, he called, and his partner joined him. We progressed that way, relay after relay, the whole afternoon. The fog lifted at the lip of a grassy hollow, and the shelter stood there, within earshot.

units: a living culture forms from flour and water left open to the air
yeasts present in the atmosphere settle into the mixture
the baker removes a portion and tops it up with fresh flour at regular intervals
after a week the culture becomes steady
a sour smell signals that the culture can be used
the flour is sifted before the warm liquid goes in
the dough is folded over on itself between two rest periods
the fierce heat of the oven sets the structure and colors the outside
the resulting bread keeps for a week without drying out
text: A starter begins with nothing more than flour, water, and the open air of the room. Give it two or three nights and wild yeasts drift in out of that air, settle into the paste, and puff it up. From then on the baker feeds the culture on a schedule: scoop out part of what sits in the jar, stir in a measure of fresh flour, and wait. By the end of the first week the culture holds steady and gives off a sharp, sour smell, and that smell is the signal that it can raise a full dough. Sift the flour, pour in warm water, work the starter through with a spatula, and knead until the mass turns soft and supple. Let it rest, fold it over on itself, let it rest again. A blistering oven sets the crumb and browns the outside. The method asks for patience. What it returns is a dense, fragrant loaf that keeps a week without drying out.

units: a worker at an inn leaves her pot on weak embers before going to bed
she had meant to take it off before sunrise
tiredness keeps her from coming back at the planned hour
the liquid drops by half and the meat falls apart into strands
the cook skims the surface and then tastes the dish
the sauce turns out thick and slightly sweet
the low prolonged heat has changed the tissue of the meat
the customers ask for the same dish the next day
the cook repeats the accident on purpose every evening
text: A cook at a roadside inn set her heavy pot over dying embers and went up to bed, certain she would lift it off before sunrise. She slept through instead. When she came back down, the broth had boiled away by half and the meat had fallen apart into strands. She skimmed the surface, expecting to find ruin, and tasted from the edge of the ladle. What she found was thick, dark, and faintly sweet. Because the heat had stayed so low for so long, the tough tissue had melted instead of tightening. The travelers sitting at her tables asked for the same dish the following day. She could not explain the accident, so she chose to repeat it on purpose: every evening she banked the fire down and left the pot alone until morning. A recipe born of forgetfulness made the name of the house.

units: lumps form in a sauce while it cooks
the pan has to come off the heat source at once
leaving the sauce on the heat gives a scorched taste
adding a cold liquid and then whisking hard dissolves most of the lumps
the shift in temperature makes the lumps give way
a fine strainer catches the pieces that remain
the leftover bits are crushed with the back of a hollow utensil
the mixture then goes back over a low flame with constant stirring
stirring the flour into cold liquid prevents the trouble next time
text: Lumps showing up in your sauce while it cooks? Nothing is lost yet. Pull the pan off the burner right away, because leaving it there lets the flour stick to the bottom and pick up a scorched taste. Splash in a little cold water and whisk hard, right there in the pan. That jolt in temperature breaks most of the lumps apart. If a few stubborn ones hang on, tip the whole thing through a fine strainer and press the stubborn bits against the mesh with the back of a ladle. Then set it over a low flame again and keep stirring without a pause, circling out to the sides of the pan so nothing catches. Next time, stir your flour into a cold liquid before it ever meets the heat, and none of this happens. A smooth sauce comes down to that one habit, not to some knack nobody taught you. Keep the whisk where you can grab it.

units: two cooking counters face each other in a covered hall
the first counter cooks everything by plunging it into hot fat
the line at the first counter moves quickly
the second counter has been simmering its dishes since early morning
customers in a hurry choose the fast cooking
the prices at the two counters are close
their spending goes to different things
the woman in charge of the place notices that the traffic flips over the course of the week
neither counter tries to copy the other
text: Inside a covered market hall, two cooking counters face each other across the aisle and argue, without saying a word, about method. On one side everything goes down into hot fat: the heat seals the outside in a matter of seconds, and the line never stops moving. On the other, a cook has had pots simmering since the morning opened, and her service runs at a slower pace. Customers in a hurry pick the fryer, and those who sit down to eat pick the pot. The prices on the two boards land close together, though the two spend on different things, one burning through oil, the other through hours of fuel. The woman who runs the hall notices the traffic flip as the week goes on, quick early, patient by the end. Neither counter shows any interest in copying its neighbor, and the quiet rivalry keeps the hall full.

units: the goods on the stall are sorted by shade
the first group gathers dried roots and barks
the red goods give off a smell that catches at the throat
the green goods sit at the back of the stall
a stone vessel takes up the middle of the stall
the inside of the vessel is stained by past mixtures
a worn grating tool is kept for hard dried fruits
the seller refuses to sell goods already reduced to powder
he claims that powder loses its fragrance within one season
text: At the spice seller's stall the goods are laid out and sorted by shade. The ochres come first: dried roots, curls of bark, powders that smell of resin and warm wood. The reds sit next to them, harsher, sharp enough to catch at the back of your throat when you reach across the table. The greens fill the back, crumpled leaves, seeds no bigger than grit, stems tied into tight bundles. A stone mortar holds the middle of the table, its pestle leaning, its inner wall stained by mixtures long since sold. Beside it lies a worn grater kept for the hard dried nuts, which the seller will not hand over already ground. Powder goes flat within a single season, he says, while the whole seed keeps its soul. Behind him, cloth sacks slump open on brown treasures nobody knows the names of, and nobody ever asks for.

units: cooking once rested on the senses of the cook
measuring probes changed the nature of the trade
each food can now be given a set band of heat
baths of regulated heat appeared afterward
food sealed away from the air never goes past the target value
the writer judges this change a good one
opponents read it as a loss of feel
the writer holds that the instrument rules out crude error without dictating taste
what the writer fears most is the sameness of the results
text: For generations cooking ran on the senses alone: a palm held over the coals, an ear tuned to the sizzle, an eye on the color of the crust. Then the measuring probe arrived, and the trade turned into something else altogether. A cook could now assign each piece of food a narrow band of heat and hold to it without drifting. The same logic went further with baths of regulated heat, where food sealed away from the air never climbs past its target. I take that shift for progress, whatever is said by those who read it as a loss of feel. Measuring does not forbid tasting. The instrument rules out the crude failure; it has nothing to say about seasoning. What worries me sits elsewhere, in the pull toward sameness. A flawless result repeated without variation turns into a flawless kind of boredom.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the pastry cook comes from a line of millers
her father sorted grain in front of her during her childhood
she could tell one grind from another by touch before she could read a recipe
this early familiarity shaped her choice of trade
she started as an apprentice in a neighborhood workshop
the night hours built up her stamina
a wrist injury pulled her away from kneading
that setback led her toward light preparations
she puts her flour through the sieve twice to get her layered pastry
she refuses to expand her house after a mention in a trade journal
text: The pastry cook at a guest house comes from a long line of millers, and flour has never once been an abstraction to her. Her father sorted grain in front of her when she was small, so she could tell one grind from another by touch before she could read a recipe. That early ease settled her choice of trade. She started out as an apprentice in a neighborhood bakehouse, where the night hours built up her stamina. A wrist injury pulled her away from the kneading bench, and the setback pushed her toward the lighter work of fine doughs. There she found her signature: pale layered pastry whose lift comes from flour put through the sieve twice. Her own apprentices remember one rule above the rest, weigh the gesture instead of rushing it. Since a trade journal named her house, she has refused to grow.

units: the room pleases the visitor right away
the menu offers a narrow choice
the vegetables come out lukewarm although their dish was meant to keep them hot
the reviewer works out that the plates waited under a heat source
the cooking of the main course is correct
the sauce has broken because it was mounted too early
the fault lies with the layout and not with the skills
moving the pass closer to the stove would remove the wait
sending out fewer plates at a time would improve the service
the dessert made to order arrives flawless
text: The room wins you over at once, and the menu is short, which usually promises a kitchen that knows its own mind. Trouble arrives with the first course. The vegetables come out lukewarm in a cast-iron dish that should have kept them scalding hot, and you can tell the plates waited a while under a lamp. The main course confirms the weakness: the cooking is judged well, but the sauce was mounted too early and has already broken on the plate. The fault is not talent, it is layout. Move the pass closer to the stove, send out fewer plates at a time, and the wait that spoils the kitchen's own work would disappear. Dessert proves the point. Made to order, it lands clean, tight, exact. A house capable of that should not let the start of a meal go cold. We will come back, after calling ahead.

units: the reader had asked whether the writer eats better since moving
the writer finds the food different without finding it better
her aunt cooked everything in a single pot
she used the leftovers of the day before in a broth
the roommate gives every ingredient its own utensil
at the aunt's place the helpings were generous and hot
proportions were never argued about there
in the current place people taste and adjust before serving
the writer misses the smell that used to fill the hallway
the writer invites the reader to come and judge for himself
text: You asked me whether I eat any better since the move. Honestly, it is different, not better. My aunt cooked everything out of one pot, and whatever was left from the day before went into a broth and came back as dinner. My roommate works the opposite way around: every ingredient gets its own pan, its own timer, its own seasoning. At her place the food came hot and there was plenty of it, and nobody ever argued about proportions or put a thing on a scale. Here we taste, we adjust, we start over, and supper lands late. I like both, for reasons that cancel each other out. One fed me, the other entertains me. What I miss is the smell that filled the hallway the second I opened her door. This place smells clean. Come over some evening and judge for yourself. We will pick the menu together at the cupboard.

units: the woman in charge of a preserving workshop answers questions about common mistakes
she holds that the quality of the seal counts for more than the thickness of the glass
a seal used a second time often fails as things cool
the liquid has to cover the jars completely during the heat treatment
the top of the contents spoils with no visible sign if it stands clear
she recalls that salt preserves but hides the flaws of poor produce
the foam that appears on fermenting vegetables is no sign of failure
that foam comes with the start of the process
she refuses to state a general rule about how long things keep
text: We put the most common mistakes to the woman who runs a preserving workshop. On the jars themselves, she says the seal matters more than the thickness of the glass, and that a seal used a second time tends to fail as the jar cools. On heat processing she is firm: the water has to cover the jars completely, or the top of the contents spoils with nothing visible to show for it. On salt she draws a line, since it preserves but also hides the flaws of poor produce. Her answer on fermented vegetables surprises us. The foam that rises is no sign of failure, it comes with the start of the process. On how long a jar keeps, she will give no general rule at all, and sends us back to the smell, to the sound of the lid, to the look of the liquid. An attentive keeper's nose, she says, beats any label.

units: an experienced cook takes his apprentice to task over the state of his cutting tool
the dull blade bruises the herbs instead of slicing them
the crushed leaves give up their sap too early
the color of the dish turns dull as a result
the aroma of the dish is weakened as a result
the apprentice claims he sharpened the tool the day before
the fault comes from an angle badly held during sharpening
the superior asks for the operation to be done again in front of him
text: The head cook took his apprentice aside and told him the chopping blade had gone dull. Instead of slicing through the herbs, he said, it was bruising them. Crushed leaves surrender their sap too soon, the dish loses its bright color, and the aroma thins to almost nothing. The apprentice protested that he had put the blade to the stone only the day before. His superior lifted the metal edge against the window light and showed him the rounded edge. The angle had wandered during sharpening, and the apprentice never noticed. You could read the whole story on the plate, the cook said: a brown sauce where a vivid one belonged. Discipline at the sharpening stone decides the final flavor. Then he told the apprentice to sharpen the blade again, there and then, under his own supervision.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: meat from animals killed before the cold season spoiled very quickly
with no artificial cold, rural households faced shortage
salt supplied the first remedy for this problem
a heavily concentrated salt solution pulls the water out of the tissue
this drying out stops micro-organisms from multiplying
aromatics were later added to the preserving bath
preserving thus became a way of seasoning as well
smoking added a protective layer at the surface
these methods passed on from one person to the next through direct apprenticeship
text: Meat from animals killed ahead of the cold season used to spoil within days. With no artificial cold to lean on, a farming household could watch its whole store turn and then face an empty winter. Salt offered the first way out. Cooks noticed that a heavy brine pulled the water out of the tissue, and that once the water was gone the micro-organisms had nothing left to multiply in. The method grew more refined. Aromatic berries, dried peel and bitter roots went into the bath, so that keeping food and seasoning it became one and the same operation. Smoking rounded off the work, laying a protective film across the exposed surface. All of it traveled from one valley to the next by direct apprenticeship, hand to hand, and it reshaped what people ate wherever regular trade never reached.

units: the difference between the two doughs lies in their microbial population
a starter brings together wild ferments and acid-making bacteria
the yeast sold in packets holds only one selected species
starter dough gives a crumb with uneven holes
yeast dough gives a more even and more neutral crumb
fermentation with a starter calls for an overnight wait
fermentation with yeast finishes far sooner
the outer crust of the starter loaf browns more deeply
the acids thrown off during fermentation feed the browning reactions
text: So what really separates a sourdough loaf from one raised with packet yeast? It comes down to who is living in the dough. A starter carries a whole crowd of wild ferments along with acid-making bacteria, while the packet holds a single species, picked out and grown on purpose. You taste that difference in the crumb. Sourdough leaves you ragged, uneven holes, a soft tang, a smell that lands somewhere near toasted nuts. Yeast gives you something tidier, more even, frankly more neutral. The waiting is not the same either. A starter wants a whole night to do its work, and yeast is finished in a fraction of that. The crust browns deeper on the sourdough loaf too, because the acids thrown off during fermentation feed the browning reactions. Pick whichever suits you: patience, or speed.

units: a power cut struck a kitchen crew during a banquet
the ovens stopped while poultry was half cooked
the refrigerated units stopped holding the cold
the darkness forced the brigade to work under hand lamps
a backup gas burner served to finish the meats
tubs of crushed ice took over from the refrigerated cabinets
a station head improvised a faster service
the guests never noticed the incident
text: A power cut caught a kitchen crew in the middle of a banquet service, and the story they tell about it afterward is worth repeating. Three problems landed at once. The convection ovens died with the poultry still half done. The cold rooms stopped holding temperature, putting every cream and every mousse at risk. And the dark drove the brigade to work under hand lamps propped up on the shelves. The answer came from three things they happened to have. A backup gas burner finished the meats in a barely trembling broth. Tubs of crushed ice stood in for the refrigerated cabinets. A station head rewrote the order of service on the spot, sending plates out one at a time, faster than planned. The guests, management insists, never caught a hint of the panic behind the swinging door.

units: you have to choose a fired clay vessel with a firm handle
the lid must close without leaving a gap
the aromatic bath is prepared the evening before
the meat is laid piece by piece into that bath
the resting happens overnight in a cool place
the liquid darkens and the flesh dulls during the wait
the meat is then seared over a hot flame
the strained liquid serves to moisten the cooking
the covered cooking goes on beside the hearth
the meat is ready when a fork slides in without effort
text: Begin with a vessel of fired clay, one with a firm handle and a lid that settles without leaving the smallest gap. The evening before, pour in the bath: a scented oil, a mild vinegar, a handful of leaves crumpled between your fingers. Lay the pieces of meat down one by one, the way you would set stones into a low wall. Let the night do its patient work somewhere cool and dark. In the morning, uncover the vessel. The liquid will have darkened, and the flesh will have taken on a duller shade. Sear it over a hot flame, then moisten it with the strained bath. Cover the pot again and forget it beside the hearth for a long afternoon. Serve when a fork slides into the meat without meeting the least resistance, and when the thickened sauce coats the back of a spoon in a glossy film.

units: a cooperative workshop reports a rise in rejected products
the line concerned packs soups
the cooling that follows heat treatment starts too late
the product stays in a temperature band that suits resistant spores
this exposure makes the seals bulge
a sourness becomes noticeable in the product
fouling of the plate heat exchanger lowers the heat transfer
chemical cleaning scheduled too far apart is blamed
management plans an extra wash cycle
probes will be fitted at the mouth of the tunnel
text: Technical management at a cooperative processing workshop reports a steady rise in rejects on the line that packs soups. The analysis points to a single cause. Cooling after pasteurization starts with a measurable delay, which leaves the product sitting in a temperature band where resistant spores thrive. Hold it there long enough and the lids bulge, while a sourness comes through on tasting. Suspicion falls squarely on the plate heat exchanger. Fouling builds up and drags down the transfer coefficient, and with chemical cleaning scheduled too far apart, the flow of chilled water no longer makes up the loss. Managers have announced an extra wash cycle, along with probes fitted at the mouth of the tunnel. A check on how the vats close will round out the package of measures.

units: the ripening room sits in a cellar under a stone vault
the cheeses rest on boards of resinous wood
the humidity falls whenever the entrance stands open
the surface of the cheeses hardens because of this drying
a shallow basin of water was set along a cold wall
evaporation from this basin makes up the loss of humidity
the wooden door was replaced by a soft-closing leaf
a hanging gauge warns the team before the critical threshold
text: The ripening room lies in the cellar of an old building, under a vault of gray stone. Spruce boards hold the wheels, sorted by size, and the air smells of hazelnut and damp straw. One difficulty threatens the place. Whenever the entrance stands open, the humidity falls away, and the rind hardens at the surface until ripening stalls underneath. The cellarmen settled on two practical measures of their own. Along the coldest wall they set a shallow basin of water, whose evaporation makes up what the room loses. They also took out the old wooden door and hung a leaf that closes softly, fitted with a low handle you can work with an elbow. A gauge hangs from the vault now and warns the team before the critical threshold is crossed, and the wheels nearest the entrance are turned more often.

units: the defense of cooking at home often rests on sentimental attachment
the writer suggests comparing two meals of equal worth
the meal cooked at home costs little in raw ingredients
how much salt goes in depends on whoever does the seasoning
this meal demands someone stay watchful at the stove
the factory dish hands back a whole evening
the factory dish keeps without any special care
the factory dish imposes a fixed recipe and additives the eater puts up with
the decisive gap is about control, not about taste or price
text: Standing up for home cooking against factory meals usually starts as a matter of sentiment, and the argument deserves a cooler look. Set two comparable meals side by side. The first comes out of a family pot. It costs little in raw ingredients, its salt depends entirely on the hand doing the seasoning, and it demands that somebody stay watchful at the stove. The second comes out of a sealed tray. It hands back a whole evening, it keeps without any special care, but it locks in a fixed recipe and a list of additives the eater never chose. The gap that matters is not taste, and it is not price. It is control. Cooking for yourself means keeping a say in what goes down your throat. That freedom is paid for in attention, and each of us can judge whether the trade is worth it.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the pastry cook reaches her workshop before sunrise
she grates the colored part of the peel straight over the dough
she keeps the candied rind in jars
her dented mold came down to her from her mother
she keeps her scoring knife on her at all times
she turns away any machine she could not take apart herself
she trains one apprentice every season
she hands the baking over to her apprentices very early
she says she listens to the dough instead of imposing her will on it
text: You have to see her push open the workshop door before the sun is up, apron tied high, sleeves shoved back to the elbow. The pastry cook down the street has three loves, and she will tell you about all of them. Citrus first. She grates the colored part of the peel straight over the dough so the scented oil falls where it belongs, and she keeps the candied rind in jars lined up along a shelf. Then old tools. Her dented mold came down from her mother, her scoring knife never leaves her pocket, and she turns away any machine she could not take apart herself. Then apprentices. She trains one every season, with no complicated paperwork, and she hands them the baking early. Ask her for a secret and she shrugs her shoulders: she listens to the dough instead of laying down the law to it.

units: the plain look of the room gave no hint of the quality of the meal
the first course is a clarified broth of root vegetables
that broth is striking for its depth despite being clear
the second course pairs a crisp-skinned fish with a purée of bitter herbs
the cooking of the fish is judged remarkably precise
the main course disappoints because the sauce is reduced too far
the meat in that dish was of good quality all the same
the dessert puts the whole meal back on its feet
the dessert pairs an ice cream scented with peel and a crisp tile
the service is described as quiet and sure
text: Nothing about the plain room, as you come through the door, prepares you for how carefully the meal climbs. The first course arrives without a word: a broth of root vegetables, clarified, nearly clear, and startling in its depth. A piece of fish follows, skin crisp, set on a purée of bitter herbs, cooked to the second and worth every word of praise. The main course lets things down. The sauce has been reduced too far, and it flattens a cut of meat that deserved better while burying the aromatics with it. Dessert puts the evening back on its feet: an ice cream scented with bitter peel, on a thin tile that cracks under the spoon. Portions stay modest, which keeps the whole meal light and lets the dessert land. The service, quiet and sure, follows the rise without ever getting ahead of it.

units: the writer of the message is taking a pastry course
the mixture swells properly while it rests
the mixture collapses once it goes into the oven
the writer says she followed the given instructions to the letter
the writer tried a different leavening agent
an experienced acquaintance offers an explanation
that explanation blames the fault on too much handling
the neighbor advises cutting the last rise short
the writer asks for a meeting before changing her method
text: I am writing about the pastry course you run in the shared hall. Since I signed up, one problem has defeated me and I cannot sort it out on my own. My dough swells beautifully while it rests, then sinks the moment it goes into the oven. I have followed your instructions to the letter. I weighed every ingredient. I even switched to a different leavening agent. A neighbor of mine, who has kneaded bread since she was a girl, offered an explanation of her own. The dough gets worked too hard, she says, and the structure holding it up eventually gives way. She suggests I knead with a lighter hand and cut the second rise short. Before I try anything, I would value your judgment, since nobody knows the ovens in that hall as well as you do. If you could spare me a few minutes after the next session, I would be truly grateful.

units: the text sets two ways of cooking fish against each other
cooking over coals dries the surface and colors it
steaming keeps the moisture in the flesh
coals add a smoky aroma that the other method lacks
steam lets the clean smell of the product come through
cooking on a grill calls for a thin film of fat
cooking under a lid needs no fat at all
firm flesh suits fierce heat better
delicate flesh falls apart and has to be watched closely
text: Should a fish go over hot coals or into steam? The gap between the two is narrower than people assume, though the results never match. Coals dry the outside and color it, and they drive the juices deep into the flesh. Steam works the other way around, plumping the fibers and holding the moisture exactly where it started. What about flavor? Charcoal leaves a smoky note that steam will never produce, while steam lets the clean smell of the fish come through unmasked, with nothing laid over it. And fat? A grill wants a thin film of it, or the skin welds itself to the bars. Cooking under a lid wants none at all. So which one? Whichever suits the piece in front of you. Firm flesh takes the hard heat and comes off whole. Delicate flesh falls apart above boiling water and has to be watched closely from the first minute to the last.

units: a vegetable seller gives advice on cutting
he says the cut changes with the plant
onion has to be sliced into thin strips so that it melts
herbs are cut fine without being crushed
garlic is reduced almost to a paste so that it spreads better
carrot is prepared either in shreds or in even cubes
he warns against anything in between for that vegetable
he warns that a dull blade damages the vegetables
he advises putting an edge on the blade before a long session
text: The vegetable seller looked up from his stall last night and told me that nobody cuts everything the same way. That, he reckons, is where most people go wrong before they even light the stove. Onion has to be sliced into thin strips, thin enough to see through, or it will never melt down in the pan. Herbs you snip with the tip of the blade, never crushing them, since crushed leaves go dark and lose their smell. Garlic he likes chopped almost to a paste, because it spreads right through a sauce that way. And carrot? He laughed at that one. Shred it, or cut it into even cubes, but nothing in between. Then he handed me my change with one last piece of advice. A dull blade bruises vegetables far worse than a clumsy hand, so put an edge on it before any long session of chopping, on a wet stone, and never in a rush.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: keeping food comes before the arrival of artificial cold
drying in the air was the first technique
salt pulls the water out of flesh and halts decay
smoke above a fire makes meat keep longer
smoked meat takes on a harsh taste
traveling sellers spread these stores along long roads
kitchens far apart took up identical methods
sinking meat in melted fat seals it away from the air
these methods survive in the recipes of today
text: Long before artificial cold, keeping food edible meant a running fight against damp and rot. The earliest cooks hung their catch out in the moving air and let the wind dry it through. Later they learned that salt pulls the water out of flesh and halts decay before it starts. Then came smoke. A cut of meat left hanging above a fire took on a harsh taste and kept for whole seasons afterward. Traveling sellers carried such stores along longer and longer roads, until kitchens that had never met were working by identical methods. Later still, cooked meat sunk in melted fat sat sealed away from the air. Every step pushed back the day a food would spoil, and every one of them left a mark in the recipes we still use, repeated by cooks who never stop to wonder where the habit came from.

units: a pale foam appears on the surface of a liquid as it cooks
that foam comes from proteins released by the heat
the released particles are too light to sink back
the bubbles carry these particles upward
leaving that foam clouds the broth
a clouded broth turns gray and tastes heavier
the cook lifts it away with a ladle again and again
beating an egg white stretches the same proteins
the net that forms holds the air
a trace of salt weakens the bonds and makes the foam firmer
text: When water shivers in the pot, a pale foam climbs to the surface and clings to the sides of it. That is scum, made of the proteins the heat has driven out of the food. It rises because cooking loosens the fibers and frees particles too light to sink again, and the bubbles carry them up with them. Leave it there and it falls back into the broth and clouds it. The liquid turns gray, the taste grows heavy and dull. So a careful cook lifts it away with a ladle, patiently, as often as it forms again. Something very close to this happens under a whisk in a bowl of egg white. The beating stretches those same proteins into a supple net that traps the air. A trace of salt hurries the change along, because it weakens the bonds and lets the foam set sooner, firmer and far steadier under the spoon.

units: a fish stock had a metallic bitterness
the cook first suspected an acid ingredient and then his pot
he went back through every step of his preparation
the carcasses had boiled far too long
a short infusion without a rolling boil is what is needed
a long extraction releases sulfur compounds
the gelatin breaks down past that limit
he now rinses the carcasses and takes out the gills
he keeps the pot below boiling point
the stocks he gets are clear and free of bitterness
text: It began with a fish stock that gave off a bitter, metallic edge, the day before a service in a staff canteen. The cook blamed the vinegar first, then the pot he had used, before he walked back through his own recipe step by step. The fault lay in the bones. He had let them boil for close to an hour, when a carcass takes only a short infusion that barely trembles. Past that point the bones give up sulfur compounds and the gelatin breaks down. So he rewrote his method. He now rinses the bones in cold water, pulls out the gills, heats the pot without ever letting it reach a boil, and stops the extraction before the liquid can bubble. He strains it through fine cloth. His stocks come out clear since that correction, the bitter note is gone, and his team reports no further fault.

units: the recipe offers two tools for grinding herbs
the leaves have to be washed dried and stripped of their stems
with the mortar the salt and garlic are crushed first
the leaves go in a little at a time and are not pounded
the mortar gives a thicker and more fragrant texture
the color holds better by that route
the electric machine is used in short pulses
the bowl has to be chilled so the heat does not cook the herbs
the oil is poured in a thin stream at the end
a dry cheese may be added in fine shreds
text: Before making an herb paste, decide between the mortar and the electric machine, because the two of them do not give the same texture at all. Begin by washing the leaves, drying them thoroughly, and stripping away the tough stems. If you choose the mortar, crush the salt with the garlic first, add the leaves a handful at a time, and turn the pestle rather than pound with it. The paste will come out thicker and more fragrant, and its color will hold better. If you prefer the electric bowl, work in short pulses and chill the bowl beforehand, or the heat of the blades will cook the leaves and dull the whole thing. Either way, pour the oil in a thin stream right at the end. You may then grate a dry cheese over the top and fold it in with a fork, lightly, until the paste is even throughout.

units: a covered market has opened again after renovation work
the hall takes its light through the roof
the vegetable stalls now hold the middle of the space
the fishmongers aisle has cooling that needs no ice
part of the building is set aside for producers who transform food
a baker shapes his dough in front of the customers
a shared kitchen is offered for rent by the hour
the traders approve of the ventilation and the drainage
those two faults used to force repeated closures
future rents worry the sellers because the amount is not known
text: The covered market in the northern district opened again this week, after a refit that ran for the better part of a season. Visitors step first into a hall lit from the roof, where the vegetable stalls now hold the middle ground. Beyond them runs the fishmongers aisle, cooled by a quiet system that has replaced the trays of melting ice. A third of the building has gone to producers who work on site: a baker shaping dough in front of the customers, a seasonal cannery, a cutting room. Management also announces a shared kitchen, rented by the hour, open to caterers with no premises of their own. Traders questioned there praise the ventilation and the drainage, two faults that used to force repeated closures. What worries them is the rent, whose final figure has yet to be announced.

units: steam makes it impossible to see on entering the room
the fat melts in the bottom of the pot
the pieces of meat start to brown along their edges
a caramel smell signals that liquid has to go in
the stuck juices are scraped loose and the flame is lowered
a fragrant steam escapes from under the lid
that smell travels as far as the hallway
the sauce darkens and coats the spoon
the meat gives without any effort
the heat is turned off and the smell lingers in the house
text: You walk into the kitchen and you can barely see a thing, because the steam has covered everything in sight. At first the pot says nothing. It heats, the fat melts down in the bottom, and the pieces of meat start to brown along their edges. A little later there is a burnt sugar smell in the air, and that is your signal. Pour in the liquid, scrape the stuck juices loose, drop the flame. After that everything slows. The lid shakes, one bubble breaks, another follows, and a thick fragrant steam escapes through the gap and drifts out into the hallway. Toward the end the sauce has darkened and coats the spoon, and the meat gives under the fork without any push at all. You taste, you fix the salt, you add a turn of pepper. Then you kill the heat, and the smell keeps hold of the whole house.

units: the writer refuses to treat home cooking as an optional pastime
where handing the skills down disappears industrial food takes the place
the consequences show up later at the doctors
with no adult to pass it on the child never handles a blade
the child does not learn to judge when something is cooked
grown up he buys dishes to reheat
spending on food goes up
the range of foods narrows
added sugar becomes the reference flavor
the writer judges that the cost at school would be offset by savings on care
text: We should stop treating home cooking as an optional pastime. Where the handing down of these skills fades, industrial food fills the gap, and the results turn up later in the doctors surgeries. The chain is almost mechanical. With no adult to pass on the order of operations, a child never handles a blade, never tastes a dish while it is still cooking, and never learns to judge when something is done. Grown and on his own, he buys what can be reheated, because that is the only route he controls. Spending on food climbs, variety collapses, and added sugar becomes the flavor everything else is measured against. Making such workshops compulsory at school would cost a great deal, and nobody denies it. But the savings on long term care would outrun the bill, and the generation after would win back an independence it had lost.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman described runs the kitchen of a country inn
she started out on a very cramped cooking station
at first she followed written instructions to the letter
she weighed every ingredient and was afraid of getting things wrong
she now trusts her palate rather than a timer
she has given up fierce heat and prefers a very gentle simmer
her old way of cooking leaned on an abundance of spices
her current way of cooking leans on the worth of the raw ingredient
she passes this change on to the beginners she trains regularly
she holds that mastering the hands comes before mastering the wait
text: The woman who runs the kitchen at a country inn learned her trade on a cooking station barely wider than her shoulders. Back then she read recipes line by line, weighed out every ingredient, and lived in fear of getting something wrong. These days she tastes, adjusts, and lets a pot sit without once glancing at a timer, since her own tongue tells her sooner than any clock would. Heat used to be her tool for speed; now she wants the barest tremble on the surface, because a slow simmer draws out flavor that a hard boil tears apart. Her old cooking leaned on a heavy hand with spices. Her cooking now leans on what the ingredient itself is worth. She hands that shift to the beginners who come through her kitchen each season, telling them the same thing every time: waiting is harder to learn than the work of the hands.

units: the place described sits beside a waterway
the staff put down the dishes quietly and without explanation
the list of dishes is short and fits on a single sheet
that list shifts with what comes in
the shortness of the offering suggests nothing is kept in store for long
the cooking methods are of uneven quality
the fish is right on the surface and right inside
the root vegetables are spoiled by a sauce that weighs too much
the last sweet dish rescues the impression left by the vegetables
the closing verdict urges a visit despite too much sauce
text: Three things stand out in this dining room set beside a canal. Start with the service, spare to the point of silence: plates come down quietly, set in front of you without a word, and nobody offers to tell you what is on them. Then the menu, a single sheet that shifts with whatever comes in from the growers, listing so few dishes that clearly nothing sits waiting in a cold room. Last, the cooking, which is where the kitchen wobbles. Fish comes off the pan with crisp skin and flesh that holds together, while the roots beneath it drown in a thick sauce that blurs every edge. Dessert wins the argument back and rights what the roots had spoiled: a smooth cream, barely sweet, with fruit poached in its own juice. Worth the trip, then, as long as you accept that sauce here sometimes takes up more room than it ought to.

units: the writer of the message tells about a cooking attempt from the evening before
he browned sliced bulbs in a wide flat pan
he stirred without stopping so the fat would not turn black
he then added pulses and water
the pot cooked slowly while he cleaned up
the first taste had no flavor at all
he set the seasoning right with a sour fruit and crushed seeds
he covered the dish with a tart milk product
someone from the same building took three helpings
the writer admits he made the dish up with no model to follow
text: You will never guess what came out of my tiny kitchen last night. Onions went into a wide pan first, sliced thin, and I stood over them the whole time, stirring, because the fat was one moment away from turning black. In went the lentils, then cold water, and the pot ticked along on a low flame while I dealt with the washing up. A taste later: nothing. Flat as paper. So I squeezed in citrus juice, crushed a pinch of seeds over the top, and the whole thing woke up at once. I poured off the extra liquid, spooned soured milk across the surface, and carried it to the table with no faith in it at all. A neighbor from two doors along, asked over at the last minute, went back for a third helping and wanted to know how it was made. I owned up: there was no recipe behind any of it, and I had made the whole thing up as I went.

units: the text explains where the golden shade of a bread crust comes from
the color arises from a meeting between sugars and matter bearing nitrogen
very dry air sets that meeting going
a pale surface points to an oven that is not hot enough
too much water in the dough holds the color back as well
damp keeps the surface from reaching the temperature it needs
heat pushed too far turns the sugars black
that drift brings a bitter taste
a very dark crust is not necessarily a fault
one and the same change yields pleasant scents and burnt ones
text: What turns a crust amber? Apprentice bakers ask it constantly, and the answer lies in a meeting between the sugars of the dough and the proteins alongside them, a meeting that only the dry heat of the baking chamber can set going. And when the surface stays pale? Usually the air lacks bite, or the dough carries too much water: steam holds the color back, since damp keeps the surface from climbing past the point where the change begins. Push the heat harder, and what happens? The sugars caramelize, then blacken, and a bitter edge settles over everything. Does a very dark crust mean, then, that somebody got it wrong? Not at all. The shade you aim for depends on the smell you want, because one and the same change gives you the scent of toasted nuts and the scent of scorching alike.

units: a spice seller sees his shop falling quiet
visitors smell the goods but walk out with nothing
their holding back comes from not knowing what to do with these products
his student reckons a scent on its own does not bring a sale
she suggests keeping a tasting pot on the counter
plants would steep in it in a seasoned liquid
the seller worries at first about the lack of room
he ends up taking up the idea
sales climb from the following week on
visitors come back with sharper requests
text: On a wet evening the spice seller was complaining that his shop was going quiet for want of curious customers. He told his apprentice how people wandered in, leaned over the jars, breathed deep, and then walked out with nothing, put off by powders they had no idea what to do with. She answered that a smell convinces nobody until it belongs to a dish. Her idea was plain enough: keep a pot at one end of the counter with roots steeping in a seasoned broth, so anyone could taste before buying. He balked, sure it would swallow the little space he had, and then gave way. By the second week he admitted the jars were emptying and that the same faces kept coming back with sharper questions. His shop, he said with dry amusement, had stopped selling powder and started selling suppers.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the text sets two great ways of keeping food against each other, both older than machine-made cold
the first way takes the water out of the food
salt, sugar and a spell in dry air belong to that way
denying the tiny living things their water stops them from spreading
the second way changes the matter through souring or fermenting
the ferments themselves build a setting that germs cannot bear
taking the water out stiffens the texture and forces a soak before use
changing the matter plainly alters the taste of the food
it raises scents the raw matter never held
cold halts spoiling without adding anything to the flavor
text: Long before anyone could make cold on demand, two families of technique competed for the work of keeping food, and the contest still lights up the kitchens of today. The first works by taking away: salt, sugar or a spell in dry air pull water out of the tissue, and the small living things that spoil food lose the medium they cannot do without. The second works by changing: matter steeps in a sour brine, or ferments are left to build a setting no intruder survives. Taking away leaves the first taste mostly alone, yet it hardens the flesh and forces a soak before anything can be done with it. Changing rewrites the flavor outright, souring, rounding, raising scents the raw thing never held. Cold came last, and it halts decay while creating nothing, which explains both its reign and its blandness.

units: the text lays out four ways of carrying heat in cooking
boiling water spreads a steady heat that goes no higher
it softens the tough parts and draws out the aromas that dissolve
cooking with steam avoids washing the substance out of the food
it holds the color and the firmness of vegetables
heated fat climbs above the temperature water can reach
it serves to brown the surface before the flame comes down
the dry heat of a closed chamber dries the outside and concentrates the sugars
the piece has to be moistened with its own cooking juices
chaining these ways in a thought-out order gives results no single one can reach
text: Four ways of moving heat cover nearly everything done in a home kitchen, and each obeys a logic of its own. Boiling water gives an even, moderate heat: it softens tough tissue, pulls out whatever aromas dissolve, and suits any dish meant to yield a broth. Steam is gentler and cooks without washing the substance out of the food, which is how greens keep both their color and their bite. Hot fat climbs well above the temperature water can reach and builds a browned surface, which is why cooks sear in it before dropping the flame. The dry air of a closed oven, last of the four, parches the outside and concentrates the sugars, provided the piece gets basted with its own juices along the way. String the four together in a thought-out order and you get textures that no single one of them will ever hand you.

units: a large wedding feast is put at risk by a cooking mishap
the woman in charge of the sauces left her pan on a source of heat
she had stepped away to see to a helper who had hurt his hand
the bottom of the pan had taken on a blackened deposit
the guests were already waiting to be served
she brought the deposit back by pouring pale wine over it
the deposit gave off a smell of nuts
she strained the liquid and enriched it with cold fat
a relative of the bride asked how it had been done
she would not set the method down in writing
text: A wedding feast came close to collapse over one forgotten pan. The cook in charge of the sauces had left her reduction sitting on a hot plate while she saw to an apprentice who had opened his finger on a blade. She came back to a dark, sticky crust welded to the bottom, and the hall out front was already waiting. Rather than start over, she poured in a glass of pale wine, scraped hard with a spatula, and found that the burnt layer was giving off a warm smell of nuts nobody expected. Through a sieve it went, a knob of cold butter beaten in, and the sauce reached the tables with nobody the wiser. The bride's father was asking for the recipe before dessert. She told the story to the other cooks at length, but write the method down she would not: an accident, she said, cannot be ordered up.

units: the instructions cover the roasting of a whole farmyard bird
it has to come out of the cold well before it is cooked
without that wait the outside would be done before the middle
the skin has to be wiped, because water blocks the browning
as long as water is leaving it, the surface does not get hot enough
the bird has to sit on a support with gaps in it
left flat in its own juices, the underside would cook in water
the piece has to be moistened with its fat while it roasts
a rest after roasting is needed before carving
carving too soon loses the juices and leaves the meat dry
text: Take a whole farmyard bird and set it out of the cold a good long while before it goes anywhere near heat, or the outside will be done long before the middle even warms. Wipe the skin dry with a cloth: damp skin will not brown, because the surface cannot climb past the temperature browning needs while water is still leaving it. Salt it well and stand it on a rack, never flat in its own juices, or the underside boils instead of roasting. Spoon the fat that melts out of it back over the skin as it roasts, since hot liquid carries heat into the hollows that air reaches badly. Then let it rest away from the flame before you carve, because tightened fibers give their juice back as they cool. Cut into it too soon and the whole of it runs out onto the board, and what you serve is dry.

units: amounts of damaged vegetables were thrown out when the market closed
the sellers were sorry about the loss and could do nothing about it
the goods were still fit to eat despite the way they looked
no arrangement existed to take them away before closing time
a group of people living nearby put forward an answer in three steps
the unsold stock is gathered in the closing hour
a room lent by the town is used for sorting
the vegetables are cooked and put into jars that same evening
the food is handed to households named by the welfare service
the shortage of room and the want of cold storage hold the scheme back
text: Whole crates of bruised vegetables went into the dumpster every week when the covered market shut, under the eyes of the stallholders themselves, sorry about it and out of ideas. The produce was sound, only dented or a shade too ripe to sell, and nothing existed to carry it off before nightfall. A residents' group put forward an answer in three moves: gather the unsold stock in the closing hour, sort it in a room lent by the town, and turn it into soup and preserves right away. Volunteers simmer the vegetables that same evening, sterilize the jars, and pass them on to families sent their way by the welfare service. The traders say their bills for waste collection have come down. What holds the scheme back now is room: the lent space is full, and a cold store is still missing.

units: a short cooking time is needed to get a firm bite
too much sauce softens a firm preparation
low, drawn-out heat loosens the fibers without drying them
patient sieving gives a smooth preparation that coats the palate
a smooth texture takes the edge off harsh flavors
liquid poured in cold makes lumps in a purée
flesh full of fibers points to a badly chosen cut
batter that is too wet gives a cake that sinks like a sponge
texture registers before taste does
text: Three textures rule the plate of a careful cook, and each answers to rules of its own. Crunch comes first. It calls for brief cooking, firm material and restrained seasoning, since a heavy sauce softens it at once. Melting texture takes second place, and it grows out of low, drawn-out heat that loosens the fibers without drying them. Smoothness closes the set. Patient sieving is what gives it that coat on the palate, and it rounds off flavors that would otherwise bite. Alongside those three families sit the accidents every cook dreads. A lumpy purée gives away liquid poured in cold. Stringy meat announces a badly chosen cut. A spongy cake tells of batter soaked with moisture. Knowing the faults is worth as much as mastering the successes, because texture registers before taste does.

units: talk about cooking shifted as households cooked less
the speed of a meal was prized first
the food industry claimed to free whoever prepared the meals
ready-made dishes were then blamed for having no taste
they were faulted for carrying too much salt
cooking shows put the work of the hands on display
what happened in home kitchens never matched that display
a recent line of talk weighs a plate by its price and its origin
each phase corrected the excess of the one before it
text: Public talk about cooking has changed shape as households drifted away from their own stoves. Speed was prized first of all. A meal had to fit inside a narrow slot, and the food industry promised to set whoever cooked entirely free. Then the mood turned, and the ready-made dishes were blamed for their flat taste, their overwhelming saltiness, their dreary sameness. Cooking programs answered by putting the work of the hands on display, though what went on in home kitchens never quite matched the picture. A third line of talk takes over now, weighing a plate by what it costs and by where it came from. Nothing about that sequence is absurd. Each stage trimmed back the excess of the one before it. One question stays open all the same, and nobody has settled it. Who is left with room enough to cook without pressure?

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the baker credits her skill to a childhood spent beside a family mill
she turned down flour blends mixed in advance
that refusal cost her customers early on
her dough ferments at its own pace
the slow fermentation thickens the crust
her bread gives off a faintly sharp smell that throws off newcomers
many disappointed customers come back because the bread keeps for a week
her batches are gone before the middle of the day
she puts her success down to stubbornness rather than to a gift
text: Ask the baker on the corner where that dense loaf of hers comes from, and she will tell you she had almost nothing to do with it herself. Her parents ran a mill, so she grew up with her hands in flour, and the habit settled everything that came after. Since she had told grains apart by touch from childhood on, she turned down the ready-mixed flours, and that cost her customers early on. Her dough rises at its own pace, so the crust thickens and the loaf carries a faintly sharp edge that throws off newcomers. Plenty of people walk out disappointed, then come back, because this bread keeps for a whole week. She has never needed a sign over the door. The batches are gone before midday, and the line of customers spills out onto the walkway. Her success, she laughs, rests on stubbornness, not on any gift.

units: this establishment listed more dishes than its kitchen could handle
the broth had no flavor at the first service
a heavy sauce buried a delicate fish
the chocolate dessert felt gritty in the mouth
the staff out front did their job properly
the manager cut half the dishes from the list
a cook hired from a country inn took over the long cooking
plates arrived hotter and the wait shrank from the following week
a short menu is presented here as the condition of sound cooking
text: The place that just opened at the end of the shopping street had a familiar trouble. Its menu ran far too long, and it listed preparations the kitchen could not handle. The opening service made that plain enough. The broth came out flat, a heavy sauce buried a delicate fish, and the chocolate dessert felt gritty under the spoon. Out front, the staff did their job well enough. The manager settled matters by cutting the list in half and by handing the long, slow cooking to a second cook hired away from a country inn. The difference showed within the following week. Plates left the kitchen hotter, waits grew shorter, and the evening shift stopped calling for extra hands. A short menu is no confession of poverty. Here it is the very condition under which a kitchen finally cooks the way it should.

units: the woman written to describes the kitchen she now has as nothing like the old one
the old kitchen smelled of damp wood and baked fruit
the recent one gives off a smell of metal and soap
the copper pan heated unevenly
the sauce had to be watched without a break
the recent burner answers the dial at once
the writer sees a trade in this rather than an improvement
the old soups had a cloudy color and a deep flavor
vegetables cooked in the recent kitchen keep some firmness
text: You write that the kitchen you now have is nothing like the one we used to share, and I think I follow you. Ours smelled of damp wood and baked apples. Yours, you say, smells of cold metal and soap. In ours the copper pan heated in patches, and a sauce had to be watched the way you watch a small child. In yours the burner answers the dial and nothing boils over. What I see there is less a step forward than a straight trade. You gained precision and you gave up the waiting. Our soups turned cloudy and tasted deep, and your bright kitchen will never reach anything like that. Yours, on the other hand, leave the vegetables a firmness we knew nothing about. Write and tell me what you cook in the evenings. I would like to picture the steam on your windows the way I still see it on ours.

units: whether an emulsion holds depends on three separate things
an egg yolk or some mustard wraps the droplets of fat
that wrapping keeps the droplets from running together
oil added little by little gives the binder time to work
a heavy splash of oil tears the preparation apart
very cold liquid sets part of the fat and makes a lumpy mass
a split sauce is rescued by starting from a fresh yolk in a clean bowl
the failed mixture is worked back in a little at a time
an emulsion that has held looks nearly clear at its rim
text: What separates an emulsion that holds together from one that splits apart? Three separate things govern it, and each can be examined on its own. The first is the binder. An egg yolk, or a dab of mustard, wraps every droplet of fat and keeps the droplets from running together. The second is the pace of the pouring. A thin thread of oil gives the binder the leisure to do its work, while a heavy splash tears the whole preparation apart. The third is temperature. Liquid straight out of the cold sets part of the fat and leaves a lumpy mass behind. So how do you rescue a sauce that has already split? Start over with a fresh yolk in a clean bowl, then work the failed mixture back in a little at a time. An emulsion that has held looks nearly clear at the rim and velvety in the middle.

units: the head waiter tells the young cook the dining room will be full
the cook says he put the garnishes together as soon as the doors opened
only the herbs are missing
the purchasing manager reports a late delivery
she suggests using a sharp condiment kept in a jar
the head waiter agrees on condition that the menu says so
a guest finds his dish too salty halfway through the evening
the cook owns the mistake and offers to make the plate again
in the end not one order was lost
text: At the start of service the head waiter reminded the young cook that every table in the room was booked. The cook answered that he had put the garnishes together as soon as the doors opened, and that only the herbs were still missing. The purchasing manager then reported that the delivery would run late, and she offered to stand in a sharp condiment kept in a jar for the fresh herbs. The head waiter hesitated, then agreed, on condition that the menu said so. Halfway through the evening a guest sent word that his dish tasted too salty. The cook owned the mistake at once and offered a fresh plate, which went out again with no real delay. As the night closed, the buyer summed things up for the gathered staff. Not one order had been lost, and everyone had been equal to the work in hand.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: keeping food once rested on salt, smoke and sugar
those limits shaped tastes that lasted
salt pulls the water out of meat, which forced people to soak it before cooking
root vegetables went into broths to balance a flavor that pushed too hard
smoke left sharp compounds on the surface of the cuts
cooks rubbed those cuts with herbs and fat to soften that attack
sugar was kept for fruit because it was scarcer
mechanical cold made these techniques unnecessary
the techniques lived on as tastes people prefer
text: Long before mechanical cold ever reached the kitchen, keeping food meant salt, smoke and sugar. That single limit shaped whole tastes. Salt pulled the water out of meat, so the meat had to be soaked before it could be cooked, and broths filled up with root vegetables to balance a flavor that pushed far too hard. Smoke left sharp compounds on the outside of every cut, so cooks learned to rub the surface with herbs and fat and take that attack down. Sugar, being scarcer, was kept for fruit, whose flesh it turned clear and yielding. Once the icebox and then the cooling machine had spread through kitchens, none of this was needed any longer. It did not go away, though. By then these had become tastes that people actively looked for, and they cost more today than anything sold fresh.

units: sticky rice clumps into a pasty mass as it cooks
the main cause is not the pot you use
the grain lets go of starch the moment it heats in water
that starch works like glue
rinsing the grain until the water runs clear solves part of the trouble
measuring the water keeps the cooking from dragging on
cooking that drags on crushes the grains
cutting the heat before the end lets the steam finish the job
salting the water at the start fixes a taste that falls flat
text: Your rice clumps up into a pasty mass? It happens more often than anyone admits, and the pot is rarely responsible. The grain releases its starch the moment it heats in water, and that starch behaves exactly like glue. First fix: rinse the rice under cold water until the water runs clear, then leave it to drain. Second fix: measure the water instead of pouring it by eye, because too much drags the cooking out, and cooking that drags on crushes the grains. Third fix: cut the heat before the end you were told to wait for, put the lid on, and let the steam finish the job without any stirring at all. If the taste still falls flat, salt the water at the start rather than the plate at the end. What you end up with is separate grains, firm to the bite, ready to accept any sauce without disintegrating.

units: an oven breakdown upset a caterer's evening
the crew moved the whole menu onto fierce heat
the guests thus compared two ways of cooking without thinking about it
the root vegetables roasted the day before had a soft center and a sweet surface
the same vegetables seared in a pan kept a sharp firmness and a plain bitterness
the fish from the oven had loose, airy flesh
the fish cooked over the flame had brittle skin and denser flesh
the guests who were asked split into two camps of about equal size
the caterer now offers both ways of cooking
text: An oven that quit turned a caterer's evening into a demonstration that nobody had planned. With no dry heat left, the crew moved the whole menu onto fierce burners, and the guests ended up comparing two ways of cooking without once thinking about it. The day before, the same root vegetables had roasted without hurry. Their centers went soft, their surfaces turned sweet, their smell came out round. That night, seared in a pan, they held a sharp firmness and a plain bitterness much closer to the raw vegetable. The fish followed the same swing. Out of the oven its flesh was loose and slightly spongy. Over the flame the skin turned brittle and the inside sat denser. Asked on the way out, the guests fell into two camps of about equal size. The caterer took the lesson and now offers both.

units: a hard surface sends a short jolt back into the foot as it lands
that jolt travels up through the ankle joint and then the joints of the leg
the muscles soak up part of the impact, which brings on exhaustion sooner
stride length shortens on its own over that kind of surface
the foot then lands closer to the hips
a shorter stride covers less ground and brings the pace down
the body speeds up its step rate to make up for it, at the cost of heavier breathing
coaches advise rotating training surfaces
repeating one identical movement on one identical surface injures more than the distance covered
text: Land on a hard surface and the foot takes back a short, sharp jolt. It climbs from the sole up into the ankle, and from there on into the knee and the hip. Because the muscle soaks up part of that energy, tiredness shows up a good deal sooner than it would on soft ground. The stride then shortens all by itself. The foot comes down closer to the hips, and the joint takes less strain for it. Shorter steps mean less ground covered per stride, so the pace falls off. To make that up, the body turns the legs over faster, and the extra turnover costs more breath. Coaches therefore tell their runners to rotate surfaces from one session to the next. Soft footing gives a tendon room to recover, while firm footing builds up bone. What injures a runner is not the distance covered. It is doing the same movement over and over on the same surface.

units: the club coach kept warning that ankles would give out before lungs
ground hardened by the cold kept the shoes from gripping
half the squad limped when the season started up again
the players blamed their gear, then the man who ran the gym, then bad luck
one player who works as a physical therapist suggested a balance drill on one foot
the drill is done on a soft cushion, with no hand on the wall, before every session
the players thought the drill was ridiculous at first
sprains grew rarer once the habit took hold
the routine now opens every session, whatever shape the ground is in
text: Our coach kept telling us our ankles would quit before our lungs did, and he was right. As soon as the cold hardened the ground, the shoes stopped biting, and half the squad limped through the first weeks back. We blamed the shoes. Then we blamed the man who ran the gym. Then we blamed plain bad luck. One of us, a physical therapist by trade, offered a deal: a quarter of an hour balancing on one foot before every session, on a soft cushion, with no hand on the wall. Nobody bought it. At first we laughed at each other wobbling like badly planted fence posts. Then the sprains thinned out, and coming back after the break stopped feeling like a sick ward. The drill has opened every session since, frozen ground, soaked ground or dry. Our coach never once admitted he had not thought of it himself.

units: three kinds of sole stand apart when you shop
the thick, soft sole cushions the impact and suits long outings on the road
the thick sole wears out fast and leaves the foot unsteady going downhill
