the thin sole brings the foot closer to the ground and passes the push through better
the thin sole leaves the tendon open to repeated jolts
the studded sole is meant for soft ground and turns uncomfortable on a hard track
trying models on is advised once the foot has already swollen
you should jog on a firm surface before closing the sale
ankle support is tested by pivoting in place
text: Buying an athletic shoe comes down to weighing three kinds of sole, say the salespeople trained for the job. The first runs thick and soft. It cushions the impact and suits long outings on pavement, though it wears out fast and leaves the foot unsteady on a downhill. The second one is thinner. It brings the foot nearer the ground and passes the push through better, but it leaves the tendon open to jolt after jolt. The third carries studs and belongs on soft ground. On a hard track it turns loud and awkward underfoot. The method the sellers advise takes three moves. Try the models on once the foot has swollen from a long walk. Jog on a firm surface before you reach for your card. Then pivot in place and compare how each one holds the ankle. A shoe that fits draws far less notice than one that pinches.

units: the gym reopens after its equipment was overhauled
the tumbling floor has been rebuilt from scratch
a springboard stands in front of the vaulting table
the bars carry the chalk left on them by the athletes
the hanging rings serve mainly for upper-body strength work
a pit filled with foam blocks catches the falls of those still learning
beginners show up late in the evening
attendance has risen since the reopening
the people who run the place credit the renewed equipment
text: A smell of varnish still hangs over the mats in the entrance of the overhauled gym. The tumbling floor, rebuilt from scratch, gives back a flat sound under a visitor's shoe. Then comes the springboard, a curved plank the vaulters test with a heel before they trust it. Farther along, the bars carry the white streaks of chalk that every athlete leaves behind in passing. The rings hang from the ceiling on long cables and serve mostly for upper-body strength work. At the far end, a pit of foam blocks takes the falls of anyone still learning, and the dull thud it gives off marks out the hours of the evening. Beginners turn up late, when the room still belongs to quiet. Attendance has climbed steadily since the doors opened again, and the people who run the place credit the renewed equipment.

units: the run-up sets the speed of arrival on the board
the jumper builds speed gradually while keeping the chest upright
the second-to-last step serves to lower the center of gravity
the last contact with the ground lasts less time than the ones before
that last contact turns forward speed into an upward push
the board bends under the load and then gives back the energy it stored
the arms rise at the moment the board returns the jumper
the rotation starts during the rise and not after the high point
a landing that is too stiff passes the shock into the ankle joint
text: Everything starts with the run-up, whose length sets the speed of arrival on the board. The jumper builds pace gradually, chest upright, stride even. On the second-to-last step, the supporting leg bends further and the center of gravity drops. The final contact with the ground lasts less time than the ones before it. That is the contact that turns forward speed into an upward push. The board bends under the load, then hands back the energy it stored. The arms come up at that exact moment, or the drive leaks away. Rotation begins during the rise, never after the high point of the flight. The landing takes both feet, knees bent, chest tipped slightly forward. A landing too stiff passes the shock straight into the ankle and the tendon, which accounts for most of the injuries seen at this stage.

units: nothing requires a child to settle on one discipline before adolescence
early specialization piles the same movements onto the same joints
that concentration brings on tendon overload before growth is finished
a narrow movement repertoire makes adapting hard when the ground changes
boredom is put forward as the leading cause of dropping out
clubs push specialization because early results attract funding
the writer proposes delaying selection in the youth categories
he recommends requiring a second activity of every competitor
text: Nothing requires a child to settle on a single discipline before adolescence, yet clubs press for it anyway, and the effects can be measured. Early specialization piles the same movements onto the same joints, so tendon overload appears well before growth has finished. It also narrows the movement repertoire. A teenager who has known one apparatus, or one kind of footing, adapts poorly the moment the ground changes. Then comes boredom, the leading cause of dropping out between late childhood and adulthood. Clubs persist because results that arrive early attract funding. We would gain by pushing selection later in the youth categories and by asking every competitor to take up a second activity. An athletic career rests on the variety of the supports it is built from, not on their repetition.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the strength coach was a competitive swimmer when she was young
a torn tendon cut her athletic career short
she went back to school after that injury
she noticed that injuries mostly happened on the return after a break
she set up a build-up spread over three weeks
that build-up begins with light loads and slowed-down movements
heavy loads come in only at the end of that period
the number of injuries fell at her club
neighboring clubs have taken up her method
text: They call her the club's strength coach, and her whole office fits inside a single gym bag set down at the edge of the pool. She swam in competition as a young woman, until the evening a tendon tore and her career ended on the spot. She went back to school after that injury, then came back to the water with a question in her head. Watching her athletes closely, she noticed that injuries rarely struck in the middle of the season. They struck on the return, after a break. So she imposed a build-up spread over three weeks, made of light loads and movements deliberately slowed down. Heavy weights enter only at the end of that stretch, once the ankle and the shoulder have their full range back. The injury count at her club fell away, and the clubs nearby now copy what she does.

units: the writer went to two gyms over the same season
the first gym is fitted with guided machines and with screens
the guided machines force the movement along a fixed path
the second gym sits in a poorly heated shed
the second gym offers mostly bars, free weights and apparatus
the coach at the second gym fixes your position without being asked
the writer made more progress in the less comfortable gym
he still recommends the plush gym to anyone the iron intimidates
text: I went to two gyms this season, and they have almost nothing in common. The first one gleams: guided machines, screens everywhere, soft music, carpet that swallows the sound of the weights. It feels good in there, except the machine picks the path for you, and the shoulder never learns to hold itself. The second one sits in a badly heated shed, with bars, free weights and a couple of squeaking apparatus. The floor rings, people talk loudly, and the coach walks straight over to fix your position without waiting to be asked. Guess where I got stronger. In the shed, obviously, because a whole movement beats one that is steered along rails. I would still send anyone the iron intimidates to the plush place. A reassuring machine beats giving the whole thing up after a single week.

units: the writer reports to her reader on the club she joined
the adult section's sessions last an hour and a half
the warm-up takes the first third of the session
the equipment includes thick mats, a springboard and two sets of weights
the membership fee covers the loan of studded shoes
the staff is made up of two volunteers and one paid employee
the paid employee follows up on the athletes who get hurt
newcomers sit in on two sessions before paying
the writer invites her reader to come one weekday evening
text: Dear neighbor, you asked me for a proper report on the club I joined, so here it is. Sessions in the adult section run an hour and a half, and a full third of that goes to the warm-up, which surprised me at first and won me over later on. The equipment holds up well: thick mats, a springboard in good shape, and two sets of weights, from the lightest to the heaviest. The fee covers the loan of studded shoes, which matters a lot if you would rather buy nothing until you are sure. Staffing rests on two volunteers and one paid employee, and she is the one who follows the athletes who get hurt, a twisted ankle, an angry tendon. Newcomers sit in on two sessions before they pay a thing. Tuesday evenings are quiet, so come along to one and I will introduce you to the whole group.

units: the first question is about what happens as the wall comes up
the swimmer judges the distance left without lifting his head
he adjusts the reach of his arm strokes to arrive at the right spacing
the flip starts with the chest tipping toward the bottom
the feet land on the wall, set hip width apart
the push off the wall produces a speed higher than swimming does
the tucked position underwater holds that speed
the stroke has to start again before the speed falls away
a badly placed foot costs more than a badly swum length
text: What happens to a swimmer in the second just before the wall? He measures, without ever lifting his head, the distance he has left, and he stretches or shortens his arm strokes so as to arrive neither too close nor too far out from it. And after that? The chest tips over toward the bottom, the flip goes round, and the feet land flat on the wall, set about hip width apart. Does the turn really matter as much as people claim? It does, because the push off the wall throws him forward faster than he will ever swim under his own power. The tucked position underwater holds on to that speed, provided that nothing sticks out. And when should the stroke start again? Just before the speed begins to fall away. A foot set wrong on the wall costs him more than an entire length swum badly.

units: a woman coaching a group asks her students about aches that keep coming back
a boy describes a burning feeling in his thighs two days afterwards
that boy often gave up on the sessions at the end of the week
another student reports a comparable discomfort across her upper back
the coach puts these aches down to a sudden demand made on an unprepared muscle
she recommends a longer warm-up that begins with brisk walking
she advises closing the session with stretches free of any jerking
after a fortnight the aches ease and the absences stop growing
text: The coach asked her group about the aches that kept coming back after practice. One boy said his thighs burned two days later, and he owned up to dropping the sessions at the end of the week more often than not. A girl beside him reported the same discomfort, only across her upper back. None of that surprised the coach. Soreness turns up, she told them, when a muscle nobody has prepared is suddenly asked to give everything at once. So she stretched the opening of each practice, a good deal longer than before: brisk walking first, then slow circles of the arms and shoulders, then the drills themselves. She changed the closing minutes as well. Every session now finishes with quiet stretching, held steady and never yanked. A fortnight of that was enough. The aches eased off, and the empty spots along the wall stopped multiplying.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: contests of long ago were held with no measuring device and no markings on the ground
an elderly villager acted as judge through his word alone
the end of a match depended on the players wearing themselves out
in matches today the smallest irregularity is flagged and checked on video
athletes of long ago entered the game with no muscular preparation
that lack of preparation brought on repeated joint injuries
athletes today set aside a sizeable part of their training for warming up
the pull of movement and the wish to outdo the other person have not changed
text: Picture a match from long ago. No whistle, no clock, no lines painted on the ground. An old man from the village called it all, and whatever he said stood. The game ended when the players ran out of legs, and not a moment sooner. Now look at a match today. Shove somebody half a step too hard and it gets flagged, measured, and played back on a screen. The other gap is the getting ready. Back then you walked in cold and went straight at it, and you paid for that hurry with knees and ankles that wore out early. Players now hand over a solid slice of every training session just to wake the body up. One thing sits in both pictures, though. People run because running feels good, and because they want to beat whoever is next to them. The measuring changed. The wanting never did.

units: three signs give warning that an effort has outrun the resources on hand
the involuntary clenching of a muscle comes above all when water and minerals are short
a sharp pain under the ribs comes from breathing that has been handled badly
trembling in the legs shows an energy store that is close to empty
each of these signs calls for a different response
the first is answered by drinking and by lengthening the muscle gently
the second is answered by easing the pace and breathing more fully
the third is answered by stopping, taking in food and waiting
brushing these warnings aside opens the way to an injury that is slow to heal
text: Three signs warn an athlete that the effort has outrun the resources on hand. The first is the cramp: a muscle clamps down on its own and will not let go, and it turns up above all when water and minerals have run short. The second is a sharp jab under the ribs, and it comes from breathing that has been handled badly. The third is a tremor in the legs, which says the store of energy is close to empty. Each of the three calls for a different answer, and mixing them up only drags out the recovery. Against the first: drink, then lengthen the clenched muscle gently. Against the second: ease the pace and pull the breath deeper. Against the third: stop, take in food, and wait it out. Reading these warnings costs an athlete a pause. Brushing them aside opens the way to an injury that is slow to heal.

units: a smell of chalk and warm rubber fills the hall as the player walks in
this player had gone unused for the whole season
the person in charge of the team waves her onto the floor with a simple hand signal
her first plays go wrong and she misses two catches
a deflected ball strikes the edge of the hoop and drops back high in the air
she recovers the ball after its bounce by throwing herself to the ground
her roll ends with the ball sent back up by a single hand
the play earns her one point without changing the gap on the score
from that moment she stops staring at the ground and feels lighter
text: Chalk and warm rubber, that was the smell of the hall when the substitute finally set foot on the floor. She had gone the whole season unused, counting other people's passes. At the restart the man running the team waved her on with a flick of the hand, no words at all. Her first plays went wrong. She missed two catches and felt the quiet draw tight around her. Then a deflected ball clipped the edge of the hoop and dropped back high in the air. She followed the bounce, threw herself to the ground, rolled across one shoulder and sent the ball back up with a single open hand. The point counted. The gap on the scoreboard stayed exactly where it had been. Something else shifted, though: she stopped staring at the ground. The rest of the game felt short, and oddly light, as if the floor had agreed at last to hold her.

units: the item has to be pulled onto a limb that is straight and not bent
an item fitted over a folded joint slips away within the first few strides
the sleeve is drawn up from the lower leg and never rolled
a fold of fabric hampers the circulation and leaves the end of the limb numb
the central opening has to ring the kneecap without pressing on it
weight resting straight on the bone brings on a spread-out ache after the workout
the straps are tightened working from the bottom towards the top
tightening done the other way round makes the lower joint of the leg swell
wearing it at length for no reason weakens the muscles it covers
text: Pull the brace onto a straight leg, never onto a bent one. A support fitted over a folded joint slips away within the first few strides and stops holding anything at all. Draw the sleeve up from the lower leg, and never roll it, because a fold of fabric squeezes the vessels underneath and leaves the whole foot numb. Check next that the central opening rings the kneecap without pressing anywhere on it. Weight resting straight on the bone brings on a spread-out ache once the workout is over, and that ache can last the evening. Tighten the straps working from the bottom towards the top. Done the other way round, the pull drives blood downward and the lower joint of the leg swells. Take the brace off once the session ends. Worn at length for no reason, it weakens the very muscles it covers.

units: the management of a sports facility closes two halls for the time being
the buckled coverings of the floor had caused accidents
the relatives of the enrolled children protested against this decision
the facilities nearby had no free slot at all
a meeting open to the public was arranged
specialists pointed to an old water leak as the source of the trouble
that leak made the floorboards lift under the impact of jumps
the sports played with a racket or over a net move to a gymnasium brought back into service
the dance and strength sessions are held in a multipurpose hall
text: The management of the sports facility has closed two of its halls for the time being. The coverings on the floor there had buckled, and several people had come down hard on them. Relatives of the enrolled children protested at once, since the youngsters lost their slots and every facility nearby was already full. So a meeting open to the public was arranged. Specialists laid out what they had traced: an old water leak, never fully dealt with, which lifts the floorboards each time a jump lands on them. The answer comes in two parts. Everything played with a racket or over a net moves across to a gymnasium brought back into service. The dance and strength sessions go into a multipurpose hall. Repairs to the floors should be finished before the cold months, and the lost slots handed back.

units: two kinds of floor are fitted in most sports halls
these two floors answer differently under the weight of the foot
the boarding mounted on flexible supports sinks slightly with every step
this boarding hands part of the energy back to the leg
it spares the joints and forgives landings that come down badly
its pale shade holds the marks of shoes and calls for regular upkeep
the artificial floor grips more and helps the push at the start
it puts up with water, with wheels rolling over it and with shoes worn outdoors
it makes slides painful and takes none of the shock out of impacts
text: Most sports halls are floored in one of two ways, and the two do not answer the weight of the foot in the same manner. Boarding laid over flexible supports sinks a little under every step, then hands part of that energy back to the leg that produced it. It spares the joints, and it forgives a landing that comes down badly. Its pale shade, on the other hand, holds every mark a shoe leaves behind, so the upkeep has to be regular and thorough. The artificial floor grips harder and gives a cleaner push at the start of a sprint. Water does it no harm, wheels roll across it without leaving a trace, and shoes worn outdoors are welcome on it. What it will not do is soften anything: a slide across it hurts, and the shock of each landing travels straight up the leg with nothing taken out of it.

units: the writer holds that the mania for counting spoils the pleasure of physical activity
he sets out the effects of that mania one after another
he likens running to a graded test because of the devices worn on the arm
he notes that the setting of people against each other reaches even friendships
an easy outing turns in this way into a contest of figures
whoever falls short of the weekly target feels at fault despite having been active
night-time rest is submitted in its turn to the reading of graphs
the writer does not reject the indicators but blames them for filling the whole space
he wishes physical activity to remain a desire and not an obligation
text: Honestly, the mania for counting has eaten a good part of the pleasure out of moving. Look at what it has brought, one piece at a time. Running turned into a graded test: you set out with a device strapped to your arm and come home with a mark. Then the setting of one against another crept in everywhere, friendships included, so an easy outing turns into a contest of figures. After that comes the guilt. Whoever falls short of the weekly target feels at fault, though he walked, swam, and laughed with the people close to him. Even the sleep of the night goes into the graphs now, as if resting were something you could pass or fail. I am not saying the readings are worthless. I am saying they have filled the whole space between us. Moving ought to stay a desire, and never a debt you owe.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: this caregiver began her working life in a small local facility
there she eased the shoulders of swimmers during their training
she specialised in shoulder complaints, a specialty little sought after at the time
a women's squad at a high level then took her on
she watched the throwing movements through a whole season before stepping in
her way of going about it rested on video, on comparison and on talking
shoulder complaints fell within the group
she now leads the medical staff of a training centre
she credits her results to listening to the injured athletes and to checking what they said
text: The therapist began her working life in a small local facility, easing the shoulders of swimmers between one length and the next. From there she went deeper into shoulder complaints, a specialty few people were chasing at the time. A women's squad at a high level took her on, and she spent a whole season watching how the players threw before she stepped in with a single exercise. Her way of going about it caught everyone off guard. She filmed, she compared, she talked things over with the athletes rather than handing down orders. Shoulder complaints fell within the group. She now leads the medical staff of a training centre and teaches younger therapists. She says she invented nothing: she listened to the athletes who were hurting, then checked what they said, one claim at a time.

units: the performance leaves the viewer with an unsettling feeling
the performers were trained as athletes and not as stage artists
that background gives them an uncommon physical staying power
they dance for sixty minutes without their breathing showing any fatigue
that reserve lends an unexpected scale to the closing part
the same background produces the failing of the evening
trained to reach a goal, they favour movements that make a display
the gestures made for nothing, proving nothing, are what they lack
the string of feats leaves no room for a pause
the audience comes out impressed but barely moved
text: The performance leaves you unsettled, and the reason stands there from the opening minute: the performers were trained as athletes, not as stage artists. That background gives the evening its finest quality, a staying power you rarely see. They dance a full hour without their breathing showing any fatigue, and that reserve lends the closing part a scale no technique on its own would reach. The same background produces the failing of the evening. Trained to reach a goal, they go for the movement that makes a display: the high leap, the controlled fall, the shape that pulls a gasp out of the room. Gestures made for nothing, proving nothing, are what they lack. So the piece becomes one feat after another with nowhere to draw breath. You come out impressed, and barely moved by what you have watched.

units: the writer sends his message right after a training session
he used to believe the two sports called for the same abilities
both call for holding a steady pace
the burning breath of the first minutes turns up in both
when running, the joints take the shock against the ground
when swimming, the sense of weight fades away
the runner fights the slope of the ground
the swimmer fights the drag of the water
trading one for the other eased the writer's joint aches
the writer urges his reader to give it a try
text: I am writing this with my breath still ragged, straight off the session, because something clicked out there and I wanted you to hear it first. For season after season I was convinced that running and swimming asked exactly the same things of a body. They do overlap in one place: both of them want a steady pace held from start to finish, and both set your lungs burning through the opening minutes. What caught me off guard was everything else. On the road, every stride slams into the ground and my joints swallow the shock of it. In the water my weight seems to go somewhere else entirely, and all that is left is the pull of the shoulders. A runner fights the slope of a hill. A swimmer fights the water pushing back. Since I started trading one for the other, my knees have quit aching. Give it a try, then tell me how it feels.

units: the text answers the questions beginners ask most often
the warm-up should work the ankle and the hip
costly shoes are not needed
a gripping sole guards against slipping on wet ground
the early shortness of breath clears up on its own
a sharp pain signals damaged tissue
muscle repair happens during rest
outings should be lengthened in small weekly steps
the pace chosen must still allow talking
text: So you want to move more without wrecking a knee. The same handful of questions reaches me every single week, so here they are, answered in order. Warm up or not? Warm up, and not with a lazy shake of the legs, because the ankle and the hip both need waking up before you push off. Do you need costly shoes? No, you really do not. What you do need is a sole that grips, since one slide on wet ground will cost you weeks. Should it hurt? No. The gasping at the start settles by itself, but a sharp stab is tissue telling you something has torn. Train every single day? Bad idea. Muscle rebuilds itself while you rest, not while you sweat. And how do you actually get better? Stretch each outing by a handful of strides a week, hold a pace that still lets you talk, and write down how you felt.

units: the coach breaks the race into three stretches
the favorite went out far too fast
the chasing pack let her go without responding
the turn came on the steep climb of the second lap
the coach's runner passed her rivals one by one
the chaser crossed the top of the climb in front
she opened a lead on the downhill part
she accepted a slide through a muddy bend the others refused
she dropped her last rival on the closing stretch
the coach credits the win to composure rather than power
text: Caught at the finish line, the coach splits the race into three stretches. Off the line, she says, the favorite went out far too fast, and the pack behind her simply watched her go without lifting a finger. Then came the steep climb on the second lap, and the whole thing turned over. “I watched my runner pick them off one by one, and right then I knew she was going to close that gap,” she says. Her own runner crested the top of the climb in front, then stretched her lead on the way down, where the rest of them braked out of caution. “She took the slide through that muddy bend. The others refused it,” the coach adds. On the closing straight, with the crowd roaring her in, the young athlete pulled clear of her last rival. “Power did not win that race. A cool head did,” she says, her voice catching.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: running was at first a duty tied to survival
it served to chase game, to carry word, or to escape a threat
the reliance on endurance favored legs able to hold a pace for long
that pressure shaped a springy tendon at the heel
it also produced heavy sweating
a ligament holds the neck steady during the stride
the spread of settlements and pack animals cut that need
effort then turned into measured and rewarded spectacle
our bodies keep the imprint of a use that is no longer needed
text: In the beginning, running was no pastime at all. It was a duty: you ran to chase down game, you ran to carry word, you ran to get away from something that meant you harm. Because staying alive rested on endurance, our forebears kept, without ever once choosing it, legs that could hold a modest pace across enormous stretches of ground. Out of that need came a strange sort of body, with a springy cord at the heel, skin that sweats freely, and a head held level by one thin band of tissue. Then the settlements sprawled, the roads opened, beasts carried the loads we used to carry ourselves, and the need drained away. Effort turned into show. We began to time it, to compare it, to hand out crowns for it. That shift explains an oddity: our flesh still remembers a use our lives no longer ask of it.

units: the pain in the side ends many outings
a muscular sheet separates the rib cage from the abdomen
that sheet drives the breathing of the lungs
short, hurried breathing keeps it from letting go completely
its lasting contraction hauls on its anchor points
the pain shows up mostly under the ribs on the right side
easing the pace and drawing out the exhale is the first remedy
pressing the sore spot while folding the chest forward slackens the anchors
a heavy meal before the effort makes the trouble more likely
text: A stitch in the side ends more outings than most runners will admit, and its workings are easier to grasp than they sound. Under the lungs sits a broad sheet of muscle that walls the rib cage off from the belly, and that sheet is what pumps the air in and out. When breathing turns short and hurried, the sheet never fully lets go. It stays clenched and starts hauling on the places where it attaches. That is when the ache arrives, low under the ribs, usually on the right. Three fixes cover almost every case. First, ease the pace and drag out each exhale, blowing steadily as the foot opposite the ache lands. Second, press a hand into the sore spot and fold the chest forward, which slackens the attachments. Third, skip the big meal beforehand, since a full stomach shoves the sheet upward.

units: the athlete interviewed now plays in goal
she began her career in an attacking position
it took her seasons to see how opposed the two roles are
the forward moves toward open ground
the forward must drop her misses at once
the keeper falls back toward her own line
the keeper must hold on to every detail, since her lapses are paid for on the spot
in her first match in goal, she turned aside a low shot
the crowd rose to its feet after that save
she holds that both positions ask for equal courage
text: A goalkeeper once shared a memory with me that lays her trade bare. She had come up through the ranks as a forward, and it took her several seasons to see that the two positions obey opposite laws. A forward, she explained, moves toward open ground: she has to break at the right instant, slip past a defender, and drop every miss the moment it happens. A keeper does the reverse. She retreats toward her own line and has to hold on to every last detail, because a lapse there is paid for on the spot. On the evening of her first match in goal, she threw herself at a low shot and turned it away with her wrist. The whole crowd came to its feet. She understood something she had never felt as a forward: a team thanking her for an act of defense. Both roles, she now insists, ask for the same courage.

units: getting a session ready runs through four parts in order
the first part covers the gear and its condition
a rubbing seam or careless lacing brings on a skin injury
the second part is waking the body up
it combines brisk walking, joint circles, and short bursts of speed
the third part alternates quick stretches and easy ones
the pace chosen must stay bearable without tightening the breathing
the fourth part is winding down, drinking, and lengthening the legs
noting the tiredness felt in a notebook records the progress
text: Build your session in four parts, and keep them in this order. Part one is your gear. Check the laces, check that the sole is holding, and run a finger along the seams, because a blister starts with one rough edge that nobody bothered to look at. Part two wakes the body up. Walk briskly, roll the joints of the legs through their range, then finish off with a few short bursts of speed before the real start. Part three is the body of the session. Trade quick stretches for easy ones, holding a pace you can carry without your breathing going tight. Part four brings you back down. Slow in stages, drink, then lengthen the muscles of the thigh and the calf with no jerking. Last, note in a notebook how tired you felt. Week by week, that record tells you whether you are truly improving.

units: rain was falling when the first competitor reached the platform
people feared the event would be called off
the wind dropping left the water perfectly still
the organizers then sent off the first heats
the opening diver entered the water with almost no splash
the strictest judge handed her a high mark
a competitor slipped on the wet board and chose to withdraw
the setup was wiped dry before the restart
the defending champion pulled off a figure never tried at this site
she finished ahead of every one of her rivals
text: Rain was already coming down when the first competitor climbed up to the platform, and honestly, half of us figured the whole thing would be scrapped. It was not. The wind died off, the surface went perfectly still, and the organizers sent off the opening heats. That first dive shut everyone up: she slid in with barely a splash, and the judge nobody can please handed her a high mark. Then it got messy. One competitor slipped on the soaked board, caught himself at the last second, and decided he was done for the day. Crews wiped everything dry and the diving picked up again. Late on, the defending champion went for a figure nobody had ever tried at this pool, a tucked reversal, and she landed it clean. Climbing out, still laughing, she had beaten every rival in the field.

units: a smell of resin and chalk meets the visitor at the door
the climbing wall runs the full height of the building
the colored holds trace routes that are hard to read
thick mats cover the floor and swallow the noise of falls
all you hear is rubber squeaking and the breathing of the climbers
the openings stay shut to keep fingers from going cold
keeping them shut makes the heat build in the room
a teenage girl hesitates, then throws herself at a distant hold
her foot skids and the rope stops her halfway up
repeating the attempts is what brings the progress
text: The smell reaches you right at the door: resin, and the dry chalk that everyone carries on their hands. The climbing wall runs the full height of the building, and its colored holds trace paths the eye follows without ever making sense of them. Because thick mats swallow the floor, a fall lands without a sound. All you hear is rubber squeaking on stone and the breathing of the climbers overhead. The room grows warm, since every opening stays shut against the drafts that turn fingers stiff and useless. At the base of the wall a teenage girl hesitates, then throws herself at a hold well out of reach. Her foot skids, the swing spins her sideways, and the rope stops her halfway up. She lowers off, blows on her palms, starts over. Those attempts repeat, and that is where progress comes from.

units: the writer finds it wrong to file movement away among amusements
children now spend their afternoons seated in front of a screen
that stillness harms the skeleton, the eyesight, and the sleep
blaming families is convenient and unfair
the streets have closed to play
school yards have shrunk
the adult timetable no longer leaves a free gap
the writer calls for places where noise and falling are tolerated
he proposes opening the covered yards outside teaching hours
he argues that physical tiredness is the mark of an active life
text: We filed movement away under amusements, and the bill for that decision has come due. The child who used to climb, to jump, to roll down a grassy bank now spends the whole afternoon seated, a screen within reach. His bones show it, his eyes show it, his sleep shows it worst of all. Blaming parents is easy and unfair. The street shut its doors to play, the school yards were shaved down, and the adult timetable no longer leaves a single loose hour. Getting out of this costs no great budget and calls for no untried doctrine. Give children back places where noise is allowed and falling is expected. Open the covered yards outside teaching hours. Accept that a walk on foot is worth more than a parking spot saved. And stop treating a tired body as an accident: it is the mark of a life being used.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the specialist works with athletes who swim
she starts by watching the athletes launch themselves from the edge
she looks for the movements that waste strength
she spends the second half of the day in a room full of machines
she teaches beginners to take hold of the load without tightening the upper back
she ends with a study of the session notebooks
she ran middle distances before she taught
she says her know-how comes from her own physical injuries
she rejects programs that are the same for everyone
she believes suppleness brings more progress than rigid strength
text: The strength coach at a swimming club splits her week into three clear jobs. She crouches at the pool edge first and watches her swimmers drive off the wall, following how the knees fold before the push, hunting for the small motions that burn effort and give nothing back. Afternoons belong to the weight room. There she corrects footing and teaches the youngest ones how to take hold of the bar without locking up the shoulders and the upper back. Evenings she reads the training notebooks, marking them line by line with a copyist's patience. She is short and solidly built, a former middle-distance runner, and she says her craft came from listening to her own injuries. She will not copy one athlete's program onto the next one, and she keeps repeating a single claim: a loose swimmer improves faster than a strong, stiff one.

units: the narrator tells of her visit to an indoor place devoted to climbing
her first impression of the reception was bad
the clothes lockers worked badly
she thought about giving up and leaving
an instructor taught her the right way to take hold of the grips
she lost her balance coming back down and nobody mocked her
the crowd made the place noisy later on
the way the climbers helped each other made her forget the noise
she finds the price fair and the walls well designed
she criticizes the changing rooms and means to come back
text: Right, let me say it straight: that climbing gym won me over. The front desk looked like a mess when I walked in, the lockers jammed on me, and I nearly turned around and left. Then an instructor came over and showed me how to hold the grips without crushing my fingers, and the whole session flipped. I got up an easy route, lost my footing on the way down, and nobody laughed. Later the place filled up, the noise went up a notch, and I grumbled to myself. But the climbers kept passing advice around without shoving past each other, so the racket melted into the effort. I walked out with my forearms on fire and that daft grin beginners wear once a movement finally makes sense. Fair price, smart walls, changing rooms that need gutting and rebuilding. I am going back next week, no hesitation.

units: the writer writes to a member of her family to give news
a structure that crosses a waterway was closed for works
that closure made the training circuit unusable
the person in charge moved the sessions to an old stone works
the soft ground there forces the lower joints to bend more
the pains at the back of the foot have clearly gone down
the grainy ground softens the impacts better than the hard surface
people passing saw the group from the road and signed up
the number of members has doubled
the reader is invited to come and try with borrowed equipment
text: Dear cousin, you asked how the neighborhood running club was doing. It is thriving, and the reason behind that is almost funny. The footbridge over the canal shut for repairs, which chopped our usual loop into two useless stretches. With no route left, the coach shifted our sessions out to the old stone quarry, where loose ground forces the ankles and knees to bend much more. The heel injuries fell away almost at once, because the grit soaks up the shock that concrete used to throw straight back. And since the quarry sits in plain view of the road, walkers slowed down to watch, then signed up, so we are twice the size we were. I am telling you all of this because you said you wanted to start again. Come along one morning; someone will lend you shoes, and you will find the slope loses its bite.

units: the text deals with a joint at the top of the arm left inactive
inactivity brings on a stiffening according to the fitness specialists
the discomfort felt discourages movement even further
a violent strain is not advised because it wakes the suffering again
the answer put forward consists of very small ranges repeated
the first exercise lets the limb swing freely
a very light weight such as an empty container is then brought in
if the trouble comes back one has to go back to an earlier step
the improvement does not come in a steady way
whoever rushes the process fails over and over
text: What happens to a shoulder you stop using? It seizes up, the rehab specialists answer, and the discomfort that follows discourages the movement even more. The circle closes on itself. So should you force it? No. Rough handling wakes the pain and drives the joint further into stiffness. What is left, then? A tiny range of motion, repeated without hurry, held over weeks. You begin by letting the arm hang and swing on its own, a pendulum that nothing pushes. Then you add a laughable load, an empty bottle, and after that something barely heavier. And if the ache comes back? You drop down a step without making a drama of it, since progress here almost never runs in a straight line. Whoever accepts that slowness gets a supple shoulder back. Whoever tries to skip ahead keeps staging the same disappointment over and over.

units: a specialized caregiver describes two techniques for coming back to the ground
the first technique keeps the lower limbs straight
that first option carries the shock up as far as the top of the legs
the middle joint of the leg then takes the load
the second technique bends hips and knees at the moment of contact
the muscles at the front of the leg then cushion like an elastic device
the patient finds the second option more demanding
the caregiver grants that tiredness but judges it better than wearing out the joint tissue
a noisy return to the ground points to a badly controlled cushioning
a quiet return to the ground reveals a mastered movement
text: The physical therapist was laying out for his patient two different ways of meeting the ground after a jump. The first one, he said, means coming down on straight legs: the shock then travels up with nothing in its way, right to the hips, and the knee joint has to take in almost the whole of it. The second one asks you to bend the hips and the knees the moment your feet touch, so that the muscles of the thigh brake the descent the way a spring would. The patient objected that the second method felt more tiring to him. The therapist granted him that readily, then added that tired muscle costs a great deal less than worn cartilage. He closed on a difference that beginners tend to blur: a loud landing tells you the ground took charge, while a quiet landing shows an athlete steering the whole thing himself.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: old physical activities are sorted into categories by the specialists
the sorting rests on the aim pursued
the first category sets two wrestlers against each other on a narrow surface
such contests are found in almost every society that settled for good
the second category gathers the speed trials over various lengths
these trials put the honor of the community at stake
the third category concerns throwing an object far away
the vocabulary of those movements survives in the disciplines of today
the fourth category brings together the ball games with local rules
these practices combined exercise ceremony and the settling of quarrels
text: Old games of movement sort themselves into distinct families, which researchers tell apart by their purpose. There are, to begin with, the trials of strength, where two opponents grapple and try to unbalance each other inside a narrow space; they turn up almost everywhere that societies settled down for good. Next come the races, run over lengths that varied widely, often barefoot, and loaded with prestige for a whole settlement. A third family gathers the throws, in which a stone, a shaft or a disc is hurled as far as the arm allows, and whose movements have handed their vocabulary down to the sports we practice now. A fourth brings together the ball games, whose rules shifted from one valley to the next. Historians add that such practices mixed exercise, ceremony and the settling of quarrels, with no clean line between them.

units: the contraction of a muscle obeys an ordered series of steps
the thinking organ sends an electrical impulse when an intention appears
that impulse travels along a nerve conductor
a chemical product is released at the contact zone with the fiber
very fine elements slide past each other and shorten the fiber
the attaching cord then pulls on the bony piece
the limb moves because of that pull
the filaments loosen once the movement is over
the whole process takes a very short span of time
breathing speeds up when the fibers run short of energy
text: A muscle that contracts follows a strictly ordered set of steps. It all starts in the brain, which fires an electrical signal the instant an intention to move takes shape. That signal runs down a nerve, reaches the junction where the nerve meets the fiber, and releases a chemical there. The fiber answers at once: minute filaments slide past one another and pull the whole thing shorter. The tendon, dragged by that contraction, hauls on the bone it grips, and so the limb travels. As soon as the movement ends, the filaments let go and the fiber stretches back out. The whole sequence takes a fraction of a second, and it repeats thousands of times over a single run. When it races, the runner begins to gasp, because the fibers are calling for fuel faster than breathing can bring it.

units: the narrator was coming back from a swimming session in the evening
he chose a narrow path running past a storage building
the recent rain made the slope slippery
he thought he would gain speed by going down rather than avoiding the slope
his foot skidded on a hidden root
he fell and landed in the mud
his open bag let his things spill out
he had to drag himself along the ground to gather his things one by one
a passer-by handed him back a cloth without speaking
he now takes the paved route
text: The other night, heading home from the pool, I had the bright idea of cutting along the path that runs past the warehouse. It had rained, the slope was greasy, and I told myself I would get down it faster than I would get around it. So I let my legs go, and my left foot skated off a root I never saw. I stumbled, flailed like a puppet, and landed flat in the mud with my bag hanging open. Because the bag was open, my things rolled off everywhere, and because my things rolled off everywhere, I had to crawl around gathering them one at a time. A man out for a stroll handed me my towel without a word, working very hard at not laughing. I got home soaked, caked in drying mud, and thoroughly humiliated. Now I take the paved road around, and I put a lot less pride into my shortcuts.

units: going back to running after an ankle injury worries ordinary practitioners
a badly rehabilitated joint gives way at the first badly placed step
coaches put forward an approach in four phases
the first phase consists of holding oneself up on the injured leg
that posture lasts about thirty calm breathing cycles
the second phase repeats the exercise with the eyes closed
closing the eyes removes the visual cues and calls on the receptors of the joint
the third phase brings in short hops in place with rotation of the hips
the last phase offers gentle strides with a gradual lengthening
any sharp pain calls for a stop and a return to the earlier phase
text: Going back to running after a sprain frightens most amateur athletes, and the fear is well founded: a foot joint that has not been retrained properly gives way the first time you land crooked. The routine coaches recommend comes in four stages. Start by balancing on the injured foot, arms loose along your sides, for roughly thirty calm breaths. Move on to the same position with your eyes shut, which strips the balance of every visual cue and forces the deep sensors of the foot to wake up. Then add short hops in place, turning the hips as you go and keeping the heel from drifting outward. Finish with slow strides on even ground, stretching the distance out from one session to the next. Stop everything the moment a sharp pain shows up, and pick the previous stage back up the day after.

units: two groups of runners share the same sports facility at the end of the day
the training goes on as night comes closer
the speed runners have a massive build and thick legs
they put out a violent effort over a short run of strides
they then come to a stop with their breath short
the long-distance runners are thinner and go round without a break
their breathing follows a steady rhythm
the speed specialists recover by walking
a woman in charge of the training watches both camps
she notes that one side stares at the measuring device and the other at the sky
text: The track smells of wet dust, and two groups of runners share it as the daylight goes. On one side, the sprinters: thick-set, heavy through the thighs, waiting dead still, then bursting into some thirty strides and stopping short, chests heaving, hands planted on their hips. On the other, the distance runners: leaner, looser, circling without a break, their torsos quiet, their breathing metered out like a clock. The first spend everything in one brief flare, then walk the fatigue off along the railing. The second hoard every movement and hardly ever stop. A coach watches both camps from the finish line and remarks that the sprinters keep their eyes on the timing device while the distance runners keep theirs on the sky. What they run, she says, shows in the way they carry their tiredness.

units: the hall can be entered before the sun comes up
the person in charge lays out equipment on the floor before the group arrives
the participants leave their belongings near the partition
the warm-up pairs a walk with a run
handclaps set the pace of the jumps
a ball-returning drill is done in pairs
the session ends with seated stretching
each student's progress is written down
text: The gym unlocks its doors while the sky is still dark, and the wooden floor gives off a faint damp shine. A short, thickset coach lays out hoops along the center line, then sets a row of low cones beside them. Students file in, drop their bags against the partition, and pull on shoes with pale soles. Warm-up starts with a wide, swinging walk, arms stretched toward the ceiling, and turns into an easy jog around the room. Jumps follow: feet together first, then alternating, while the coach claps out the beat. Next come passes in pairs, each player sending the ball straight back without ever holding it. At the close, everyone sits in a circle and stretches the calves. The coach writes down what each student has managed, then opens the windows to air the room before the next group turns up.

units: the writer finds it contradictory to demand activity while removing open space
school play areas are shrinking in size
empty ground is turned into parking
trips on foot vanish in the name of traffic danger
young children run out of breath on the first flight climbed
the writer blames the surroundings rather than any lack of will
a child with no practice on rough ground absorbs falls badly
the fear of falling deepens the stillness further
the writer asks above all for school surroundings that can be walked
text: We tell children to move more, and then we take away the places where moving is possible. That contradiction wears on me. Schoolyards keep shrinking, empty lots turn into parking, and walking anywhere has been ruled out because the streets count as dangerous. So we get kids who wheeze on the first flight of stairs and tense up the moment an unfamiliar effort is asked of them. Call it what it is: not laziness, but a result. A child who has never run over broken ground cannot absorb a fall. He lands badly, hurts himself, and grows afraid. Fear pins him down harder still, and the loop closes. By all means, add supervised sessions. But make the streets around the schools walkable first. Movement is learned by walking, climbing, and tripping, not only inside a slot penciled onto a timetable.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the head of the swimming group first failed as a competitor
her uneven stroke lost her ground at the turns
she considered leaving the sport
a medical practitioner found a fault in her shoulder position
that fault came from growing too fast
she spent a whole season reworking her technique with video support
her race times came down after the correction
she forbids heavy repetition while the posture is wrong
text: Before she ever ran a group, the swimming coach at the town pool went through a long run of failures. As a teenager she swam length after length without improving, held back at every turn by a jerky, uneven stroke. Her results flattened out, and she came close to leaving the water for good. It took a sports doctor to spot the trouble: a shoulder sitting wrong, the leftover of a growth spurt. Rather than push harder, she gave a whole season to relearning her catch, filmed from below the surface, adjusting where her hand entered the water by fractions. The stroke grew long and steady, and her times fell. Now she puts the same method to work with the swimmers she trains. Film, show, fix one thing per session. She bans endless sets until the position is right, and her group has real staying power.

units: the writer used two different climbing sites in the same season
the first occupies an old and poorly lit building
its holds are smooth from constant use
the routes of the first site call for balance more than pulling
the second site is colorful and its routes change every week
the second encourages bounding and showy movement
the writer prefers the dark site without calling it better
he explains that choice by the attention he must give his feet
text: Two climbing halls took my money in the same season, and nothing about them matches. The first sits under an old market roof and keeps the gloom of a place nobody bothered to repaint. Its holds are worn down, polished by countless palms, and the routes force you to hunt for balance far more than to pull. You climb there slowly, almost without a word, and come down with your forearms burning. The second hall bursts with color. The walls run high, the mats lie thick, and fresh routes go up every week. Everything there invites a leap, a lunge, a movement worth watching. A seasoned climber will find patience in the first and a playground in the second. My preference goes to the dark hall, though I would not call it the better one: it makes me listen to my feet, while the other flatters my arms.

units: the writer sets out on request the method followed since taking the sport up again
he records the length and the speed of every outing
he takes his heart rate on waking while still lying down
he does strength work twice a week without heavy loads
he uses two pairs of shoes according to how long the outing is
he advises drinking before thirst appears
he halts his progression when two sessions in a row feel like a burden
he credits this tracking with the absence of new injuries
text: You asked me to lay out the routine I have followed since starting up again, so here it is, item by item. Load first: every outing goes in the book, total time, average pace, how the last stretch felt. Recovery next: I watch my sleep and take my pulse the moment I wake, still flat on my back. Strength work comes twice a week and no more. Side planks, calf raises, hip extensions, never anything close to a maximum weight. Shoes: two pairs in rotation, a light one for the short outings, a cushioned one for the long ones. Food holds no surprises, apart from one habit, which is drinking before thirst shows up. Mood, last of all: two outings in a row that feel like a chore and I stop pushing. The notebook is an ugly thing, but it holds me upright and has kept me clear of any fresh injury.

units: one question concerns the youngest age for carrying a load
before school age no added weight is needed
the very young child works with his own weight by climbing
the next stage puts the quality of movement above resistance
a light object and a reflection are enough at that stage
the gear has to match the child's build
an adult's equipment must not be taken over
two short training sessions are worth more than one very long one
the exercise stops as soon as the hold of the back gives way
text: A listener writes in to ask how young a child can be and still lift a load safely. The answer runs in stages, and taking them in order is what matters. Before school age, no outside weight serves any purpose whatsoever. The child already has his own body, and he shifts it around well enough by climbing and by rolling. Then comes a stretch of years where learning the movement itself outranks any question of resistance. A light stick and a mirror will do far more good than a loaded bar. A second question concerns the gear, which has to fit the child's own frame and must never simply be borrowed from a grown-up. A third asks about frequency, and a single rule covers it: two short, regular sessions beat one that drags on and on. Watchfulness comes last, and it has to stay sharp. The moment the back starts to round, the exercise ends.

units: a young athlete reports knee pain after three climbs
he had doubled the length of his routes within a week
the coach explains that tendons come along more slowly than breathing capacity
the pain comes from that gap in adaptation
the young man believed himself able to take more
the coach points out that the feeling of ease comes before the tissue grows strong
they agree on a lighter restart and a modest weekly increase
the coach weighs the cost of an ignored injury against that of a short pause
text: A teenager told his coach that his knee began to burn as soon as he reached the third climb of the day. The coach asked him what had changed in his training, and the boy admitted that he had doubled the length of his runs inside a single week. Tendons, the coach said, come along a good deal more slowly than lungs do, and the pain sat right there in the gap between them. The boy answered that he still felt perfectly able to take on more. What feels easy, he was told, arrives well before the tissue is ready for it, and that is exactly what fools beginners. So the two of them settled on a lighter restart, with only a small step up from one week to the next. The boy wanted to know how long that would go on. An injury waved off costs you a season, the coach answered, while caution accepted costs you a handful of outings.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: mail carriers once crossed high ground with no path and no pack animal
one man alone wore himself out before reaching the far end
the letter risked arriving late or being lost
the answer found was to pass the load on
stopping places were set at equal distance
each stop held a rested carrier who left without waiting
the overall speed of the transport was doubled
the carriers stopped holding back since their share was short
this principle of splitting an impossible effort still serves elsewhere
text: Picture messengers who had to cross whole valleys on foot, with no road cut for them and no animal to carry the weight. The work broke bodies, and the flaw in it stated itself plainly enough: one man alone collapses short of the far end, and the letter comes too late or never comes at all. The answer they found was the relay. Shelters went up at an even spacing, each one holding a fresh runner who took the leather pouch and set off again at once. The stretch to be covered in one go turned bearable, and the speed of the whole doubled. Better still, the runners quit saving themselves. Knowing their share was short, they ran it flat out. And there the idea appears that still serves us, from hauling goods to racing in teams: cut an impossible effort into portions a body can hold.

units: what tells the two runners apart is how muscle energy is used
the speed runner has mostly fast-contracting fibers
those fibers are powerful but burn out within moments
the distance runner has fine and slow fibers
those fibers use oxygen without tiring
the speed runner builds a breathing debt that he repays after the effort
the distance runner sets his pace to keep that debt from opening
their training differs between repeated starts and long outings
how the fibers are shared out depends partly on inheritance
text: What sets a sprinter apart from a distance runner, if not the way the muscles spend their energy? The sprinter draws on fast fibers, thick ones, good for a contraction that is short and powerful but dies out almost at once. The distance runner carries slow fibers instead, finer and less quick, which burn oxygen and hardly tire at all. A sprinter produces his force with next to no air, and pays the debt afterward, gasping at the line. The other one holds a pace that never lets that debt open up in the first place. Training shows the split as well. One piles up starts and full recoveries, the other stacks long outings at a steady effort. Work tips the balance one way or the other without ever turning it over, because the share of each fiber type is handed down in part at birth.

units: the narrator recalls a walk along a soaked ridge line
the soles made a sucking noise in the mud
a stone came down the face during the climb
the walk was led by an elderly woman at a steady pace
the other walkers came up scattered
reaching the top happened all at once
a strong wind dried the clothing in a moment
the way down took a gentler side and passed without a word
text: Up on the ridge the mud made every footfall slide out from under us, and that outing has stayed with me above all the others. There was the noise first of all. The suck of soles pulling free, the breath cut short, a single stone rolling off the face into empty air. There was the woman out in front, well past retirement age, climbing without once altering her rhythm, as though the slope had nothing whatever to do with her. There was the group strung out behind her, each of us matching the pace to our own tiredness. And there was the crest, arriving all at once, with a wind that dried our jackets in a handful of seconds. We went down the far side, gentler, telling each other nothing. That silence was worth more than any story, and it comes back whenever a climb looks too steep.

units: a wall painting decays because its support soaks up water
the colored layer flakes away from the wall
the damage comes from the support and not from the paint
the first step is to draw the moisture out of the wall
compresses pull the salts out of the wall
the loose fragments are set back down with a liquid adhesive
the losses are filled with fine hatching that can be spotted up close
the missing decoration is not painted back in
text: Picture a painted wall shedding itself while you watch. The plaster drinks in the damp, the color lifts, and the wall painting some long-gone workshop laid down there crumbles into dust. Blame almost never falls on the paint. The trouble sits behind it, in a support that swells and shifts. So the conservators dry the wall out first, slowly, laying on compresses that pull the salts up out of the masonry. Then they go after the flakes, one at a time, slipping a thin liquid adhesive under every lifted chip until it settles back down. Brushes come last, and barely. They fill the losses with fine hatching, close-set strokes that anyone leaning in can spot for what they are. No serious workshop paints the lost decoration back in. You stabilize, you fill, you leave the wound legible, and the work stands there owning up to what happened to it.

units: an exhibition separates the finished work and its preparatory drawings into two rooms
the finished painting is shown alone on a dark wall
visitors speak quietly in front of the finished painting
the preparatory drawings are hung close together and show second thoughts
the public stops longer in front of the preparatory drawings
the preparatory drawings start conversations between visitors
a teacher believes her students finally grasp that creation happens step by step
the organizer of the exhibition hesitated to show the working documents
text: The split hits you at the door. One room holds the finished painting and nothing else, hung alone on a dark wall, lit hard from above, and people drop their voices as they walk in. The next room does the opposite. The preparatory drawings crowd the wall, pinned edge to edge, full of second thoughts, lines abandoned halfway, thumb smudges along the margins. The guards will tell you where the crowd actually stops. The finished canvas gets silence. The sketches get talk, strangers pointing things out to one another. A teacher who came with her class put it plainly. Her students had finally understood that a picture is not handed over whole, that it gropes and fails and starts again. The man who built the show admits he nearly kept that second room shut, afraid of stripping the wonder off the thing he was showing.

units: the modeling material must first be softened under the hands
the air bubbles are driven out by slamming the mass on a hard surface
a dull sound shows that the air has been forced out
the thumbs hollow the piece out from the center
the fingers draw the wall upward
the drying happens in the shade under a damp cloth
drafts must be avoided while the piece dries
the cut base must be wider than the piece
a plaster cast makes it possible to copy the shape once the surface is dry
text: Wake the clay up before anything else. It comes out of the bag cold and closed, and it gives way only once your palms have worked it over, slowly, without forcing. Air comes next. Slam the mass down on a hard bench, again and again, and listen for the ring to go flat and dull, which is how you know the bubbles are gone. Now open the form. Your thumbs sink in at the center while your fingers travel up the outside and coax the wall taller. Then comes the part that impatience ruins. Dry the piece in the shade, under a damp cloth, well away from any draft that would pull the water out of one side first. Cut the base wider than the body, because anything meant to stand needs an honest footing. Want a copy? Take a plaster cast, but hold off until the surface feels dry against your hand.

units: the window was taken down panel by panel
every element was plotted on a measured drawing before it was removed
the glass was cleaned with demineralized water in the workshop
the cleaning had to spare the dark painted layer
the broken glass was joined with resin under a magnifying instrument
a resin bond cannot be undone afterward
a second window was set in front of the original to shield it from swings of heat
the new metal network is thinner than the previous one
the reinstallation has to be finished before the cold season
text: Work opened with the window coming down, panel by panel, every piece plotted on a measured drawing before it was eased out of its lead frame. The glass then traveled to the workshop, where a wash of demineralized water lifted the crusted deposits without touching the dark painted layer underneath. The hard part followed. Fractured pieces were joined with resin under a magnifier, a bond that nobody will ever be able to take apart again. The team then settled, after some argument, on an outer glazing, a second window set in front of the original to shield it from swings of heat and from condensation. Reassembly came after that, in fresh lead drawn narrower than the old strips, so the drawing could read again as it once did. The site office says the panels will be back in place before the cold season.

units: the performance room sits on the top floor of an old building
its wooden frame is left exposed
the wood soaks up part of the low sounds and softens harsh tones
the side walls lean slightly
the lean of the walls sends the sound back toward the middle rows
listeners far from the stage hear almost as well as those at the front
the low ceiling shortens the reverberation
spoken voices come through more clearly while large ensembles lose their fullness
the programming mostly holds small groups and readings
text: The room sits under the roof of an old building, and the bare timber frame decides how everything sounds inside it. Wood answers to low notes, taking a share of that energy out of the air and rounding off whatever is harsh in a tone. The side walls lean in a little, which throws the reflections back toward the middle of the seating, so a listener at the rear hears roughly what the front row hears. The low ceiling cuts the other way. It shortens the tail of the reverberation, which sharpens spoken words and thins out anything played by a large group. The programming follows from all of that without much argument. Small ensembles, solo recitals and readings fill the calendar, while heavy forces stay away, because the room would only turn them into a blur. Here the building chooses the repertoire.

units: the largest share of museum collections stays out of the exhibition rooms
a shortage of space and of means explains this situation
one answer is to digitize the stored holdings on a large scale
digitizing makes a piece shut in a drawer visible from far away
another answer is to lend works out for a limited term
these loans help institutions that cannot afford to buy pieces
the writer holds that both answers must be carried out together
the two answers meet different needs
text: Almost everything a museum owns sits in storage, and almost none of it ever comes back up the stairs. This is no secret. What hangs on the walls is a sliver of what the building holds, and the reason is dull rather than sinister: too little room, too few hands, too little money. Two answers keep circulating. Digitize the stores on a large scale, so that a print shut in a drawer can be studied by someone who will never walk through the door. Or send the objects out on loan, for a fixed term, to smaller places that could never afford to buy anything comparable. Both are worth doing, and doing at once, because they satisfy different hungers. One feeds study and curiosity at a distance. The other puts a person in a room with the object itself. Refusing to choose has a price. Letting a whole store sleep has a steeper one.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the craftsman compares his trade to a discipline of patience
he used to draw on a screen
a mistake made on a screen was undone with no consequence
the metal he engraves allows no correction
this constraint made him more demanding, as he sees it
on a screen he worked fast and dropped his difficult ideas
on the plate he thinks before every cut
a cut driven too deep ruins weeks of effort
his daughter is learning to draw on a computer and teases him about his method
text: The engraver in the back workshop calls his trade a patience sport. He spent years drawing on a screen, where a wrong line vanished with a keystroke and cost him nothing whatever. The burin put a stop to that. Metal forgives nothing, he says, laughing, and that is exactly what made him better at the work. He likes setting the two side by side. On the screen he turned out plenty and turned it out fast, but he dropped any idea the moment it fought back. On the plate he sits and thinks before every cut, because one stroke driven too deep throws away weeks of work. His daughter, who is learning to draw on a computer, teases him for it and calls him a cave dweller. He tells her he will teach her engraving once she has learned to wait, and that waiting will look less like a punishment then.

units: the writer keeps three successes and one flaw in this exhibition
the low picture rails force the visitor to step close to the works
this closeness changes how the small formats are perceived
the labels are short and free of jargon
the labels describe a technique instead of commenting on a feeling
a quiet sound track carries workshop noises
these noises stand in for background music
the lighting is too even and flattens the relief of the thick materials
the writer advises a visit late in the day when the sun comes through the high windows
text: Three things carry this show, and one thing drags it down. Start with the hanging itself. The rails sit low, low enough that you have to step in close, and that short distance rewrites how the smaller formats read. Then the labels, cut short and scrubbed of jargon, telling you how a thing was made instead of instructing you on what to feel about it. Then the sound, kept faint, a blade scraping across a palette, the creak of an easel being shoved aside. Workshop noise, in other words, and it makes far better company than any piped music. The flaw is the lighting, spread so evenly across the walls that it flattens every ridge of paint on the heaviest pieces. Come back late in the day, when raking sun reaches in through the upper windows, and you will see what the hanging failed to give you.

units: the writer is writing from a performance hall that is still empty
he arrived late at his first class in the fall
he had sworn never to go back on stage
he came back every week through the cold season
his loyalty came first from stubbornness and then from pleasure
the director of the troupe gave him the part of an old caretaker
that part says little and watches the others
the performance the evening before played to a full house
the person he is writing to had urged him to sign up for the class
the writer invites the person he is writing to the closing performance
text: I am writing to you from the empty hall, before the others arrive. Do you remember my first class, back in the fall? I turned up late, coat still buttoned, swearing afterward that nothing would ever drag me onstage again. Through the cold months I kept turning up regardless, week after week, out of sheer stubbornness at first and afterward out of genuine pleasure. When we began staging, the director of the troupe handed me the old caretaker, the one who says almost nothing and watches everybody else. Last night we played to a full house. I felt the silence close over my first line like water going still. This is not boasting. I am writing because you pushed me toward that class, one evening when I insisted nothing amused me anymore. Come to the closing night. I am keeping you a seat down front.

units: the browning of old paper comes from the raw material itself
a pulp made from wood holds a substance that oxidizes in light and air
this oxidation gives off acids that break down the cellulose
the round brown stains come from excess damp together with spores
a fungus feeds on the size held in the sheet
washing lifts these stains only in part
an alkaline bath cancels the acids that are present
this bath leaves a protective reserve in the sheet
a sealed frame mount limits the warping that travel causes
text: People ask us all the time why an old print turns brown. The answer sits in the fiber. Once the pulp carries wood, it carries lignin along with it, and lignin reacts to light and open air, then gives off acids that eat away at the cellulose. What about the brown stains, the ones with a ring around them? Those need damp air and a few spores. A mold settles in, feeds on the size in the sheet, and leaves a mark that washing will only lighten. So what does a conservation workshop do about it? It deacidifies in an alkaline bath, which cancels the acids already at work and leaves a small buffer stock behind in the paper. And if the work has to travel? It goes into a neutral mount inside a sealed frame, since every shift in the surrounding damp makes the fiber move and deepens the cockling.

units: a neighbor tells about an evening spent in a theater
she sets two theaters she goes to regularly against each other
in the first theater, the stage elements are painted on wide canvases
in the second theater, movable panels are shifted in front of the audience
the neighbor prefers the theater that makes her forget she is watching a performance
her brother prefers the theater where the stage machinery stays visible
the two of them often argue about this question without ever agreeing
the neighbor ends up granting that each of the two methods calls for a skill of its own
she invites the person she is talking to to come and judge for himself at the next showing
text: My neighbor came back from the theater last night and could not stop comparing the two houses she goes to. At the first one, she said, the scenery is painted on huge canvases, and the moment the curtain lifts you believe you are standing in an old square. At the second, everything rides on rolling panels that the crew pushes around in full view, so the audience sits and watches the change happen right in front of them. She loves the first house more, because it lets her forget she is watching something made up. Her brother takes the other side, the one where the machinery stays out in the open. The two of them come back to the argument constantly, and they never settle it. In the end she granted that each way asks for a skill of its own. Then she offered to take me along next time, so I could decide for myself.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
