units: ancient builders handed down a set of forms that architects still reuse
the upright support carries the load and divides up the space inside
the rounded vault answers the need to roof a wide room with no support in the middle
the curve of this vault carries the thrust out toward thick walls
the carved band runs under the roof
this band puts into pictures the stories the community wanted to pass on
the grand staircase serves to stage the arrival of the visitor
specialists explain the spread of these forms by the travels of masters and apprentices
text: Across almost every continent, ancient builders left behind a stock of forms that architects still put to use. The column comes first: it carries the load, gives rhythm to the space inside, and offers the eye something to rest on. The dome follows, born of the wish to roof a wide room with nothing holding it up in the middle; its curve pushes the thrust out toward the thick walls that ring it. The frieze fills the narrow band running under the roof, and in repeated figures it tells the stories a community meant to pass on. Last comes the grand staircase, which does more than carry people upward: it stages the arrival of the visitor. Scholars who study these buildings point out that such elements traveled from one workshop to the next as masters and apprentices moved around.

units: the making of a woven hanging goes through several steps in a row
a painter first makes a small drawing that settles the colors and the composition
this drawing is then copied out at full size on a guiding sheet
this sheet is set behind the threads to steer the hand of the craftsman
the wools are dyed before the weaving
the craftsman writes down the recipe of each dye bath so as to find the shade again later
the weaving is done on the back of the piece
the threads are cut and the edges bound when the piece leaves the loom
the workshop only discovers the final look after turning the work over
text: A tapestry never comes out of a single gesture. It starts with a small drawing, where the painter settles the colors and the placing of the figures. That drawing is then blown up onto a full-size sheet, which the weaver hangs behind the threads to guide the hand. Before any weaving, the wools go through the dye vats, and the craftsman writes down the recipe for each bath so the same shade can be found again much later. The weaving is done from the back, which forces the weaver to picture a front she will not see until the end. She moves along row after row, unhurried, following the outline that shows faintly through the work. When the piece leaves the loom, the threads are cut, the edges are bound, and the work is turned over at last. Only then does the workshop see what it has made.

units: the instrument of a student had lost its biting sound
the maker first ruled out the heaviest damage to the instrument
the belly had no crack and the pegs held the tuning
the examination then moved to the bow, whose hair had been drawn too tight
too much tension cuts down the contact between the hair and the string
this reduction makes the attack soft and thins the sound in the upper registers
the maker loosened the frog, sanded the stick and laid on fresh rosin
the student found the sound again from the first notes
the workshop wrote the case down because this fault returns when a quick adjustment stands in for a full examination
text: A student's instrument had lost its bite, and nobody could say why the voice had gone dull. The maker she took it to began by ruling out the worst possibilities: the belly showed no crack, the soundpost stood straight under the bridge, the pegs held the tuning. He then turned his attention to the bow, whose hair had been drawn far too tight after a rehairing. Too much tension cuts down the contact between hair and string, so the attack turns soft and the tone thins out in the upper registers. He loosened the frog, sanded the stick lightly, and laid on fresh rosin. From the first notes the student recognized the sound she thought she had lost. The workshop wrote the case down in its records, because this same fault comes back whenever a quick adjustment stands in for a full examination.

units: playing a stubborn piece all the way through again makes the difficulty worse instead of solving it
the advised method is to cut out the passage that causes trouble
the exact bar where the hand hesitates must be found and marked
the fragment must be played very slowly and with each hand apart
attention goes to the position of the fingers and not to the page
the speed grows by successive steps
one must drop back to the previous step as soon as a mistake occurs
the fragment must then be joined to the neighboring bars because the difficulty often sits in the seam
this approach keeps one from fixing a wrong motion that would have to be unlearned
text: When a piece of music resists, playing the whole thing over and over makes the trouble worse instead of clearing it. The advised method is to cut out the passage that fails and treat it as a thing apart. First find the exact bar where the hand hesitates, and put a pencil mark beside it. Then play that fragment very slowly, hands apart, watching where the fingers land on the keys rather than following the page. Raise the speed step by step, and drop back to the previous step the moment a mistake shows up. Finally join the fragment to the bars on either side, since the trouble often sits in the seam. Close the session by playing the whole thing through without stopping. The whole approach takes patience, but it keeps you from fixing a wrong motion that would later have to be unlearned.

units: two neighboring concert halls have chosen opposite strategies to renew their audience
the first hall has shortened its programs and dropped the break in the middle
tickets there cost less and dress is left free
the players of this first hall introduce the works themselves from the stage
the second hall has lengthened its break and turned it into a meeting with the audience
the listeners of the second hall may come down to question the performers
both managements report attendance on the rise
the first hall draws occasional visitors while the second builds up subscribers
a regional study will compare these results at the end of the season
text: Two concert halls in the same town have taken opposite routes to renew their audience. The first has cut its programs short and dropped the interval, on the view that listeners who have just discovered the form sit poorly through a broken evening. Tickets cost less there, dress is up to you, and the players introduce the works themselves from the stage. The second went the other way: it stretched the break in the middle and turned it into a meeting, where the audience comes down to the pit and puts questions to the performers. Both managements claim attendance is up, yet the crowds are not the same. The short-format hall pulls in one-off visitors drawn by curiosity, while the other builds a body of subscribers. A regional study will compare the two records at the end of the season.

units: an old market hall has been turned into an arts house
the entrance lobby holds posters and an upright piano open to everyone
the pottery room houses shelves loaded with unfinished bowls
the makers of these bowls come back in the evening to finish them
the dance room has kept its original floor, which creaks underfoot
a narrow room at the back serves as a recording studio
rugs fixed to the walls stand in for soundproofing the place could not afford
the upper floor holds a collection of sheet music lent out against a signature
benches have been put on the roof to give a place to rest
text: Push open the door of the old market hall that became the arts house, and the first thing you meet is the lobby, cluttered with posters and an upright piano anyone can try. To the left, the pottery room smells of wet clay; the shelves sag under unfinished bowls that their makers come back to finish in the evening. Across from it, the dance room kept its original floor, and the boards creak so loudly that the students count their steps by the sound. At the back, a narrow room serves as a recording studio: rugs nailed to the walls stand in for the soundproofing nobody could ever afford. Upstairs sits the sheet-music library, whose scores go out on a signature and no deposit. And up on the roof, someone put in benches, because people needed somewhere to breathe between two sessions.

units: in the older forms of song, the storytelling part came first
the repeated part held a short and secondary role there
broadcasting turned this order upside down
a listener with half an ear had to be able to name a track very quickly
the repeated part grew until it opened the song
listening platforms have pushed this shift further
their payment kicks in after a very short stretch
the writer of the text judges this shift to be impoverishing
the writer holds that stubborn creators are already showing that the constraint can be escaped
text: Take the popular song and follow it forward from its oldest shapes. At the start the verse carried the story and the chorus was a place to rest: short, almost an afterthought. Then broadcasting over the air flipped that order, because a listener with half an ear had to know a track within a few seconds, and the chorus swelled until it opened the song. Streaming services pushed that logic further still, since payment kicks in after a very brief stretch of listening. What we get now is a body of work where the hook comes before everything else and the story fades out. You can welcome this and see a sharper efficiency in it. What I see is a loss: a form that gives up on lasting gives up on surprising too. The most stubborn writers among them are already proving that the constraint can be escaped.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the workshop calls this specialist the restorer of wall paintings
her mother cleaned the display cases of a regional museum
she went along with her mother as a child
those hours gave her a taste for damaged surfaces
she studied the chemistry of solvents before taking up drawing
she refuses to act as long as the source of the damage has not been found
her colleagues fault her for her slowness
she answers that haste has destroyed more paintings than damp
her methods have been spreading among the younger ones since a whole room was put in her charge
text: In the workshop they call her the restorer of the wall paintings, and the title says little about the stubbornness the work demands. As a child she tagged along with her mother, who washed the display cases in a regional museum; and those hours gave her a taste for damaged surfaces. Because she could not bear to watch faces vanish under grime, she learned the chemistry of solvents before she learned to draw. That detour explains her manner: she treats each wall like a patient and refuses to touch it until she has found what caused the harm. Her colleagues complain that she works too slowly, and she answers that haste has destroyed more paintings than damp ever did. Since a whole room was put in her charge, her methods have been spreading among the younger hands who work in the house.

units: a retrospective given over to the art of glass raises an objection of a technical order
the pieces on show sit on low plinths and are lit from above
this lighting flattens the thicknesses instead of bringing them out
the visitor loses the reading of the inner layers of the objects
the cases have been lined up against the partitions
glass calls for a neutral ground and light coming from behind
the critic suggests pulling the plinths away from the wall and adding diffusing panels
he also advises bringing down the color temperature of the sources
he recommends going over the hang again before the announced tour
text: The retrospective given over to glass raises a technical objection the general reviewers let pass. The pieces sit on low plinths and are lit from above; that grazing light flattens the thicknesses instead of bringing them out, and the visitor loses the reading of the inner layers, which is what this work has to offer. The fault lies in the layout: the cases have been lined up against the partitions, when glass calls for a neutral ground and light coming from behind. A remedy exists and has been tried elsewhere. It would be enough to pull the plinths away from the wall, put diffusing panels behind each object, and bring down the color temperature of the sources. The route would gain as well, since visitors are now forced along a single wall. The hang deserves a second look before the announced tour.

units: the writer of the message answers a question about what he is doing
a first workshop teaches him to shape hollow figures in clay
the instructor finds his movements still too hurried
a second room is used for casting and smells of damp material
the writer spends whole afternoons there smoothing surfaces
one space is devoted to making jointed puppets
the room at the back hosts rehearsals and heats up under its lamp
the writer invites his correspondent to come and see for himself
text: You asked what I actually do at that arts center, so here is the whole rundown. First comes the clay room, where I am learning to build hollow figures; the instructor keeps telling me my hands move too fast. Next door is the casting room, which smells of damp plaster and has buckets lined up along the wall. I spend entire afternoons in there, sanding surfaces until they turn smooth under my palm. Then there is the puppet corner: we carve heads out of soft wood, paint the eyes on, stitch tiny clothes together. And at the very back sits a room for stage runs, with a lamp overhead that heats up so badly we crack the window between scenes. I never expected to get attached to a place like that, and now I cannot stand to miss a session. Come by and see it for yourself, and you will understand right away.

units: a restoration specialist is questioned about a damaged painting
she noticed the poor condition of the work as soon as it arrived
the yellowed protective layer flattened the light colors
the work begins with a careful examination lasting several weeks
this examination locates the places where the paint layer is lifting
the cleaning advances in very small portions
the added retouching can be removed and does not cover the original
the features of the face became legible again after a single session
the work is then placed in a space where humidity is controlled
text: When did you realize the painting was in trouble? The conservator says she knew the moment it came out of its crate: the varnish had yellowed so badly that it flattened every light color. Where do you start with a case like that? With the examination, she answers, weeks of work under a magnifier, mapping every spot where the paint layer has begun to lift. Cleaning follows, done in very small patches, with cotton swabs rolled fresh and thrown away constantly. Then the retouching, which never covers the original: fine strokes, all of them removable, laid only into the losses. Did the outcome surprise you? She smiles and admits that the features of the face, once lost in a brown haze, came back in a single sitting. And where does the painting go now? Behind glass, into a room where the humidity is watched around the clock.

units: a sculptor stops working to question his student
the student finds that the block of stone resists her
each of her blows detaches an unexpected chip
the master explains that stone has veins running in one direction
striking across these veins makes the surface split
he advises drawing the shape in charcoal first
he recommends removing material in layers while walking around the block
the student judges this method exhausting
the next day the shape advances and the chipping has stopped
text: The sculptor set down his mallet and asked why she had gone quiet. The stone was fighting her, the apprentice said; every blow she landed tore off a flake she had not expected. He explained that the block ran in veins, and that striking a vein at an angle would split the whole surface open. Because she was cutting without listening to the grain, the stone took its revenge. He told her to lay the outline down in charcoal first, then to take the material off in thin layers, walking around the block as she went. The apprentice complained that working that slowly wore her out. The sculptor smiled: stone forgives nothing you remove, he said, so haste costs more than patience. She picked up her chisel and said nothing. The next day she reported that the flaking had stopped and the shape was finally rising. He nodded without looking up, because he had heard it coming in the ring of the metal.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: reproducing images once required a draftsman for every copy
two copies made by hand were never alike
cutting a metal plate solved this problem of fidelity
ink held in the grooves is laid on the paper under pressure
cutting the metal with a burin took weeks and an expert hand
the plate was then covered with a protective coat and the metal attacked with acid
a light needle was then enough to open the line
this method made the line more supple and the tones came from the density of the cuts
text: Getting pictures into circulation once ran into a hard physical limit: every single copy needed the hand of a draftsman, and no two copies ever came out alike. Engraving was what settled the matter. A polished metal plate was cut into with a burin, loaded with greasy ink and then wiped clean, and whatever ink stayed down in the grooves transferred onto the sheet under the press. Fidelity was solved, but another difficulty opened up in its place, since carving a plate that way took weeks of labor and a very steady hand. So the metal was eaten away with acid instead, under a coat of varnish that a light needle could scratch through. Someone clumsy with a burin could now engrave in his own handwriting. Lines grew supple, tones came from how densely the hatching was packed, and the image traveled at last far from whoever had made it.

units: two distinct methods are used to decorate a wall
the first consists of painting on plaster that is still damp
the color sets into the lime as it dries
the painter has a single session before it hardens
the drawing is prepared in advance and transferred from a pricked model
the second method sets colored fragments into mortar
the craftsman can stop and take the work up again later
rounded shapes are built there in very fine stages
both techniques withstand damp but decay in different ways
text: Two methods share the job of decorating a wall, and they ask for different hands and different patience. The first has the painter work on plaster that is still damp. Pigment sinks into the lime, the color locks in as the surface dries, and there is one sitting only before everything hardens. The drawing therefore has to be settled beforehand, then transferred from a model pricked with holes. The second method sets colored fragments one by one into a bed of mortar. Nothing is urgent here: the craftsman can break off, leave the work, and pick it up a week later without harm. The curve of a face, though, has to be built out of tiny steps, and a soft gradation is paid for in countless cuts. Damp troubles neither method, but one ages by going pale and the other by shedding pieces.

units: a group of amateur singers rehearses in an abandoned industrial building
the place brings them three distinct discoveries
low sounds carry on there under the steel framework
the woman in charge has to slow her entrance signals because of this echo
a single lighting unit leaves half the group in shadow
the singers at the back work by ear without seeing the direction
passersby come in listen to one piece and leave in silence
a regular audience forms without any invitation
the group finally chooses to perform there rather than in the planned hall
text: An amateur choir was rehearsing in an abandoned factory hall, and the place handed them three surprises, one after another. The first was acoustic: under the steel roof frame, the low voices hung on for a full second, which forced the director to slow down every entrance she gave them. The second was visual. A single lamp clamped to a beam cut the group in half, one side lit, the other sunk in shadow, and the singers at the back learned to work by ear without ever seeing the beat. The third surprise came from the neighborhood. People wandered in, sat down on upturned crates, listened to one piece, and left again without a word. By the end of the season the hall had a regular audience nobody had invited, and the choir decided to give its concert there rather than in the room it had booked.

units: the flexible plate is first warmed so that it cuts easily
the design is drawn then gone over in ink so it will not disappear
the wide areas are removed with the thickest tool
the tool must be pushed away from the hand holding the plate
the details are opened with a fine tool
the rough edges are smoothed once the relief is obtained
the ink is spread with a roller until it makes a steady sound
the sheet is rubbed from behind with a smooth curved object
one corner is lifted to check the result before removing the sheet
text: Take a sheet of linoleum and let it warm up near a radiator, because warm material gives way under the tool instead of fighting back. Draw your design in soft pencil, then go over the lines in ink, or you will lose the shape with the first curl of waste. Clear the big open areas with your widest gouge, always pushing away from the hand that holds the block. Switch to the fine gouge for details, hatching, and the edges of your shapes. Once the relief looks clean, sand the fuzzy ridges down a little. Roll out ink on a slab of glass, load the roller until you hear a steady hiss, then ink the block with crossing passes. Lay your paper down, rub the back with the curve of a spoon, and lift one corner to check. If the tone looks weak, drop the sheet back and work it again before you pull it.

units: a neighborhood theater reopens after three winters of closure
cracks in the vault had first raised fears of demolition
the survey concluded that the structure was sound
damp was rising from the foundations and eating the ornaments
the work was redirected toward drying out and gluing the decorations back
the company was able to rehearse in the lobby during the work
the neighborhood got into the habit of attending these rehearsals
every seat for the season is sold at the reopening
the management explains this reversal by the continuous presence of the actors
text: Closed for three winters, a neighborhood theater has just reopened, and its return comes down to a decision the management hesitated to make. Cracks in the vault had first raised the fear of demolition. The survey found the opposite: the structure was sound, but damp was rising out of the foundations and eating into the plaster ornament. So the work changed its aim. Instead of rebuilding the hall, crews drained it and glued the moldings back one at a time. That choice had a consequence nobody planned. Because the craftsmen worked on site, the company could rehearse in the lobby, and the neighbors got in the habit of dropping in on the sessions. At the reopening the box office was sold out for the whole season, in a hall that had closed in front of empty rows. Management credits the turnaround to the actors never leaving.

units: a dirty skylight leaves the studio in a dull light
this atmosphere falsifies every color laid on the canvas
the painter discovers her mistakes only by taking the picture outdoors
she gives up opening a window in the back wall because the stones are too thick
the bulbs she tries give a yellow cast that is more troublesome still
she puts a wide tilted mirror on the opposite wall
the outside light thrown back by this mirror reaches the easel without harshness
she now begins her drawings as soon as the studio opens
her colors hold up once the picture hangs elsewhere
text: Under its grimy skylight the studio sat in a gray light that drained the life out of every tone. The painter complained about it each winter: her blues turned to ash, her reds lost their warmth, and she caught her own mistakes only after carrying a canvas out into the open air. She thought about cutting an opening through the back wall, but the masonry turned out to be far too thick for that. She tried a set of harsh bulbs, whose yellow cast proved worse still. The answer came from a mirror. She fixed a broad panel of it to the opposite wall, tilted down toward the floor, and the daylight it threw back spread over the easel at last with no hard edge to it. Now she starts drawing the moment the shutters open, and her colors keep their promise once the canvas hangs somewhere else.

units: the author considers it wrong to equate an image file with the work itself
this confusion weighs on the budgets of collections
a photograph renders the lines and the values if the lighting is set
it does not restore the thickness or the relief of the painted material
the look of a protective layer changes with the position of the viewer
a file depends on a format a support and a reading program
each of these elements ends up unusable
a print stored in a box can be consulted without a device
the author acknowledges that the digital copy protects the original and spreads it far
the author concludes that the copy documents the work without replacing it
text: Setting an image file beside the work it records confuses two different kinds of object, and collections pay for the confusion. A photograph gives back the contours, the values, often the hue, provided the lighting has been calibrated. What it drops is the thickness of the material: the ridge of heavy paint, the tooth of the paper, the depth of a varnish that answers the eye differently every time the viewer shifts. The file also ages worse than people assume. It depends on a format, on a magnetic support, on a program that reads it, and each of those links expires. A print forgotten in a box can be read again with no machine at all. Does that mean refusing the digital copy? No, it spares the original from handling and carries the image where nobody will travel. But it documents a work, it does not replace it.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a woman recounts the path that led her to painting restoration
her interest begins while she cleans the workshop of a family member
at first she watched the cleaning of yellowed layers
little by little she is allowed to work on parts of a painting
she sets up her own premises in a courtyard after her training
her equipment includes a magnifying instrument and colors kept in jars
she has treated a pierced family painting and a wall painting faded by water
she can spend several weeks on a very small surface
she says she struggles to consider a job finished
she teaches two beginners that the work must be imperceptible
text: It started with a broom. As a girl she swept out her uncle's workshop, where damaged canvases came in to be saved, and she stayed on to watch. A swab of damp cotton would travel across a yellowed varnish, and the dullness simply lifted, which struck her as a kind of witchcraft. By her teens she was asking to hold a brush. They gave her frames first, then a corner of sky, then a face. Once her training was over she rented a tiny room at the back of a courtyard, with a swing-arm magnifier and pigments in glass jars. Work trickled in: a family portrait with a hole punched through it, a stairwell mural gone gray where damp had climbed the wall. One painted palm can keep her busy for weeks, she says, and the hard part is stopping. Two apprentices work beside her now, and she keeps telling them that good retouching is never seen.

units: the performance ends with a lukewarm reception from the audience
the staging comes down to a dark rug and two seats
no painted element appears on the stage
the lack of scenery leaves the audience without indications of where the action takes place
the text does not make up for this missing information
the musical accompaniment is played on the spot, hidden by a hanging
the sound covers the lines spoken faintly
one sequence carried by an actress is judged successful
the reviewer blames the failure on excessive austerity
text: The audience filed out with only scattered applause, and the coldness is easy to account for. Everything rests on a bare stage: a dark rug, two stools, not a single painted flat. Stripping it down might have thrown the focus onto the performers. It does the opposite, because nothing up there tells you where any of this is happening. So you start hunting the dialogue for clues, the dialogue withholds them, and the plot slides out of reach. The music, played live behind a hanging curtain, makes matters worse: it swallows the quieter lines, and whole speeches disappear under it. One passage deserves rescuing, a woman playing a scene of grief almost without moving, where the emptiness of the stage finally earns its keep. The evening fails through too much austerity, not through any shortage of ambition.

units: the writer is writing from a workshop where wood is worked
a piano had been damaged by water
the keys were sticking and the sound was altered
a specialist had judged tuning impossible in that state
the writer considered getting rid of the instrument
a neighbor who works with wood offers to take it apart and dry it
the padding spoiled by damp is replaced
the repair took the two people a whole cold season
the instrument now holds its tuning
the writer invites the reader to come and play it
text: I am writing from the joinery shop, wedged between two planks and the smell of warm glue. Do you remember the old piano I told you about, the one the rain got into? I had given it up for lost. The keys were sticking, the strings gave back a cracked note, and the man who came to look at it said there was no tuning an instrument in that state. I nearly let it go for firewood. Then a neighbor who works in wood offered another road: take the soundboard apart, dry the pieces flat under clamps, replace the felts the damp had eaten. The two of us spent a whole winter on it, with no plan worth the name. Since the day before yesterday it holds its tuning. I sit down in the evening and improvise clumsy things that nobody else will ever hear. Come and try it whenever you like; it is waiting for you.

units: the text contrasts sculpture obtained by removing material with sculpture obtained by pouring
carving does not allow what has been taken away to be put back
the pouring process starts from a clay model
a hollow impression is drawn from this model
metal or plaster is then poured into it
a cast piece can be reproduced as long as the model survives
the carver must examine the structure and the flaws of the block before starting
the caster must watch the tightness of the mold and the speed of setting
the carved surface keeps the mark of the tools
a cast piece shows lines where the parts of the mold joined
text: What separates a carved sculpture from a cast one? In the first, the maker takes material away and can never put it back, so every stroke of the chisel is final. In the second, he shapes a model in clay, pulls a hollow mold from it, then pours in metal or plaster: the form can be run again for as long as the model survives. Do the two ask for the same preparation? They do not. Carving demands that you read the block first, its grain and its hidden cracks, or it will split under the tool. Casting moves the trouble onto a tight mold and onto a cooling rate you have to master. And does the result look different? It does. Cut stone keeps the tracks of the tool, while a cast piece carries thin ridges where the parts of the mold met. What you pick follows from the effect you are after.

units: a museum official explains to visitors how a collection is formed
purchases follow the logic of completing an existing body of work
gifts raise the difficulty of the conditions set by the donor
some works are lent by another institution for a limited period
a visitor asks what becomes of the pieces that are never shown
the objects not on display are kept in crates with controlled air
these pieces remain available for research work
a student asks what share of the collection can be seen
the official admits that the share on show is small
text: Standing before the central case, the curator set out for his listeners how a collection comes together. He began with purchases: an institution rarely buys at random, and each piece that comes in has to round out a body of work already assembled. He turned to gifts, which raise a delicate matter, since a donor commonly expects the bequest to stay on permanent view. He mentioned loans as well, entrusted by another institution for a fixed term. A visitor asked what becomes of the pieces that are never shown. They sleep in storage, the curator answered, in crates with the air held steady, and researchers go on working with them. A student wanted to know how much of the holdings can be seen. The curator granted that the share is small, and that no room, however vast, could reveal it all at once.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the first tapestries answered practical needs of insulation and division
they also served to signal status
the earliest patterns were geometric and repetitive
specialist workshops appear near noble courts
the hangings then begin to tell stories in pictures
the figures were known by the objects that went with them
dyeing improves and offers brighter colors
the trade in these cloths enriches merchant towns
a model painted by an artist was reproduced by anonymous workers
mechanization reduced this craft to a narrow luxury market
text: The earliest figured weavings answered needs that were wholly practical: to line a cold wall, to shut one room off from another, to mark a rank. The patterns of those first hangings were geometric, easy to repeat and easy to keep in the memory. Specialist workshops then grew up around the noble courts, and the hanging turned into a story, whole scenes read from left to right, each figure known by the object that went with it. Demand pushed the dyers to widen their range, and the glowing threads drawn from insects and from roots made the fortune of several trading towns. After that came the painted cartoon, laid out by an artist and then followed stitch by stitch by weavers who never signed their work. The mechanical loom cut this painstaking craft down at last to a narrow luxury trade.

units: the text explains the darkening of old paintings
the protective layer laid on the surface breaks down on contact with air
this layer takes on a yellow tint that changes all the colors
the resistance of coloring matter varies with its origin
coloring matter of plant origin fades under too strong a light
the loss of one color can change the tint of a whole area
deposits from burning form a greasy film on the work
what is visible today differs from the original appearance
careful cleaning is justified by these changes
text: You have surely stood in front of an old painting at some point and wondered where that brownish haze over it comes from. Blame the varnish first. A coat of it goes on to protect the surface, but the film oxidizes with the air, it turns yellow, and in the end it tints the whole picture the way dirty glass would. Then there are the pigments themselves. Some colors hold for generations; others, drawn from plants, fade as soon as they take too much light, so a blue sky can drift toward green once the yellow that warmed it has gone. Add the smoke of lamps and hearths, which leaves a greasy skin over everything. The upshot is that the painting in front of you barely keeps the color it had on the day it left the workshop. That is exactly why a careful cleaning is worth the trouble.

units: a water leak flooded the dressing room the night before the first performance
the costumes ended up soaked
the colors of a thick fabric bled onto light-colored clothes
giving up the performance would have meant a financial loss
playing in rehearsal clothes was judged unacceptable
the technical manager suggests deliberately unifying the spoiled tints
all the cloths are dipped again in a single pale bath
the lighting is changed to match these new shades
the audience knew nothing of the accident and enjoyed the result
the company has kept this version born of a mishap
text: On the night before the opening, a pipe burst backstage, and the company found the dressing room under water, costumes lying in soaked heaps on the tiles. The velvet of the coats had bled onto the pale shirts, and the stiffened collars hung limp. Calling it off would cost a fortune; going on in rehearsal clothes felt beneath them. The stage manager offered a way out nobody expected: since the dyes had run anyway, why not let the whole stage look washed out on purpose? The team spent the night dipping every piece of cloth in one pale bath until the range settled into an even pinkish gray. The lighting crew cooled their lamps to match. The audience, knowing nothing of the flood, praised a look both bold and coherent. The company has kept that accidental version ever since.

units: the text sets out two printmaking techniques to choose between
the first consists in cutting into a metal support
the metal is covered with a protective film before the drawing
a corrosive liquid deepens the lines opened with a point
the second technique calls for clearing from a block of wood the parts meant to stay white
this second method allows no correction
both processes involve inking and then wiping the surface
the paper used must be dampened before it goes under the press
the sunken process gives a thick line that can be felt with a finger
the wood process gives flat areas with clean edges
text: Choose your road before anything else, for two hands are open to you and they do not ask for the same kind of patience. To cut into metal, take a plate coated with a thin varnish, draw your design on it with a needle, then lower the plate into a biting bath: the acid deepens the lines you have opened. To cut in relief, take a block of soft wood and clear away instead everything that must stay white; here nothing at all can be taken back. Either way, ink the surface, wipe it clean, lay down a sheet of damp paper and roll the whole thing under the press. The eye tells the two apart: the sunken line holds a heavy charge and stands up under the finger, while the wood gives flat fields and clean edges. Pull one sheet, look hard at it, correct what needs correcting, and begin again.

units: a center for conserving recordings has opened in a converted industrial building
a first bench deals with magnetic tape
these tapes go through an oven before they are played
this heating stops the recording layer from sticking
a second bench reads discs with a contactless optical device
a third service writes the description of the sound documents
this description calls for listening to each recording in full
the backup copies are spread over two sites
the head of the center holds the documentation to matter more than the carrier itself
a recording without a description can no longer be found
text: A center for sound conservation has just opened in a converted industrial hall, and the man who runs it walked us through the work bench by bench. The first bench handles magnetic tape: the reels go into an oven before playback, so that the recording layer stops clinging to itself. The second reads cut discs, whose grooves an optical sensor traces without ever touching them. A third service writes the description of each recording, slow work, since indexing means listening to every piece from end to end. A separate room holds the backup copies, kept in two different buildings. The man who runs it presses one point above all: the carrier matters less than the description filed with it, because a recording nobody has described cannot be found again and has all but stopped existing.

units: the smell of the damp material strikes the visitor before anything else
a fine dust covers the floor of the room
the fast spinning of the wheel is the cause of this dust
unfired vessels are piled on the shelves
their grayish tone will change once they have been through the kiln
the presence of the kiln speeds up the drying of the pieces
the craftsman therefore protects certain pieces with a wet cloth
the walls have never been given any paint
every object set down in the workshop has a practical function
text: Push the workshop door open and the first thing that reaches you, before anything else, is the smell of wet clay. A fine dust lies across the whole floor, and the reason is the wheel: it scatters droplets in every direction the moment it picks up speed. Shelves sag under bowls that have not been fired yet, a dull gray that will turn warm brown once they come out of the kiln. The kiln sits at the back, and the heat it throws dries the pots far faster than anyone wants, so the potter keeps a damp cloth draped over the ones he is not touching. The walls are rough and have never seen a coat of paint, so they hold the dust instead of shedding it. Stay an hour and you understand that nothing here is decorative. Every tool on the bench does one particular job, and the order you think you see comes out of use, not out of tidiness.

units: the closing of a venue happens in successive stages
the usual explanation blames the public for losing interest
the crowds at nearby stages contradict this explanation
the level of the rent swallows the margin of the takings
a first solution is to share technical costs between venues
these venues wrongly consider one another as rivals
a second solution rests on long leases
this guarantee demands affordable prices and original creations given a stage in return
text: A theater rarely closes all at once. It dims in stages: a season trimmed, a subscription put on hold, a technical crew cut back. The standard verdict blames audiences for drifting away, yet the lines outside the halls down the street make that verdict look lazy. What actually squeezes these houses is rent, which swallows whatever margin the box office still produces. Two remedies exist, and neither one calls for a miracle. The first is to pool the heavy costs, the sets, the lighting boards, the insurance, among venues that treat one another as rivals while courting the very same audience. The second is to lock in long leases, tied to something firm in return: seats people can afford and original creations given a stage. Otherwise we will go on mourning closures we arranged ourselves.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a specialist repairs old paintings
her manner recalls that of a repairer of watches
both trades call for tiny movements repeated over and over
she lifts the darkened varnish with a swab of cotton
she halts her hand as soon as the tone underneath looks doubtful
the material of a movement responds in a predictable way
a painting instead puts up old touch-ups and deposits of smoke
the aim of the repairer of watches is to get the object running again
the aim of the specialist is to keep the painter's gesture readable
text: The painting restorer bends over a canvas the way a watchmaker bends over a stopped movement. For both of them the motions are tiny and endlessly repeated, and a slip forgives nothing. She lifts yellowed varnish in patches no wider than a fingernail, with cotton rolled onto a slim stick, and she stops her hand the moment the color underneath looks uncertain. The watchmaker straightens a toothed wheel that a knock has bent, and metal answers her plainly, while paint answers with buried changes of mind, with old touch-ups, with layers grimed by lamp smoke. The difference lies in the aim. The watchmaker wants the machine running again. The restorer wants nothing running at all. She only wants some later eye to still read what a hand laid down there, one evening, on stretched cloth.

units: the exhibition shows prints
the deep inks do not clog the dark areas
the paper used has a grainy texture
this texture softens the contrast of the light areas
the order of hanging follows the successive states of the plates
this arrangement makes the progress of the engraved drawing visible
the labels lack any indication of the technique used
this absence leaves the uninformed visitor at a loss
text: Three things go right in this hanging of prints, and one thing goes wrong. Start with the inking: the blacks stay dense without ever filling the hollows, which lets the finest lines breathe and gives some sheets a startling depth. Then the support, a coarse-grained paper that feels almost felted under a fingertip and takes the edge off the whites, so the contrast never turns harsh. Then the sequence, since the plates hang by successive states and a visitor watches the image assemble itself, from a half-finished sketch to the final pull. What goes wrong is the labeling, silent about the process, the tool, the bite of the acid. Anyone who already knows the craft can piece it together alone. Anyone meeting it for the first time leaves with a vague admiration and nothing learned.

units: the writer thanks the woman who led an engraving course
he came to the studio with no earlier experience
the first session dealt with preparing the plates
he then learned to control how long the bite lasts
one of his plates was ruined during the attempt
the woman in charge offered to let him start again right away
the last session yielded a successful pull
the writer wishes to enroll in the following course
text: I am writing at the close of the engraving course you led, and I want to thank you for it. I came to the studio with no practice whatever, uneasy about holding a needle in front of people who plainly knew what they were doing. The opening session, given over to degreasing and grounding the plates, put that worry to rest. Your instructions were plain and exact, and nobody in the room was left behind. We moved on to controlling the bite, and I understood that the time spent in the bath decides nearly everything. My second plate was ruined by too long a soak, and you told me at once to prepare another, without a word of reproach. The last session produced a clean pull that I am proud of. So I would very much like to enroll in the course that follows, if there are any places still left.

units: a technician explains how old recordings are brought back
the hiss comes from the wearing down of the original medium
filtering too hard also wipes out useful sound
the high end of the string instruments goes first
the technician therefore prefers a measured correction
he compares several copies of the same recording
this comparison tells a flaw in one copy from a flaw shared by all
he always keeps an unaltered version of the file
text: People keep asking the sound technician where that haze over old recordings actually comes from. His answer is a short one: the medium wore down, and wear lays a steady hiss over everything, a hiss the microphone never picked up. Can it be wiped away for good? No, he says, and it should not be, because heavy filtering carries off the topmost overtones of the strings along with the noise, and what is left sounds dull. What does he do instead? He applies a restrained correction, then sets several copies of the same disc side by side. A crackle on one copy belongs to that copy. A crackle on all of them belongs to the cutting itself. One rule governs the whole job: the original stays archived untouched, because a listening choice that felt right yesterday can look wrong tomorrow.

units: an actress tells a stage manager about a sound problem
her voice cannot be made out at the back of the hall
the stage manager first assumes the microphone is failing
the wooden set is in fact throwing the sound back toward the stage
a thick rug is laid on the floor to soak up the reflections
the speakers are turned toward the far seats
the actress checks the result from the last row
the trouble is gone by the next rehearsal
text: The actress caught the stage manager at the edge of the platform and told him that nobody past the third row could make out a single word she said. He figured the microphone was going flat, and said he would swap the battery out and see what happened. She pushed back. The trouble started earlier than that, before the mic ever got involved, because the plank set was throwing her own voice straight back at her and pushing her to shove harder. He granted she was right, then suggested a heavy rug at the foot of the panel to soak up those returns. After that they tilted the speakers toward the far rows, which had been sitting in a dead patch. She went back there to listen while an understudy read her lines, and came up saying it was clear at last. At the next run, nobody craned forward.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: two old ways of fixing images are set against each other
wall painting addresses a large audience
the decorated manuscript is meant for a single reader
wall painting is carried out quickly on plaster that is still damp
the illuminator can break off and take up the work again at will
wall painting suffered from changes in what the buildings were used for
manuscripts came through better because they were stored out of harm's way
the two techniques used comparable pigments
text: Two ways of fixing an image lived side by side for a long while, and they disagree about almost everything. Painting on a wall speaks to a crowd. It takes a whole surface, reads from a distance, and forces its figures on anyone who steps through the door. A decorated page speaks to one reader, alone and stooped, turning leaves at whatever pace suits him. Part of the gap comes from the craft itself. Damp plaster gives the painter one working stretch and no more, which rules out second thoughts and demands a sure hand, while the illuminator shuts his volume and takes it up whenever he likes. Their fates parted as well. Walls were whitewashed, cut through and put to other uses as the buildings changed, while volumes shut in a cupboard came through whole. The pigments, though, were ground from the same stuff.

units: the colorants used in painting come from three distinct sources
the first source is mineral and comes from crushed rock
these mineral powders hold their tone for a long time
the second source is vegetable and comes from roots or berries
vegetable colorants fade under a bright light
the third source comes from insects or shells
these last ones were scarce and expensive
a binder turns the colored powder into a paste that can be used
text: Three families of color share the painter's palette, and each one of them carries a tale of where it came from. The first comes out of stone. Crush a pebble, sift the powder, and down falls a deep blue or a warm ocher that will hold its note for ages, since rock keeps no memory of the light thrown on it. The second is born of plants, of roots torn up, of berries crushed, of wood left to steep, and those tints are airy, almost afloat, lovely at first sight, yet they pale under a strong light and end up shadows of themselves. The third comes from living creatures, from gathered shells and dried insects, and its scarcity kept it for lavish commissions. One gesture runs through all three: powder is nothing until a binder takes hold of it and turns it into a paste that can be worked.

units: a tuner works on an instrument before a concert
the hall was too warm when he arrived
the heat had slackened the strings unevenly
he first set a reference note against the tuning fork
he then adjusted the other notes by successive fifths
a bass string gave way during the operation
he replaced that string and then stretched it by hand
he measured the temperature before checking a second time
text: The tuner walked into the hall a good hour before the concert, and he knew from the doorway that the air in there was far too warm. The heat had slackened the stringing unevenly, the bass having drifted further than the middle register. He began by setting a reference note against the fork, by ear, with no device at all, then climbed in fifths, narrowing each interval by a beat he counted off. The work turned rough. On the third pass a bass string gave way outright and the wire coiled itself onto the soundboard. He fitted a fresh one, seated it firmly on its pin, and pulled it by hand so it would settle before the players showed up. Then, with a thermometer in his palm, he waited for the air to drop and then took the whole instrument through again, starting over from the very first note.

units: a neighborhood has two distinct ways to put a request to a local authority
the first way rests on a document taken around for people to sign
this way calls for very little in the way of materials
the administration is obliged to keep the written request
a signed document reflects neither disagreement nor shading
the second way means gathering people in a hall open to all
the meeting lets opposing views answer each other directly
people who cannot travel are shut out of the meeting
background noise puts quiet speakers at a disadvantage
the two ways complete each other, one measuring the discontent and the other explaining it
text: A neighborhood that wants a local authority to listen has two very different routes open to it. The first is a written request, carried door to door for signatures. It costs almost nothing, it can be put together in one evening, and it leaves a paper record the administration is obliged to keep. Its weakness is that it says nothing back: a signed sheet shows no shading, and nobody argues an objection out on it. The second route is a meeting in a hall open to all comers. Everyone states a case, opponents answer each other directly, and a compromise often takes shape before the room empties. But a meeting shuts out anyone who cannot travel, and the background noise buries the quiet speakers. The two go together: signatures measure how wide the anger runs, and the meeting shows where it comes from.

units: a repair truck came regularly to the square of a very small village
the children arrived first, drawn by the noise and the smell of the workshop
people brought damaged objects, among them a seat and a faulty lamp
a woman insisted on keeping a coffee mill despite its condition
each owner told the story of how the object had broken
the craftsman listened without looking away from his cutting bench
the square emptied little by little while the craftsman packed his crates
the narrator reads in these visits the proof that nothing was thrown out without argument
text: Week after week the repair truck pulled up at the edge of the square, and the whole small village seemed to open at once. The children came first, drawn by the racket of the grinder and by the smell of hot metal. Then came the objects: a chair whose seat had given way, a lamp with a bare wire, a coffee mill its owner refused to give up. Then came the stories, because nobody left without saying where the crack had come from. The repairman listened without lifting his eyes from the cutting bench, nodding in the right places. When he shut his crates, the square emptied slowly, the way a hall empties once a concert has ended. What he carried off was not only a load of scrap metal. It was proof, renewed week after week, that nothing here was thrown out before somebody had spoken up for it.

units: preparation starts with an inventory of the water points and outlets available
a notice goes up at the entrance a week before the operation
this notice gives the time, the expected length and the equipment to bring
the division of tasks is written down the day before
the lane running along the building has to be checked clear of bins
the cleaning starts with the high parts and works down toward the ground
starting from the bottom would mean redoing part of the cleaning
the equipment is put away before the last break, while the volunteers are still there
a written record of the damage goes to the manager at the end
text: Before you run a cleaning day in a shared courtyard, walk the ground and note which taps and power outlets actually work. A week ahead, put a notice at the entrance giving the start time, how long the job should take, and what tools people ought to bring. The evening before, write the jobs down with a name beside each one, because spoken instructions get forgotten. On the day, gather the volunteers by the gate and check that the lane along the building is clear of bins. Start high, with gutters and ledges, then work down toward the ground. Do it the other way and you will clean the same surfaces twice. Put the equipment away before the last break, while the volunteers are still together. Finish by writing down the damage you found and handing that note to the building manager.

units: a retaining wall collapsed in an old part of town
the collapse closed the road serving the foot of the slope
with no alternative route, traffic was pushed onto a narrow lane
buses cannot pass each other in that lane
people living nearby report repeated delays
a crowd formed outside a hall that was too small when a meeting was announced
technical services blame the damage on an old seepage made worse by rain
the repair will take several weeks because the ground has to be tested first
a temporary footbridge has cut the detours without ending the congestion
text: A retaining wall gave way at the end of the week in an old part of town, and the road serving the foot of the slope was shut at once. With no route to fall back on, traffic shifted onto a narrow lane where two buses cannot pass each other. People living nearby report the same delays over and over, along with a crush at the one stop still in service. When a public information meeting was announced, a crowd gathered outside a hall far too small to hold everyone who turned up. Technical services blame the collapse on seepage that had gone on for years and was made worse by weeks of steady rain. Repairs will take several weeks, since the ground has to be tested before a fresh footing can be poured. A temporary footbridge is now in place, which has cut the detours without clearing the congestion.

units: the reception hall is on the lower floor of a low building
the light comes from a grimy skylight
a single reception counter works behind a pane with a hole in it
the line stretches as far as the front door
people coming and going in search of a form cut across the line
the wait sets off arguments about who goes next
colored tokens are now handed out on arrival
a board announces the color being called and seats have been installed
the counter works at the same rate but the quarrels have almost stopped
text: The reception hall sits on the lower floor of a squat building, and its light comes from a grimy skylight overhead. A single counter is open, behind a pane of glass with a round hole cut in it. The line in front of it stretches all the way to the front door, and it keeps getting broken by people wandering off to hunt for a form. Waiting sours the mood: someone questions who was there first, someone accuses a newcomer of pushing in. Since last season the desk has handed out wooden tokens at the door, each one marked with a color. A board shows which color is being called, and benches have been lined up along the wall. People sit, watch the board, and stop watching one another. The counter works at the same speed it always did, but the arguments have all but stopped in that once noisy room.

units: the author disputes the idea that help between neighbors has disappeared
in the building of his childhood, tools were borrowed from the door across the hall
an older resident watched the children without being asked
in his present building, people pass on the stairs without speaking
that same building produced volunteers to repaint a bike room
a list of people willing to wheel the bins out was drawn up there
the author puts the change down to the channel used and not to selfishness
help now travels through written messages and a notice board
the author prefers reserved but reliable neighbors to nosy ones
text: People keep telling me that neighbors have stopped helping each other out. My answer is that the help has only changed shape. In the building where I grew up, you knocked across the hall to borrow a wrench, and the woman on the top floor watched the children without ever being asked. Where I live now, nothing like that happens. We pass one another on the stairs without a word. So what? That same staircase turned out two volunteers last season to repaint the bike room, and a list of people willing to wheel the bins out. The difference is not selfishness, it is the channel. Help used to depend on closeness. Now it travels through a written message and a board hung by the mailboxes. I will take reserved neighbors who show up when it matters over chatty ones who keep score.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman described keeps her paperwork in a cupboard
she pulls out a bulky binder every week
she holds the post of treasurer in a neighborhood association
she takes in the members' contributions and chases the latecomers
she writes the sums by hand before entering them on a computer
she obtains the loan of a hall and a discount from a printer
she decides between competing costs such as sewing and the repair of a machine
she turns down the top post she is regularly offered
a member holds that without her the funds and the projects would both be empty
text: Her whole office fits inside a cupboard, and once a week she pulls out of it a binder as thick as a brick. As treasurer of a neighborhood association, she takes in the dues, chases the members who forget, and writes every figure by hand before copying it into a spreadsheet. She bargains too: the loan of a room next door, a discount from a printer, a bill put off a month, the patience of an annoyed landlord. And she decides, because the spending competes for one small pot. Supplies for the sewing workshop, a repair to the copier, refreshments for the open meetings. She turns down the top post she is offered at every renewal, saying that accounts kept straight weigh more than a title. Without her, one member says while stacking chairs, the pot would be empty and so would the plans.

units: the opening of the performance looked unpromising
the stage held only a bare platform and mismatched seats
the amateur performers seemed tense
the first scene suffered from a script that was too written and badly embodied
the room settled when an actress picked up a fallen ring of keys without breaking her line
the show gained pace from that incident onward
short scenes followed one another and the poor set stopped being a problem
the closing sequence ran without speech and showed neighbors ignoring each other
the critic holds that the script has to be shortened
the critic reckons the company would deserve a bigger hall
text: Nothing at the start of the evening promised much: a bare stage, three mismatched chairs, amateur players visibly stiff with nerves. The opening scene suffered from a script that had been written rather than spoken, and the voices recited it instead of carrying it. Then the room went quiet on its own when one actress, playing a caretaker, dropped her ring of keys and picked it up without breaking off her line. From there the show found its pace. Short scenes followed one another, the weariness of some answering the stubbornness of others, and the poor set stopped mattering. The final sequence, played without a word, struck me as the truest of all: neighbors crossing paths in a stairwell and failing to recognize each other. The script needs tightening. The company deserves a bigger house.

units: the sender announces a water shutoff affecting two stairwells
the cut is planned for the following afternoon
a shutoff valve in the basement is eaten by corrosion and stuck
this part controls the whole riser
no work on the upper floors is possible before it is replaced
the corrosion comes from a slow leak that ran into a drain
residents are asked to fill containers the night before and close their own taps
the return of pressure will bring a loud purge that is harmless
a whistle from the water heater must be reported to the manager
the cost will be met by the shared contribution already paid
text: To everyone in the building: the water will be off in both stairwells tomorrow afternoon. The cause is a corroded shutoff valve in the basement whose handle no longer turns. Since that one part controls the whole riser, nothing can be done on the upper floors until it is replaced. The corrosion came from a slow leak that took a long time to spot, because it ran straight into a drain. So, in practical terms: fill two containers per household the night before, and close your own taps while the water is off, to avoid damage when the pressure comes back. The plumber expects a loud purge on start-up, since the air being pushed out will rattle the pipes, and that is harmless. If your water heater whistles afterward, report it at once. The cost is covered by the dues already collected.

units: the question asked concerns a rise in the members' annual contribution
current income no longer covers the upkeep of the hall
the treasurer finds the rise moderate but fears shutting out members of small means
the board proposes opening the hall to outside uses in return for payment
the quiet periods are what this opening targets
an unused hall costs as much as a used one
bookings would be handled by members taking turns
a single register would prevent conflicting commitments
a review would be discussed in a general meeting if income still fell short
the chosen answer combines a limited rise with partial letting
text: Should the annual membership fee go up? The question arises because the income no longer covers the upkeep of the hall. The treasurer answers that the rise would be a small one, but that it would push out the members who can least afford it. Is there another way? Yes, the board replies: open the hall to outside users in return for a payment. The quiet stretches of the calendar are what it has in mind. An empty room costs no less than a busy one. Who would handle the bookings? A desk staffed by members in turn, working from a single register so that nobody promises the same evening twice. And if the money still falls short? Any revision goes back to a general meeting rather than being settled by the board alone. The chosen answer pairs a limited rise with partial letting, which spreads the effort instead of loading it onto a few.

units: a spokeswoman for a neighborhood group lays out their demands
she sorts these demands into three headings
the first heading concerns street lamps that stop working at night
the second heading deals with waste left on the ground
the third heading targets the danger of a crossing that is too narrow
an occupant of a nearby dwelling reports a work site barrier that blocks the view
a public official announces that a study has begun
a meeting open to the public is promised for soon
every household that signed will receive a written reply
text: Speaking for the neighborhood group, the woman at the microphone sorted the complaints under three headings. Lighting came first. Every other lamp along the lane behind the old workshop, she said, goes dark as soon as night falls. Cleanliness came second: cigarette ends piled at the foot of the benches, sacks dumped beside the bins instead of inside them. The crossing came third, where bicycles and delivery vans fight over a roadway too narrow to hold both. A tenant from the corner building spoke up as well. The hoarding around the work site next door, he said, blocks what you can see from the sidewalk. The official handling the file answered that a study is already under way, and that an open meeting will be held before the season ends. Every household that signed the register left out last week will get a written reply.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the first communities gathered near a source of water
that place gave rise to the notion of common ground
a well was dug first, then ringed with a low rim
a stone seat there took in the oldest members
shared business was argued out beside the well
as the settlements spread, arcades rose around the open ground
trade came to stand alongside public speech
a roofed building then kept the traders out of bad weather
the place served to announce and to challenge common decisions
text: Long before streets carried names, people came together where the water was, and out of that habit grew the idea of ground belonging to everyone. A well was sunk first. A low rim went up around it, and after the rim a bench of stone, where the oldest of the settlement sat through the afternoon. Whatever touched the whole community came to be argued beside that well. As the settlements spread, arcades rose along the edges of the open ground, and goods began to change hands where only words had. Later a roofed hall was raised, its pillars keeping the stalls dry when storms broke at dusk. The square ended as the place where shared decisions were read out, listened to, and shouted down when they displeased. Out of that slow layering comes the stubborn attachment people still feel for an emptiness ringed by walls.

units: the tiredness caused by noise at night depends above all on the shape of the surrounding walls
hard surfaces send sound back instead of soaking it up
a shout in a closed courtyard returns as an echo to the sleeper
an abrupt change in level breaks deep sleep
the sleeper can wake without keeping any memory of it
exhaustion lowers the capacity to put up with noise
sharper annoyance leads to complaints
designers use absorbent materials and planting
a soft surface takes energy out of the sound wave
text: What wears people down about noise at night has less to do with how loud it is than with the shape of the walls around the bed. Smooth stone and glass throw sound back rather than soaking it up, so a shout let loose in a closed courtyard returns as an echo to the ear of whoever is trying to sleep. Deep sleep breaks at the slightest jump in level, and the sleeper surfaces without ever recalling it, so the night loses its continuity. The effects stack. Tiredness lowers what a person can put up with, worn tolerance turns an ordinary sound into a nuisance, and the nuisance turns into a complaint. Planners answer with porous materials, hedges set along the fences, and paving that damps the roll of wheels. Every soft surface strips energy from the wave, and a weakened wave stops crossing walls.

units: a dispute grows out of a waste bin left open in a shared courtyard
the residents of one building blame the others for leaving sacks on the ground
those others answer that the passage is blocked by bicycles
the written exchanges turn hostile
two households break off all contact
a building employee suggests drawing a sketch of the courtyard together
each participant was to mark their routes and their drop-off spots
the sketch shows that a sealed doorway forced every route through the same point
reopening that doorway and putting up a low fence end the quarrel
text: It began with a complaint about a bin left standing open in the shared courtyard of a housing block. Residents of the north wing accused those in the south wing of setting their sacks down on the ground, and the south wing answered that the north wing filled the passage with bicycles. Voices rose, letters turned curt, and two households stopped speaking altogether. The caretaker then put forward an odd proposal: bring both sides together, not to argue the matter, but to draw the courtyard. Each person was to mark where things got put down and which way they walked. What the drawing showed was a sealed doorway that pushed everyone through one single point. The doorway was opened again, a low fence divided the ground, and the complaint was withdrawn without any formal proceeding.

units: two ways exist to consult the residents of a housing block
the first sets a voting box in the entrance hall for a week
a slip is dropped into every mailbox
the count takes an evening and two witnesses
having witnesses keeps the result from being challenged
the second way uses an open book where each person writes and signs
a private vote keeps opinions to oneself
the open book puts the reasoning on display and shifts positions
the private vote is chosen for questions that set residents against each other
text: There are two ways to take the opinion of everyone living in a housing block, and they do not serve the same purpose. The first is to stand a voting box in the entrance hall for a week, with a slip dropped into every mailbox. Allow a whole evening for the count, and line up two witnesses so that nobody can argue with the outcome afterward. The second swaps the box for an open book, left on a table by the stairs, where each resident writes an opinion and signs it. A closed vote keeps opinions to oneself and suits subjects that raise tempers. An open book puts the reasoning on display, and people do shift their position once they have read it. Take the box when the question splits households, and the book when what is wanted is a shared view of the matter before anything gets decided.

units: a covered market is described through its different phases
the stalls go up very early
the sellers scrap over the empty wooden supports at that hour
the busy stretch pulls the aisles very tight
parents with strollers give up the visit and leave by the back
the evening clear-out is reckoned the hardest
it means packing up the goods that went unsold
the traders help one another out by lending equipment
one of them keeps an eye on the stall of a trader who has stepped away
text: Push through the swinging door of the covered market and the first thing you hear is the clatter of carts. The place runs on three tempos, and the traders will tell you so straight out. First comes the setup, before dawn, when everyone builds a stall and scraps over the empty pallets. Then comes the crush, when the aisles pull in so tight that strollers give up and head back out the rear door. Last comes the teardown at night, the worst of the three, the one nobody wants to talk about, because the crates that went unsold have to be packed away again. Between those three a quieter life slips in. They save one another a parking spot, lend out a scale, watch a neighbor's stall while he goes off to eat. One seller sums it up laughing. We bicker all day, she says, but we never let go of each other.

units: the cleaning crew has the space to itself at sunrise
they gather the leaves that came down in the night
delivery drivers and then office workers arrive after them
those workers cross the place without paying it any attention
a loud procession of cyclists cuts the space in two
the public seats fill up in early afternoon
a water basin has been out of service since the cold season
its rim does duty as a ledge for setting bags down
late in the evening the eating places carry their seats outside
text: At sunrise the plaza belongs to the sweepers, who push the night's fallen leaves ahead of them in long dry heaps. The delivery vans come next, then the office workers, who cut across on the diagonal without once looking up. A column of cyclists splits the open ground down the middle, horns and whistles all mixed together, and vanishes down the lower avenue. By early afternoon the benches have filled: retired men, teenagers perched on the backrests, a mother keeping watch on a stroller. The fountain in the middle has been shut off since the cold set in, and its rim now does duty as a ledge for bags. When the sun drops behind the roofs, the color of the place changes and so does the crowd. The eating places carry their chairs out, windows light up one by one, and the stone still gives back the heat it took in.

units: public seats have been taken away in front of a building
the place now stands empty
that emptiness follows directly from taking the seats away
the removal answered late gatherings and litter
a smell that would not clear was invoked as well
the seats also served people who caused no trouble
an elderly woman used to break her walk there
with nothing to sit on, the usual presence of passersby disappears
the presence of seated people kept the spot safe
text: The benches in front of the building were carried off, and now everyone wonders why nobody stops there anymore. That is no accident. It is a result. Whoever decided to pull them out started from a real grievance: crowds gathering late, empty bottles, a smell that would not clear from under the arcade. Take away the seat and you take away the crowd, and the arithmetic looked sound. But the seat had never served only the people who caused trouble. It served the old woman who breaks her walk in two, the delivery man catching his breath, the boy waiting on a friend. With nothing to sit on, those people no longer stop, and the space empties of its ordinary witnesses. And it was the eyes of seated passersby that kept the forecourt safe. In driving out the use nobody wanted, we drove out the mild watch that held it in check.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a professional practices mediation in a very crowded district
she takes on disputes that the courts will not look into
most complaints concern noise, waste and parking
punishment sharpens tension without changing habits
she starts by listing the complaints building by building
she marks the spots where one household's movements disturb another's rest
she holds short meetings given over to a single question
the commitments people make are written down
a check follows about six weeks later
text: She handles mediation in a densely built district, taking on the disagreements that neither the police nor the courts care to open a file on. The starting problem is one of numbers: most of the conflicts reported turn on noise, on how the waste gets moved around, and on parking, and none of those three yields to punishment, which hardens positions without altering habits. Her method works in steps that can be measured. She lists the complaints building by building, then marks the points where one household's comings and goings run into another household's rest. After that she calls short meetings, each given over to a single question, and writes down what people commit to. A check follows six weeks later. Files that reopen after that check, she says, make up a very small share of her year's work.

units: two makeovers of nearby spaces are set side by side
the first concerns a school yard given a cushioned surface
that spot also holds planters and wooden tiers
the children spread across it unevenly
every fixture imposes one single way of using it
the second job took over an abandoned lot for far less money
it looks unfinished, with rough low walls
a wider range of activity is seen there
the absence of any imposed use accounts for that range
text: Two makeovers a few steps apart invite comparison, and the verdict is not the one the drawings promised. The first gave the school yard a cushioned surface, planters, and wooden tiers to sit on.
