The work is careful, yet the children spread across it badly, since every fixture assigns one posture and leaves little room for invention. The second went up on abandoned ground nearby, cost a good deal less, and looks unfinished: packed earth, rough low walls, young trees fenced off behind temporary panels. And yet the range of what happens there beats anything the first one manages, for the plain reason that nothing on the site tells you what a surface is meant for. Designers would do well to keep the lesson. The most polished scheme is not always the one that takes in the richest life.

units: workers put up a metal structure in front of the building next door
the din of the assembly disturbs the flats on the floor
a sheet stretched over the front wall takes the tenants' view away
the caretaker warns the residents that the call system will be cut off
three households voice their displeasure
a temporary stand-in device is adopted
contact between neighbors becomes more frequent
the longest-standing resident finds the situation unheard of
text: Dear neighbor, here is an account of the week, exactly as I observed it unfolding from my window. It began with workmen bolting a steel framework together outside the neighboring building, and the clanging metalwork awakened everybody on our floor. Then a green tarp went up over the front wall, eliminating our view of the courtyard. Next morning the caretaker went door to door: the entry buzzer would be off while the lobby is redone. Three households complained loudly, and something came of it, a spare bell screwed onto a plank, standing in for the real one. By the end of the week the work had quietly rearranged us. We run into each other on the sidewalk, our conversations last longer nowadays, and the woman who has lived on our staircase longest swears she has seen nothing like it since she moved in. Love,

units: neither the designer nor the residents decide on their own what a district looks like
the shape of a district comes out of a long argument between opposing sides
a piece of abandoned ground usually sets off that argument
the emptiness of the place draws proposals for what to build there
the proposals bring shared memories back up
what one side asks for cannot be squared with what the other asks
the local body has to choose between those demands
the public clash usually deepens the bond to the place
text: Who decides what a neighborhood looks like? Not the designer alone, and not the people living there alone either. The answer comes out of a slow argument that sets them against one another as much as it brings them together. What sets that argument off? A patch of abandoned ground, most of the time, fenced in, thick with nettles, claimed by nobody. Because the emptiness unsettles people, it attracts plans, and because it attracts plans, it wakes up what everyone remembers. And then? One side wants vegetable beds, another wants a room for music, and the council has to rule on wishes that cannot be squared with each other. Does the quarrel damage the street? Rarely, say those who have been through one. Contradicting each other in public is how people come to know their neighbors, and the place ends up mattering more.

units: a maintenance worker lays out a fault before a meeting of occupants
water getting in eats away at the connections of the outdoor box
every spell of rain cuts the link
an occupant asks whether the whole thing has to be replaced
the worker reckons a cover, fresh sealing and new ducting will do
the woman in charge of the accounts asks what the work will cost
the sum he gives is below the price of a complete unit
an occupant from the top of the building reports a crackle in her handset
text: The maintenance man stood up and laid the fault out for the committee of residents. Water has been getting into the entry panel, he said, and it eats the contacts, so any rainfall kills the line immediately. A resident asked whether complete replacement was necessary. No, he answered: a stainless cover, fresh sealing, and replacement ducting run up from the basement would keep the circuit dry. The woman who keeps the accounts wanted to know what that would cost. He gave a modest sum, well under the price of a complete door unit, provided the way into the service room is cleared for him. A tenant from the top floor mentioned that her handset had been crackling since the fall. He wrote the remark down and offered to look at her cable that same afternoon, before he closed the box up again.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: older communities were organized differently depending on where they settled
some grew up beside a spring, others where two trading roads crossed
beside the water, authority served to share out a scarce resource
households there were counted and the turns of use written down
cheating there cost a person standing among the rest
at the crossing, the assembly saw above all to making trade safe
it set the measures and settled disputes
shared memory still differs according to those two beginnings
the institutions we have keep the mark of both patterns
text: Older communities did not arrange their common life the same way, and where they had settled accounts for much of the difference. Some grew up beside a spring, others where two trading roads crossed. Beside the water, authority came down to sharing out what there was too little of. Households were counted, turns at the channels were written down, and whoever took more than his share sank in the regard of the rest. At the crossing, wealth came with the traffic, so the assembly cared less about dividing than about keeping exchange safe. It fixed the weights, ruled on disputes, punished cheating. The two patterns left different memories behind. Where water gave the orders, people recall dry years and feuds; where trade did, they recall fairs, ruin, and the alliances that followed. Our institutions still carry both marks.

units: a neighborhood group rests on supports anyone can name
its members begin by listing what is needed and who can give what
a place to meet is needed if anything is to get done
meetings on a fixed date are worth more than enthusiasm that comes and goes
bringing in new participants keeps the active core from burning out
clear accounts keep mistrust away
newcomers must be taken in without an unspoken pecking order
a group missing one of these supports goes on, but attracts no newcomers
text: A neighborhood group stands on supports anyone can name. The first is the survey. Before acting, the members write down what is lacking around them and what the people nearby can offer: ages, languages spoken, trades, spare hours. The second is a room. With nowhere to sit down together, good intentions evaporate. The third is rhythm, because a meeting held on a fixed date is worth more than a burst of eagerness that comes and goes. The fourth is fresh hands: when the same few carry everything, they wear thin and the group dies out. The fifth is open accounts, since anything kept dark breeds suspicion. The last support is the hardest to see, which is taking newcomers in without laying an unspoken pecking order on them. A group that lets one of these go still goes on, but it attracts no newcomers.

units: a musical instrument is taken out through an opening high up in a building
it hangs from a brightly colored strap
at first there are very few onlookers
a crowd of the curious ends up filling the roadway
the workman moving it does not answer the comments
he braces the load against the frame set up for redoing the front wall
a resident fears for her vehicle parked underneath
the arrival on the ground sets off applause
the owner offers a drink to those who watched
she has loathed the object since her marriage
text: You will not believe it: a piano emerged from a third-floor window on an orange strap. Initially maybe three of us stood watching, heads tipped back. Then somebody stopped, then somebody else, and before long a crowd was filling the roadway, calling out judgments on the operation as though it were street theater. The mover said nothing back. He hauled on his rope, braced the case against the frame put up for redoing the front wall, let it down a notch, began again. A woman upstairs kept fretting over her car, parked right underneath. When the thing touched the ground the crowd clapped, which finally got a grin out of him. The best came later. The owner, a very dignified lady, asked the whole sidewalk in for a drink, to mark the going of an object she had loathed since her marriage.

units: clearing a piece of neglected ground calls for planning beforehand
the owner's permission is what makes the work lawful
without that permission nothing that gets damaged is covered
probing the soil prevents injuries from buried waste
the jobs must be handed out before the participants show up
with no jobs handed out, part of the group stands around waiting
thick gloves and plenty of containers are needed
a heap left behind draws further dumping
food shared at the end brings the participants back
text: Clearing a piece of neglected ground calls for a method worked out beforehand, or the volunteers drop away after the very first outing. Begin by getting the owner's permission, since without it the work is unlawful and nothing that gets damaged is covered. Probe the soil next, because an old dump can hide broken glass or leaking drums, and a work party thrown together ends at the first-aid post. Hand out the jobs before the group shows up, because if people learn what to do only once they arrive, half the hands stand waiting at the gate. Bring thick gloves and more containers than seem necessary, since a heap left at the roadside pulls in further dumping. Close the day with food shared on the spot. Tiredness goes down better when it ends together, and the volunteers turn up again at the next outing.

units: an electrical failure leaves a residential sector without light
with the lifts stopped, elderly occupants are shut in at home
those occupants are left with no heat and no way to call
the failure itself is put right quickly
the real obstacle was that nobody knew which occupants were on their own
an employee of the library thinks up a cheap answer
a voluntary register of vulnerable homes is drawn up with the caretaker
two neighbors per floor are named to check the apartments when an alert comes
two later incidents passed off without panic
text: A failure on the network dropped the upper quarter into darkness, and the news climbed the stairwells landing by landing. With the elevators stopped, older residents stayed shut in their apartments, no heat, no charged phone. The hard part was never the outage, which was put right soon enough, but the blankness: nobody knew who lived alone behind which door. A woman who works at the library came forward with an answer that cost little and has lasted. Together with the caretaker she drew up a voluntary list of the homes where someone might have to be helped, then gave every floor a pair of neighbors charged with knocking when the next alert came. The list sleeps in a sealed envelope. Two alerts have passed since, neither with any panic, and the street claims to feel less anonymous.

units: two staircases in the same block share nothing but their height
one is built on a concrete frame
its wide straight steps throw sound back
its landings open onto corridors lit by a band of glass
the other, more worn, turns around a stone core
its steps are hollowed by use and its metal rail shifts
its light comes from a glazed opening at the top
the newer staircase carries noise from one end of the building to the other
the older one swallows sound but holds the damp
being narrow, the second forces the people using it to meet
text: Two staircases stand facing each other inside the same residential block, and nothing makes them comparable but their height. The one in the east wing rests on a concrete frame. Its steps are straight, wide and loud, and every landing opens onto a corridor lit by a band of glass. The one in the west wing is older and winds around a stone core. Its steps are hollowed in the middle from use, the wrought-iron rail shifts under the hand, and the light falls from a glazed opening right at the top. The first carries noise so effectively that a slammed door below resounds upstairs. The second swallows it, but it holds the damp, which means painting the walls over and over again. The people living in the old wing see more of each other, because the narrow turns oblige them to slow down.

units: protecting common life means naming what makes it fragile
the loss of ground open to free use is the first threat
what is left are places meant for buying
that shift cuts down the meetings between people unlike one another
a body that debates without ever concluding cheapens public speech
walling the generations apart separates childhood from old age
alarming stories turn the neighbor into a danger
the writer holds that this decay can be undone
modest acts such as backing a beginner mend the social bond
text: Defending our common life means naming, without flinching, everything that makes it fragile. First, the loss of ground open to everyone: once the benches go, what is left are places meant for buying, and we stop rubbing shoulders with anyone unlike ourselves. Then the heaviness of decision, because a body that debates and never concludes teaches its own members that public speech weighs nothing. Add the walling apart of the generations, which files each of us in a separate pen, childhood here, old age elsewhere. Add fear too, kept alive by stories that make the neighbor a danger before they make him a support. None of this, however, is settled for good. A society mends through ordinary acts: opening a room, backing a beginner, agreeing to lose an evening listening to a disagreement.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the manager runs a neighborhood drop-in center
she grew up next door to a noisy workshop
quarrels between neighbors marked her childhood
she decided to face conflicts instead of avoiding them
she began by listing what people argued about
she set up a weekly drop-in session
so many people came that the room grew too small
the local council granted her a larger space
she credits her experience rather than any inborn gift
text: From a glass-walled office looking onto the courtyard, the woman who runs the neighborhood drop-in center watches families come and go. Her method makes sense once you know her history. As a child she lived in an apartment that shared a wall with a noisy workshop, and the quarrels between neighbors left a lasting mark on her. Grown up, she chose to deal with conflict rather than walk away from it. She knew those everyday grudges from the inside, so she began by listing what people argued about, then opened a drop-in session once a week. Families poured in by the second week, and the room quickly grew too small. That turnout persuaded the local council to hand over a much larger space next door. None of it comes from any inborn gift, she says. She simply turned an old wound into a useful skill.

units: the covered hall was remodeled recently
the designers wanted one open volume with no partitions
the din of the stalls disturbs those who come to read
children moving about unsettle people looking for quiet
thick hangings on rails now divide the space
these dividers can be moved as needs change
the fix cost little and built nothing permanent
the writer prefers this correction to the original design
text: Walking into the remodeled covered hall feels like entering a sentence that never comes to an end: the eye hunts for something to rest on and finds nothing to hold it. The flaw shows itself at the threshold, well before you have crossed the first aisle. The designers wanted one continuous volume, no partitions anywhere, every use blending softly into the next. Instead the din of the stalls swallows the readers sitting at the back, and children weaving between the tables unsettle anyone who came in looking for quiet. What has been done since deserves praise. Nothing heavy was built. Thick hangings on rails now cut the nave into rooms, and they slide along to wherever the day requires. The place breathes at last. It gains in warmth what it loses in purity, and that owned-up flaw beats the fine idea that made the building unlivable.

units: the writer compares two waste collection systems
the first system gives each dwelling its own bin
this first system is expensive to maintain
it makes sorting mistakes traceable
the second system is a shared container sunk below ground
this container costs less and keeps the smell in
its anonymity encourages illegal dumping
the writer recommends the second system with clear signage
the decision will be made at an upcoming residents meeting
text: Here is my answer about the two sorting systems our building is weighing up. The first gives every apartment its own bin, emptied once a week by the contractor. Upkeep runs high, but it keeps each household honest, since a sorting mistake can be traced back to a door. The second costs far less: everything goes into one shared container sunk below ground, on the strip of land beside the parking area. It holds plenty, and the lid keeps the smell in. The trouble is that nobody can be identified, so people dump whatever they like. Compare them and it comes down to this. One fixes habits, the other fixes clutter. Since bags piling up by the entrance is our real headache, I lean toward the buried container, provided we add signage anyone can read. Tell me what you think before the residents meeting.

units: the head of an urban services department is asked about public consultation
she believes consultation exposes uses that clash
three topics come up at almost every meeting
people living on the street want traffic slowed
shopkeepers fear losing customers
noise complaints run against the need for places open late
terraces cut into the room left for people on foot
the department head denies that consultation settles disputes
the final decision belongs to the elected representatives
text: Asked what a public consultation is really good for, the head of the urban services department answers that it brings clashing uses out into the open. Three themes surface at nearly every meeting she attends, she notes. The first one is traffic: people living along the street want it slowed down, while the shopkeepers fear their customers will drift away for good. The second concerns the hours after dark, where she sets the need for somewhere young people can go late against the steady complaints about noise. The third is the sidewalk, where the terraces eat into the room left for strollers and for wheelchairs. Does the consultation settle these disputes? She says plainly that it does not. It gives them a shape, sorts them by weight, and then hands the burden of choosing to the elected representatives.

units: the president of an association asks a volunteer about the state of the lobby
the volunteer reports overflowing mailboxes and parcels on the floor
the caretaker has been out sick for two weeks
no stand-in was arranged
a tenant had already reported it in writing without any reply
the treasurer suggests paying for a temporary replacement
the tenant objects that the fund is meant for something else
the president decides to visit the apartments the next day
a general meeting will be called if nobody steps forward
text: Near the end of the meeting, the president of the association asked the young volunteer what exactly he had seen in the lobby. The mailboxes were overflowing, the volunteer said, and parcels had been sitting there on the floor since the day before. The president wanted to know what lay behind such an unusual mess. The caretaker had been out sick for two weeks, the volunteer explained, and nobody at all had taken over his rounds. A tenant spoke up from the back: she had already reported the whole thing in writing and had never heard back. The treasurer offered to pay for a stand-in, just this once. The tenant objected that the money was set aside for something else entirely. The president settled it there. He would knock on every door the next day, and call a general meeting if no one stepped forward.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: streets did not carry posted names from the start
people once found their way by shop signs and trades
this worked as long as the neighborhood stayed small
the spread of the outskirts made spoken directions useless
the authorities could no longer collect the taxes
they could no longer find the people they were after
numbering the housefronts grew out of this trouble
the mail carrier daily round follows from it as well
residents pushed back against the measure at first
they saw it as an intrusion into their private life
text: Believe it or not, streets did not start out with their names posted on a plate. People found their way by painted signs and shopfronts. You lived by the well, or across from the tanner, and that did the job as long as the whole neighborhood fit into a handful of lanes. Then the outskirts spread, newcomers arrived in crowds, and directions passed along by word of mouth stopped working. The authorities reacted for a very practical reason. They could no longer collect the taxes, and they could no longer put their hands on the people they were after. That is where numbers on housefronts come from, and the mail carrier daily round along with them. The odd part is that residents pushed back at first. An address handed to them felt like a stranger walking into their private life.

units: a rumor of a break-in spreads through a residents group chat
the message is twisted and blown up in one evening
an alarming story travels faster than a denial
fear makes people warn those close to them
setting the record straight takes patient checking
some neighborhood groups appoint two verifiers
these verifiers check every alert before it goes out
a waiting period is imposed before anything is shared
the number of alerts drops and trust climbs back
text: A rumor swells inside the residents group chat: intruders got into the basement. Within a single evening the message has been passed on, twisted, and blown out of all proportion. Researchers who study how information travels know the pattern well. An alarming story outruns any denial, because it feeds on fear, and fear makes each of us warn the people we care about. One message is enough to put a whole building on edge, while setting the record straight takes slow and patient checking. Some neighborhood groups are trying out a fix that actually works. They name two people whose job is to verify every alert before it goes out, and they impose a waiting period before anything at all is shared. The result comes as a surprise. Alerts drop off, trust climbs back, and the exchanges turn useful again.

units: the narrator watches two lines form in a single week
the first stands at an administrative counter
this first line stays silent and packed tight
everyone in it keeps an eye on the spot they hold
the second waits outside a community canteen
people there talk loudly
they hold the place of a neighbor who has stepped away
the difference comes neither from the wait nor from the weather
it comes from what each person hopes for at the end of the line
text: I came across two crowds in the same week, and they had nothing in common. The first was waiting at an administrative counter: packed tight, silent, shuffling under an awning too short to cover anyone. Each person kept an eye on the spot he had. Nothing passed between them but sighs and sideways looks, as though waiting there ruled out speech. The second had formed outside a community canteen open to all. It shuffled just as much, under the same drizzle, but voices carried, and someone would hold a place for the neighbor who had stepped away for an umbrella. The gap had nothing to do with the wait or the weather. It came from what each person hoped for at the end of the line. At the counter they feared a refusal. At the canteen they expected hot soup and a familiar face.

units: the procedure applies before a community space opens to the public
measure the width of the entrance door
check the slope of the ramp
a wheelchair must turn without awkward maneuvering
the emergency exits must be located and cleared
the charge on the extinguishers and the electrical inspection must be verified
the furniture must be entered in a register with its condition
seats that sag under weight must be pulled out
a felt panel cures the echo of a bare ceiling
the compliance papers must be requested from the owner after a renovation
text: Before you open a community space to the public, run these checks in order. Start with access: measure the width of the entrance door, check the slope of the ramp, and make sure a wheelchair can turn without awkward maneuvering. Move on to safety. Locate the emergency exits, clear whatever blocks them, and verify the charge on the extinguishers along with the inspection of the electrical panel. Then handle the furniture: enter every chair and table in a register, note the condition of each, and pull out any seat that sags under weight. Finish with sound, which people tend to forget. A bare ceiling throws voices back and makes talking tiring, while a felt panel is enough to cure it. If the building has been renovated lately, ask the owner for the compliance papers and file them with the register.

units: a job placement association asked to occupy an idle warehouse
the warehouse belongs to a public housing landlord
the request drew no reply at first
a technical meeting brought together the landlord the safety services and the people behind the project
the project planned a repair workshop and a shared kitchen
the experts required the roof structure to be reinforced
the landlord agreed to pay for the bracing
the association pledged to handle upkeep and keep watch over the place
the agreement was signed at the end of autumn
a building next door is now the subject of a similar request
text: It began when a job placement association applied for temporary use of an idle warehouse owned by a public housing landlord. The request drew no reply at first. Two weeks later, a technical meeting brought the landlord together with the safety services and the people behind the project, who wanted to put a repair workshop and a shared kitchen under that roof. The experts concluded that the roof structure had to be reinforced, and that without it the doors could not open to the public. The landlord put forward a compromise. It would pay for the bracing, while the association would handle day-to-day upkeep and keep watch over the place. The agreement was signed at the end of autumn. The workshop has opened since, and the idle building next door is now the subject of a similar request.

units: a covered market is in poor condition
the roof lets water through
the sellers are short of space
the aisles are crowded with shoppers
inspectors have declared the place unhealthy
a group of sellers puts forward a three-part answer
the requests concern the roof, the aisles and the drainage
a local body has approved the idea but lacks money
the work would be done in the slow season
the sellers hope the buyers will come back
text: The market hall down in the lower streets no longer keeps anything dry. Its timber frame is rotting, broken panes let the rain straight in, and the concrete floor turns slick the moment the damp rises. Sellers complain of cramped stalls that press against one another, while shoppers shuffle along an aisle packed shoulder to shoulder. A traders' group has put forward an answer in three parts. They want the roof rebuilt first, then the central walkways widened, and finally a drainage system laid in, since inspectors have called the building unfit and unhealthy. The district council backs the idea and is still hunting for the money. Work would begin in the slow season, so that no stall has to shut. The traders will put up with the mess, sure that a repaired hall will win back the buyers who had been drifting away.

units: two public spaces are set side by side
one is old and the other recent
trees surround the older one
you can stay there without spending
the new space is bright but has no shade
the noise puts off anyone who would like to stay
the old one was designed for pausing and the recent one for moving through
the writer holds that a place is judged by those who stay in it for no reason
text: People like to set the old square against the recent forecourt, as though one belonged to the past and the other to what comes next. The contrast is worth a closer look. The old square, ringed by close-planted trees, invites you to sit down without buying anything: an idle old man, children at a run, a stallholder dozing in the warmth. The recent forecourt gleams with pale paving and hard-edged benches, yet it throws no shade at all, and its clatter drives off anyone who might want to linger. One was drawn for the quiet halt, the other for passing through. We are too quick to judge a shared space by how it shines. It should be judged by how many people stay in it for no reason. A place that works is not one you cross. It is one you inhabit for a moment, then leave with regret.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a mediator works in a defined district
her work falls into four parts
she handles disputes between neighbors
she receives both sides in a neutral place
she helps people with official paperwork
she runs meetings and trains volunteers
she records closed cases with great care
her colleagues praise her warmth and her helpfulness
she studied social law before taking the post
text: Four strands make up the work of the mediator assigned to the northern district, each of them set out in a written protocol. The first covers quarrels between neighbors: she takes in the complaint, checks whether it can be handled, and then calls both sides into a neutral room. The second deals with rights and entitlements, so she helps people fill in forms and points them toward the office that can rule on it. The third is prevention, since she runs meetings in the housing blocks and trains the volunteers who will go on to lead them. The fourth is record-keeping, and here she is exacting, because every closed case has to be coded. Colleagues describe her as warm with the public and quick to help newer staff. She studied social law before taking the post, and added a course in active listening.

units: a redevelopment scheme is assessed phase by phase
the consultation of residents was serious
the documents and the objections were made public
an option preserving a courtyard was rejected without explanation
the work went ahead quickly
the signage hindered the oldest residents
the finished result looks solid and clear
the final judgment is mixed
the writer hopes the early method will be used again elsewhere
text: Following this redevelopment scheme stage by stage is the surest way to weigh what it achieved. The opening phase, an open consultation with residents, was handled with real rigor: minutes were circulated, objections recorded, deadlines met. The second stage disappoints, because the client dropped the option that would have preserved the inner courtyard and gave no adequate reason for doing so. Construction followed, carried out at a speed that deserves credit, though the signage badly confused the older residents. Handover, at last, reveals a plain ensemble whose materials look durable and whose walkways read clearly. The verdict is therefore divided: an exemplary method at the start, an opaque ruling in the middle, a respectable outcome. One would like the next scheme to keep the first of those qualities without repeating the second failing.

units: the writer has just moved somewhere else
the building looked in good condition in the pictures
the shared areas turned out to be damaged
the lack of upkeep had discouraged the occupants
that discouragement made the decay worse
the writer called a meeting between neighbors
few people came for lack of information
those present shared out the cleaning and wrote to the landlord
the state of the building has improved since
the writer asks for news from the person addressed
text: I am writing to you from the place I have just moved into, and I think you will see straight away where my head is. The building looked perfectly sound in the photographs I was shown. When I got here I found a battered stairwell, mailboxes that had been pried open, and an entry phone that made no sound at all. Since nobody was looking after the shared areas, the neighbors had given up trying, and that giving up let the damage spread further. So I called a meeting. Word never really got round, so few people came, but we were enough to settle on two things. We split the cleaning floor by floor, and we wrote to the landlord together. Since then the stairs are lit, the front door shuts properly, and the neighbors say hello on the stairs. Now tell me how your own move went, because I would like to hold it up against mine.

units: vehicles take up the sidewalk of the street
people have to walk in the lane used by cars
the writer holds that action is possible without waiting for the authorities
the residents logged the blocked crossings for a week
they took pictures and wrote a short document
a local committee must give an opinion on a car-free scheme
two bollards were put in at a street corner
the roads department promised to paint markings
the writer sums up the method in three moves
text: You asked me what has gone wrong on our street, so here it is, straight. The trouble is that the whole width of the sidewalk gets used as parking, which means we walk in the roadway with the strollers. The next question answers itself: can we do anything without waiting for some ruling from above? We can, and we started. For a week we logged every blocked crossing, we took pictures, we put together a short note. Then you will say: who ever reads a note like that? The district committee does, as it happens, because it has to give an opinion before the plan for a street without cars goes forward. The upshot is two bollards on the corner and a promise from the roads department to paint markings. It has not worked everywhere, granted, but the method holds: watch, count, ask in writing.

units: a volunteer compares two districts outside a community center
in the lower district people come in person
in the upper district they phone instead of travelling
the manager puts the gap down to distance
a woman using the service describes a packed waiting room below
the matching room above is almost empty
the number of staff differs between the two places
the volunteer finds the comparison incomplete without that fact
the speakers agree on the part played by available staff
text: Asked for her view outside the community center, a volunteer weighs up the two districts she knows. Down here, she says, people knock on the door when they need a form; up the hill they phone first and rarely make the trip in person. The manager softens that: the gap comes from distance, he argues, not from any difference in the people. An older woman using the service cuts in to say the waiting room down here is packed from opening time, while the one up the hill struck her as nearly empty. The manager grants the difference and puts it down to staffing, two workers below and one above. The volunteer concludes that the comparison would be unfair if that detail were left out. All three settle on the same point: what gets done depends less on the district than on how many hands are free.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: farming communities managed their own water
this management covered several aspects
the upkeep of the water point fell to every household
the basin was cleaned and the leaks checked
the sharing followed an order of turns that was respected
that order decided whether the crops did well
a gathering of elders punished those who broke the rule
the punishment was the loss of a watering turn
these rules were handed down by word of mouth
they lasted as long as the mutual dependence did
text: Long before water ran from a tap, farming communities took charge of it themselves, and that work fell into several separate parts. There was the spring first of all, kept up by every household: the basin was scoured, the loose stones reset, the seepage watched closely. There was the sharing next, governed by turns that nobody dared jump, since the order of watering decided how the crops came in. And there was punishment, handed down by a gathering of elders who stripped the offending household of its next turn. None of these rules were ever set down in writing. They passed from one mouth to another, held in the use and the memory of neighbors. What strikes you, looking back from a distance, is how long they lasted, as long as the mutual dependence that had brought them into being.

units: a shared budget runs through ordered stages
residents first put in their proposals
every proposal follows the same form
technical staff then judge what can be built
requests that cost too much or fall outside the scope are dropped
the proposals kept are costed and then grouped by area
the vote is held at reception points spread around
the highest placed projects enter the works program
progress is made public at regular intervals
the procedure runs again from one year to the next
text: A scheme for a shared budget runs through a fixed sequence, and it is easy to set out step by step. It opens with a call for ideas, so any resident writes a proposal on a standard form, with a short description and the place it would apply to. Technical staff then look at whether each submission can actually be built, and they throw out whatever belongs to another budget or goes past the ceiling that was set. Next comes the appraisal stage, where the surviving proposals are costed and then grouped by area. Voting follows, over a short window, at reception points spread across the territory. The proposals that come out on top are written into the works program, and a progress table is published at every stage. The whole calendar repeats from one year to the next with no real change.

units: an elevator broke down in a building
two occupants were stuck between two floors
one of them was elderly and the other very young
the repair was slow in coming
neighbors spoke to them and brought them something to drink
one resident kept phoning the firm in charge
the two occupants were freed during the night
the residents then drew up an internal contact list
they called for stricter servicing
the manager agreed to replace the worn cables
text: It took nothing more than a broken elevator for the building to discover something about itself. The car came to a halt between two floors on an evening of driving rain, with an elderly resident and a teenager shut inside. No repair crew came quickly, so the wait stretched on and on, and word of it travelled from landing to landing. One neighbor went down to talk through the door, another brought a bottle of water, a third kept phoning the firm that held the contract. The consequence was not only that the two were freed, late into the night. Because they had finally spoken to one another, the residents drew up a list of contacts the following week, and then they demanded that the servicing be carried out far more strictly. The manager, named in writing, agreed to replace the worn cables.

units: the price of a handmade piece of furniture comes from several sources
the raw material bought from the supplier counts toward the total
the joiner's tools wear down and have to be replaced
the solid wood bench used for shaping deteriorates with use
the craftsman's hand is acquired through long practice
the beginner copies that hand imperfectly
the customer's wait matches a stretch with no money coming in
no single one of these sources justifies the sum asked on its own
text: Walk into a joiner's workshop and the price of a finished piece turns out to come from many places at once, each worth naming on its own. Start with the material: timber chosen, dried, and paid for at the supplier's counter. Then the tools, the planes and clamps that lose their edge and have to be swapped out. Then the bench itself, a heavy slab of solid wood that wears away season after season while nobody thinks about it. Then the hand of the craftsman, slow to acquire, and the hand of the beginner still copying it clumsily. Then the waiting, the stretch of time a buyer sits through while nothing comes into the till. Not one of these sources, taken alone, explains the sum on the label. A buyer who calls it steep sees a smooth board. The maker sees the whole chain of spending behind it.

units: the head of the crew kept a record of operations
the foundations advanced on schedule during the first week
a steel delivery arrived incomplete the following week
the load calculations had to be redone beam by beam
the supplier blamed a break in supply
an engineer offered to replace the section with an equivalent one held in stock
the substitution was approved on condition that the slab be strengthened
output dropped before settling again
the extra cost showed up on the final invoice
text: The site foreman opened his logbook on the first morning of the job and set down the order of operations. Through the opening week the foundations went up on schedule, and the crews rotated without a hitch. The week after, a steel delivery turned up short, so the load calculations had to be redone beam by beam. The supplier blamed a break in his own supply, which the client refused to swallow without applying a contractual penalty. A technical meeting was called, and the structural engineer offered to swap in an equivalent section already sitting in stock. The substitution cleared review on one condition: the topping slab had to be thickened. When work resumed, output fell a notch, then held steady. The logbook kept the trace of that gap, and the final invoice turned it into an overrun.

units: a written estimate must be requested before any repair starts
an agreement made only in speech protects neither side
the document must state the work, the materials and the time announced
money paid in advance binds the customer to the contractor
the contractor cannot keep that advance if the work never began
proofs of payment form the basis of a claim
any change decided while work is under way must be notified in writing
the final bill must be set against the accepted estimate point by point
text: Before any sizeable repair begins, ask for a written estimate, because a spoken agreement leaves neither side protected once a quarrel starts. The document should spell out what will be done, which materials go in, and how long the work is announced to take. Read the deposit clause closely. Money paid up front binds you to the contractor, and the contractor has no right to keep it if the job never started. Hold on to every proof of payment, since that is what a claim will rest on later. Put any change agreed while the work is under way in writing, or the closing bill will climb above the first estimate and leave you no recourse. Last of all, set the bill you receive against the estimate you accepted, point by point. A gap with no reason behind it is fair grounds for refusing to pay.

units: a storage building has been running slowly since it lost its main client
orders have dropped sharply
part of the staff has moved to reduced hours
seasonal hiring has been halted
the freight companies nearby fear the consequences
sharing the building among several shippers is being considered
converting the floor space requires automated sorting equipment
the local council would pay for half of that equipment
a first occupant is said to have signed a promise to lease
text: A storage building on the freight park has been running at half speed since it lost its main client. Managers describe a sharp fall in orders that has emptied the loading bays and left the forklifts standing. Part of the staff has moved onto reduced hours, and the seasonal hiring that usually starts about now was called off. Freight companies nearby fear the knock-on effect, since their runs have already thinned. One idea is on the table: share the building among several mid-sized shippers instead of hanging everything on a single customer. Management points out that converting the floor space calls for automated sorting equipment, half of it paid for by the local council. A first occupant is said to have signed a promise to lease, which would reopen hiring in time for the busy season.

units: the two aisles of the covered market do not run at the same pace
the fruit seller calls out to passers-by and announces his prices aloud
he drops a price as soon as goods risk spoiling
the cheese shop ages its products in a cellar
its posted prices seldom change
perishable goods force a sale in a hurry
a product that improves with age allows waiting
the first business takes on seasonal hands during the glut
the second keeps the same employee all year
text: Take a look at the two aisles of the covered market, because they do not run on the same clock at all. Down the first one the fruit stall spills over with crates. The seller calls out to anyone walking past, shouts his prices across the aisle, and drops one the moment a crate looks ready to turn. Down the second, the cheese shop ages its stock in a cellar, keeps its labels quiet, and hardly ever moves a figure. The first man sells freshness, so he lives in a hurry. The second sells patience, so he can wait for his buyer. You will notice too that one takes on extra hands when the harvest pours in, while the other keeps the same employee all year round. Two shops side by side, two opposite ways of earning a living. The goods set the pace, and the pace decides the takings.

units: the argument over funding social protection overlooks three aspects
the deduction from wages is felt as a tax imposed from outside
that deduction in fact pays for shared cover
the uneven earnings of the self-employed make any fixed scale unfair
the protection of the self-employed remains incomplete
some employers escape the deductions by using short contracts
farming assignments out to others feeds the same avoidance
the writer holds that the matter belongs to fairness and not to bookkeeping
text: Three blind spots hang over the argument about how social protection gets paid for, and they are seldom raised together. The first is the contribution itself. Taken straight out of wages, it looks like a tax imposed from above, when what it actually buys is shared cover. The second concerns the self-employed, whose earnings arrive unevenly, which makes any fixed scale unfair, and whose protection is still full of holes. The third is the quietest: employers who slip out of paying by stacking up short contracts and farming assignments out to others. Each of these leads back to a question of fairness rather than bookkeeping. Those calling for across-the-board relief dodge the first. Those defending things as they stand dodge the third. The argument would gain from naming all three before anyone settles it.

units: the oldest hand in the bindery came in very young as a trainee
she was put first on cleaning and then on folding the gatherings
mixing the glues was handed to her after that
she spent long seasons at the same shaping bench
she bought out the client list when the house nearly disappeared
that buyout was paid for with her savings and two loans
she trained about a dozen young people
several of her pupils now run shops of their own
she handed the business to her last pupil, asking her not to sell the work cheap
text: The oldest hand in the bindery came in very young, as a trainee, back when the leather was still sewn entirely by hand. They gave her the sweeping first, then the folding of the gatherings, and a season later the mixing of the glues. She spent long seasons at the same shaping bench, whose worn top still carries the marks left by her tools. When the house came close to going under, she bought out the client list with her own savings and two modest loans. After that she trained a dozen young people, several of whom now run shops of their own. Too tired at last to work the press, she handed the business over to her final pupil, asking her one thing only: never sell the work cheap. She still comes in to sit by the window, and puts a word to a stitch that has been pulled loose.

units: the equipment recently fitted to the assembly line draws a mixed verdict
the tightening is controlled electronically and its accuracy is beyond dispute
that accuracy does away with the rework caused by tightening by hand
the machine now sets the pace for the operator
a badly seated part locks the station and blocks the ones before it
the workshop has gained in steadiness and lost in flexibility
upkeep calls for electronics skills the team does not have
every breakdown means waiting for an outside technician
the share of faulty parts has fallen markedly
text: The equipment recently fitted to the assembly line deserves a mixed verdict. Its tightening accuracy is beyond dispute, since the torque is controlled electronically, which does away with the rework that tightening by hand used to cause. That accuracy, though, brings a pace set by the machine rather than by the operator. Because the cycle no longer pauses, one badly seated part locks up the whole station and the stoppage travels back down the line. What the workshop has gained in steadiness it has lost in flexibility. A less visible effect comes with it: upkeep now calls for electronics skills the team does not have, so every breakdown ends in waiting for an outside technician. The balance still tips the right way, because faulty parts have grown much rarer. Operators ought to be trained to read common faults themselves.

units: the writer ordered a kitchen and signed a detailed estimate
a deposit was paid when the order was placed
no word about delivery has come since
three dates in a row were announced and then missed
the writer's last message went unanswered
the writer has to rent a furnished home, which raises his expenses
he asks either for a written commitment to a firm date with compensation
or else for the deposit to be returned in full within two weeks
he states that the file will go to a consumer association if no agreement is reached
text: I am writing to you once more about the kitchen I ordered from your showroom at the start of the season. I signed a detailed estimate and paid the deposit you asked for, and since then not one word about delivery has reached me. Your advisers have named three delivery dates in turn, every one of them missed, and my last message has gone unanswered. Because of this I am having to rent a furnished place of my own, which adds to my expenses week after week. Let me put a reasonable way out of this to you. Either you commit in writing to a firm installation date, with a reduction covering what the wait has cost me, or you return the deposit in full within two weeks. Failing an agreement, I will hand the file to the consumer association already following my case. I look forward to your reply.

units: the choice between an employee and an outside contractor comes up often in small firms
the contractor's invoice takes the place of a wage and the employer's charges
the contractor looks cheaper in the short run
the contractor bills for each job separately
the employee takes on unplanned work at no extra charge
the training an employee receives then serves the firm that paid for it
an exclusive, long-running tie with a contractor risks being reclassified
the advice is to keep service contracts for one-off, specialized needs
the advice is to hire for the core activity
text: Is it better to hire an employee or bring in an outside contractor? The question comes up again and again in small firms, and the answer depends on what you are measuring. On immediate cost the contractor looks cheaper, since one invoice takes the place of a wage plus the employer's charges. Over time the gap narrows: the contractor bills for each job separately, while an employee soaks up the unplanned work at no extra charge. And loyalty? That leans clearly toward hiring, because the training an employee receives goes on serving the firm that paid for it. Legal risk runs the other way. An exclusive, long-running tie with a contractor can be reclassified. So what should you choose? Keep service contracts for one-off, specialized needs, and hire for whatever sits at the heart of the business.

units: a shopkeeper looks back on her early days at a wholesale market
at the start she had bought too many perishable goods
unsold crates piled up behind her stall
an experienced middleman suggested she split her orders
he told her to watch the buyers before purchasing anything
she wrote down in a notebook the requests she could not meet
she started her trade again with a narrower range
her profit doubled without her selling space changing
text: The woman who ran the counter talked me through her first season at the wholesale market. She had bought far too much soft fruit at the start, she said, certain that the buyers would follow. The crates nobody wanted stacked up behind the stall, and by evening the smell of ripe pulp caught in her throat. An older broker told her to cut every order in half and to spend her mornings watching the aisles before committing to anything at all. She kept to that for a whole season. In a cloth notebook she wrote down what shoppers asked for and could not find, and what they walked past even when the price was low. When winter came she opened again with a shorter list of goods, chosen this time. Her margin had doubled, she added with a smile, and the stall had not grown by a single shelf.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: better roads transformed the economy of the countryside
poor harvests once caused local shortages that could not be filled
heavy wagons became able to travel even in the bad season
the surplus of one region made up for what another lacked
the price of grain stopped varying sharply from place to place
growers began to raise a single crop
they kept the crop that paid them the most
the hands thus freed were taken on by the workshops of the market towns
text: Better cart roads reshaped the rural economy far more deeply than the men who had paid for them ever expected. As long as harvests moved along muddy tracks, every farming basin had to feed itself, and a failed harvest left behind a shortage that nothing from outside could fill. Once heavy wagons could roll through the wet months, the surplus of one valley made up for what the next one lacked, and the price of grain stopped swinging violently from district to district. That steadiness brought a result nobody had planned for. The growers narrowed their fields down to a single crop, dropping the side plantings and keeping whatever paid them best. The hands that this narrowing set free drifted down to the market towns, where the workshops took them on without the least trouble.

units: a workshop can hold orders and still lack ready money
suppliers and staff are paid before the customers pay
an invoice sent out is a sum owed but not received
payment often arrives after the spending has already happened
financial health depends on the pace at which money comes in
asking for a payment up front brings funds in early
steady reminders sent before the due date help payment along
a body can advance the money and take on recovering the sums
text: A small workshop can hold a full order book and still run out of money by the following week. The whole trouble lies in the timing of it. It pays its suppliers and its staff long before its customers pay it. Every invoice it sends out is money owed but not yet in hand, and the day it falls due sits well past the day the costs were met. Financial health, then, rests less on profit than on the pace at which cash comes in. Three remedies are open to a workshop in that position. The first is to ask for a payment up front when the order is placed, which brings funds in from the outset. The second is to send steady, courteous reminders ahead of the agreed date. The third costs more: hand the unpaid invoices to a body that advances the money and takes over the work of collecting it.

units: two workshops in the same trade stood on the same street
the first kept about ten workers and took every order
the second was run by a couple who turned down ordinary work
the larger workshop coped badly with the slack periods
its fixed costs ran on while its machines stood idle
the couple came through those periods with no financial harm
when demand returned the big workshop raised its output fast
the couple could then take on no extra order
each of the two approaches won in one season and lost in the other
text: Two binding workshops stood on the same street, only a few doors apart, and lived off the same trade. The first kept about ten workers on the floor and took every order that came through the door, however plain the work. The second belonged to a married couple who turned away any job that called for neither gilding nor chosen leather. Through the slack months the larger shop struggled, since its fixed costs ran on while its presses stood idle. The couple crossed the same weeks unharmed, because what they spent went on materials and on their own labor. When demand picked up, the picture flipped. One of them doubled its output inside a week. The other hit a ceiling and had to turn away the extra work. Each of the two ways of trading won in one season what it gave back in the next.

units: it is wise to read an employment contract before signing it
the section on hours may hold a duty to stay reachable
you must ask what pay is set for those periods of availability
the bonus announced may be guaranteed or left to the manager's choice
the length of the trial period and the terms of ending it are worth checking
a mobility clause forces a change of site if the employer decides so
you may ask for a copy of the document and take it home
an employer who pushes the candidate to sign gives away some flaw
text: Before you sign an employment contract, put the pen back down and read it slowly. Start with the section on hours. That is where on-call time tends to hide, meaning stretches when you have to stay reachable without being at work. Ask straight out how those hours are going to be paid, and have the answer written into the document. Move on to pay, and find out whether the bonus you were promised is owed to you or left to your manager's say-so. After that, look at the trial period, how long it runs and how either side can end it. Then check the mobility clause, which ties you to moving sites whenever the company decides. If something is unclear, ask for a copy and take it home. A sound employer will not mind. One who pushes you to sign on the spot is telling you plenty already.

units: a stoppage began early outside a logistics warehouse
the night shift staff broke off their work first
machine drivers and truck drivers joined them before midday
the strikers want a frozen bonus scale reopened
they demand the scrapping of a computer program that tracks every movement
management refused at first to talk under pressure
a delegation was received in the evening with no result
the vehicles were sent on to two nearby depots
deliveries to neighborhood shops ran late
the dispute is spreading to another site of the same company
text: The walkout began at first light outside the gates of a logistics warehouse. The night-shift sorters dropped their work first, and by late morning the forklift drivers and a part of the truck crews had joined them. They want a bonus scale that has been frozen for three seasons reopened, and they want the firm to drop a pacing program that, they say, tracks every movement a worker makes. Management said at the outset that it would not bargain under pressure, then agreed to see a delegation early in the evening. That meeting produced nothing whatsoever. Stranded trucks were rerouted to two nearby depots, which held up deliveries to the neighborhood shops. A mediator is due to take the talks up again tomorrow, while the action spreads to a second site belonging to the same firm.

units: a smell of grain reaches you before you enter the building
the stacked sacks give off a heat that raises a haze
the lack of ventilation forces the doors open very early
birds come in through those openings and cannot be driven away
constant use has hollowed out the pans of the scales
the passing of carts has cracked the brick floor
the jolting spills what is inside the badly tied sacks
the workers give up sweeping because the dirt comes back quickly
text: You catch the smell of grain dust well before you reach the doorway. Under the dark roof beams the sacks rise up in uneven walls, and the warmth coming off them lifts a haze that blurs and thickens the air. Because nobody ever thought to ventilate the place, the handlers swing the doors wide at daybreak, which draws in a flock of gray birds that no one there manages to chase back out. The scales sit in the middle, heavy, polished smooth by hands, and since they never rest, their pans have worn into a bright shallow bowl. The brick floor, ground down under the hand trucks, has split in a star beneath every pillar, so the carts jolt and the overflow from loosely tied sacks spills out in pale trails. Nobody bothers to sweep here. Everyone knows the dust will be back before dark.

units: grading a help desk by the number of calls handled is a mistake of method
the measure appeals because it is easy to work out
it turns harmful as soon as it sets what the teams are paid
an employee judged on speed cuts short the awkward exchanges
he passes the files on or closes requests he has settled badly
the quantity rises while satisfaction falls
the cost shifts onto the fresh calls from the same customers
it is proposed to weight the pace by the share of problems settled at once
an outside check ought to confirm that share
part of the work escapes any measure and belongs to the judgment of supervisors
text: Judging a help desk by the number of calls it handles is a mistake of method, and an expensive one at that. The measure appeals because it costs nothing to work out. It turns harmful the moment it sets what the teams take home. An adviser graded on speed learns fast to cut short the awkward conversations, to push the file over to another department, to close a request he knows was settled badly. Volume climbs, satisfaction falls away, and the real cost moves to the calls those same customers make again. There is a way out, though it takes nerve. Weight the pace against the share of cases resolved at first contact, and have an outside audit confirm that share. It also means owning that part of this work resists measurement, and leaving that part to the judgment of supervisors.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman now running a depot comes from the field of purchasing
her predecessor had been trained on the workshop floor
he judged performance by the quantity shipped
she judges performance by how stock moves and whether deadlines hold
the former manager settled tensions by talking and by his own standing
she prefers written rules put up for all to see and the same for everyone
he allowed private arrangements while she bargains for gains that cover all
the two ways of managing gave comparable financial results
the mood of the place changed between the two spells of leadership
text: The woman now running a materials depot took the job after a long career in purchasing. Her predecessor had come up from the workshop floor. He knew the machines, the movements, the tiredness of the crews, and he judged a week by what had gone out through the loading bay. She, trained in trade, looks first at how fast the stock turns over and at whether the delivery dates hold. The former manager settled trouble by talking and by the weight of his own standing. She prefers rules that are written, posted up, and the same for everyone. Where he allowed private arrangements, she bargains for gains the whole crew shares. The two methods brought in much the same margin, but not the same mood. Under him, people stayed late and nobody counted. Under her, they leave on time and talk more.

units: a retraining scheme meant for workers is judged uneven
the guidance stage is valued for its searching interviews
those interviews are led by people who come from the trade
they end in a written plan and not in a list of options
the equipment of the technical training is old and poorly suited
the machines of the employers differ from those used in training
the administrative help works well because compensation claims are dealt with on site
the follow-up after hiring stops too soon
most people who drop out do so after the opening stage of the contract
the yearly budget rules out any lasting planning
text: The retraining scheme offered to workers in an industrial area deserves a mixed verdict, since its parts differ so widely in quality. The guidance stage is strong. The interviews run long, they are led by people who have worked the trade themselves, and they end in a written plan rather than a list of possible paths. The technical training suffers from aging equipment, inherited from the shops that closed, which prepares people badly for the machines employers actually run. The administrative help convinces more, as the compensation claims are handled on site. Follow-up after hiring, by contrast, stops far too soon, when most of those who give up do so once the opening stretch of the contract is over. Funding, finally, hangs on yearly budgets, which rules out any lasting planning.

units: the writer lost his source of income after a plant shut down
he moved into restoring old furniture
he is writing from the place where he practices his new trade
his savings are shrinking
that decline forces him to sell his pieces sooner than planned
he is learning to haggle over prices without embarrassment
every mended object brings him new buyers
he states that dread has left him since the change
he asks the woman he writes to for a reply
text: My dear friend, I am writing from the workshop where my tools now live. When the factory closed, my livelihood vanished with it, and that loss pushed open a door I would never have leaned on alone. Waiting felt worse than starting over, so I turned to the restoration of antique furniture. Wood demands patience, and it has handed mine back to me. My savings keep thinning, which forces me to sell each piece sooner than intended, so I am learning to haggle over a price without blushing. Every chair I restore seems to deliver two further buyers, and that modest chain keeps me upright. You will ask whether I miss the steady pay. I will tell you the dread is gone, and that quiet is worth more than the security I surrendered. Write back soon. I need your voice the way glue needs a hand pressing down on it.

units: a company can run short of cash even with a full order book
the lag between takings and payments to suppliers creates the trouble
negotiating a deposit at the order eases the accounts at once
short-term credit suits only a passing shortfall
borrowing against a lasting imbalance merely hides the problem
contracting out occasional work lightens the fixed costs
the margin must be examined product by product
one line sold at a loss can swallow the profit of the others
the gap between money coming in and going out must be checked every week
text: What can a firm do when the money from its sales lands long after the suppliers have been paid? That lag drains the cash and chokes the business, even when the order book is full. Which move works fastest? Reworking the terms: a deposit taken at the order eases the bank balance straight away. Should the owner borrow, then? Short-term credit suits a passing shortfall, never a settled imbalance; used on a structural weakness, it only hides the fever. How can the fixed costs be lightened? By contracting out the occasional work instead of keeping a workshop that sits idle. And if the trouble holds? Then the margin has to be read product by product, because one line sold at a loss swallows the profit made on the rest. Which figure deserves watching? The gap between money coming in and money going out, checked weekly, not once a year.

units: a head of human resources sets out two options to the staff representative
the first option is to take on seasonal hires
the second option is to give the extra load to the crews already in place in exchange for higher pay
the representative reckons that hiring costs more in training
he reckons that the second option wears down the existing crews
the manager grants that quick dismissals would damage the reputation of the company
the representative objects that exhaustion cannot be ended like a contract
both sides settle on a middle course made of limited extra help and a bonus
a further meeting is planned before the season ends
text: The head of human resources set out his thinking to the staff representative and laid two routes before him. The first was to take on seasonal hires and absorb the rise in orders that way. The second was to hand the extra load to the crews already in place, in exchange for higher pay. The representative answered that hiring would cost far more in training, while the other route would wear down the people who were already there. The manager granted that letting workers go at the first slowdown would leave the company with an ugly name, whereas a heavy week can be put right in a week. The representative countered that exhaustion, unlike a contract, cannot simply be ended. The two of them settled on a middle course: a limited amount of extra help, along with a bonus for the longer shifts. They will meet again before the season closes.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the porter moved bales between the harbor and the storehouse
his pay depended on the weight he carried
the broker brought sellers and buyers together without touching the goods
the sworn weigher vouched for the accuracy of the scales
the money changer swapped coin brought from elsewhere and kept a share
the crier announced fresh arrivals in public
the scribe kept the record of debts
these trades have vanished or taken another name
each of these roles answered a lasting need of commerce
text: Before machines came in, trade rested on a set of callings whose names have faded away. The porter moved bales between the quay and the storehouse; his pay hung on the weight he carried, and his back deteriorated well before old age. The broker never laid a finger on the goods. He merely introduced an impatient seller to a suspicious buyer. The sworn weigher vouched for the accuracy of the scales, without whom no bargain would have held. The money changer exchanged coin brought in from elsewhere and retained a share as it passed through his hands. The crier announced fresh arrivals in the square, since nothing else made them known. The scribe, last of all, kept the record of debts, because what one man remembered rarely suited the other. Such callings have vanished or taken another name, yet each answered a need that trade has never stopped feeling.

units: at the start the owner lives on savings and waits for buyers
the first visitors look around without buying anything
a hard stretch follows in which money going out beats money coming in
half the shops close during that stretch
a group of regular buyers eventually takes shape
these regulars come back every week
word passed between neighbors then draws in new buyers
the owner ends up taking on some help
the text stresses how slow the process is and that there is no magic recipe
text: Wondering what happens to a corner shop once the doors open? At the start the owner lives on savings: rent goes out, shelves get filled, and then comes the waiting. Those early weeks bring mostly browsers, people who step in, look around and walk out without buying a thing. Then comes the rough stretch, when money leaves faster than it arrives, and that is where half the shops pull the shutters down for good. If the owner holds on, a core of regular buyers takes shape, the sort who come back every week. From that point on the neighbors carry the shop along, one telling another. In the end, if the slope eases, the owner takes on some help and can breathe again. There is nothing magic in any of it, and no recipe that spares you the effort. It is a long climb, and it wants a solid pair of legs.

units: a fire gutted a textile warehouse without injuring anyone
the rolls of cloth meant for three nearby workshops were destroyed
the workshops stopped their machines for want of material
the seamstresses paid by the piece went unpaid
a distributor canceled its seasonal order
that cancellation removed the main income of the workshops
a manager describes a week of unbroken telephone calls
the insurance covers the goods but not the lost contracts
owners in the trade now split their stock between two distant warehouses
text: A fire in a textile warehouse brought a whole supply chain to a halt, and the shock caught out everyone who had thought it solid. Nobody was hurt, but the blaze destroyed the rolls of cloth meant for three workshops nearby. With no fabric, those workshops shut their machines down; with nothing coming off the machines, they could not pay the seamstresses who earn by the piece. Further along the line, a distributor canceled its seasonal order, wiping out the main income those same workshops had counted on. A manager at one of the sites says the phone rang without a break for a week, every call bringing one more consequence. The insurer will cover the cloth, not the contracts that melted away. Owners in the trade now split their stock between two warehouses far apart, a cost they used to dismiss as waste.

units: the difficulty comes from the awkwardness of saying a sum out loud
the advice is to gather your results onto a single sheet
those results must be measured in output or in customers won
the request should be made during a quiet stretch
the evening before a deadline must be avoided
the request is put in one short sentence followed by silence
the silence must be left to the other person
if the answer is no you must ask what conditions would make agreement possible
the asker comes back on the agreed date with his notes
text: Asking for a raise is like crossing a narrow footbridge: the run-up counts as much as the handrail. Everyone knows where the trouble lies. It sits in the awkwardness that grips the voice the moment a sum has to be spoken aloud. Here is how to go about it. Gather onto a single sheet what you have achieved since you took the post, counted in output produced or in customers won. Pick a quiet stretch of the calendar, never the evening before a deadline. Put your request in one short sentence, then stop talking. The silence that follows belongs to the person across from you, so do not fill it. If the answer is no, do not argue. Ask instead what conditions would make agreement possible, and write them down with care. Come back on the day agreed, your sheet in hand. Patience is not shyness. It holds the rope taut without snapping it.

units: two neighboring employment areas reacted differently to the same industrial decline
the first drew in vast logistics warehouses
that first area shows activity restored but low wages
its workforce turns over quickly
the second area funded workshops that repair equipment
recovery there was slower but median earnings are higher
both areas received an equivalent amount of public support
the length of training explains the gap between the two models
elected officials are now studying the method they used to criticize
text: Two neighboring employment areas met the same industrial decline and came out of it in opposite states, to the plain surprise of the analysts. The first went after vast logistics warehouses. Its activity has climbed back to where it stood, but wages there are crushed and the workforce turns over quickly. The second put its money into modest workshops that repair equipment. Recovery came slower, and yet median earnings have now passed those of its neighbor. Both areas drew public support of a comparable size, which rules out any budget explanation. What separates them is the training a post demands: a sorting job is learned in a week, while mending equipment takes two seasons. So the second area keeps its workers, where the first watches them leave. The officials who once mocked that slow method are studying it now.

units: the hall rests on a slab worn down by passing traffic
the vegetable growers hold the north side with their crates stacked up
the cheese and preserve stalls run along one of the side walls
those stalls are held by families settled there for generations
the sellers of cloth and haberdashery gather under a patched glass roof
a coffee counter takes the opposite side and serves as a place to talk over prices
a central aisle wide enough for two carts runs through the building
a glazed office houses the steward who assigns the pitches and takes the fee
the sloping floor carries the wash water out to a channel outside
text: The covered market hall rests on a broad stone slab, worn smooth by the passage of carts and shoe leather. Along the north side stand the vegetable growers, their crates stacked behind them like a low wall. Down one side wall run the stalls of cheese and preserves, held by families settled there for generations. Opposite, beneath a patched glass roof, gather the sellers of cloth, thread and buttons. The far side holds a coffee counter where the traders settle up and talk over prices. A central aisle, wide enough for two carts abreast, divides these quarters and carries the buyers through. At the back, a glazed office houses the steward, who assigns the pitches and takes in the fee. The floor, laid on a gentle slope, sends the wash water out to a channel beyond the walls.

units: the working week at first had no legal limit
employers announced the ruin of the workshops if a limit came
after the limit output rose
the writer explains that rise by the cost of tiredness
the weekly day of rest was fought with the same arguments
paid periods of rest met the same opposition
none of the collapses announced at each step happened
the same arguments now serve against a shortened week
the writer grants that an old line of reasoning can stop being accurate
he demands that those who repeat a disproved forecast explain why it failed
text: Shorter hours are forever set against the survival of firms, and the quarrel gains from being put back in its own order. At the outset the working week ran on with no legal limit at all, and employers swore that any limit would ruin the workshop. The limit came, and output rose, because tiredness cost more than absence ever did. Next came the weekly day of rest, denounced in the very same terms, and after it paid rest, fought with equal heat. Every step arrived with a forecast of collapse across the board, and every forecast proved false. Now we hear those same sentences aimed at a shortened week.
