A word of caution: nothing promises that reasoning sound yesterday is sound still. But anyone repeating a forecast disproved three times over owes us, at the very least, an account of why it failed.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the manager runs a food warehouse
the winter deliveries kept arriving incomplete
the shops she supplied ran short of goods
she blamed the hauliers and the suppliers first
she realized the mess came from her own building
the heavy goods were moved close to the doors
painted lanes on the floor now organize the movement
the handlers laughed at the change at first
the crews walk shorter distances
not one order went short the following season
text: The woman who ran the food warehouse knew the smell of damp cardboard better than anyone. Every winter brought the same ordeal back to her door. The trucks pulled in half empty, and the shops she was meant to supply cleared their shelves faster than she could fill them. She blamed the hauliers first, then the suppliers, before admitting that the mess started inside her own building. So she sat down and rethought the whole place. Heavy stock went by the doors, rare items to the back, and she painted colored lanes across the floor that nobody crossed without a reason. The handlers laughed at her, then came around, because their walking shrank. The next season, not one order went short. She tells it without pride, the way you describe something obvious that took you several winters to see.

units: two assembly shops are set against each other
the first put its money into one costly machine
that machine cuts and folds with no operator
the second shop lines up three modest stations set by hand
the integrated line runs faster than the three stations
the single machine takes many seasons to pay for itself
one breakdown of the single machine halts all production
the modest stations are mended with ordinary parts
the integrated setup pays off when demand stays steady and high
the writer concludes that the choice depends on the customers
text: Setting the two assembly shops side by side means weighing two ways of putting money to work. The first backed one costly machine that cuts and folds with nobody standing over it. The second chose three modest stations, set by hand, watched in turn by a single worker. On paper the integrated line wins. It runs faster than the three stations together, and the man on the floor merely confirms the settings. Watching the shops work softens that verdict. The one machine takes many seasons to pay for itself, and a single breakdown freezes everything behind it. The three stations rarely fail together, and ordinary parts put them back to work. The integrated shop pays off as soon as demand holds steady and high. The split shop takes ragged orders better. What decides the matter is who buys from you, not the spec sheet.

units: the writer answers a request for advice in writing
the reader is starting out in the same trade
he urges reading contracts down to the termination clauses
a shaky engagement shows itself in its annexes
he advises checking that the employer really pays the contributions
he recommends keeping your pay slips
he warns against rushing the pay talk out of embarrassment
a wage set badly at the outset weighs on you for a long time
he urges keeping company with others in the trade to hear about bad employers
the writer offers his help if trouble comes
text: You asked what I would tell someone just starting out in our trade, and I am glad to answer in writing, so that nothing of it gets lost. First of all, contracts. Read them through to the termination clauses, because a shaky engagement shows itself in the annexes rather than in the title. Second, social cover. Make certain your employer really pays in the contributions owed on your behalf, ask for your pay slips, and file them away. Third, money. Never rush a pay talk out of embarrassment, since a figure set badly at the outset will weigh on you for a long time. Fourth, company. Keep company with others who do the same work, and they will tell you which houses to steer clear of. Last of all, spare your own strength. I wish you a calm beginning, and my help is yours should trouble come.

units: an employment adviser answers a run of questions
she puts the starting point in taking stock of your own skills
the second stage is spotting employers who hire without saying so
then come applications shaped to each place
she warns that many refusals are to be expected
discouragement often arrives before the first interview
she advises writing down every step taken in a notebook
keeping that notebook turns waiting into actions you can measure
she advises preparing the interview by studying what the firm does
she warns against mistaking slow hiring for unfairness
text: Where does a job search begin? The adviser brushes the expected answer aside. You do not begin by writing, you begin by taking honest stock of what you can actually do. And then? Then comes the stage of spotting the employers who are hiring without having said so yet. After that you approach them, one letter at a time, shaping each one to the place it goes to. How many refusals lie ahead? More than you picture, she grants, and the weariness usually sets in before the first interview. What holds a person together? A notebook, with every step written into it, which turns waiting into a run of actions you can measure. And the interview itself? You prepare for it by studying what the firm does, instead of reciting your own past. Her closing word is short. Hiring is slow, and slow is not the same as unfair.

units: a neighbor tells the narrator about his picking season
he had been taken on for the length of the harvest
his pay hung on the number of crates he filled
the crop came in heavy right across the region
the buyers forced the price down to half the usual one
the growers sold cheap rather than let the fruit rot
the rate paid per crate fell
the pickers took home less for gathering more
he means to go back next season
he will insist on a rate written down before he leaves
text: Back from the picking season, the neighbor downstairs held nothing back. He had been taken on for the harvest, paid by the crate, in an orchard where the work ran from first light until dark. The crop came in heavy right across the region, he told me, so the buyers set the terms. They offered half the usual price, and the growers let it go cheap rather than watch the fruit rot on the branch. The rate per crate dropped, and the pickers took home less for gathering more. He shrugged his shoulders at that. When an orchard overflows, he said, nobody comes out ahead, not even the man doing the selling. He means to go back all the same, since he knows the ground and knows where to sleep for nothing. But he will not leave again, he told me, without a rate written down and signed beforehand.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: before common funds one accident ruined a craftsman's family
the workshop hung on the bodily strength of a single person
archives tell of widows forced to sell the tools
apprentices were sent back to the countryside they came from
the answer came from the workshops themselves with no help from those in power
every member paid in a small sum at regular intervals
the fund replaced a ruined tool and kept an injured man fed
it also paid for the burial of a master craftsman
historians stress how slowly the idea took hold
the arrangement was later taken over by the public authorities
text: Before the trades built up common funds, one accident was enough to ruin a craftsman's family. The danger was plain to everybody. A workshop hung on a single pair of hands, and hands got broken. The old trade archives tell of widows who had to sell the tools in order to eat, and of apprentices sent back to the countryside they came from. The answer grew out of the workshops themselves, with no help from anyone in power. Every member paid in a small sum at regular intervals. The fund replaced a ruined tool, kept an injured man fed, and paid for a master's burial. What strikes historians is how slowly the thing was invented. Whole generations passed before people would accept that a risk falling on one man is easier to carry among many. Once accepted, it spread fast, and the public authorities took it over much later.

units: a fixed wage is likened to a running stream
the earnings of a self-employed worker are likened to rainfall
the wage earner can plan his spending because the money comes in evenly
the self-employed worker knows fat stretches and empty ones
the difference lies in the evenness and not in the amount
on the same yearly earnings the self-employed worker is lent money less readily
the lender is after evenness rather than wealth
the self-employed worker has to make that evenness himself
he does it by holding back what the fat seasons leave him
text: A wage is a stream. What a worker earns on his own account is rainfall. The stream carries no more water than the rain does, yet it keeps running. Whoever draws steady pay can plan what to spend, sign a lease, promise to pay a sum back, because he knows in advance how much will pass under his feet. Whoever lives off showers goes through fat weeks and then dry ones. The money pours down, then nothing falls at all. So the difference lies in the shape and not in the sum. That is what lights up a fact that looks strange at first. On the same yearly earnings, the second is lent money far less readily than the first. A lender is not buying wealth, what he is buying is evenness. And whoever lives on rain has to make that evenness himself, by holding back whatever the fat seasons leave behind.

units: a routine inspection was aimed at a packaging plant
the inspector wrote up faults of four different kinds
pallets of resin were stored too close to the ovens
that heat explained why some batches came out warped
the dosing unit had gone far too long without calibration
the setters corrected its drift by hand and wrote nothing down
half the night crew lacked the certificate the post called for
the scrapped parts appeared in no accounting record
the head of the site blamed the pressure of the orders
the inspector puts these faults down to checking let slide again and again
text: It was supposed to be nothing more than a routine call at a packaging plant, and the inspector came away with faults of four kinds. Take the materials first. The pallets of resin sat close enough to the ovens to pass the heat limit, which explained the warped batches. Machines next. The dosing unit had gone far too long without calibration, and the setters had been correcting its drift by hand, writing nothing down. Staffing after that. Half of the night crew held posts they had no certificate for at all. Records last. The scrapped parts turned up in none of the production accounts. The head of the site pleaded the pressure the orders were putting on him. The inspector answered that nothing she had just written up came from haste. It came from checking let slide, season after season.

units: the procedure covers the opening of a retail shop
the steps must not be swapped around
the first is to gauge what the neighborhood wants
that gauging is done by watching the passers-by and the storefronts nearby
the business must be registered before any goods are ordered
the lease has to carry an exit clause
the first range of goods is kept narrow on purpose to spare the cash
a trial week with no advertising serves to adjust the prices
a record of what comes in and goes out is kept from the first sale on
text: Work through these steps in the order they are given here, because opening a retail shop allows no swapping around. Begin by gauging what the neighborhood wants. Count the people going past, note the storefronts already there, ask those who live nearby. Register the business next with the office appointed for it, since no goods may be ordered before that formality is done. Negotiate the lease after that, and insist on an exit clause, because a badly chosen space is harder to leave than to take. Put together your first range of goods, narrow on purpose. Better to run out of an article than to tie up your cash. Open the doors quietly for a trial week, with no advertising, so that prices and hours can be adjusted. Keep a record of what comes in and goes out, from the first sale on.

units: the closing of a cannery has been announced
the plant used to buy the catch of the fleet nearby
the skippers put to sea less and sell straight to customers at a loss
the boatyards have cut their staff
the shops on the main street are seeing fewer customers
the wages that were cut are no longer spent locally
elected officials are calling for an investor to take the site over
nobody has come forward because rebuilding the cold chain costs too much
an association of workers proposes buying the plant together
the outgoing management has not answered that proposal
text: Since the cannery announced it would close, the working district around it has taken one blow after another. The plant used to buy the catch from the fleet nearby. With that outlet gone, the skippers put to sea less often and sell straight to customers, at a loss. The boatyards that lived off their orders have cut staff in turn. The shops on the main street already count fewer customers through the door, because the wages that were cut are no longer spent locally. Elected officials are calling for an investor to take the site over, yet nobody has come forward, since rebuilding the cold chain would cost too much. An association of workers is pushing another way out: buying the plant together and turning it to small runs of goods. The outgoing management has said nothing so far.

units: two woodworking shops stand on the same street
the first shop shapes wood by hand with plain tools
the second shop uses machines and employs three workers
the workers in the second shop mostly watch screens
the hand shop turns out little but sells at a steep price
the mechanized shop turns out a lot and sells cheaply
the hand shop depends on its reputation to survive
the mechanized shop depends on the flow of orders
the two owners greet each other in the evening
text: Two woodworking shops stand on the same street, barely a doorway apart. In the first, a seasoned joiner shapes every board by hand at a workbench holding nothing beyond plain, unremarkable tools. In the second, machinery slices identical planks throughout the day, and the three workers there watch screens considerably more than they handle timber. The handmade shop produces very little, yet each piece departs at a steep price, since the buyer purchases patience alongside the wood. The mechanized shop dispatches crate after crate cheaply, counting on volume to cover heavier overheads. One survives as long as people keep praising the work of the hand. The other survives as long as orders keep arriving. At closing time the two owners nod across the street, aware that they sell the same object by opposite routes.

units: the writer names three weaknesses in stock management
the first weakness concerns forecasting demand
forecasts rest on old records with no correction
warehouses fill up with goods nobody buys
the second weakness concerns the costing of goods
a surplus of goods ties up cash needed elsewhere
the third weakness concerns how buyers behave
managers order too much for fear of running short
the writer holds that fixing the forecast alone will not do
text: Three weaknesses eat away at the way midsized manufacturers handle their stock, and they deserve plain names. The first is forecasting. Demand gets projected from old records, with no correction for the supply breaks that distorted them, so warehouses fill up with goods nobody buys. The second is costing. A surplus batch ties up cash that will be missing elsewhere, and a crowded storeroom soon costs real money to keep. The third is behavior. Managers order heavy rather than face an empty shelf, an instinct anyone can understand and one that quietly drains the accounts. A losing year rarely comes from a single mistake. It comes from three habits that feed one another. Fixing the forecast while leaving untouched whatever rewards the buyers will bring nothing but brief relief.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the person described runs a weaving cooperative
she started out as an apprentice at a hand loom
her first job was mending broken threads
the experienced weavers gladly handed that job to her
she was then moved to the receiving of raw materials
that post taught her about prices and delays
she trained in bookkeeping away from the workshop
she proposed selling without going through a middleman
takings climbed and the workshop hired more staff
text: The woman who runs a weaving cooperative began there as an apprentice at a hand loom. Her first job was tying broken threads back together, painstaking work that the more experienced weavers were glad to hand off to her. After two seasons she was moved to the receiving dock, where the raw materials came in, and that post taught her about prices, delays, and margins. She left the workshop for a spell of training in bookkeeping, then came back with one clear proposal: sell straight to the shops instead of going through a middleman who took his cut. The cooperative hesitated, then agreed to a small trial. Takings climbed, and the workshop hired two more spinners. She now heads the place she knew as a child, and she gives the delicate orders to the apprentices, the way it was once done for her.

units: a training scheme for jobseekers is under review
the scheme is judged useful but poorly calibrated
the modules teach motions that are too narrow
employers want people able to move from one station to another
trainees find work but leave it quickly
the reviewer blames the departures on the narrowness of the training
the stretches spent inside a company give better results
the reviewer calls for those company stretches to be lengthened
text: The training scheme under review delivers a genuine service, but its calibration invites serious argument. Its modules teach narrow motions, tailored to a single task, while employers are asking for people who can move from one station to another as the order book shifts. The mismatch produces an effect you can measure: trainees land a job quickly enough, then walk away before the probationary period ends, unable to cope with the secondary duties dropped on them. The stretches spent inside a company turn out far better, probably because the trainee watches the whole chain there rather than one isolated link. The review therefore calls for those stretches to be lengthened, even at the cost of the classroom hours, which look redundant beside the manuals handed out on the very first day.

units: the writer writes to a friend about his soap business
making the soap by hand swallows all his evenings
the profits stayed too thin at the start
the shipping costs ate up the margin
the writer cut his catalogue down to three scents
he now delivers to a shared depot instead of sending each parcel
the business has turned profitable since these changes
the writer invites his friend to come and see the workshop
text: I owe you news about the soap business, and this letter arrives considerably late. You remember what I used to complain about: making everything by hand swallowed all my evenings, and the profits remained stubbornly thin. I finally identified the culprit, and it was shipping. Every parcel went out on its own, with its own box and its own paperwork, and the margin melted away before the order ever reached the buyer. So I cut. I brought the catalogue down to three scents, the ones that always moved, and I stopped chasing single orders. My crates now go to a shared depot, and the retailers come and take what they need. Since then the business is genuinely profitable, and I sleep. Come and see the workshop when you pass through. You will judge the difference, and you will go home loaded up.

units: an economist answers questions about how young firms raise money
she compares a bank loan with bringing an investor into the capital
a loan must be repaid even when trade falls off
a loan leaves the founder in command of his own decisions
an investor asks for nothing if the venture fails
an investor demands a share of the decisions and of later profits
she advises a loan for businesses with steady takings
she advises opening the capital for uncertain and costly ventures
text: An economist specializing in the financing of young firms agrees to take questions. Borrow, or bring in a partner? She refuses to settle it in a word and sets the two side by side. A loan, she explains, imposes a due date that arrives whether or not sales hold up, yet it leaves the founder in full command of every decision. Bringing an investor into the capital demands nothing should the venture fail, but it sells off a share of the decisions and of whatever profit comes later. So which does she advise? A business with dependable takings carries a fixed due date easily and does well to borrow. An uncertain venture, expensive to launch and slow to repay, rarely holds up without a partner willing to wait. The real question, she says, is how regular the incoming receipts will be.

units: two market women talk after the covered market closes
the fruit seller lists her troubles
she mentions the rent on her stall
she mentions the crates of damaged goods
she mentions the supplier who arrives late
the cheese seller answers that her own troubles differ
the cheese seller mentions the cold she has to hold steady
the cheese seller mentions the falling number of customers
the two women agree to share a van
text: The shutters of the covered market had just come down when the fruit seller began her inventory of troubles. She talked about the rent on her stall, which climbed every season while the aisle remained as shabby as ever. She talked about the battered crates, the bruised peaches that no customer would ever take and that she would carry home at night. She talked about her supplier, whose van pulled in after opening, once the shoppers had already come and gone. The cheese seller heard her out, then said her own troubles answered to entirely different names: the cold, hard to hold steady, the power bill that followed from it, and the line of customers thinning week after week. The two of them fell silent for a moment. Then they agreed to rent a van together and go for their crates before dawn.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the text traces the rise of the trade associations
the first craftsmen were scattered and had no common rules
neighboring shops first agreed on matching measurements
the next agreement covered the length of apprenticeship
the associations then set floor prices
the floor prices sheltered members from competing on rates
the associations also decided who could open a shop
that closing of the door ended up holding back untried methods
the associations lost their power as the manufactories grew
text: Before any organization existed, the craftsmen of a single trade worked in isolation, each on his own, with no shared measure and no rule in common. The first agreement between neighboring shops covered size: a board, a pot, a length of cloth had to match one gauge, or else a buyer had no way to compare. Apprenticeship came next, and its length and its stages were duly established. The trade associations, thriving by then, extended their grip further and fixed a floor beneath prices, which sheltered their members from ruinous undercutting. In the end they took for themselves the right to say who could open a shop, and that closing of the door, protective at the start, discouraged untried methods. Once the manufactories gathered hundreds of workers under one roof, these associations lost their hold.

units: the text explains why a farm product rises in price after a poor harvest
a thin harvest shrinks the quantity on offer
the buyers turn up in the same numbers as before
the scarcity drives up the price paid to the grower
the processors pass that rise on to their own charges
some buyers turn to a replacement product
the added demand drives up the price of the replacement too
prices come back down when the next harvest is plentiful
text: A meager harvest does more than merely empty the barns. It sets off a chain of effects that reaches all the way to the market stall. The available quantity dwindles while just as many buyers turn up as before, so each of them agrees to pay more to get a share, and the price paid to the grower climbs. The firms that transform the crop watch their own invoices swell, and they pass the weight on to what they charge. Part of the trade gives up at that point and switches to a neighboring product. That migration carries a consequence that few people anticipate: the replacement, suddenly in heavy demand, grows dearer in its turn, even though its own harvest was perfectly ordinary. Equilibrium returns only with a generous season, when the barns fill again and the pressure on prices eases.

units: a village bakery threw away part of its output every evening
the baker baked the same quantity without regard to sales
the waste threatened the finances of the shop
the apprentice wrote down the unsold loaves for several weeks
the record showed that the losses piled up at the end of the week
the end-of-week batch was cut back
the leftover loaves are sold cheaply before closing
the waste fell sharply
a neighboring shop copied the method
text: Every evening the baker in a valley village filled a sack with the loaves nobody had bought, and the sack went off to a farm nearby. He had baked the same quantity since the day he opened, without once looking at what sold, and the waste was devouring a margin already thin. The apprentice suggested counting. For several weeks she wrote down in a notebook how many loaves went unsold, their shape, the flour used. The record was merciless: the losses piled up at the end of the week, when families baked at home. So the last batch of the week was cut by a third, and whatever sat on the shelf half an hour before closing was sold off at a knockdown price. The waste shrank, the till breathed, and the shopkeeper across the way, who had been watching, began keeping an identical notebook.

units: a newly learned idea leaves a trace that is at first unstable
that trace settles mainly during sleep
the nerve circuits replay the learned sequence during that phase
reviewing too soon after learning brings almost no benefit
a little forgetting before the review strengthens its effect
recalling without help fixes the material better than rereading it
specialists advise stretching the gap between two passes
writing the idea down and then trying to say it back from memory produces lasting knowledge
text: Understanding an idea in class is not the end of learning it. At first the brain turns what it takes in into a faint trace, and that trace wipes out easily. The slower work comes later, mostly while you sleep: nerve circuits replay the sequence you picked up and settle it into place. Go back over the material right away and you gain almost nothing, because the trace is still fresh. Wait until a little of it has slipped away, and the review forces your memory to rebuild what it lost. Pulling the answer back with no help does far more than reading the page again. That is why people who study learning tell you to stretch the gap between one pass and the next. Write the idea down, put the card away, then try to say it back with nothing in front of you. What you keep that way stays.

units: a bookbinding shop nearly stopped operating
its last craftsman lost the use of one of his hands
the moves of the trade had never been written down
the woman in charge had him recorded while he described each operation
an apprentice carried out the moves while he corrected her out loud
the outcome was a manual naming the most common fault at every step
the shop kept working and drew applicants from far away
one man's accident set off the writing down of a practice that had been spoken until then
text: A bookbinding shop came close to shutting down when its last craftsman lost the use of one hand. Nobody had ever written the small maneuvers of the trade down, and the woman running the place was afraid the whole repertoire would vanish along with him. So she set a recorder running and had him talk through every operation: sewing the folded sheets, gluing the spine, setting the headbands, paring the leather. An apprentice did the work with her hands while his voice caught her mistakes as they surfaced. Out of that arrangement came a manual nobody had planned, with a note beside each step naming the error people make there most often. The shop stayed open, and the manual brought in applicants from distant regions. One man's injury had pushed a craft that lived only in speech onto the page.

units: the words are missing at the moment of saying back what has been noted
the method proposed rests on a notebook kept for this alone
each page is divided into two columns of unequal width
the wide column takes the word met and a whole sentence that carries it
the narrow column takes a definition written by the learner himself
a mark is added every week the word still slips away
the words piling up too many marks are copied apart and gone over out loud
at the end of a season the notebook forms a word list belonging to its author
text: Your notes accumulate and nothing fastens itself to them. The moment you have to say any of it back, the words desert you. The remedy is modest: a single notebook, reserved for nothing else. Rule every page into two columns of unequal width, a broad one and a slender one. In the broad column, set down the word you ran into and a whole sentence that carries it. In the narrow one, write a short definition in your own wording, never lifted from somewhere else. Any week the word still slips away from you, add a mark beside it. Once a page carries too many marks, copy those stubborn words onto a fresh sheet and work through them standing up and out loud, with the definition kept out of sight. By the end of a season the notebook has turned into a glossary that belongs to nobody but you.

units: two neighborhood workshops announce the same goal of repairing on your own
the first workshop runs in the shape of a lecture
the people at the first leave with papers they will never open again
the second workshop is built around the machines brought in by those who come
there you move ahead by sitting next to someone who has already taken a similar machine apart
the organizers of the second admit that their approach is confused and noisy
the people at the second come back while those at the first grow scarce
the gap between the two workshops comes from where the question starts
text: Two neighborhood workshops make the same offer: learn to repair on your own whatever breaks down at home. The first runs like a lecture. An instructor stands at the front, holds up the tools, hands out a printed guide, and everyone leaves with a stack of paper they will never open again. The second runs like a work site. You show up with your own broken machine, sit down beside a person who has already taken one like it apart, and follow the thread of your own breakdown until it loosens. The people behind the second workshop are the first to admit their setup is loud, disorderly, and hard to measure. Their crowd comes back the following week, though, while attendance at the lecture thins out by the third session. The gap has nothing to do with the equipment. It lies in who asks the question.

units: a smell of white dust catches you as soon as you enter the room
a worn raised platform carries a narrow table and a chair that does not match
a dark board covers the full width of the wall and keeps lines that cannot be wiped off
the school desks lined up keep a hollow groove now out of use
notches were cut into the wood by impatient hands
boxes of yellowed writings are piled on the ledge of the openings
a glass cabinet holds rolled maps a skeleton and jars
the room now serves as storage without anything having been taken out of it
text: Push the door open and the smell of chalk dust reaches you before anything else. At the back, a low platform worn smooth by shoe leather carries a narrow table and a chair that never matched it. A black slate runs the whole width of the wall, streaked with pale lines no cloth will take off anymore. The desks stand in rows of six, each one keeping its hollow groove for ink, dry for years now, and its notches cut by restless hands with a knife. Boxes of yellowed exercises are stacked along the window ledges, every page covered in careful writing. Behind glass, a cabinet holds rolled maps, a wooden skeleton, and dusty jars whose labels are peeling off. Nothing was thrown out and nothing was replaced. The room is a storeroom now, and people step into it the way you step into a memory left open.

units: the ease of deleting a word harms the teaching of writing
the pupil of earlier days left the mark of his hesitations on his page
the first draft counted as proof of a path of thought
the coming of electronic supports made correction invisible
a deleted mistake can no longer be read again by its author
you get better by going back over what you missed and not by handing in a clean copy
the teacher deprived of the first draft judges nothing but an endpoint
the writer argues for giving correction marks their standing back
text: Deleting a word costs nothing now, and the teaching of writing has lost more by that than anyone reckons. A pupil used to write in ink, so the page held on to every hesitation: a crossed-out line, a word called back in the margin, a sentence begun again two lines further down. The draft was not waste. It was evidence that thinking had happened. Then came the electronic screens, where a correction leaves no scar at all. The mistake goes, and the chance of ever reading it again goes with it. Nobody gets better by handing in an immaculate copy. You get better by going back to what you missed. A teacher who sees only the finished version has no view of the mind at work; he grades an arrival and forfeits the journey. Give the crossing-out its standing back and you give error its use as a tool.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman teaching the workshop worked earlier as a potter
a joint condition forced her to give up the wheel
that injury is the reason she moved into teaching
she can no longer show a movement over a long stretch
she therefore cut every movement into short steps named with precision
her students get a vocabulary that other workshops leave unspoken
her apprentices move ahead faster than those trained by imitation alone
being able to describe a fault before correcting it explains that lead
text: The woman who teaches the pottery workshop spent the greater part of her working life at the wheel herself. Inflamed wrist joints put an end to that, and it was the injury that pushed her toward teaching. Since she can no longer sustain a demonstration over any length of time, she had to break every movement into short steps and give each of them an exact name: centering, opening, raising the wall, smoothing. Her students walk away with a vocabulary that most workshops leave unspoken. This insistence on words has had an effect she never planned on. Her apprentices come along faster than apprentices trained by imitation alone, because they can put a name to what went wrong before they fix it. The physical trouble of a single woman changed the way an entire trade gets taught.

units: the book of exercises is aimed at apprentice carpenters
its physical making and its drawings are judged to be of good quality
the rising order of difficulty looks carefully thought through
the book shows nothing but successful moves and never failed ones
a learner who gets it wrong finds no page describing his fault
that absence leads the learner to lay the failure on himself alone
the reviewer suggests adding a picture of the botched piece on the facing page
he also suggests joining to that picture the question to ask in front of it
text: The book of exercises written for apprentice carpenters has a flaw that its handsome manufacture does not buy off. The binding holds, the drawings are clean, the climb in difficulty has clearly been thought through at length. Where it fails is decisive: it displays the cut that works and never the cut that goes astray. An apprentice whose line wanders off finds no page telling him what a mistake looks like, or what it does to the joint once the pieces meet. Too often he concludes that the failure belongs to him alone. Putting this right would be straightforward and inexpensive. Facing every plate, add a picture of the botched piece, and under it the question to ask yourself when you are looking at one. That much would turn a handsome object into an instrument you could genuinely learn from.

units: the reader is torn between evening lessons and going straight into an apprenticeship
the writer of the letter took both roads
the evening teaching announces its program and marks the exercises
on that road a failure costs nothing but a harsh comment
the workshop announces nothing and there you learn by starting over after failing
a mistake made in the workshop is paid for in wasted material
the writer advises beginning with the evening lessons
he recommends noting down what you fail to understand in a notebook before turning up at the workshop
craftsmen gladly take in a newcomer who carries precise questions
text: You asked me whether to sign up for the evening class or go straight into a workshop. I took both roads, and the difference has stayed with me. In the class you move lesson by lesson: the program is laid out in advance, the exercises come back marked, and failing costs you nothing worse than a hard comment. You pick up the principles quickly, but the material stays at arm's length. In the workshop nothing is announced. You watch, you ruin things, you start over, and every mistake is paid for in wasted stock. What you gain there is a confidence no lesson hands you. My advice is short. Begin with the class, keep a notebook of everything that stays unclear, then turn up at the workshop with those pages. Craftsmen open right up to anyone who arrives with a real question. Write and tell me what you decide.

units: the question asked bears on what separates a trainer who marks you from a trainer you forget
the woman running a retraining center puts the difference down to patience with repetition
she names first the listening that lets the learner finish his wrong statement
she names next the cutting of the task into pieces small enough to keep failure away
she names the negative example where the trainer himself performs the faulty move in front of everyone
she names last the silence held while the learner is searching for the answer
the poor trainer talks too much and moves ahead too fast
he takes the clarity of his own explanation for the understanding of his audience
she states that you turn into a trainer by watching other people get it wrong
text: What makes one trainer stay with you for years while another leaves nothing behind? The woman who runs a retraining center answers without a pause: patience with hearing the same thing twice. Then she breaks it down. Listening comes first, since a good trainer lets the learner finish the wrong sentence instead of cutting in. Next comes the slicing: the task is cut into pieces so small that failure hardly gets a chance. Then the bad example, performed by the trainer in front of everyone and owned. Last comes the silence, held while the learner is closing in on it. And the poor trainer? He talks too much, pushes ahead too fast, and takes the clarity of his own explanation for understanding in the room. She adds one thing. Nobody turns into a trainer by reciting. You turn into one by watching other people go wrong.

units: a teacher points out to her student that the tool warps whenever the applied force changes
she asks him to run the movement again in slow motion
the student says he followed the written instructions
the student admits he did not understand the wording of the last point
the teacher explains that heat expands the metal and throws off the measurement
she states that the origin of a fault is rarely found where it shows
the student notices that the cutting waste curls badly
the student concludes on his own that the angle of the tool must change
the teacher considers this reasoning transferable to other machines
she holds that a trade is handed on through an understanding of cause and effect
text: The instructor tells her apprentice that the blade warps the moment his wrist presses harder. She has him set the tool down and repeat the entire movement at half speed. He protests that he followed the written sheet exactly, though the final instruction never quite made sense to him. She unpacks it: the hand leans in early, the workpiece overheats, the metal expands, and the measurement comes out false. A fault, she adds, seldom begins where it eventually becomes visible. The apprentice studies the shaving emerging from the groove and remarks that it curls badly. Then he reaches the conclusion himself, that the cutting angle must change. She approves, and promises that once such reasoning becomes habit, it transfers to every machine in the workshop. A trade, she concludes, passes from one person to another through cause and effect, never through imitated gestures.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: knowledge once rested on human memory alone
the death of a teacher meant that part of his doctrine disappeared
learned communities looked for a lasting safeguard
reciting as a group spread the effort of memory across several people
an error by one reciter was caught by another
writing under dictation then secured what speech preserved badly
the method called for trained copyists and a term by term check of the text
copying mistakes became the new danger
checking by two readers comparing aloud corrected that flaw
piling up these precautions made the doctrine transmissible over long stretches of time
text: Before writing, learning survived in human memory alone, and that left it badly exposed. When a teacher died, part of what he taught went into the ground with him. Communities of scholars looked for a safeguard that would outlast any single life. They settled first on reciting in chorus, which spread the burden of holding things across many mouths instead of one. Where a voice faltered, another voice held the line, and the whole came through. Dictation followed, fixing on a surface what speech kept so poorly. The method called for trained copyists and for a check made term by term against the text. Mistakes of the hand now replaced mistakes of the tongue as the chief danger. Against that, two readers would take the copies and compare them aloud. Precaution laid on precaution is why a body of teaching could cross many lifetimes without warping.

units: two ways of teaching hand skills exist side by side
the first has the trainer perform before the learner who then copies
this route suits continuous movements that words convey badly
it leaves the learner helpless once conditions change
the second names and justifies every step
it demands more effort at the outset
it supplies a rule that can be reused in other settings
seasoned trainers blend the two approaches
they ask the learner to describe for himself the movement he has just seen
alternating between watching and speaking anchors the learning more firmly
text: Two ways of teaching hand skills sit side by side, and neither one wins everywhere. The first is showing. The trainer does the work, the learner watches, then tries it. This carries smooth flowing movement quickly, the kind that words handle badly. Its weakness shows up as soon as the setting shifts, since the learner is left with nothing to steer by. The second is telling. Every step gets a name, a place in the order, and a reason. It costs more at the start, but it hands the learner a rule that travels to other jobs. Trainers with years behind them use both. They run through the movement, then make the learner tell it back in his own words. Swinging between the eye and the mouth holds the learning down far better than either route on its own. So the comparison names no winner. It names a mixture.

units: a neighbor recounts his early days in the workshop of a relative
he arranges his account around three memories
he had been given the most unsteady workbench
he understood that the faulty furniture was part of the trial imposed on him
he reversed a pattern he was meant to copy and ruined a stack of boards
the blunder still amuses the crew
no colleague gave him any explanation unprompted
everything came unstuck once he started questioning the old hands
the old hands would answer provided they were asked
he now passes this lesson on to the beginners he supervises
text: The fellow down the hall described his first week in his uncle's workshop, and it reduces to three memories. The bench, first. They handed him the wobbliest one available, the one that rocked whenever he leaned on it, and he understood soon enough that the bench belonged to the trial. The stencil, second. Sent to mark a stack of boards, he laid the pattern down backwards and ruined the entire pile, which the crew still recalls with amusement. The silence, third. Nobody explained anything. They put a tool in his hand and waited. Eventually he began asking questions, and everything opened at once. The old hands answered willingly, they simply wanted the question first. He passes that lesson to the beginners under his supervision, that whoever stays silent learns twice as slowly.

units: the session opens with the handing out of materials to the participants
each one receives an untreated piece of wood and a stiff card template
the participants check that the corner is true with a measuring instrument
warped pieces are pulled out at this stage
the outline of the template is traced in one unbroken line
the teacher makes uneven tracings start over
after a break the measurements are carried over to the other face
this transfer brings any drift into the open at once
the session ends with a shared showing of the corrected mistakes
the cutting is put off until the next meeting
text: It opens with the handout, in the training rooms where marking out is taught. Each person gets a rough board and a template cut from stiff card. Next comes the square. The participants set it against the edge and make sure the corner is true, and any board that has twisted is pulled out right there. Then the line. The template is traced with a fine point, and the hand never lifts partway through. The trainer walks the aisles and sends anyone whose line wanders back to the start of it. A break follows. Afterwards each person carries the measurements over to the far face, which brings any drift into the open at once. The session closes with everyone gathered round, each participant holding up a board and naming the mistake he put right. Nothing gets cut until the group meets again.

units: adults take up writing again in the basement of a former storage building
they had given up writing a very long time ago
an association of neighbors lends the premises for nothing
the absence of official oversight spares newcomers the feeling of going back to school
the woman in charge holds that embarrassment discourages more than the difficulty of the subject
the layout of the room makes voices carry
the participants therefore hear one another read
this mutual listening breeds a rivalry among them
a former factory worker moved from copying to writing on her own
every stage of her progress rests on the one before it
text: In the low room beneath an old storehouse, a handful of adults are writing again after letting decades pass without it. A neighborhood association lends the space and asks nothing in return, and that plain generosity accomplishes what no budget could. Because the room answers to no authority, nobody entering feels she is returning to school. The woman running the evening states it plainly, that embarrassment drives more people away than difficulty ever does. The tables are broad, the ceiling high, so voices travel, and because voices travel, everyone hears the others reading aloud. Out of that listening a quiet rivalry emerges. A former factory worker copied first, then dictated to the woman beside her, then wrote unaided. The chain advances slowly, yet each link holds because the previous one held.

units: this training workbench has an adjustable height
its top is drilled with holes at even spacing
beginners hold their piece badly and it drifts under the tool
pegs dropped into the holes lock the piece with no hand clamping
the top is made of a hard wood that is not abrasive to blades
a side rail stores the measuring instruments
this storage frees up the working surface
a container set underneath catches the cutting waste
this collection limits the risk of falls
a slot at the front takes the learner's instruction cards
text: The first thing you notice about a training bench is that it rises and drops to fit the worker, and that its top is drilled with holes at even spacing. Those holes answer an old trouble. A beginner grips the work poorly, it wanders under the tool, and the cut runs off the line. Drop pegs into the holes and the piece sits still, with no vice and no straining fingers. The top is solid beech, dense enough to take a knock, soft enough to leave a cutting edge alone. A rail along one side holds the square and the rule, so they stay within reach instead of littering the surface. Underneath, a tray catches the shavings and offcuts, which keeps the floor from turning slippery. A groove across the front takes the learner's instruction cards. Every part of it answers something a beginner was seen struggling with.

units: learning by heart and learning by inquiry are often presented as incompatible
the author judges this rivalry to be groundless
with nothing held in mind the learner only tries at random
the learner who stops at memory recites a table of contents without knowing what it holds
these two figures fail because they pull apart operations that belong together
memorizing demands an effort at the start and then frees one
it makes attention available for more demanding operations
inquiry stays costly at every stage
it teaches one to state a claim, to test it and to give it up
the author recommends combining the two rather than choosing
text: Learning by heart and learning by inquiry are set against each other far too readily, as though one had to drive the other out. The quarrel strikes me as badly framed. A learner holding nothing in mind does not inquire at all. He gropes, having no material to put together. A learner who has only committed things to memory recites a table of contents for a book he never opened. Both fail, and for one reason, that they pull apart operations the mind keeps joined. Weigh what each of them demands. Memorizing takes its toll early and repays later, since it frees attention for work of a higher order. Inquiry charges at every stage, yet it trains a person to state a claim, put it to the test, and give it up. One yields speed, the other caution. A serious training measures out both and declines to choose.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: none of her relatives had practiced a craft trade before her
her path breaks down into three parts
she began her apprenticeship while her friends were still studying
she learned above all by watching an older practitioner who said little
she repairs damaged books and remakes the worn parts
she turns down orders that call for too short a deadline
she first builds a model in ordinary paper to test her decisions
she deliberately limits her teaching to two students a season
this limit lets her correct movements on the spot
she refuses to write a book, holding that the craft passes from hand to hand
text: No one in her family had worked with their hands before her. The life of this bookbinder falls into three parts. Training came first. She signed on as an apprentice at an age when her friends were still sitting in classrooms, and she learned by watching the hands of an older woman who said very little. Then the work itself. She brings damaged volumes back, resews the gatherings, rebuilds the worn headbands, and turns away any order that comes with a rushed deadline. Before a delicate repair she builds the whole volume again in ordinary paper, so she can test a choice without risking the original. Teaching came last. Two students a season enter her workshop, never more, because she means to catch every movement as it happens. She will not write a manual. One hand, she says, teaches another hand.

units: the author comes out of this woodcraft course with a divided judgment
the opening sessions won him over
a booklet handed out at the start announced a route one could follow
the instructor moved at a pace the novices could bear
the number of participants grew because sign-ups were accepted too late
the trainees had to wait for want of enough tools
a good share of the sessions went by watching the others
the person in charge split the group to put things right
the author holds that this decision came too late
he recommends the course only if numbers are capped in advance
text: Honestly, I came out of that woodworking course in two minds about it, so let me take it in order. The early sessions won me over. We were handed a booklet whose contents page laid out a route you could follow, and the woman teaching kept things moving without leaving the raw beginners behind. Then the group swelled, because sign-ups were still being taken far too late. From that point on you queued for the one saw in the room, and half the session went by watching other people work. The organizer did react and split us in two, which I was glad of, but it came late. The last few sessions clawed back a little of what had been lost. I would send someone there on one condition, that the numbers be capped when the sign-up opens. The material is sound. The running of it is not.

units: the person the message is addressed to teaches a manual trade to beginners
the beginners lose control of the movement as soon as they are no longer guided
the writer blames the way the trade is taught rather than the learners
the demonstration is currently run straight through, with no pause
the proposed remedy is to break the run of movements into three parts
each part ends with a cue the learner can perceive and check alone
a short scoring sheet, filled in by the learner, separates a good movement from a rough one
the writer advises keeping the split in writing for the next group
text: Dear colleague, I owe you an answer about the beginners who lose the movement the moment you let go of their hands. The fault sits in the method, not in how hard they concentrate. You run the whole sequence through in one go, then ask them to copy it in a single sweep, and the memory of the motion cannot keep up. Break the run into three stretches, and end each one with a cue they can check on their own, the tool resting at a set angle or a sound you only hear when it goes right. They stop, they check, they carry on. Add a short scoring sheet they fill in themselves, one that tells a movement done right from a movement done roughly. Give them a week of fumbling and most will hold the whole run unaided. Keep a written copy of your split, since the next group will need it. Tell me whether it survives your bench and I will mend it.

units: the first question sets one-to-one teaching against teaching a whole group
one-to-one teaching matches the pace to the learner and catches a mistake as it appears
the group setting puts the learner in front of how the others reason
the group setting forces each learner to say out loud what he thought he had mastered
one-to-one teaching costs a great deal because it ties up one instructor per learner
the group setting shares the effort but thins out the instructor's attention
the managers questioned advise alternating the two arrangements
one single marking scheme applied to both arrangements distorts the comparison
text: A listener asks whether teaching one to one beats teaching a whole group. That turns on what you measure. Tutoring matches the pace to the learner and catches a mistake before it hardens into habit, so practical skills come on quickly. A group does something else. It sets each learner in front of the way the others reason, and it forces them to say out loud what they assumed they had mastered. A second question concerns cost. Tutoring ties up one instructor per learner, which keeps it scarce, whereas a group shares the effort and thins the instructor's attention. So must one be picked? The managers questioned advise alternating: the group session lays down the common markers, and the private one clears the blockages a group leaves untouched. A last question turns to assessment. One marking scheme for both arrangements distorts the comparison, since they do not aim at the same gain.

units: an employee at a bookbinding workshop recounts an exchange with a visitor
the visitor wanted to know what the training covers
the employee sorts the learning into three groups
the first group covers knowing the materials and the marks left by old workshops
the second group covers carrying out the movements
the third group comes down to stamina, and that is the one that makes people give up
half the apprentices give up before their first season ends
people leave at the point where the apprentice is asked to decide with nothing to copy
the employee judges success by the absence of fingerprints on the leather
text: An attendant at a bookbinding workshop recounts an exchange with a visitor. She wanted to know what the training covers. He told her it sorts into three groups. The first has to do with the stuff itself: telling one paper from another, picking a glue, reading the marks an old workshop left behind. The second is the hands: folding without crushing, stitching at an even pitch, pressing a cover without bruising it. The third, he said, comes down to stamina, and that is the one that wears people down. She asked how many apprentices give up. Half of them leave before their first season ends, he answered, usually at the point where nobody shows them anything anymore and they have to decide with nothing to copy. She asked what the surest sign of success is. He pointed to the leather: an apprentice sure of his hands leaves no fingerprints on it.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: at the outset the learner lodged with his master to learn a trade
the learner watched for several seasons before being allowed a tool
trade bodies then imposed stages and a fixed length of training
the learner had to submit a finished piece to the judgement of seasoned craftsmen
a refusal forced the learner to start his piece over
as workshops grew, the master could no longer follow each learner
the tricks of the trade were then set down in written manuals
technical schools took over next, with syllabuses and examinations
the shift brought steadiness and cost some of the attention given to one learner
text: To begin with, learning a trade looked nothing like school. You moved in with a master, slept under his roof, and watched him work for whole seasons before anyone let you touch a tool. Then came the trade bodies, which set out stages, tests and a fixed length of training. A learner had to hand in a finished piece for the seasoned men to judge, and if they turned it down, he started over. Workshops grew, and no master had the time to follow each learner, so the tricks of the trade were written down in manuals and the learner had to puzzle them out alone. Technical schools arrived last, with their syllabuses, their classes and their examinations. At every step something steady was gained, and a little of the attention the old master gave his one learner was lost. The argument is far from settled.

units: reading a chapter again wrongly convinces you that you own it
how familiar the text feels gets mistaken for having memorised it
rereading calls on recognition while the test calls for recall
recognition comes so easily that the learner breaks off revising too soon
the learner then finds out what he is missing while sitting the test
saying the content back from memory with the book shut exposes the gaps
the difficulty felt during recall strengthens the memory
the practical consequence is turning each page into a question put to yourself
learners trained this way hold on to more a year later without revising any longer
text: Reading a chapter again gives you the feeling that you own it. The text turns familiar, your eyes slide along, and that ease gets mistaken for real memory. Researchers on learning explain where the muddle starts: rereading calls on recognition, while the test calls for recall. Those are two different operations. Recognition comes easy, so the learner breaks off revising too soon and finds the gap only once the paper sits in front of him. Shut the book, try to say the content back from memory, and the opposite happens. The effort hurts, it exposes the holes, and that very difficulty sets the trace deeper. One practical consequence follows: turn each page you have read into a question you put to yourself. Learners trained that way hold on to more a year later, without having revised any longer than the rest.

units: a pupil was stuck on the same line for the whole lesson
his voice grew fainter as his embarrassment grew
the usual teacher took him for a slow pupil
a teacher passing through looked at the way he held the page
the pupil tilted the sheet and followed the line with his fingernail
the teacher gave him a strip of card with a slot cut into it
the slot laid over the line stopped the words from jostling one another
the pupil first said the letters one by one, then read a whole sentence
the teacher left a description of the method on a card in a drawer
text: The boy had been stuck on the same line since the lesson began. He droned out the syllables, went back, lost his place, and his voice dropped as his embarrassment rose. The schoolmaster saw nothing but a slow pupil. A stand-in teacher, there for a week, watched the way he held the page: he tilted the sheet and traced the line with his fingernail. She handed him a strip of card with a slot cut into it. The boy slid the slot over the line, and the words stopped jostling one another. He said the letters one by one at first, then joined the syllables, then read a whole sentence without stopping for breath. She said nothing about it, but she wrote the method on a card and left it in the drawer of the platform desk. Two seasons on, the boy was reading aloud to his class without a stumble.

units: the reader must settle on one of the two methods and stay with it
the first method rests on writing the list out again and again
once the list is covered, you write it back from memory and then check it
the first method suits runs that are short
the second method means making up cards with a question and an answer
you answer aloud and set aside the cards you have got right
the second method holds off forgetting better on long runs
one identical mock test after a week decides between the two methods
using both together would make it impossible to tell which one worked
text: Before you set out to memorise a list of terms, pick one of two methods and stay with it to the end. First method: copy it out. Write the list in full, cover it, then write down again whatever you can call up. Compare, cross out what went wrong, and start over on a clean sheet. This one puts the hand to work and suits short runs. Second method: question yourself. Cut the list into cards, one item per card, question on one side and answer on the other. Shuffle them, answer aloud, and set aside every card you have got right. This one holds off forgetting better on long runs. Put them side by side after a week, on the same mock test, and keep whichever leaves you hesitating less. Whatever you do, avoid running both in that first week, or you will never know which one did the work.

units: a training centre fitted out in a former market hall received journalists
the woman in charge set out three pieces of work under way
the first covers taking in adults who are switching trades
half of these adults have not studied since they left school
the second reorganised the workshops so that every bench is in view
that clear view makes hazardous handling easier to watch over
the third brings forward the check on what has been learned, judged far too late
a short check now closes every session and gives a marker to measure against
one-to-one support entrusted to former learners is meant to cut the number who drop out
text: Housed in a former market hall, a training centre opened its doors to the press. Its director set out three pieces of work under way. The first concerns intake: the centre now takes in adults switching trades, half of whom have not studied since they left school. The second concerns the premises. The workshops have been laid out so that every bench stays in view from the central aisle, which makes hazardous handling easier to watch over. The third targets assessment, which instructors judged to come far too late; a short check now closes every session and gives the learner a marker to measure himself against. Asked about the people who drop out, the director admitted the numbers stay high through the first season. She announced one-to-one support entrusted to former learners, who know the obstacles because they cleared them themselves.

units: a low room with whitewashed walls serves as a writing workshop for adults
each table is laid out with a sheet, a pencil and a book of models
the leader draws a letter of unusual size on the board
the participants go through the book of models before writing anything at all
each of them then copies the letter ten times over, watching the tilt of the pencil
halfway through the session the leader corrects the position of their wrists
the strokes grow steadier as the session goes on
each of them cuts out his best line and glues it into a shared notebook
the shared notebook hangs near the door of the room
text: A low room with whitewashed walls serves as a writing workshop for a group of adults. Before they arrive, each table holds a blank sheet, a sharpened pencil and a book of models. The leader opens the shutters, then draws a single letter on the board at an unusual size. The participants come in, settle down, and start by leafing through the book of models without writing anything at all. Each of them then copies the letter ten times over, watching the tilt of the pencil. Halfway through the session the leader walks between the rows and straightens their wrists. The sheets fill with strokes, uneven at first, then steadier. At the end, each of them cuts out his best line and glues it into a shared notebook that hangs near the door. The room empties, the pencils go back in their box, and the notebook keeps the record.

units: the writer disputes the idea of replacing general subjects with short courses
these short courses are cut to fit one particular job
what a job consists of changes over the course of a working life
training that fits too snugly turns useless once the equipment changes
the abilities that last are reading a stiff manual and reasoning over a drawing
putting a clean question to a colleague is one of these lasting abilities
these abilities come by a long detour and look pointless while they are taught
looking pointless is what makes them easy to cut from a syllabus
the writer holds that practice with no theoretical detour turns out interchangeable hands
text: Everyone keeps saying that school ought to prepare people for work, and a hasty conclusion gets drawn from it: swap the general subjects for short courses cut to fit one particular job. The intention makes sense, the result is a disaster. A job changes what it consists of over a working life, and training that fits too snugly turns useless the moment the equipment moves on. What lasts is the ability to read a stiff manual, to reason over a drawing, to put a clean question to a colleague. Those abilities come by a long detour, and they look pointless at the very moment they are being taught, which is what makes them easy to cut. So we save on what prepares people best and pay later in failed career changes. I am not defending theory against the workbench. I say that the workbench with no detour turns out interchangeable hands.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a workshop supervisor uses two ways of teaching
the first one shows the movement and then has it copied
the second one lets the learner work it out alone before any correction
imitation gives clean results within the first week
what is picked up by imitation is poorly retained
working it out alone multiplies mistakes and wastes material
the learner who searched understands the reason behind every movement
faced with an unfamiliar task, the imitator stalls and the searcher adapts
the trainer blends the two approaches according to how dangerous the operation is
text: The workshop supervisor trains his apprentices two ways, and he never stops setting one against the other. The first runs on demonstration. He performs the movement in front of the learner, slows every stage down, then stands back and lets it be copied. The second, which he trusts more, makes the beginner fumble alone with the material before anyone corrects a thing. Demonstration pays off quickly, with clean work inside the first week, but the memory of it wears thin. Fumbling wrecks a good deal of stock and turns out one mistake after another, and yet whoever comes through it has grasped for good why every movement goes where it does. On an unfamiliar job the gap shows. The imitator, however careful, stalls, while the one who searched adapts. So the supervisor mixes the two, saving demonstration for the dangerous operations and free exploration for the assemblies that carry no risk.

units: the reviewer finds three strengths and two weaknesses in this beginner's manual
the notions are introduced in short linked stages
this progression keeps the reader from feeling out of his depth
difficult movements are broken down across several pictures
rival handbooks make do with one picture per movement
the author keeps away from obscure vocabulary while staying exact
the exercises offered are judged far too few
the answers at the back of the volume say nothing about the reasoning
the book is recommended to anyone who works in an orderly way
it suits badly the reader who needs to be corrected at every turn
text: Three strengths set this beginner's manual apart from comparable handbooks, and two weaknesses temper the praise. Its progression comes first. The book advances in short stages, each fresh notion resting on the one before it, so the reader takes in the material without ever feeling out of his depth. Its illustration comes next. Awkward movements are broken down across a run of pictures, where rival handbooks make do with a single one. Its language comes last, turning away from obscure vocabulary while conceding nothing in accuracy. The reservations bear on two points. The exercises closing each chapter remain far too few for anyone hoping to practice in earnest, and the answers, pushed to the back of the volume, keep silent about the reasoning that produced them. The book therefore suits an orderly reader, and suits much less the one who needs his errors caught at every turn.

units: the writer of the letter addresses his former trainer
he let a long stretch of time pass before writing
at the start he followed the instructions without grasping their sense
he said them over to himself from memory in the evening
the workshop then handed him a whole order
he ruined his first three pieces and thought of giving up
repairing the fourth piece showed him what patience was worth
he now lays out his equipment the night before and writes his mistakes down
he has been asked to train a newcomer
he finds that what he inherited above all is a way of looking at a mistake
text: I am writing at last, after letting far too long go by, to tell you what your teaching has become in my hands. At the start I followed your instructions without grasping any of them, and I said them over to myself in the evening like a lesson learned by heart. Then the workshop handed me an order of my own. I ruined the first three pieces and came close to walking away. It was while repairing the fourth that what you said about patience meant something at last. Now I lay my tools out the night before, I write my mistakes down in a notebook, and I read that notebook again before every fresh batch. Last season the manager asked me to break in a newcomer. I heard your own words coming out of my mouth, almost without choosing them. That is when I understood: what you handed me was a way of looking at a mistake, not only a trade.

units: explaining a notion to someone else improves retention
a lesson left sitting in a notebook demands no effort of memory
putting it into words out loud makes the brain hunt for every element
that effort of recall hardens the memory
an unexpected question brings out a gap nobody had noticed
a gap once noticed can then be filled
too wide a difference in level pushes the explainer to cut his account down too far
cutting it down that far warps what he thought he had a firm hold on
the ideal listener is slightly less advanced but able to push back
text: Do you hold on to something better once you have said it out loud to someone else? You do, and the reason is short. As long as the lesson sits in a notebook, nothing forces your memory to build it again. The moment you have to put it into words, your brain goes hunting for every link, and that hunt hardens the trace. And what if the other person asks something you never saw coming? So much the better. The question opens up a gap you would never have spotted on your own, and a gap you have spotted can be filled. Does that mean explaining anything to anybody pays off? No. When the difference in level runs too wide, whoever explains trims the whole account down too far, and that trimming ends up warping what he thought he had a firm hold on. So the right partner stands a step behind you, close enough to follow, fresh enough to push back.

units: the woman running a shared workshop describes a problem of keeping people
the newcomers were giving up after three sessions
they went home every evening with a botched piece of work
a volunteer craftsman saw the beginners tense up at their first cut
the team changed the way a session runs
a newcomer now finishes a piece that somebody else began
he takes care only of the finishing touches
the beginners leave with a finished object and they come back
the craftsman reckons that this choice slows down the learning of the cut
he grants that the learners stay long enough to end up learning it
text: The woman who runs the shared workshop made no secret of the trouble when we asked her about it. Beginners were dropping out after three sessions, she told us, because they went home every evening with a botched object in their hands. A volunteer carpenter, sitting over by the bench, backed her up. He had watched hands tighten at the very first cut. So the team rebuilt the way a session runs. Every newcomer now ends up on a piece somebody else began, she explained, with nothing left but the sanding and the smoothing. The beginner walks out holding a finished object, she added, and he turns up again the week after. The carpenter tempered all this a little. The arrangement slows down the learning of the cut, he said, but it keeps people around long enough that they end up learning it anyway.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: knowledge passed on by mouth and by hand before writing
spoken storytelling rested on the return of the same turns of phrase
the group put right whatever the teller got wrong
learning with the hands did almost without words
no rule in the abstract was taught to the beginner
the apprentice copied what he watched and was corrected on the spot
the right movement settled into muscle before it was understood
writing keeps the exact words but loses the voice and the presence
workshop teaching dies out if the craftsman trains nobody to follow him
the two ways of passing things on ended up completing each other
text: Long before writing froze what people knew, everything passed from mouth to hand, and that double road had laws of its own. Spoken story lived on repetition. The teller came back again and again to the same turns of phrase, and the memory of the listening group pulled him straight whenever he strayed. Handwork barely used speech at all. Nobody taught the beginner a rule in the abstract. He watched, he copied, he got his knuckles rapped, and the right movement settled into muscle long before it reached the mind. Once carved signs spread about, the comparison turned around. The written page kept the words untouched and lost the voice, the shading, the presence of the master. The workshop kept the movement alive and went dark with the craftsman who had trained nobody to follow him. In time the two roads came to answer each other.

units: the author describes four levers of lasting memory
going back over a notion at widening intervals fixes it better
a recall that comes a little hard hardens the memory
questioning yourself works better than reading again
reading again creates a misleading feeling of command
mixing exercises of different kinds slows the session down
that mixing teaches you to identify the problem before choosing the procedure
the brain replays the learned sequences during sleep
the most useful sequences move toward stable memory
these levers do not spare you repetition but make it pay better
text: Four mechanisms hold a piece of learning in place for good. The first is spacing. A notion gone over again at widening intervals settles deeper than the same notion drilled in one sitting, because every recall that comes a little hard hardens the trace. The second is self-testing. Questioning yourself beats reading the page again, since a second reading hands you a feeling of command that nothing checks. The third is interleaving. Alternating exercises of different kinds slows the session down, yet it trains you to name the problem before you pick the procedure for it. The fourth is sleep, during which the brain replays the sequences it has learned and moves the most useful ones into stable storage. Not one of these levers stands in for repeated practice. Each of them raises what that practice returns.

units: a beginner in bookbinding is given an instruction that strikes her as senseless
her trainer forbids her to sew before folding an enormous quantity of sheets
she carries out the order without believing in it
she feels she is losing a whole season
her folds grow even as the weeks go by
her fingers end up feeling the thickness of the paper without measuring
once allowed to sew, she gets a straight spine and clean seams
