the trainer admits he went through the same ordeal and hated it
he explains that this dreary task trains the hand and not the craft itself
a hand already trained picks up the next movement easily
text: The apprentice bookbinder was given, in her first winter, an instruction that struck her as senseless. The master of the workshop forbade her to sew a single gathering until she had folded a mountain of sheets by hand. She carried out the order without believing in it, sure that she was throwing a whole season away. Week after week her folds grew even, and then her fingers gave up measuring altogether. They felt the thickness of the paper and stopped where they had to. When she was allowed to sew at last, she found the thread following a spine already straight, with no seam buckling anywhere. The master admitted then that he had gone through the same ordeal and had hated every hour of it. That dreary labor, he added, teaches nothing about binding. It trains the hand, and a hand already trained picks up the next movement without effort.

units: the procedure starts with cutting the piece into short fragments
an overloaded memory holds on to nothing
a fragment of two bars settles better than a full page
each fragment must first be played at a slow pace
a repeated mistake beds in as firmly as a correct movement
you join two fragments when one comes out clean three times running
the breakdowns happen above all at the joins between fragments
the session ends with a run through the whole thing however rough
the next day it is better to start from the joins than from the opening
ignoring this advice makes the beginning solid and the ending shaky
text: Start by cutting the piece into short segments, because a flooded memory holds on to nothing: two bars settle where a whole page melts away. Then work each segment through at a slow pace, since a mistake played over and over beds in as firmly as a correct movement, and going slowly keeps the fault from being written in. Once a segment comes out clean three times running, join it to the segment beside it, because a piece gives way at the joins far more often than in the middle of a phrase. Close the session with a run through the whole thing, rough as it may be, so that your memory keeps a trace of the shape as a whole. The next day, start from the joins and not from the opening. Skip that, and the first bars will gleam while the ending stays shaky right up to the concert itself.

units: a converted shed houses a neighborhood workshop
the people living nearby saw the retired craftsmen carrying their trade away
the young people of the area had nowhere to learn
an association set up a very plain arrangement
each retired volunteer puts in two half sessions a week
he takes on two beginners at the most
there is no program and no assessment
you start straight from a repair a neighbor has asked for
half of the beginners carry on from one season to the next
the old hands say that explaining forces them to pull apart their automatic movements
text: Sanding, sawing and loud talk fill the converted shed at the bottom of the street, home now to a workshop for the whole street. Everybody living nearby knew the problem. Craftsmen going into retirement carried their trade off with them, and the young people around here had nowhere to learn anything. An association put together an arrangement with nothing clever about it. Each retired volunteer turns up two afternoons a week and takes on two beginners, never more. No program, no assessment. You start straight from whatever a neighbor has asked for, a wobbly chair, a shutter that sticks, and the old hand shows you as the job goes along. Half the beginners carry on from one season to the next. The old hands gain something too, since explaining forces them to pull apart movements that had gone automatic.

units: the training space is laid out as four separate stations
the opening station is where raw stock is sorted and cleaned
marking out calls for careful checking so that assembly does not go wrong
the assembly step uses clamping tools worked by two people
the final station brings together sanding, finishing and checking of measurements
a posted sheet gives the order of operations, the tolerances allowed and the safety gear
the instructor moves around to correct how the students handle their hands
you have to go through every station before you are allowed to work unsupervised
text: A hands-on training workshop breaks down into four stations, and each one covers its own family of movements. The opening station handles raw stock: the apprentice weighs, sorts and cleans whatever will pass through later. At the second, everything is marked out, and careful checking of those marks heads off costly trouble at assembly. Third comes the bench, fitted with vises, clamps and a screw press that two students work together. The last station, which most people find tedious, brings together sanding, finishing and measuring to spec. A sheet pinned to the wall lists the order of operations, the tolerances allowed and the protective gear required. The instructor moves from bench to bench, adjusting a grip here, straightening a shoulder there. Every student passes through all four stations before earning the right to work unsupervised.

units: teaching happened first through watching an elder and repeating
the arrival of writing froze the procedures into books
moving pictures later promised a clearer explanation
the writer disputes the idea that this sequence is steady progress
each medium gains in reach what it loses in human presence
the written book reaches distant readers but corrects no movement
the moving image shows a movement from every angle without sensing the hesitation of the person watching
the conclusion argued for is that no medium replaces the presence of an elder
text: Once, teaching was almost wholly a matter of imitation. The learner watched an elder, copied, failed and began again. Then writing arrived and locked the procedures into manuals, turning something alive into something dry. Screens came later and promised clarity of a fresh kind: animated diagrams, explanations cut into steps, a smooth path forward. I would argue that this sequence is no ascent at all. Every medium has gained in reach exactly what it has given up in presence. A manual reaches readers the workshop would never have taken in, yet it cannot steady a shaking hand. Moving pictures show a movement from every angle and never once feel the hesitation of whoever sits watching them. The conclusion takes few words: no medium stands in for an elder leaning over unfinished work.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: an injury to her hand marked the start of her path
she had to work out unusual grips to hold her tools
that constraint made her alert to how each person handles an instrument
she built a reputation as a very fine teacher
she breaks every movement into steps for beginners
her workshop took in students who had been turned away elsewhere
she cut back her own output in order to teach more
that choice lowered her income
her former students, now experts, still use her method
text: The bookbinder in question lost the use of two fingers while she was still young, and that injury shaped the whole course of what came after. She could not hold the folder the way her classmates did, so she was forced to work out grips of her own, and that made her alert to the way other people take hold of a tool. The same alertness later earned her a reputation as a superb teacher. Since she had broken every movement down into steps to make it possible for herself, she could break down a beginner's clumsy attempt just as readily. Her workshop drew students whom other workshops had turned away at the door. As demand grew, she cut back her own output and gave her afternoons over to teaching. The choice cost her income, but it spread: her former students, seasoned now, still work by her method.

units: the beginner's manual is irritating from the opening pages
the author piles up definitions and breaks off his demonstrations with digressions
the reader finishes a chapter without being able to name what he took in
the content itself is judged to be good
the criticism bears on the arrangement and not on the substance
reading it in reverse, starting with the exercises, cleared up the difficulty
the exercises are graded and honest about how hard they are
the book then becomes a resource where you look for what is missing
the advice is to open the theory only when you get stuck
text: Honestly, this beginner's manual annoyed me from the very opening pages. It is a tangle. The author piles up definitions, doubles back on himself, drops a digression into the middle of a proof. You finish a chapter unable to say what you picked up. Worst of all, the material itself is good; it is just served in a jumble. So I tried something: read the thing backwards, starting with the exercises. That cleared everything up. The exercises are superb, graded, honest about how hard they get. Work them first and you find out what you lack, then go hunting for the definition that is missing. The book turns into a store you draw from rather than a corridor you get pushed down. So yes, I would recommend it, with one instruction: start at the back, and open the theory only once you are stuck.

units: the writer reports on two training courses taken during the same term
the first gathered a large group in a tiered lecture room
the speaker there talked without being interrupted
the second brought a very small number together around a table
the woman running the second fell silent as soon as a question came up between participants
the first covered a wide syllabus and left the participants passive
the second moved more slowly and drew out exchanges
a newcomer there got further than a seasoned practitioner
the writer recommends the second arrangement despite its narrower syllabus
text: Dear colleague, here is the account I promised of the two courses I sat through this term, since they contradict each other point for point. The first packed a good thirty of us into a tiered lecture room: the speaker talked, we took notes, and nobody broke in. The second gathered a handful of us around one table, and the woman running it fell silent the moment a question passed between us. The first covered a wide syllabus and left us diligent but idle. The second inched along and made us talkative, muddled at times. Where the first rewarded a tidy page of notes, the second rewarded a mistake said out loud. A newcomer got further there than a seasoned practitioner, because he dared admit what he had not followed. If you must pick for the team, take the second, even at the cost of ground covered.

units: a student asks a stoneworker what learning is
the answer comes as an ordered list
the first item is accepting dullness
the movement made endlessly is compared to water wearing away rock
the second item is accepting difficulty
an obstacle overcome leaves a mark that ease does not leave
the third item is taking account of what the material will allow
another item is putting up with harsh correction from an elder
the last item is forgetting what was learned so that the hand comes before thought
the craftsman refuses to put a number on how long it takes
text: What does it mean to learn? The student puts the question to the stonecutter, who answers with a list, the way a man lays out his tools along a bench. To learn, he says, is first to consent to dullness: a movement made endlessly wears its way in as water wears limestone. It is next to accept what is hard, not from any taste for pain, but because an obstacle beaten leaves a mark that ease will never press. It is to listen to the stone, which refuses one curve and asks instead for another. It is to bear the eye of an elder who corrects without comforting. It is at last to forget what was learned, so that the hand moves ahead of the mind. How many seasons, the student asks, does that road take? The stonecutter smiles, wipes his chisel and says such a span is crossed, never counted.

units: the instructor first asks for the power to the device to be cut
the trainee reports that the indicator light keeps blinking
the instructor explains that a residual charge stays in the capacitor
you have to wait for that charge to drain away
the cover comes off by loosening the screws crosswise
uneven tightening warps the sealing gasket
the trainee then measures a residual voltage of nothing
the instructor requires the operation to be logged in a register before reassembly
the procedure only holds good if every step is dated and signed
text: The instructor began by telling the trainee to cut the power to the device and watch for the indicator light to go out. She answered that it was still blinking. He explained that a residual charge lingers in the capacitor and that you have to wait until it has drained away entirely. Next he had her take off the cover, loosening the screws crosswise rather than one after another around the rim. She asked what lay behind that rule. Uneven tightening warps the sealing gasket, he told her. She then measured the residual voltage and reported a reading of nothing at all. The instructor accepted the measurement and had her log the operation in the register before anything went back together. He finished by saying the procedure is worthless unless every step is dated and signed.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the spread of town workshops changed the way trades were taught
families were no longer enough to supply the hands needed
masters took children from elsewhere into their own homes
living together this way gave rise to written agreements
the agreements set the term, the upkeep and the secrecy
the ban on teaching outside the workshop protected the worth of the trade
that ban held back the spread of technique
the guilds never settled the contradiction between secrecy and renewing the workforce
travelling workers carried the skills from one workshop to another
text: As workshops multiplied in the towns, the passing on of a trade changed in kind. Families could no longer supply the hands that were wanted, so masters began taking children from elsewhere into their own homes. Living under one roof led to written agreements: how long the bond would run, what food was owed, which methods were never to leave the premises. Secrecy guarded the worth of the trade, so teaching outside the workshop was forbidden, and that ban slowed the spread of technique. Out of it came a contradiction the guilds never managed to settle, since guarding a method meant starving the trade of fresh arms. When traffic between regions picked up, travelling workers carried the skills from one workshop to the next all the same. Secrecy gave way through movement, then, not through any decision of the masters.

units: material read again feels familiar and that familiarity is mistaken for command of it
the student thinks he is ready and then finds himself helpless later on
recognizing a statement takes less effort than producing it from memory
the brain confuses these two sensations
the answer is to question yourself without looking at your notes
the effort of recall strengthens memory even when it fails
the recalls have to be spaced further and further apart
the spacing stretches to the point where forgetting becomes likely
this method leaves a feeling of failure although it works
text: Anyone studying alone runs into a familiar trap: material read a second time feels familiar, and that feeling passes for command of it. The reader shuts his notebook confident, then finds himself helpless a week later. The mechanism is well established. Recognizing a statement costs less effort than producing it from memory, and the brain mistakes one sensation for the other. The fix is a reversal. Instead of rereading, you ask yourself the question and hunt for the answer with your notes shut. The effort of recall strengthens the trace far better than a pleasant reread does, even when nothing comes. You then space those recalls out, close together at first, wider and wider after that, up to the point where forgetting starts to threaten. The method feels thankless, because it makes you feel unsuccessful while it works.

units: the narrator showed the same knot to two learners
the younger one got it after a single demonstration and two failed tries
she asked no questions
the grown man listened closely and took notes
he questioned the narrator about the logic of the crossing
he did not get the knot all evening
the man was trying to understand where the young one simply copied
the narrator took his notebook away and covered his eyes
the man succeeded quickly once he could not see
the narrator concludes that his explanations got in the way of the man's hands
text: I taught the same knot to two learners last season, and the comparison has been nagging at me ever since. The younger one needed a single demonstration: she grabbed the rope, botched it twice running, then got it right without my saying a word, and without asking me a single question. Her neighbor, a grown man, listened to me with perfect courtesy, took notes, asked sharp questions about why the crossing works the way it does. And he failed at it the whole evening. It was not that he learned worse; he learned differently, wanting to understand first what the girl was content to copy. When I finally took his notebook away and tied a cloth over his eyes, his hands found the answer in three tries. The lesson stings a little: my explanations had fed his head and frozen his fingers.

units: the steam produced while cooking moves through the room
on touching the cold glass this steam turns back into liquid
the water left on the pane blocks the view outside
the condensed water slides down and gathers at the bottom of the window
standing water swells the wood and lifts the paint
an unpleasant smell ends up spreading through the kitchen
the root of the trouble is the moisture made inside the home
changing the air while cooking breaks the process
it is better to open up before the film appears than after
text: Steam rising from a pot of boiling water does not simply vanish into thin air. It drifts across the room until it meets the cold glass of the window. Against that chilled surface it turns back into water and leaves a thick film that blurs whatever lies outside. The droplets slide down the pane and gather along the bottom rail of the frame. Let them sit there and the wood swells, the paint lifts in blisters, and a sour smell works its way through the kitchen. So the fault does not lie with the rain falling outside. It lies with the damp air that people make themselves while they cook. Open a window while the pans are on and the chain breaks: wet air leaves, dry air comes in, and the condensation has nothing left to feed on. Anyone who has learned that opens up before the panes turn white, not afterward, once the damage has taken hold.

units: a sharp knock came with every closing of the kitchen cabinet
the door struck the frame instead of settling flat
the tenant first suspected that the wood had warped
sanding the edge changed nothing
a lamp held close revealed play in the upper hinge
the screws were spinning in holes that had grown too wide
glued wood splinters made it possible to build a solid grip again
once dry the screws went back into fresh material
the door closes quietly again
the episode shows that the source of a noise rarely sits where the ear places it
text: A sharp knock came every evening as the kitchen cabinet was shut: the left door struck the frame instead of settling flat against it. The tenant blamed the wood first, certain that damp had crept in and warped the panel. She sanded the edge back with care. Nothing changed. Then she held a lamp close to the joint and saw it at once. The upper hinge had worked loose, two screws were spinning freely in a hole that had widened around them, and the door hung askew. A cabinetmaker's trick fixed it: pack the tired holes with splinters of wood soaked in glue, let them set hard, then drive the screws into fresh material. Since then the door swings shut without a sound and the handle no longer scrapes the frame beside it. The whole business left her with a rule. When furniture complains, the source is rarely where your ear puts it.

units: the two cleaning cloths do not serve the same purpose
the kitchen cloth is thin and dries without leaving marks
the kitchen cloth suits dishes and cooking surfaces
the floor cloth soaks up a large puddle
the floor cloth leaves a damp film behind it
the two must be stored apart
the floor cloth needs rinsing in scalding water after use or it will smell
the kitchen cloth goes into the machine with the rest of the wash
the deciding test is contact with food
text: Want to clean fast and clean well? Start by telling your two helpers apart, because they were never meant for the same job. The dish towel is thin and tightly woven; it holds little water but wipes dry without leaving streaks, so keep it for plates, glasses, and the cooking surface. The floor cloth is thick and loose. It drinks up a whole puddle, yet it leaves a damp film behind wherever it passes, and it belongs to the floor, never the table. Get into the habit of storing them apart, one folded in a drawer, the other hanging over the bucket. Rinse the floor cloth in scalding water after every pass, or it holds on to a stale smell. The towel goes into the machine with the sheets. One last test, the only one to keep if the rest slips away: ask whether the surface touches food. Yes, take the towel. No, take the other.

units: a group has set up a repair workshop in an old covered market
a first bench is given over to clothes and cloth accessories
trousers are taken up there and fallen hems are stitched back
a second bench handles electrical devices
damaged power cords make up most of the electrical requests
a third bench looks after furniture
legs are glued back there and fittings or handles are replaced
a fourth space lends out tools for a modest membership
the waiting line has not grown shorter since the opening
a mobile service is planned for outlying districts
text: Inside an old covered market, a local group has opened a workshop where things once thrown out are given a second life. The first bench takes in cloth: a pair of trousers shortened, a fallen hem stitched back into place, a torn bag strap swapped for another one. The second is kept for electrical devices, and broken power cords make up most of what comes through the door. The third, far noisier than the rest, works on furniture: a loose leg glued back on, a hinge reset, a fresh handle screwed into place. A quieter fourth corner runs as a tool library, where anyone can borrow a drill in return for a small membership. The volunteers press one point above all others. The line has not grown any shorter since the doors first opened, which says the know-how is missing more than the will. A mobile service is due to reach the outlying districts before long.

units: at sunrise the courtyard smells of wet stone
washing done the day before hangs on a line strung between two walls
the water dripping from the washing runs into a groove cut in the ground
by midday the air dries out and the sheets swell
a cat settles on the warm rim of the well
a wooden panel bangs on an upper floor before falling back against the wall
late in the afternoon a neighbor comes for her washing
she leaves the pins clipped to the line
in the evening the courtyard empties and a smell of soap lingers
night brings the damp back onto the flagstones
text: At sunrise the inner courtyard still smells of wet stone. Yesterday's wash sags on a line strung between two walls, and the water falls drop by drop into a narrow groove cut along the paving. Toward midday the air dries out, and the sheets swell and snap like sails. A gray cat settles on the warm rim of the well, its eyes half closed against the light. A wooden shutter bangs on an upper floor, then falls back slackly against the wall. Late in the afternoon a neighbor comes down for her wash, folds each piece over her arm, and leaves the pins clipped to the line behind her. Once evening comes the courtyard empties, the groove dries out, and nothing is left but a smell of soap hanging between the walls. Then night brings its chill, the damp creeps back onto the flagstones, and the courtyard quietly gets ready to begin the round again.

units: welding a casing shut instead of screwing it down cuts off access to the inner parts
with no access the independent shop cannot work out what has failed
with no diagnosis no price is quoted
the owner ends up buying a replacement device
each step of the reasoning looks sound taken on its own
the sequence leads to throwing out an object that a minor part would have saved
as repairers grow scarce the handing on of technical skill breaks off
the know-how is missing where demand is rising
the useful move is on design and not on sorting waste
text: Turning a repair away costs far more than it looks, and the mechanism is worth setting out with some care. A maker who welds a casing shut instead of screwing it down cuts off every route to the parts inside. With no way in, the independent shop cannot work out what has failed. With no diagnosis, it will not quote a price. With no quote, the owner goes and buys a replacement. Each link looks sound on its own, and the whole chain ends with a discarded object that one hinge or one seal would have kept in use. A second effect runs beneath it, harder to see: as repairers grow scarce, the handing on of technical skill breaks off, so the know-how is missing at the very place where demand keeps rising. Reversing that means working upstream, on how devices are designed, rather than downstream, on how the waste is sorted.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the alterations seamstress keeps a narrow shop in a neighborhood
she began as an apprentice in a clothing workshop
she put linings together there one after another
the closing of the workshop left her without a job
she owned only a secondhand machine and had no customers
she changed scale by mending single pieces instead of producing runs
each repair costs less than a replacement garment
her order book shows a wait of two weeks
she is handing the trade on to an apprentice
text: Behind a narrow shopfront, the neighborhood seamstress keeps up a trade that most people had written off. She began as an apprentice in a clothing workshop, running linings together one after another, day after day. When that workshop closed its doors she was left without a job, holding a secondhand machine and not a single customer of her own. Her answer was to change scale. Rather than sew long runs, she offered to rescue single pieces instead. A hem taken up, a sandal strap sewn back on, a pocket restitched, a broken fastener swapped out: every job of that kind costs less than the garment it saves. Her shop is never empty and her order book shows a wait of two weeks. She has taken on an apprentice of her own, sure that the trade dies unless it is handed over out loud, with a hand laid on the work.

units: two clothes racks are sold in the same place at very different prices
the steel model opens easily and carries a heavy load
its feet skid on a smooth floor
the aluminum model weighs half as much
the aluminum model packs into a slim sleeve
its drying surface is smaller
the heavy one suits large households
the light one suits cramped homes
one corrodes at the joints and the other bends under a wet load
the choice turns on the room the buyer has
text: Two clothes racks share the same shelf and carry a wide gap in price between them, yet daily use settles the matter far less sharply than the packaging claims. The first, in coated steel, opens out with a single pull and takes a heavy load without sagging in the middle. Its side wings lock on a firm catch, but its feet skid on a smooth floor. The second, in aluminum, weighs half as much and packs away into a slim sleeve, which suits a cramped home. Its drying surface stays smaller, though, and two sheets barely fit on it at once. Put to work, the heavy one serves a large household while the light one serves a small place. Neither deserves the enthusiasm of its own leaflet: one corrodes at the joints, the other bows its bars under a wet towel. What settles the choice, above all else, is the room the buyer has to spare.

units: the writer of the message is leaving and gives instructions to the housemate
the kitchen faucet drips if it is shut too sharply
a tool for pouring oil sits under the sink
the wardrobe door has to be lifted to close
a hanger for a coat has been cleared
the hot water takes a while before it can be used
the mailbox fills up fast and has to be emptied
the recycling bag has to go out at the start of the week
the neighbor below knocks on the ceiling when people walk heavily in the evening
that neighbor sleeps while the residents are awake
text: Hey, I head off tonight, so here is how the place works, with nothing left out I hope. Kitchen: the faucet drips if you shut it too sharply, so turn it slowly, and the funnel for oil sits under the sink beside the floor cloth. Bedroom: the wardrobe closes badly, you have to lift the door as you push it, and I have cleared a hanger for your coat. Bathroom: the water heater takes an age to warm up, so switch it on well before you undress. Mail: the box fills up fast, so empty it on your way in and leave the lot on the low table. The recycling bag goes out at the start of the week, so remember to carry it down. One more thing, the man below knocks on his ceiling as soon as anyone walks heavily after the evening meal. Do not hold it against him, he sleeps while the rest of us are still up.

units: a building caretaker describes how his week runs
he starts at first light with the cleaning of the shared areas
he checks the lighting in the stairwell
he puts the bins out before the collection truck comes
he brings the washed bins back once the collection is done
the lower fitting on the bike room door gives way regularly
he straightens that door every other week
he gives a whole stretch of time to repairs reported by the residents
he makes a round at the end of the day to check the locks
he reckons that the steadiness of the routine keeps him going
text: We asked the building caretaker to walk us through his week, one task at a time. He starts at first light with the shared areas: sweeping the hall, running a mop across the entrance, checking the bulbs in the stairwell. Asked what follows, he explains that he wheels the bins out before the truck arrives, then brings them back washed once the collection has moved on. We ask him which problem turns up most often. He names the bike room door, whose lower hinge gives way under the weight and which he has to straighten every other week. Midweek he gives a whole stretch of time to the repairs that residents have reported. Then comes the evening round, when he tries every lock in turn. Asked whether the work tires him out, he answers that the steady routine keeps him going more than it wears him down.

units: a resident from an upper floor warns the caretaker that a door no longer locks
the closing mechanism gives way as soon as the handle is released
water seeps in through a damaged drainpipe above the door
the caretaker had already entered the fault in his logbook
he says he can undertake nothing without the building manager's approval
the resident stresses that the delay encourages rust in the lock
the two agree to wedge the door leaf with a piece of wood
a canvas sheet is planned to divert the flow toward the street drain
the caretaker promises a written reminder before the end of the week
the resident wants to collect written backing from the other occupants
text: A resident from one of the upper floors stopped the caretaker in the hallway to report that the door of the bicycle room would not lock any more. The catch, she said, slid back the moment anyone let go of the handle, and rain was working its way in through a split drainpipe just above the doorway. The caretaker answered that the fault already sat in his logbook, but that he could start nothing on it until the building manager had signed off. Every day of waiting feeds the rust in the lock, she pointed out. The two of them settled on a stopgap. A wooden wedge would hold the leaf of the door in place, and a stretch of canvas would send the water out toward the street drain. He promised to put a reminder in writing before the week was out, and she offered to collect the backing of the other occupants on paper.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: households once drew their water from a dug shaft or a holding tank
a vessel had to be hauled up and the grit left to settle at the bottom
the supply was kept in a ceramic pot standing somewhere cool
these days one movement at the household fitting delivers the water
the flow no longer depends on the physical strength of whoever draws it
the old shortage forced people to reuse the water they had washed with
every loss of water was watched closely back then
today's abundance makes a seepage hard to notice
progress removed the carrying but concealed the waste
text: Before running water reached the home, a household built its whole day around a dug shaft or a holding tank. Someone hauled the vessel up, waited for the grit to settle at the bottom, then kept the supply in a ceramic pot standing somewhere cool. Set beside that routine, an ordinary kitchen now looks almost effortless: one movement at the household fitting, and the flow no longer depends on the bodily strength of whoever draws it. Comfort is not the whole of the difference, though. Shortage used to enforce a discipline of its own. Washing water went back into scrubbing the floor, and every loss was watched closely. Abundance has loosened that watchfulness, and a seepage can run for weeks on end before anyone notices it. Progress took away the carrying, and hid the waste in the very same stroke.

units: a kitchen drawer holds tools whose purpose is often forgotten
the tool with a long handle and a deep bowl lifts hot liquid
the perforated utensil holds the food back while the water runs away
its holes must be narrow so that nothing is lost
the dish rack allows drying by air with no help from anyone
the citrus press keeps the liquid apart from the flesh and traps the seeds
the bendy blade wipes the side of a bowl clean without harming it
each utensil answers one particular movement
text: You pull open a kitchen drawer and there they are, a whole crowd of tools whose purpose most of us have quietly forgotten. Take the ladle. That long handle and that deep bowl are there so you can lift boiling liquid out of a pot without scalding your knuckles. The strainer holds the pasta or the beans back while the water runs away, and its holes have to be narrow, or half your supper goes down the drain with it. The rack works on its own, over time: you stand the rinsed plates in it and the air alone does the drying. The citrus press keeps the juice well apart from the flesh and traps the pips at the bottom. And the bendy scraper wipes the side of a bowl clean without harming it. Each one answers one movement of your hand, so mixing them up only makes the job harder than it needs to be.

units: the incident happens just before the bread shop opens its doors
the cooking appliance can no longer reach the heat required
the woman in charge suspects the burner first, then the ignition sensor
the first bake comes out too pale and the display stays nearly bare
a young employee decides to inspect the flue opening
burnt bread debris was blocking the duct and starving the flame of air
clearing the duct takes about half an hour
the next bake recovers its normal color and smell
the woman in charge adds this check to her weekly habits
the story then spreads through the neighborhood by word of mouth
text: It began in the last quiet hour before the bread shop opened its doors. The woman in charge found that her oven would not climb to the heat she needed for the morning. She suspected the burner first, then the sensor that governs the ignition. The first bake came out pale, with no crust worth the name, and the display stayed nearly bare. Customers came in, went away again, came back without understanding. It was a young employee who thought to open the flue hatch: burnt scraps of bread had packed the duct tight and were starving the flame of air. Clearing it took about half an hour, dust and all. From the next bake on, the loaves had their color back and their smell with it. She wrote that check into her weekly habits, and from counter to counter the story crossed the whole neighborhood.

units: shoes must be kept away from any heat source because the material dries out
the lower part has to be brushed to remove the dried mud
hardened dirt holds water and attacks the stitching
an interior that feels cold and soft shows the fabric has taken in water
crumpled paper serves to draw that dampness out
the wax goes on in small amounts and in circular movements
a layer laid on too thick is not taken in and spoils the look of the surface
polishing with a woolen cloth warms the wax and closes the pores
neglect brings a split at the point where the foot bends
text: Because leather dries out when it sits beside a radiator, begin by carrying the pair well away from any source of heat at all. Brush the sole next, for caked mud holds the water against the stitching and slowly eats away at it. Slide a hand into the lining: if it feels cold and soft to you, it has drunk in yesterday's rain, and crumpled paper must be pressed inside to draw that dampness back out. Now the wax, a mere trace of it, worked in patient circles, since a thick layer never sinks in and merely dulls the surface. Let the pair rest a while, then bring the shine up with a woolen cloth. The rubbing warms the wax, which settles and closes the pores behind it. Neglect these small attentions, and the leather will split exactly where the foot bends, and no repair will bring it back.

units: the body in charge of water has made public a review of its network
a notable share of the water sent out never reaches the homes
the old metal pipes crack because of movements in the ground
pressure swings during the night add to the cracking
the first measure cuts the network into stretches that valves can isolate
meters read the overnight flow in order to spot a loss
a flow that does not drop at night reveals a leak
the second measure lowers the pressure because high pressure breaks pipes
a household leak counts for little beside a main split open under the road
text: The body that runs the water supply put out a review of its distribution network this week. The finding is blunt: a notable share of the water it sends out never reaches the homes it is meant to serve. The old metal mains, laid down before flexible joints became usual, crack as the ground beneath them shifts, and the pressure swings of the night widen what has already cracked. Two measures follow from that diagnosis. The first cuts the network into short stretches that valves can isolate, while meters read the overnight flow, which betrays a loss whenever it refuses to drop. The second brings the pressure down, since too hard a push breaks one pipe after another. A dripping tap in a household kitchen, the technicians add, counts for very little beside a main split wide open beneath the road.

units: the space in front of the building has uneven paving
containers there hold green and scented plants
a pale wall coating spreads a soft light toward the lower windows
the space at the back is covered with an even concrete surface
a wall without any opening blocks the view there
wooden seats and a water point invite people to stop in the first space
the second takes the bins and the delivery vehicles
one aims at pleasure and the other at function
both spaces belong to the same building
text: The space in front of the building rests on paving that never quite lies level, and along its edges stand containers where ferns and scented herbs are growing. A pale coat spread over the walls sends a soft light back toward the lower windows. Behind that same building the ground tells a different story: an even concrete surface, poured in one piece, with a wall that has no opening at all and blocks the view entirely. The first of the two invites you to stop, since wooden seats are ranged along the wall and a water point stands ready for the planting. The second takes the bins and the delivery vehicles, and nobody lingers in it for a moment. One of them aims at pleasure, the other at plain function. Both belong to the same building, and the contrast between them shows how a place divides its uses.

units: the author defends mending a damaged appliance rather than replacing it
the cost of a spare part is far below that of a replacement product
the saving made benefits the household budget
giving up a purchase avoids the digging of material, the shipping and the packing
taking an appliance apart teaches how it works inside
that skill then travels among the people around you
mending is blamed for demanding a patience few people have
shared places offer the help of a volunteer and the loan of tools
the main difficulty comes from sealed making that stops appliances being opened
text: Mending a damaged appliance rather than replacing it is a choice, and the choice holds up on several fronts at once. Money comes first: a spare part costs a fraction of what a replacement costs, and the saving stays inside the household budget. Then the materials. The digging of the ore, the shipping, the packing all vanish along with the purchase you decide to give up. Then the skill: whoever takes a casing apart learns how the thing works inside, and that understanding travels on among the people around you. Mending, runs the objection, demands a patience that few people have. The objection forgets the shared workshops, where a volunteer guides your hands and lends you the tools you lack. The one serious difficulty lies in the making itself, glued and sealed shut so that nobody can open it.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman who sells fresh produce began as a child at her mother's side
she sorted the crates before selling started
she told how ripe a fruit was from the sound it made in her palm
her first sales point was boards laid across supports
it was replaced later by a wooden counter sheltered by a canvas
she guides undecided buyers according to what they are looking for
one customer wants a fruit whose central stone comes away easily
another asks for grapes with no seeds
she now passes her trade on to her niece, who takes notes
she says she never wrote anything down and trusts the memory in her hands
text: The woman who sells fresh produce at the covered market started out as a child, at her mother's side, sorting the crates before the selling began. She could already tell how ripe a plum was, she says, from the sound it made in the palm of her hand. Her own first stall was a couple of boards laid across supports; a wooden counter with a canvas stretched above it came a good deal later. She learned to guide the buyers who cannot make up their minds: this one wants an apricot whose stone comes away on its own, that one is after grapes with no seeds in them at all. Lately she has been passing the trade on to her niece, who takes careful notes on every scrap of advice she is given. She never wrote a thing down herself, she says, laughing, and her hands remember the work better than her head does.

units: the shared eating place occupies a former market building
a single dish is offered at each service
that limit produces a quality rarely met
not spreading the buying thin gives access to vegetables grown in open fields
preparation starts very early in the day
the one broth can reduce to an unusual thickness
the bread served alongside has a crackling crust
the hard surfacing of the room amplifies noise and hampers conversation
nothing is provided for those who refuse root vegetables
text: The shared eating place set up in the old market building is well worth the walk, and that comes down to one rule the cook stands by: a single dish offered at each service. Out of that limit comes a quality you very rarely meet. Because he is not spreading his buying thin, he gets vegetables grown in the open fields, and he starts work on them very early in the day. Because he has only one broth to keep watch over, he lets it reduce to a thickness you will find nowhere else. The bread served alongside it has a crust that crackles under the tooth. The room, on the other hand, works against the meal: the bare tiling throws the voices straight back, and talking soon turns into an effort. Nor is anything at all provided for those who refuse root vegetables. None of this cancels the merit of the place.

units: the writer is writing to a neighbor about their two homes
the neighbor's home sits directly under the roof
the neighbor closes a wooden shutter to keep the sun out
the writer's home takes up the lowest level of the house
the writer deals with damp that lifts the wallpaper
the neighbor has to wipe away a fine grit that comes through the gaps
the writer watches a crack widening behind a radiator
the two neighbors air out their homes in opposite ways
the writer suggests bringing in a tradesman for both levels
text: Dear neighbor, I am writing about our two homes, because keeping them up turns out to be two different jobs. Yours sits right under the roof, so the heat builds the moment the sun hits the tiles, and you have to swing the wooden shutter closed before noon. Mine takes up the bottom level of the house, where a cold damp lifts the wallpaper away from the baseboard. You fight dry air. I fight wet walls. You wipe off a fine grit that drifts down through the gaps in the roof frame, while I keep an eye on a thin crack that widens a little more each month behind the radiator. Even the cures pull in opposite directions: you air out in short bursts, whereas I have to warm the room before I open anything. So here is my thought. Let us bring in a tradesman together and have him look at both levels in one visit.

units: delicate laundry is best washed by hand
the water should be lukewarm and the soak short
a small amount of soap saves repeated rinsing
the fabric must not be wrung out hard
a dry towel draws off the water still held in the cloth
drying is done flat and away from any heat source
stretching the damp garment does away with ironing
an old stain is soaked before any wash
scalding water would set the color of the stain
text: Should delicate laundry be washed by hand? In most cases, yes. Lukewarm water and a short soak treat the fibers far more kindly than a drum spinning at full tilt. How much soap? Very little. Pile on the suds and you will end up rinsing the same load over and over. Should the water be wrung out hard? No. Press the fabric between your palms, then roll it in a dry towel to draw off whatever water is still trapped in it. Where should it dry? Flat, well away from any direct heat, on a surface that lets air move underneath. And the ironing? Skip it. Stretch the garment while it is still damp and set the crease with your fingers. What about an old stain? Soak it before it ever goes into a wash, and keep it clear of scalding water, which would set the color instead of dissolving it.

units: the caretaker asks the narrator about noises in the night
the narrator was asleep and heard nothing
the caretaker glimpsed a shape near the mailboxes
a wooden shutter banged on the upper floor
the caretaker found a key outside a door at the back
the caretaker had no idea whose key it was
a tenant came later to claim the key
that tenant had locked herself out while taking the trash down
the caretaker advises leaving a spare with someone trusted
text: The caretaker stopped me in the entryway and asked whether I had heard anything during the night. I told him no, that I had slept straight through. He said he had first caught sight of a shape over by the mailboxes, and then heard a wooden shutter bang somewhere on the upper floor. After that, he told me, he went down the stairs with his flashlight and found a key lying on the mat outside the back door. I asked him whose it was. He shrugged and admitted he had no idea at all. A while later, the tenant from the upper floor came down looking for it. She had let her door swing shut behind her while carrying the trash down, and had not wanted to wake anyone. The caretaker laughed, then told me to leave a spare with someone I trust. I think I will do exactly that before the week is out.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: households once depended on a well or a fountain
water had to be carried in bucket by bucket
washing clothes was concentrated into a single operation each week
the arrival of indoor pipes changed household habits
washing spread out into more frequent rounds
clothes were changed more often
the making of light fabrics grew
floors could be cleaned with plenty of water
smooth coverings took the place of rough boards
text: Before running water reached the home, hauling it governed everything else. A household drew on a well or a public fountain, and that dependence set the rhythm of the week: laundry happened once, in a single long push, because every bucket had to be carried in by arm. So the day a pipe entered the house, far more changed than comfort. Once water came without effort, washing broke into smaller and more frequent rounds, clothes were changed more often, and the making of light fabrics grew to keep pace. A second effect followed. Floors that had once been swept dry in a cloud of dust could now be sluiced with as much water as anyone liked, which made smooth coverings far more appealing than rough boards. Plumbing, in the end, reshaped the furniture indoors and the clothing people wore on their backs.

units: dough that tears puts beginners off
flour packs into tight lumps while it is stored
sifting the flour lets air into it
butter straight from the cold is a solid block
dough does not take in fat that is too hard
grating the butter scatters it into fragments
fingers can also crumble it
dough worked too roughly pulls back during baking
a rest in the cold under a damp cloth loosens the mixture
text: Dough that tears under the rolling pin puts off plenty of beginners for good. The fault is rarely in the hands. It starts in the flour, which packs itself into tight lumps as soon as it sits in a bag. The cure is an old and simple one: sift it over the bowl so that air runs through it and lifts it. Butter creates a similar snag. Straight from the cold it comes out as a solid block, and dough will not take in fat that hard. Grate it on the wide side of a grater, or crumble it between your fingertips, so that it scatters into tiny flakes throughout. Then comes the matter of rest. Dough worked too roughly pulls back in the oven and leaves ragged edges. A spell in the cold, under a damp cloth, loosens the strands, settles the mixture down and makes the pin surprisingly easy to handle.

units: the tradesman shows the narrator two tubes of glue
the first glue is water based and hardens as it dries
the first glue calls for a long clamping time
the second glue sets on contact with moisture in the air
the second glue grabs very fast
the second sticks to slick surfaces such as metal
the joint made by the first glue stays flexible
the joint made by the second breaks under a twist
the tradesman keeps the slow glue for the load-bearing piece
a thick layer of glue holds less well than a thin film
text: The man who came to fix the shelf set two tubes of glue side by side and told me they did not work the same way at all. The first one is water based. It soaks into the grain and hardens as the water leaves, so it wants a clamp held on for hours in a warm room. The second one sets by pulling moisture out of the air, grabs in a matter of seconds, and takes to slick surfaces such as metal or glazed tile. You pay for that speed elsewhere. The first leaves a joint with some give in it, one that follows the wood as it swells from season to season, while the second dries to a stiff ridge that snaps clean under a twist. So he put the slow one on the rail that carries the weight, the quick one on the trim. The usual mistake, he added, is loading the joint: a thick bead fails before the fibers it holds.

units: the furniture must be emptied out completely before starting
the shelves are wiped with a damp cloth
the surfaces have to dry in open air
the clothes are sorted into three groups
one group gathers the pieces that need altering
everything kept has to be washed even if it looks clean
a trace of sweat draws insects in during storage
it is better to fold clothes flat than to hang them
a sachet of scented wood is tucked between the layers
every box gets a label saying what is inside
text: Moving a wardrobe from one season to the next goes a great deal better when it follows a set order. First, empty the closet down to the last hanger and wipe the shelves with a damp cloth, then leave every surface to dry in open air. Second, sort what you own into three piles: what you still wear, what needs altering, and what you are letting go. Third, wash everything you keep, even the pieces that look clean, because an invisible trace of sweat will draw moths in over the months in storage. Fourth, fold each garment flat rather than hanging it, which spares the shoulders from stretching out of shape. Fifth, tuck a sachet of scented wood between the layers, and never anything liquid. Last, write what is inside on a label for every box, and stack the heavy ones at the bottom.

units: a main water pipe gave way before dawn
the break happened on a street running along a covered market
residents first noticed a warmish puddle
water pushed into the cellars of the buildings next door
an on-call crew shut off the supply to the district
the traders moved their stalls to a nearby hall
the technicians found that a root had loosened a joint
the repair was finished by nightfall
the water stayed cloudy through a whole evening
pumps will drain the cellars the following week
text: The main pipe gave way shortly before dawn, on the street that runs along the covered market. Residents noticed a warmish puddle at the foot of a lamppost first, and then the paving lifted and water pushed into the cellars of the buildings next door. An on-call crew reached the site before the shops opened and shut off the supply to the whole district. Traders wheeled their stalls over to the neighboring hall, where a couple of taps still ran. By mid afternoon the technicians had cleared the broken iron and found that a root had worked its way in and loosened an old joint. The repair wrapped up at nightfall, though the water stayed cloudy through the evening, and the utility told people to run the tap a while before cooking with it. Pumps are due to drain the flooded cellars next week.

units: the house described belongs to the narrator's uncle
the entrance hallway is narrow so as to hold the heat
the kitchen takes up the largest room
the household eats there and fixes bicycles there
soaked coats dry there as well
the green paint came out of a leftover pot
the upper part of the walls stayed paler for want of paint
the floor slopes toward the garden door
that slope was there to let wash water run out
a mirror throws light back onto the table
text: Walk into my uncle's house and you see at once that it was built with its back to the wind. The door opens on a narrow hallway, because whoever put the place up wanted to hold the heat near the hearth. That is why the kitchen took the biggest room and swallowed all the traffic: people eat there, they fix their bicycles there, they hang soaked coats there to dry. The walls carry a dull green that came out of a leftover pot, and since it ran short, the upper stretch stayed a good deal paler. The tiled floor tilts toward the garden door, an old trick for letting wash water run out, which is why the children's marbles all roll the same way. And because the back window faces a blank wall, my uncle hung a mirror across from it, to throw a little light onto the table where his family gathers each evening.

units: homes pile up things that are barely used
putting things away has become an occupation in itself
the trouble lies in objects that never circulate
a machine bought for one precise use sleeps in a cupboard
a neighbor is sometimes looking for the same machine
the writer rejects the moral call to own less
tool stores already exist inside apartment buildings
the loans are written down in a notebook by the tenants
these stores rest on a small deposit and a short loan
the writer asks landlords to set aside a room for such exchanges
text: Our homes fill up with things that earn their keep one season a year, and putting them away has quietly turned into a job of its own. The trouble is not that we own a lot. It is that nothing moves. A machine bought for one recipe sits asleep in a cupboard while the neighbor down the hall hunts for the very same machine. No amount of moralizing about owning less will fix that. What fixes it is quiet arrangements that make borrowing as easy as buying. Tool stores already run inside apartment buildings, kept by tenants who write down every loan in a notebook. Where they work, they rest on three rules: a small deposit, a short loan, and repairs shared out. Landlords ought to set aside a room in the building for that kind of exchange, the way they already set one aside for strollers.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: an employee lives on the lowest level of the building, next to the front door
his duties fall into three separate categories
the first category covers the cleanliness of the shared areas
he puts a lubricant on the closing mechanisms that make noise
the second category concerns the delivery of letters
he carries the mail to the doors of the oldest residents
the third category consists of calming quarrels between neighbors
he hears the parties to a dispute one after the other
he does not pass on what he learns about the residents' lives
he almost always tracks down the owner of a mislaid object
text: The caretaker of the building lives in a ground-floor unit, right up against the front door. His duties fall into three separate categories. The first is cleaning: he sweeps the stairwell, wipes the glass in the entrance hall, and oils any lock that squeaks. The second is the mail, which he sorts every week and leaves at the doors of the oldest tenants. The third is smoothing over quarrels. When neighbors fall out, he hears each side on its own and then puts forward a settlement both can live with. What earns him his standing, though, is how little he says. He knows the habits of every household and repeats none of it to anyone. Tenants also praise his memory for lost property: a key, a glove, an umbrella left behind in the elevator almost always finds its way back to the owner.

units: the piece of furniture under review was bought secondhand
on arrival its surface was under a sticky coat the seller had not mentioned
that old finish had to be stripped off completely
the supports of the piece began to wobble the following week
simply tightening them cured the fault without taking the whole thing apart
after a season of use the overall verdict is favorable
the material stands up to very hot vessels
one drawer jams when the air turns damp
no adjustment cures that jamming
the piece is judged worth having given how little it cost
text: This low table came secondhand, and the honest verdict on it has come from using the thing. It turned up looking dull, the top under a tacky coat of varnish the seller had said nothing about. Stripping that old finish off completely came first, before there was any hope of a decent result. The following week the legs began to wobble, and tightening them cured it, with no need to pull the whole thing apart. After a season of family use, the verdict leans the right way: the wood shrugs off scalding mugs, scuffs wipe out with a cloth, and the height suits reading as well as a meal taken in front of a screen. One flaw does hold out, though. The drawer jams as soon as the air turns damp, and no adjustment touches it. For what it cost, the table earns its place, so long as you can live with that.

units: the kitchen refit has just been finished
a workman uncovered a cracked pipe behind the washing basin
the seeping had been going on for several weeks
the damp left the wall covering crumbly to the touch
the leak had to be sealed before any finishing work
the water supply had to be shut off during the repair
the dishes were washed at a neighbor's for five evenings
the spending went up and the timings stretched out
the writer invites the person she writes to come and see the room
text: I am writing because the kitchen is finished at last, and you will never guess what held the whole job up. Digging behind the sink, the workman came upon a split pipe. Water had been seeping for weeks, so the plaster crumbled the moment you laid a hand on it. The crack had to be sealed before anyone could think about paint. Since the repair meant shutting off the water, we spent five evenings washing dishes at the neighbor's upstairs. She lent us her basin, and we carried the plates back up the stairs still warm. The upshot: the budget swelled, the timings stretched, and my temper along with them. Now that it has all dried out, the room smells of fresh paint and I sit in there for no reason at all, just to look at the smooth wall. Come and see it for yourself as soon as you can.

units: workshops open to everyone take in household appliances that no longer work
a woman who runs one of these workshops answers what visitors ask
the main obstacle is not that parts are scarce
owners give up because they believe the inside of an appliance is out of reach
the chosen method is to have the visitor carry out the action
the visitor lifts the lid himself and cleans the clogged part
a helper steps in when the repair goes beyond what the visitor can do
this help takes place in front of the owner of the appliance
more objects leave in working order than are left behind
text: What is to be done with a household appliance that has stopped working? The question comes up over and over at repair workshops open to everyone, and the woman who runs one of them answers it readily. The obstacle, she explains, has nothing to do with parts being scarce. Owners give up, sure that a closed casing is out of bounds to them. How do you overturn a belief like that? By having them do the thing instead of describing it: the visitor lifts the lid himself, spots the clogged filter, and scrubs it clean under water. And when the fault runs past what he can manage? A helper takes over, always in front of the person who brought the appliance in, who watches every stage. You measure the outcome in objects that leave in working order, far more of them than are left behind.

units: a resident held that the countryside was better than the noise of an apartment building
her neighbor had lived in both settings
the neighbor disputed that preference
she described the sounds of wood and wind in a house standing on its own
she said that no voice covers those sounds in the countryside
she liked knowing the occupants by their step on the stairs
the first wanted a planted plot and warm water at the outside tap
the second told quiet, which you choose, from company, which you take in
the two women reached no agreement
they greeted each other the next day all the same
text: The tenant below held that the quiet of a country house was worth more than the stir of an apartment building. Her neighbor answered gently that she had known both and believed nothing of the sort. Out there, she said, the wind rubs at the shutters and the floorboards creak with no human voice to cover the sound. You sit and listen to your own solitude. Here, she went on, the stairs ring with steps you know, and each step carries a face: the nurse coming home, the student going out, the child dragging a backpack. The first woman pressed her case all the same. She wanted a garden, the smell of cut grass, water gone warm in the tap outside. The second smiled and said that quiet is chosen, while company is taken in. They parted without agreeing, and greeted each other the next day.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: before running water arrived, three techniques served to wash cloth
the first technique used water mixed with strained ashes
this alkaline solution dissolved greasy matter
the second technique rested on blows struck with a wooden tool
the beaten cloth was then rinsed and left to run off on a hard surface
the third technique spread the cloth out on damp vegetation
damp and radiance together took out the soiling
these methods damaged the fibers, whose weave turned coarse
the wear explains why cloth was counted, mended and handed down
text: Before water arrived under pressure, keeping cloth clean rested on three methods that the old manuals set out in careful detail. The first was an alkaline soak: pieces were stacked in a tub and water strained through ashes was poured over them, and the dissolved potash went to work on grease. The second was mechanical and called for a wooden beater: the fiber was struck against a sloping board, then rinsed under running water and left to drain on a flat stone. The third was sun bleaching. Spread out over wet grass, the cloth gave up its stains to the damp and the light working together. All three wore the material down, and the weave turned coarse to the hand after ten washes or so. That wear is why cloth was counted, mended and handed on from one household to the next like something of value.

units: the observation bears on a kitchen window over one cold night
preparing food gives off steam into the room
this moist air meets a pane that the outside has chilled
the steam turns into droplets settled on the glass
the droplets run together and then travel down the panel
the water gathers against the horizontal piece of wood, which soaks it up
by daybreak the condensation is gone from the glass surface
the wood stays soaked with water in spite of that disappearance
repeating the process lifts the paint and favors fungus
airing the room briefly after cooking halts the process at its start
text: Let us watch what happens at a kitchen window over the course of one cold night. Early in the evening, cooking gives off steam and the room takes on a moisture you cannot see. Toward the end of the meal, that warm air reaches the pane, which the outside has chilled. The steam loses its energy and turns liquid again, and fine drops settle across the glass. Later, drops lying side by side run together, gain weight and slide toward the foot of the frame. They gather against the horizontal rail of wood, which soaks up part of that water. By daybreak the mist has gone from the surface, yet the wood stays soaked through. Repeat that cycle across a whole season and the paint lifts away and fungus gets its opening. Airing the room briefly after cooking halts the chain at its very first link.

units: a bicycle was left against a railing after a change of home
repeated rain attacked the drive, which had seized up
the workshop in the area was quoting a wait of two weeks
so the owner set about the repair with no help
he cleaned every link with a solvent and a stiff brush
the noise of the work drew a neighbor carrying tools
the neighbor trued the back wheel, which had worked loose
that help gave rise to a weekly meeting
the two men repair the objects the building has abandoned
the bin room holds no more hulks
text: The bicycle had been propped against the railing since the end of summer, forgotten after a move. Rain after rain had eaten into the chain, whose links would no longer turn. Because the workshop in the area was quoting a wait of two weeks, the owner decided to set about it alone. He laid the machine on a sheet, poured solvent over the metal, and worked every link with a hard brush. The old grease, gone tacky by then, came away in flakes. The rasp of the bristles drew a neighbor, who came down with an oil can and a open wrench. For want of the right tool, the back wheel had worked loose; the man trued it in a handful of movements. Out of that one favor grew a habit. Once a week the two of them repair whatever the building abandons, and the bin room has emptied of its hulks.

units: a door gives out a shrill noise each time it is moved
the procedure saves calling in a tradesman
you first work out which hinge is at fault by moving the door slowly
a cloth laid underneath protects the floor from runs
you use a thin oil and not a thick paste
a thick paste picks up dirt and makes matters worse
a single drop laid on the pin is enough
moving the door several times spreads the product
you wipe off the excess once it has run down
if the noise carries on, the upper fixing of the hinge has to be tightened
text: So your door shrieks every time it moves, and the noise wakes you up at night? Here is how to be done with it without calling anyone in. Start by working out which hinge is at fault: ease the door open very slowly and listen for where the sound is born. Next, slip a cloth underneath, because what runs off will mark the floor. Take an oil can filled with thin oil, never a thick grease: grease holds dust and the trouble comes back worse. A single drop is enough, laid right on the pin. Swing the door back and forth a dozen times so the liquid works its way down. Let the rest drip out, then wipe the surplus off with the same cloth. If the sound carries on, the top screw has shifted: drive it home, or the door hangs crooked on its hinges. The quiet comes back before the evening is out.

units: two districts side by side have taken opposite approaches to reviving their shops
on the high bank, a sheltered market was built with public money
the pitches there go at a low rent to growers from nearby
attendance at this market reaches its peak at the end of the week
on the lower bank, no building received funding
local people banded together and use an old school yard
each seller sets up a folding stand of his own
the sheltered market draws passing buyers attracted by settled hours
the yard holds a nearby clientele that puts up with bad weather
in both districts, the shops on the streets nearby get more visitors
text: Two districts side by side have taken opposite roads to reviving their local shops, and the contrast leaps straight out at you. On the high bank, a covered market was put up with public money; pitches go at a low rent to growers from nearby, and the crowds peak at the end of the week. On the lower bank, not one building of any kind was funded. Local people banded together into an association and took over an old school yard, where each seller brings a folding stand of his own. The returns differ as much as the settings do. The covered market draws passing buyers, who want shelter and settled hours. The yard holds a nearby following that puts up with rain and improvisation. One point brings the two together: in either district, the shops on the streets nearby have seen more people come through.

units: the caretaker unlocks the courtyard gate at sunrise
the courtyard floor is swept in front of the mailboxes
the planters under the awning are watered after the sweeping
parcels are stacked against a wall around midday
the children of the building use the courtyard as a play area in the afternoon
the children's racket is tolerated until dusk
a single lamp with chipped glass lights the way to the stairs
the gate is shut again and the emergency exit checked before night
this arrangement has never been set down in any written rule
text: At sunrise the caretaker unlocks the gate, and the inner courtyard wakes up slowly. He sweeps the rough paving in front of the mailboxes, pushing the grit toward the drain. Then he waters the two planters that sit under the awning. By midday the delivery drivers have stacked parcels against the far wall, and the passage narrows into a cluttered corridor. In the afternoon the children of the building take the yard over, rolling a ball from step to step, and he puts up with the racket until dusk. Once the windows light up one by one, the quiet comes back. A single lamp, its glass chipped, throws a thin beam over the way to the stairs. Before night falls he shuts the gate again and checks the emergency exit. Nobody has ever set this routine down in writing, yet it comes around the same way every day.

units: repairing an appliance now costs more than buying another one
the steep price of spare parts puts people off going to a repairer
appliances in working order are thrown into the sorting bins
the pile-up of discards raises the bill for treating waste
that expense is carried by the community
the cheapest choice for one person brings the heaviest cost for everyone
bringing the price of parts down would be part of the cure
making repair manuals available is the second measure put forward
text: Getting a broken appliance fixed now costs more than buying another one, and that reversal has quietly reshaped what we do. Spare parts sell at a steep price, so the owner gives up on the repairer the moment a lid cracks or a handle works loose. The outcome sits in plain view in the sorting bins, where machines barely worn lie beside wobbly chairs that a screwdriver would have saved. All that discarded metal and plastic pushes up the bill for treating waste, and the community foots it in the end. So the loop closes. The cheapest choice for one person turns into the heaviest expense for everyone. Breaking it would mean bringing the price of parts down and putting repair manuals within reach of anyone who asks for them. Until that happens, a workshop where things get mended will stay an oddity.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a neighbor mends the other tenants' clothes for nothing
she has sewn since she was a teenager and was never trained
her sewing machine came down from her mother
the table holding the machine wobbles and is propped up with cardboard
the ceiling light was too weak to tell a dark thread from a dark cloth
the poor light made her seams go wrong
a tenant from downstairs found her an adjustable lamp at a secondhand market
the lamp gathers the beam exactly where it is needed
she refuses to be paid and asks for a hot drink instead
text: Every stairwell seems to have one, the neighbor who takes in everybody's torn clothes and hands them back mended, without asking for a thing. She has been sewing since she was a teenager, and nobody ever taught her. The machine came down from her mother, and it stood on a wobbly table she kept level with a folded piece of cardboard. Light was her trouble. The ceiling bulb burned too dull to separate a dark thread from a dark cloth, so her seams wandered off and she had to unpick them and start over. A tenant from downstairs turned up with an adjustable lamp he had found at a secondhand market, its shiny reflector gathering the beam right where her hands were. Now a frayed hem takes her two stitches. She waves the money away, asks for a hot drink, sits down and tells workshop stories, and the whole corridor gains by it.

units: two food shops stand face to face at the entrance to the neighborhood
the first one fills a cramped and badly heated room
the fruit in the first shop is weighed by hand
the owner of the first shop calls out his prices
the second one carries a far wider range and clear labels
the second one offers a checkout with no employee
the fruit from the cramped shop has a straightforward smell
the fruit from the shop next door is even but tastes of nothing
the shopper settles it by mood and hardly ever by reason
text: Two food shops stand face to face at the entrance to the neighborhood, and the contrast is worth a pause. The first one fills a cramped, badly heated room where crates climb toward the ceiling. The fruit gets weighed by hand and the owner calls out his prices across the counter. The second one gleams behind its windows, with a far wider range, labels you can actually read, and a checkout where no employee stands. Use them both for a while and the gap in quality turns out not to follow the gap in comfort. Tomatoes from the cramped room ripen on the shelf and smell of something. The ones next door are firm, even in size, and taste of nothing at all. On one side you pay for discomfort and flavor, on the other for ease and blandness. Shoppers settle it by mood, hardly ever by reason.

units: the writer of the letter writes from the table where the meals were eaten together
the floor by the window is cracked and has not been replaced
the rug in the hall has lost its fringes
the teapot chipped at the spout is still used every evening
one armrest of the chair is worn down to the weave
a shawl left behind by the reader lies on that chair
the drawer holds keys, postcards and a worn stub of pencil
the plants on the ledge hang on despite careless watering
the door creaks and still shuts badly
text: I am writing from the kitchen, at the table where the two of us used to eat. Nothing here has changed, and that is precisely what I wanted to describe. The tiles beside the window remain cracked. I abandoned any idea of replacing them, since they belong to the room now. The hallway rug has lost its fringes, and I step over it without noticing. That teapot you detested, chipped at the spout, still appears every evening. One armrest of the armchair is worn down to the weave, and the shawl you left behind lies across it. The drawer holds your keys, a stack of postcards, and a pencil worn to a stub. On the outside ledge the plants survive my careless watering. I tidy very little, as you know. But I keep these battered objects the way you keep familiar handwriting. Come back whenever you like. The door creaks, and it shuts no better than before.

units: a dark ring low on a partition wall points to damp coming through
what to do about it depends on how far it has gone
at the first stage the plaster darkens but still feels dry to the touch
airing the room and pulling away the furniture that blocks the air is enough at that stage
a cheap measuring device confirms the trend
the coating turns spongy and gives under pressure as the damp works inward
the wall then has to be tapped and a seal or a pipe checked
at the late stage the plaster lifts away in patches
painting over it hides the sign without removing the cause
text: What should you do when a dark ring creeps up the bottom of a partition wall? It depends on how far the damp has already gone. Early on, the plaster darkens without coming loose, and the surface still feels dry under your fingers. Open the windows, pull away the cabinet that blocks the air, and that will usually do it. A cheap moisture meter confirms the trend in a couple of readings. Later, as the damp works inward, the coating turns spongy and gives under light pressure. Now you have to tap along the wall, trace the water back, and check the seal of a joint or the run of a pipe. At the late stage the plaster lifts away in patches and leaves a gritty face behind.
