Treating the surface will not do any more. And painting over it? That hides the sign and lets the damage work on underneath.

units: a tenant reports to the manager a dripping tap going back to the fall
the manager points to the lack of a written request
the tenant says he called three times and got no answer
the manager grants that the switchboard was swamped and the messages went missing
with no report on record no tradesman was sent out
the drip therefore carried on and stained the ceiling of the home below
the tiles under the sink have split
the repair will run higher than a seal changed at the start
the two settle on confirming every call in writing the same evening
text: The tenant told the manager that the tap in the washroom had been dripping since the fall. The manager answered that no written request had ever reached his desk, and that nothing gets ordered without one. The tenant reminded him he had called three times and never got hold of anyone. The manager granted that the switchboard had been swamped and those messages had gone missing. With no report on record, he said, no tradesman had been sent out, so the drip had simply carried on. The tenant pointed out that the ceiling of the home below now carries a brown ring, and that the tiles under the sink have split. The manager conceded that the repair would run higher than a seal changed back at the start. The two settled on a rule, that every call gets confirmed in writing the same evening.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: before running water every household had to fetch its water outside
the chore fell mostly to the children and to the servants
the buckets were carried up worn and slippery steps
the water stood in containers nobody scoured properly
illness passed from one person to another through this stored water
the local authorities began by opening more places to draw water
that step shortened the walk without making anything cleaner
piping under pressure together with treatment settled the problem
putting a tap in the kitchen did away with the household store
text: Before water ran into homes, every household sent someone out to a well or to a fountain in the neighborhood to fetch it. The chore fell mostly to the children and to the servants, who hauled heavy buckets up steps worn smooth and often slick. Tiredness was the smaller part of the trouble. The water stood for days in containers nobody scoured properly, slimy at the bottom, and illness passed from one person to the next through it. Local authorities began by opening more places to draw from. That shortened the walk, but it left the stored water no cleaner. What settled the matter was piping under pressure, together with treatment of the supply before it reached the houses. Once a tap stood in the kitchen, the household store vanished, and the main source of contamination went with it.

units: bread and a dry cracker left out overnight change in opposite directions
the bread goes hard while the cracker goes limp
the single cause behind both changes is water on the move
fresh bread holds a great deal of water, most of all in the crumb
the water in the bread drifts off into the room and the starch settles anew
the cracker comes out of the oven with almost no water
the cracker pulls moisture in from the air and loses its snap
a damp cloth laid over the basket keeps the crumb supple
shutting the two foods away brings about two opposite effects
text: Leave a slice of bread and a dry cracker out on the table overnight, then look at what has happened. The bread has gone hard and the cracker has gone limp, two opposite outcomes with one cause behind them, water on the move. Fresh bread holds a great deal of it, most of all in the crumb. That water drifts off into the air of the room, the starch settles into a different arrangement, and the crumb is left dry and brittle. The cracker comes out of the oven with almost none, so it absorbs moisture from the air instead, its sugars soften, and the snap gives way to a spongy limpness. Each one reaches for a balance with whatever surrounds it. A damp cloth laid over the basket keeps the crumb supple. Shut the bread away to hold its water in, shut the cracker away to keep water out. One tin, two opposite jobs.

units: a bunch of keys was left behind on a low wall near a bus stop
a student photographed it and then handed it in at the kiosk nearby
the kiosk keeper listed the objects hanging from the ring
the ring carried a mailbox key and a token for a cart
a building badge with nothing written on it hung there as well
the photograph stayed up on the kiosk window for two evenings
the neighborhood put forward several guesses about who owned it
the caretaker of a block knew the badge model and worked out the floor
the owner had not yet noticed that her keys were missing
text: It started with a bunch of keys left behind on the low wall by a bus stop. A student photographed them, and then took them along to the kiosk a few steps away. The kiosk keeper laid out everything hanging from the ring, a mailbox key, a dull token for a cart, a scuffed leather fob, and a building badge with nothing written on it. The photograph stayed taped to the kiosk window for two evenings running. Then came the guesses from all sides, a nurse from the block across the way, a delivery driver in a hurry to finish his round, a retired man who walks his dog on that same corner. The badge decided it. The caretaker of that block knew the model on sight and worked out which floor it came from. The owner, told late in the afternoon, had not yet noticed that her keys were missing.

units: rainwater does not soak into paved surfaces
fast runoff reaches the stream all at once
these surges push the river out of its bed
the banks lose their fine silt to the current
bare cropland erodes in the same way
perforated paving replaces the asphalt of parking lots
cover crops open root channels that drink the downpour
planted ditches store the runoff before returning it to the subsoil
text: Rain that lands on paved ground has nowhere to go. It sheets across the asphalt, fills the drains, and reaches the stream in one hard surge instead of seeping in slowly. The river swells, jumps its banks, and strips the fine silt from the edges as it goes. Bare cropland behaves the same way, since the soil packs down and no root holds it against a downpour. The remedy is not complicated. Give the ground back its power to drink. Planners now lay perforated paving across parking lots, so grass grows through the gaps and the water sinks between them. Farmers sow cover crops between harvests, and those roots bore channels that swallow a heavy shower. Elsewhere, shallow planted ditches catch the runoff, hold it among the reeds, and let it slide down into the ground water without haste.

units: the narrator returns to a jetty she knew as a child
she remembers damp and quiet air on her old visits
the hard wind of her recent visit nearly tore her bag away
sheets of water now came over the low wall
the lighthouse keeper describes storms closer together than before
he used to count a single big warning each season
he now counts three or four between two spring tides
the narrator finds that the place of her childhood has changed character
text: I went back out onto the harbor jetty during the storm season, and I barely knew the place. As a child I used to walk out along it in a soft damp hush that smelled of salt, with the spray hardly wetting my face. That week the wind nearly ripped my bag off my shoulder, and sheets of water were coming clean over the low wall. The lighthouse keeper told me the blows arrive far closer together now, with troughs that run much deeper. Back then, he said, you logged one big warning a season. He counts three or four between two spring tides. It is not the same stretch of coast at all, honestly. The sand has melted away beside the steps, the fishermen have shifted their traps into the shelter of the mole, and the shore I carry in my head has turned into an old map you keep out of fondness.

units: a home compost bin fits into a small space
the method breaks down into three parts
the bin must sit on living soil and out of full sun
wet waste and dry material have to be alternated
meat scraps are kept out of the mixture
the pile must be turned at regular intervals to air it
moisture like that of a wrung-out sponge is what you want
the end product is a dark crumbly material that feeds the soil
text: Composting at home takes up less room than most people would expect, and the whole job breaks into three parts. Start with the container. Set a slatted bin straight onto living soil, in the light shade of a hedge, so that worms can climb up into it on their own. Then the material. Alternate a wet layer, peelings or grass clippings, with a dry one, fallen leaves or torn brown cardboard. Keep meat scraps out. They draw rodents and stall the whole process. Upkeep comes last. Turn the pile with a fork every couple of weeks, and check that it stays as damp as a wrung-out sponge. Too wet, it reeks. Too dry, it goes dormant. After two seasons you pull out a dark, crumbly material not far from the humus of a woodland floor. Spread it around your plantings to feed the ground and hold the water there.

units: a dike broke before sunrise
a night worker was the first to raise the alarm
the residents left with very little in hand
the water reached the upper floor of the low houses
the current dropped during the second half of the following night
a layer of gray silt covered the streets once the water drew off
the rescue crews set pumps on the central square
an engineer blames the break on runoff from the hillsides
text: The dike gave way just before dawn, quietly, the way a seam lets go. A night worker watched it split open from the footbridge and sounded the siren. A thick fog was still lying over the village when people came out with a bag in one hand, leaving their kitchen lights burning behind them. The flood climbed to the upper floor of the low houses, held that mark through the following night, and slackened only toward morning. What it left as it drew off was a smooth gray silt, poured through the streets like varnish. Rescue crews set pumps on the central square, and the drone of the motors took over from the silence of the water. An engineer from the river service blames the break on the runoff coming down off the stripped hillsides, which loaded the channel far past anything it was built to carry.

units: the treeless plateau loses its heat as soon as the sun goes
the heat stored in the ground rises toward a clear sky
the air against the ground falls below the dew point
the water vapor then settles as beads on the plants
a deposit of crystals forms when the surface drops below freezing
this frozen deposit draws a white rim along the edge of the leaves
cold air gathers in the hollows of the ground
the dips therefore freeze before the slopes above them
text: On a treeless plateau the surface begins shedding heat the moment the sun drops. All through the sunlit hours the ground stores energy, and it sends that energy straight up to a cloudless sky, which hands none of it back. The thin layer of air pressed against the ground therefore chills faster than the air above it. Once that layer falls under its dew point, the vapor it carries can no longer stay invisible. It settles out in fine beads on stems and spiderwebs, and we call it dew. Should the surface drop below freezing, the deposit changes character and becomes frost, a rim of white crystals along the edge of every leaf. Cold air weighs more than warm air, so it slides down the slopes and gathers in the hollows. The dips whiten well before the ground standing above them.

units: the author holds it unreasonable to cover fertile ground with buildings
a productive soil takes thousands of years to form
a sealed surface removes that resource with no way back
built surfaces make flooding worse downstream
the author would tie any further project to the repair of a derelict site
he asks that the price of land carry its power to feed people
he wants the stripping of abandoned sites made compulsory
he holds these measures to be administrative rather than technological
text: There is no sound argument left anywhere for burying our best growing ground under buildings. A fertile layer takes thousands of years to build, one crumb of humus at a time, and a concrete slab cancels it inside the space of a single building season. The loss runs well past farming. Sealed surfaces throw the rainfall downstream, where it feeds the floods that towns end up paying for. Three measures would turn this around. Tie each further project to the repair of a site already built on and since abandoned. Write the power to feed people into what a parcel of land is worth, rather than what may be put up on it. And require that derelict ground be stripped back open, so the water can reach the subsoil again. None of this waits on some invention still to come. It waits on a decision.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the warden watches over a waterlogged marsh
she reads the height of the water off graduated staffs
she likens her work to that of a nurse
she explains that a patient and a marsh are both mended by small corrections
the man before her wanted above all to drain the site
she had the old drainage ditches filled back in
the spongy growth came back after that work
the marsh now holds the water of heavy rain
text: The warden of a marsh at the bottom of a valley spends her weeks watching ground that breathes. Graduated staffs stand in the peat, and she reads the water off them, presses the moss flat with her palm, listens for frogs. She likens the work to that of a nurse. You cure nobody by shaking them awake. You adjust a little, watch, and try again. The comparison also marks how far she stands from the man who held the post before her. He wanted the place dry, cut straight ditches, and won himself a little ground that could be plowed. She had every one of those cuts filled back in. The spongy moss came up again over the peat, the brown layer thickened, and the hollow of the valley began drinking in the downpours instead of flinging them all at once at the houses lying below it.

units: the visitor expected nothing from this exhibition about climate
she came out of it delighted
a first room throws a fine spray of water over the visitors
a wind machine there works up a storm wind
a second room shows hailstones kept in the cold
a third room carries the smell of damp woodland
the visitor finds the explanatory panels far too crowded
she recommends the visit in spite of that flaw
text: Honestly, I walked into this exhibition about climate expecting nothing at all, and I came out of it delighted. Three rooms, three ideas, and no filler anywhere. The first one soaks you. Nozzles throw a salty spray over you while a wind machine works up a gale, and you grasp at once what a battered shoreline puts up with. The second room plays the cold. Behind a pane of frosted glass lie hailstones gathered after a squall, big as walnuts, sliced open to show off the rings inside them. The third goes after your nose. You step into a rebuilt patch of woodland that smells of soaked moss, with a blower pushing the scent of wet leaf mold at you. My one complaint is the panels, wordy and cramped, which nobody reads standing up. Go anyway, and save some breath for the last room.

units: the writer writes to her cousin with news of a stream
the watercourse was shut inside a concrete pipe
a group of neighbors won its return to open air
the machines opened the pipe at the start of the cold season
willows and rushes were planted along the banks
a hard rain came before the young plants had rooted
the banks held through that rise of water
dragonflies have been seen over the reopened stream
text: Dear cousin, you asked how the stream was getting on, so here is the story of the season. It began when the group of neighbors finally won the right to bring the water back into open air, after decades shut inside a concrete pipe. The machines showed up as the cold weather set in and split the slab open the whole length of the common meadow. We planted willows and rushes along the edges, mud to our knees, and by the second week the water had found a winding line of its own. Then a hard rain fell before the roots had taken hold, and we were sure we would lose the lot. The banks held, barely nicked. Dragonflies patrol the shallows over the pebbles now, and the children come hunting larvae under the flat stones. Come and see us before the thaw, you will not know the meadow.

units: the moisture laid on the leaves comes from the air itself
the nighttime cooling of the surfaces brings on that deposit
air loaded with vapor can no longer hold it in suspension
mist forms when the condensation happens in the air rather than on a surface
a cover of cloud keeps that deposit from happening
soil rich in organic matter holds more moisture
that moisture sustains the organisms that break down dead plant matter
removing the plant cover dries out this reserve
text: What lays that wet film on the leaves before daybreak? Nothing fell out of the sky. The air simply gave back what it was holding. Losing its heat to the empty dark, the skin of every plant turns colder than the air washing over it, and the invisible vapor gathers there in beads. That is dew. And when the chill takes hold of the whole body of air rather than one surface? Then the beads hang where they are, and mist spreads across the meadow. A blanket of cloud sends the warmth back down and cancels the business entirely. Where does the water go afterward? The ground drinks it, and drinks it better the more rotted plant matter it holds. That store keeps alive the countless creatures that chew through dead leaves and hand them back to the soil. Strip the cover off, and you dry out the water first, then the quiet life leaning on it.

units: two adjoining plots are set side by side by the person who runs the fruit trees
one of the plots is sheltered by a living hedge and a bank of earth
the other plot is open and exposed to the push of the wind
the sheltered plot keeps its water longer after a rainfall
the open plot dries out quickly once the sun returns
the neighbor blames the living hedge for shading the young plants
the neighbor also blames it for housing small mammals
the manager judges these faults minor next to the water saved
helpful insects lodge in the low growth on the bank
both speakers reckon that the harvests must be recorded over several cycles
text: The orchard manager says she weighed two neighboring plots against each other before deciding. A thick hedge runs along one of them, and a low bank of earth slows the water down. The other lies open, and the wind sweeps across bare soil right up to the fence. She insists the sheltered plot holds its moisture long after a downpour, while the open one dries out the moment the sun comes back. Her neighbor sees it differently. He argues that the hedge steals light from the young plants and gives shelter to rodents. She has thought about that, she says, and it weighs little against the water she saves. Useful insects nest in the scrub on the bank, she adds, and drift down toward the blossom. On one point the two of them agree: unless each of them records his harvests over several seasons, the comparison proves nothing.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: thoughtful use of trees is not a recent practice
past generations told apart many uses for a single tree
the shoots rising from a stump cut to the ground served as fuel
the covering of the trunk was taken when the inner flow starts again
this covering was used to prepare animal hides
foliage gathered at the end of the cycle fed the herds when grazing fell short
the woven living hedge served as a barrier and gave fruit
the trenches at the foot of the earth banks drained the crops and stored water
this landscape was in fact a set of tools and not mere scenery
text: Think careful use of trees is a modern idea? Not at all. Earlier generations had already sorted through what a single tree could give them, and their list ran longer than we tend to assume. First came the firewood, cut from the shoots that spring back out of a stump felled to the ground. Then came the bark, stripped off when the sap starts moving again, and used for curing hides. Leaves came next, gathered at the end of the season and fed to the herds whenever the grazing ran short. Add the living hedge, woven in place, which stood in for a fence and bore fruit as well. Do not forget the ditches dug at the foot of the banks: they drained the fields and held a reserve of water. Every piece had a job, and nothing was left lying about. What looks to us like scenery was in truth a working set of tools.

units: the process begins on a plot left without upkeep
in the first cycle tall grassy growth rules the ground
in the next cycle thorny plants take hold
these thorny plants keep the young shoots safe from browsing animals
the first trees to settle spread by seeds carried on the wind
these first trees grow fast but bear a lack of light poorly
slower growing species then develop under their cover
the edge of the woodland shows the stages of the change to the eye
a fire, a violent gust or a felling brings the plot back to the start
text: It starts with a patch of ground that nobody mows anymore, and that the eye reads as empty. Through the first season, tall grasses take charge and close the soil over. In the next one, brambles and thorny scrub move in and shield the young shoots from grazing mouths. Then the pioneer trees arrive, light things with seeds that travel on the wind; they shoot up fast, but they cannot stand shade. Under that cover, slower species germinate and wait out long seasons before they push through the canopy. At the edge of the wood the whole sequence reads at a glance: low shrubs in front, tall trunks behind. Foresters call this a succession, and they point out that it has no fixed end. A fire, a storm or a felling sends it back to the beginning, and the same order plays out again.

units: the structure protecting against the water broke during the night
the keeper of the water works was very close by
he heard a low sound followed by the bank sinking into the flow
an earlier clearing of the bed had removed the roots that held the shore firm
without those roots the sediment was carried off at every rise of the water
the flood covered the low fields and buried the crops under mud
people from nearby first blamed the rainfall
the keeper blamed the break on the loss of the plants along the shore
plants with spreading roots were put back in the following cycle
the new plantings now withstand the current and hold the bank
text: On the night the dike gave way, the lock keeper was asleep close to the breach. He recalls a dull sound, then the bank sliding into the current. What lay behind it came out later: the roots that had bound the shore were torn away the autumn before, during a careless clearing of the channel. Stripped of that frame, the silt had nothing left to grip, and each rise of the water carried off its share. The flood spread through the low meadows, drowned the fences and laid a sheet of mud over the crops. People living nearby blamed the rain at first. The keeper pointed instead at the bare stumps along the edge, and kept saying the works had lost their living skeleton. Shrubs with creeping roots went in the following season. Since then the young stems bend under the current without breaking, and the bank holds.

units: a bank of earth crumbling under the rain blocks the trench below
the first step is to find where the water arrives and where it stands
without that survey the plantings will be washed away
plant waste must be cleared and dead stems cut at ground level
the base of the trunk is kept because its roots still hold the ground
short terraces are laid out in staggered rows to break the slope
shrubs with tight roots are planted and the ground is covered with chipped branches
watering is limited to the first cycle so that the roots go down for water
after two cycles low growth covers the slope and the water no longer gathers
text: A bank that crumbles with every shower ends up choking the ditch below it. Here is how to hold it in place for good. Start by working out where the water comes from and where it collects; skip that survey and your plantings will simply wash away. Clear the debris next, then cut the dead stems back flush with the ground, leaving the stump where it stands, since its roots still bind the soil. Dig short level terraces, offset from one row to the next, so that the slope is broken up. Set shrubs with dense root systems at the back of each terrace, then mulch with branches chipped on the spot. Water through the first season only, or you will end up with lazy roots. Check how the plants have taken after every heavy rain and replace the ones that dried out. Two seasons on, scrub covers the slope and the runoff spreads.

units: two settlements on the banks of the same watercourse chose different strategies
the floods of the previous year prompted these decisions
the first settlement raised its protective structure and hardened the shore
the second bought farmed land in the low ground to take in the overflow
basins were dug on this bought land
measurements show a steadier flow leaving the second settlement
the underground store of water builds back better in the second settlement
the leaders of the first cite the protection of a heavily built area
the specialists hold that the two methods complete each other
text: Two riverside towns on the same watercourse settled on opposite answers after the floods of last year. The first raised its dike and faced the foot of the shore with stone, on the argument that protection ought to be visible and immediate. The second chose to buy up low farmed plots, dig ponds there and let the river spread out across them when it overtops. Readings presented at a public meeting show a clear gap between the two: the flow leaving the second town is far better spread out, and its groundwater builds back more fully. Officials in the first town reply that their choice shields a densely built quarter, which the other method could not have done. The engineers brought in conclude that the two approaches complete each other rather than compete, and advise combining them along the basin.

units: a water logged area sits below the path and is crossed on boarding
the ground is soft and dark water rises between the plants
three settings follow one another with no marked border
a strip of tall hollow stems lines the entrance and hides the view
a mass of low shrubs holds the middle part
still water remains under this mass
an open sheet of water holds the central part
birds, water dwelling creatures and many insects use the place
the plants catch particles and substances before they reach the underground store
text: Below the path lies a wetland, crossed on a run of boards. The ground there is spongy, soaked with a brown water that rises between the tussocks. Three habitats follow one another with no clear line between them. Along the entrance a belt of reeds shuts off the view and rustles at the least breath of air. Further in spreads a thicket of low shrubs, and under it the water stands in dark pools. At the center lies open water, mirroring the sky, ringed by a soft edge that gives way underfoot. Nesting birds, frogs and a swarm of insects all make their living here. The place works as a filter too, since the plants trap particles and dissolved matter before any of it reaches the water table. Nothing about the spot looks dramatic. It is still one of the richest habitats anywhere nearby.

units: the writer was doubtful at first about a plot left untended near housing
a building project meant to destroy the growth and build on the plot
the project stopped for lack of money
the plot was overrun by thorny plants after two cycles
the people nearby complained about this spread
a group of residents suggested making paths and mowing the middle part only
this suggestion was first met with mockery
the winged wildlife came back and the children made the place their own
the local authority ended up formally protecting the plot
the writer now prefers this barely tended space to a laid out garden
text: Honestly, I had no faith in that scrap of waste ground behind the housing blocks. We were told at the start that a developer would flatten everything and pour concrete over the lot. Then the work stopped for want of money, and the ground was left exactly as it was. Two seasons on, brambles had taken the whole thing over and the neighbors were grumbling. A residents' group suggested cutting paths through it, keeping the scrub around the sides and mowing the middle only. People laughed. Then the birds came back, the children got into the habit of running there, and the local council ended up listing the plot as protected ground. My own view shifted along the way. I used to want a park laid out with a ruler; now I stand up for that useful mess. It costs next to nothing to keep and gives back more than a clipped lawn.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a long shortage of rain caused this grower of young trees to change trade
she farmed grain before that
her harvests collapsed two cycles running
she turned her driest plots into a place for growing trees
she had to learn to name trees and to judge the health of a seedling
her first customers were neighbors
people managing watercourses then ordered plants from her to hold the shores firm
her plants root better elsewhere because they grew on poor ground
she now has staff and takes in people who are training
from her earlier trade she kept the habit of writing everything down
text: A long drought decided the career of the woman who runs the local tree nursery. She was farming grain at the time, and watched her yields collapse two seasons running. With nothing to harvest, she turned her driest fields into a nursery for native trees. The switch forced a second trade on her: reading bark, judging the vigor of a seedling, sowing at the right moment. Her first orders came from the neighbors, then from the people who manage rivers and were hunting for plants able to hold a shore. Because her stock grows on poor soil, it takes root more readily once it is moved elsewhere. She now has three people on the payroll and trains apprentices who come from far away. One habit survives from her earlier work, and it is a stubborn one: she writes everything down, season after season.

units: the quiet where the machines were is the first impression left by this reworked valley
the site had earlier been laid out in a very rigid way
the bed of the watercourse had been made straight and its shores covered with stone
the meadows had been dried out by a network of trenches
the wild animals had left this site
those behind the restoration gave the stream its bends back
trunks were placed in the bed on purpose
the wooded edge was allowed to gain on the meadows
visitors struggle to move about without getting wet
the cover of the trees keeps the air cool and the flow is slowed before the town
text: What strikes you in this valley given back to the water is the silence where the machines used to be. The site had been straightened past all reason: the stream pulled into a line, the shores walled, the meadows drained down to the last ditch. The result read as a corridor rather than a landscape, and the wildlife had cleared out. Whoever planned the restoration went the other way. They gave the stream its bends back, dropped whole trunks into the bed, let the wood creep out over the grassland. You could accuse them of indulging disorder, and walkers often struggle to find a dry way through. It convinces all the same. Under the canopy that has grown back the air stays cool, dead trunks feed the insects, and the current sheds its load before the town. A quiet success, measured less by what it built than by what it made possible.

units: the writer sends news to a close acquaintance about a plot of ground taken back in hand
a layer of plant matter has been spread over the soil to hold the moisture
the hedge has been filled out with cuttings taken from shrubs
the plants chosen can stand a shortage of water
building rubble has to be hauled away because it blocks water from soaking in
the writer notices that rain is held better since the work was done
the roots reach farther down than they used to
the writer asks after the food garden of the person written to
text: Dear friend, I finally have something to tell you about the plot we took back in hand behind the house. Three jobs have kept me busy, and here they are in turn. The ground came first. I spread a thick blanket of dead leaves over it, which holds the damp in and slows the drying out. The hedge came second. I filled its gaps with cuttings pulled off the shrubs that shrug off a dry spell. The third job is the dreary one, hauling away the rubble the old shed left behind, since it keeps water from soaking in. Already the leaf layer drinks up the rain better, and the roots are reaching farther down than they used to. If the weather keeps swinging the way people warn it will, these small chores will beat regret. Write back soon, and tell me how your vegetable patch is coming along.

units: a heavy fuel escaped from a storage yard into a watercourse
the leak went unnoticed through the first week
fishermen then saw fish that had gone weak
a colored film spread across the surface of the water
the technical services moved only once the drinking supply was threatened
floating devices were put in place to hold back the slick
the fouled sediment was scraped off after the pumping
wildlife is coming back to the site little by little
a smell lingers on the bank when the heat builds
text: So you want to know what has gone on in the river since the trouble at the fuel storage yard? Here it is, in order. Through that whole first week nobody caught on at all. The heavy oil was seeping out under a cracked slab, and from the bank there was nothing to smell and nothing to see. Then the anglers began pulling up listless fish, and a rainbow film crept out across the flat water. Did anyone move fast, you ask? Honestly, no. The crews turned out only once the slick had reached the drinking water intake. After that it all went quickly. Floating booms went in, the oily layer was pumped off, and the fouled silt underneath was scraped away. And now? Now the wildlife is drifting back, slowly, though the bank still gives off a tarry smell whenever the heat builds. That is where things stand.

units: the spring that feeds an upper district is running dry
the water drawn for crops has emptied the underground table
a grower fears losing his harvest without irrigation
a schoolteacher asks the manager about supply brought in by truck
the manager admits that this would become necessary the following summer
the council intends to cap the volumes it allows
the leaking pipes will be repaired
the watering of ornamental ground will be forbidden
those present admit that their own habits add to the shortage
text: The woman who runs the water service put it plainly to the residents gathered in the lower hall. The spring that feeds the upper district is running dry. Farm pumping had emptied the table underground through the dry months, she said, and one thing was dragging the next along behind it. A grower shot back that without irrigation his crops would burn. A schoolteacher asked whether the children would end up drinking water trucked in from somewhere else. That, the manager admitted, was what the following summer would bring unless something changed. The council would cap the volumes it allowed, patch the leaking mains, and forbid the watering of lawns. The meeting ran late, and by the end everyone could see that the shortage came not from the sky alone but from what every household drew.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the channel of a harbor was filling with deposits season after season
ships could no longer work their way up to the quays
the merchants believed wrongly that the sea was pulling away
the river was in fact carrying down sediment torn off the slopes
the felling of trees had left the hillsides with no cover
engineers tied the ruin of the heights to the decline of the harbor
plantings were ordered along the ridges
works of woven brushwood were set into the gullies
basins were dug to trap the mud before the shore
the depth of the navigable passage was won back
text: A thriving harbor town once watched its channel fill in, season after season. Ships loaded with salt and timber scraped bottom, then gave up on reaching the quays. The merchants worried, sure the sea was pulling away from them, when in truth the river kept carrying down into the roads a load of silt torn off the slopes above. Timber felled for roof beams had left those slopes with nothing on them, and rain now cut the soil with nothing to slow it. A generation of engineers finally tied the skinned hillside to the failing harbor. They had the ridges replanted, brushwood woven along the gullies, and basins dug where the mud could settle before it ever reached the shore. The channel won back its depth, and the lesson outlived those who learned it. No one heals a shore without tending the heights above it.

units: two roofs sharing a wall behave in different ways under the sun
the first carries a dark bituminous covering
that surface takes in nearly all the sunlight that reaches it
the heating damages the insulation laid beneath
the cooling equipment then runs without a break
the second pairs a pale coating with a cover of plants
that roof throws back part of the sunlight and stores rainwater
the pale one stays cooler when both are read at the same hour
the planted roof weighs more and calls for steady upkeep
text: Two roofs share a wall and answer the sun in opposite ways, and the covering is what explains it. The first wears a dark bituminous membrane, close to tar, which soaks up almost every bit of sunlight that lands on it. The surface climbs so hot that the insulation laid beneath it ages early and the cooling equipment never shuts off. The second carries a pale mineral coating topped with a mat of thick-leaved plants. It throws back a good share of the sunlight and keeps rainwater in its growing bed. Read at the same hour, the pale roof stays markedly cooler than the dark one. The gap turns up on the energy bill of the building as well. On the other hand, a planted roof weighs more and asks for steady upkeep, which the membrane never does. So the choice rests on the framing as much as on the weather.

units: the keeper of a high mountain station tells of a stretch of his last measuring season
the packed snow was covered with a grayish deposit
that deposit had come from fires burning far away
a darkened surface takes in more heat and melts faster
the buried instruments had to be dug out twice in the same week
the slope was strangely quiet at night
the usual nighttime trickle of water had gone
the observer wrote down what he saw in a notebook
the readings of the seasons that followed bore out his impression
text: The keeper of a high mountain station tells of one stretch of his last measuring season that he has never shaken off. He starts with the color of the old packed snow. Instead of the white he expected, a gray veil of soot lay across the whole of it, carried in from fires burning far away. He goes on to the melt, which ran fast, because darkened snow takes in more heat than clean snow does. He describes the buried sensors too, dug out twice in a single week as the pack sank under them. Last he brings up the quiet, a slope stripped of the night trickle of meltwater that used to keep him company. Back at the shelter he wrote it all into a bound logbook, aware that one man's story proves nothing. The readings of the seasons that followed bore him out, and his notebook seeded a far wider study.

units: the roof must be looked over and clean before any water is collected
a screen goes into the mouth of the gutter to hold back leaves
the tank is set on firm footing and out of the sun
a collector fitted with a filter joins the downspout to the tank
the overflow must run off toward planted ground and not toward the street
the water of the first week serves to rinse and is then thrown out
the seal of the lid is checked every season
an open container helps mosquitoes breed
the store is drawn down partway before the frost to keep the wall from splitting
text: Before you start collecting rainwater at home, look the roof over. A clean covering, free of moss and grime, will give you clearer water. Next, drop a strainer into the mouth of the gutter so that the leaves stay out. Set the tank on firm footing and well out of the sun, since warmth feeds algae. Join the downspout to it with a collector that carries a filter, and make sure the overflow can run off into a planted bed rather than onto the street. Open the tap through the whole of the first week to rinse the tank, then throw that water out. Every season, check that the lid still seals, because an open container breeds mosquitoes. Last of all, draw the store down partway before the frost sets in, or the ice will split the wall. Water of this kind suits the garden and the washing of tools.

units: an old shore path has been closed off with a fence
the sea is hollowing out the foot of the rock wall
storms have come around more often
each swell carries off soft rock at the base of the bank
the upper part ends up giving way
a house was pulled down over the cold season before
its rubble still litters the beach below
an official explains that pulling back and holding on both come dear
researchers find the pace quickening as the water rises
the parking areas are being shifted inland
text: What hits you first up on the cliff is the orange mesh strung across the old shore path. The people who live here will tell you straight off that the sea is eating the foot of the wall and the top follows. Storms come around more often now, and every heavy swell tears another bite of soft rock out of the base, until the harder stuff overhead tips forward. One house had to be pulled down over the cold season before, and its rubble still litters the beach below. The official in charge of the shore makes no secret of his bind. Pulling back comes dear, and holding on comes dearer. The researchers who came to measure the retreat find the pace quickening as the water rises. For now the parking areas get shifted, access gets closed off, warnings get posted. And each winter the fence moves farther inland.

units: a wet meadow looks from a distance like an ordinary field
straight ditches were cut long ago to drain the marsh
that draining was meant to win grazing ground
the water runs off toward a canal instead of sitting in the hollows
the peat laid open to the air gives up its carbon
the birds that nested in the rushes have left the place
a crew of managers stops the ditches with clay
the water table is lifted and the reeds come back
walkways keep visitors away from the tender ground
frogs and newts moved into the pools by the second season
text: Seen from the towpath, the wet meadow could pass for an ordinary field, grassy and cropped short. Walk closer and the straight ditches show up, cut long ago to dry the marsh out and win grazing ground for livestock. The water now slides off toward the canal instead of sitting in the hollows, and the peat, laid open to the air, breaks down and gives up its carbon. The birds that nested in the rush clumps have gone. A crew of managers is working to tip the balance back. They stop the ditches with clay plugs, lift the water table and let the reeds crowd in again. Wooden walkways steer walkers away from the tender ground. By the second season the refilled pools had taken in frogs and newts, and the soaked peat had stopped smoldering. The ground looks messier, and that is the sign they were waiting for.

units: the writer disputes the sporting image used to describe work on the climate
a race is run alone and closes at a set finish
the writer offers instead the image of ground worked in common
each person there takes over the soil the others left behind
whoever neglects a patch in a garden harms the plot alongside
changing the image changes the kind of commitment expected
a promise with a figure on it differs from a promise of steady upkeep
the writer calls for talk of care rather than of performance
the generations to come will judge what has lasted
text: We like to talk about work on the climate as a race, with winners out front and stragglers behind. The picture is appealing, and it misleads. A race is run alone and it closes. Climate sits closer to a shared garden, where each of us takes over the soil the last hands left behind. Slow down in a race and you lose your place. Let your patch go in a garden and the weeds walk straight into the bed alongside. That difference is no decoration. It changes what we ought to expect from the commitments people make. A runner promises a score. A gardener promises to keep showing up. One measures an arrival, the other a continuity. We would do better, then, to speak less of records and more of care, less of standings and more of seasons. Those who come after us will not ask who ran hardest. They will look at what is still growing.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman running the restoration site grew up beside a wetland
her father taught her how to turn the peat
she had noticed the decline of the birds that bred there
she trained at a university in ecology
her first crew replanted bare banks
the young trees set too deep in the soil died off
she then picked species that tolerate standing water
the passing birds came back once the reed cover closed over
she passes her method on to crews from elsewhere
she says a damaged habitat is healed by patience and not by machine power
text: The woman who now runs the restoration site grew up a short walk from a marsh. Her father put a spade in her hands early and showed her how to turn the peat. She watched the brackish water rise and fall each year, and she kept count of the nesting birds as their numbers thinned. Ecology at the university came next. Her first crew was sent to replant stripped banks, and the work failed: the saplings went in too deep and rotted in the sodden ground. So she changed the approach, picking species that shrug off standing water and setting the holes farther apart. Many seasons on, the reed bed has closed over itself and the passing flocks are back. She trains crews who come from other regions now, and she tells them the same thing every time: a broken habitat mends through patience and close watching, never through the force of machines.

units: the narrator finds the shared compost yard worth attention
the rules of the yard turn away thick woody stems
a shredding machine was therefore brought in
waste reduced to chips breaks down twice as fast as before
the number of people using the yard has risen
the noise of the machine disturbs the ground floor homes
the compost is not screened before it is handed out
users therefore carry home useless bits of wood
the quality of the product changes from one bin to another
the writer holds that a screen would correct most of the flaw
text: Honestly, the shared compost yard is worth a look, even if the running of it limps in places. Whole branches are not allowed in the bins, so somebody had to bring in a shredder, and that machine is what changed everything: chipped up, the scraps break down in one season instead of two. Word got around, and now people show up with their buckets and wait their turn. The catch is the racket. The motor screams, and the folks on the ground floor keep their windows shut all morning. Someone also told me the finished compost ought to be screened before it goes back out, or gardeners walk off with lumps of wood they cannot use. That step simply does not happen, so what you get depends on which bin you dig into. My verdict is short: fine idea, sloppy execution, and one screen away from being a model of its kind.

units: the writer is staying at a water treatment works
the incoming water carries nitrogen compounds
the level climbs after rain falls on the neighboring crops
the metal pipes suffer chemical attack
the repairs are expensive
a planted wetland was laid out upstream
the plants clean the water before it reaches the tanks
the pollutant load drops by about a third
the power use of the works falls as well
the crew intends to enlarge the filtering area
text: I am writing from the treatment works where I am spending the week, and what goes on here should catch your interest. The intake basin takes in water loaded with nitrates, and the readings climb as soon as rain washes off the fields next door. That worries the operators, because the metal piping has started to corrode and every repair costs a fortune. What surprised me was how plain the answer is. Upstream of the works, someone dug a shallow pond and planted it thick with reeds, and those plants scrub the water before it ever reaches the tanks. The load comes down by roughly a third, and the power bill has eased along with it. No extra pump, nothing added. The crew is already talking about stretching the filter pond out toward the meadow. The rest can wait until my return, so keep an evening free for me.

units: the text sets the lack of water against too much water in a river
the nature of the ground decides the answer
silty ground holds back the rising water then releases it slowly
a slope stripped of plants sheds the water at once
the specialists do not clearly name the worse of the two
the rising water lays down feeding deposits despite the damage it does
the lack of water hardens the surface and squeezes the roots
the specialists rule out hard structures and deep wells
they call for land that mixes water holds plant barriers and soils that drink
text: Which should we fear more, a river run dry or a river out of its bed? The question keeps coming back, and the answer lies in the ground you happen to be standing on. Silty flatland drinks the flood like a sponge and gives the water back over weeks; a stripped slope throws it all downstream at once. Ask which wound heals better and the water scientists start hedging. A flood tears things loose, true, and yet it also lays down feeding silt, while drought bakes the surface hard and clamps down on the roots. So what should be built? Neither a wall nor a borehole, they answer, but a stretch of land that can swing both ways: ponds that hold, hedgerows that slow, loose soil that drinks. Only then does the comparison mean anything, since one trouble eases with a slow water table and the other with the memory of runoff.

units: a technical manager sets out the procedure to people in training
her deputy speaks after each explanation
plant waste is no longer placed under a cover layer
breaking down deep in the pile it gives off a gas that warms the air
sorting takes out the metals by magnetic pull
the plastics are separated by a jet of air
the glass passes through a moving screen
the dark liquid from the rows must be pumped off before it reaches the groundwater
a cover that lets air through holds down the smell
protective gear and a ban on working alone are imposed
text: The engineer in charge of the site walked the trainees through the procedure, and her deputy filled in the gaps after each point. She began with what has changed: green waste no longer goes under a cover layer, because breaking down deep in the pile it gives off a gas with a fierce warming effect. Her deputy took over on sorting. Magnets pull out the metal, a jet of air lifts the plastic away, and the glass drops through a shaking screen. She came back to the dark liquid that seeps under the rows, which has to be pumped off before it reaches the water table. Her deputy added a word on smell, held down by a breathable sheet and a fine spray. She closed on safety: helmet, heavy gloves, and never walking alone between the skips. The trainees asked what becomes of the rejects, and the crew promised them a look at the furnace.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the first settled groups opened modest growing plots at the edge of the woods
the trees took the ground back once a group moved on
making metal called for enormous amounts of wood fuel
whole stands of trees were then removed
the slopes left without trees began to slump under the rain
official orders required cutting branches instead of felling whole trunks
the slides of earth pushed those in charge to plant the slopes again
these plantings often rested on a single species
that sameness left the woodlands open to insects
a mixture of species is now held to be the best protection
text: The earliest settled groups cut into the edges of the woods, opening clearings just wide enough to sow. Whenever a hamlet moved on, the trees crept back over the ground it had left, and the forest outlived what had been taken from it. Smelting metal changed that. It swallowed charcoal in quantities nobody had needed before, whole stands came down to feed the furnaces, and the stripped hills began to slide with every heavy rain. Rules followed. Written orders called for cutting branches rather than felling trunks, and left the coppice time to ripen. Later, alarm at the mudflows drove those in charge to plant the slopes again, usually with one species and nothing else, which left those young stands defenseless once insects found them. What has been learned since comes down to a single word: variety. A mixed hillside takes both the pests and the dry spells better.

units: part of the carbon dioxide in the air passes into the seas
this taking in changes the chemistry of the water
the sea surface turns more acid
the living things that build a chalky shell are struck first
their thinnest rims are eaten into and break down
these tiny creatures feed fish and seabirds
the weakening carries through the whole food web
warmer water holds less dissolved gas
part of the carbon therefore works its way back to the air
the shallow stretches near shore react before the rest because of farm inputs and water heavy with silt
text: As carbon dioxide builds up overhead, the sea takes in a large share of it, and what it takes in alters its chemistry. The dissolved gas forms a weak acid, and the surface water turns steadily sharper. Creatures that build a chalky shell feel it first: the shell knits together poorly, and its thinnest rims begin to eat away. Since those tiny animals feed fish and seabirds alike, a weakness at the bottom travels up through the whole food web. A second effect piles onto the first. Warmer water holds less dissolved gas, so part of the carbon that went in works its way back out to the air, and the process keeps itself going. Readings taken close to shore show that the shallow stretches shift first, because they also take in muddy runoff and the fertilizer washed off the fields behind them.

units: the shared garden came close to being given up
water sat between the rows from the first heavy rain
the young plants rotted without reaching maturity
turning the soil deeper changed nothing
the layer of clay pushed the water back up
an experienced gardener found the real cause
the runoff came from the sloping parking area
a planted ditch was cut along the edge of the plot
trees that drink water were put in and the beds were raised
the harvest of the following season was heavy
text: We came within a hair of walking away from the neighborhood garden, and the letdown stung. The first real downpour left water sitting between the beds, the whole plot turned into a swamp, and the young plants rotted where they stood. A neighbour said dig deeper, so we dug deeper; nothing came of it, because the clay underneath pushed everything straight back up. It took a retired gardener to tell us we had been looking in the wrong place: the parking area sloped, and all its runoff was landing on us. So we cut a shallow ditch along the fence, put in willows to drink the excess, and raised the beds on salvaged planks. The season after that, squash sprawled over half the ground and the lettuce finally held. We laugh about it now, about the boots stuck fast and the drowned rows.

units: the text compares two ways of handling kitchen scraps at home
the space available guides the choice
the first answer uses a ventilated container
wet material and dry material are layered in it
the mixture has to be turned once a week
the finished product appears after two seasons
the second answer means burying the scraps in a dug trench
the depth of cover keeps small animals away
the second answer costs nothing but yields nothing you can take back out
the reader is asked to measure the space and count the meals cooked at home
text: Anyone who wants to deal with kitchen peelings without handing them to the collection truck has two routes to choose from, and space is what decides between them. The first is a ventilated bin: you lay down a wet layer, then a dry one, turn the pile once a week, and at the end of two seasons you pull out something dark and crumbly. The second route is plainer still. Dig yourself a trench, tip the scraps in, and bury them under enough soil that rodents lose interest. Set side by side, the bin needs watching but hands you a soil improver ready to spread; the trench costs nothing and feeds the ground where it lies, though you will never lift a single spadeful back out. To settle the matter, measure your balcony or your plot, then count the meals you actually cook at home in a week.

units: the shore described here is retreating under the waves
the posts driven in recently already lean
the water drawn from the wells has taken on a salty taste
the salt water is moving in under the growing land
the growers have given up the most delicate crops
they are turning to hardier plants that ask for less water
the cellars suffer damp and salt eats at their walls
the yard of the school was built up higher after a flood
the residents argue over holding the shoreline or moving the houses uphill
no decision has been taken locally
text: At first light the wind drops over the seawall, and you can finally hear what this place is going through. Out front, the sea gains: every storm carries off a piece of the dune, and the posts driven in last year already lean inland. At the wells, the water pulled up tastes of salt now, a sign that the salt wedge is climbing under the gardens. Farther along, in the fields, the growers have given up on the tender vegetables and fallen back on tough varieties that ask for less water. Behind the embankment, in the cellars, damp rises and salt crust chews at the foot of the walls. At the end of the lane sits the school yard, built up higher after the last flood. And everywhere the same low talk: hold the shoreline, or move the houses up the hillside? Nobody here settles it, and nobody pretends any longer that the question is absent.

units: still water fills the bottom of a hollow ringed with reeds
its surface was clear before and now carries a greenish film
lasting heat speeds up the loss of water to evaporation
the dissolved minerals grow denser in what is left
the ground nearby dries out and splits into brittle pieces
plants rotting at the bottom give off a foul smell
the water insects disappear from the place
the birds that fed there quit the shore
the spring downhill barely supplies the growing plots any water
the growers bore deeper wells and pull the buried water lower
text: Still water lies in the bottom of a hollow ringed with reeds. It ran clear once; now a greenish film sits across it and the wind barely creases the surface. Long stretches of heat are the first cause: the water leaves faster as vapor, and the minerals dissolved in it grow denser in whatever is left behind. Around the rim the ground bakes and splits into brittle plates that crumble underfoot. With nothing to stir it, the plant matter rots down below, and the smell that rises off the hollow turns the stomach. The water insects go first. The birds that used to feed on them quit the shore altogether. Farther downhill, the spring that once soaked the growing plots barely wets the soil now. So the growers bore deeper wells, and each one they sink pulls the buried water lower. Each drying spell sets up a harder one behind it.

units: the streets overheat because they are paved with asphalt and concrete
the air there turns hard to breathe as soon as the sun hits
heat related collapses are becoming more frequent
air conditioning is offered as the answer to the problem
an air conditioner throws outside the heat it pulls from inside
that equipment eats a huge amount of power
the writer proposes planting thick trees along the busy streets
he proposes making schoolyards soak up rain and laying pale surfaces
he calls for water where people stand and wait
he claims these measures need no untried technology but a budget
text: Let us be blunt for a second. Our streets bake because we paved them over with asphalt and concrete. The moment the sun hits, the air turns thick and hard to breathe, and then we act surprised that people keep going down in the heat. Air conditioning, we are told, is the fix. It fixes nothing. It shoves outdoors the very heat it pulls from indoors, and it eats power at a rate nobody wants to look at. There is a way out, and none of it is clever. Line the busy streets with trees thick enough to throw real shade. Break up the schoolyards so the rain soaks in. Swap black paving for pale surfaces that bounce the light back. Put water where people stand and wait. Not one of those waits on an invention nobody has made yet. They wait on a budget. Comfort is not something you cool. It is something you plant.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman running a measuring station climbs weekly to a ring of rock walls
her predecessor logged ice thickness by hand
she now receives readings sent up automatically by sensors
the ice was once hard and bluish underfoot
the surface today is soft and gives under crampons
the glacier snout was once a clean edge and is now a thinned tongue
crumbling gravel streaks that tongue
she also watches two facing slopes of the same range
the slope that takes the sun loses its ice far faster than the other
she finds that gap more telling than an overall average figure
text: Once a week the woman who runs a measuring station hikes up to a ring of rock walls to take the readings off her instruments. The job is the one her predecessor held, but almost nothing about it has stayed put. He wrote ice thickness into a notebook by hand. She opens a screen and finds the readings waiting, sent up by sensors on their own. He walked on a hard bluish crust. She crosses a soft skin that gives under her crampons. Where his notes described a clean wall of ice at the snout, hers describe a thin tongue streaked with gravel that crumbles at a touch. She watches two facing slopes of the same range as well. The one that takes the sun head on gives up its ice far faster than the shaded one. That gap, she says, teaches her more than any average figure for the glacier as a whole.

units: the review covers a set of photographs devoted to drought
the first part shows split ground covered with whitish crust
the second part shows horizons veiled by heat
a third part gathers emptied riverbeds and abandoned watering equipment
the last part shows the people who stayed on
the reviewer calls that last part the finest
the whole set avoids complaint and moral lessons
the pictures are hung so that each one pulls you into the next
the reviewer holds that the quiet in the frames carries more weight than an argument
text: Seldom has a set of photographs handled drought with so light a hand. The opening sequence stays low, on the ground itself: clay split into plates, a chalky crust, pale dust that lifts at the smallest breath of wind. The next group leaves the earth for the air, where heat smears the far edge of things and the horizon dissolves into haze. A third gathers what the water left behind, riverbeds paved with stone, dry basins, watering hose coiled and forgotten like dead root. The last group, and the finest, turns to the people who stayed: dusty hands, weathered faces, eyes tipped up toward the sky. Nothing here complains and nothing preaches. The pictures are hung so that each one pulls you into the next, and the quiet inside those frames carries more weight than any argument could.

units: the writer sends word from a measuring post to describe a repair
he opened the case at the start of the week
a mineral crust covered the temperature probe and skewed the readings
he cleaned that probe in an acid bath while watching the time
he then put the unit back together and checked the gasket seal
the curve sat a fixed step off once the post restarted
so he recalibrated the unit against a reference probe
he cleaned the dirt covered solar panel and the charging voltage climbed back
the readings have come in without a break ever since
he invites the person he writes to over to see the monitoring board now in place
text: Writing from the measuring post, as promised, to tell you how the repair on the sensor turned out. I took the case apart at the start of the week and found the temperature probe under a hard mineral crust that was skewing every reading. I soaked it in an acid bath and stood over it with a timer, since the stuff chews through metal if you forget it. Next morning I put the unit back together and checked the gasket for a tight seal. Transmission picked up again, but the curve sat a fixed step off the true value, so I recalibrated against the reference probe. The day after that, I wiped the solar panel, gray with dust, and the charging voltage climbed right back. Nothing has dropped out of the record since. Come by the post whenever you like and take a look at the monitoring board now running.

units: a common question concerns the damp spreading through the walls of older housing
that damp comes from groundwater rising under the foundations
harder rain falling closer together feeds that rise
packed downpours saturate compacted soil that takes in nothing
the water then heads for the cellars
a waterproof coating seals the damp inside the masonry
masonry sealed that way turns friable and sheds in patches
specialists advise drainage around the building
they also advise renders that breathe and open ground nearby that takes water in
the answer on cost states that acting late comes to more
text: A question comes up at nearly every public meeting: where does the damp climbing the walls of older housing come from? It comes from groundwater rising under the foundations, and that rise is fed by rain that now falls harder and closer together. A second question follows: what has any of this to do with the climate? Downpours packed into an hour saturate compacted soil that takes in nothing at all, and the water goes looking for the cellars. Third question: is a waterproof coating not enough? It is not. Such a coating seals the moisture inside the masonry, which turns friable and sheds in patches. What is advised instead? Drainage around the building, renders that let a wall breathe, and open ground alongside that takes water in. The last question turns on cost, and the answer is blunt: waiting comes to more.

units: a fisherman tells an engineer the water has smelled wrong since the cold season
a brown scum clings to the stones on the bed
the smell sharpens when the level of the river drops
the engineer explains that a sewer line upstream spills over during storms
the fisherman objects that the trouble has run through too many seasons
the engineer also names the runoff from an animal operation on the plateau
the plan calls for a holding basin upstream
it also calls for a thick strip of planting along the banks
steady checks on what gets released are scheduled
the engineer says the insects coming back will signal the change
text: On the bank, a fisherman tells the engineer sent out to look into it that the water has smelled wrong since the cold season. She asks whether the color changed as well. He points to a brown scum stuck on the stones of the bed and says the stench climbs as soon as the level drops. She explains that a sewer line upstream spills over whenever a storm runs past what the pipes can hold. He is not satisfied: the trouble has run through too many seasons to hang on a few storms. She grants him that, and brings up the animal operation on the plateau, whose runoff drains down toward the bed. Then she lays out the plan, a holding basin upstream, a thick strip of planting along both banks, steady checks on what gets released. He asks when the water will run clear. The insects, she says, will tell him first.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: in one valley wood was once burned for every purpose
the air smelled of smoke and the walls went black with soot
people took that state of affairs for granted
a dark fuel was then cut out of the rock
the energy yield rose sharply
workshops spread and the sky over the working valleys hazed over
the real turning point lies in the change of scale
a burned forest can grow back over generations
carbon drawn from a buried seam cannot be put back there
the old fires lived off what grew around them while the later ones drew on a store
text: Picture a valley where wood went into every fire, from the supper pot to the forge. The air smelled of smoke, the walls went black, and nobody thought twice about it. Set that beside what came after, once people started cutting into rock for a dark fuel. The heat you got out of a single load of it jumped. Workshops spread. The sky over the working valleys hung hazy from dawn to dusk. The real break, though, was one of scale. Burn a forest and it comes back, given enough generations of patience. Burn a seam out of the ground and the carbon it held has nowhere to go back to. The old fires lived off what grew around them, while the ones that followed drew down a store. Watch nothing but the flame and you will miss the difference. It shows only when you look at what feeds the flame.

units: three mechanisms account for the changes in the oceans
the first mechanism has to do with the heat the water soaks up
warmed water swells and raises the level with no ice melting
the second mechanism is chemical and comes from dissolved carbon dioxide
water turned acidic works away at shells and chalky skeletons
the third mechanism concerns the mixing of the water layers
the surface layer mixes less with the layers beneath it
that lid keeps nutrients from below away from the plankton
the three mechanisms feed one another
a sea with less life in it draws down less carbon
text: Three mechanisms are enough to account for what is happening to the oceans. The first is heat. Seawater soaks up a huge share of the warmth building up, and warm water swells, so the level climbs even where no ice has melted at all. The second is chemistry. As the sea takes in more carbon dioxide it turns slightly corrosive, and it works away at the shells and the chalky skeletons that shellfish and corals build for themselves. The third is stirring. A warmer surface layer mixes less readily with the cold water beneath it, and that lid keeps nutrients from rising, which leaves the plankton hungry. Each one bites on its own, and together they bite harder. Warmer, more acidic, more layered water carries less life, and a sea with less life in it draws down less carbon than before.

units: the keeper of a mountain refuge barred her shutters before the sky changed
a warm breath came down from the pass in the middle of the afternoon
a curtain loaded with sand then moved up the trail
sand settled even on the tables
the keeper knew the wind had carried that dust from dry country far off
rain stained the color of ochre fell at nightfall
that rain left hardened streaks on the windows
the snow on the nearby glacier had turned rust red by morning
that snow melted faster than the keeper had ever watched snow go
she wrote the event into her log without expecting it to happen again
text: The woman who kept the mountain refuge had barred her shutters before the sky gave any sign. Around the middle of the afternoon a warm breath slid down from the pass, close and heavy. Then the whole slope went blurred and dim. A curtain of sand came up the trail, and grit settled everywhere, even along the tabletops inside. She knew the wind for what it was: it had carried that dust off dry country far beyond the ridgelines. The rain came at dusk, thick and stained the color of ochre, and it dried on the windows in hard streaks. By morning the snow on the glacier below was no longer white but rust red, and it melted while she stood watching, faster than she had ever seen snow go. She wrote the whole of it down in her log. It did not once occur to her that it would happen again.

units: fear has an identifiable trigger
fear stops once the danger is gone
anxiety points at a future and uncertain danger
anxiety shows up as muscle tension and damp hands
fear is compared to a brief alarm signal
anxiety is compared to a faulty, continuous alarm signal
both emotions start out with a protective function
telling the two states apart helps you respond appropriately
text: You are walking down a dark hallway when a door slams shut behind you. Your heart pounds, a chill travels down the back of your neck, your shoulders go rigid. That is fear. It has a precise cause, it arrives abruptly, and it subsides the moment the threat has receded. Anxiety operates on another principle entirely. Nothing definite ever stands before it; it looks ahead, toward whatever might happen. You feel it in a clenched jaw, in damp palms that stay damp for no reason you can point to. Fear is like an alarm that rings and then stops. Anxiety is like a badly wired alarm that hums underneath everything else. Both of them start out protecting you. What separates them is how long they last and what they are aimed at. Naming which of the two is traveling through you already sharpens the response you choose.

units: adults gather every week in a room used for stage practice
the workshop is aimed at people whom speaking in front of an audience blocks
the woman leading it previously worked in care
the session is divided into three categories of exercises
the first set of exercises works on breathing
the second set works on facial expressions
the third set consists of looking at each other in silence
this silent face-off often triggers a burst of laughter
the leader reads that laughter as a release
text: A handful of adults meet once a week in a studio whose wooden floor is scuffed and scratched. The workshop is meant for people paralyzed the moment they must address an audience. The woman who runs it worked in care before she turned to directing, and she builds every session around three families of exercises. The first set works the breath: draw the air in, hold it, release it in one prolonged sigh, until the throat finally loosens. The second set works the face: pull a grimace, hold it, drop it, and feel the gap between a tension you suffer and one you choose. The third set works the eyes: two participants stare at each other wordlessly, and one of them usually ends up laughing. That laugh is no failure, she says. It signals that a knot of awkwardness has just come undone.

units: the first step is to settle somewhere away from demands
you must rest your hands on your legs and breathe without forcing
the next step asks you to spot where the anger shows up physically
you are advised to name that area mentally
you then loosen the joints one by one
each release comes with a full breath
you must wait until the intensity drops on its own
the last step is to state briefly what you were trying to protect
that need is most often the need to be heard
text: Begin by sitting somewhere no one is asking anything of you. Lay your palms flat on your thighs, let the air sink to your belly, and do not try to push it along. Then look for the exact place where the anger has settled: a heat climbing into the cheeks, a tightness under the ribs, a stiffness in the fists. Name that place silently, the way you name the rooms of an unfamiliar house you are discovering. Loosen the joints one after another, the jaw, the neck, the fingers, granting each a complete breath. Wait for the surge to subside of its own accord; it always does, whatever route it takes. Then say aloud, quietly, the shortest sentence that describes what you were trying to defend. Often it was neither an insult to avenge nor a position to defend, merely a need to be heard.

units: volunteers were kept awake for a whole night
the study combines brain observation with measurement of sweating
the brain area in charge of detecting danger becomes more reactive
its reaction lasts longer than usual
the cause put forward is weakened control by the frontal area
frontal activity drops as the sleep deficit grows
participants perceive expressionless faces as threatening
they react sharply to low-intensity sounds
the resulting irritability damages the next night and restarts the loop
text: A research team has just released the measurements taken from volunteers who were held awake through an entire night. The protocol pairs brain imaging with continuous readings of the skin's conductance. Sleep deprivation reaches first the deep structure charged with appraising threat: it fires harder, and above all far longer, at perfectly ordinary images. The cause lies in the loosened grip of the frontal region, whose activity falls off as the sleep debt mounts. The consequence can be read directly in behavior. The volunteers take blank faces for hostile ones, flinch at barely audible sounds, and report clammy hands that linger well past the session. The authors close on a return effect: the irritability that builds up wrecks the following night, so that the cycle feeds itself.

units: the waiting area was set up in a cramped passage
the seats faced each other in two lines
a swing door produced unpredictable bangs
the ceiling lighting was dull
users left more tense than they arrived
the seats were regrouped into clusters turned toward the windows
a soft floor covering was installed to soften noise
a device was added to the door to prevent banging
the expected waiting time is now displayed
signs of irritation have decreased since
text: The waiting area of the department took up a narrow corridor, furnished with two rows of seats set face to face. Whoever sat there had nowhere to look but at a stranger, a swing door banged at unpredictable intervals, and the ceiling fixture cast a wan and colorless light over everything. Users came in tense and went out more tightly wound still. The care team therefore reworked the layout. The rows were broken into clusters angled toward the windows, a soft covering was laid over the floor to swallow the sound of footsteps, and the door was fitted with a damper. A wall panel now shows the expected wait, which lifts the most trying uncertainty of all. Since then the staff have reported a clear drop in gestures of irritation, and a calmer welcome for appointments that run late.
