units: the text compares tracking by a digital tool with talking to a professional
the human exchange rests on a direct relationship
the professional notices cues the patient does not put into words
the digital tool captures neither shifts in the voice nor silences
the tool records assessments as data
the tool's strength is the reliability of its record keeping
human memory distorts and flattens recollections
the tool can reveal a pattern that went unnoticed
the author holds that the two approaches fill distinct roles
text: Should you hand your moods over to a digital journal? The question deserves better than the flat answers it tends to draw. A session with a practitioner rests on a living relationship: the voice wavers, a sigh escapes, and the listener catches what the account leaves out. Automated tracking hears neither the tremor of the voice nor the uneasy pause. It records ticked boxes and plotted curves. Its strength lies elsewhere, in a faithful memory, where recollection warps and flattens. A patient convinced he has been low for weeks opens the record and finds a pattern he had never noticed. The two devices, then, do not fill the same place. The journal measures and reminds; the conversation reads and accompanies. Setting one against the other means choosing between a scale and a gaze.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: she staffs a night-time telephone line
her post is in a room with no opening
she has held this job for many seasons
she names three qualities her role requires
the first is to bear the callers' silences
the second is to catch the audible signs of distress
the third is to detach once the shift is over
she walks home to shed what she has heard
a caller apologized for calling over a minor matter
she told him a minor matter deserved just as much attention
text: She takes calls on a crisis line late into the night, in a room without a window, and she has held the post for a good many seasons. Three qualities make the work, she says with a laugh. Patience comes first: she lets a silence stretch out, because a caller in tears needs someone who will not fill the emptiness for him. Then the ear: she catches a tremble in the voice, a breath held back, a sentence that breaks off at the same word every time. And distance last: when her shift is over she walks home and leaves behind what she has heard, or she would never get through the week. She recalls a caller, the other night, apologizing for troubling anyone over so small a matter. She answered that on this line, the smallest thing has the same right to be listened to as the worst.

units: the film begins with a long still image of an empty seat
this opening deliberately creates unease
the first part follows a family after a death
this part has neither narration nor added soundtrack
grief specialists speak in the middle part
the reviewer judges that these contributions weaken the film
the final part returns to the silence of the opening
the scene judged the most successful shows two relatives holding each other without speaking
the reviewer praises the absence of sentimentality
text: The film opens on a fixed shot of an empty chair, held long enough to leave the viewer uneasy. That opening choice announces everything that follows. The first stretch tracks a family through the weeks that follow a death, with no voice-over and no added score; you hear only household noise and, now and then, a stifled sob. The middle stretch shifts gear as grief specialists come in, and there the film loses its grip, because their explanations paper over what the faces had already said. The closing stretch returns to the silence of the beginning and delivers the truest scene of all, an awkward embrace between two relatives who cannot find their words. You leave the theater without any lift, and yet with the rare sense of having watched a sorrow handled without indulgence.

units: the writer explains to her addressee the reason for her long silence
she stopped replying after bad news
her withdrawal did not come from a lack of affection
every conversation forced her to go back over her pain
the isolation worsened her state more than the sadness itself
she has taken up walking in the evening again
the neighbors' questions still make her physically uncomfortable
she answers anyway and it is becoming easier
she invites her correspondent to get back in touch
text: I am writing because my silence over these past weeks must have hurt you, and you deserve to know where it came from. After the news you already know about, I stopped answering messages. It was not indifference. Every call required me to retell the story, and retelling it reopened the identical wound, so I went quiet, and that retreat cut me off far more surely than the grief itself. Here is what I understand now: the withdrawal, not the sorrow, is what made me so heavy to carry. I have started going out to walk again in the evenings. My face still burns when a neighbor stops to ask after me, but I answer, and each answer costs me a little less than the one before it. Write to me whenever you feel inclined. I promise nothing about cheerfulness. I do promise to answer the telephone.

units: a frequent question concerns whether slowed breathing really works
the explanation rests on a nerve linking the brain to the internal organs
lengthening the exhale activates that nerve
this activation lowers the heart rate
the protocols recommend a cycle longer than natural breathing
the exhale must last at least as long as the inhale
many patients give up after a failed first attempt
the initial failure is explained by breathing too deeply
you must reduce the volume taken in while stretching the cycle
it is advised to practice outside of tense situations
text: One question keeps coming back in consultations: does slowing the breath really settle anything, or is it a comforting belief? The mechanism is established. A drawn-out exhale stimulates the nerve that runs from the brainstem to the inner organs, and that stimulation brings the heart rate down. Second question: what pace? The accepted protocols stretch the cycle well past its spontaneous rhythm, giving the exhale a length at least equal to the inhale. Third question: what about failure? Many patients give up because a first attempt sharpens the alarm instead of easing it. The trouble comes from unintended overbreathing, brought on by pulling in far too much air. The fix is to shrink each breath while drawing it out, and to practice in calm before reaching for it under strain.

units: an acquaintance of the narrator records her inner states in a notebook
she writes down the moral exhaustion that arrives at the end of the week with no clear cause
she spots her irritation in the way she slams the cupboards shut
she also notes the worry that comes before a dreaded exchange
she marks down feeling relieved, since that state fades from memory too quickly
she records the embarrassment that reddens her cheeks after an unfortunate remark
the narrator asks her what this record is good for
the woman answers that she wants to recognize herself, not reform herself
she claims that naming an inner state by its name already calms it
text: A friend told me the other evening that she keeps a notebook of her moods, and she walked me through what goes into it. Weariness comes first, the kind that drops on her at the end of the week for no reason she can name and leaves her wanting nothing. Then irritation, which she catches in the way she slams the cupboard doors shut. Worry gets a line of its own, the sort that circles the kitchen with her before a conversation she dreads. She writes down relief as well, she said, because that one slips out of memory as soon as the fear lifts. Last comes embarrassment, the prickle in her cheeks after she says something clumsy. I asked her what the whole list was good for. She said she is not trying to correct herself, only to recognize herself, and that putting a name to a feeling usually takes the sting out of it.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the way low spirits are accounted for has changed over the generations
the earliest healers put dejection down to an imbalance of the blood
they treated that dejection by drawing blood off
a later stage consisted in shutting the sick away from public view
that confinement was not aimed at curing them
physicians then began gathering and writing down what their patients told them
the houses of care were fitted with gardens, walking paths and workshops
it was assumed at the time that steady occupation settled the mind
conversation became a means of care in its turn
today's listening rooms carry the mark of those successive stages
text: The words people use for low spirits have shifted from one generation to the next, and the shifts fall into stages that can be read in order. The earliest healers filed dark moods under disorders of the blood and drew blood off to correct them. Confinement came next: the afflicted were shut away, not to be cured but to be kept out of common sight. A generation later, physicians began listening to what their patients told them and copying the complaints into ledgers. Houses of care were then given gardens, walking paths and workshops, on the assumption that steady occupation settled a restless mind. Closer to our own time, talk itself turned into a remedy, and listening became a craft that had to be taught. Every one of those stages has left its mark on the rooms where people are heard today.

units: a grievance that repeats and is never spoken leaves a lasting imprint on memory
silence turns into a store where what went unsaid piles up
that pile breeds a stubborn grudge
the grudge makes old memories sharper than they truly were
the person replays the scene in his mind through the night
that chewing burns the energy meant for the people close to him
a quiet withdrawal from company sets in afterwards
the solitude allows no contradiction and so strengthens the grievance
getting out of the circle means saying the thing aloud, clumsily if need be
text: An annoyance that keeps coming back and is never spoken wears a groove into memory. Silence feels comfortable at first, then turns into a storeroom where everything left unsaid gets piled up. Out of that pile grows a stubborn grudge, and the grudge lends old scenes an edge the events themselves never had. At night the sleeper goes back over them, stages the exchange again, supplies the lines that should have been delivered. The chewing wears him down, since the mind spends on an absent opponent the energy the people close to him deserve. Withdrawal follows, quietly: an invitation is turned down, a call is cut short, solitude gets chosen and blamed on tiredness. And because solitude leaves nothing to contradict the grievance, it confirms it instead of putting it out. Getting free means saying the thing aloud, clumsily if need be.

units: a trainer in charge of a night team described this case in a report
the verbal clashes happened mostly at the close of the shift
a look at the data ruled out production load as the main cause
the busiest stretches fell earlier in the shift
the tensions broke out after the second scheduled break
alertness and resistance to frustration both drop at that moment
the handover meeting was moved to the opening of the shift
its length was cut and an order of speaking was imposed
a form on inner state, filled in on arrival and on leaving, served as the indicator
the reported incidents fell after one full cycle
text: A trainer responsible for a night team wrote the following case into an internal report. Verbal incidents clustered at the close of the shift, where operators lost their tempers with one another again and again. A look at the logs ruled out production load as the main driver, since the busiest stretches fell much earlier. What the records did show was that exchanges soured after the second scheduled break, the point where alertness drops and tolerance for frustration goes with it. The protocol adopted moved the handover meeting to the opening of the shift, cut its length, and imposed a fixed order of speaking. A mood form, filled in on arrival and again on leaving, supplied the measure. One full cycle later the reported incidents had fallen, and the team described a calm that held.

units: two calming methods must be told apart before being used against a surge of anxiety
the first method means controlling the breath while seated, one hand on the belly
the breathing out must last longer than the breathing in, and the cycle repeats
this method takes hold very quickly and calls for no equipment
its effect fades as soon as the irritation shows up again
the second method means writing the fear down and setting beside it what makes it unlikely
the page must be read again at the end of the day
this second method asks for more effort and comforts less on the spot
its benefit, on the other hand, holds for several weeks
combining the breath for the emergency and the writing for the underlying trouble is advised
text: Two calming methods deserve to be told apart before either is turned on a rising wave of anxiety. The first works on the breath. Sit down, rest one hand on the belly, draw air in slowly, then let it out over a longer count, and repeat the cycle until the pulse eases. Its strength is speed: it takes hold within moments and calls for no equipment at all. Its weakness is how long the effect holds, because it fades the moment the irritation comes back. The second method works on words. Write down the exact fear, set beside it whatever makes that outcome unlikely, and read the page again at the end of the day. It asks for more effort and gives less comfort on the spot, yet what it gives holds for weeks. In practice, pair them: breath for the emergency, writing for the underlying trouble.

units: a place for people to be heard has been fitted out in a former storage building
its staff set out several uses of the site
the first use is the walk-in welcome, with no appointment and no paperwork
group meetings bring together visitors touched by the same ordeal
those shared ordeals include the death of someone close, a break-up or the loss of a job
a movement workshop lets tension come loose through walking and stretching
a fourth use consists in sending the heaviest cases on to a specialist
the manager reports that attendance has doubled since the opening
half of the visitors come back again
text: A listening center fitted out inside a former storage building has opened to the public, and the staff there set out several distinct uses for it. The first is the walk-in welcome: anyone can push the door open and talk to a trained listener, with no file to fill in and nothing to justify. The second covers the group meetings, which bring together people carrying the same ordeal, the death of someone close, a break-up, or the loss of a job. The third is a movement workshop, where tension is worked loose by walking and stretching rather than by telling a story. The fourth use, a quieter one, is referral: distress too heavy for a short talk gets passed on to a practitioner. The manager says attendance has doubled since the doors opened, and that half of those who come come back.

units: a child goes down in the middle of the room and the noise takes over the home
the fit starts with a rigid back, balled fists and a locked jaw
the first sob cuts the breathing off
an odd hush follows that first sob
the crying then carries on in wave after wave
the slightest clumsy word sets the wave going again
the face turns red and the hair sticks to the temples
the calm arrives with nothing you can point to and the hiccups come further apart
the child ends up slumped against a shoulder, worn out and surprised at the quiet
he then asks for water as if nothing had happened
text: You have seen it happen: a child goes down in the middle of the living room and the noise takes over the whole place. It starts with the back going rigid, the fists balled, the jaw locked. Then comes the first sob, huge, cutting the breath off and leaving an odd hush behind it. After that the crying settles into waves, up and down and up again the second anyone says the wrong thing. The face turns red, the hair sticks to the temples, the hands grab at whatever cloth is near. Then, with nothing you can point to having changed, the swell weakens. The breath breaks into hiccups that come further and further apart. The shoulders drop at last. The child ends up slumped against a shoulder, worn out, warm, half surprised at the quiet, and asks for a glass of water as if none of it had happened.

units: people are now required to keep an even mood at all times
that demand delivers the opposite of what it aims at
a dark inner state reads as a flaw of character
whoever feels one therefore hides it from those around him
by hiding it, he loses the sharing that would have eased it
the loneliness that results adds still more to the load
the inner state sets hard instead of running its course
a shame at failing then comes on top, heavier than the original hurt
this chain explains the growing number of consultations begun too late
the writer judges it cheaper to let sadness be spoken than to treat it afterwards
text: People are now expected to hold an even mood whatever happens, and the demand delivers the opposite of what it sets out to do. A dark feeling reads as a flaw of character, so whoever carries one keeps it hidden from the people around him. Kept hidden, it gets shared with nobody at all, and the one mechanism that might have eased it goes missing. The loneliness that follows adds to a weight already heavy, so the feeling hardens and settles in rather than running its course. Then comes the shame of not coping with it, heavier by far than the hurt it grew out of. That whole chain is why so many people reach a consulting room late, once the trouble has thickened past what ordinary talk can undo. Letting sadness be spoken aloud would cost a great deal less than treating it after seasons of silence.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman who runs a bookbinding workshop did not take up the trade out of a liking for the material
she spoke little and went to pieces in front of a counter clerk
she called off appointments out of fear of being looked at
her life had narrowed until it fit inside two streets
an acquaintance offered her to come and sew sections with no obligation to speak
the change came from the work of the hands itself
her voice came loose while her hands were busy
she first served customers in short sentences, then explained her craft
she ended up training an apprentice
she says the fear is still there but no longer decides how her weeks are spent
text: The woman who runs the bookbinding workshop at the back of the courtyard did not take up the trade out of any love of paper. She spoke little, went to pieces at a counter, and called off appointments rather than be looked at. Her life had narrowed until it fit inside two streets. One season an acquaintance offered her a bench and some sections to sew, with no requirement to say a word to anyone. She stitched whole evenings without lifting her head, and that suited her. What changed things was the work of the hands: with them busy, her voice came loose before she noticed. She answered customers in short sentences at first, then explained what she was doing, then trained an apprentice. The fear has not gone, she says, and it still meets her at a stranger, but it no longer decides how her weeks are spent.

units: two instruments for gauging mood are in use in clinical practice
the first instrument is a short questionnaire the patient fills in himself
its items ask about the week just gone
its internal consistency holds up and the form takes little attention to complete
that lightness allows the measure to be repeated
it is hit by a desirability bias that flatters the profile the respondent reports
the second instrument is a structured interview run by a trained professional
its scoring rests on observed signs as much as on what the person says
it stands up better to the bias but costs a great deal of time and depends on the rater's training
the writer recommends the questionnaire for close follow-up and the interview for settling a diagnosis
text: Two instruments for gauging mood are in circulation in clinical practice, and comparing them repays a close look. The first is a short questionnaire the patient fills in alone, its items asking about the week just gone. Internal consistency holds up well, and the form takes so little attention to complete that the measure can be repeated as often as the follow-up requires. Against that, it carries a desirability bias: respondents paint a rosier picture than they live. The second is a structured interview run by a trained clinician, scored on observed signs as much as on what is said aloud. It stands up better to the bias, but the time it eats makes it expensive, and its reliability rests on how well the rater was drilled. For close monitoring, take the questionnaire; for a diagnosis, the interview.

units: the writer answers a close person who was worried about how she was doing
a move to a new home came before a stretch of broken sleep
the ringing of the phone made her body clench
someone she knows suggested she write her fears down at the end of the day
she thought the advice was pointless before she followed it
the writing brought up a recurring fear of being left behind
a specialist tied that anxious bond to her early years
she now tells the people close to her instead of shutting herself away
text: You asked in your note whether I was doing any better, so let me start where it started. The week we moved, sleep came apart, and every time the phone rang my shoulders locked up. A woman I know told me to write down, each evening, whatever had tightened my throat that day. The advice struck me as pointless. I did it anyway. Ten evenings in, the same fear kept surfacing on the page: that the people I love would leave me behind. A psychologist told me this anxious kind of attachment takes shape early, in the first years, and that it eases once you dare to ask for help. So now I tell my friends when I am sinking, instead of vanishing without a word. It still costs me something, I will not pretend otherwise. Last night I laughed out loud without watching myself do it. Write soon, and tell me about your week.

units: a mental health specialist takes questions about thoughts that keep repeating
the brain meets a threat to a bond almost the way it meets a threat to the body
the scene is played again in the hope of finding a way out
the replay keeps the alarm on rather than settling it
the alarm in turn sets the repeating thoughts going again
sleep breaks up because the inner watch does not stop at night
the people nearby tire of the same complaint and pull back
that withdrawal deepens the loneliness of the one who broods
the specialist advises writing the whole episode out a single time
text: What becomes of a slight you cannot put down? We put the question to a clinical psychologist who studies thinking that will not stop repeating. Her answer starts with the brain, which meets a threat to a bond almost the way it meets a threat to the body, and so it runs the scene again, hoping this time to reach a way out. Does the replay help? Not at all. It keeps the alarm switched on, and the alarm sends the thoughts round once more. Why does sleep break up? Because the watchman inside never goes off duty at night. And the people nearby? They hear the same complaint until they are worn thin, and they pull back, which leaves the brooder more alone than before. Her advice is to write the episode out end to end, one single evening, then close the notebook. A thought put into sentences stops turning on itself.

units: a young girl admits she cannot put what she feels into words
her aunt does not push and pours her something hot to drink
the aunt says she kept quiet at the same age out of reserve
the aunt holds that such silence shuts a person in rather than shielding her
the girl is afraid her words will make her mother cry
the aunt suggests locating the sensation instead of naming the sorrow
the girl points to two places on her neck
her breathing loosens once she has described them
they agree on a flat hand on the table as an arranged signal
the mother sits down beside her and asks nothing
text: The girl said she could not put what she felt into words, and she said it to the carpet rather than to her aunt. Her aunt let it sit for a while and poured out something hot to drink, then admitted that at that age she had held her tongue as well, out of reserve. Silence, she said, shields nobody at all. It only shuts you in alone. Her niece answered that words felt too heavy, and that hers would make her mother cry. So the aunt offered a way round: do not name the sorrow, find where it lodges. The girl pointed to her throat, then to the back of her neck, and her breathing loosened once she had said it. They settled on a quiet sign. A flat hand on the table would mean it was time to talk. That evening the hand came down, and her mother sat beside her and asked nothing at all.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: with no instruments to hand, early practitioners went by what patients told them
their approach joined long listening to the matching of similar cases
later practitioners took readings from the body
those readings included the beat of the heart and the length of sleep
the early approach caught the fine grain but missed the regularities
the instrument based approach caught the regularities but lost the fine grain
a feeling pushed out of awareness yields no measurable sign
the two approaches were later brought together
each one covers what the other cannot see
text: Before recording instruments were available, physicians described disorders of mood from what patients told them and nothing else. They listened at length, then set one case beside another to see what held across both. Clinicians trained later worked from the body instead, taking readings of the heartbeat, of the sweat on the skin, of how long a night of sleep ran. The older way caught the fine grain and missed the regularity; the instrument based way found regularities and let the fine grain slip. The split follows from the object itself. A feeling pushed out of awareness leaves no reading behind, while a reaction of the body writes itself down. The two traditions were eventually braided together: the patient is questioned while his inner reactions are tracked, and the two records are then compared. Neither one replaces the other, and each covers what its neighbor cannot see.

units: three kinds of signs give away that someone is uncomfortable
the first sign lies in the posture, with the shoulders drawn in
a hand carried toward the face goes with that posture
the second sign lies in the voice, whose pace weakens
the third sign lies in the eyes, which settle nowhere
discomfort bears on the picture one presents to others
fear, by contrast, bears on a danger coming from outside
shame stands apart because it runs longer and cuts deeper
an observer who notices can soften his voice and look away
text: Three kinds of signs give away that the person across from you is uncomfortable. The first lies in the posture: the shoulders draw in, the chin drops, and a hand rises toward the face as though to cover it. The second lies in the voice, whose pace weakens, whose sentences break off, and which loses its footing. The third lies in the eyes, which slide away, come back in short touches, then settle nowhere. What separates these signals from those of fear is their target, since discomfort bears on the picture one presents to others, whereas fear answers to a danger coming from outside. They differ from shame as well, which runs longer and cuts deeper and drives a person to withdraw entirely. Reading them serves the observer above all: he can soften his voice, look away, leave a gap in the exchange. Such restraint often makes the conversation bearable for the one who feels exposed.

units: a singer who is not a professional auditions in a borrowed hall
he had rehearsed for several weeks
a wave of dizziness took him as soon as he reached the platform
his hands went cold and his voice missed the opening
the panel granted him a second try
that second attempt came out worse than the first
a musician suggested he stand with his back to the audience
the performance then came out true and easy
afterward he took the ending again facing the room
he puts his trouble down to being watched rather than to the singing
text: An amateur singer turned up for an audition in a hall lent out by a society of musicians. He had rehearsed the piece for weeks and believed he was ready. The moment he reached the platform, the room tilted under him. The ceiling seemed to come down, his hands went cold, and his voice missed the opening note. He asked to start over, and the panel let him. The second attempt came out worse than the first. One of the players at the keyboard then suggested he sing with his back to the room. He laughed, and then he tried it. The piece came out whole, true, very nearly easy. They asked him afterward to turn round and take the last verse again, and he sang it without a tremor. What had frightened him, he decided, was never the singing but the eyes on him, and a tiny detour had been enough to disarm it.

units: the first step is to spot the bodily signal of anxiety
putting a word on the feeling takes some of its force away
you have to write down precisely the outcome you dread
you then set the harm you imagine against how likely it really is
stretching the outbreath slows the beat of the heart
arriving early spares you the tension of a room already full
planting your feet on the floor tells the brain the body is steady
asking for a drink breaks the runaway if panic takes hold
text: Start by catching the moment your stomach knots up before a meeting, because a feeling with a word on it loses some of its force. Then put down in your notebook exactly what you dread: being cut off, coming across as useless, sitting through an awkward silence. Write the harm you picture, and beside it the odds that it happens. The gap will jump out at you. Breathe after that, stretching the air on the way out, since it is the outbreath and not the intake that slows the heart. Come early, because walking into a room already full winds you up, while taking your seat before the others lets the tension drop away. Through the meeting, keep both feet planted flat on the floor, since that contact tells the brain the body is steady. And if panic climbs anyway, ask for water. The gesture gives you something to hold and breaks the runaway.

units: a place offering psychological support opened on a street of shops
the men who came in flared up during the first session
those men did not turn up for the sessions that followed
the team first put these departures down to a lack of willingness
the front room could be seen from the street through a pane of glass
being exposed to onlookers turned discomfort into aggression
the entrance was moved round to the courtyard side
a curtain went up and the lighting was brought down
the number of people breaking off treatment fell by half
the director advises studying the place before explaining a behavior
text: In an old quarter, a house offering support opened at the end of a lane lined with shops. The staff kept meeting the same wall. Men who came in for help flared up during the first interview, and then never turned up again. The team put it down at first to a lack of willingness. Closer watching told another story: the front room was glazed toward the lane, which left visitors on show to anyone walking past, and their discomfort came out as anger. What worked was a change of building before it was a change of treatment. The entrance was moved round to the inner courtyard, a heavy curtain went up, the lighting was brought down. Within one season, the number of people breaking off after the first appointment had fallen by half. The director repeats the lesson to her trainees: before you read a behavior, study the place that produced it.

units: a waiting room stands apart from the other spaces in the building
its walls are a muted green against a very bright corridor
the seats in it are turned toward one another
in the corridor the seats are lined up along the wall
a thick floor covering smothers the sound of footsteps
the hard floor of the entrance, by contrast, throws the noise back
worn magazines lie on a low piece of furniture
those who arrive show a sharp restlessness in voice and gesture
they leave the room walking at a steadier pace
text: The waiting room at that practice is like no other space in the building. Its walls carry a muted green, while the corridor beside it snaps with white. In here the armchairs turn a little toward one another, as though they expected a conversation. Out there the chairs run flat along the wall. A thick rug swallows the sound of footsteps, whereas the hard floor of the entrance throws every heel back at you. On the low table lie tired magazines, scruffier than the ones at the front desk, and perhaps it is that untidiness that reassures. Those who come in are often keyed up, the voice pitched high, the hands quick. They go out again at a steadier pace, the jaw unclenched. The room cures nothing, of course. Like an airlock, it only prepares the crossing from one inner state to another.

units: the writer disputes the idea that sadness is a fault to be put right
an emotion reports what holds value for the person feeling it
the pace of digital exchange makes a lasting mood look suspect
that pressure leads people to dread their own inner slowness
methods of assessment favor whatever can be counted
inner experience therefore escapes the studies, since it cannot be coded
a feeling pushed down comes back as irritability or exhaustion
the writer grants that pain which drags on calls for treatment
treating ordinary sorrow as an illness robs people of the words to speak of themselves
text: We ought to stop handling sadness as a breakdown in need of repair. First point: an emotion is no fault in the manufacture, but a report on what holds value for the person feeling it. Second point: the pace our screens demand casts suspicion on any mood that lasts, so that people end up dreading their own inner slowness. Third point: protocols of assessment favor whatever can be counted, and inner experience, hard to code, drops out of the studies altogether. Fourth point: a feeling pushed down does not fade away, it comes back elsewhere, as irritability or as a tiredness that will not lift. Someone will object that pain which drags on calls for treatment, and the objection is sound. But to fold ordinary sorrow into illness is to rob everyone of the words for saying what they are living through.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the main figure answers calls from people in distress
early in her career she raised the volume of her voice
that approach pushed callers to break off the exchange
she completely overhauled her way of speaking
she now leaves pauses and slows her delivery
she repeats the last word the caller has said
the caller's breathing eventually falls in with hers
her colleagues have taken up the same method
she says this work has changed how she hears the people around her
text: The woman on the helpline takes calls from people in trouble, and she keeps her voice low on purpose. Early on she did the opposite: she pushed her voice up to cover the panic at the other end. It backfired. Callers stiffened, cut her off, hung up before she got anywhere. So she turned the whole thing around. Now she leaves silences, she slows down, she takes the last word a caller says and hands it back. Little by little the breathing on the line falls in with hers, and the tightness on the line eases without either of them naming it. She shrugs when she explains this, as if it were plain. Her colleagues copied her once they saw their own calls holding longer. One thing still makes her smile: the work taught her to hear the people at home, and she had thought she knew them already.

units: the piece passes judgment on an exhibition devoted to the emotions
the first part of the route piles up video installations
that accumulation wears out the attention of visitors
the emotions are presented there in a distant and didactic way
the second part offers a space with no screen at all
there you listen to accounts of grief spoken by strangers
the public slows down there and shows feeling
the final stage invites you to set down on paper the emotion hardest to name
the reviewer advises walking the place in the opposite direction
text: You come out of this exhibition about the emotions with mixed feelings. The trouble starts with the layout. Screen after screen, room after room, the video installations pile up, and the visitor, worn out well before the halfway mark, ends up skimming past every one of them. Anger, shame and joy get the same cool, explanatory treatment, so nothing ever stirs. The people who built it seem to have worked that out, because the second half pulls the show back. One bare room, no screen anywhere, asks you to listen while strangers describe a grief. The quiet in that room does the work on its own, and the crowd slows down, lingers, doubles back. The last stage goes further still: you write on a slip the emotion you find hardest to name. Worth the trip, then, provided you begin at the end and walk it backward.

units: the addressee has asked a question about the kinship between two feelings
the writer describes fear as a pressure applied to the back of the neck
fear dampens the palms and shortens the breath
grief is compared to a wet weight that covers you
fear pushes you to move whereas grief holds you still
both feelings slip away when you try to look at them head on
both settle when you put them into words in front of someone
the writer explains in this way why he writes so often
the writer says he prefers an awkward sentence to a piece of advice
text: Your question has stayed with me since your letter came: is grief anything like fear? I turned it over by the window, and here is what I think. Fear is a hand laid on the back of your neck. It grips, it presses, it wants you up and moving. It leaves your palms damp and your breath short. Grief presses nothing. It settles. It lies over your chest like a soaked blanket and asks you to stop. One speeds you up, the other slows you down, and that is the clearest line between them. On one point, though, they are twins, and that point has occupied me all winter. Both slip away the moment you look straight at them, and both loosen their hold once you say them out loud to somebody. That is why I write to you so often. Write back. Your clumsiest sentence steadies me better than advice.

units: specialists draw a line between an emotion and a mood
three criteria underpin that distinction
an emotion is brief whereas a mood stretches out further
an emotion relates to a target you can pick out
a mood has no addressee you can assign to it
the third criterion concerns the traces you can observe in the body
you cannot shut down the firing of an emotion by will
you can on the other hand shape how it shows
fear sends blood toward the muscles to make the body ready to act
text: Is an emotion the same thing as a mood? The question comes up again and again. Specialists say no, and they set out three criteria. The first is duration: an emotion flares and dies away fast, while a mood stretches over a far wider span. The second is the object. An emotion aims at something you can point to, whereas a mood drifts with nothing to land on and nobody to fasten itself to. The third is the mark left in the body, which shows up in heart rate, sweating and muscle tension. Can an emotion be shut down by willpower? The answer has to be qualified. You can shape how it shows, you cannot cancel the moment it fires. And what is fear good for? It gets the body ready to act by pushing blood toward the muscles, which is why your hands clench and your throat goes tight without your ever deciding on it.

units: the practitioner opens the session with a harmless question about meals
the young boy claims he cannot remember
the young boy closes up and folds his arms
the practitioner switches subject and mentions the sound of the rain
the young boy admits that he dreads family meals
he explains that the people at the table stare at him
the practitioner asks him which seat he would rather take
he points out the far end of the table, next to the door
the practitioner suggests he raise the subject at home
he ends up agreeing and announces that he will come back
text: The session opened on a question that seemed to lead nowhere: the psychologist asked the boy what he had eaten the evening before. He said he could not remember, then went quiet and folded his arms tight across his chest. She let it go without pressing him and talked instead about the rain hitting the window and the color the sky had taken. After a while he said that family meals frightened him, because everyone around the table watched him the whole time, from the first dish to the last. She asked where he would sit if the choice were his. He said he would take the far end of the table, right beside the door. She suggested he bring it up at home, in his own words. He hesitated, and then he agreed. On his way out he said he would be back, and he smiled without turning around.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: healers of long ago put the states of the soul down to inner fluids
that theory appealed because it offered a remedy people could carry out
low spirits were treated through diet or through the drawing of blood
one failure after another weakened the belief
direct observation took over from the theory
some healers noted identical signs for fear and for rage
they tied those states to the nerves rather than to a fluid
suffering of the mind stopped being seen as a stain to be driven out
out of that reversal came the idea that speech given a hearing can heal
text: Long before anyone thought to measure, healers explained the states of the soul by inner fluids that had to be brought back into balance. The theory held because it handed people something to do: if low spirits came from an excess, then a change of diet or an opened vein ought to drain it off. One failure after another wore the belief thin, and looking closely took over from reasoning. Physicians noticed that fear and rage left the same marks on patients who had nothing else in common, and they concluded that such states belonged to the nerves and not to any liquid. The consequence ran deep. Suffering of the mind stopped being handled as a stain to be flushed out, and people began to question it instead. Out of that turn grew the idea that speech, carefully heard, could heal.

units: speaking in front of an audience speeds up the heart and dampens the hands
the voice turns shaky in that situation
fear itself is not to blame since it makes the body ready to act
the trouble comes from the thoughts added on top of the fear
you picture the humiliation ahead and watch for unfriendly faces
that watching drives the alarm higher still
the first countermove is to make the out-breath longer than the in-breath
that lengthening settles the pace of the heart
the second countermove is to put your attention on a receptive listener
moving attention outward breaks the vicious circle
text: You know the feeling. You stand up to speak in front of a room, your heart starts pounding, your palms turn cold and damp, and your voice comes out with a wobble in it. Fear is not the culprit here, since fear gets the body ready to move. What sinks you is everything you stack on top of it. You picture yourself making a fool of yourself, you scan the room for a hard face, and the alarm inside you climbs another notch. Two small moves get you out. Breathe out longer than you breathe in, because a long exhale pulls the heartbeat down. Then look after somebody other than yourself: find the most attentive face in the room and speak to that person. Turn your attention outward and the loop has nothing left to feed on. Your hands may still shake a little. You will get to the end anyway.

units: two men have been waiting for the same medical test since the same hour
the first reads a magazine and mentions his vegetable patch
the second checks the display board over and over
the second half rises each time a name is called out
both men say they feel the same worry
the first tells himself he will soon be given some information
the second expects the worst outcome
a nurse predicts that the second will walk out wrung dry
the nurse reckons that a word can turn the experience of waiting around
text: Two men have been sitting in the same waiting room since the same hour, booked in for the very same test. One leafs through a magazine with his shoulders loose and says he is thinking about his vegetable patch. The other keeps checking the board above the door, and he half rises every time a name carries down the corridor. Ask them and both will tell you they feel the same dread. The difference sits somewhere else entirely. One is telling himself he will soon know where he stands, the other is telling himself he will soon hear the worst. A nurse who has watched this play out for years says the second man will walk out wrung dry, while the first will walk out merely relieved. She adds that a single sentence, dropped at the right moment, can tip a wait from one side to the other.

units: get hold of a thin notebook and keep it on you for a week
each evening you write three lines and no more
the first line names the dominant feeling with a precise term
you set aside vague terms in favor of exact words
the second line gives the place in the body where the feeling showed up
the third line names the event that came before the feeling
you forbid yourself any rereading before the week is out
rereading too soon bends what you noticed
at the end you spread the pages out to spot what keeps returning
the exercise is run again in the following season
text: Pick up a thin notebook, the kind that slides into a back pocket, and keep it on you for a whole week. In the evening, open it on your knees and write three lines, no more than that. On the first, name the feeling that took over, using the sharpest word you can reach for: not bad, but tightness, or heaviness, or lift. On the second, write where in the body it settled, whether the throat, the neck or the stomach. On the third, name whatever came just before it, even if the link looks thin to you. Read nothing back until the week is out, because rereading too soon bends what you saw. On the last evening, spread the pages in front of you and look for what keeps returning. You will find repeats that memory alone would never have held. Close the notebook without judging it, and run the whole thing again next season.

units: a research team ran a protocol in two similar hospital wards
the first stage consisted of measuring without stepping in
the measures covered the pulse and the sweating of the nursing staff
peaks were recorded at the moment of the spoken handovers between teams
the second stage imposed a short break before every handover
the instruction asked for the breathing to be slowed during that break
the third stage set the readings of the two wards against each other
the ward given the break showed better pulse variability
the authors stay cautious because the load on each team differs
text: A research team started its protocol at the beginning of the cold season, in two hospital wards chosen for how closely they matched. The first stage recorded heart rate and sweating in the nursing staff across their shifts, with nobody stepping in to change anything. When the readings came back, the spikes clustered around one moment: the spoken handover between teams. The second stage put a short, compulsory pause before every handover, with instructions to slow the breathing while it lasted. The third stage set the figures from the two wards side by side. The gap widened week after week, and the ward with the pause showed steadier heart rate variability along with fewer damp hands. The authors stop short of claiming much, since the two teams do not carry the same load.

units: the heart races and the hands sweat before speaking in front of a group
the person going through it believes she is fragile and judges herself clumsy
the fear pushes her to avoid meetings where she would have to speak
avoidance strengthens the fear instead of reducing it
breathing out more slowly than you breathe in slows the heartbeat
rehearsing the opening line aloud at home helps with getting started
it is better to put up with the early trembling than to fight it
a relaxed friend can serve as a practice audience
the panic wears down after several repeated attempts
text: You know the feeling. Your heart takes off, your palms go damp, and your throat locks shut right before the first word to a room full of people. Anyone who goes through it decides she is fragile, that she comes across as clumsy, and soon she is ducking every meeting where somebody might call on her. That is where the trap shuts. Dodge the room and the fear grows instead of shrinking. What gets you out is dull and practical. Breathe from the belly, letting the air out more slowly than you drew it in, and the heartbeat settles on its own. Say your opening line aloud at home until your mouth already knows the road. Let the early trembling happen rather than wrestling it down. A friend who is easy company makes a fine practice audience. After enough tries, the panic simply wears out.

units: two opposite positions go around about the place of feelings in a team
the first one demands complete restraint and admits nothing but arguments
the second one prizes the open expression of anger and grief
imposed silence sends the unease around underground
compulsory restraint leaves colleagues quicker to take offence
expression without limits wears out the people listening
a middle way is to name your own state without demanding that it be repaired
this balance sounds obvious to state but has to be learned
text: Raise the place of feelings in a team and two camps start shouting past each other. The first wants them held back altogether: the steady professional parks his moods at the door and brings nothing to the table but arguments. The second cheers for saying it plainly, anger out loud, grief owned in front of colleagues. Each camp is right about its rival and wrong about itself. Enforced silence does not clear the unease away, it drives it underground, where it spreads and where the mildest remark leaves everyone quick to take offence. Pouring it out without limit wears the listeners down until no one is listening at all. What holds is narrower than either: name what you feel without asking anyone to repair it. Saying you are worn thin obliges no colleague to console you. Easy to state, slow to learn.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the listener works evenings with a headset on a helpline
the people who call stay anonymous
her voice stays low and never rises
her first quality is putting up with long silences
her second quality is holding on to details given early in the call
her third quality is a welcoming tone that promises nothing
one caller who said little took an hour before producing a whole sentence
she will never know what became of the people she listened to
text: The voice comes first, low and level, and it never climbs, not even when the line is jammed. She spends her evenings at a helpline with a headset on, taking calls from strangers in pieces who give no name at any point. Three gifts hold the work together. Patience is the first: she lets silences run on where anyone else would hurry to fill them. Memory for small things is the second; a dog mentioned in the opening minute comes back out of her mouth much later. The third is warmth without false closeness, a tone that steadies while promising nothing at all. She tells of one guarded caller who took a whole hour before a full sentence arrived. What became of him she will never learn. That is the heaviest part of the work: shelter for a single evening, and then the line goes dead.

units: the program under review is made of four successive stages
the opening session serves to list what sets the anxiety off
the self-rating scale stays understandable with no training behind it
the breathing work locks every participant to one and the same pace
that single pace ignores the differences in lung capacity
graded exposure is the best designed part of the program
the ladder of feared situations is built together with the patient
the last session handles relapse prevention on a single sheet
the final judgement is mixed: rigorous middle, rigid opening, rushed ending
text: The program under review runs through four stages, and each earns a verdict of its own. It opens with a structured interview in which the practitioner lists whatever sets the anxiety off. That part is sound: the questions stay open, and the self-rating scale reads clearly to someone with no training behind him. The breathing work that follows is harder to defend, since the instruction locks every participant to one pace while lung capacity plainly differs from person to person. Stage three, graded exposure, is where the design holds best: the ladder of feared situations gets built with the patient rather than handed to him. The closing session then disposes of relapse prevention on one photocopied sheet. The judgement comes out mixed, rigorous through the middle, rigid at the door and rushed at the exit.

units: the writer is explaining a long absence he has never justified clearly
the death of his sister happened a short while ago
the grief did not fade the way he had assumed it would
the writer turned inattentive and let files slip his mind
he would read the same page over without holding on to any of it
this scattering damaged the quality of his reports
out of that grew a sense of being no longer capable
that sense led him to turn down the invitations of his team
his silence was taken for contempt
he is starting treatment and wants to come back in stages
text: I am writing to you about my long absence, which I have never explained with any clarity. My sister died a short while ago, and the effect on me was not the one I had assumed. I expected the grief to settle in and then thin out; it took quite another road. First it left me inattentive. Files slipped my mind, and I would read the same page over and over without holding on to a line of it. My reports suffered for that scattering, and out of the poor work grew a conviction that I was no longer capable. From the conviction came avoidance: I stopped answering the invitations of my team, and the silence was read as contempt. I can see how opaque that chain must have looked from where you sit. I have begun treatment with a specialist, and I would like to resume my duties in stages.

units: the question raised is whether sleep can be learned when the mind will not settle
insomnia feeds itself through the dread of not sleeping
the long waking hours then prove that dread right
the first piece of advice is to cut down the time spent in bed
the window is then widened step by step once falling asleep turns quick again
leaving the bed when the night drags on is advised
this instruction keeps the bed from standing for a struggle
the effect of screens is real but it is overstated
a racing mind counts for more than screens do
text: One question keeps coming back in consultations: can a person learn to sleep when the mind refuses to switch off? The accepted answer opens on an unwelcome note. Insomnia feeds itself. Dread of a sleepless night keeps you awake, and the waking hours then prove the dread right. So what is to be done? The first piece of advice startles people, since it asks for less time in bed rather than more. You narrow the window until falling asleep turns quick again, then widen it step by step. A second question comes up often: get out of bed when the night drags on? Yes, say the protocols, so that the bed stops standing for a struggle. And screens? Their effect is real but overstated; a racing mind weighs heavier. One rule holds throughout: a restless head settles better upright than lying down.

units: the older brother tells his sister he cannot make sense of their mother
their mother flares up over a tiny mishap but stays calm at bad news
the sister describes their father as working the other way around
the father says nothing during a crisis and turns pleasant once things are quiet
the mother lets the anger out fast and forgets it fast
the father stores it up and then caves in weeks later
the brother finds the loud way more hurtful because the words land straight
the sister prefers that way because you know where you stand
both of them admit they were handed a model without choosing it
text: The older brother told his sister he had given up making sense of their mother. She would shout over a spilled glass, he said, and then take bad news without a flicker. His sister answered that their father ran the other way around: not a word out of him while things fell apart, then all charm once the house went quiet. One lets it out fast and comes down fast, she said, and forgets it within the hour. The other stores it, holds on to it, and caves in weeks later out of nowhere. The brother argued that the loud way cuts deeper, because the words land straight in your face. His sister thought the opposite: at least you know where you stand, while a long silence leaves you guessing at anything. Neither way was better, they agreed, and neither of them had picked the one they were handed.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: three readings of mental suffering came before the scientific discipline
these readings piled onto one another rather than replacing one another
the supernatural reading put the trouble down to a force from outside
it treated through ceremonies meant to drive that force back out
the reading by inner fluids explained melancholy by an imbalance of the body
it reached for bleedings, purges and strict diets
the moral reading held the sufferer answerable for his own disorder
it prescribed fixed hours, work with the hands and removal from other people
each reading brought forth its own institutions and its own words
phrases born of these readings live on in everyday speech
text: Long before the study of the mind turned into a discipline, mental suffering was read in three ways, and the later ones piled onto the earlier rather than clearing them off. The first reading was supernatural: something from outside had taken hold, so the cure lay in ceremonies meant to drive it back out. The second put the fault in the body, blaming melancholy on inner fluids gone out of balance; patients were bled, purged and held to strict diets. The third was moral. It held the sufferer answerable for his own disorder and bet on discipline, on fixed hours, work with the hands and removal from other people. Each reading raised its own houses, its own trades, its own words. Everyday speech carries them still, in talk of black moods and possessed minds. Careful clinical observation came last, and took generations to win.

units: the newborn has only three signals of feeling at his disposal
these signals are distress, calm and a wide awake curiosity
near the close of the first year comes fear of unfamiliar faces
that fear shows the child now sorts the close ones from the strangers
in front of a mirror the child works out at last that the smudge is on his own forehead
out of that recognition come embarrassment, pride and shame
school teaches that a feeling can be kept out of sight
the child discovers that a soothing face can lie
in adolescence the charge of feeling swells before the power to hold back does
that gap explains how hard the outbursts of that age break
text: Watch a newborn and the whole repertoire fits into three signals: distress, calm, and a wide awake sort of curiosity. Everything that follows grows out of there. Near the close of the first year comes unease at an unfamiliar face, proof that the child now sorts the close ones from the strangers. Then the self arrives. Put in front of a mirror, the child works out at last that the smudge belongs to his own forehead, and out of that recognition come embarrassment, pride and shame. School lays down a further layer: a feeling can be kept out of sight, a soothing face can lie, tears come less freely with an audience nearby. In adolescence the charge swells while the brake matures late, which is why the storms of those years break so hard. The finished structure takes decades to raise.

units: an incident on a hospital ward illustrates how a state of feeling spreads
the nurse in charge of the ward took bad family news as her shift began
she told no colleague about it
her speech quickened and her instructions came out clipped
the team changed its behaviour within two handovers
exchanges grew shorter and cross-checks fell away
the number of preparation errors doubled
the review afterwards ruled out fatigue and patient load as explanations
the cause settled on is the silent passing of a state through posture, gaze and pace of speech
a short debriefing meeting put the coordination back
text: An incident on a hospital ward gave a clean illustration of how a state of feeling spreads. The nurse in charge, unflappable as a rule, took bad news about her family just as her shift began. She said nothing about it to any colleague. Her speech quickened all the same, and her instructions came out clipped. Within two handovers the whole team had shifted: exchanges grew shorter, cross-checks fell away, and the mood on the floor turned heavy. The measurable consequence showed up in the incident log, where preparation errors doubled. The review afterwards ruled out fatigue and patient load, both of which had held steady. What was left was the silent passing of a state through posture, gaze and the pace of speech. A short debriefing meeting was enough to put the coordination back.

units: the frame that carries the roof can be timber or steel
this frame passes the weight of the roof down to the load-bearing walls
thin strips of wood are nailed crosswise to take the covering
the covering described is a dark rock split into flat leaves
this covering lets the space under the roof breathe
a channel set at the foot of the slope catches the rainwater
this water is then sent into a vertical downpipe
an opening cut through the slope lights and airs the floor under the roof
this opening weakens the weathertight skin if it is badly fitted
a trained tradesman checks the whole of it before the wet months
text: A roof is an assembly of parts, and every one of them does a job you can name. The frame comes first, timber or steel, holding the whole thing up and handing the weight down to the walls that carry the load. Onto that frame go the battens, slim strips nailed crosswise, ready to take the covering. Slate does the covering here, a dark rock that splits into flat leaves, shedding rain while it lets the space beneath breathe. Along the foot of the slope a gutter catches what streams off and feeds it into a downpipe, so the face of the building stays dry. Higher up, a dormer cuts through the pitch to bring light and air into the room under the roof, and its surround has to be fitted closely, since any hole weakens the skin that keeps the water out. Before the wet months, a trained roofer goes over each of these parts.

units: the workmen were taking up a damaged floor at the top of an empty house
a workman's tool struck something hard under a board
an old timber covered with notches came to light
the man in charge of the site halted the work
a restoration specialist came to look at the find the next day
she recognized marks cut by the builder who raised the house
these marks showed in what order the structure had to be put together
the owner gave up the idea of replacing the structure
he chose instead to have it strengthened
the timber is left in view and protected by a pale coating
text: The work began on the top floor of a house nobody had lived in for two winters, where a rotten floor was coming up board by board. Under the third plank the workman felt his bar strike something that would not give. He brushed the dust away and uncovered an old beam, blackened, its hidden face cut with a row of even notches. The foreman stopped the job on the spot. A restorer of old buildings arrived the next morning. She ran her palm along the grain, recognized joining marks scored by the carpenter who had raised the house, and said they told whoever came later in what order the frame went back together. Each piece had been marked before it was lifted, the way words are numbered in a sentence taken apart. The owner, told at the end of the week, dropped the idea of replacing the frame and asked for it to be strengthened. The beam still shows overhead under a pale wax.

units: you have to check how wet the wall is before putting up a light partition
a damp backing keeps the covering from holding
the skim coat lifts away in flakes at the first heating if the backing is wet
the layout line is marked with a taut string
a floor track out of level throws off every upright and ripples the finish
the bonding compound is mixed in small amounts because it stiffens fast
a screw driven too deep tears the face and weakens the board
tape bedded onto a wet joint swells and then splits
a gap left at the foot of the partition keeps rising damp off it
text: Before you put up a light partition, take a moisture reading on the wall behind it. Plaster will not grip a damp backing, and the skim coat lifts away in flakes as soon as the heating comes on. Snap the layout line with a taut string, then set the floor track down: run it out of level and every upright inherits the error, so the finished face ripples along its length. Mix the bonding compound in small batches, since it stiffens fast and whatever is left over goes to waste. Drive each screw until the head sits flush and no deeper, because a torn face weakens the very board it was meant to hold. Let the work dry before you skim. Tape bedded onto a wet joint swells first and splits later, which shows through the paint. Leave a gap along the bottom edge as well, or the first trace of rising damp will stain the foot of the wall you have just built.

units: neighbours in a low-lying district had their cellars flooded after heavy rain
the trouble had been going on since the end of summer
a survey was ordered by the local authority
the drainage system had been laid out for ground that soaked up water
yards covered in concrete have done away with that soaking
the water reached the doorways of the houses and worked under the doors
the paths will be laid with a loose stony material that lets water through
channels running along the walls will carry the water to a basin dug further off
the money comes from a grant and from a share paid by the owners
a first stretch will be finished before the rainy season
text: Since the close of summer, people living in a low-lying district have reported cellars under water after every heavy downpour. A survey ordered by the local authority put the blame on the drainage system, laid out for ground that once soaked up the rain. Yard after yard has been covered in concrete, and nothing sinks in any more: the run-off slides toward the doorsteps and works its way under the doors. Two measures have now been settled on. The paths will be lifted and laid again with loose gravel, which lets rain pass through instead of throwing it back against the buildings. Stone channels will then follow the exposed walls and carry the flow to a holding basin dug well away from the houses. A grant to the authority covers most of the cost, with the owners paying the rest between them. One stretch is due before the rains come.

units: two houses look at each other from either side of a narrow street
they have nothing in common
the house on the left has a pale render on its walls
its openings are closed by painted wooden panels
over each opening on the left runs an oak lintel left in view
the house on the right has stone walls left bare
its openings are narrower and capped with a lintel of hard rock
it is shut by metal slats that slide rather than swing
the first gives a sense of welcome, the second a sense of closure
the doorsteps differ too, one of wood hollowed by use, the other a heavy slab
text: Two houses stand across a narrow street from each other, and they share nothing at all. The one on the left wears a pale lime render, broken by tall windows that painted wooden shutters close at dusk. Over every one of those windows sits an oak lintel left in plain view, barely curved, softening the flat run of the wall. The house opposite answers with bare stone, its joints raked deep, its openings pinched narrower and capped with a thick block of granite. No shutter swings there. Metal slats run down instead, sliding in a groove cut for them. The first house looks open-handed, a little worn by weather. The second looks shut, heavy, cut to stand up to the wind that comes along the street. Even the doorsteps part company, a wooden one hollowed by generations of feet on one side, a cold and heavy slab on the other.

units: the writer holds that we pull buildings down too readily instead of repairing them
his first charge is the waste of materials that could still be used
taking a building apart with care costs more than knocking it down quickly
his second charge concerns the loss of hand skills
these skills die out along with the places that passed them on
his third charge is aimed at the disappointing comfort of new buildings
the new building bakes in the warm season and whistles in the cold one
the bill lands on whoever lives in the place
his fourth charge is that what the occupants feel for the place counts for nothing
he is not asking that everything be kept but wants proof that no repair was possible
text: Let us be blunt: we knock buildings down far too fast and mend them far too rarely. Charge one, the waste. Sound roof timbers, tiles good for another lifetime, an oak staircase, all of it goes into the skip because taking a house apart with care costs more than swinging a bucket at it. Charge two, the hands that knew how. Who can still point a wall with lime, ease a sagging lintel back up, split a slate without cracking it? Those skills go out with the workshops that handed them on. Charge three, the comfort we were promised never turns up. What goes up in their place bakes in the warm months, whistles in the cold ones, and whoever lives there pays for both. Charge four, what people feel about a place they have lived in weighs nothing at all in the decision. I am not asking that everything be kept. Show me first that no serious repair was possible.

units: the woman in question was brought up beside a place where rock is quarried
her father worked there cutting stone out of the ground
she watched blocks being split before she split them herself
she went into training in a workshop that repairs old buildings
her first commission of note was cutting a fresh doorstep to replace a worn one
she went on to harder work, a cracked lintel and a vault to reset
she opened a workshop of her own about ten years after she started
she employs two workmen
she now teaches beginners, several of whom had never used a tool
she holds that this material calls for patience
text: A quarryman's daughter, the stone carver grew up beside a limestone pit, watching blocks come apart under the wedge long before she held a chisel of her own. At sixteen she took a place in a workshop that repairs old buildings, learned to read the grain of a block, and landed her first real commission, cutting a fresh doorstep for a roadside inn whose own had worn hollow. Harder work followed, a cracked lintel to make good, a vault to reset stone by stone. Ten winters or so after she began, she opened a workshop of her own and took on two men. Lately she gives part of every week to beginners from every sort of background, several of whom had never picked up a tool. Stone, she says, forgives impatience very badly, and what she really teaches them is how to slow the hand down.

units: the visitor leaves this refitted building feeling hemmed in
the feeling comes from choices of construction rather than from a quarrel over taste
an insulating skin has been added in front of the old walls
this addition has sunk the windows into a deep recess
the view outward is now blocked
a stretched ceiling hides the timber frame that used to be in view
hiding it takes away the sense of size the place had
the floor of loose stone has been replaced by a smooth surface
this surface throws sound back and makes the noise hard to bear
the reviewer approves of keeping the doorstep worn down by passing feet
text: You come out of this refitted hall short of breath, and the reason has less to do with taste than with what was built. The old walls have been lined throughout with an insulating skin, which drops each window to the end of a deep shaft, so the eye runs aground well before it reaches the daylight. The roof frame, once readable from one end of the hall to the other, has gone behind a stretched ceiling, and with it went the measure that made the room feel generous. The floor of packed gravel gave way to a smooth screed, which throws every voice back off bare surfaces and turns ordinary talk into a din. One decision consoles. The doorstep was kept as it was, worn into a hollow by feet beyond counting, a reminder that the place was in use before anyone thought to improve it.

units: the writer is addressing his neighbour in writing
he brings up the channel that catches water along the wall they share
this channel has been spilling over since the recent rains
the water is eating into the wall covering and laying the mortar bare
a look at it showed a blockage of leaves and an empty nest
one fixing bracket has given way and tipped part of the channel over
the writer offers to clear the channel himself shortly
he offers to replace the broken brackets and put the fall right
he suggests fitting a guard so that the trouble does not come back
he asks his neighbour whether she agrees to all this
text: Dear neighbour, I am writing about the gutter that runs along the wall our two houses share. Since last week's downpours it has been spilling over halfway down its length, and the water is eating into the render, which is going soft and letting the mortar show through. I put a ladder up to look at it. The channel is packed with matted leaves and an abandoned nest, and one of the brackets has given way, which tips that whole length backward. Three things would sort it out. A thorough clear-out first, and I can do that myself before the week is over. Then the two broken brackets replaced, cheap enough as parts go, with the fall eased a little toward the downpipe. Last, a guard over the mouth of the channel so that the same thing does not build up again. Tell me whether that suits you.

units: the text sets timber-frame building against building in concrete
the comparison comes up when a client looks at two tenders
timber goes up fast because the parts are shaped in the workshop beforehand
its lightness allows shallower foundations
timber suffers from water and calls for wide roof overhangs
the points where timber meets the ground need watching closely
concrete stores warmth and flattens the swings of temperature
it also cuts down the noise from outside
making it costs the environment dearly and its drying stretches the work out
the common answer joins a concrete base to a timber frame
text: Timber frame or concrete? The question comes up the moment a client sets two tenders side by side. What does timber offer? Speed above all, since the parts arrive shaped from the workshop, the site stays clean, and a light structure sits happily on shallow foundations. What is held against it? Water. Timber wants a roof that oversails well beyond the walls, and every point where it meets the ground has to be watched year after year. What does concrete offer? Mass, which soaks up warmth, flattens the swing between day and night, and muffles the noise coming off the street. What is held against it? A heavy toll in the making, and drying times that stretch the work out. So which of them wins? Very often both, a solid base carrying a light frame, a pairing that serves the building better than either on its own.

units: the job began as an ordinary check
a loose roof element was spotted from the metal working structure
the roofing specialist flagged a crack hidden under the coating
that crack was hard to see from below
the owner demanded a full survey before any work
the mason laid bare a binder crumbled by the weather
the timber frame was not damaged
the wall was strengthened with a binder made of sand and lime
the roofing elements were put back in place
the front wall is judged stable for what follows
text: The site foreman says the whole thing started out as an ordinary check, nothing more. He had climbed the scaffolding to look at the gable end when he noticed a roof tile working loose. The roofer with him caught more than that: a thin crack ran beneath the render, and from the yard below almost nobody would have picked it out. They called the owner, who refused to let anyone patch anything until a full survey had been done. The mason brought in later scraped the surface back and found the binder crumbling and soft, washed out by the weather. The timber frame, he says, had come through untouched. The crew then packed the wall with a mix of sand and lime, and once that had set they laid the covering back in place. The owner now says the front wall will hold without anyone watching over it.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the exhaustion of the nearby deposits forced the builders to change material
brick took over because it weighed less and was made on the spot
the walls grew thinner
the openings gained in width
curved coverings were replaced by ceilings carried on beams
the new material stood up badly to water
a lime based coating served as breathable protection
the craftsmen had to learn to judge a firing instead of a quarried block
the old buildings still keep the mark of that change
text: When the quarries near the building sites ran dry, the men who raised walls had to think again. Stone grew scarce, and brick took its place, since it was lighter to lift and could be fired in kilns a short walk from the work itself. The change reached all the way into the shape of the buildings themselves. Walls grew thinner. Openings widened. The vault gave way to flat ceilings carried on beams. Brick, though, drank water badly, so a lime coating went over it, one that let damp escape rather than trapping it. The trade shifted too. A mason no longer read the grain of a quarried block; he learned to judge a firing by its color and its ring. Out of that shift came a way of building that rose faster and cost less, yet flinched at every long rain. The oldest walls still standing carry the mark of it.
