units: the breaking of a poured floor almost always has a traceable origin
an uneven settling of the support unbalances the spread of the load
water working in makes the inner metal bars swell
that swelling widens the gap
the change is followed with a measuring device fixed on the surface
a gap that stops moving is treated at the surface
the treatment means opening the gap at an angle then filling it with a hardening product
a gap that keeps opening reveals a problem in the ground
the ground is then stabilized by injecting a product under the footings
text: A poured slab hardly ever splits without a reason you can trace. The ground under it settles unevenly, one side drops, and the load stops spreading the way it should. A gap opens, hair thin at first, then wider as water works in and swells the steel bars buried in the concrete. Anyone assessing the damage starts by tracking that gap: a gauge is glued across it and read at set intervals. If the reading holds steady, the repair stays shallow. You cut the crack open at an angle, clear the dust out, and pour in a resin that hardens cold. If the gap keeps growing, the fault lies in the ground rather than the slab, and a binder has to be injected beneath the footing to even the bearing out. Skip that step, and you will go on dressing the same wound forever while the soil keeps giving way beneath the patch.

units: a craftsman took charge of restoring an old farm building
he spotted two building techniques stacked in one and the same wall
the lower part joined uneven stones and a yielding binder
the upper part had been built later with rigid elements and a hard binder
the older part had followed the movements of the support without harm
the recent part showed breaks in several places
the cause of the trouble was not the age of the material but the pairing of two techniques
the craftsman advised taking down and rebuilding the recent part with a compatible binder
the owner ended up accepting the cost
text: The craftsman who agreed to restore the old farm building took the work on out of plain curiosity, and little else. On his first walk through it he found two ways of building stacked one above the other inside a single wall. Down below, earlier hands had set uneven stones in a fat, yielding mortar that still gave a little under the thumb. Above, added long afterward, sat hard blocks bedded in gray cement. The lower courses had shifted with the ground and taken no harm; the upper work had torn open in several places. What had failed, he concluded, was not the older material but the pairing of two techniques that answered to opposite logics. He advised taking the later section down and raising it again in a mortar close to the original. The owner balked at what that would cost, and in the end agreed to it.

units: you first gather the tools you need including a one wheeled carrier and a mason blade
the crumbling zones of the wall must be taken out and the dust removed
the surface must be wetted without excess
the mix joins sand, lime added little by little, and water
the paste obtained must stay firm enough to cling to the tool
it goes on in three successive coats
each coat has its own job: to grip, to fill, to level
a coat must dry away from any draft before the next one
the tools are cleaned straight after use
the binder is kept in a dry place
text: Before you set about rendering an old wall, put your kit together on the ground: a wheelbarrow, a bucket, a wide trowel, a float, and a sieve. Then get the wall ready. Rake out the crumbling patches, brush every trace of dust away, and damp the surface down without soaking it. Mixing comes next. Tip the sand into the barrow, work the lime in a little at a time, add water, and turn it until the paste clings to the blade instead of sliding off. Lay it on in three passes. The first grips the wall, the second fills the hollows, the third brings everything level. Let each coat dry right through, out of the draft, before you start the one above it. Finish by looking after the kit. Rinse the tools right away, empty the barrow, shut the binder in a dry store, and throw a cover over the sand heap.

units: the week began with an incident on the site
the metal working structure had been shifted by the night wind
taking it down took two working days
a young worker found a blocked opening under the roof
people in the area knew that story without putting any faith in it
the head of the project stopped the demolition
the site turned into a rescue operation
onlookers come by regularly to look at the find
the man in charge accepts the delay in handing the work over
text: The week got off to a rough start over on the site in the old quarter. The crew showed up to find the scaffolding leaning sideways, since one windy night had been enough to shove it out of true. Down the whole thing came, two full working days of it, and not one of them grumbled. Next morning, clearing out the loft, an apprentice came across a sealed hatch tucked under the rafters. People around here had heard talk of it for years and never really bought it. The architect came over, called a halt to the demolition, and just like that the job turned into a rescue. Since then, folks drift by at the end of the day for a look down the dark hole they reopened. The boss just grins about the whole business. He meant to hand the place over fast; now he knows it will be late, and it hardly bothers him.

units: the outside of the building gives an impression of good condition
the floor under the roof space is buckling
a damaged drainage pipe has been throwing water against the wall for a long time
the coating on the wall is coming away in patches
a brown stain spreads with every spell of rain
the concreted surface of the passage has lost the sand it rested on
the occupants tried to hide the fault under a coat of paint
that paint blistered quickly
the survey recommends dealing with the roof before anything else
text: Seen from the yard, the house looks perfectly sound. Pale front wall, straight gable, shutters all in line, and a visitor would walk in without a second thought. The inside tells quite another story. The floor under the roof space has begun to hump, because a split gutter has been emptying itself against the wall season after season. Damp has crept into the timbers, lifted the render off in flakes, and left a brown ring that grows a little wider with every downpour. Lower down, the hallway slab rings hollow: the sand it once rested on has washed out from underneath. The owners painted over the stain first, hoping to bury it. The paint blistered before the next winter was out, showing a wall soaked right through. The survey is blunt about it: start at the roof, or whatever you mend below will rot again.

units: the writer finds the spread of smooth front walls worrying
a cement based coating stops the wall from letting damp out
the trapped water ends up breaking the stone from within
the writer holds that a sealed surface was mistaken for a protected one
he proposes using binders that let vapor through
he advises keeping cement for the buried parts
he invites us to accept the visible aging of a wall
he calls for training craftsmen to examine old building work
a properly coated wall lasts several generations with light upkeep
text: Street after street is going over to smooth front walls that age badly, and the drift ought to worry us more than it does. A wall skinned in cement has stopped breathing. It holds water against the stone, and in time the stone bursts from within. We mistook a sealed surface for a protected one. The cure asks for no brilliance at all. Go back to binders that let vapor pass, keep cement for what sits below ground, and let a wall weather instead of demanding that it stay untouched. Craftsmen should be taught again how to read old masonry, a slow discipline that the rush of modern building has all but rubbed out. A wall coated the right way lasts generations on nothing more than an occasional wash of lime. We would rather keep redoing every so often what earlier hands managed to get right the first time.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman heading the roofing was trained by a practitioner who drew nothing
her master judged pitch and tightness through his senses
she works from measurements and preparatory drawings
her master repeated the trips carrying materials
she groups her loads so as to go up only once
she grants her master one advantage: the feel for the state of a frame
no set of readings replaces that feel
she has kept the habit of walking a roof before touching it
her jobs are shorter than in her early days and just as sound
text: The roofer who runs the site learned her trade from an old hand who never drew a single line. She likes to set the two schools of work against each other. He laid tile by eye, walked the pitch to correct it, and told whether a roof was tight by the sound rain made on it. She measures first, notes the angles, and works the layout out on paper before she climbs. He went up and down all day with the barrow; she makes up her loads on the ground and carries them once. On one point, though, she grants him the advantage. He could feel a tired frame flex under his boots, and no set of readings will give you that. So she kept one habit of his: walk the whole roof over before laying a hand on any of it. Her jobs now run shorter than they did in her early years, without losing anything in strength.

units: the verdict on this conversion falls into three parts
the original frame was kept and quietly strengthened
that choice is praised because the span of the frame can still be read
the finishing disappoints the writer
the coating chosen is too rigid and is already cracking near the bearing points
the unbroken concreted surface takes no account of the movements of the support
moving through the building is judged pleasant and clear
the sound was dealt with without any visible fittings
the writer regrets that the level under the roof is closed to the public
text: This conversion calls for a divided verdict, one that falls readily into three parts. The first is structure. The carpenters kept the original trusses and doubled them so quietly that the eye passes over the work, and the span still reads clean from one end of the hall to the other. The second is the finishing, and here the praise thins out. The render chosen is too hard, and it has already cracked where the loads come down, while the slab, poured in one unbroken sheet, takes no account of a ground that moves. The third part concerns use. The place is a pleasure to walk through, the way in and out stays obvious, and the sound has been tamed without a single panel on show. One regret remains: the floor under the roof is kept for staff alone, which denies visitors the finest view of the vault.

units: the writer is writing from a room fitted out under the roof
the roof had been leaking since the cold season
the water that seeped in warped the beams
the warped wood kept the landing door from closing
the tradesman took the door off and trimmed the jamb
two pieces of the roof frame were strengthened
the writer invites the reader to come and sleep in that room
the room has no heating yet
text: I am writing to you from the room up under the roof, the one we called the loft when we were small. Rain had been getting through the covering since the cold months, and the soaked beams swelled until they twisted out of line. That is why the landing door stopped shutting: the wood had shifted, the hinge pulled sideways, the frame went out of square. The carpenter lifted the door off its pins, planed the jamb down, and hung it back. He doubled two rafters as well, since the roof was pushing its weight the wrong way. Now the slope runs clean, the stairwell smells of resin, and rain overhead sounds friendly again. The upstairs room is yours whenever you come. Bring heavy blankets, though, because the warmth does not climb that far yet, and the view over the valley is worth a cold night.

units: an old wall is not plastered the way a recent wall is
the professional compares the old wall to something that breathes
a waterproof coating traps the water coming up from below ground
that trapped water brings salt deposits to the surface
the coating ends up peeling away in pieces
lime laid on in thin passes lets vapor through
a surface that is too smooth must be rubbed back and wetted before coating
this method slows the job down but spares the wall from ruin
text: Should an old wall be plastered the way a recent one is? The builder we put the question to says no, and he sets it out in one image: the old wall breathes, the young one sweats. So what happens if you seal the first of them under a waterproof coat? Damp rising from below stays locked inside, salt works its way out to the face, and the coating blisters and comes away in sheets. What does he offer instead of that? Lime, laid on in thin passes, so that vapor can travel out freely through the masonry. And if the backing is too smooth to grip? Then you rub the face back, wet it down, and brush on a very liquid first pass that bites into it. Work of that kind goes slower, he grants, but the wall stops rotting quietly behind its skin. A face treated so will stand a whole generation with no patching.

units: the manager asks the tradesman how the floor should be fastened
a nail goes in quickly
a nail bends without snapping under shaking
a screw holds better when something pulls on it
a screw breaks if the structure moves
laying a heavy board on joists calls for a fastening that tolerates the wood moving
the screw costs more in tools and in care
the parts meant to come apart will be screwed
text: The site manager asks the joiner whether the upstairs floor ought to be nailed down or screwed down. Nails go in quickly, the joiner says, and they take shaking well, because the shank bends rather than snapping under it. A screw holds a great deal better against pull, he adds, but it shears clean off as soon as the frame shifts under its load. A heavy board bedded on joists wants a fastening that lets the timber keep moving as it dries. The manager weighs up what each way costs him: screws mean a power tool and a careful hand, nails mean a hammer and a steady rhythm. So you nail down whatever swells and shrinks, the joiner sums up, and you screw down whatever you may want to take apart again. On this job, he says, the battens get nailed and the access hatches get screwed.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: three broad methods came before metal was used everywhere
the first method piles up stones with no mortar
the steadiness of that pile comes from the mass of the blocks
the second method uses clay bricks dried without firing
the third method joins a timber frame to a filling that is then coated
each way of building depended on what lay close at hand
these ways forced thick walls and low buildings
villages built that way are still lived in and kept up the same way
text: Before metal came into common use, the building trade rested on three broad families of method. The first piles up chosen blocks of rock with nothing at all between them, and stands on the sheer weight of its courses. The second shapes raw clay into bricks dried in the open air, bedded in a mud of the very same stuff. The third raises a timber frame, packs it out with a light filling, then has the whole face coated over. Each answered to a resource lying close by: rock breaking the surface, silt from the river beds, the woods along the ridge. Each set its own limits too, in thick walls, low roofs, and steady upkeep. Builders worked around them by turning the openings, deepening the footings, steepening the pitch. Whole hamlets built so are lived in yet, and patched with the old gestures.

units: the stages of a building job follow an order that cannot be changed
a board fence marks out the edges of the plot at the start
the footings are poured into trenches cut in the ground
the walls go up with gaps left for the doors and windows
the roof frame goes on once the masonry has dried
the covering puts the job out of the weather
the pipe runs go through the partitions while they are still open
a coating laid on a damp backing comes away
text: Nothing goes up at random on a plot made ready for a house, because each stage settles what the one after it can do. A board fence marks the edges first, guarding the turned soil and giving the machines a line to work to. Then the footing trenches are cut and filled with reinforced concrete. The walls climb course by course, with gaps kept open where the doors and windows will sit. The roof frame waits until the masonry has cured. The covering then closes the volume and puts the job under shelter. Water and air runs are threaded through the partitions while they still stand open. Coating comes last, then floors, then paint. Swap two of those stages and the bill climbs, since a coat spread on a damp wall lifts away, and a partition closed too soon has to be opened again.

units: a jammed lock set the whole business going
the residents forced the door and made a joke of it
one shove too hard tore the metal piece out of the frame
the bottom hinge gave way under the weight of the door
the dropped door scraped along the tiles
the caretaker wanted to replace the whole thing
a resident who restores furniture won a few days to try mending it
she took the door off and knocked the frame back square
the neighbor came out of it with a name as a woodworker in the building
text: It began with a sticky lock down in the basement of our building. At first we shoved a little, laughed it off, said the door had a temper. Then a neighbor put his shoulder in too hard, the strike plate tore out of the frame, and the bottom hinge ripped loose. The leaf was heavy, so it dropped on a slant and scraped the tile the whole way across. Nothing would budge after that, and nobody dared lean on it. The caretaker wanted the lot replaced and had a quote ready, but the tenant on the ground floor, who mends furniture, asked for a week. She lifted the leaf off, knocked the frame back square with a mallet, hung a fresh hinge, greased the works. The lock snaps shut now. That job gave her a name as a cabinetmaker across the whole building, which she had never gone looking for.

units: an opening that rubs makes a room unpleasant to use
the cause is rarely in the glass
rubbing low down points to wood that has swollen
rubbing high up points to fixings that have worked loose
the shiny patch left by the contact must be sanded
an oil is then wiped on and left overnight
the brackets go back with the holes shifted slightly
a level held on the sill checks that the frame stands plumb
a shim corrects a frame that is still twisted
text: A window that catches spoils the use of a whole room, and the fault lies hardly ever in the glass itself. Start out by watching the gap along the edge. Rubbing low down means the wood has swollen. Rubbing high up means instead that the fixings have worked loose. In the first case, swing the sash wide open, find the shiny band that the contact has left behind, and sand that strip with medium paper until it runs free again. Dust it off, wipe on a light oil, and leave it overnight. In the second case, drive the brackets home once more, moving the holes a shade so the screws bite into sound wood. Then check plumb with a level laid flat on the inner sill. If the frame stays twisted, slide a thin shim behind the upper hinge. Patient adjusting will spare you the price of a replacement.

units: two building jobs are going on facing each other
one of them is a tall block of flats
the balconies of that block arrive ready made
lifting machines set whole face panels in place
that block gains one floor a week
the other job is the repair of an old house
the workers there take the roof off piece by piece
they check the walls and change the timber that has gone bad
the neighbors like the space promised but hold to the mended front
text: Two building jobs face each other along one street, and nothing binds them but the dust. On one side a tower of flats climbs, its balconies turned out of the works already cast, rounded lip and all. Cranes set whole face panels down, and the elevation gains a floor a week. Across the way an old house lies open like a patient on a table. The crews take the roof off tile by tile, sound the masonry, cut out the lengths of frame that have died. Where the first job makes a virtue of speed, the second keeps faith with the joints it uncovers. People on the street watch both and cannot settle it. They admire the room the tower holds out, yet their fondness goes to the scaffolded old front, which will hand them back a street they thought lost. Neither one calls the other useless.

units: the frame that carries the building can be seen from outside
the upright posts were cut with a hand tool
each post carries a horizontal piece that takes the roof frame
the walls are made of three layers one over another
air is left to move within the thickness of the walls
the windows have a sloped sill that sheds water
the ground around the building is covered with draining stones
the roof reaches out beyond the wall and shelters the timber
no surface has been painted
text: Seen from the yard, the shed shows its bones before anything else. The posts, squared off on all four faces with a hand axe, each carry a horizontal beam that takes the trusses above. The walls themselves run in three layers, lapped boarding outside, a vented gap of air, then insulating panel fixed on battens. The openings all share one drawing, a low apron below, a jutting sill cut on the slant to throw water clear, a lintel in one piece. Inside, the floor is a smoothed slab. Outside, a band of draining gravel follows the walls around. The roof falls away both ways and ends in a wide overhang that keeps driving rain well off the timber. Nothing here has ever been painted. The boarding is going silver, the ironwork is taking a patina, and the whole shed ages with no heavy care.

units: building has slowly given up on lasting
soft mortars were replaced by a harder binder
that binder was taken up because it sets quickly
heavy roof frames gave way to lightened structures
those lightened structures cannot be mended and have to be swapped out
thick coatings were replaced by very thin layers
the guarantee on those coatings runs out before the wall wears
each of these choices was aimed at a saving in the short term
the writer calls for materials that can be mended
text: We have stopped building to last, and the drift settled in one careful step at a time. Masons let the soft binders go first, in favor of a stiff cement that sets faster and carries better. Heavy roof frames gave way next to light trusses figured right to the bone, which nobody can mend and everybody must swap out whole. Thick coatings gave way in turn to films so thin that the guarantee on them runs out well before the wall behind them grows tired. Every one of those steps paid for itself on the day it was taken. Their sum leaves us a stock of buildings that will have to come down before they can ever grow old with any grace. A building worth the name will take repair after repair. Asking for materials we can mend is no builder's longing for the past. It is simply plain prudence.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the site manager learned her trade through an apprenticeship
her crew works on old buildings
clients mostly ask for surfaces made to look new
the footings of the buildings give way under the stories added on
the floors are held up by temporary props before anything else
the ground is probed to find hollows
the gaps in the masonry are closed only after the building is made safe
she turns down decorative finishes while the frame is still weak
she takes the client under the floor to show him the damaged beams
text: She started out as an apprentice on repair jobs, and today she runs a crew that puts old buildings back on their feet. Wherever she goes, the trouble is the same. Owners want fresh walls, while the footings underneath sag beneath the stories that somebody added on over the years. Her answer is a strict order of work. Her men prop the floors up with temporary posts first, then probe the ground for hollows. Only after that do the masons close the cracks and rebuild the bearings. This site manager turns down decorative work for as long as the frame is still weak, and the talks that follow can get sharp. When a client hesitates, she hands him a lamp and walks him under the floor, where the beams have gone soft and spongy with damp. The look on his face usually puts an end to the argument.

units: two neighboring buildings stand at the end of the same street
the first is all glass and hands back the sky
the second is low and laid up in fired brick
the old front keeps the marks of the hands that raised it
the tower is judged too regular in its geometry
the house offers worn thresholds and uneven corners
the old building is faulted for being cramped and run down
the low rooms hold the warmth better
the heavy walls soften the noise
text: Two buildings share the far end of one street, and the taller one looms over its neighbor without ever winning the argument. The first is glass from foot to roof; it hands the sky back at you like a cold mirror, holds the eye a moment, then lets it go. The second sits low and heavy, laid up in fired brick that the wind has smoothed, and it keeps you looking. Its face still carries the marks of the hands that raised it. The comparison soon favors the humbler one. The tower offers a flawless geometry; the old house offers worn thresholds, corners that lean, a porch that shelters. One you visit, the other you live in. People call the old building cramped and run down, forgetting that its low rooms hold warmth and its heavy walls take the edge off noise. Beauty here comes from use, not from line.

units: the writer sends his sister news of the work
three jobs are running at the same time
the broken tiles have been swapped out by the roofer
the joints around the flue have been filled with a soft mortar
every window opening has been sealed against drafts
a strip of tape has been laid along the fixed frame
the tradesman offers to partition the back room into a study
the added wall will be light board with no contact with the ceiling
the walls will take a lime wash before the cold season
text: Dear sister, here is the update on the house at last, just as I promised you. Three jobs are running at once, so I will take them one at a time, in order. On the roof, the roofer swapped out the tiles that had broken, then came back to fill the joints around the flue with a soft mortar that can move a little. On the windows, I decided to seal every opening against the drafts: foam pressed into the recess, a strip of tape along the fixed frame, and they are gone. Inside, the tradesman wants to partition the back room off into a study. The added wall would go up in light board and stop short of the ceiling, without touching it. The walls still need a wash of lime before the cold weather sets in. I will write to you again as soon as the roof frame has been checked. Give the children a hug from me.

units: the lead designer is asked to retrace how the operation went
a detailed record of the standing building opened the project
that survey took a whole season
the tests brought out a weakened timber frame
the schedule had to be rewritten after that finding
only the frailest part was taken down
the rebuilding went up on the footings that had been kept
the tightness of the site made the trades harder to organize
bringing the pipework back into service was the trickiest phase
text: Asked to retrace the stages of the operation, the lead designer begins with the survey work. Everything, she says, started with a full record of the standing building, taken room by room and carried across an entire season. What came next? The tests, she explains, showed a weakened timber frame, and the schedule had to be rewritten around that finding. On the technical choices, she reports that only the frailest wing was taken down, and that the rebuilding went up on the footings that had been kept. Asked about the obstacles, she points to the difficulty of keeping the trades apart on so tight a site. And what does she take away from the whole stretch? Not the heavy work, she answers, but bringing the pipework back into service, a phase finished well past the date that had been announced.

units: a carpenter explains to his apprentice that the door is rubbing
the fault comes from the movement of the shell and not from the door
fitting another door would give the same jamming
a mark on the threshold proves the settling is still going on
the apprentice offers to plane the bottom of the leaf
the carpenter accepts that stopgap
the bearing under the wall will have to be rebuilt afterwards
the rubbing will come back if the ground drops further
text: The carpenter told his apprentice that the door was rubbing because the shell of the house had shifted. The apprentice asked whether they should fit another one. No, the carpenter said: the fault sat in the ground, so a fresh door would jam in exactly the same way. He pointed to the scar the leaf had worn into the threshold, proof that the settling had not stopped. The apprentice offered to plane the bottom of the leaf. His teacher agreed, though he warned that the cut would ease the trouble without curing it, and that the bearing under the wall would have to be rebuilt afterwards. Since the ground was still dropping, he added, the door would catch again within a season or two. The apprentice wrote down the lesson: treat the cause, or the repair keeps coming back, and the bill with it.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: old builders wanted to roof a wide hall with no support in the middle
a flat stone cover snaps under its own weight
the answer found was to lean the blocks against one another
this shape sends the load out to the side walls
wooden supports carried the work while it was going together
those supports were taken away once the middle block was in place
the sideways push shoved the walls outward
masses of masonry were added against the walls to hold them
text: Picture builders who want to roof a huge hall without setting a single column in the middle. Their trouble is easy to see: stone is heavy, and a flat cover snaps as soon as you stretch it across. So they looked for another way. What they found was the vault. Lean the blocks against one another and the load slides out to the side walls instead of dropping straight down. Of course the thing has to be held while it goes together, which is why they set wooden frames underneath to carry the stonework until it closed on itself. Once the middle block dropped into place, the timber came away and the vault stood on its own. That left the sideways push, which shoved the walls outward, so they answered with thick buttresses. Clever, no? Every obstacle called for one more piece, and in the end the hall held.

units: the choice between timber and masonry turns on how the building is used
a brick wall banks the heat before giving it back
a timber wall warms quickly and cools just as quickly
the heavy answer suits rooms in use all the time
the light frame suits premises used now and then
masonry calls for drying time and a crew of many hands
timber parts turn up cut to size and go together without water
the costs of the two methods end up close
designers advise deciding on the feel wanted indoors
text: Timber or masonry? The question comes up on every project, and the answer turns mostly on how the building will be used. A brick wall banks heat: it warms up late, then hands it back when the night comes down. A timber wall does the opposite, climbing quickly in temperature and losing it again just as quickly. For a room that is in use around the clock, weight wins the argument. For premises opened only now and then, the light frame wins instead. The work on the site splits the two families as well. Masonry has to dry and calls for a crew of many hands, whereas timber panels turn up cut to size and go together without a drop of water on site. Costs, in the end, tend to meet somewhere in the middle. So designers suggest choosing on the feel you want indoors, and not on whatever is in fashion this season.

units: an elderly tenant is allowed to walk through the building before it comes down
the hall floor is broken and holds the print of the furniture carried out
the apartment doors are shut and marked with a chalk cross
a thin partition had already been torn into by the workmen
an old wall paper shows behind the split board
the roof frame at the top lets a thread of air through
the stair rail worn by use moves her more than the rest
she thanks the caretaker on her way out
she refuses to lift her eyes toward the front of the building
text: The day before the demolition, the oldest tenant in the building was allowed one last walk through the condemned building. She pushed open the hall door first, where the broken tiling still held the print of the furniture carried out weeks before. Then she climbed on toward the landings, counting the shut doors, each one of them marked with a cross in chalk. On the third floor she stopped at a thin partition the workmen had already torn into; behind the split board lay an old paper that nobody had ever scraped off. She finished under the roof, where the tired frame let a thread of air through. Nothing moved her quite like the stair rail, polished smooth by hands long gone. On her way out she thanked the caretaker, and then she refused to lift her eyes toward the tall gray front.

units: the crack must be opened down to sound material
the dust is taken out with a brush
the edges are wetted before the filler goes on
the powder must be tipped into the water and never the other way round
the paste is pressed into the hollow to drive the air out
the surface is smoothed with a wide blade running past each side
drying lasts at least one whole night with no heating
the hardened patch is then sanded and dusted off
a mineral paint is brushed on in two crossed coats
text: Start by opening the crack along its whole length with the point of a trowel, cutting back until you reach sound material underneath. Brush the groove clean of dust, then wet the edges lightly, because a filler laid on a dry face will let go later on. Mix the paste in a clean bucket, tipping the powder into the water and never the other way round. Work it in straight away, pressing hard so that the air is driven out of the hollow. Smooth it off with a wide blade, running a little past the crack on each side. Leave it to dry overnight at least, and do not heat the room to hurry it. Sand the hardened patch with a fine abrasive, dust it off again, and run your hand across to check that the join no longer catches under your fingers. Only then brush on a mineral paint, in two crossed coats.

units: entry to several buildings of a low lying district has been banned
the families put out of their homes have been moved into a communal hall
an underground body of water has been swollen by rain that would not stop
the sand carrying the footings has been washed out by that water
the ground has settled unevenly
stepped cracks have opened across the fronts
the experts judge that the old fabric could not take such a movement
the stairwells have been declared dangerous
resin injections are announced to avoid demolition
text: Access to several buildings in the low lying district was banned yesterday, and the families put out of their homes were moved into a communal hall. Technical services have known the cause for seasons. An underground body of water, swollen by rain that would not stop, has washed out the sand on which the footings rest. The ground has settled unevenly, opening stepped cracks across the fronts. The experts called in judge that the fabric, already tired, was in no state to take a movement of that size. The stairwells were declared dangerous as a direct result, and the evacuation was ordered on the spot. Owners are demanding a second opinion, since putting the buildings right would mean underpinning the footings. The local authority has announced resin injections, failing which demolition would become unavoidable.

units: two neighboring homes show opposite characters
the older one has thick stone walls and few openings
the newer one offers wide glazed surfaces on a light frame
the old building holds its coolness better when the air is hot
the recent building follows outdoor temperature swings quickly
the occupants of the old home report a coating that soaks up water rising from the ground
a waterproof layer was laid under the outer cladding of the recent home
the occupants of the recent home worry when air renewal stops
a building tradesman holds that each construction answers a different purpose
text: Two homes sit side by side along the same road, and you tell them apart at a glance. The older one squats behind thick stone walls, under a low roof, with hardly any openings. The newer one stands taller, lining up wide panes of glass across a frame of pale timber. When the air turns hot, the old walls keep their coolness and warm up slowly. The recent one tracks whatever the outdoors does and answers the smallest shift. People in the older home complain that the render drinks up damp rising from the ground. Their neighbors praise the sealed layer laid under their cladding, yet they worry about stale air whenever the ventilation stops. A tradesman who works on both kinds refuses to pick a winner. One was raised to stand for ages without upkeep, the other to burn far less energy.

units: the writer holds that fast building work spoils the look of the streets
he regrets that heavy hand-worked materials give way to light elements
he notes the loss of homes with irregular shapes
those irregular shapes came from crooked plots or from split inheritances
buildings put up now repeat matching volumes stacked without hesitation
the size of a home was once judged by its extra spaces such as attics and cellars
it is now judged by the room count that is advertised
the writer refuses to call for a return to the past
he asks that a building be judged on what it will offer the next generation
text: Building at speed has become a habit, and the habit is making our streets poorer. Consider the losses one by one. Materials first: the heavy block, worked by chisel and by a patient hand, gives way to lightweight panels that no palm has ever touched. Shape next: the odd-angled dwellings, born of a crooked plot or of an inheritance split among heirs, vanish behind matching volumes that get stacked without a second thought. Use, last of all: a roomy home once meant nooks, an attic under the beams, a cellar below the boards. Now it means a room count printed in a listing. I am not asking anyone to turn back, and I distrust easy longing for what is gone. I ask only that a building be measured by what it will hand to the generation after us, and not by how quickly the site was finished.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the craftsman started out sorting beams on a renovation job
he was learning to tell sound timber from a piece ruined by damp
he then joined a workshop that put wood together without glue or metal parts
there he took up layout, cutting and fitting against irregular walls
a fall from scaffolding kept him off building sites while he healed
during that break he drew roof frames for other crews
on his return he opened his own workshop and took on two apprentices
he teaches that a measurement taken on the spot beats a plan sent from afar
text: The carpenter started out as an apprentice on a renovation job, where sorting the beams fell to him. He had to tell rough but sound timber from a crumbling piece that damp had eaten through. After a few seasons he moved to a workshop that cut its joints by hand, using neither glue nor metal fasteners. There he picked up layout, full-scale drawing, angled cuts, and at last the fitting of pieces against walls that never stood true. A fall from scaffolding kept him off sites through a long recovery, and he filled the break by drawing roof frames for other crews. When he came back he opened a workshop of his own and took on two apprentices. He tells them again and again that a measurement taken on the spot beats a plan mailed in, because an old wall keeps moving and no frontage runs plumb.

units: cracks ran through the building from its base to its top
a broken gutter had soaked the foundations over a long period
the water seeping in had dissolved the mortar and shifted the stones
the staircase had lost its steadiness
the site manager put the cause right before the appearance
he drained the foot of the wall, made the binders good and changed the worn steps
that order of work explains the soundness gained and the plainness of the result
some visitors find the result disappointing for want of a visible effect
the writer faults the uniform windows that wipe out the trace of older openings
the writer still holds the choice defensible because a finish laid over shifting walls would have split
text: What this restoration deserves credit for is largely what it refused to do. Cracks ran through the building from footing to ridge, because a broken gutter had been soaking the foundations for season upon season. Water seeping in dissolved the mortar, stones slid out of line, and the staircase turned wobbly underfoot. So the site manager went after the cause before the appearance. He drained the foot of the wall, made the binders good again, and swapped out the worn treads. That order of work explains why the structure now stands sound. It also explains how plain the outcome looks, plain enough that some visitors leave disappointed for want of anything to admire. The windows are too uniform, and they wipe out the record of older openings. Still the choice holds up: any finish laid over shifting walls would have split.

units: the writer lives above a former workshop
the floor creaked under every step and disturbed the neighbor below
shims, screws and thick rugs had settled nothing
a joiner found the source of the noise in a single visit
the joists were resting on a sagging beam
the hollow under the floor made every footfall louder
the joiner put a sturdy prop in the cellar and fixed the boards down again
the noise stopped that same evening
the neighbor and the writer made peace after the repair
text: I finally have a quiet moment, so here is how the floorboard saga ended. Ever since I moved into this apartment above a former workshop, every step set the boards creaking and woke my downstairs neighbor. Shims, screws, carpets thick enough to trip over: nothing improved matters. Then a joiner came up to look and identified the reason during a single visit. The joists were resting on a beam that had sagged, and the hollow underneath turned every footfall into a drum. He wedged a sturdy prop into the cellar and refastened the boards onto fresh battens. By that evening the apartment had gone completely quiet. My neighbor brought me a potted plant to celebrate, and we laughed about two miserable seasons spent resenting each other. Come and stay soon, the spare room is ready.

units: heating costs come from what the walls are made of and not from the age of the building
a thick wall stores heat and gives it back through the night
a light partition loses its heat as soon as the heating stops
insulation works differently on an old wall and on a recent one
an old wall has to let vapor through or water builds up inside its thickness
a recent wall needs an unbroken barrier and controlled air renewal
tradesmen advise picking what you can mend yourself
render is patched with a mason's tool
a panel made in a factory has to be swapped out whole
text: So does an old house cost more to heat than a recent one? Mostly it depends on what the walls are made of, not on the age of the building. A thick wall absorbs heat and releases it overnight, whereas a thin partition surrenders everything the minute the boiler shuts off. And insulation, what does that change? Enormously, though not in the same manner on either side. On an old wall the vapor has to pass straight through, otherwise water accumulates inside the thickness and the wall deteriorates. On a recent wall you want the opposite: an unbroken barrier, plus air renewal kept under control. So which should you choose? Whichever you can repair yourself, the tradesmen answer. Render you patch with a trowel. A panel assembled in a factory you replace in one piece, or not at all.

units: the site manager set out the renovation plan to the local residents
he sorted his answers around three worries
knocking down the partitions will take two weeks and the loud machines will stop in late afternoon
a fine sheet will wrap the scaffolding to hold down the dust
the rubble will be wetted before it is carried out
the sidewalk will be routed around the work but the ground-floor shop will keep its entrance
one woman living nearby worried about the wall she shares with her yard
the engineer promised shoring and then repointing at the builder's cost
a father raised the passing of trucks at the hour when children come home
text: The site manager presented the renovation plan to the residents who had come to hear him, and he arranged his answers around three worries. Noise came first. Demolishing the partitions would take two weeks, he said, and the noisiest machines would fall silent by late afternoon. Dust came next. A fine sheet would wrap the scaffolding, and the rubble would be dampened before it was carried out. Access came last. The sidewalk would be diverted around the works, though the shop on the ground floor would keep its own entrance. One woman asked what would become of the wall she shares with her yard. The engineer present promised it would be shored up and afterwards repointed, at the builder's expense. A father then raised the question of the trucks, and the hour when children walk home.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: lasting homes appear once groups stop moving from place to place
the first walls were branches packed with mud and made again after the rains
a silt paste hardened in the sun proved tougher than a fresh coating
the molded block could be made again exactly the same
a wall became a sum of matching pieces, which changed the builder's trade
firing in a kiln gave a block the rain could not touch
builders then grew bold enough to stack levels
the arch and then the vault freed openings from heavy timber crossbeams
every step forward rested on a repeated gesture and on a material taking over from the last
text: Homes built to last show up once a group stops wandering and decides to keep its stores in one place. The earliest walls were branches packed with mud, thrown up quickly and patched again after every rain. Then came the finding that changed everything: silt paste left to harden in the sun holds far better than a fresh coating, and a molded block can be made again and again exactly the same. From that point a wall was a sum of matching pieces, and the builder's trade shifted as much as the shape of the houses did. Later, firing in a kiln yielded a block the rain could not touch, and builders grew bold enough to stack one level on another. The arch, and after it the vault, freed openings from their heavy timber crossbeams. Every step forward rode on a gesture repeated and a material taking over from the last.

units: an inside wall can turn damp with no leak at all
the air of a heated home carries vapor given off by cooking, by showers and by breathing
the vapor turns to droplets when it meets a cold surface
cooled air holds less water than warm air
the cold spot usually comes from a local flaw in the insulation
the covering soaked with water ends up spread with dark stains
warming the surface by fixing the flaw takes the cause away
carrying the vapor off through steady ventilation also takes the cause away
drying the stain on its own settles nothing because the cold surface stays
text: An inside wall can go damp with no leak anywhere, and the physics behind it is well understood. The air in a heated home carries vapor, given off by cooking, by showers, and by the breathing of everyone inside. That vapor drifts freely until it meets a cold surface. There it turns to droplets, because cooled air holds less water than warm air does. The cold spot usually traces back to a flaw in the insulation: a concrete lintel, a badly protected corner, a window sill running clean through the wall. Moisture settles there, the covering drinks it up, and dark stains spread out over time. Two remedies reach the cause. Warm the surface by fixing the flaw, or carry the vapor away with ventilation that never stops. Wiping the stain dry changes nothing, since the cold spot stays put.

units: a property of three buildings ran into trouble while its roof was being redone
the firm stripped the covering off one wing before checking the frame
the inspection turned up rafters eaten hollow along their whole length
the work stopped
the temporary sheeting gave way in a downpour and water wrecked the ceilings on the top floor
the residents meeting in assembly refused to settle a second estimate
a mediator offered to share out the spending
the firm made the ceilings good at its own cost and the owners funded the replacement rafters
the house rules now call for an examination of the structure before any covering is stripped
text: A property of three buildings ran into an instructive mishap while its roof was being redone. The firm hired for the work stripped the covering off a whole wing before anyone checked the frame beneath, and the inspection turned up rafters eaten hollow along their entire length. Work stopped. The temporary sheeting gave way in a downpour, and water wrecked the ceilings on the top floor. Meeting in assembly, the residents refused to settle a second estimate. A mediator offered a way out. The firm would make the ceilings good at its own cost, and the owners together would fund the replacement rafters, which nobody could have foreseen in so old a structure. The deal held. The lesson now sits in the house rules: no covering comes off before the structure under it has been examined in full.

units: the young deer is born as the cold season ends
at birth it wears a coat covered with spots
through its first weeks it stays motionless in the vegetation
its pale fur makes it hard to tell apart from the ground
its mother moves off to feed and comes back to nurse it
this distance keeps scent from gathering around the hiding place
once its legs grow firm it follows its mother along the trails
the spots fade when the warmth returns
before the next cold season it joins a group of its own kind
text: The cold season loosens its grip, and the fawn arrives in a clearing, too weak to trail its mother more than a few steps. For weeks it lies where the tall grass conceals it, chin flat, ears low, motionless even when a shadow crosses. Its dappled coat borrows the color of dry leaves, so the eye slides past it. The doe drifts off to graze and returns at regular intervals to nurse, and her absence keeps scent from gathering around the hiding place. Once the legs firm up, the young animal finally walks behind her and learns which trails carry the least risk. Warm weather arrives, the spots fade, the coat darkens. Soon it grazes alone, choosing tender shoots by instinct. Before the cold circles back, it falls in with a herd and follows it toward the sheltered slopes. The clearing means nothing to it now.

units: the mare had been limping since the day before
the assistant first blamed the trouble on a simple knock
a stone had in fact wedged itself under the animal's foot
this stone crushed the tissue at every step
without quick action a pocket of pus would have formed
the caregiver pared out the cavity and protected the wound
the animal was moved onto soft ground that cushions its weight
the neglected state of its mane revealed poor upkeep
the team now checks the feet before every outing
text: The mare had been limping since the previous day, and the stable assistant put it down to a bruise. The examination told another story. A sharp stone had wedged itself between the frog and the wall of the hoof, and it crushed the tissue with every step the animal took. Left in place, that pressure would have driven a deep inflammation and then a pocket of pus that drains badly. So the practitioner pared out the cavity, disinfected the wound, and packed it under a thick dressing held by adhesive tape. Since the mare tolerated confinement poorly, she went into a sandy paddock whose loose footing cushioned her weight. Her tangled mane, a sign of grooming let slide, pushed the team to rethink its routine. Weeks later the gait had evened out, and a hoof check now comes before every outing.

units: a claw left to grow too long ends up breaking the skin under the paw
one must pick a moment when the animal is dozing
press the base of the toe until the claw slides out
a colored zone marks where the blood vessels run
the cut must stop short of that zone
going past that limit brings on bleeding
a tool with a curved blade serves better than an ordinary clipper
it is advised to interrupt the session if the animal stiffens
a treat makes every subsequent session easier
text: A claw left to grow too long presses against the pad beneath it and eventually breaks that soft skin. The procedure below corrects the trouble without alarming the cat. Choose a quiet moment, some while after a meal, when the animal lies dozing across a lap. Take one paw gently, press the base of the toe until the claw slides out of its sheath, then locate the pink zone where the blood vessels run through it. The cut must stop well short of that mark; beyond it, bleeding follows immediately, and the pain is considerable. A tool with a curved blade serves far better than an ordinary clipper, whose jaws crush the horn instead of severing it cleanly. Should the animal stiffen, interrupt the session and resume the following day, one paw at a time. A treat afterward makes every subsequent session easier.

units: two neighboring shelters take in abandoned animals
the first gives every resident a pen of its own
the second settles compatible animals into small groups
keeping them apart slows the spread of disease
grouping them cuts down the habits that boredom brings on
adoptions close faster in the shelter that groups its animals
fights, on the other hand, break out more often there
both teams keep the same health record
they send animals to each other as spaces open up
text: Two shelters on either side of a valley take in the animals that the region abandons, and the two of them run on opposite ideas. The first gives every resident a pen of its own. A keeper defends the choice on the grounds of contagion: mange travels slowly when no muzzle ever touches another. The second reads temperaments and settles the compatible ones into small groups, and its director reports a sharp drop in compulsive licking and in the barking that plain boredom brings on. The adoption records bear the difference out. Animals leave faster from the group shelter, where visitors get to watch them interact. Fights break out more often there, and a bitten resident has to be pulled aside on the spot. Both teams keep the same health record, and each one sends animals over to the other as soon as a space opens up.

units: the farmyard belongs to an uncle of the speaker
the rooster carries a red growth on top of its head
a hard spike stands out behind each of its legs
the hens roll around in the dry dust
the ducks have a shallow pond of their own
the geese announce visitors with their cries
a cat sleeps on the woodpile
the uncle hands out grain before nightfall
text: You really ought to see my uncle's farmyard, the whole thing is a spectacle. The rooster runs the place: that red comb goes straight up the second the gate swings open, and the spur behind each leg makes him worth avoiding. The hens spend entire afternoons rolling around in the dry dust, feathers puffed right out, and they come up gray from beak to foot. Down the slope a little, the ducks have a shallow pond of their own that they empty and refill all day long with those flat bills. The geese you hear long before you ever see them, and the moment a car turns onto the lane they start hollering together. Up on the woodpile, an orange cat sleeps straight through the racket. And my uncle comes by with his bucket of grain before dark, the same hour every evening, and the whole yard settles.

units: the first animal collections were there to dazzle the visitor
the animals were shut behind narrow bars
wider cages came later and echoed the original habitats
the parks then set out to breed threatened species
releases back into the wild were attempted
captivity weakens the habits that keep an animal alive
the writer holds that protecting wild land should come first
he grants that a few species hang on only under human watch
text: Once, a collection of animals was there for one purpose, to dazzle the visitor. A big cat behind narrow bars stood for power, and nobody stopped to ask what those bars did to it. Wider cages came later, planted with trees and dug out with pools, meant to echo the habitats the animals had come from. Then the parks claimed a purpose of another order: breed the rare species, keep the bloodlines on paper, send captive-born animals back out to the wild. That last step deserves a hard look. A predator fed at a fixed hour loses the habits that keep it alive, and its release fails far more often than it works. Those budgets would do more for the land itself, for wooded corridors, for rivers freed of their weirs. Still, a handful of species now hang on nowhere but under human watch, and pretending otherwise helps nothing.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the trainer grew up on a farm far from any neighbor
an accident took her father's sight
she then taught a dog to guide her father
that success drew other requests
she converted a barn into a training floor
she picks her puppies for their calm in the face of noise
she rejects anything built on fear
her former pupils still come back to ask for her advice
text: The trainer grew up on a farm far from any neighbor, among plow horses and herding dogs. When a farm machine took her father's sight, she set about teaching a young bitch to walk him from the house down to the barn. The dog learned to slow at the steps and to press her muzzle into his hand before every obstacle. Word spread, and families began knocking at the farm door. Lacking room indoors, she converted the barn into a training floor, with ramps, slick patches, and heavy doors that swing back at you. She picks her puppies for indifference to noise rather than for spark, because a fearful animal freezes at the worst possible moment. Having seen firsthand what fear produces, she rejects any method that leans on it. Her former pupils still return regularly to ask for her advice.

units: the new tank of a public aquarium comes under review
the curved panes warp the outlines of the fish
lighting that runs too harsh throws glare off the scales
the fish bunch into one corner of the tank
an artificial current was added to spread the fish out
filters have taken the edge off the lighting
the visitor route stays too narrow near the entrance
the writer calls for that passage to be widened
the installation is judged a success in spite of these flaws
text: The tank that opened in the mild season deserves a hard look before any praise is handed out. Its curved panes flatter from across the hall, but they warp the outlines as soon as you step up close: a tail fin reads far broader there than it truly is. The first lighting ran too harsh, and the scales threw off so much glare that the dark markings along the back simply vanished. The fish, put off by it, bunched into one blind corner and dropped out of sight altogether. The staff answered. An artificial current now spreads them through the whole volume, and tinted filters have taken the edge off the beams. One serious flaw remains, the visitor route, so narrow near the entrance that groups jam up there. It needs widening. Even so, the installation holds up against the best of them.

units: the writer asks a breeder for advice
he cannot settle between two animals to keep at home
the rabbit needs room to run every day
the bird takes long absences without harm
the rabbit gnaws through any cable within reach
the bird keeps up a steady noise that is hard to bear
the writer lives in a cramped home
he asks for an answer before the visit he has planned
text: Madam, I am writing to ask your advice, since your years of breeding will guide me better than the pamphlets I have been reading. I cannot settle between a rabbit and a pet bird, and each case seems to me as strong as the other. The rabbit needs room to run every evening, or else its muscles waste away; the bird takes my long absences without any harm, which counts for a great deal given how often I travel. On the other side of the ledger, a rabbit gnaws through any cable left within its reach, while a bird keeps up a steady whistling that my neighbors are unlikely to forgive. My home is cramped, and no balcony extends it, so that weighs heavily in the balance. Would you be kind enough to write back before the visit I have planned for next week? Please accept, madam, the assurance of my respect.

units: the antlers of deer drop off and build back over each yearly cycle
the horns of cattle and their kin lengthen without ever coming away
antlers are made of plain bone
horns wrap a bony core in a hard sheath
building antlers back demands feed rich in minerals
males settle their rivalries with these appendages
the females of some species carry horns as well
shed antlers are gnawed down by small mammals
text: Walkers ask the same thing over and over again: are antlers and horns one and the same? They are not, and the clearest split between them lies in what becomes of each. A deer's rack drops off once the rut has ended, then builds itself back over the cycle that follows, while the horn of a bull or a goat lengthens without pause and never comes away at all. What are they made of? The first is plain bone, fed during its growth by a covering of velvet skin; the second wraps a bony core in a hard fibrous sheath. Does all that regrowth cost anything? It does, and it demands feed rich in minerals. What good are they? Males settle their rivalries with them, and in some species the females carry horns as well. And afterward? The racks left lying on the ground get gnawed down by voles and squirrels.

units: a herder explains that his flock stopped feeding
he blames the change on the wetness of the vegetation
a woman who keeps animals nearby describes a different reaction in her own stock
the goats crowded against the fence
the herder admits he moved the watering point
the shade of the hedge made the water too cold to drink
the young animals drank less and lost weight
the herder judges that the fault is his own and not the weather's
the woman nearby confesses she made the same mistake earlier
text: The shepherd said his flock had stopped grazing the moment the wind picked up. He put it down to wet grass, which sits heavy in the mouth, and to the way an uneasy animal chews badly. The woman on the far slope, who keeps goats, told him hers had done the opposite: they crowded up against the fence and stayed there. At that the shepherd owned up. He had shifted the water trough closer to the hedge, and the shade there kept the water cold. Since the move, he said, the lambs drank less, lost weight, and their mothers wore themselves out calling them back. The blame lay with his own hand, he decided, and not with the weather. She laughed quietly at the confession, then admitted she had done the very same thing in the cold season before, and had watched it end the same way.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: harnessing a draft animal pressed on its throat
that pressure got in the way of the animal's breathing
the animal could not deliver its full power
craftsmen shifted the bearing onto the shoulders by means of a padded collar
this change raised the load the animal could pull
a head piece served to steer the animal without injuring it
a guard over the mouth kept the handlers safe from bites
these inventions spread from one valley to the next by copying
text: In earlier times, harnessing a draft animal ran up against a blunt mechanical problem, and it went unsolved for a long while. The strap crossed the throat, and the harder the beast pulled, the tighter it squeezed the windpipe. Breathing gave out before the load had properly moved, so most of the animal's strength was simply thrown away. The remedy lay in moving the point that took the strain. Craftsmen built a padded collar to rest on the shoulders, which let the animal breathe freely while it pulled, and the weight it could shift rose sharply. A soft head piece came next, giving the driver a way to steer without cutting into the muzzle, and a light guard over the mouth kept handlers clear of bites during awkward turns. Workshops copied one another from valley to valley, and the design traveled on with no name attached to it.

units: birds and mammals feed their young in different ways
nestlings come out of the egg almost bare
a fine insulating down protects them from the cold
the parent birds carry food in from outside the nest
these trips back and forth are very frequent
young mammals take a food made by their mother
young mammals press against one another to keep their heat
both methods answer the same feeding need
text: Set a clutch of hatchlings beside a litter of young mammals and what you see is two different answers worked out for one and the same demand. In the nest, the chicks break out of the shell almost bare, and only a thin, insulating down stands between their skin and the cold. Every mouthful has to be carried in from outside, so the parents shuttle back and forth from first light until dark, with barely a pause between one trip and the next. Among mammals the food comes from the mother's own body, so it is there whenever it is wanted, and no journey is needed to fetch it. The young pile in against one another and hold on to their heat while the adults are away. What differs, then, is where the food comes from and how far the parents have to roam. The need being met is exactly the same on either side.

units: a naturalist made an inventory of the shelters on a wooded slope
a tunnel dug under a stump housed a rodent
she never once caught sight of that occupant
a hollow under roots served as a den for a carnivore
birds had built their nests in the cracks of a fallen wall
insects lived under the loosened bark of dead trunks
the shelters changed occupants over the course of the season
she handed her notes to a research team, which published them
text: A naturalist spent her days on a wooded slope, setting down in a list every shelter she could find and whatever was housed in it. She began with the burrows that had been cut into the hillside. One of them opened under a rotting stump and belonged to a rodent she never once laid eyes on. Further along she found a den wedged beneath a knot of roots, lined with hair and dry twigs, and in use by a carnivore of middling size. Then came the cracks in a fallen wall, packed with birds' nests, and the loose bark of dead trunks, alive underneath with insects too small to count. What struck her hardest of all was the turnover of the tenants. A shelter left empty was taken over again before the season was out. She handed her notes over to a research team, and they put the whole lot into print without delay.

units: you must first pick a spot sheltered from the wind
the feeder is fixed high up, out of reach of predators
dry seed is poured into it
salty leftovers must be kept out
a shallow dish of water is set beside it
the water must be changed as soon as it turns cloudy
the feeder must be washed regularly to stop disease from spreading
the animals should be watched from a distance without going closer
the feeding must not be broken off suddenly in the cold season
text: So you want to feed the birds in the orchard, and you would rather do it properly than badly. Start by finding a corner out of the wind, open enough to see across, and awkward for a cat to climb. Hang the feeder high, well clear of any low branch, then fill it with dry seed. Never any salty scraps left over from a meal. Set a shallow dish of water beside it, a wide saucer will do, and change the water the moment it turns cloudy. Every other week, scrub the whole thing out with hot water, because droppings build up and pass disease along, and a dirty feeder does more harm than no feeder at all. Watch your visitors from a distance and stay back, or they will quit the orchard altogether. One last thing, and it matters more than the rest: once the cold season has set in, do not cut the food off all at once.

units: the level of a body of water fell after a dry season
a strip of mud linking the shore to the islet was laid bare
predators from the land took that crossing
the nests set on the ground were raided
the adult birds abandoned the breeding site
part of the colony settled on a steep bank
the wardens had a channel cut to isolate the islet
some pairs came back to lay the following season
the original numbers were never recovered
text: A dry season pulled the water level down, and that drop on its own was enough to undo the whole bird colony that had been nesting on the islet out in the middle. As it fell back, the water laid bare a tongue of mud running from the shore out to the islet, and carnivores prowling the edge were across it on the first night. Nests sitting on open ground were raided, the eggs lost, and the adults walked away from a site their kind had used for generations. Part of the colony moved to a steep rocky bank, harder to reach but open to the spray, where almost nothing hatched. Volunteers raised the alarm, and the wardens who look after the place had a narrow channel cut, so that the islet could no longer be reached on foot. The next season some pairs came back to lay. The old numbers, though, were never seen again.

units: a shelter is dug into a bank between roots
brambles hide its entrance
the rains used to flood the tunnel
the soaked bedding turned icy for the animal
a second opening was cut higher up the bank
a dry chamber was hollowed out above the level the water reached
dry grass lines the floor of that chamber
the old tunnel now carries the rain away
text: Low in the bank a dark mouth runs in between the roots, screened so well by brambles that a walker would go straight past and notice nothing. The passage slopes down, its walls rubbed smooth by fur going through, over and over. When the rains came, water ran along the slope and gathered at the bottom of the tunnel. The soaked bedding turned icy, and the animal lay shivering on it. So a second mouth was cut higher up the bank, and from there a shaft climbed to a dry chamber, hollowed out above the line the water had reached. Brittle grass, dragged in from the meadow next door, covers the floor of it now, and the warmth of a sleeping body holds there without trouble. The old passage carries the rain instead, swallowing it and letting it out lower down, well away from the bed.

units: the writer compares rearing in a closed space and rearing on open range
a closed space makes each animal easy to tell apart and to examine
an injury is picked up early there
confinement helps parasites move around
open range builds up the muscle of the animals
open range cuts down joint trouble
the scattering of the animals makes health checks hard
the writer advises running both systems by age and by season
he asks that the choice rest on measurements and not on beliefs
text: Pitting closed housing against open range settles very little in the end, and the demand from both camps for a single verdict only coarsens the argument. Shut in, an animal can be told apart from the rest, weighed, handled, looked over, and a wound shows up while it is still small. That same closeness gathers parasites and hands them around the herd. Out on open ground the account turns over: muscle builds, joints give less trouble, but the animals scatter, and keeping a check on their health becomes a matter of luck. A sensible holding will run both systems, then, sorting the stock by age and by season instead of raising either method into doctrine. What is still wanting is the habit of settling such choices by what has been measured, and not by what the keeper happens to believe in his own heart.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman running a care center looks after injured animals
she worked as a veterinary assistant before setting up her shelter
the shelter sits in an abandoned farm
she feeds the nestlings with tweezers at short intervals
she holds fractured wings still and watches them mend
she teaches volunteers to take hold of a frightened animal without hurting it
she writes down every arrival in a register
she releases the healed animals well away from busy roads
she refuses to give a name to the animals she takes in
text: The woman who runs the care center gives her days to animals that will never be hers. She started out as a veterinary assistant, learning how to hold a struggling creature, how to set a splint, how to read a picture of a broken bone, and later she opened her own shelter in a farm that had stood empty for years. The work falls into fixed tasks. She feeds the nestlings with tweezers, a little at a time, from first light until dusk. She binds broken wings, watches the weight come back onto them, changes the dressings. She trains volunteers, showing them how to take hold of a frightened animal without hurting it or getting bitten. She writes down every arrival in a thick register: the species, the injury, how it ended. The ones that mend she lets go well away from busy roads, and she gives none of them a name.

units: a factual book about animals that live by night is assessed
the opening sets down observations made in the field
that opening convinces the reviewer
the middle chapters lay out measurements from work on captive animals
that part is judged too dry to read
it still brings solid knowledge about hearing and finding one's way
the closing pages give protective recommendations that stay too vague
the drawn plates are held to be the great success of the book
the reviewer advises reading it all the same
text: The book opens with notebooks kept after dark, and that opening wins you over at once. The author waits out long stretches for nothing, sets down hopes that come to nothing, and records brief meetings with animals that sense her long before she can make them out. Then the tone shifts. The middle chapters lay out run after run of measurements taken from captive animals, in prose so dry that the reading bogs down completely. Solid material sits in there all the same, on hearing and on how such animals find their way. The closing pages offer a list of protective measures, too broad, unhappily, to commit anyone to anything. The drawn plates are another matter: they catch posture and movement so well that they carry the book on their own. Worth reading, then, soft middle and all.

units: the writer is keeping the dog of a close friend who has gone traveling
the animal whined at night behind the bedroom door
it refused to eat its ration
it damaged the floor with its claws whenever she moved away
the writer first read this behavior as a reproach
a training specialist explained that the animal was looking for a steady reassuring landmark
she was advised to keep the outings regular and to put the bedding near the entrance
the dog now sleeps against a cloth that carries the smell of its owner
text: Your dog stayed with me while you were away, and I am writing at last with the relief of someone who has found the way out. The first nights were bad. He whined behind my bedroom door, left his ration untouched, and raked the floorboards with his claws the moment I stepped away from him. I took it as a reproach for your leaving. Then a trainer set me straight: the animal was hunting for a steady landmark, not for a punishment he had earned. She told me to walk him at the same hours every day, to hang his lead where his nose could reach it, and to push his bedding against the wall by the front door. He settles there now as soon as the light goes, curls into the cloth that still holds your smell, and waits for the lock to turn without a sound. He eats, he runs, he sleeps hard. You will find a calm companion, and a friend rather pleased with herself.

units: specialists in animal behavior refuse to treat the two kinds of group as one thing
in a herd of grazing animals each beast adjusts to its nearest neighbors
no member of that group holds an overall view of the movement
among bees the scouts come back and pass on directions through their movements
the colony keeps the site that gathers the most support
the first group exchanges body postures and changes of pace
the second group exchanges content comparable to a reasoned proposal
the first reacts almost instantly while the decision of the second takes several days
text: Ask whether a herd and a swarm run on one and the same machinery, and researchers who study animal behavior will tell you no. In a herd, every beast trims its own path to the ones moving beside it, and the shape of the whole comes out of nothing but those local corrections. No single animal holds the plan of the movement. A swarm works on another principle altogether. Scouts fly back and spell out directions through the way they move, and the colony settles on the site that draws the most backing. So what separates the two systems? The kind of signal each one carries. A herd passes along a stance, a burst of speed, the turn of a head. A swarm passes along content, something close to a case being argued. And what about speed? A herd answers within a fraction of a second. A swarm weighs the matter for days on end before it lifts off.

units: a livestock keeper set out her worries to a veterinary practitioner
she reported that the animals had been eating less grass for a week
she added that the chewing of the cud lasted less time than usual
the practitioner examined the teeth of the animals
he then checked the quality of the water on offer
he also judged the fodder too poor in fiber
he recommended keeping the weakened animals apart from the group
he promised to come back and check the state of the herd
text: The keeper laid out her worries to the vet who had come to look over her animals. She told him her cows had been grazing less for a week, that they stopped chewing the cud earlier than usual, and that one had lain down in the middle of the pasture. The practitioner answered that he would work through three leads in order. He began with the teeth of each animal, since one broken tooth is enough to put a cow off her chewing.
