He moved on to the trough, drawing water from a pipe that struck him as fouled. He finished with the fodder, which he judged too poor in fiber and badly suited to their digestion. Before leaving, he advised her to keep the weakened animals apart, to note every refusal of feed, and to call his office if intake did not climb back. He promised to come by again and check the herd.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the coming together of humans and wild animals began with a mutual acceptance
predators came to look for the waste left around the camps
the least fearful individuals ended up being fed
hunting groups mixing humans and dog like animals took shape
grazing animals were then penned as a living store of meat
those beasts were sorted for their calm and for their fleece
the rise of crops created a need for animals able to pull loads
cats were tolerated to keep rodents away from the grain stores
text: Domestication begins with no decision at all. It begins with a truce that neither side ever spelled out. Meat eaters prowled the edges of the hunting camps, drawn by the scraps thrown aside there. The warier ones bolted at any noise. The bolder ones lingered, and in the end they were fed by hand. Out of that closeness came the mixed pack, human and animal running down the same game together. Next came the penning of grazing beasts, held at first as meat kept alive, then picked over for a quiet temper and for a thick fleece. Tilled ground raised a demand of another kind, and the sturdiest animals were harnessed to drag the loads. Later, cats were suffered in the grain stores, where they held the rodents off the harvest. Every stage lengthened the list of species bound to us, and reshaped their bodies as much as their tempers.

units: one sometimes finds on the ground a thin see through casing left by a reptile
the outer layer of a snake skin does not stretch as the animal grows longer
that stiffness forces the reptile to get rid of its old casing
a fresh layer builds up underneath the old one
a fluid slips between the two layers and lifts them apart
the eyes of the animal turn cloudy during this phase
the snake hunts little and stays hidden while its sight is poor
it rubs its snout against a stone to start the peeling
text: Ever picked up one of those see through husks at the edge of a path and wondered what animal could have left it lying there? That is a snake skin, and the whole business comes down to a simple flaw in the design. The casing that shields the reptile will not stretch. It stays stiff while the animal underneath keeps getting longer. So it has to shed. A fresh layer builds up below, then a fluid works its way between the two and lifts them apart. While that is going on, the eyes turn a milky blue and the snake can barely see a thing. So it hardly hunts, and tucks itself away under a stump. Once the split is complete, it scrapes its snout against a rough stone, catches the lip of the old casing, and crawls straight out of it the way you peel off a sock. What you find lying on the ground is that worn out coat.

units: a print left in the mud near a pen set off the alarm
ewes had been killed during the night
the sheep farmers blamed the losses on a wild meat eater
a naturalist judged the print too broad for that idea
cameras that fire on movement were put in place
the pictures showed two dogs running loose without an owner
the owners of the dogs were traced and held to account
an electrified fence and a night watch put an end to the attacks
text: The alarm went up over a single print in the mud, a few steps from a pen where three ewes had been killed during the night. Sheep farmers up the valley named a wild meat eater at once, and asked for leave to go out and shoot it. The naturalist sent to the spot refused to sign off on that. The pad printed in the mud looked too broad to her, and the bites sat wrong for a practiced killer. On her word, cameras that fire on movement were strung along the fences and left there. The pictures, collected a week later, showed two dogs running loose across the field, collars still around their necks. Their owners were traced without much trouble and held to account for the losses. The local council paid for an electrified fence and for a watch through the dark hours, and the killing stopped dead.

units: two ways exist of watching wild birds
the first is to put out food that draws them in
this way quickly brings the bolder species close
it changes the behavior of the birds one claims to study
the second is to sit motionless inside a screen of branches
it demands staying quiet through a long wait
it shows behavior that food never brings about
it is advised to begin with the first way and then take up the second
text: Before you carry your binoculars down to the hedge, settle on one of the two ways of coming at birds, because they will hand you very different things. The first lays out bait: a scatter of seed on a board, a lump of fat tied to a low branch. The bolder species turn up fast, counting them is easy, and what you end up watching are guests at a table rather than free birds. The second asks you to build a screen of branches, to sit down inside it before first light, and to hold still. The wait runs long and the cold creeps in through everything you wear. In return you catch the display, the squabble over a dry stem, the heavy flight of a bird carrying nest material home. Start with the bait until the shapes are familiar. Move to the screen once the names come to you without a pause.

units: a team of researchers is finishing the yearly count of a sea bird colony
the count covers occupied nests and not the adults in view
the breeding numbers have fallen against the previous campaign
the fish these birds live on has moved into deeper water
the adults range further out to feed
the eggs are left alone more often than before
gulls take advantage of these absences to plunder the nests
the team recommends limiting the access of walkers to the foot of the cliffs
text: A team of researchers has wrapped up the yearly survey of a colony lodged on the coastal cliffs, and their findings come in four parts. Numbers first. The count rests on occupied nests, a steadier measure than the adults in view at any one moment, and the total has dropped sharply against the previous campaign. Feeding next. The fish the species lives on has moved into deeper water, which stretches out every trip the birds make. Breeding after that. The adults range further from the rock, eggs sit uncovered that ought to be brooded, and gulls with an eye for the gap plunder the exposed nests. Access last. The team urges closing the foot of the cliffs to walkers through the sensitive weeks, a modest step by its own account, but one that can be taken without any delay at all.

units: the mare leaves her stall when the gate opens
she halts and reads the air before going on
she shakes her whole coat to rid it of the damp
she rolls on her back in a sandy hollow
she eats the grass of the pasture for a long stretch
she heads for the trough set under a tree
she stays on her feet and dozes in the shade of the leaves
she waits near the rail for someone to come and bring her in
text: The moment the gate swings open, the mare steps clear of her stall and stops, nostrils flared, to read the air of the pasture. She goes three paces on, then shakes herself from crest to tail until the damp of the night leaves her coat in fine drops. The roll follows. She folds her forelegs, tips onto her flank, works her back into a sandy hollow, and rises with a thrust of the loins. Then she grazes without lifting her head, moving in short even shifts along the fence, tearing at the rich growth of the margins and passing over the coarse tufts of the middle, until the heat turns her toward the trough standing under the tree. There she drinks, stays on her feet, one hind leg resting, eyelids heavy, ears turning. Late in the day she comes back to the rail and waits, still, for someone to lead her in.

units: wildlife parks justify their existence by the saving of species
their opponents hold that confinement unmakes the animals
the ground on offer is far smaller than the range covered in freedom
this restriction brings on repeated movements in meat eaters
the food handed out removes any active searching
animals born in captivity survive badly once released
the writer proposes keeping these parks for species genuinely at risk
the writer suggests funding the protection of wild habitat with the gate money
text: Wildlife parks defend themselves by pointing to the species they save. Their critics answer that confinement unmakes the very animal it claims to shield. The argument deserves to be followed to its end, because one effect pulls the next along. An enclosure, however generous, offers ground that bears no comparison with the range a meat eater covers when it is free. Out of that shrinkage come the mechanical journeys back and forth along the bars, familiar to every keeper. Food handed over at fixed hours then wipes out the search, and with it any schooling in the hunt. It follows that beasts born behind a grille rarely last long when they are turned back into the wild. The conclusion holds, to my mind. Keep these parks for species genuinely at risk, and turn the gate money over to the defense of wild habitat.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the main figure looks after the animals at a shelter
she walks into the enclosure before the sky lightens
she likens her work to that of an interpreter
a thick-furred mammal states its needs differently from a bird
she raises motherless newborns on a bottle
she keeps her distance when a grown animal is hurt
she compares her patience to that of someone tending a plot of ground
her colleagues credit her with sensing pain before any visible sign
she puts that reputation down to close and repeated watching
text: The keeper crosses the enclosure before the sky begins to lighten, a bucket of feed braced against her hip. Her work, she likes to say, is closer to an interpreter's than anyone expects: she has to listen to languages that carry no words. A shaggy mammal rubbing itself along the fence asks for something quite different from a bird beating its wings behind glass. With the newborns she learns to bring up orphans on a bottle once the mother has gone; with wounded grown animals she does nothing but watch from a distance. Her patience belongs to someone tending a plot of ground, since a recovery cannot be hurried, only walked beside. The rest of the staff swear she can sense pain before the animal ever limps. She laughs at that and says she simply looks harder, and more often, and never in a rush.

units: the text weighs up a film about wildlife
the assessment falls into three aspects
the steadiness of the long takes is judged excellent
one sequence follows a bird of prey settling on a branch
the added music drowns the sound recorded on the spot
the commentary mixes up two different bodily states
one passage shows young that have just left the teat
that passage is held to be the best in the film
the crew never stated how long the watching sessions lasted
text: The wildlife film that went out last week deserves to be weighed on three separate counts rather than one. Visually it is faultless: the long takes hold rock steady, without a tremor, while the camera tracks a bird of prey coming down to settle on a branch. The sound is another matter altogether. Recording made on the spot keeps giving way to a wash of music that flattens the rustle of leaves and the scrape of feathers. Scientifically, the commentary blurs two states that are nothing alike, the animal sunk in winter sleep and the one that merely dozes off in spells, and the slip weakens an argument otherwise carefully built. What saves the picture is the long stretch given to the young the female has just weaned: no cutting tricks, only gestures handed on. A pity the crew never said how long it sat waiting in the field.

units: the letter is addressed to a woman living in the house next door
it concerns a ginger cat that moves from one plot to the other
the writer saw it at dusk hidden under a hedge
the animal was watching birds that had come to drink
the next day it settled on a window ledge
the writer first assumed it belonged to a tenant
the worn collar and the animal's thinness proved her wrong
she leaves it water but refuses to feed it
the animal walks badly on one hind leg
text: Dear neighbor, I am writing to you about the ginger cat that comes and goes between our two gardens. Late last week I caught sight of him at dusk, flattened under the hedge, keeping watch on the birds that come down to drink at the basin. The next morning he cleared the low wall and settled himself on the ledge of my window, quite at his ease. My first thought was that he belonged to the tenant at the far end, until I noticed the worn collar and how thin he has grown since. I have been leaving fresh water out for him, though I will not feed him, as I would rather he did not attach himself to my yard. Should you know who owns him, I would be grateful if you would pass the word along, since he favors one hind leg and walks poorly on it. I am happy to talk this over in person. With kind regards.

units: the wall of the egg grows thinner from the inside
the embryo draws off the calcium meant for its skeleton
a longer incubation yields a more finished young one
that young one moves about as soon as it leaves the shell
other species are born without feathers and without sight
this strategy shortens the time the female stays still over the clutch
it therefore lowers the risk of being spotted by a hunter
the adults must then feed young that cannot move
neither strategy is presented as the better one
text: What goes on inside an egg in the last hours before it opens? The shell grows thinner from within, because the embryo is drawing out the calcium that its skeleton needs. Why do some chicks arrive in down and others arrive bare? It turns on how long the sitting runs: the longer it lasts, the more finished the chick, ready to run about the moment it works its way free of the shell. And what does a species gain by hatching young that are naked and blind? It cuts short the stretch of time the female must hold still over the clutch, which lowers her chances of being picked out by a hunter. The bill comes later, when the parents have to feed a whole brood that cannot yet stir. So does one method win out over the other? No. Each answers what its surroundings demand, and neither would pay off elsewhere.

units: someone from the neighborhood tells of his troubles with keeping animals
his rabbits were digging under the fence and getting out
the runaways headed for the vegetable patch at the far end
the man had already sunk the wire mesh deeper
the animals were slipping through a gap he had not found
his daughter suggests laying a wide board flat against the fence
a digging animal starts its hole at the foot of the barrier
it gives up once it meets a hard surface
the family nailed boards down and then poured gravel over them
there has been no escape since
text: My neighbor stopped me at the gate to tell me the whole saga of his rabbits. They kept digging under the wire, he said, and heading straight for the vegetable patch at the far end. I asked whether he had tried sinking the mesh deeper. He had, he told me, and they still squeezed out through some gap he had never managed to find. His daughter was standing there listening, and she said, why not lay a wide board flat on the ground, right up against the fence. It struck me as sharp: an animal that digs goes at the base of whatever stands in its way, and once it meets something hard it quits. So they nailed the boards down and tipped gravel over the wood. Not one has got out since. He still laughs about it, because he was picturing a wall and she settled it with scrap lumber.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: two ways of taming animals existed at the same time
the first came about with no human intent
animals drew near the camps for the food scraps
they bred there alongside people
the second way rested on a choice made by keepers
the keepers held on to the calm animals and put aside the aggressive ones
this sorting produced bloodlines that do not exist in the wild
bones found in refuse heaps bear witness to the first process
pens and tethers bear witness to the second
the first process gave companions and the second gave herds
text: Two paths to taming ran side by side long before writing, and researchers still tell them apart. The first owed nothing to human intent. Animals drifted toward the camps for the scraps, put up with people at close range, and went on breeding right there, so the sorting happened with nobody meaning it. The second path was a matter of choice: keepers held on to the quietest beasts, weeded out the ones that turned on them, and within a handful of generations shaped bloodlines the wild had never produced. Bones dug out of old refuse heaps tell the first story. Pens and tethers tell the second. Specialists point out that one road delivered companions and the other delivered herds. The two overlap, of course, since an animal that came close by accident is one evening kept on purpose.

units: the text describes what a coat reveals
an even shade hides the animal in a stretch of sand or grass
a coat marked with spots mimics foliage shot through with light
those spots break up the animal's outline
tousled hair traps air against the skin
such hair keeps the body warm without weighing it down
swimmers wear a dense pelt that holds water off the skin
every coat also gives off a smell
a dog nosing a trunk picks up there that one of its own went by
the newly born wear a down that a breath will shift
text: A coat tells a story, and the eye has to work at it before the story comes clear. Start with plain color, which melts an animal into a wide stretch of sand or dry grass. Then the dappled coat, whose shadows mimic leaves punched through with light and break up the line of the back. Then the shaggy hair, tousled by wind, holding a layer of air against the skin and keeping the body warm with no weight to it. Then the sleek thick pelt of the swimmers, packed so tight that water slides straight across and never once reaches skin. Every coat carries a smell as well, and the smell travels: a dog nosing a trunk reads there that one of its own went by. Last of all comes the down of the newly born, so slight that a breath will shift it. Together they make up a language that nobody speaks aloud.

units: a team strung a fine net between two poles at the edge of a copse
the birds caught were measured and weighed and then let go
one bird marked the season before was taken again at the same spot
that second capture allowed a comparison of mass from one season to the next
the bird had lost a marked amount of weight
the loss fitted with a hard winter
the technician added two measurements to the protocol
she recorded wing length and the state of the plumage
the final report calls for longer watching of the site
the gear was left standing for the following season
text: At the start of the ringing season the team strung a fine net between two poles along the edge of a copse. Every bird that came in was measured, set on a field scale, and let go again in under a minute of handling. On the third evening a bird ringed the season before turned up in the same net, and that opened the way to comparing its mass from one season to the next. The figures showed a marked loss of weight, in keeping with a hard winter behind it. The technician changed the protocol on the spot: from then on she also took wing length and noted the state of the feathers, both of them signs of wear. By the close of the campaign the file held dozens of usable lines. The final report argues that the site deserves watching without a break, and the gear was left standing where it was.

units: a wall sheltered from the prevailing wind should be chosen
an exposed entrance lets rain in and chills the eggs
the support must be firm because a box that sways frightens the occupants
the entrance hole must stay narrow
a wide opening makes it easy for predators to get in
the box must hang beyond the reach of cats
no branch alongside should serve as a foothold
the inside should not be lined because the occupants bring their own material
a damp lining rots the brood
a clean-out at the end of the season clears parasites that would harm the next clutch
text: Before you put up a nesting box for small birds, pick a wall that lies out of the prevailing wind, since an exposed entrance takes in rain and chills the eggs inside. Screw the back plate to something solid and unmoving, because a box that sways unsettles the occupants and they will leave it at the first alarm. Cut the entrance hole narrow, as a wide one makes life far too easy for predators. Hang the whole thing beyond the reach of cats, shoulder height at the very least, and with no branch alongside that could serve as a foothold. Do not line the inside of it: the birds bring their own material, and a damp lining holds a moisture that rots the brood. Clean the cavity out once the season has ended, since the parasites piling up in the debris will spoil the clutch that follows.

units: walkers reported that the young ducks along a canal were disappearing
an association of naturalists looked into what was happening
the concrete slope kept the young from getting out of the water
the bread thrown in by passersby drew rodents
those rodents wrecked the nests
the local authority put in sloping wooden ramps that run below the surface
the young can climb these ramps without help
signs tell people that bread harms the birds
a later count found more surviving young
those in charge judge one season too little to draw a conclusion
text: Along the banks of a canal in town, walkers had been reporting for weeks that the duck broods were vanishing. An association of naturalists looked into it and came back with two causes. The concrete slope gave the ducklings no way out of the water, and rats drawn by the bread that passersby toss in were raiding the nests. The local authority began by fitting wooden ramps, set at a steep angle and running below the surface, which the young can climb up without help. Signs went up next, explaining that bread does the birds no good at all and feeds the rodents instead. A count taken when the warm season came round again turned up more surviving young than the year before. Those running the project are staying careful: one season proves nothing, and the watching will go on.

units: different groups of animals share the same shore without clashing
the web-footed birds search the mud with their bills
these birds leave star-shaped prints in the mud
squat rodents live in the reed belt
these rodents dig tunnels and eat the young stems
their soft coats keep the damp away
the insects hold to the dry part of the slope
the insects feed the animals that fly
the shore reads as three levels stacked one above another
text: Three kinds of creature share the pond's edge, and none of them crowds the others. Web-footed birds work the soft mud, probing the silt with their bills and stamping star-shaped prints wherever they pass. Higher up, where the reeds lie flattened, squat rodents burrow tunnels and gnaw the tender stems down to the pith; their downy coats shed the damp and hold in warmth. On the dry slope the insects take over, smaller, harder to spot, past counting. They spin, they bore, they haul, and they feed everything that flies overhead. Watch long enough and the bank sorts itself into three floors stacked one above another: water, mud, cropped grass. Each floor sets its own food, its own hours, its own quiet. The edge is no single stretch of scenery but a pile of narrow territories, stitched together.

units: the writer holds that public argument has not kept up with tracking methods
counting was first done by eye and written down on paper
colored marks then made it possible to follow one animal
those marks unsettled the species least willing to be approached
shrunken transmitters now record movement without a break
these devices also measure how deep a dive goes and how fast a heart beats
the writer judges that each advance shifts the moral problem instead of settling it
a light device still changes what a bird spends in energy
the writer asks that an outside body approve every fitting
text: Let it be said plainly: watching wild populations has become a different practice, and public argument has not kept pace. At first people counted by eye, notebook in hand, with every bias such a method carries. Then came bands and colored marks, which let a single animal be followed but unsettled the shyest species. Shrunken transmitters came after, reading movement without a break, down to how deep a dive goes and how fast a heart beats. Every technical step has shifted the moral question instead of settling it. A sensor weighs almost nothing, yet it alters how a migrating bird cuts the air and what the flight costs it in energy. My own stand is firm. Nothing should be fitted unless it answers a stated question, unless an outside body has cleared it, and it should come off once the data stops being usable.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman who looks after the horses had not aimed for this job
a knee injury pushed her out of her first trade
that injury forces her to move without haste
the fearful animals came close to her before the others did
she names each move aloud before any contact
stubborn animals turn biddable within a season
nearby places send her the animals written off as hopeless
she credits a limit set on her body rather than a gift
she forbids the beginners she trains to move at a run
text: The keeper in charge of the horse stalls never set out to hold that post. A knee injury had ended her work in the harness shop, and the same injury steered her toward the boxes. Because she limped, she moved slowly, and the nervous animals, used to quick hands, came to her before any of the calmer ones did. Out of that forced slowness a method grew. She learned to name each move aloud before her hand reached out, and within a single season the balkiest of them turned biddable. Word spread to the shelters nearby, which began sending her the cases everyone else had given up on. She refuses the word gift. Her advantage, she says, comes from a limit set on her body, and anyone willing to slow down would get the same result. She trains apprentices now, and forbids them to run down the aisles.

units: the reviewer finds the pictures in the film a success
the reviewer faults the narration for handing the animals human motives
that shortcut suggests survival comes from weighing options
the viewer leaves moved but no better informed
the last part of the film runs without narration
those sequences were shot at night with a thermal camera
they follow a pack of wolves crossing a wooded corridor
having no speech makes that sequence truer than the opening of the film
text: Nothing is wrong with the pictures in this wildlife film: the framing holds, the patience shows, every surface comes through with precision. The narration is what lets it down. It hands the animals human motives, the she-wolf decides, the hawk chooses, the colony takes revenge, and that shortcut weakens the case, since it suggests survival comes down to weighing options. You leave moved and none the wiser. The cure was already at hand, and the director found it in the closing stretch: the night footage, caught on a thermal camera, runs almost without a word. A pack crosses a wooded corridor, halts, moves on, and no sentence arrives to tell us what the silence means. All at once the scene is truer than everything before it. The lesson holds for the whole genre. Filming is enough, explaining betrays.

units: the writer writes to someone he knows about two cats
the striped cat was already hanging around behind the workshop
a second cat with ginger fur turned up not long ago
the striped cat barely hunts and sleeps on the warm sheet metal
the ginger cat is thin and eats greedily
the ginger cat keeps its distance from people
the writer tried feeding them in one place from two bowls
the ginger one ate what was in both bowls
the writer is thinking of staggering the meals of the two animals
text: Remember the striped cat that hung around behind the workshop? He has a rival now, and the gap between the two is worth a letter. The striped one barely hunts. He sleeps on the warm sheet metal and waits to be served, and he purrs the moment a door creaks. The newcomer is ginger, thin, ravenous, and will not let anyone within three steps of him. One of them has worked out that people are a supply, the other has them down as a threat. Where one begs, the other steals. I tried feeding them together, two bowls set well apart, and it was a poor idea. The ginger one emptied both, and the striped one stared at me as though I had sold him out. So I will stagger the meals, one at first light and one after dark, and let them settle it. Come by some evening and watch, you will laugh. Write if you want me to keep the ginger one until autumn.

units: a specialist in animal behavior answers the reporter's questions
the subject is the massed flights of birds above river mouths
the specialist puts forward three explanations
living in a crowd lowers the odds that any one bird is taken
the birds find food by watching those that come back full
the flock locates the fish without a leader pointing the way
birds pressed close hold their heat better through the night halts
the specialist denies that these flights have a ranking
each bird matches its speed to whoever flies nearest
text: We put the question of massed bird flights above the river mouths to a specialist in animal behavior. Is there any organization behind those drifting clouds? Her answer came in three parts. Safety comes first: a crowd spreads the risk around, and any single bird stands less chance of being taken while it travels inside a shifting mass. Information comes second: the ones arriving late follow those coming back full, and the whole flock learns where the fish are without any leader pointing the way. Heat comes third, for pressed close through the night halts, the birds lose far less of it. Is there a ranking all the same? She will not have it. What she describes are local rules, each bird matching its speed to whoever flies nearest, and a shape over the whole that nobody ever intended.

units: the herdsman comes to warn before sunrise
he reports that one animal is missing
the neighbor holds that the fog makes any search pointless
the herdsman answers that the animal has been moving badly since the day before
three people set out together to look for the animal
the herdsman explains that the animal follows smells instead of its own kind
the neighbor hears breathing behind some brambles
the animal is found lying down and alive at the foot of the slope
the herdsman carries the animal back on his shoulders
text: Before sunrise the old herdsman knocked at the shutter and said one of the animals had not come in. My neighbor, still in her shawl, told him nobody goes looking for a horned beast in fog, and that waiting would serve better. He answered that it had been limping since the day before and could not have gone far. The three of us set out. On the path he explained he had seen it drift toward the ravine, and that it had the fault of following smells rather than its own kind. Then my neighbor said she could hear breathing, down there, behind the brambles. The herdsman climbed down, pushed the branches apart and called up that she was there, lying still and alive. He carried her back on his shoulders without one word of complaint. Walking home he said only that the next outing would be hers alone, and he laughed under his breath.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: taming reached first for the species that put up with human presence
a herd species already lives inside a ladder of rank
such a species grants an outsider the top place
a solitary territorial species never concedes that place to an outsider
human groups held on to the lines whose young could bear being close
individuals that could not be approached bred poorly behind fences
the sorting therefore happened with no plan behind it
tamed animals show a shorter jaw and drooping ears
these traits show up together because they trace back to the same cells of the embryo
text: Taming did not begin with the most useful of the wild species but with the most tolerant ones. A herd animal already lives inside a ladder of rank, so it will readily grant an outsider the top place, something a solitary, territorial animal never concedes. One consequence follows at once: human groups held on only to the lines whose young could bear being close. The wary ones fled or struck out, and they bred poorly behind fences, so the sorting happened with almost no plan behind it. Build and temper changed together as a result: the jaw shortened, the ears drooped, aggression fell away, adulthood arrived later. Those traits show up as a set because they trace back to the same cells in the embryo. Tameness, then, was never taught to anything at all. It was simply harvested.

units: amphibians leave the woods for the ponds where they hatched
their route often crosses a road
these web-footed animals advance in short hops
they freeze in the glare of headlights
they travel mostly after sunset
a local population can die out within three seasons
one answer is a low fence steering the animals toward a duct
the structure costs a lot but works with nobody watching it
a second answer closes the road on the nights of heaviest migration
both answers call for the usual crossings to have been mapped beforehand
text: When the mild season comes back, amphibians leave the woods for the ponds where they hatched. Their route often crosses a road, and the losses there run high: these web-footed creatures advance in short hops, freeze in the glare of headlights, and travel mostly after sunset, when traffic is still moving fast. A local population can die out within three seasons. Two answers have been tested. The first is a low fence set along the roadside, steering the night travelers toward a duct that runs beneath the surface. The structure costs a great deal, but it works with nobody watching it. The second, far lighter, closes the road on the nights when the migration is heaviest. Both call for the usual crossings to have been mapped beforehand, and only patient watching makes that possible.

units: two young dogs of the same age reached the shelter on the same evening
the first dog is heavy-set and flecked with gray
the first dog puts up with handling and asks for contact
the second dog flinches at noise and comes out only once it is dark
the staff thought the first dog would be taken very fast
it was the second dog that left the shelter first
a family kept her precisely because she stayed out of sight
that family found their home too quiet for a restless animal
the first dog waited until autumn
the manager concludes that the friendliest animal is not the one taken first
text: Nobody would have bet on the pup that hid at the back of its kennel. Two dogs of the same age had been left at the shelter on the same evening, and the staff never tired of comparing them. The first was heavy-set and flecked with gray, and she put up with any handling. She ate everything, slept anywhere, and asked for a hand on her head each time a door opened. The second flinched at the clatter of a bucket and came out of her shelter only once it was dark. The keepers reckoned the first would be gone in a week. It was the second who found a home first. A family chose her exactly because she stayed out of sight, saying a quiet household suited a restless animal badly. The flecked one waited until autumn, passed over by visitors who found her pushy. The manager draws a lesson he keeps repeating: the friendliest animal is not the one who leaves first.

units: a resin applied to the hair increases its grip
the hair drags and then releases the string over and over
this repetition produces a steady oscillation
the speed of the oscillation sets the note that is heard
a string on its own moves too little air
the vibration travels through a piece standing on the body
the body of the instrument begins to move in turn
widening the vibrating surface makes the sound louder
text: Draw a bow across a tight string and the sound starts with a grab so small that the ear never notices it happening. Rosin rubbed into the hair leaves it faintly sticky. So the hair takes hold of the string, drags it a whisker's distance sideways, then lets go. The string springs back, the hair seizes it again, and the cycle repeats without a break. That steady catch and release sets up an even vibration, and how fast it repeats is what fixes the pitch you hear. A string on its own pushes far too little air to carry across a room. It hands its motion instead to the bridge, a thin slip of wood standing upright on the belly. The bridge rocks that broad panel, which in turn shoves a much larger body of air. The sound swells because the surface doing the vibrating has been made wide.

units: the head of the percussion instrument sounded dull at the end of the session
the music director halts the session and sends for the repairer
the dry air had shrunk the animal skin
tightening the fixings would have made things worse
the repairer chooses to add moisture to the room
containers full of water are set around the platform
the group carries on rehearsing in another room
with the suppleness back, a slight adjustment restores the true pitch
text: The rehearsal was nearly over when the timpanist noticed that her drum had stopped answering. Under the stick the head gave back a flat thud, no depth in it, as though every trace of tension had drained away. The conductor stopped the players and sent for the craftsman who looked after the instruments. He found that the very dry air of the hall had shrunk the natural skin, stretched for weeks over the copper bowl. Turning the screws down would only have deepened the imbalance, and it might have split the skin outright. He suggested something gentler: damp the room little by little and let the head slacken on its own. Wide basins of water were set around the platform, and the players moved to another hall to finish. By morning the skin had its give back, and two turns of a key brought the pitch home.

units: you should examine two blades before fitting one
the soft blade bends under the pressure of a finger
the stiff blade keeps its shape when you press it
the blades must be wetted before they are fitted
the fastening must not be tightened too far
you test a low note and then the same note high up
the soft blade answers quickly but weakens in the upper register
the stiff blade asks for more effort and carries loud playing
the choice rests on how tired you feel after a long held sound
text: Lay two reeds side by side and look them over before you fit either one to the mouthpiece. The softer one gives under your thumb; the harder one keeps its curve and pushes back. Each of them suits a different job, so trust the trial rather than the reputation. Wet both blades in a little warm water, then set the first on the table of the mouthpiece and tighten the ligature only just enough to hold it. Blow a long note down low, then the same note up high. The soft blade speaks quickly and the tone comes out sweet, but the high note slips away as soon as you press harder. The hard blade needs more support to start, gives a thicker sound, and holds together when you play loud. Keep whichever tires you least after a long held tone, not the one that charms your ear on the first breath.

units: the place where the instruments are made has taken visitors only lately
a smell of glue and cut wood meets you at the door
the space is divided into four working areas
the first area is where boards are split and joined
a student shapes a piece there by hand with no powered tool
the finishing area is sheltered from moving air
each coat of finish dries before the next one goes on
the last area lets the instrument be tried by playing it
the manager promises that nothing leaves without being tested
the same wood yields instruments that sound different
text: Warm glue and fresh-cut wood hit you the moment you step through the door of the workshop, which opened to visitors only lately. Four stations share the floor. At the back sits the cutting bench, where maple boards are split, folded open, and glued up into the backs of the instruments. On the right comes assembly, and there a young trainee shapes a bridge with a knife, no machine anywhere near her. Further along is the varnish room, kept clear of any draft, where each coat has to dry before the next goes on. The last station, the busiest one, is for trying things out: strings go on, a bow goes across, everyone listens. The manager warns visitors that no piece leaves the shop until it has been played. Most of them go away having learned something odd: two instruments cut from one board never sound alike.

units: the space stands empty late in the day before the session
the technical crew lays the cable and hangs two pickups
the players settle in and tune their instruments
the first take begins once night has fallen
one player fits an accessory that softens the tone
the sound engineer moves a pickup back in response
stray noises can be heard during the pauses
the last take is the best one despite the exhaustion
the gear is packed away before the sun comes up
text: Late in the afternoon the hall stands completely empty, and the quiet inside it feels thick. The technicians come in first, running their cable along the walls and hanging a pair of microphones above the platform. The players drift in afterward in small groups, settle themselves without hurry, and tune their instruments in a calm sort of disorder. The first take starts once night has fallen. A cellist fits a mute onto his bridge to soften the tone, and the engineer at once pulls one microphone back. Between takes you hear paper rustling, a cough, a chair grinding on the floor. Near midnight the tiredness shows on every face, and yet the last take is the one that holds together. The cable is coiled again before dawn, and the hall goes back to its silence, a little warmer than it was.

units: the absence of noise is now sold as a product
the hum of machines makes the ear sort things out very early
this protection of the hearing costs us fineness of listening
attention goes to masses of sound rather than to detail
sound recordings are made to survive the noise around them
those recordings in turn deepen the listener's inattention
the writer describes a loop that feeds itself
bringing back the absence of noise is no longing for the past
text: Quiet has turned into something you buy, and that transformation is worth a moment of thought. Because machines hum everywhere, the ear learns early to filter, to push the drone into the background, to expect nothing from what it takes in. That defense carries a cost of its own. Guarding itself, our listening loses its fineness: it picks out fewer shades and settles for broad blocks of sound. Music follows along, built to survive the noise, squeezed flat, evened out, shaped for half an ear in a corridor. And since that music is what surrounds us, it trains the ear toward still less attention, so the loop closes on itself. Giving silence its place back is no longing for an older time. It is what has to happen if sound is to become an event again rather than scenery nobody notices.

units: the specialist opens the instrument before doing anything else
the middle register gives a sound that is too harsh
she checks the tuning by working on the fastenings of the strings
the trouble stays once that check is done
the padding of the striking parts has packed down with use
grooves have been worn by the contact of the strings
she refuses to replace the parts and would rather restore them
she pierces the padding with points to give it back its spring
she then adjusts the control worked by the left foot
text: Before she touches the keys, the tuner takes off the front panel and studies the inside without a word. The instrument handed to her sounds hard through the middle, as though every note there were struck too bluntly. She checks the tuning first, string by string, with a lever that turns each pin an eighth of a turn. The fault stays. So she looks at the hammers and finds the cause: the felt, packed down by years of playing, has gone hard and carries grooves worn into it by the strings. Her answer is not to swap the parts out but to nurse them. She pricks the felt of every hammer with fine needles to give it back its spring, then sands the surface smooth. Last she sets the left pedal, which brings the hammers closer to the strings, and plays the middle again: the roundness is back.

units: two recordings of the same string work are set against each other
the older recording was made in a space of large dimensions
the echoes there overlap and soften the beginnings of notes
the listener feels placed far away
the other recording was made with pickups very close in
each group of instruments becomes possible to pick out
this precision costs the feeling of space
neither version is declared better than the other
the distant recording suits the calm passages
the close recording suits the fast passages
text: Setting two recordings of one string orchestra score against each other tells you more than an argument about taste ever will. The older one of them, captured in a wide hall, lets the echoes blend as they please; attacks come out rounded, edges a little blurred, and you seem to be listening from the far end of a long room. The other, made with microphones set close in, lays out every section: you can catch the scrape of the bows, the breathing of the players, the grain of the lower strings. That sharpness costs something, since the whole loses the depth that gave the earlier version its breadth. Neither one of them wins outright. The distant recording persuades in the slow movements, the close one takes over in the fast passages, where the clarity of the line decides everything.

units: the writer answers a request for news of his learning
the first sessions went on holding the instrument without making a sound
that early constraint spared his shoulders
the teacher asks for a breath that comes from the belly
an uneven stream of air makes the note waver
the nimbleness of the fingers comes along by itself once the basics hold
hearing is the faculty that takes longest to form
the writer now catches his own tuning mistakes before they are pointed out
he invites the reader to come and listen the following week
text: You asked me how the lessons were going, so here is what a whole season of them has taught me. Posture came first: I spent the early sessions just holding the instrument without playing a single note, which felt completely ridiculous at the time and which saved my shoulders. Then breathing. My teacher insists the air start from the belly and reach the mouthpiece steadily, or else the note wobbles and fades out into nothing. Fingers come third, and they sort themselves out on their own as soon as the other two points hold up. The ear ripens slowest of all: I am starting to hear that I am out of tune before anyone tells me, and that turns out to be more encouraging than it sounds. Come round next week, bring your own instrument along if you like, and judge the result for yourself.

units: she started out with cleaning and tidying jobs
she had no access to the mixing gear during her first year
she was then given the placing of pickups on the drums
an accessory badly fitted on a brass instrument can spoil a take
the hardest thing was keeping her remarks to herself
she ran a session alone to cover for a missing colleague
that successful session put an end to the menial jobs
she now teaches the trade to newcomers
her main advice is to trust the ear and not the eye
text: The first question put to her is where she began. She swept the studio, she says, coiled cable and carried crates of equipment around, and never laid a hand on the desk for an entire year. And after that? After that they let her set microphones on the drums, then on the brass, where a single badly placed mute can ruin an entire take. And the hardest part of those early days? Keeping quiet whenever she could hear a fault that the others were letting slide. In the end she ran the desk on her own one night, standing in for a colleague who had fallen ill; the session went perfectly well, and nobody ever handed her a broom again. And now? Now she trains up beginners, and she keeps repeating the one rule she believes in: you place a microphone with your ears, never with your eyes.

units: the takes recorded in the room come out muddy
the engineer blames the hard surfaces of the walls
a sound takes too long to die away in the room
the player reports a hum coming from the air system
the first fix is to hang absorbent material near the microphones
the second fix is to rest the air duct on flexible mounts
the player fears the tone of her instrument will be altered
the engineer promises a gain in the high frequencies instead
text: The studio engineer kept saying that the takes recorded in that room came out muddy, and he laid the blame squarely on the walls. Nothing there soaked up anything: every note hung on far too long, and the wash of it smeared the attack of whatever was being played. The cellist had a complaint of her own. Whenever the air system started up, she could hear a low hum sitting under everything. So the engineer set out two fixes. Hang absorbent panels close behind the microphones, first of all, to break up what the bare surfaces kept throwing back. Then rest the air duct on flexible mounts, so its shudder stopped traveling through the floor. The cellist worried about what all that would do to the tone of her instrument. The engineer told her the opposite would happen: take out the stray echo and the top end comes back, the part the room had been eating.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: two ways of passing music on coexisted over long stretches of time
the first way rests on a pupil copying a master by ear
in that way nothing is set down on any material support
every performer freely alters the piece he has learned
the second way uses written signs giving pitch and duration
writing fixes the work and lets it travel far from its author
transmission by ear breeds many versions
specialists find that the two paths have combined
copyists set down only a framework that performers filled in
text: Over long stretches of time, music traveled by two routes at once, and the contrast between them still shapes how players work today. The first route asked for nothing but the ear. A master played, a pupil copied, and the piece moved on through patient repetition. Nothing was set down on any material support, so every performer bent the tune a little, adding a turn here, cutting a repeat there. The second route used written signs that told the eye how high a note sat and how long it lasted. Writing pinned the work down and let it travel far from whoever had made it. Music carried by ear breeds versions without end. The written page breeds faithful copies. Yet scholars have shown that the two never stood apart. What the copyists set down was a framework, and the players filled in the silence the pages left them.

units: every sound comes from a fast motion that stirs the surrounding air
the first family gathers strings pulled tight between two supports
these strings are set moving by plucking, bowing or striking them
a hollow body strengthens the motion passed on by the string
the second family gathers hollow tubes driven by the breath of the player
the pitch obtained in a tube depends on the length of air left free
the third family gathers skins stretched over a frame
the fourth family gathers metal bars and plates that are struck
each family is known by its tone color, tied to the material used
text: Sound begins with a fast motion that stirs the air around it, and the objects able to make that motion fall into families. In the first are strings pulled tight between two supports. You pluck them, you draw a bow across them, or you strike them, and the shaking passes into a hollow body that strengthens it. The second family is built from open tubes: the breath of the player sets a column of air moving inside, and how high the note sits depends on how much of that column is left free. The third gathers skins stretched over a frame, which answer a blow with a short, dark ring. The fourth holds bars and plates of metal that sound on their own the moment something hits them. Each family has a voice you learn to know, because the material doing the moving filters the overtones in its own way.

units: a neighbor takes the narrator down to the basement of their building one evening
the neighbor claims the pipes give out a kind of song
the two women go down with a lamp and a recorder
at first they hear only the boiler and the metal door
when the pump stops a low held note appears
a faint high sound rides above that low note
the neighbor admits she has been hearing this for several weeks
playing the take back reveals a regular throbbing
a repairman later blames a valve left badly closed
text: One evening the neighbor from the floor below dragged me down to the basement of our building, swearing that the pipes sang down there. We went with a lamp and a borrowed recorder. At first there was nothing worth the trip: the boiler grumbling, the metal door creaking shut behind us. Then the pump cut out, and the whole cellar began to ring. A low note came up out of the plumbing, steady and held, with a thin whistle riding above it. She laughed and owned up that she had been hearing it for weeks without daring to mention it. We let the machine run for half an hour. Playing the take back upstairs, we heard that note plain, throbbing with an even beat that made it tremble. The repairman who came the week after needed one look: a valve left badly closed, a pipe whistling like a flute.

units: capturing the sounds of a street calls for a careful method
you have to pick a spot sheltered from moving air
air striking the microphone membrane makes an overwhelming rumble
the machine has to be clamped to a steady support
a hand holding the microphone passes on audible rubbing
you should switch your phone off to avoid interference
a take should start before the event aimed at and run on past it
you have to listen to the take on headphones before leaving the place
text: Recording a street takes more care than people expect, and every shortcut shows up later in the edit. Pick a sheltered spot first, because moving air slams into the microphone membrane and lays a rumble over everything else. Then clamp the machine to a stand. Hold it in your hand instead and every shift of your fingers turns into a steady scrape running the whole length of the take. Switch your phone off as well, or it can drop a short burst of interference into the file that no amount of cleaning will lift. Start rolling before the thing you came for and keep rolling well past it, or the cut will land too early and the passage will be useless. Last of all, listen on headphones while you are still standing there. A fault caught late means coming back; a fault caught on the spot takes one step sideways to fix.

units: a rail line runs right along the yard of a school
passing trains cover the voices of the children
the teachers describe lessons broken off again and again
protective work was carried out over one season
a thick tilted wall throws the sound wave back toward the track
the windows of the building were given reinforced glazing
absorbent cladding was laid over the exposed face
the noise remains but seems clearly further off
the children now hear the bell without straining
text: Stand in the school yard and the first thing you hear is not the children but the rail line running along the wall. Every so often a train comes through, and the squeal of wheels on the curved rail swallows the voices, the games, the bell itself. Teachers talk about lessons chopped into pieces, dictations started again from the top, pupils raising their voices without noticing. The work took a whole season. A thick wall, tilted toward the track, now throws the wave back down onto the ballast instead of letting it clear the fence. The windows were fitted with reinforced glazing, and absorbent cladding covers the exposed face of the building. The roar has not gone. It has moved off, as though pushed behind a heavy curtain. Out in the yard the bell rides over the voices again, and nobody has to shout to be heard.

units: two rooms in the same music school sound different
the lower room is lined with wood mounted on a hollow frame
its walls drink up the high frequencies and soften the attack
the upper room is built of polished stone and has no drapes
its walls send the sound wave back almost without loss
quick notes pile onto one another there
a brass section gains fullness in the upper room
a string quartet loses clarity there
the teachers keep the lower room for sessions of fine adjustment
text: The lower room and the upper room of the music school do not sound alike, and the ear picks it up in the opening bar. Wood panels line the lower room, mounted on a hollow frame. Those walls give a little with the instrument, drink up the high end, and hand back a warm, faintly veiled sound in which the bite of a bowed string rounds off. Upstairs it is polished stone, with no drapes and no rugs. The walls send the wave back almost whole, so the ring hangs on and quick notes pile onto each other before any of them has died out. A brass section swells there and fills the space, while a string quartet turns cloudy and loses its edge. That is why the teachers keep the lower room for the sessions where fine adjustments get made, and send the larger groups upstairs when what they want is weight.

units: the writer disputes the idea that music played without a break is harmless
he puts forward three objections one after the other
the first objection concerns the drain on the attention of the customer
this drain brings on a tiredness whose cause escapes the person feeling it
the second objection concerns the staff exposed to the same sound loop
these staff have no control at all over what they hear
the third objection concerns the way music itself loses its worth
the writer holds that silence is what makes a sound audible
text: Treating the music that runs without a break in shops as a harmless little comfort is a mistake. Three objections deserve a hearing. The first has to do with attention. An unbroken stream of sound takes a cut of whatever mental resources a customer brings through the door, so he listens without listening and tires out without ever placing the cause. The second concerns the people who work under it. The clerk, the server and the one at the register take the same loop from the start of a shift to the end of it, with no dial anywhere within reach. The third bears on the music itself, which stops counting as an event the moment it becomes a curtain hung behind every activity. Silence is not a hole waiting to be filled. It is what makes a sound audible at all, and it deserves defending the way anything scarce deserves defending.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the tuner of the theater began his apprenticeship very early
he sorted felts in the workshop of an instrument maker
he was first taught to listen for the beats between neighboring strings
he then spent a year replacing hammers
he also set the travel of every key on the keyboard
once he was a tuner he made the rounds of concert halls
the heat of the stage lights threatens the steadiness of the instrument
he says one wrong note is enough to shake the confidence of an orchestra
he now passes his trade on to two apprentices
text: The tuner who works for the theater started young, in the workshop of an instrument maker who had him sorting felts. Long before anyone handed him a key, he was taught to listen for the beats that rise between two strings tuned close together. A whole year then went on swapping out hammers and setting the travel of every key on the keyboard, fussy work that asks for a hand which never wavers. Once he had the trade, he followed it through concert halls, where an instrument has to hold steady against the heat pouring off the lights and the air a full house stirs up. One sour note, he says, heard from the stands, is enough to shake the confidence of a whole orchestra. He now teaches two apprentices, telling them that the ear is built by patience, and that the hand follows on after.

units: the concert under review took place in an old covered market
the metal roof and the concrete floor throw the sound back hard
this layout gives a tinny return
the trio cut its volume to suit the place
the gaps left between musical phrases became noticeable
the double bass suffered from too much low end in that space
the drums on the other hand gained from the acoustics
the reviewer advises standing close to the stage
text: Honestly, the show in the old covered market was worth the trip, and what stayed with me had as much to do with the building as with the playing. Sheet metal overhead, raw concrete underfoot: every note comes straight back at you with a tinny edge, which means a loud band would turn to mush in there within a minute. The trio had clearly worked this out. They played soft, then softer, and the gaps between the phrases ended up carrying as much weight as the notes did. The double bass took the worst of it, since low frequencies gather in a shed like that and thicken into a paste. The drums came out ahead: each stroke shot up into the roof beams and came back wider than it left. One tip if you go. Stand down front, right against the platform, or what you hear will be roof and metal and very little of the players.

units: the writer answers a question his correspondent raised earlier
two string instruments are sitting in a place where instruments are made
on the first one, a finger pulls the string aside and releases it to start the sound
on the second, a bow drawn across the string produces the sound
the tone of the first dies away as soon as it appears
the tone of the second can be held for as long as the movement lasts
the first allows several strings to sound together
the second hardly manages more than two strings at a time
the writer recommends the first one for backing a singer
text: You asked me a while back to sort out the two string instruments sitting in the workshop, so here goes. On the first one, a finger pulls a string aside and lets it snap back, and that release starts the sound. On the second, you drag a bow across the string and the tone builds up under it. Everything else follows from the way the sound begins. Pluck a string and the note dies the moment it appears. Bow a string and you can stretch the note out as long as your arm keeps moving, swelling it or letting it fade whenever you choose. One more gap is worth knowing about. The plucked instrument takes several strings at once, so a whole chord sits under your hand, while the bowed one barely manages two together. Backing a singer, take the plucked one. Carrying a single line, take the other.

units: the text sorts noises into three categories
the first category covers sounds that never break off
the ear stops noticing those steady sounds
the second category gathers sounds that come back at intervals
the third category concerns very short and violent impacts
an impact of that kind can damage hearing in an instant
how long the exposure lasts weighs as much as how loud the sound is
three protections are named: move away, put up a barrier, shorten the exposure
hearing cells that have been destroyed never grow back
text: What exactly counts as noise? The answer sorts the phenomena into three families. The first covers steady sounds, the hum of a machine among them, which the ear stops registering after a while. The second gathers sounds that come back at intervals, an alarm chiming over and over, never letting you forget they are there. The third holds the short, violent impacts that can wreck hearing in a second. Should the racket of a building site worry anyone more than the murmur of a wide street? Specialists answer that how long you stay exposed weighs as much as how loud the source is. What protection works? Three measures come recommended: move away from the source, put an absorbing wall in between, cut the listening short. Does damaged hearing mend itself? Destroyed cells never grow back, and prevention remains the only route.

units: a learner recounts out loud a lesson he was given
the specialist asks him to listen in silence to a struck key
at first the learner hears only one sound
several strings in fact belong to a single key
the specialist deliberately slackens one of the strings
the learner then hears a regular throbbing
removing that throbbing is the point of the operation
the specialist plays a run of neighboring notes
the learner tightens the moving part too far during his own attempt
by the end, two strings no longer produce any throbbing
text: The student went back over his lesson out loud, step by step, in the order it had actually happened. The tuner had asked him first to say nothing and just listen while she struck a single key. He told her that all he could hear was a single note. She pushed back: three strings vibrate behind that key. Then she slackened one of them on purpose, and he said a slow throb had come up, like a wave rising and dropping away. Tuning, she explained, means getting rid of that throb. After that she played a whole scale so he could hear the neighboring notes. She handed him the wrench at last and let him turn the tension pin himself. He cranked it too far, the throb sped up, and she told him to work with a lighter hand. By the close of the session, two strings had fallen silent for each other.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: old rooms were low and hung with cloth
sound died away quickly in them
that quick fade allowed fast successions of notes
taller stone rooms were built afterwards
sound lingered there long after it was made
fast passages turned confused in those rooms
the writers of music then spaced their notes out and lengthened them
adding padded seats and an audience cut the lingering sound down
musical writing grew fast again after that
the text concludes that materials shaped music as much as taste did
text: Look at what happens to a piece of music when the room it is played in changes size and shape. Players once worked in low chambers hung with heavy cloth, where sound died almost as soon as it left the strings. With nothing left hanging in the air, they could run fast notes together and keep them clean. Then tall halls of bare stone went up, and every sound dragged a long tail behind it. The same quick passages turned to mush, so composers slowed their writing down, stretched the chords out, and traded quick ornament for long held tones. Later those halls filled with padded seats and packed listeners, and the echo shrank again. Writing picked up speed once more, and the pace tightened. Stone and fabric, in other words, shaped the scores as much as any taste of the people listening did.

units: students sitting at the back catch only part of the instructions
the cause lies with the surfaces of the room rather than with the speaker
bare walls throw back sounds that then mix together
everyone speaks louder, which raises the noise further
specialists call that mechanism a spiral
absorbing panels are put up on the ceiling
pads under the chairs do away with the scraping
the layout of the tables turns voices toward the listeners
teachers strain their voices less once those changes are made
the money spent stays modest
text: In plenty of classrooms, the students sitting at the back catch no more than half of what they are told. The trouble rarely starts with the teacher's voice. It starts with the surfaces of the room. A bare space throws sound back, the returns pile onto each other, and syllables blur. So everybody speaks up, and the level climbs higher still. Acousticians call that a noise spiral. Breaking out of it takes surprisingly little work. Porous panels go on the ceiling and soak up part of what bounces. Felt pads fixed under the chair legs kill off the scraping. Tables get turned so that mouths face ears. Where those steps have been taken, teachers push their voices far less than they used to. The outlay stays small, and you can hear the difference from the very first lesson onward.

units: a woman upstairs plays a plucked string instrument
a man on the ground floor plays a worn guitar
the narrator likens the two kinds of music to two kinds of rain
the music from upstairs makes separate notes parted by silences
the music from below forms a continuous fabric that cannot be counted
the power fails during a storm
the two neighbors then play at the same time without having agreed on it
the narrator listens from the stairwell of the building
the blend makes a music unlike either of the first two
the neighbors stop playing when the power returns
text: The woman who lives above me plays a harp, and the man on the ground floor works at a battered guitar. In the end I came to compare the two the way you might compare two kinds of rain. Hers falls in separate drops, each note clean, each one held apart from the next by a polite silence. His comes down as a sheet, strings answering strings, fingers scraping, nothing you could ever count. During a storm one evening the power failed across the building, and the two of them began playing at the same moment, with no word between them. From the stairwell I heard the drops land on the sheet. It was neither of their musics but a third one, which neither could have written down. When the lights came back they stopped, doors closed, and the building went back to being two apartments stacked up.

units: the preparation follows three ordered steps
the room holding the most furniture is the one to choose
any device making a background noise has to be switched off
a thick cloth is hung behind the person speaking
the microphone goes at chin height and slightly off to the side
the tilt keeps expelled air from striking the diaphragm
the stand belongs on the floor rather than on a piece of furniture
a short stretch of silence is recorded to gauge the room noise
monitoring is done on headphones and not through a speaker
one whole take is kept before any editing
text: Before recording a voice at home, get the room, the microphone, and the take ready, in that order. The room: pick whichever one holds the most furniture, shut the windows, switch off anything that blows or hums, and hang a thick blanket behind where you will stand. The microphone: bring it up to chin height, a hand's width from your mouth, tilted off to one side so the breath behind consonants never strikes the diaphragm. Set it on a weighted stand resting on the floor, never on the table, since wood carries every bump straight through. The take: record a short stretch of silence first, which gives you a measure of the room noise. Keep your volume even, without drifting closer or farther away. Monitor on headphones, never through a speaker. Save one whole spare take before you cut anything.

units: work on a concert venue has just been finished
complaints had piled up over a whole season
low sounds became inaudible from the far rows back
an acoustic study was commissioned and then handed to those in charge
the decision was made to open up the vaulted ceiling
the panels that threw the sound back were taken down
the armchairs were replaced by seats whose absorption never varies
the stage floor was given a slope
a musical ensemble played with no audience to test the venue
those in charge will wait a whole season before drawing conclusions
text: Renovation work at the concert venue wrapped up at the end of last week, at the end of an operation the musicians followed closely. It had begun after a full season of complaints: ever since the ceiling was redone, the low instruments vanished for anyone sitting in the far rows back. An acoustic study was commissioned and then handed to the management, which decided to open the vaulted ceiling back up. Crews took down the panels that threw the sound back, swapped the old armchairs for seats whose absorption never varies, and put a slope into the stage floor. An ensemble played behind closed doors to measure how the room now answers. Management has announced that performances will resume, warning at the same time that no final verdict will come before a whole season of use.

units: you hear the workshop before you catch sight of it
the craftsman strikes a heated piece of metal
each blow makes a short sound thrown back by the metal walls
the pitch of the sound shifts because the metal cools
the sound turns higher as the material stiffens
the sandy floor soaks up part of what bounces back
a blower keeps the fire going and makes a steady noise
the ear grows used to that steady noise and keeps only the blows
the silence after the stop seems sharper than it really is
text: You hear the forge well before you ever catch sight of it. The smith hammers away at a bar pulled hot from the fire, and each blow tears out a short, near-shrill sound that comes straight back off the sheet-metal walls. Because the bar cools under the hammer, the pitch shifts: it climbs as the metal stiffens, and it drops when the flame softens the bar again. Sand on the floor swallows part of what bounces, so the din stays bearable for whoever works there. At the far end of the shop, a blower breathes steadily on the coals, and its steady drone lies under everything else. The ear settles into that drone and ends up hearing only the blows. When the hammer stops, the silence seems deeper than it really is, because hearing holds on to the trace of the sound a moment longer.

units: the listener has no say in the music played in public places
that music is played to slow customers down
the writer locates the problem in the absence of any prior agreement
no way of stopping the music is offered
people who hear poorly are put out more than others
background music covers voices and makes conversation tiring
a first measure sets up stretches of time with nothing playing
those stretches would be posted at the door and would cost nothing
a second measure lowers the volume until talking becomes possible
a third measure hands the setting over to the staff of the place
text: Hardly anyone gets to pick the music they hear in public anymore. Walk into a store, an elevator, a waiting room, and a chorus greets you, tuned to slow your step along the shelves. The problem is not taste, it is consent. Nobody asked whether you wanted to listen, and nobody offers you a way to shut it off. For people who hear poorly it runs worse: the wash of sound covers voices and turns a conversation into hard work. So what could actually be done about it? First, make silence available. A stretch of the day with nothing playing, posted at the door, costs nothing at all. Second, drop the level until two customers can talk without raising their voices. Third, hand the dial to the staff, since they are the ones stuck with the loop from open to close. None of this calls for a law.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the man described builds pipe instruments
he picks out dried wood without flaws
he melts a metal mixture into thin sheets
these sheets are rolled to form the pipes
the pressure of the bellows must be adjusted
too much pressure gives a harsh tone
too little pressure weakens the tone
tuning slightly alters the length of the pipes
he stops working when his hearing tires
text: An organ builder works slowly, and every motion he makes answers to a measurement. Wood comes first. He picks out boards that have dried for years, throws aside any board with a knot in it, and planes them down until the thickness holds steady from one end to the other. Metal comes second. He melts tin and lead together, pours the alloy out into thin sheets, and rolls each sheet into a pipe that speaks the moment air crosses it. Air comes third. He sets the pressure of the bellows with care, because too strong a wind turns the note shrill, while too weak a wind smothers it altogether. Tuning comes last, and it is the hardest part of the whole trade. He shaves or draws out each pipe by a hair, until the high voice stops beating against the low one. His ears give out long before his hands, he says, and that is the moment he puts the tools down.

units: the evening opened with a short piece for low strings
the first sound filled the space without excess
a lone singer then performed a work with restraint
the writer points out how young this performer is
the second half of the program convinced less
the brass instruments buried the wooden wind instruments
a string instrument out of tune made an unpleasant noise
the conductor flagged the mishap with a single look
the last chord hung under the ceiling of the hall
the writer judges this group uneven against its ambitions
text: The evening opened with a short piece for low strings alone, and their thick sound filled the hall without ever crowding it. A singer followed, unaccompanied, shaping every phrase with a restraint you seldom hear from a performer that young. The second half of the program went less well. The brass sat too far forward and buried the woodwinds, so the middle of the texture simply went missing. One violin had slipped out of tune, and a brief scrape cut across the room, which the conductor put right with a single look. The closing section drew every desk together at last, and the final chord hung under the vaulted ceiling for what felt like a suspended stretch of time. You come away with the impression of an uneven group, superb once it stops chasing effect, shaky the moment it reaches for sheer power.

units: the writer is writing from a rehearsal room
the room has no heat and the air is damp
the damp warps the wood and slackens the strings
the instrument loses its tuning after half an hour
the retuning eats up half of the session
the leader has seen the same trouble on his bow
his request for a heating unit was turned down
the group falls back on a tighter room next door
the bare walls of that room swell the low sounds
the writer asks the reader to bring a tuning fork
text: I am writing from the room where we rehearse, since I got here well ahead of everyone else. The place has no heat at all, and the damp cold works away at my instrument. The wood shrinks, the strings go slack, and the tuning falls apart after half an hour. Retuning eats up half the session, which wears the rest of the group down as well. Our leader finally worked out why, once his own bow had begun rasping in the same way. He asked for a portable heater and was turned down flat.
