So we squeeze into the room next door, which is tighter, with bare walls that throw the sound straight back and set the low notes humming. I will take that over the cold. If you come by at the end of the week, bring your tuning fork. Mine has rung false ever since I dropped it, and I no longer dare trust it.

units: a sound professional is asked about her hearing health
she blames the wear on quiet drawn out mixing sessions
listening at low volume forces sustained attention
she gave up on the ear protection she had bought
that protection skewed how she heard the high frequencies
she breaks off her listening at regular intervals
she holds herself to a volume ceiling she never crosses
she sometimes turns down a session when she feels drained
the ringing in the evening has dropped off sharply
text: What is it that wears down the hearing of a sound engineer fastest? She answers without pausing at all. Not concerts, she says, but the long quiet mixing sessions that stretch on for hours, where the ear strains at low volume to catch the smallest details. And the remedy? She bought earplugs first, then let them sit unused in a drawer, because they smother the high frequencies and skew her judgment. What she does now rests on three habits. She kills the sound at regular intervals so that her ears can rest for a while. She holds herself to a ceiling she never crosses, however hard a client pushes her. The third habit is the hardest of all, and it means turning a session down whenever she feels her hearing giving out. Since then, she says, the ringing that used to fill her head at night has all but stopped.

units: two professionals judge the same place differently
the man finds the sound of the stage too flat
he blames the drapes for soaking up the high frequencies
the singer feels held up there by her returning voice
the side walls send her own singing back to her
both of them notice that the floor shakes with low sounds
that shaking throws off the readings of the technician
it works as a rhythmic marker for the singer
she hums under her breath in the other place for reassurance
the technician prefers a place that adds no color
text: The technician and the singer do not describe the same hall at all. He finds the stage flat and dull to his ear, and he blames the heavy drapes, which soak up the highs and hand him back something soft and shapeless. She feels held up there instead, since her own voice comes back to her off the side walls. On one point, at least, the two of them agree. The floor shakes as soon as the low notes begin to rise. He calls that a flaw, because the tremor blurs the readings he takes. She calls it a support, because she feels the beat under her feet before she hears it at all. Asked about the wider hall next door, she admits that she hums under her breath there just to reassure herself, the silence feels so hollow. He much prefers that one. A room that adds nothing, he says, finally lets you hear what is being played.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the writer traces early music back to three motions of the hand
the first motion is to strike
a skin stretched over a hollow box gives a low carrying sound
the second motion rests on breathing
a hollow plant stalk with holes turns breath into a note
closing or opening the holes shifts the pitch
the third motion is to pluck
a tight string let go gives a short lived sound
a cavity was added to draw out the vibration
these three beginnings still show in the shape of instruments
text: All early music comes down to three motions that the hands learned apart from one another. The first of them is the strike. A skin stretched over a hollow frame answers the blow and shakes the air around it, which is where drums come from, and their rumble carries farther than any voice. The second is the breath. A hollow stalk, bored through with uneven holes, turns plain air into a note, and fingers that close or free the holes push the pitch up or down. The third is the pluck. A string drawn tight between two fixed points sounds only briefly when you pull it aside and let it go. A hollow box was soon added underneath, so that the shaking would last longer and grow louder. The three families later mixed together, yet their beginnings can still be read in the shape of the instruments.

units: a string pulled aside swings around its resting place
that swinging squeezes then frees the air beside it
the disturbance travels along from one point to the next
the air particles themselves barely move
the outer ear guides the wave toward a canal
a thin membrane starts swinging at the end of that canal
three small bones strengthen that motion
a coiled organ full of fluid then takes in the vibration
cells topped with hairs turn the motion into nerve signals
the rate of the swings sets the pitch that is heard
text: A plucked string leaves its resting place behind, comes back to it, then overshoots it once again. That back and forth is what we call vibration. It squeezes the air molecules beside it, which bunch up and then spread out in turn, passing the shove along to the ones beyond them. The wave travels outward that way, step by step, while the air itself barely moves at all. The outer ear funnels it into a narrow canal, and at the far end of it a thin membrane starts swinging at the very same rate. Three tiny bones pick up that motion, strengthen it, and hand it on to a coiled organ that is full of fluid. Inside, cells topped with fine hairs bend over and fire off a nerve signal. The nerve carries that signal to the brain, which hears a high or a low note depending on how fast the swings arrive.

units: a flaw in the casting had cracked a bell
the crack could not be seen without examination
it split the vibration into two parts out of tune
the ringing gave a beating instead of a clean sound
neighbors complained without grasping where the noise came from
the local assembly had the bell taken down
a specialist declared the repair impossible
she explained that welding changes the density of the metal
the bell was cast again with its own alloy
putting it back in service stopped walkers in their tracks
text: A flaw in the casting, invisible to the naked eye, had cracked the bell up in the tower. The split ran under the lip of the bronze and broke the vibration into two parts that no longer agreed with each other. Every peal gave a dull beating instead of the full tone people expected, and neighbors complained about a grating ring without ever knowing where it came from. The local assembly voted to take the bell down, a long and costly job. A founder was called in, and she ruled out any repair at all. Welded metal no longer holds the same density, she said, and the tone suffers for it. She offered instead to melt the whole thing down again with its own bronze. The recast bell went back up as the cold season ended, and its first peal rang so cleanly that walkers stopped where they stood.

units: the text speaks to whoever plays in an overly echoing room
the notes pile up and blur the fast passages
the stiff surfaces send the sound back without taking it in
a clap of the hands serves to gauge how long the tail lasts
a rug on the floor treats the bounce between floor and ceiling
a thick cloth is hung on one wall only
covering every wall would leave the room lifeless
shifting the music stand to an angle keeps low sounds from building
a second clap lets you check the result
text: You practice in a room where every note drags on behind the next one, and fast passages turn to mush. Hard surfaces are the cause, since they send the sound straight back at you instead of taking it in. Work through this in order. Clap once in the middle of the room and listen to the tail. The longer it hangs on, the more correction you are going to need. Lay a thick rug on the floor first, because the bounce between floor and ceiling is the most stubborn one of all. Hang a heavy blanket on the wall your instrument faces, and on that wall only. Cover all four and the room goes lifeless, with the highs swallowed. Then swing the music stand to an angle, because a square placement builds up the low notes and sets them droning. Clap again. If the tail has come down by half, stop right there.

units: a student survey compares two neighboring urban areas
the workshop area puts up with steady machine noise
that constant noise ends up slipping past the attention of residents
the area of the wide streets shows a lower average level
abrupt traffic sounds break out there without warning
it is those sudden peaks that cut into rest
one resident sets the steady hum against the biting sound
the survey also covered the nighttime hours
night deliveries bring on ringing ears and exhaustion
the authors conclude that the unexpected tires more than the intensity
text: Two neighboring districts live with noise in opposite ways, and a student survey has just borne that out. On the workshop side, the machines never stop, but their drone is steady, and residents say they grow so used to it that they stop hearing it at all. On the avenue side, the average level is lower. It is the horns and the squealing brakes that come out of nowhere, and those short spikes are what pull people out of their rest. One resident put it plainly. A steady hum you end up forgetting, a sound that stings, never. The students also looked at the nights. Where the activity stops, sleep repairs itself. Where deliveries run through, people report ringing ears and heavy exhaustion. Their conclusion fits into a single sentence: it is not the volume that wears you out, it is the surprise.

units: a mold is built out of clay before the pouring
the molten metal is poured without a break
the piece cools for a whole night without being moved
the mold is broken once the metal has cooled
the surface looks reddish and unpolished when it comes out
a tuning specialist adjusts the pitch at the end of the process
material is taken off the inside to change the note
the craftsman adds a personal mark when the result satisfies him
text: The workshop heats up long before any metal moves. The founder starts by building a mold out of clay, building it up by hand, one layer over the last, then leaving it to dry beside the furnace. Once the alloy runs, he pours it in a single steady stream and watches the bubbles come up to the surface. Cooling takes the whole night after that, and nobody touches the piece until it has gone lukewarm. When the shell breaks under the mallet, out comes a coppery flank, reddish and still rough. The tuner works last. He strikes the rim, listens to the note, shaves thin curls off the inner wall, and strikes again. Every pass lifts the pitch a shade. Once the tone rings clear and the vibration dies away without a beat, the craftsman puts his tool down and cuts a small mark of his own into the metal.

units: shared places have grown too noisy
shops play music to hold on to their customers
household machines give off unpleasant sound signals
each source taken alone seems harmless
it is the sum of the sources that makes the din
concentration scatters and talking costs more effort
vulnerable people now stay away from public places
doctors report lasting exhaustion among those exposed
the writer holds that an individual answer would not work
the writer asks builders and manufacturers to protect quiet
text: One quiet shift deserves a moment of attention: the places we share have grown far too loud, and the fault is spread across many hands. Shops pipe in music tuned to keep customers browsing. Household machines announce every finished task with a shrill little tone. Taken one at a time, each of these sounds is harmless. Stacked together they build a roar that nobody ever chose. Attention breaks apart, a plain conversation costs more effort than it should, and the frailest users simply stop coming to public places. Clinicians report a lasting exhaustion among people who cannot step away from the racket. Because the cause is collective, no private remedy will do: plugging your ears only shifts the burden onto you. The people who design buildings and the firms that build our machines should treat quiet as a resource worth keeping.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: she began her trade in a country workshop
her first specialty was mending cracked soundboards
the bodies she repaired gave a muffled sound
neither the wood nor the varnish nor the strings explained the fault
she blamed a layer of glue laid on too thickly
she tested hanging samples that she struck
the samples with the least glue sounded better
she changed her preparation and corrected the instruments already delivered
she passes this method on to students who come from far away
text: The woman who restores old instruments learned her trade in a country workshop, where most of her work was mending cracked soundboards. One puzzle held her for whole seasons: the bodies she glued back together came out muffled, as though a blanket lay over them. The wood was sound. The varnish had not lifted. The strings pulled at the right tension. In the end she turned on the glue itself, laid on too thickly, holding the soundboard back from its own vibration. To test the idea she made up sample panels, hung each one from a thread, and tapped it. The heavily glued ones answered with a dull thud, the lighter ones rang out. So she thinned her mixture, warmed it gently, and called back every instrument she had already handed over. Her customers heard the change at the first playing. She now teaches the method to apprentices who travel a long way for it.

units: the narrator compared two recorded versions of the same set of pieces
the two listenings were a week apart
the first group takes a fast and very confident pace
that first version ends up wearing the listener out
the second group slows down and blends the tones more
one passage of the fast version is out of tune between two instruments
one piece of the slow version loses its coherence
the narrator picks the second version
his reason is that it stands up to repeated listening
text: I listened to two recordings of the same set of string pieces, a week apart, and honestly the gap between them threw me. The first group plays fast, with a swagger you can hear in every attack, right down to the players breathing. Brilliant stuff, and wearing after a while, like a light too bright to look at for long. The second group takes its time. Tempos stretch out, the tones melt into one another, and what sounded angular turns round. The first record grabbed me. This one kept me. Neither is spotless. On the fast one, a middle passage goes sour because the viola and the cello never quite agree. On the slow one, a single piece sags and loses the thread. Asked which of the two I would keep, I say the second without pausing, because it survives a replay and the fatigue never arrives before the end.

units: the writer is staying in a rented house beside an estuary
he chooses to describe the sounds rather than the views
the water strikes the supports of the building at a steady beat
the boats scrape when the level rises
a bird lets out an evening call he takes for a creaking door
human noises come from the quay and from a radio set
the wooden frame creaks during the night
those creaks make up a kind of tune
the writer records what he notices with the hour and the wind
he means to play his recordings when he gets back
text: I am writing from the low house we have rented near the estuary, and what I want to hand over to you here is what I hear, rather than what I see. Begin with the water: a steady slap against the posts under the floor, then the scrape of hulls as the rising tide lifts them straight. Then the birds. One of them lets out a thin call at dusk that I still take for a door swinging on a dry hinge. Then the people: voices carrying up from the quay, a radio playing somewhere far off, a cart rolling over the boards. The last one caught me off guard. The timbers themselves creak after dark, and the creaking settles into something close to a tune. I am writing it all down in a notebook, with the hour and the wind behind it. Once we are back home, I will play you the takes that came out well.

units: the origin of the phenomenon is older than the keeper can remember
her grandmother already knew this echo
the first returning sound she caught seemed weakened to her
she first put the cause down to the wind
she then suspected the work of water on the rock
a specialist in rocks explained to her the part played by the shape of the ground
she accepts that explanation and still comes to listen
the curious go away pleased once they have shouted
she waits until she is alone to say a short sentence
the voice that comes back to her sounds lower and altered
text: When did the cliff first answer? The keeper of the path waves the question off: the thing was there before she was born, and her grandmother knew it as a girl. What did she hear the first night? A call that came back to her worn thin, as if the rock gave it up unwillingly. Did she look for a reason? She blamed the wind, then the water that eats at the face, until a passing student of rocks spoke to her about the curve of the hollow. What does she do with that answer? She keeps it, and she still climbs up alone at dusk to hear her own voice return to her deeper than she sent it. And the visitors? They shout, they laugh, they go home pleased. She waits for them to walk off, then says a short sentence and lets the wall hand it back, rough and slightly changed, and she goes down telling nobody.

units: the technical manager explained the source of the shrill noise to the performer
the microphone was picking up the sound coming out of the speakers
that sound went back into the circuit and built itself up
the performer thought the sound level alone was to blame
the technician answered that the aim of the microphone weighed more
he advised moving the speakers behind the performer
he offered to cut the high frequencies and the input level
he recommended never aiming the microphone at a speaker
the test worked apart from a brief moment during a move toward the audience
text: The stage manager took the singer aside to explain where the shriek was coming from. Her microphone, he said, was picking up the speakers set out in front of her, that sound went back into the amplifier, and the loop fed itself until it howled. She asked whether the volume alone was to blame. Not really, he told her. Where the microphone points matters more, because a capsule aimed at a speaker hears its own echo. So what could be done? Move the speakers behind her, he suggested, pull down the high frequencies that flare up first, and take a little off the input as well. He added one rule for the stage: never swing the microphone toward a source, not even while bowing. The singer tried it through the sound check. The shriek stayed away, apart from one second, when she leaned out over the hall.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: passing melodies on by ear made them drift from one relay to the next
learning went by copying a sung model
after three relays two neighboring groups sang differently
the first scribes wrote signs above the sung words
those signs showed the direction of the voice but not the gap between the notes
you still had to know the tune to read those signs
the answer was to draw reference lines
the height of the sign then showed the pitch of the note
a performer could from then on sing a piece he had never heard
that invention opened the way to writing for several voices
text: Handing a melody down from one generation to the next raised a problem that memory alone could not settle. Singers learned by copying a model they had heard, and every copy drifted a little from the one before it. Three hands along, two settlements side by side no longer sang the same tune. The earliest copyists tried marks above the words, sketching where the voice rose and where it fell, without saying by how much. That helped, but not enough: you had to know the melody already before the marks meant anything. The answer turned out to be a plain piece of drawing. Rule one line across the page, then a second, and set each mark at a height you can measure. From then on the space of the page stood for the pitch of the sound. A singer could work out a tune he had never heard, and writing for several voices at once became possible.

units: in air the particles are far apart and carry the vibration poorly
sound fades quickly as it travels through air
in water the packed particles pass the vibration on with no delay
the vibration moves much faster in water than in air
a swimmer under the surface cannot tell where an engine noise comes from
that confusion comes from the signal reaching both ears too close together
metal carries the vibration better still than water
a wall of wool soaks up almost all of the vibration
the same blow gives a different sound depending on what carries it
text: Put two ways of carrying a sound side by side. In air the wave spreads out fast: the molecules sit far apart, they hand the shock along lazily, and the message fades within a short distance. In water those same molecules almost touch. The shock passes from one to the next with no delay, and sound travels far quicker there than it does through air. That is why a diver hears a distant engine yet cannot tell where it lies: the signal reaches both of his ears too soon for him to compare them. The comparison holds for solids too. A steel bar carries a vibration better still than water does, while a wall of wool soaks up nearly all of it. One blow struck on those three gives three results: a bright crack on the metal, a dull ringing under water, a short flat thud in the wool.

units: the narrator expected a long session but not a failed one
the injured pianist had to play with one hand
the borrowed room belonged to a dance school
its floor threw the sound back hard
the singer had a cold and a ragged voice
she refused to soften her part in spite of it
noisy building work broke into a quiet passage
the group carried on anyway out of stubbornness
the final result turned out to be good
the musicians kept those choices for the performance
text: They warned me the run-through would drag on. Nobody warned me it would turn into a run of disasters. First blow: the pianist shows up with a bandaged finger and announces he will play with the left hand only. Second blow: the room, lent to us by a dance school, has a floor that throws everything back, so the smallest note cracks and returns doubled. Third blow: the singer has caught a cold, her voice comes out raw, and she flatly refuses to lighten her part. Fourth blow, the best of them: somebody drills through the shared wall during the quietest passage. We kept going out of sheer stubbornness. And the thing held up. That left hand laid down a rocking bass none of us had imagined, the ragged voice fit the words, and the floor pushed us to play softer than usual. On the night, we asked for rugs and kept it all.

units: the access roads clog because drivers all set out at the same hour
each driver believes that pushing ahead alone serves his own interest
traffic specialists see sensible choices whose sum produces the opposite effect
a first solution spreads the start of work across the morning
staggering the departures thins out the crowding at the peak
a second measure gives one lane to cars carrying several riders
that reserved lane rewards the sharing of a vehicle
applying both measures together raises the speed and the punctuality of public transit
the main obstacle is the lack of coordination among independent decision makers
text: Roads into the middle of a city clog for a plain reason: nearly every driver pulls out at the same hour. Each one figures that pressing ahead alone will save time, and the line grows longer for everybody. Traffic engineers describe a pile of reasonable decisions that adds up to an absurd outcome. Two remedies come up again and again. The first spreads the departures out: employers stagger when shifts begin, and the peak thins across a wider stretch of the morning. The second sets aside one lane for cars carrying more than one rider, which pays off the trouble of sharing a trip. Where both have been tried together, average speeds climb back and the buses hold to their timetables. So the barrier is not a technical one. It comes down to coordinating people who each decide on their own.

units: a bicycle courier had ridden the same machine for seven years
his old two wheeler felt heavy and rattled over rough ground
the bike lent by the shop was slimmer and quick on the flat
he expected to be won over but felt uneasy at first
the old machine forgave a sloppy line of travel
the borrowed one reacted harshly under braking
after a week he decided that each machine had an advantage of its own
he gave the loaned model back
he simply replaced his braking system
text: Seven years on the same machine, and the courier finally consented to try another. His old bicycle sat heavy underneath him, the wide handlebars forced his shoulders open, and the rear fender rattled over every broken patch of road. The replacement from the shop was its opposite: a slender frame, additional spokes, deep rims that rolled across flat ground almost without effort. He anticipated delight. What arrived instead was plain discomfort. His old bicycle forgave a wobbly line; this one punished the slightest drift of the wheel. The pads bit so fiercely at the first junction that he nearly pitched over the front. A week later he reckoned it up: the lighter machine triumphed on speed, the older one on confidence. He returned the borrowed bicycle and replaced nothing except his brakes.

units: setting aside an hour for checks before a long trip is advised
the front glass has to be cleaned on the inside as well as the outside
the mirrors are set once you are sitting in the driving position
tire pressure is measured while the tires are not hot
the state of the brakes can be seen through the opening in the wheel
the fluid levels under the hood have to be topped off
a level that drops quickly points to a leak in the circuit
the bulkiest bags go at the bottom of the luggage space
writing the checks down makes later departures easier
text: Before a long drive, allow yourself a full hour and work through the car one area at a time. Begin with visibility: wash the front glass on both faces, run the wipers briefly to confirm they leave no smear, then settle into the driver seat and adjust each mirror from there. Move to the wheels: read the tire pressure while the rubber remains cold, examine how evenly the tread has worn, and inspect the pads through the gap in the rim. Open the hood and top off the washer fluid, the coolant and the oil; a level that sinks quickly means a leak, never a thirst. Load last: heavy bags flat across the floor of the trunk, nothing loose on the rear shelf, straps around whatever protrudes. Record everything you inspected in a small notebook. The following departure will feel calmer.

units: the first train came out of the depot before sunrise
people from the neighborhood watched the departure from behind barriers
the recently built rail link serves the warehouse area and the station
the work had started four years earlier
moving the buried pipes was the most expensive phase
laying the power cables was held up by a shortage of parts
test runs without riders brought a faulty track switch to light
the opening to the public was pushed back twice
shopkeepers in the area grew annoyed at these delays
text: The first streetcar rolled out of the depot just before sunrise, watched by people from the neighborhood who had gathered along the barriers to see it go. The freshly laid line now ties the warehouse district to the train station, four years after the first crews arrived. They spent the opening months moving buried pipes, an invisible job and by far the priciest of the whole build. Rails came next, then the overhead wiring, which stalled when the parts ran short. Test runs without riders turned up a faulty switch at the entrance to the depot, and putting it right took three weeks. The start of paid service slipped twice, and shopkeepers cut off from their customers made their irritation heard. The head of the project now says the promised frequency will hold from the coming weeks onward.

units: a narrow strip of grass runs along the roadway
vehicles squeezing past each other have damaged the edge of the road
two parallel ruts have been dug into that border
rain sits in these hollows instead of reaching the ditch
the trapped water softens the ground and breaks up the edge of the surface
vehicles hugging the right make the rutting worse
stakes driven in by people living along the road are knocked flat by wide trailers
the low light of evening makes these deformations easier to see
this old lane carries far heavier traffic than the one it was built for
text: A thin band of cropped grass runs beside the narrow road, and it is the grass that gives the story away. Cars squeezing past one another have bitten into the shoulder until the ground gave way and sagged into two parallel ruts. Rain collects in them instead of draining off toward the ditch; it seeps down, softens the soil, and the edge of the hard surface cracks away in flakes. Every vehicle that hugs the right cuts the groove a little deeper. People living along the road drove in stakes to mark the limit, but the stakes lean now, torn loose by trailers too wide for the space they are given. When the light comes in low at dusk, every hollow stands out and the lane looks stitched with dark scars. From that one ruined margin you can guess what a cart track is asked to carry today.

units: the wearing out of a road depends above all on the weight carried by each axle
the damage grows far faster than the mass under a power law
one loaded truck harms the top layer as much as a very large number of cars
engineers understand this mechanism
the rules on paying a share ignore this mechanism
the sum asked of haulers depends mainly on the declared dimensions
a first correction would charge for the load measured under each axle
sensors set into the road surface would make that measurement possible
a second correction would spread the freight over more axles
text: Nothing wears out a road like the weight riding on a single axle. The damage does not rise in step with the load; it climbs by a steep power, so one fully laden truck chews through the top layer as fast as many thousands of cars. Highway engineers have understood this mechanism for a long time. The rules on who pays what take no notice of it at all: a hauler is billed mainly on the size he declares for his vehicle. Two corrections follow from that. Charge for the real load under each axle, read by sensors set into the road surface, rather than for a tonnage stated on paper. Then push the freight onto a greater number of axles, something trailer builders already know how to do. A road priced by the wear it takes would cost far less to keep up than a road priced at random.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the head of the depot first worked as a driver
she drove on night runs
she holds that the two jobs differ in almost every respect
behind the wheel the attention goes to what is happening right now
in management the effects of a decision show up much later
as a driver she judged her success by arriving on time
as a manager she judges it by the steadiness of every route
she has kept the habit of listening to the sounds of the vehicles
she values what a driver reports more than the readings of instruments
text: The woman who runs the bus depot started out behind the wheel herself, on the night runs. Two jobs people assume are close, she says, and almost nothing about them lines up. Driving, your world ends at the windshield: a signal, someone stepping off the curb, a door that will not close. From a desk the view stretches over weeks, and a call made at the start of a week shows what it was worth a season later. As a driver she measured herself by whether she reached the last stop on time. As a manager she measures the steadiness of a whole network. One habit stayed with her from the road, and she prizes it: listening to the bodywork. A groan from an axle, reported by a driver, tells her more than a whole page of gauges. Her old colleagues fault her only for growing strict about schedules.

units: the assessment covers a shared bicycle service opened not long ago
the mechanical design of the machines is judged sturdy
the parts that wear can be swapped without special tools
such repairability is unusual for a fleet of this kind
the drop off points are bunched too tightly in the central area
slots grow scarce in the districts up the slope
a rider who goes down early finds no space on the way back
the pricing favors short trips and penalizes long rentals
the saddle setting and the height of the bars are judged comfortable
text: Three things stand out about the shared bike service that opened not long ago. The build comes first, and it earns real respect: a thick frame, reinforced rims, a fender welded on rather than bolted, brake pads you can swap out with ordinary tools. What wears can be repaired, and that stays rare on a fleet of this kind. The spread of the docks is the weak point. Stations bunch up in the center and thin out as soon as the ground starts to rise, so a rider who coasts down at dawn comes back to find every slot taken. Pricing rewards quick hops and hits long rentals hard, which suits an errand but talks you out of a ride taken for pleasure. One last point in its favor deserves a mention: the saddle adjusts with a single hand, and the bars sit high enough to spare a tender back.

units: the writer sends his message from a seat on a train
the train follows a tight valley
he left his starting point very early with an overloaded bag
the bus at the start of the trip had a flat tire
the driver fixed it while complaining about the sloping shoulder
the passengers had to help move the vehicle
that incident made him miss his rail connection
a ticket clerk put him on a train that halts at every stop
he finds the experience worthwhile in the end despite the piled up delay
text: I am writing from a seat aboard a train, a tight valley sliding past the window, and I will recount the whole business in order, because this journey deserves it. I departed at first light with an overloaded bag and altogether excessive faith in my connections. An hour beyond town, the bus blew a tire. The driver hauled out the jack, grumbled about the tilt of the shoulder, and enlisted every passenger to push. So of course I missed the train I had booked. At the following halt, a woman behind the ticket window transferred me onto a slow service that stops everywhere, and hamlets slid past that I would otherwise never have noticed. Around midday I shared my lunch with a couple in the middle of moving house. The delay accumulated without troubling me. Please do not pity me. I came out ahead.

units: the question raised is whether to close the stops that few people use
the planning specialist holds that the question is badly framed
she blames the thin ridership on how far apart the runs are
a service that comes rarely drives riders away
the fall in ridership is then used to justify further cuts in service
she believes that travel by booking can break this circle
she insists that booking be possible by voice call as well as online
she points out that a vehicle without riders costs nearly as much as a full one
she concludes that removing a stop treats the effect and strengthens the origin of the problem
text: Should the stops that almost nobody uses be shut down? The engineer responsible for planning replies flatly that the question has been framed the wrong way around. Thin ridership, she explains, originates in how far apart the runs are: a service that comes rarely drives riders away, and departing riders push the counts lower still, which is then read as grounds for further cuts. We ask her whether booking a ride on demand breaks the loop. She believes it can, on one condition: the booking must work by voice over a telephone as readily as on a screen, otherwise the remedy excludes the very people it claims to serve. On cost, she notes that an empty vehicle runs up nearly the bill of a full one. Closing a stop, she concludes, treats the symptom and nourishes its underlying cause.

units: a depot supervisor lays out two routes for a newly hired driver
the expressway has a recent safety barrier and a toll point where you get on
the surface of the expressway is smooth and barely shakes the vehicle
the second route runs through small towns whose pavement has broken open
speed humps rise before the intersections of the second route
the driver objects to the direct run on grounds of cost and boredom
the supervisor holds that a broken road wears the mechanics more than the toll costs
the driver comes around to her supervisor and picks the expressway
text: The depot supervisor laid out both routes for the newly hired driver and told her straight off that they were not equal. The first runs along an expressway with a fresh safety barrier the whole way and a toll point where you get on. The surface there stays smooth, so the cab barely shudders. The other cuts through small towns where the pavement has broken open into holes, and a speed hump rises before every intersection. She pushed back: the direct run costs money, and the sameness of it wears you down. Her supervisor answered that torn-up pavement chews through suspension far faster than any toll eats into the day's takings. A swerve caused by an unmarked hole, he added, comes dearer still. In the end she granted that safety weighed more than the saving, and she settled on the expressway.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: trade called for surfaces able to carry heavily loaded wagons
the width of the way had to let two teams pass each other
military needs produced straight lines and evenly spaced stopping places
ordinary travelers gained places to rest and points to draw water
carved markers announced the distance still to be covered
upkeep forced itself in because a neglected way breaks down and closes over
these old concerns turn up in the networks still being built
text: Organized road networks grew out of needs that had little to do with one another. Commerce came first. The builders had to lay down a surface firm enough that a loaded wagon would not sink into it, and wide enough that two teams could pass without either one halting. Warfare pushed next, and it pushed differently: straight lines, and stopping places set at even intervals so a column could move without scattering. Only later did anyone think of the ordinary traveler, who gained wayside inns, watering troughs, and carved markers announcing how far was left to go. Upkeep settled the matter on its own, since a way nobody tends will rut, fill with brush, and shrink back to a footpath. Every one of those old concerns turns up again, barely altered, in the networks we are still building today.

units: marks on the ground show where the doors will open
you have to wait for riders to get off before stepping on
two streams meeting in the doorway slow the whole exchange
once aboard it is better to work toward the middle of the car
the entry step turns slick in rain and brings people down
you are advised to get ready to leave one stop before the one you want
forcing the door is a bad idea and you can come back on the other track
text: You step onto the platform, and the first thing to do is spot where the doors will line up. Painted marks on the ground tell you. Then let people off. Sounds obvious, but two streams meeting in the doorway obstruct the whole exchange and cost the entire carriage a solid minute. Once you are aboard, work your way toward the middle instead of stationing yourself beside the entrance. The boarding step deserves some attention when it rains, because the surface turns slick and passengers go down fast. On the way out, get yourself ready one stop early: bag closed, one hand free. And if you miss it, whatever you do, don't wrestle with the door. Ride to the next one, cross over, and come back on the other track. Nothing dramatic happens, unless you insist on fixing your mistake in a rush.

units: a front tire tore open on the edge of a hole in the surface
the steering yanked hard and the coach left its line
the driver gave up on hard braking so as not to unsettle the heavy truck behind him
he let the side barrier take the friction of the vehicle
the riders heard the body grinding along the metal for a long stretch
the inquiry showed that the repair of the surface had been botched
the top layer had peeled loose after a wet season
what the riders take away is that the barrier held
text: A single blown tire was enough to turn a routine run into an emergency. The coach was holding the right lane when the front wheel tore itself open against the edge of a badly patched hole. The steering yanked hard, and the vehicle began veering off toward the shoulder. The driver did not stand on the brake, a maneuver that would have swung the trailer of the truck riding behind him. He eased off the accelerator instead and let the side barrier absorb the friction. The passengers, shaken about, heard the bodywork grinding along the metal for a long stretch before the whole thing came to rest. The investigation established afterward that the surface had been patched in haste after a wet season, and that the top layer had peeled loose. What the riders take away is simpler: the barrier held.

units: loading a luggage bay is a matter of method and not of muscle
the bags arrive in no order while the space available is fixed
you are advised to sort the bags on the ground before opening the hatch
hard cases and soft bags are split into two groups
the heaviest pieces go against the back wall
the soft bags fill the hollows the cases leave
the bags for the first stop go near the opening
a well built load does not shift under braking
text: Loading a luggage bay calls for method rather than muscle, and the trouble comes from one thing only: the bags arrive in whatever order they arrive, while the space forgives nothing. So begin on the ground, unhurried, before you ever swing the hatch open. Set the rigid cases to one side, the collapsible bags to the other, and keep apart whatever will have to come out along the way. Then stand the heaviest pieces against the back wall, flat, edge toward you; they will form a base that does not shift. Push the soft bags into the hollows the cases leave, the way straw is packed into a mattress. Save the space by the opening for what gets off at the first stop. A bay built this way stays motionless under braking, and the unloading runs its course without anything tumbling onto the stones.

units: two ways of collecting tolls work on the same road corridor
the barrier setup forces vehicles to come to a full stop
the queue stretches as soon as traffic thickens at the barrier setup
the repeated pull-aways drive up fuel use among heavy trucks
the overhead reader lets vehicles through without any break in pace
throughput measured at the reader runs well above that of the barriers
the loss of the braking cuts wear on the surface
automatic reading fails when plates are dirty
collecting after the fact brings a heavier load of paperwork
text: Two ways of collecting tolls now operate along the same corridor, and the readings taken at the recently opened interchange show just how far apart they sit. The barrier plaza, with its sorting lanes, forces every vehicle to a full stop. Throughput there hits a ceiling, the queue stretches as soon as traffic thickens, and the repeated pull-aways drive up the fuel consumption of the heavy trucks. The overhead reader mounted on the access ramp lets vehicles through at an unbroken pace. Throughput measured there triples, and wear on the surface drops, since the repeated braking has disappeared. Technicians point to one weakness in exchange: the reader fails on dirty plates, and collection then falls back on billing after the fact, which is considerably more expensive to process. Smoother flow, in short, is bought with paperwork.

units: the moored vessel takes up the whole length of the pier
a row of round openings ringed in brass runs level with the water
the level given over to vehicles looks like a wide metal hall
the access ramps clatter under passing wheels
the cabin floor is known by its narrow passageways and numbered doors
the topmost deck takes the walkers and holds benches bolted down
a lowered gangway joins the stern of the vessel to the pier
two thick lines hold the vessel against the swell
text: The moored vessel takes up the full length of the pier, and its construction reads level by level. Down at the bottom, the dark hull barely breaks the surface of the water, and a row of round portholes runs along it, each one ringed in brass that the salt air has tarnished. Above that opens the vehicle deck, an immense metal cavern where the ramps clatter under passing wheels. Next comes the cabin floor, known at once by its narrow passageways and the numbered doors that follow one another without a break. The topmost deck belongs to walkers: benches bolted down, an unbroken railing, a signal mast, a funnel as broad as a tower. Astern, a lowered gangway reaches the concrete of the pier, and two thick lines, drawn tight on the diagonal, hold the whole vessel steady against the swell.

units: roadways were widened in the name of easy driving
shops were moved out to the edges where parking was plentiful
that move stretched the distances each of us has to cover
doubling the lanes was followed by an even thicker jam
a recent reversal narrows the roadways and hands space back to people on foot and on bicycles
the writer refuses to read that reversal as a passing fashion
the old mistake lay in treating traffic as a fixed volume
traffic in fact answers to the lanes it is offered
text: Before judging the state of our streets, it helps to walk back through the decisions that made them. Roadways were widened first, on the belief that easy driving would serve everyone. Shops were then pushed out to the edges, where parking was plentiful, which stretched the distances each of us has to cover. Jams showed up anyway, so the lanes were doubled, and the jams came back thicker than before. Lately the order has reversed: roadways are narrowing, trees are going in, space is handed back to people on foot and on bicycles. Call it fashion if you like, but fashion is not what it is. It corrects a mistake several generations old, one that treated traffic as a fixed volume of fluid rather than a demand shaped by the lanes offered to it. Worth remembering before the next job starts.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the woman driving the evening service did not choose this work at the start
she worked as a mechanic in a shop that closed
the closing of the shop pushed her to take the heavy-vehicle license
her time with engines lets her catch a worn suspension at the first speed hump
she calls out faults before they can cut the service short
knowing the frame lets her ease over obstacles gently
she had the entry step replaced because its worn edge troubled older riders
her line logs fewer incidents than the others
the company has handed her the training of incoming drivers
text: The woman who drives the evening service never set out to do this work. She started as a mechanic in a repair shop. The shop closed, and she took the heavy-vehicle license because nothing better came along. Her years with engines ended up serving her well. She feels a worn suspension at the first speed hump, and she calls the fault in before it can strand the line. Knowing the frame by heart, she eases over the humps so gently that her riders no longer bang into the seat in front of them. She also got the entry step replaced, since a worn edge made climbing aboard risky for older passengers. The outcome is plain: her line logs fewer incidents than the others, and the company now hands her the incoming drivers to train. She laughs about it, having only ever wanted to repair motors.

units: the recently opened bus terminal was met with polite praise
the boarding bays run in a line along a single corridor
nothing hung overhead helps the traveler find his coach
a rider in a hurry has to walk the whole row before spotting his departure
the hall throws back an echo and makes spoken announcements impossible to follow
panels hung above each bay would settle the question of direction
absorbent material set under the roof beams would help hearing
the number of benches ought to be doubled
the writer finds the structure sound but its use badly thought out
text: The recently opened bus terminal deserves better than the polite praise that greeted it. Its main flaw hits you at the door: the boarding bays run down a single corridor with nothing hung overhead to mark them, so a rider in a hurry walks the whole row before spotting his coach. The hall, for its part, rings hollow and stretches the announcements until nobody can follow them. All of this would amount to failure if the building gave us nothing to work with. The remedies exist, though, and they come cheap. Lit panels hung above each bay would settle the question of direction. Absorbent material fixed under the roof beams would give the voice back its edges. As for the benches, too few of them, doubling the number would do. The frame is sound. It is the use of it that nobody thought through.

units: the writer has settled not far from a harbor area
he lists the vehicles he has at hand
the boat belongs to his neighbor
he has learned to free the line that holds the boat
his bicycle is old and needs weekly upkeep
he uses it to reach the market
an animal pulls the cart
the craftsman strengthened the pulling gear
the shared boat leaves a trail on the water
the load he must move guides his choice
text: Dear friend, I am writing to set out for you the means of travel I have had at hand since settling close to the harbor. There are four of them, and each has its hour. The first is a boat that belongs to my neighbor, and I have learned to slip its mooring line free without fumbling at the knot. The second is an old bicycle, heavy in the frame, which I service every week without fail and ride down to the covered market. The third is a cart drawn by a donkey, whose harness the wheelwright strengthened for me before the cold weather set in. The fourth is the river ferry, which leaves a broad and quiet wake behind it. I confess that my choice depends above all on the load I must carry and on the state of the tracks. Please accept my sincere regards, and believe in my wish to welcome you here before long.

units: training opens with a spell of watching from the landing stage
the newcomer first learns to work the helm
he then sails as second hand on real crossings
approach drills happen over still water at first
a head wind is added to raise the difficulty
the examination includes a crossing made in the dark
a breakdown is staged on purpose during the test
the final landing is carried out without power
the certified pilot works under a veteran for one season
shipping owners distrust pilots who lack experience
text: How does anyone begin training as a river ferry pilot? It starts at the landing stage, where the trainee spends his days watching the maneuvers and learns to hold the helm without forcing it. What comes after that? The candidate ships out as second hand and repeats his approaches on real crossings, over still water at first, then against a head wind. Which tests close the course? A crossing made in the dark, a breakdown staged on purpose and a landing brought off without power. Why does that last one matter? It forces the crew to read the current and to watch the wash thrown up by passing vessels. Is the certificate enough to take command? No, the holder must still shadow an old hand through a whole season. Shipping owners welcome such caution, for they rarely hand a deck over to a beginner.

units: the courier takes off his head gear before speaking
a slippery layer covered the road surface
his two-wheeler lost its grip on a bend
the driving wheel spun without biting the ground
he insists that he did not fall
he weaved between heavy trucks to keep out of the ditch
a parcel came off the rear rack
he turned back to pick the parcel up
his delivery round ran late
he took a picture of the wheel to convince his boss
text: The delivery rider set his helmet down on the table and started talking. He told me the road had been coated all over with a thin slick of mud and that his scooter had slid out on the lower bend. The back wheel, he said, would spin without biting as soon as he opened the throttle at all. I asked him whether he had gone down, because he was limping a little on his way in. He said no, but he had weaved between two heavy trucks to keep himself out of the ditch. A parcel had worked loose from the rear rack, so he doubled back to pick it up, and the whole round ended up running late. His boss, he told me, never believes a word about mud. That is why he took a picture of the dirty wheel before setting off again, just to have something solid in hand. Then he shrugged and put the helmet back on.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: switching tracks once called for heavy hand labor
workmen had to lift the rolling stock and shove it across
the growing number of lines made the problem sharper
a workshop hand thought up a device with swinging blades
one pull on a lever was enough to move those blades
from then on the train changed course while still rolling
the system had few parts and was easy to mend
this invention helped lines grow into a network
students of technical history see it as a turning point
text: Long ago a train on rails could change course only at the cost of painful labor. Workmen levered the wheels up with a bar, then shoved the frame across by hand, so every branching point ate up real effort. Operators wanted a way out, for lines were multiplying and crossings came thick and fast. A mechanic in a repair shed hit on the idea of two hinged steel blades, held against the fixed rails, which a lever swung aside in a single motion. From then on the train swung onto the other track while still rolling. The method spread fast, because it used few parts and could be mended where it stood. It changed the shape of the lines themselves: builders stopped laying single stretches and wove webs in which each branch met the next. Historians of technology call it a founding gesture.

units: the two ways of moving look alike but spend energy differently
the walker must lift his own weight at every stride
his energy drains away in a movement he keeps repeating
the cyclist lets the saddle carry his weight
he keeps up a turning motion that the wheel holds on to
for the same effort the bicycle covers a greater distance
walking calls for no machinery at all
it gets over obstacles that a wheel cannot clear
the machine offers speed but stays fragile
the kind of ground should guide the traveler in his choice
text: Walking and cycling look like near neighbors, and yet they spend their energy in wholly different ways. The walker lifts his own weight at every stride, sets it down and lifts it again. His effort drains away into a stubborn beat. The cyclist hands that weight over to a saddle and has only to keep a circle turning, which the wheel carries on for him. Out of this comes a striking gap. For the same effort the bicycle takes its rider far beyond what his legs alone would manage. Walking keeps a quieter advantage. It asks for no chain, no inner tube, no smooth roadway, and it climbs the stair, the bramble, the loose sand. One buys speed and pays with a fragile machine. The other buys freedom and pays in slowness. A wise traveler reads the ground before he settles the question.

units: the customer reports a sway that shows up at high speed
the diagnosis is worked through station by station
the coupling part had too much play in it
that play set off jolts on a crowned road surface
the tires showed slanted wear along the inner edge
such wear points to wheels that are out of alignment
one suspension clamp had lost its grip
the braking system worked but was clogged with grime
the road test after repair showed no sway at all
the driver had been running like that for weeks
text: A driver left his trailer with us on a wet evening, reporting an odd sway that showed up as soon as the speed climbed. We worked through it station by station. First station: the coupling ball, whose play ran well past the allowed tolerance, enough on its own to set the whole rig lurching over a crowned road surface. Second station: the tires, worn on a slant along the inner edge, which is the classic mark of wheels out of alignment. Third station: the leaf suspension, where one clamp had lost its torque altogether. Fourth station: the brake circuit, sound in itself but clogged with grime. We fitted a fresh ball, reset the axle, drew the clamps up again and bled the lines. On the road test the sway had gone, and the driver admitted he had been running like that for a whole season.

units: the first check bears on how hard the tires are inflated
a soft tire slips on wet ground
the drive train must be looked over next
the braking surfaces have to stay free of damp
the saddle is set so the leg comes almost straight at the bottom of the stroke
the bags are spread on either side of the rear wheel
an uneven load makes the ride unsteady on a slope
you take along what is needed to mend a puncture
a brake test comes before you join the traffic
text: Before setting out, kindly work through the following steps in the order given here. Begin with the tires and squeeze each one firmly between thumb and forefinger, since soft rubber slips on a wet road surface. Look the chain over next and check its tension along its whole run, then turn to the brake pads, whose faces must stay clean and dry. Set the saddle height so that the leg comes almost straight at the bottom of the pedal stroke. Load the bags on either side of the rear wheel and balance the weight carefully between them. An uneven load will set the machine weaving on the very first descent. Take along a spare inner tube, two tire levers and a hand pump. Finish with a short trial run on level ground, squeezing the brakes gradually as you go, and only then join the traffic.

units: a crossing structure has been taken out of service for repair
vehicles now use a narrow road along the heights
trucks have trouble passing one another there
the time spent commuting has doubled
the buses that carry people together are running late
shops in the lower quarter are losing custom
the local authority has put link boats into service
this arrangement does not settle the matter of freight
the metal frame had been eaten away by corrosion
completion is expected before the cold season ends
text: Closing the bridge for repairs has thrown traffic across the whole town into disorder. Vehicles now climb a narrow ridge road where heavy trucks struggle to pass one another. The effect came at once: journeys between home and workshop take twice as long, and the buses that gather workers arrive behind schedule. Shopkeepers in the lower quarter report a clear drop in custom, since people give up on the detour. The local authority answered by chartering two river shuttles, which link the banks at close intervals. The stopgap takes in a share of the walkers, but it leaves the question of deliveries untouched. An engineer on the site explains that the steel frame had been eaten away by corrosion and that no partial repair would have held. Work should finish before the cold season ends.

units: the access track is made of gravel and looks to be in poor shape
it climbs steeply and forks at the top
the hollows in the ground shake vehicles violently
rain makes the surface slippery
the wheels lose their grip as the bend comes up
a man living nearby decided to act
he brought in crushed stone to fill the holes
he opened a drainage ditch along the bank
the ground now dries out quickly
dust rises when towed vehicles go past
text: Honestly, our gravel track has never been much to look at. It climbs steeply, it turns hard at the fork up top, and the ruts run so deep that the car pitches about like an old rowboat on a swell. In the rain the surface turns to soap and the wheels let go just before the bend, so you grip the wheel with both hands and hope that nothing is coming down at you. The man at the bottom of the hill finally had enough of it. He hauled in a whole load of crushed stone, filled the hollows one by one, then cut a channel along the bank to carry the water off. Since then the slope dries out fast and the mud no longer builds up. It is not perfect. Dust flies up the moment a trailer goes past, but at last we drive up there without fear. The mail carrier still leaves his van below and walks up.

units: the piece sets road widening against the growth of rail
a line of cars takes up a wide strip for few passengers
a train on rails moves as many people in less space
those who defend the car point to its being always available
that advantage counts above all where few people live
towns that widened their main roads see congestion return
this return of saturation happens very quickly
a service running at steady intervals takes in the rise in numbers
the writer urges spending first on the lasting answer
text: Should we widen the expressways once more, or pay for extra train sets? The question deserves a cool head. A line of private cars takes up a great width of ground to shift a handful of people, while a train on rails carries the same crowd within a far narrower strip. Drivers reply that a car goes anywhere, at any hour, with no connection to catch and no waiting about. The point holds, above all outside the crowded districts. Yet towns that have doubled their main roads watch the flow fill the widened lanes to the brim within a single season. A service running at steady intervals, by contrast, takes in the growth without choking. Our stand is plain: widening relieves briefly, frequent service relieves for good. Public money would do better to fund what does not clog up again.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the future barge pilot grew up beside a waterway
as a child she watched the boatmen tie their vessels to the quay
she began her working life as a helper on a sand barge
she learned to read the movement of the current
her training covered approach and slowing maneuvers
she learned to bring a heavy hull alongside despite the wind
after many seasons she was given command of a convoy
that convoy could tow two more craft
she now teaches the trade to beginners
she tells them to think ahead to the next maneuver
text: The woman who would one day pilot a barge grew up in a cluster of houses along a narrow canal. As a child she watched the boatmen tie their vessels to the quay and push off again at dawn toward the next lock. In her teens she took a helper's job aboard a barge loaded with sand, and there she learned to read the current. Her training was demanding. She had to master the approach, slow down without scraping the bank, and lay a heavy hull alongside while a crosswind shoved against it. After many seasons on the water she was given command of a full convoy, one that could tow two more craft behind it. She teaches beginners now, and she repeats a single rule to them: a careful boat handler is already thinking about the next maneuver, because water forgives nothing done in haste.

units: a funicular now serves a very steep slope
a winding road used to provide that link
the climb now costs travelers less effort
the shops at the top of the slope draw more customers
ridership runs past what the operators forecast
the cars are packed at peak times
the wait at the foot of the slope turns some users away
dropping the road shuttles leaves isolated residents without service
the installation is judged sound technically but badly sized
text: The funicular put in on the hillside deserves a mixed verdict. Its car climbs a steep face that a winding road used to serve, and swapping one for the other has pulled in two directions at once. Since the climb now costs a traveler no effort at all, the small shops at the top of the slope draw customers they had given up on, and their takings have risen sharply. Ridership, though, has run so far past what the operators forecast that the cars leave packed through the afternoon peak, and the line building up at the foot of the slope turns away part of the crowd, who give up and stay below. One more consequence is still argued over: the road shuttles were dropped, and the residents living farthest out have no service at all. The engineering side convinces. The sizing plainly does not.

units: the writer of the message moved far from where he works
his coach trip took a very long time
traffic jams made the arrival time impossible to predict
he arrived worn out before he had even started
a coworker suggested a combined solution to him
he now reaches the station with a folding bike
he finishes the trip on a regional train
the bike lets him get around heavy traffic
he saves half a period on his old run
he invites the person he is writing to come try the route
text: You asked whether the move had wrecked everything, and at first, honestly, it had. The coach crawled, it sat behind a line of cars that never seemed to end, and I could never tell what minute I would walk in. I would show up worn out before starting anything at all. Then a coworker floated an idea I should have come up with myself: split the trip in two. Now I head out with a folding bike, slip past the stopped traffic all the way down to the station, and finish on a regional train, where I finally get to sit with the bike tucked under the seat. The run is half a period shorter than the old one, and I turn up cheerful instead of furious. Rain is the one drawback, but a cape handles it. Come out some morning and I will lend you the spare bike, and you can ride the route with me.

units: a planning specialist answers a reporter's questions
she compares the streetcar and the bus with a reserved lane
the streetcar carries more riders on each run
rails call for costly and lengthy works
the bus goes into service far more quickly
the bus copes badly with heavy crowds
the streetcar keeps its edge on very busy corridors
she warns against deciding without studying local demand
she holds the route to matter more than the type of vehicle
text: Lay down track, or paint a reserved lane? We put that question to a specialist in the planning of large towns. The two options never come out even, she answers, and it is the setting that decides between them. A streetcar takes on far more riders at each run, she explains, and it moves along without getting stuck behind the general traffic. Against that, laying rail means a heavy, expensive worksite, one that ties up the streets for whole seasons at a time. A bus in a protected lane goes into service quickly and can be shifted elsewhere if the demand moves, but it chokes as soon as the flows begin to swell. On the busiest corridors, then, the streetcar keeps its edge. Her conclusion refuses any clean verdict. Before you pick a vehicle, she says, study what the demand really is, because a badly drawn route ruins whatever runs on it.

units: a woman traveling asks a sailor a question on the deck of a night ferry
the sailor lists what he loves about his work
he names the smell of wet rope
he mentions the noise of the chains being worked
he brings up the brightness of the markers on dark water
he values the quiet of the sleeping passengers
he says he knows the regulars by their walk
he claims the crossing home never resembles the crossing out
text: On the deck of the night ferry, a woman traveling alone asked the sailor what still held him to the work. He rested a hand on the rail and answered her with a list, as though he had had it ready for a long while. He loved the smell of wet rope, he said, that thick scent which soaks into your palms and stays there. He loved the clatter of the chains being worked before a landing, a racket that announces the shore ahead. He loved the brightness of the markers set out on black water, told off one by one all the way to the mouth of the channel. He loved the quiet of the passengers dozing against their bags under scratchy blankets. He knew the regulars by nothing more than their careful step on the wet plating. And before he went back up to the bridge again, he added that the crossing home never once resembles the crossing out.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the first heavy loads were moved on wooden rollers
the invention of the spoked wheel made vehicles lighter
a harness bearing on the shoulders replaced the strap that pressed on the animals' throats
that change raised the pulling force available
roads laid with broken stone kept the wheels from sinking
wooden strips then guided the carts in the mines
steam removed the dependence on animal strength
each advance worked on the contact between the vehicle and the ground
text: Before any machinery existed at all, shifting a heavy mass meant levering it onto wooden rollers and carrying each roller back around to the front, over and over. The spoked wheel came later and made the bodies of vehicles lighter, so that far less effort went into getting them moving. Then the harness changed, and that mattered more than it sounds: the strap that pressed on an animal's throat gave way to a collar bearing on the shoulders, and teams could suddenly pull loads that had been well out of reach. Roads were laid with broken stone so that the rims stopped sinking down into mud. In the mine galleries, wooden strips were set down to guide the carts along their run. Steam closed the sequence out by cutting the tie to muscle. Each step worked on the same weak point, the place where the vehicle meets the ground.

units: a slowdown can appear with no obstacle and no crash
one driver brakes lightly for some small reason
the driver behind brakes harder out of caution
the amplification travels back down the line
the line ends up stopping completely
the wave of slowing moves backward while the cars go forward
keeping enough room ahead of you softens the effect
following too closely makes the spread worse
text: It happens that a line of cars comes to a standstill although no obstacle and no crash of any kind blocks the roadway ahead. The mechanism behind it can be described exactly. One driver eases off the pedal for some small reason: a clumsy merge, a glance away, a rise in the road. The driver behind him sees the brake lights come on and presses a good deal harder, out of caution. The third reacts more sharply still, and the gaps go on tightening. Step by step the amplification travels back up the column until cars a long way behind have to stop dead. The odd part is that this wave of slowing moves backward through the line while the cars themselves keep rolling forward. The remedy fits into a single instruction: keep a comfortable gap ahead of you, and never ride the bumper of the driver in front.

units: a coach of hikers turns onto a mountain track
a rockfall blocks the road above a ravine
the width of the passage rules out turning around
the driver refuses to back down through several bends
the passengers clear away the lighter stones
a farm tractor arrives from the settlement nearby
the tractor pulls the main block aside with a chain
the trip starts again with a modest delay
the woman driving the tractor refuses any payment
text: The hikers' coach had turned onto a stony track that wound its way up toward the pass. Coming out of a bend that overhung a ravine, they found fallen rock lying right across the roadway. The track was far too narrow to turn on, and the driver flatly refused to back down over that many bends on so rough a surface. The passengers climbed out and cleared away the lighter stones by hand, but the largest one would not shift at all, however hard they pushed at it. A farmer from the settlement below finally appeared with her tractor, ran a chain around the block of rock, and dragged it onto the shoulder in three unhurried pulls. The coach set off again with only a modest delay, and the whole group applauded. Asked to name her price, she shrugged, climbed back up, and drove down toward her barns.

units: the text explains how to choose between a night train and a long-distance coach
it advises comparing the price of the two options first
the night train saves you paying for a room
the coach reaches stops the railway skips
the reader should check the arrival time before booking
booking a berth away from the corridor is recommended
you have to bring a soft bag for want of storage space
the coach forces stops that break up your sleep
the final choice rests on how much you value rest
text: Torn between a night train and a long-distance coach? Work through it in order. Compare the fares first, but add to the ticket price what a room would have cost you, because the train often makes up the difference that way. Then look at the map of stops, since the coach reaches small towns that the railway skips entirely. Check the arrival time before you book, or you will land before the ticket windows open. If you go by rail, pick a berth away from the corridor and bring a soft bag, or you will sleep against your luggage with your knees folded up. If you take the road, accept in advance the required stops that will wake you in the dark, and pack something to cover your eyes. Then settle it with one question: do you want to arrive rested, or to pay as little as you can?

units: a report describes an abandoned rail line being put back in service
crews have replaced the rotted ties
a tunnel overrun by roots has been cleared
a footbridge has been added for cyclists
people living nearby dread the noise of trains after dark
local growers count on shipping their goods by rail
riders will try the line before it officially opens
the fares have not been settled yet
text: Rusted rails that the brush had been swallowing up for a whole generation are carrying trains once more. Our report from the site of the reopening holds on to several points. The track comes first: crews have pulled out the rotted ties and cleared a tunnel where the roots had grown down as far as the ballast. Access comes next: a steel footbridge now spans the cutting, so that cyclists no longer have to scramble down the embankment to reach the far side. Then come the worries, since people living nearby dread the rumble of trains after dark and are asking for sound barriers. And the hopes, last of all: growers around the area are counting on shipping their harvests by rail. Riders will travel the line before it officially opens. The fare table, for its part, has not been settled yet.

units: a mountain road grows narrower as it climbs
the slope of the ground forces drivers to slow down
cold rain makes the surface dangerous and worsens the delays
the crews in charge of the road spread sand over it
this operation aims to keep heavy vehicles from sliding
traffic runs freely again before night falls
a hamlet set high up is served by no truck
goods are carried up there by pack animals
the people living there approve of this limit, which spares the track
text: The road that climbs toward the pass grows narrower the higher it goes. Its harsh grade forces drivers to ease off, and the slowing traffic backs up into one long line at the first bend. When cold rain sweeps across it, the asphalt turns slick and the line stretches further still. Maintenance crews spread sand on the roadway then, because an iced surface would send the heaviest vehicles sliding. The effect is immediate and plain: traffic settles back into a steady rhythm well before dark. Higher up, a steep track leaves the road and ends at a hamlet no truck ever reaches. With no drivable approach, deliveries come up on the backs of pack animals, which keeps every load small. The people who live there accept the limit, since it spares the track the wear that wheels would grind into it.

units: waiting on an overcrowded platform strongly irritates travelers
transit systems were designed for fewer users
ridership has outgrown capacity without any widening of the lines
buying extra cars is costly and useless if the stops are saturated
the writer proposes spreading ridership over different time slots
he names shifting office hours as one possible measure
he also suggests reserved lanes and cheaper fares outside the rush
places that tried these measures saw peak crowding drop
most riders would agree to leave later in order to sit down
text: Nothing wears a rider's patience thinner than a packed platform with no train in sight. The cause is no mystery. City networks were laid out for a smaller population, and demand has outgrown them while the lines themselves stayed exactly as wide as before. Buying more cars costs a fortune and settles nothing while the stations choke at the very same hour. Another way in deserves a hearing: spread the demand out rather than swallow it whole. Shift the start of the workday, set aside lanes for shared vehicles, cut the fare on quiet runs. Where such steps were tried, the worst of the crush eased with no digging at all. The objection comes back fast, that everyone guards his own timetable. It weakens once you ask the riders, most of whom would trade a later start for a seat.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the driver gladly talks about the start of his working life
his old machine was in poor shape and shut badly
its rattling body warned him of a bend in advance
the vehicle he has now is far more comfortable and quiet
a camera device has taken the place of the old mirror
riders once talked with each other the whole way
today's riders look at their screens in silence
the driver admits the newer equipment is easier on his back
he misses the smell of machinery at start-up, now gone
text: Ask the shuttle driver about his first years behind the wheel and he needs no second invitation. That early machine was worn out: the door never shut properly, the floor buzzed underfoot, and the whole rattling body called out a bend before the turn signal did. What he drives today shares nothing with it. The cab is hushed, the seat backs tilt where you want them, and a camera has taken over from the blind mirror he used to squint into. He measures his riders the same way. Once the entire village boarded together and talked the length of the aisle; now each one stares at a screen, and the run goes by almost without a word. None of that leaves him bitter, he says, because the newer machine is easier on his back. What he misses is the smell of a cold engine at start-up, which nothing built since can give him back.

units: three things catch the eye at the entrance of the renovated building
the entrance area was cramped and poorly lit before the work
glazing now brings daylight all the way down to the steps
the direction signs have been redrawn in large lettering
riders in a hurry find their way without checking a display
the old grimy seats have been taken out of the place
