the perches that replaced them are few and uncomfortable
the writer finds the outcome positive on the whole
reaching the platforms no longer calls for a detour
text: Three things catch the eye the moment you step into the rebuilt stop. The first is a matter of volume: the entrance hall, cramped and dim before the work, now opens under a glass roof that carries daylight down to the steps. The second is the signage, redrawn in oversized lettering and plain symbols, so that a rider in a hurry picks out the right track without ever looking up at a display. The third point flatters less. The grubby benches are gone, and what stands in their place is scarce and hard, as though the operator would rather nobody stayed long. The account still comes out ahead. Movement through the hall reads more clearly, reaching the platforms takes no detour anymore, and the hush of the sliding doors is a pleasant shock. One rider put it plainly: you breathe better, you sit less.

units: the person written to had warned of a soaked track after the water rose
the writer set out at first light with his bags strapped down
the first part of the ride was marked by stakes driven into the ground
the ruts left by his wheels closed up right behind him
the rain stopped halfway through the ride
the ground hardened under the wind
a steep climb forced the writer to walk and push his bicycle
he reached a high shelter as evening fell
the keeper of the shelter gave him hot soup
text: You warned me the track would be a swamp once the water had risen, and you were right. I set out at first light, bags strapped down tight, the handlebars heavy as an anchor. The opening stretch, staked out with pale markers, dropped between hedges soaked through, and my wheels cut two clean ruts that the mud swallowed shut behind me. Halfway along, the rain quit and the wind dried the crust of the ground, so I rolled a long easy hour barely thinking about it. Then the climb came, steep and with no end to it, and I got off to push, counting my own steps. As evening fell I reached the shelter on the plateau, hands black, heart light, and the keeper set a bowl of scalding soup down for me. I write to you from the window. The valley is steaming, and I already want to leave again tomorrow.

units: the energy stored by a vehicle grows with the square of its speed
doubling the speed makes the braking distance four times as long
a layer of water slips in between the rubber and the road
that layer cuts the grip and reduces the slowing obtained
the grooves of the tire push the water out to the sides
worn tires can no longer clear that water away
a more heavily loaded vehicle needs more force to slow as much
specialists advise widening the gap between vehicles when these conditions change
text: So what lengthens the stopping distance of a car that is already rolling fast? The first cause is stored energy, which grows with the square of the speed: double the pace and braking takes four times the room. And once the road is wet? A film of water slips in between the rubber and the ground, grip falls away, and the same pressure on the pedal buys less slowing than before. Do the grooves of a tire earn their keep? They throw that film out toward the edges. Worn smooth, they throw nothing out at all, and the car starts to float. And what does the load change? Added mass calls for more force to shed the same speed, so the stop grows longer yet. Engineers pack their whole answer into a single short rule: open up the gap ahead of you as soon as any one of these things changes.

units: a woman traveler reports that her connecting train has been canceled
the clerk blames the disruption on a plant blocking the rails
the incident happened near the mouth of an underground passage
a replacement road vehicle is set to leave from the square
that vehicle will go around the high ground to reach the station she wants
her ticket stays valid at no extra cost
the traveler fears her belongings are too bulky for the center aisle
a luggage hold will take her suitcases
a member of staff will lend a hand stowing the bags
text: At the counter, a traveler reported that her connecting train had just been canceled. The clerk answered that the whole line was affected, since a fallen branch was blocking the rails where they come out of the tunnel. She asked whether anything at all could be arranged before nightfall. He explained that a replacement coach would leave from the square outside and would reach the connecting station by rounding the high ground. The ticket in her hand stayed valid, he added, and nothing further would be charged. She worried about her luggage, too bulky in her view for a crowded center aisle. He put her mind at rest: a hold underneath would take the suitcases, and a member of staff would help load them. She thanked him and made for the exit named on the notice, her relief plain to see.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: carriage by water ruled before wheeled vehicles rose
a boat loaded with grain moved forward with almost no effort
animals hauling the same cargo wore out fast on broken ground
the gap comes from the resistance the ground puts up
overland routes served places the current could not reach
a waterway imposes one direction and one fixed course
the two systems split the work according to the cargo
the boat suited heavy loads carried without haste
the spread of paved roads tipped the balance toward the dry route
text: Long before the wheel took over the long hauls, water carried the greater bulk of everything that moved. A barge loaded with grain slid along the current on almost no effort at all, while a team dragging that same weight over broken ground gave out before half the day was done. The gap lay entirely in resistance: water gives way, mud holds on. Overland routes had one advantage the river could never offer. They went where people wanted them to go, high ground included, whereas the stream laid down its own course and its own direction. So the two networks split the work between them, the boat taking the heavy freight that could wait, the cart taking the short and supple run. Once stone-laid roads began to spread in number, that balance tipped over for good toward the dry route.

units: the writer boils getting a bicycle ready down to three checks
he advises pumping the tires up firm
he recommends looking over the tire surface for cuts
the brake levers must be squeezed while standing still to test the lock
friction parts worn too far have to be replaced
bags hung on the handlebars unbalance the steering
it is better to carry the weight low and toward the back
taking a spare tube and a pump saves you from finishing on foot
text: Getting a bicycle ready for a long ride comes down to three checks, and not a single one more than that. Tires first: pump them up firm, run your thumb along the tread, and hunt for the small cuts where a shard of glass may have lodged. Brakes next: squeeze the levers while standing still, watch whether the wheel locks clean, and swap out any pad whose grooves have worn flat. Then the load: a handlebar hung with bags makes the steering twitchy, so drop the weight low and set it toward the rear wheel. One last piece of advice, plain and obvious as it sounds. Take a spare tube and a pump along, because a flat halfway out turns a fine outing into a long walk home. A quarter of an hour of care in the workshop, and you roll away easy in your mind, with no dread of the first slow rise.

units: the vehicle pulled out after the middle of the night with every seat taken
the engine died at the second pickup point
it came to a stop on the shoulder of a fast road
the driver reported a failure in the fuel system
a woman rider trained in mechanics offered her help
they found a clogged filter and cleared it
the journey started again after a break of about half an hour
the passengers clapped when the engine caught
the company gave the rider a free travel voucher
text: It was past midnight when the coach pulled out of the terminal, packed full, doors hissing, a smell of cold coffee hanging in the aisle. At the second pickup the engine coughed twice and then died flat on the shoulder of the fast road. The driver switched on the hazard lights and announced a fault in the fuel feed. A rider coming home from a course in mechanics offered to help, and between them they traced a clogged filter and cleaned it with a rag and a great deal of patience. The coach pulled away again half an hour later, to clapping from every row. At the far end the operator handed a free travel voucher to the woman who had bailed out its driver. She said what she had really wanted was her own bed, and that the breakdown had woken her for nothing. The rest walked off already telling the story into their phones.

units: one of the two cloths comes from the fleece clipped off a farmed animal
the other cloth is drawn from a plant after soaking and crushing
the curled animal fibers hold warmth by trapping air
the plant cloth yields a smooth yarn that feels cool to the touch
the craftsman gives the animal material to cold-season clothing
the plant material serves for shirts because it carries damp away from the skin
the animal material tightens and mats together in hot water
the plant material takes repeated washing but creases easily
text: Lay two cloths side by side on a workbench and they will tell opposite stories. One begins as a fleece clipped off a herd animal, and its crimped fibers trap pockets of air, which is how they hold on to warmth. The other starts as a plant stalk soaked until it softens, then crushed and combed into a smooth yarn that feels cool under the fingers. A weaver builds on that split. Animal fiber goes into cold-weather clothing, where a thick weave slows the heat as it escapes. Plant fiber goes into shirts, because it carries damp away from the skin. Washing tells the two apart all over again. Hot water makes the animal fiber shrink and mat together, while the plant cloth takes wash after wash and simply creases at every fold. Choosing a cloth means choosing a climate, and choosing how you will look after it.

units: the narrator visits the workroom of a neighbor who sews
the visit happens on a rainy evening
the cloth is stored by kind in the workroom
tightly knitted fabrics unravel when a pin catches them
the tools include a battered thimble, a reserved pair of scissors and a marking chalk
the maker builds a cuff and sets a jacket lining without measuring twice
customers come back with cheap jackets that sit badly at the shoulder
the maker repairs those garments rather than throwing them out
text: The woman who lives next door sews, and one rainy evening she opened her workroom to me. Until then I had understood nothing at all about the clothes I put on every morning. She started with her cloth, which she keeps stacked by kind: soft cottons, coarse weaves that scratch the palm, fine knits that unravel the moment a pin catches them. Then came the tools, a battered thimble, a pair of scissors that nobody else may touch, a flat stick of chalk for marking. After that she showed me her hands at work, and there I lost the thread completely. She builds a cuff, drops a lining into a jacket, and never stops to measure twice. Last of all she talked about her customers, the ones who come back with cheap jackets that gape at the shoulder. She laughs about it, picks up her needle, and saves the thing.

units: the first step is to put the trousers on in front of a mirror
the wanted height is fixed with pins set close together
the original edge must be opened with a seam ripper
a pass of the iron wipes out the trace of the old fold
a reserve of cloth is kept below the marked line so the work can be undone
the extra is turned inward and then fastened
the stitching must not show on the outer face
specialists advise a fitting before the pins come out
text: Shortening a pair of trousers at home demands a method, and every alterations workshop prescribes the same succession of operations, always in that order. Put the trousers on in front of a mirror, fold the cloth up to the height you want, and mark that line with a row of pins placed close together. Take them off, open the old edge with a seam ripper, then press the fold flat so that the earlier crease disappears for good. Now cut, and leave a margin of cloth below the marked line, or the whole job can never be undone. Turn the extra under, pin it down, and fasten it with stitching that stays off the outer face. A last pass with the iron settles the edge. The professionals who do this for a living always repeat the same warning: try the trousers on once more before a single pin comes out.

units: an idle textile mill set in a valley has started working again
buyers turned away from knits that pill after few washes
those buyers now ask for tougher and costlier yarn
the fleeces raised locally have found a market value again
before that, farmers destroyed those fleeces for want of a buyer
carding workshops and a dyeing house are running once more
the technical manager ties the state of the weaving to the state of the region
the shortage of trained staff holds this recovery back
text: The mill had stood silent at the bottom of the valley, and now its looms have started beating again. The cause is a quiet turn in taste, nothing grander than that. Buyers grew tired of knits that pill after a wash or two, and they began asking for longer, tighter, costlier yarn. That demand put a price back on the fleeces raised nearby, which farmers used to burn for want of anyone willing to take them. From there the effect spread outward. Carding sheds reopened, a dye house lit its vats again, and workrooms relearned how to set a neckline by hand. The technical manager puts it plainly: the weave of a sweater tells you how a whole region is faring. One shadow hangs over all of it. Trained hands are scarce, and learning the trade asks for a patience few applicants will give.

units: the work garment described takes more strain than office clothing
the arm opening is the zone that breaks first
loading the pockets pulls the front of the garment out of shape
contact with rough surfaces wears a hole at the elbows
a triangular insert is added under the arm to follow the movement
the pocket ends are locked with extra stitching
a removable reinforcing patch guards the elbow without taking the sleeve off
the inside of the garment can be taken out depending on the season
text: A builder's jacket takes strain that office clothing never has to meet. At the shoulder, the armhole opens and closes from dawn until dusk, and the seam there gives way long before anything else does. At the pockets, the weight of tools drags the cloth downward and pulls the front of the jacket out of shape. At the elbows, rubbing against rough surfaces wears the weave right through to a hole. Manufacturers answer each fault on its own terms. They widen the armhole and set a triangular gusset under the arm to take up the movement. They back every pocket and lock its corners with extra stitching. They lay a patch of heavy cloth over the elbow, and it can be swapped out without taking the whole sleeve apart. The lining stays removable, so it comes out once the cold season ends.

units: the text sets two wardrobes against each other
the first holds a small number of garments picked with care
several of those garments are more than ten years old and show visible mending
the second wardrobe is crammed with impulse buys dropped after one season
those clothes are cast aside because of a slack knit or a torn buttonhole
the writer rules out the explanation by money
the owner of the crowded wardrobe has in fact spent more
the writer puts the difference down to examining how a garment is made
he suggests teaching those checks the way we learn to read a package
text: Set two wardrobes against each other and examine them closely. The first holds a handful of garments, each one chosen slowly, and several have lasted past their tenth year and carry mending that anyone can see. The second is crammed with things bought on impulse, worn for a single season, then dropped because the knit went slack or a buttonhole tore at the first snag. People reach for the family budget as the explanation. It does not hold, since the owner of the crowded wardrobe spent more. What divides the two habits is the attention paid to how a garment was made. Look at a seam, tug a loose thread, turn back a collar to judge the lining. Such verifications cost nothing and weed out the articles that are already doomed. We ought to teach them the way we teach reading a food label.

units: the woman described mends clothes in a cramped room of a shopping arcade
her work falls into three kinds
she repairs damage such as tears and unpicked edges
fitting a garment to the customer takes the largest part of her time
factory sizes rarely suit real bodies
turning one garment into another is her favorite task
she was trained by an older professional
she sharpened her practice alone over twenty years
she turns down an apprentice who is in too much of a hurry
text: The mender works in a narrow room at the back of a shopping arcade, and her trade falls into three distinct branches. First come the accidents, a tear at the knee, a buttonhole stretched out of shape, an edge ripped open by the heel of a shoe. Then comes fitting the body in front of her, which consumes the greater part of her week, since a factory size corresponds to almost nobody's real silhouette. She takes in a back, tightens a slack neckline, shortens a sleeve by a whisker. Last comes remaking, the part of the work she likes best. A dress nobody wears becomes a skirt, and a worn coat gives up its lining to another. She learned all of it from an older tailor, then spent two decades sharpening the craft entirely on her own. She turns away any apprentice who arrives in a hurry.

units: the narrator judges his coat badly during the first cold season
at the start the collar flipped up and the back went out of shape
the color struck him as dull next to an older garment
during the second season the cloth took the shape of his frame
the third season was very rainy and the garment dried overnight
the inner part split under the arm
the repair cost a small share of the price paid at purchase
the narrator recommends this coat despite its awkward look at the start
text: Honestly, this coat had me doubting it for quite a while at the beginning. That first winter the collar kept flipping up, the gathers across the back puffed out in an odd way, and the color looked drab beside my previous jacket. By the second winter the cloth had softened and taken the shape of my shoulders, and the lapels finally hung straight on their own. The third winter was the best of them. It rained without any letup whatsoever, the surface drank the water and dried overnight, and nothing ever smelled off. Then the lining split under one arm and I thought the coat was finished. A mender charged me a tenth of what I had paid for it, and off it went for another round of service. I would tell anyone to buy one, as long as you can live with it looking ugly the first year.

units: the writer writes to his sister to announce a shipment
the crate holds a garment that belonged to their father
damp in a space under the roof was threatening the inside of the garment
the writer also feared the insects that attack stored clothing
the outer cloth has stayed sound, which is why he sent it
the end of one sleeve is worn by an arm resting again and again on a workbench
a professional offers to take material from under the collar for a discreet repair
the writer states that cloth of that kind loosens when it is worn
text: Dear sister, I am writing before the crate leaves, because what is inside it needs a proper word of explanation. You will be getting our father's blue jacket. I am not sending it along out of sentiment. Damp under the roof had begun eating away at the lining, and a garment left in a trunk ends up chewed through by moths. The outer cloth has held, and that is exactly why I decided it was worth saving. You will find the right cuff frayed. That comes from years of an arm resting on a workbench, which polished the weave away in that particular spot. A seamstress promised me that a piece taken from under the collar would make the repair invisible. Have it done, then wear it without the slightest worry. Cloth of that kind stiffens while it hangs and loosens once you put it on.

units: the text deals with the insect that damages woolen knits
the worry comes up when the knits are stored at the end of the cold season
it is the young form of the insect and not the flying adult that eats the material
traces of sweat draw that larva toward animal fibers
a washed garment therefore offers little food
storage in a closed and opaque container beats an open shelf
two nights in the cold destroy the eggs
traditional scented sachets drive the pest off without killing it and soon lose their force
regular care by airing and refolding is the most reliable cure
text: Should we fear the insect that riddles our woolens? The question comes back at the close of every cold season, when the knitted things go into storage. It is not the winged adult that eats the yarn but its larva, blind and tiny, drawn toward animal fibers and above all toward the traces of sweat soaked into them. Hence the first answer: a garment washed clean feeds that larva poorly. And the storing itself? A closed, opaque bag beats an open shelf, and two nights in the cold will kill the eggs laid along a seam. What about the scented sachets our grandmothers tucked between the piles? They drive the pest off without killing it, and the effect fades fast. The lasting cure is a thoroughly dull habit. Pull the woolens out, shake them, air them, and fold them a different way.

units: the craftswoman answers her student's questions about the fabrics in the workroom
she names first a light fiber used for warm-season shirts
she describes a second, rougher fiber meant for sacks and aprons
she states that a short-pile cloth swallows the light and suits ceremonial jackets
she points out that a pressed material never frays and spares the finishing of edges
she buys in narrow strips an openwork cloth that she fastens onto collars
the openwork cloth is the most expensive because it demands a patient hand
she asserts that the choice of a material depends on the purpose of the garment
she announces that the student will know the fabrics by touch before knowing them by sight
text: The seamstress fields her student's questions about the cloth stacked on the shelves around the workroom. Linen comes first: cool against the skin, easy to drape, and saved for the shirts worn through the warm months. Hemp comes next, coarser under the fingers, the fiber she reaches for when she cuts sacks and aprons. Velvet, she says, swallows the light instead of throwing it back, and it suits a jacket meant for ceremony. Felt never frays at the cut, so nobody has to finish its edges. Last she names lace, which she buys in narrow strips and stitches onto collars. Her student asks which one costs the most. Lace, by a wide margin, because it demands a patient hand and a trained eye. Cloth is picked for the job it has to do, she adds, never for taste alone, and before long her student will know each one by touch sooner than by sight.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: old fabrics came from fibers drawn out of plant stems
preparing those fibers called for soaking and then beating
getting enough to clothe a single chest took several weeks
harnessing the wheel to the distaff raised output
pedal looms freed the weaver's hands
the steam engine then made the workrooms bigger
the price of a shirt fell so far that people of modest means could own two
fibers born of chemistry are the most recent stage
those recent fibers dry quickly and barely crease
text: Picture a workroom where the thread is still spun by hand, strand after strand, and you have the starting point of the whole story. Old cloth began its life as fiber stripped away from the stems of plants. You soaked it, you beat it, you combed it out, and weeks went by before you had enough of it to cover a single chest. Then somebody clever hitched a wheel to the distaff, and output climbed. Pedal looms came along after that, and the weaver's hands were suddenly free for nothing but the shuttle. Steam took over next, the workrooms swelled, and the price of a shirt dropped so low that people of modest means could keep two of them at once. The latest turn you are probably wearing right now: thread that came out of chemistry, which dries again in no time and stubbornly refuses to crease.

units: the wearing out of a shoe follows mechanical causes
the foot rolls its weight from back to front
that way of bearing down wears the heel first and then the toe
the thinning of the outer layer removes the cushioning
the unabsorbed shock travels up to the knee joint
hard surfaces speed up the breakdown of the sole
a sole soaked with water loses its shape and its stiffness
makers stack layers of unequal density
the writer concludes that the stride wears the shoe more than the material does
text: A shoe wears out along mechanical lines, and never at random. The foot rolls its weight from the back toward the front, so the sole meets friction unevenly: the heel goes first and the toe follows behind it. Once the outer layer thins away, the cushioning is gone and the shock climbs straight up to the knee joint, which is why steady walkers ache there. Hard surfaces speed the whole process up, since the ground gives back nothing of what it takes. Water makes matters worse. A sole soaked through swells out of shape, loses its stiffness, and lets the foot slide around inside. Makers answer by stacking up layers of unequal density, firm underneath and softer on top. That holds up far better, though the principle stands: it is the stride that wears the shoe, not the material.

units: a tear damages the front of a borrowed dress
the dress has to be returned the next day
an edge-to-edge seam would have left a visible mark on the satin
the idea of hiding the tear under a belt is dropped
a neighbor who once kept a sewing supplies shop examines the cloth
the neighbor suggests adding an embroidered motif rather than mending
the embroidered motif shows a stem and three leaves
the owner of the dress notices the motif and asks where it was bought
text: A tear the width of a fingernail ran across the front of the borrowed dress, and the woman who had to hand the thing back the next day felt her throat tighten. Drawing the edges together would have left a ridge on the pale satin, plain to anyone. She thought of hiding the whole thing under a belt, then gave that up, since the waist sat too high. The neighbor across the landing, who had once kept a shop for sewing supplies, turned the cloth toward the window and studied it. Her idea was not to mend but to add: pale thread, a stem and three leaves, laid exactly over the wound in the satin. The work took up a whole evening, the needle moving along without hurry. The owner stopped short at the motif the next day and asked where it had been bought. Not for sale, came the answer.

units: the choice of a fastening system depends on the intended use
the lace runs through metal rings and spreads the tension over the whole height
the lace adjusts finely and can be replaced for a trifling sum
the lace calls for slow handling and comes undone if the knot is loosely tied
the metal clasp shuts in one motion and holds without supervision
the metal clasp imposes a fixed width that does not follow changes of measurement
lacing is advised for a work garment worn over layers of varying thickness
the metal clasp is advised for a formal jacket because it stays discreet
the edge must be reinforced against pulling before assembly
text: Before you settle on lacing or clasps, look hard at what the garment has to do. A lace threads through metal eyelets and spreads the pull evenly all the way up the opening. It tunes finely, and replacing one costs next to nothing. The drawback is handling: lacing is slow, and a knot pulled loosely will work itself open. A clasp shuts in a single motion and stays shut with no attention at all, but it locks you into one width, so the garment stops following the body once the measurement shifts. For work clothing, choose the lace, because the tension has to change with the thickness of whatever is worn underneath. For a formal jacket, the clasp keeps out of sight and leaves the front undistorted. Either way, check that the edge is braced against pulling before you set the lining in.

units: a trade gathering devoted to fabrics has just ended
the organizers single out four announcements
a group of workshops claims it can break cutting scraps back into fiber and feed them into fresh yarn
a woven label will state the origin of the fiber and the place of dyeing
several retail chains pledge to make the list of their subcontractors public
a machine now trims the selvedge without scorching it
that trimming does away with the hard ridge the sewers had to remove
the exhibitors expect these pledges to turn into firm orders
text: A trade gathering devoted to cloth came to a close last night, and its organizers single out four announcements from it. The first concerns recycling: a group of workshops says it can break cutting scraps back down to fiber and feed them into fresh yarn without weakening it. The second covers traceability, since every piece will now carry a woven label naming where the fiber was grown and where it was dyed. The third bears on manufacturing conditions, with several retail chains pledging to publish the list of their subcontractors. The fourth is quieter and speaks mainly to technicians: one machine now trims the selvedge without scorching it, which does away with the hard ridge that sewers used to cut off separately. Exhibitors are waiting to see the pledges turn into firm orders.

units: a coat hanging near the door changes its look as the seasons pass
at the end of the cold season the velvet collar bears the mark of the scarf
the pile of the collar stays flattened in one direction
during the mild season the garment is brushed and then stored in a cotton bag
the cotton bag takes away its smell of smoke
through the hot stretch it sleeps folded on a high shelf
it is folded with the lining outward to avoid marks
a damp cloth and a warm iron erase the crease that appeared across the back
the felt hat keeps a dent for good once the dent is pressed into it
text: The coat hangs from a hook beside the door, and it does not look the same from one season to the next. At the close of the cold months, the velvet collar still shows the place where the scarf pressed down on it: the pile lies flat one way and will not stand back up. The mild weeks arrive, and the coat is brushed, aired out, then hung inside a cotton bag, where the smell of smoke gradually leaves it. Through the hottest stretch it sleeps folded on a high shelf, the lining turned outward so that nothing marks the face of the cloth. When the chill comes back, out it comes with a sharp crease running across the back, which a damp cloth and a warm iron eventually smooth away. The felt hat above it goes through the same round, but forgives less: a dent pressed into it stays for good.

units: the writer is irritated by the flimsiness of mass-produced clothing
the seams give way at the second wash and the linings split
the customer buys again the garment he has just worn out
the labels have found that fast turnover pays better than durability
makers cut the weight of the cloth and drop the reinforcements at the stress points
an alterations shop now turns down certain repairs for lack of solid material
the writer notes that customers accept a shirt lasting a single season
the writer believes the change will come from the piled-up cost of failed purchases
text: Honestly, the state of the clothing turned out in bulk is enough to put anyone out of temper. Seams give way at the second wash, linings split open, and the buyer ends up paying twice for the very jacket he has just worn through. There is no mystery in it: the labels worked out long ago that fast turnover pays better than durability. So the cloth is made lighter, sturdy thread gives way to something thinner, and the bracing at every stress point quietly disappears. The alterations shop down the street now turns certain jobs away, because nothing is left for a needle to grip. And we adjust: a shirt that survives one season strikes us as normal. My guess is that the reckoning will come from the wallet, once the failed purchases add up to more than one garment sewn to last.

text: In a narrow room that opens straight onto the street, the shoemaker has been cutting soles since the day he left school. The trade nearly went out with him. Customers brought things in for repair less and less often, the leather suppliers would sell only in lots too heavy for one workshop to carry, and nobody came asking to be trained. He could have shut the door. Instead he changed what he made: rather than waiting on repairs, he turns custom wooden lasts for difficult feet, the ones that mass production rubs raw. His orders come from doctors and rehabilitation therapists now. He has trained two apprentices, and one of them already assembles the uppers on her own. Asked what he is proudest of, he points to a pair on the bench whose sole carries the print of an uneven stride, and says the foot gives the orders, never the model.

text: Two dresses stand facing each other in the back room, and nothing about them agrees. The first, cut from dark velvet, drinks the light; it has weight, it falls straight, it hushes everything around it. The second, in undyed lace, lets both the air and the eye pass through, so the wall shows behind it as though the cloth were unsure it existed. At first glance the velvet wins, so plainly does its mass command the room. Then the eye lingers, and the verdict turns over. Velvet offers a surface and nothing more, while the lace lays out its own drawing, every loop holding the next with no knot in sight. In the end you admire the hand that tied it rather than the dress itself. The odd part is what you carry out: the heavy piece slips away, the light one keeps pulling you back.

units: the writer is taking a garment-making class

text: I signed up for a garment-making class right when the cold weather settled in, and I have been meaning to tell you how it is going. Our teacher opened the first session by passing around scraps of fabric and asking us to hem a cotton square by hand. My stitches wandered off in every direction, crooked and uneven. I pulled them all out and started over, two evenings running. At the next session she showed us how to baste, a loose row of stitches that holds the layers still so nothing slides under the needle. It looks like pointless extra work until the day you skip it. After that came mending. I patched a worn trouser knee with a heavier piece of canvas, stitched on from underneath. Yesterday I finished a lined skirt. I am coming home with a box of pins, a metal thimble and every intention of keeping at it.

units: the little balls on a knit come from the length of the filaments

text: So what makes a sweater start pilling after barely a handful of washes? The answer comes down to the length of the fibers themselves. The short ones work their way to the surface, tangle together under friction and roll into the little balls that make a garment look tired. A long fiber spun into a tightly twisted yarn holds up much better, because the loose ends stay trapped inside the strand. Then a cheap sweater is doomed? Usually, yes, although the cut of the garment and the way you care for it count just as much. A sleeve that rubs against a bag strap all day will pill no matter how good the knit is. Can you fix it? Of course. A fabric shaver or a fine comb lifts the top layer right off. The operation does lighten the color a little, so work slowly and stop well before you have gone too far.

text: The man who runs the alterations workshop remembers a customer who walked in one morning with a coat whose lining was falling apart under the arms. “She was sure it was finished,” he says. He sees the same thing constantly. The lining is cut from a light cloth, and it gives out long before the wool around it, because it takes all the rubbing from the shoulder. Setting the whole thing right takes a single session at the machine. He opens the armhole, swaps the ruined panel for fresh satin in the same shade, then closes the seam by hand so no ridge shows through. “That coat has another ten years in it,” he adds. He turns away any job that would cost more than buying a replacement. His book is full three weeks out, which tells him that people are turning back toward repair. Bring it in, he says, at the first loose stitch.

text: Getting a clear, steady color out of cloth once demanded a kind of patience we no longer have. The dye came from pounded roots, boiled bark and crushed shells, and no two successive vats ever yielded quite the same shade. Cloth left the bath uneven and alive, marked by the hands that had lowered it in. A metal salt had to go into the bath as well, or the color simply walked away with the first rinse. Dyes made in the laboratory overturned that whole order. They hand you the same shade from one bolt to the next, they hold through washing, and they cost a small fraction of what the old ones did. The gain is real. So is the loss. Where a dyer once read a whole season and a whole harvest in a length of cloth, we read nothing but a repeatable reference. Our closets have gained in steadiness what our eyes have lost in surprise.

units: the text distinguishes three categories of textile materials

text: Three broad families of fiber share the contents of a closet. The first comes off animals. Wool, shorn from a fleece, traps air in its crimp and keeps the cold at a distance. Silk, unwound from a cocoon, gives a smooth, glossy surface. Down, plucked from under the feathers, weighs almost nothing and swells to fill a huge space. The second family grows out of the ground. Cotton, pulled from a boll, soaks up moisture readily. Linen, stripped from a stem, dries fast but creases the moment you sit down. Hemp stands up to hard wear. The third family is made in a plant, where some fibers start as cellulose and others as petroleum, and they can be spun as fine as anyone wants. Each family sets its own rules for washing temperature and for drying. Mix two of them in a single garment and those rules begin to contradict each other.

text: A tailor whose shop stands in one of the older streets received a visit from a customer whose dress had torn at the shoulder on the evening before a ceremony. He studied the tear under a magnifying glass, saw that the weave had given way across a short span, and assured her that the dress could be saved. He began by setting pins around the weakened area so that nothing in it could shift. Then he stretched the cloth over a wooden hoop, to keep the weave from drawing in on itself. From an inside seam he drew a length of thread that matched the color of the dress exactly, and he set about darning the tear one stitch at a time. The whole operation took up much of the evening. When he was done, the damage showed only under a lamp held at a very low angle. The customer went away with the dress she had planned to wear.

units: the heat of the water decides the outcome when washing a wool knit

text: Before a wool sweater goes anywhere near the sink, check the temperature of the water, because that is what settles the outcome. Water that runs hot lifts the tiny scales that line each fiber. They catch on one another, the knit mats together, and the sweater comes out smaller for good. Lukewarm water leaves the fiber alone. A mild soap is enough, since anything harsher attacks those same scales. Do not rub the wool and do not wring it out either, because the agitation felts it exactly the way heat does. Press the sweater between two towels instead, then lay it flat to dry. Hung up, it will stretch under its own weight. Brushed leather obeys a different set of rules. Soaking stiffens the surface, so brush it dry with a soft brush, always in one direction. A light surface mark lifts off with an eraser made for the purpose.

text: Inside the sorting warehouse the bags are stacked up to the rafters and the smell of damp cloth catches in your throat. “Ten tons a week come through here, and half of it is worth nothing,” says the woman who runs the place and who has been sorting here for ten years. The volume is not really the problem, she says. The blends are. A shirt that mixes cotton with a plastic fiber cannot be recycled, because there is no way to pull the two apart. So it gets burned, or it gets shipped off somewhere else. Her answer comes in three separate pieces. Make clothes out of one material. Put a readable label on them that states exactly what is inside. And set up repair workshops next to the collection points. Two towns nearby did open one, and what they send for destruction has dropped sharply. She hopes the arrangement gets copied elsewhere.

text: Two coats hanging from the same rail have almost nothing in common. The first is cut from a thick wool in a deep charcoal, with a surface that catches against the palm like felt. Its seams are doubled, its buttons sewn through four holes, its collar rises to the jaw. It sits heavy on the shoulder, and it will hold up through one cold season after another. The second, a bright blue coated canvas, crushes down inside a fist and folds away into a pocket. Its slick lining slides along the arms, and its zipper runs in a single line from hem to chin. It cuts the wind better than its neighbor, yet it lets the cold straight through the moment the air stops moving. The wool pills in patches, while the coated canvas cracks along the creases. One coat protects you by its weight, the other by its skin.

text: Nothing gives a wardrobe away like the shoulder of a jacket. Stand off to one side and look. If the seam falls in a straight line, someone thought about the garment. If it caves in, the thing was turned out by the yard. You can settle the cut in a second, before your hand ever touches the cloth. The cloth itself reads from the back of the weave, where you find out whether the threads sit packed tight or left slack. The finishing reads in the buttonholes, whose edges should be closed and even. And the upkeep is decided at the counter. A coat with a button you cannot replace and a lining you cannot restitch does not deserve your attachment. A replacement lining lasts as long as the first, provided a seam gives the needle something to grip. We wear what we could never repair, and that helplessness costs us more than we admit.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)

text: The weaver took over her family's workshop because orders for blankets had dried up. She learned the trade in stages, first sorting fleeces, then spinning, and at last weaving wide panels. That slow apprenticeship shaped the way she works now. She can name a fiber by touch alone, without so much as a glance at it. Industrial dyes struck her as harsh, so she colors her skeins in pots of boiled roots and bark. Every batch comes out a shade away from the last, and that unevenness draws buyers who have grown tired of uniform cloth. Demand climbed, and she had to take on an apprentice. The younger woman starts by learning to watch, because one thread pulled too tight warps the whole piece. Patience, the weaver says, is not a virtue in this room. It is a technical requirement.

units: the speaker was disappointed by a knit garment as soon as he put it on

text: Honestly, that sweater let me down the moment I pulled it on. The knit felt scratchy, the collar rubbed at my neck, and the tag had promised a fiber as soft as a cloud. I nearly sent it straight back. Then a friend who sews told me to wash it in lukewarm water with a splash of vinegar, and to dry it flat, never wringing it out by hand. The result surprised me. The knit turned supple, almost downy, and the collar stopped prickling. I pass the trick along now to anyone who grumbles about a scratchy sweater. My objection to the cut still stands, though. The sleeves hang too long, the shoulders gape, and no amount of washing will rescue a bad pattern. Fix that and the workshop would have a decent garment at a fair price. As things stand, I wear it around the house and nowhere else.

units: the writer is writing from a place where clothes are repaired

text: I'm writing to you from the repair shop, in the gap between two fittings, because your question about shoes deserves a straight answer. You're torn between two fastenings. One buckles, the other laces. The buckle goes on in a single motion, which suits anyone who is heading out the door in a hurry. Lacing means sitting down, pulling the laces snug, checking the tension across the instep. In exchange, it holds the ankle far better than the other one does. I watch both kinds come through here. The buckle usually snaps at the rivet, and that repair runs high. Laces you can swap out for next to nothing. If you spend your days on broken, uneven ground, take the laced pair. If your days are a string of short errands, the buckle will do. Write and tell me what you decide. I've set aside a pair of each in your size.

units: the text asks what makes one material different from another

the one who colors goes by how much it absorbs
a plant fiber keeps creases that ironing does not fully remove
the animal fiber offers a springiness that restores the shape
the most prestigious material makes those who mention it fall silent
the most common fiber stirs little enthusiasm because it is ordinary
the practitioners recognize these materials with their eyes closed
text: What separates one cloth from another, if not the hand that judges it? The weaver answers by weight, the seamstress by how a piece holds its shape, the dyer by how thirstily the fiber drinks. Each is right, and each says too little. Ask them about linen and they will talk about a dry coolness, about a crease that no iron ever quite presses out. Ask about wool and they will speak of warmth that breathes, of a spring that pulls the knit back into shape. Ask about silk and they drop their voices, as though the word alone were enough. And cotton? It stirs no poetry, because it turns up everywhere and slips out of mind. There lies the riddle of these materials. They yield to description through their uses, never through what they are. Whoever handles them long enough ends up naming them by touch, eyes shut.

units: a supervisor goes over the order of tasks before production starts

text: The floor manager ran through the order of operations before the run started. Cut the pieces first, he said, on cloth laid out flat and squared to the grain, or the jacket will twist in the first wash. The woman in charge of cutting answered that the pattern had been checked the day before and the templates were true. He went on. Shoulders get joined next, then the sleeves go in, and only after that does the lining go down. One of the operators asked whether the lining should be clipped in place before stitching. The answer came back flat. Clip it, check that it hangs straight, then stitch. The closure comes last of all. The cutter added that the whole thing has to be buttoned on a dress form before it ships, since a crooked line shows up on the hanger and can still be put right at that stage.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the color of a garment was worth more than the cloth itself

only small volumes of them were gathered
that scarcity made social position readable on clothing
the intensity of the red tones signaled the rank of a household

text: For a long stretch of history the color of a garment cost far more than the length of cloth it sat on, and that oddity shaped the whole story of dress. Stable dyes came from sea creatures, from insects, or from uncommon plants, and they were gathered only in tiny amounts. Scarcity made rank easy to read, since anyone could tell a household's standing from the depth of its reds. Rulers widened the gap by law, and forbade certain shades outright to the lowest ranks. Unable to dye anything richer, poorer workshops fell back on grays, browns, and undyed cloth, which fixed the notion of common dress as drab for generations to come. Dyes drawn from a byproduct of industry overturned that whole arrangement. Once bright color came within reach of almost anyone, hue stopped signaling wealth, and cut took over the job.

this flaw discourages recent buyers

text: A sweater fresh off the shelf picks up little balls of fiber fast, and that wear discourages anyone who has just bought one. The cause is mechanical. Short ends work their way to the surface under rubbing, tangle together, and clump into knots that catch the eye. Long yarns, spun from well-combed fiber, slide past one another and pill far less. So the fix starts at the counter, where you look for a dense, smooth knit rather than a puffy one. After that, care matters as much as the material does. Washing the garment inside a mesh bag, with no violent spin cycle, cuts down the friction that tears the ends loose. And once the knots do show up, a fabric shaver lifts them off cleanly, as long as you spread the garment flat and never tug at it. The knit comes back looking crisp, and you can repeat the whole thing without harming it.

units: a woman living on the floor above owned two outdoor garments

the other was cut from a waterproofed canvas and weighed little

she took the light garment when it was raining

text: My upstairs neighbor kept two coats in one closet, and one evening she stood there and explained the difference to me. The first was heavy, cut from thick felted wool, and it sat down on the shoulders like a suit of armor. The second, made of oiled canvas, weighed almost nothing and folded down into a bag. She took the heavy one out when the wind bit, and the light one when the rain came straight down. I wanted to settle the matter, to pick the better of the two, and I was wrong to try. One night in a downpour I borrowed the wool coat. It drank the water like a sponge, and drying it out took two evenings. The other, though, left my back frozen the moment the cold set in. Now I stand at that closet and choose by the sky rather than by preference. Learning the hard way, my neighbor called it.

text: Here is the method that professional pressers use to take the wrinkles out of a shirt without scorching it. For gear, you want a padded board, a clean iron with nothing caked on the plate, and a spray bottle filled with plain water. For prep, empty out the pockets, unfasten the collar, and dampen the cloth until it goes soft under your fingers. For the order of work, begin at the collar, move on to the cuffs, then the sleeves, and finish with the back and the fronts. Narrow areas come before wide ones, since the large panels are the ones that wrinkle last. For heat, set the iron to the most delicate fiber in the garment, and test it on a hidden seam first. For storing, let the shirt cool on a hanger before you button it up, or the trapped damp will press in fresh creases.

text: The shed smelled of damp wool when the doors slid open, a little before dawn. The shearers had come in the day before, and the fleeces were waiting in downy heaps along the wall. In the first hour a sorter pulled out the soiled locks one by one, working steadily, never lifting her head. Around the middle of the session the pressed bales went off to be washed, where warm water carried away the grease. Later the dried fibers went through the carding machine, and the white cloud pouring out of it set the visitors coughing. At the end of the line a worker knitted a sample in front of the onlookers, using the first yarn off the frame. The cooperative hopes to revive a trade that buying from abroad had killed off. Nothing is settled yet. Orders are still thin, and the shearers are getting old.

units: a thick wool jacket soaks up water in a downpour

text: Rain hits a thick wool jacket and the wool drinks it in. Within minutes the wet cloth drags heavily at the shoulders, the sleeves lose their shape and hang crooked, and the lining holds that damp all through the evening. Workshops looked for an answer that would leave the fiber alone. The first one is a hot wax, spread thin across the outer face, which fills the tiny gaps without stopping the wool from breathing. Water rolls off, and the jacket still lets air through. The second is a thin membrane, slipped between the wool and the lining. That film pushes the vapor off a warm back outward and turns the drops away. Either way the coat stays supple and keeps the line it was cut to. Brush the surface, lay down a fresh coat of wax, and the protection holds through a whole season.

units: the speaker finds the choice between natural fiber and made fiber a badly framed question

wool pills as soon as a bag strap rubs it

a loose knit forgives a heavy meal and takes another layer
a tight top draws the figure and wants the exact size

text: People keep asking me whether they ought to buy natural knitwear or a made fiber, and to my mind the question is badly framed from the start. The two families were never promising the same thing. Fine wool warms you with no weight at all, takes up the sweat off your back and lets it go without a smell, then pills the moment a bag strap rubs across it. A made fiber dries in an hour and shrugs off abrasion, holds its shape wash after wash, but sticks to your skin the second you push yourself. Look at the cut as well, because comfort really lives right there. A loose knit forgives a heavy meal and takes another layer underneath. A tight top draws the figure and wants the exact size, nothing near it. So I keep both of them on the shelf and decide by what the day ahead asks of me.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)

those clients refuse to throw their clothes away
text: The dyer works under a low ceiling, and she sorts her skeins on a bench before anything at all goes into the vat. She sums her whole trade up in three habits, without making much of any of them. First the material: her fingers tell a silky strand from a coarse tuft, and she needs no label at all to do it. Then the color. She boils her baths out of bark and root, and what comes up is a deep blue, or a red that shifts as the light moves over it. Third, memory. Every single proportion goes into a stained notebook, because a bath that turns out well will not turn out twice on luck alone. Her clients hand her tired woolens, dulled scarves, jackets gone speckled that they will not throw away. She promises little, gives back honest color, and her notebook is worth far more than her vat.

units: the narrator finds a quilted coat on a modest rack
at first he takes it for graceless
the weeks that follow argue with that first judgment
the quilting holds a layer of warm air in the rain
the high collar closes the throat against the wind without gripping it
the cloth creased by so many journeys takes on a living look
by the end of winter the coat lightens as the layers come off
the narrator concludes that a garment is judged by wear and not on display
text: I found the quilted coat on a modest rack one evening, and I wrote it off at once as graceless, too thick, too careful, sewn for people who take no chances. The weeks that followed argued with me. Under thin rain the quilting held a layer of warm air that nothing scattered, and my shoulders stayed dry the whole way home. When the wind began working through the narrow streets, the high collar showed its sense: it closed my throat against the cold without gripping it. Then came the squalls, and the cloth, creased by so many journeys, took on a living look that fresh cloth never shows. By the end of winter, stripped of the layers it had sheltered, it hung straight and light again. So I will say it plainly. A coat is not judged on a hanger. It is judged after a season of rain and walking.

units: the reader washed a sweater that shrank
a wool fiber is covered in tiny scales
heat lifts those scales up
the tumbling of the drum tangles the fibers together
tangled fibers cannot go back where they started
the shrinking is therefore beyond repair
wash in cold water with no violent spin
dry the piece flat on a towel
a rinse with a little vinegar softens the knit
text: Dear neighbor, you asked me what had happened to your favorite sweater, and the answer turns out to be purely mechanical. A wool fiber is not smooth. It carries tiny scales, laid over one another the way roof tiles are laid. Hot water lifts those scales up. The drum then shoves the fibers against each other, and the raised scales catch and lock like little hooks. The knit closes in on itself, the surface goes hard, and the sweater drops a whole size. No amount of ironing will pull it open again, because nothing can unhook what the tumbling wound together. With the next piece, use cold water and a gentle spin, then lay it flat on a thick towel to dry. A last rinse with a little vinegar softens the knit and gives it back the drape it had. Take good care of yourself, and write soon.

units: the question is whether fine knits should be given up because they pill
pilling starts with short fibers working their way to the surface
friction rolls those fibers into little balls
a long twisted yarn cuts the fault down sharply
the piece must be turned inside out before washing
loads carrying rough materials should be avoided
a fabric shaver lifts the balls off without gouging the knit
the sweater must be folded flat and never hung
a garment handled this way lasts through long seasons
text: Should fine knitwear be given up on the grounds that it pills? The answer calls for a distinction. The fault starts with short fibers that work their way to the surface, where friction rolls them into tight little balls. A long, firmly twisted yarn cuts the trouble down sharply, and the composition label tells you more about that than the look of the piece or the price shown in the window. What can be done with a garment already marked? Turn it inside out before washing, keep it clear of loads that carry rough materials, and run a fabric shaver over it, which lifts the balls off without gouging the knit. Should storage change too? It should. A fitted sweater sags at the shoulders on a hanger, so fold it flat. Handled that way, a fine woolen goes through long seasons unspoiled.

units: a customer cannot decide between two jackets

the saleswoman tells him to think about what he will use it for
the close jacket suits meetings and meals taken sitting down
the wide jacket suits walking about and carrying bags
she offers to take in the shoulders of the wide jacket
the customer leaves with the wide jacket after that offer
text: The customer stood a long while between two jackets hanging on the same rail, and he laid his trouble out plainly. The close cut flattered him, he said, but it caught his arm the second he reached toward a high shelf. The wider cut gave him back his reach, though he was afraid it would leave him looking sloppy. The saleswoman heard him out patiently, then set the two side by side for him. The first jacket, she said, serves meetings and meals taken sitting down, where nobody moves much and the outline counts. The second one goes with walking about, standing around, a bag hanging off one shoulder. She added that taking in the shoulders would tighten the second one without costing it any ease. He thought about it for a while, then left with the wider jacket and the alteration booked.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the earliest cloth comes from stalks soaked in water
those stalks give a cool fiber that creases at the smallest movement
taming herds brought a warm springy fiber
that fiber is spun by hands trained from childhood
a shiny thread is unwound off cocoons
the shiny thread travels down very long roads
a downy seed capsule yields a washable cheap cloth
better looms later turn out a ribbed velvet
every new material redrew the ordinary wardrobe
text: Have you ever wondered where our cloth actually comes from? Let us take it one family at a time, with no hurry about it at all. The oldest of them all starts with stalks soaked in water, then beaten and combed out: what comes off is a cool fiber, easy to wear once the heat sets in, and creased by the smallest movement. Next comes the fleece of tamed herds, warm and springy, spun at home by hands trained from childhood. Later a shiny thread turns up, unwound off cocoons, light enough to carry down endless roads and dear enough to be kept for finery. Then a downy seed capsule yields a washable cloth, cheap enough to clothe whole populations at once. Better looms add ribbed velvet on top of that, thick and striped. Every one of these materials went on to redraw the ordinary wardrobe.

units: the fleece comes off the animal in a single piece
a wash carries off the grease and the dust
carding pulls the tangles apart and lays the fibers in one direction
twist turns the ribbon of fibers into a yarn that holds
the yarn is then stretched on a loom to make cloth
dyeing can happen on the yarn or on the finished cloth
fulling in water draws the cloth tighter and denser
cutting and stitching finish the making of the garment
text: It all starts in a shed at the far end of a field, when the shearer works the fleece off in a single piece. That greasy mass goes straight into water: it is washed, the dust and the twigs are picked out, and it is spread to dry. Then comes carding, which pulls the tangles apart and lays every strand in one direction. The ribbon coming off the combs goes to the wheel or the machine, where twist turns it into a yarn that holds. That yarn is stretched on a loom, crossed patiently with a second one, and even cloth grows steadily under the weaver's hands. Dye can go on at this point, or earlier, on the bare yarn. Fulling in warm water then draws the fibers closer, leaving a denser surface and a softer hand. Cutting and stitching finish off the road that leads from animal to worn coat.

units: the night watchman wears a coat worn through
he lends that coat to an apprentice who is shivering
she finds a lining sewn by hand
the lining carries embroidered initials and a hidden pocket
the pocket holds a square of shiny cloth
the watchman explains that the square came off a dress his mother wore
the apprentice takes the coat to a seamstress to be mended
the watchman accepts the mending but refuses an unworn coat
text: The night watchman's coat was worn through at the elbows, and that had never troubled the man who owned it. An apprentice stood shivering outside the empty warehouse, hands pushed under her arms, and he held the coat out to her without a word of explanation. Pulling it closed, she felt a lining sewn by hand, initials embroidered in dark thread, a pocket tucked away under the seam. Inside it lay a square of silky cloth, bright, smooth against her frozen fingers as still water. He said at last that the square had come off a dress his mother used to wear, and that he kept it there to have it on him. The apprentice carried the coat to a seamstress, who rebuilt the elbows and strengthened the sleeves. He took the mending without a fuss. The unworn coat he was offered afterward he refused flatly.

units: a notebook heads the list of recommended accessories
the lamp in use must carry a red filter to spare an eye adapted to the dark
the steady mount is described as the piece people skip most often
an instrument that shakes gives no usable image
the optical instrument ranks only fourth on the list
a cheap model is judged good enough to start with
two eyepieces of different magnifications are recommended
a star chart is needed to find your way among the stars
going out regularly counts for more than the quality of the gear
text: Want to watch the night sky without spending much? Start with a short list. A notebook comes first, because what you jot down beats what you half remember later. Next, a lamp with a red filter, which spares an eye that has already settled into the dark. Then the mount, the piece almost everyone skips and the one that decides everything: a shaky instrument shows you nothing worth looking at. The telescope itself ranks only fourth, and a cheap model will carry you through your first months. Pack two eyepieces as well, one to sweep wide fields, the other to pull in a detail. Add a star chart, on paper or on a screen, or you will drift from one point of light to the next without naming any of it. Gear counts for less than habit. Go out often, even briefly, and your eye will learn on its own what moves and what stays put.

units: the turning part of the building stayed jammed on opening night

a piece of metal was wedged in the rotation rail
one technician pulled out the obstacle and the other greased the gearing
the structure began to turn again with a low rumble
the crowd first mistook that noise for thunder
the head of the site delivered an improvised speech
the press revealed the next day that the obstacle came from the building work itself
text: On opening night the dome flatly refused to turn. Guests stood about on the terrace with their drinks while two technicians climbed the inner ladder to look at the mechanism. They found a strip of metal wedged in the circular rail, dropped there at some forgotten moment. One of them worked it loose with a screwdriver, and the other greased the gearing. Half an hour later the whole frame began to swing around again, with a low rumble that the crowd took for thunder. The shutter slid open on a clear sky, and the head of the observatory, plainly relieved, put together a speech of three sentences on the spot. What he left out, and what the local paper printed the next morning, was where the metal came from: a bolt the fitters had forgotten, which had nearly wrecked an evening two years in the making.

units: your hands must be dry and free of jewelry before you start
a greasy mark attracts the particles that scratch the surface

the disk is rinsed in lukewarm water with no cloth at all
fabric moves the grains around instead of carrying them off
every grain shifted digs a groove that scatters the light of the stars
the water must run off by itself before the rim is dried
repeated washing damages the reflecting layer faster than the surrounding air
text: Before you so much as lay a hand on the mirror, dry it and take off every ring. A smear of grease pulls in dust, and dust will scratch the surface the moment anything rubs across it. Set the instrument down flat in a closed room, because one draft brings back onto the glass everything you have just cleared away. Rinse the disk under lukewarm water and use no cloth at all. Fabric shoves the grains around instead of carrying them off, and every grain you shift leaves a tiny groove that will scatter the light of the stars. Let the water run off by itself, then blot the rim alone with soft paper. If marks are still there, do not try again tomorrow. Wait out a whole season, because washing too often wears down the thin reflecting layer far faster than a year of open air ever will.

units: maneuvers meant to avoid a collision are becoming more frequent
the cause lies in the buildup of debris in low orbit
a tiny fragment can punch through a reinforced wall because of its speed
every impact produces new fragments whose course turns unpredictable
the phenomenon therefore keeps itself going
the first answer is to catalogue the objects by radar
the second requires a fuel reserve to bring the craft back down at the end of its mission
the third answer, still at the test stage, plans to capture one bulky piece of debris
text: Satellite operators report a steady rise in avoidance maneuvers. Behind it lies a growing crowd of debris in low orbit: rocket parts, bolts, flakes of paint, all traveling fast enough that a chip the size of a fingernail can punch through an armored wall. Every impact breeds fresh fragments, and their paths in turn grow hard to predict, so the whole problem quietly keeps itself going. Space agencies are currently trying three answers. The first is to catalogue what is up there by radar, so that close approaches can be seen coming. The second requires every future craft to hold back enough fuel to drop itself toward the atmosphere once its mission ends. The third, still on the test bench, sends up a chaser to grab one bulky piece with a net or a harpoon and pull it out of orbit.

units: two neighboring circular hollows show opposite appearances
the older one has a softened rim that has nearly vanished
its floor is lined with fine particles stirred by later impacts
the more recent one has a crisp wall cut into terraces
a pointed relief remains at the center of the recent formation
no bright streak surrounds the older formation
pale rays reach far out around the recent formation
those rays come from material thrown out at the moment of impact
slanting light carves a marked shadow on the recent formation alone
both formations belong to the same natural satellite
text: Two neighboring craters offer the patient observer two opposite kinds of relief. The older one has a rounded rim, worn nearly flat, and a floor buried under fine dust that later impacts have stirred over and over. The younger raises a crisp wall cut into a stack of terraces, and its floor still holds an untouched central peak. The contrast does not stop at the outline. Nothing bright survives around the older bowl, while a web of pale rays reaches an enormous distance out around the younger, marking the stuff thrown clear at the moment of impact. Grazing light widens the gap further. The old basin sinks into one flat tone, and its neighbor cuts a hard, stretched shadow across the ground. One and the same natural satellite therefore carries two faces side by side, ages apart.

units: the text asks whether lit signs should go dark after midnight
the writer refuses to treat the subject from the sky watchers' side alone
a beam aimed at the ground costs less than a scattered beam
steady artificial brightness harms the sleep of people living nearby
it also throws migrating birds off course
a whole generation reaches adulthood without seeing the milky band of our galaxy
the writer sees in that loss a landmark shared by all of humanity
not one of the arguments put forward calls for complete darkness
the conclusion argues for aimed lighting, dimmed at night, and for protected areas
text: Should lit signs go dark after midnight? The question deserves more than one angle, and the sky watchers cannot own it. Start with money: light aimed down at the ground burns less than a beam scattered upward. Then health, since steady artificial brightness breaks the sleep of people living nearby and throws migrating birds off their course. Last comes the cultural case, the one that looks weakest at first glance. A whole generation now reaches adulthood without once having seen the milky band of our own galaxy, and with it we give up a landmark every human being used to share. Not one of these arguments calls for total darkness. What they call for is plain: lighting that points where it is needed, dimmed past a certain hour, and protected stretches where the sky stays black.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
