she polished that disk through a whole night
the foreman studied the surface and moved her to a bench
she caught under her thumb flaws that no device of the day could measure
the delicate orders were kept for her
she passed on to two apprentices the rule never to force the glass
her last mirror is still in service and the team using it does not know who she was
text: She came into the optical workshop as a cleaner, very young, with no diploma and nobody to speak for her. The foreman handed her buckets and sawdust and nothing else. One evening she picked up on her own a glass disk that an apprentice had spoiled, and she polished it until daylight. The next morning the foreman held the surface up to a lamp, looked a long while, then moved her to a bench. She never left it. She learned to feel under her thumb a hollow that no device of the day could measure, and the most delicate orders ended up at her station. Near the end of her working life she trained two apprentices, repeating one rule to them: never force the glass. The last mirror she polished still serves under a mountain dome, and the team who use it have no idea whose hands shaped it.

units: the show traces the making of a star and then its end
the images are judged unusually sharp
that quality comes from the scanning of genuine archive plates
the pace never slows at any point
the lack of pauses ends up blunting the wonder of the audience
the unbroken music piles on emphasis that serves no purpose
the narration explains too much and leaves nothing to imagine
the reviewer holds that a shorter show would have left a deeper mark
text: The show impresses from the opening minute, and that is exactly what ends up working against it. The seats tilt back, the vault lights up, and in one sitting you watch a star take shape, swell, then collapse. The images are unusually sharp, because the team scanned real archive plates before setting them in motion. But the pace never eases off for a moment, and that missing breath turns the whole thing around: once one cosmic disaster follows straight on from another, you simply stop being amazed. The music runs without a break as well, piling emphasis on a subject that needed none. The narration, for its part, explains far too much and leaves you nothing to picture on your own. A shorter show, broken by silence and by a sky holding still, would have stayed with me longer.

units: the letter arrived the day before the sun was covered over
the person written to says he is giving up on watching
he pleads a lack of instrument and a lack of nerve
the writer suggests pricking a piece of card with a pin
the card held above a sheet casts a sickle-shaped image
this method rules out any risk to eyesight
a pale ring may close around the disk if cloud moves in
having no instrument is an invitation to watch the ground, the birds and the temperature
the writer asks for an account of what was felt
text: Your letter reached me the day before the eclipse, and I read it standing out in the cold. You tell me you are giving up on watching, having no instrument and, as you put it, no nerve. Let me offer you something else. Take a piece of card, prick it with a pin, hold it at arm's length over a white sheet, and the sun will draw its own thin sickle there, narrowing while you watch, with nothing risked on your side. If cloud moves in, stay where you are. A pale ring may then close around the disk, and that circle alone is worth the walk. As for having no instrument, it forces you to look around you rather than up. The color of the ground shifts, the birds go quiet, the air turns cold all at once. None of that costs a thing. Write and tell me what you felt, not what you thought you were supposed to feel.

units: the question bears on the difference between two rings seen around a heavenly body
the distinction lies in the matter crossed and in the optical mechanism
the first ring forms in high cloud made of ice crystals
those crystals bend the incoming light by one fixed angle
the ring obtained is wide, whitish and steady in size
the second ring forms in low cloud full of droplets or in a veil of fine particles
it comes from diffraction rather than from bending
that ring is narrow, colored and pressed close against the disk
its width depends on the size of the particles
a wide pale ring points to ice, a tight iridescent ring points to drops or grains
text: A reader asks what really separates a halo from a corona, given that both of them wrap the disk in a ring. The answer lies in what the light passes through on its way and in the optics at work. A halo forms in very high cloud built of six-sided ice crystals, which bend the incoming light by one fixed angle. The ring that results is wide, whitish, and comes out much the same size every time. A corona forms lower down, in cloud loaded with droplets or in a thin veil of dust, and it comes from diffraction rather than bending. That ring is narrow, colored, pressed close against the disk, and its width depends on how big the particles are. So here is a simple rule you can carry outdoors with you: a broad pale ring points to ice, a tight iridescent one points to drops or grains.

units: a neighbor tells about a night of stargazing
the instrument was set up on a balcony late in the evening
she first mistook a fuzzy streak for a plane
the sky cleared afterwards
she recognized the comet that had been announced
she woke her brother, who grumbled before joining her
she noticed the object had shifted between two looks
she plans to go out again the next night better equipped
text: My neighbor was still laughing when she told me about her night of stargazing. She had set her instrument up on the balcony around dusk, while the sky was turning purple. For a good while, she said, she could make out nothing at all, just a fuzzy smear she took for a plane. Then the haze lifted, and that was when she caught her mistake: the pale streak she had been following for half an hour was the comet everyone had been waiting for. She shook her brother awake. He grumbled, then came out in his slippers, and the two of them watched the tail stretch above the rooftops. Toward the end she noticed the thing had crept a little to one side between one look and the next. She swore she would go back out the following night with hot tea and a blanket, since she had been shivering without noticing.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: glassworkers learned to polish even surfaces
the earliest instruments stopped distorting the images
stars invisible until then became observable
observers moved from description to measurement
star catalogs grew richer and more reliable
fuzzy patches turned out to be groups of stars
steadier mounts had to be built
precision machinery was born of that need
text: The steady improvement of lenses changed the study of the sky far beyond anything the craftsmen at the bench had in mind. Once glassworkers learned to polish a truly even surface, the earliest instruments stopped bending what they showed, and stars nobody had ever managed to see came into view. That sharpness had an immediate effect: observers gave up describing from memory and began to measure. Catalogs grew thicker and steadier, and faint smudges once lumped together turned out to be clusters of separate stars. Sturdier mounts had to be built next, because a trembling tube threw away everything the glass had gained. Out of that need grew a whole craft of precision machinery, with worm screws, gears and counterweights. Step by step, the glassworker's bench reshaped the way people questioned the night sky.

units: a diffuse glow hides the stars above built-up areas
the cause is lamplight aimed upward
particles hanging in the air scatter that light
faint stars become impossible to pick out
observers have to move away from towns
tilting the lamps toward the ground and capping them solves the problem
places that have applied this measure see their galaxy again
the measure also helps sleep, birds and spending
text: A milky pallor has settled over the sky of every built-up area, and the stars are vanishing under it one by one. The trouble comes from lamps that throw part of their beam upward, where the dust and damp hanging in the air scatter it. A halo forms above the streets, and the flicker of the faintest stars drowns in it. Anyone who still wants a dark vault overhead has to travel farther and farther from the towns. The cure exists and costs little: tilt the lamps toward the ground and cap them with an opaque hood. Small towns that have done so have watched the milky band of our galaxy return above their squares. Residents sleep less fitfully, migrating birds find their bearings once more, and the lighting bill drops. The black sky is not lost; it is waiting for someone to switch off.

units: a stockman brings in a dark stone found on his land
a specialist compares it with an already authenticated sample
the two lumps look alike on the outside
cutting them open reveals internal differences
the authenticated sample holds frozen droplets and metal
the stockman's stone holds only stretched cavities
it actually comes from foundry waste
magnetic pull explains the usual confusion
analysis of the metal content settled the question
text: A stockman brought a black stone into the laboratory, picked up in his own paddock and, he was sure, fallen from the sky. The technician set it beside a reference sample, a meteorite collected in a desert and long since logged. The two lumps looked like twins: dark crust, more heft than their bulk promised, blunted edges. Cutting them apart split their histories. The reference piece showed fine frozen droplets, the chondrules found in primitive rock, and a bright metal web that came out under polishing. The paddock stone held nothing but stretched bubbles, the mark of foundry slag chilled too fast. A magnet answered to both, which is why finders are so often misled. Only the ratio between two neighboring metals settled it, and the stockman went home with a piece of old industrial waste.

units: preparing a session follows a fixed order
power and backup lighting must be checked first
a red lamp keeps night vision from being spoiled
the optics must be aligned and cleaned before dark
the finder is set on a distant target while daylight lasts
the mount must stand on stable ground
the axis of the mount must point at the northern star
the observer must plan for clothing and a hot drink
the charts and lists are gathered last
text: Preparing an observing session works best in a fixed order. Power comes first: a charged battery, coiled cables, and a red-filtered lamp so that notes can be read without spoiling night vision. Optics come next, with the mirror aligned, the eyepieces wiped on a proper cloth, the finder trained on a distant landmark while daylight lasts. Then the mount: a tripod planted on firm ground, legs spread wide, its axis pointed at the northern star so that tracking stays even. Comfort deserves the same care, since sitting still chills a body faster than most people expect, so bring layered clothing, a hot drink and an adjustable seat. Paperwork is gathered last of all, sky chart, list of targets, notebook and pencil. A wasted session rarely comes down to the gear; it comes down to something forgotten in the rush out the door.

units: the craft left its parking orbit on an order from the ground
short bursts corrected a sideways drift
the views sent back first showed a gray cratered expanse
the ground proved rougher than expected
the original landing site was dropped during the descent
angular boulders covered the intended zone
a thin signal confirmed contact with the ground
the dust raised by the thrusters fell back without a cloud
drilling is announced after a recharging phase
text: The probe left its parking orbit shortly before dawn, on an order from the control center. All through the descent its thrusters fired in short bursts to trim a sideways drift spotted the day before. The first pictures sent back showed a gray plain pocked with shallow craters, then ground far rougher than anyone had planned for. Halfway down, the team gave up on the original landing site, since angular boulders littered the chosen patch. Touchdown was confirmed by a thin signal that arrived with the usual travel delay, and the room broke into applause. A side camera then filmed the dust kicked up by the nozzle, which fell straight back without forming a cloud. Drilling will begin after a rest period, officials said, because the lander must first recharge its batteries in the sun.

units: the crew spends its breaks at the observation window
the planet looks blue and streaked with white
the speed of the craft brings sunset back over and over
weightlessness sets loose objects drifting
every piece of equipment must be fastened or strapped down
the retreating water lays bare sandbars
the glazing is thick and built of several layers
a speck of dust at that speed would pierce an ordinary wall
passing into shadow causes condensation
text: Press your forehead against the window and you understand at once why the crew spends every one of its breaks here. Below you a blue marble keeps rolling past, streaked with white, close enough that you can trace the bends of the rivers. The craft moves so fast that sunset keeps coming back, so the sky catches fire, goes dark, and does it all over again. Inside, nothing falls. Weightlessness sends pens drifting to the ceiling, so every tool has to be strapped down or stuck to a magnet. Along one coast a paler fringe shows up, because the tide has pulled back and left sandbars bare. The glazing is thick, built in layers, since a speck of debris at this speed would punch through an ordinary wall. When the station slips into shadow the pane fogs over, and you wait for the warmth to come back.

units: low orbit is filling with dead craft and fragments
every fragment travels fast enough to pierce a wall
every collision breeds new fragments
some altitudes risk becoming unusable
the absence of a binding rule keeps up the inaction
every craft should carry the means to leave its orbit at end of life
a passive tracking device would make avoidance more reliable
recovery vehicles should capture the heavy wrecks
the cost of these measures is small next to the loss of access
text: Are we really going to wait for a major collision before anyone decides to act? Low orbit is filling up with wrecks: spent rocket stages, dead satellites, and shards thrown off by destructive tests. Every scrap travels fast enough to hole a wall, and every impact breeds more scraps, which threatens to put whole altitudes out of use. Operators pass the blame around, because no binding rule forces their hand. Three measures would turn the curve around. Require first that every craft carry enough propellant to drop out of orbit when its work is done. Impose next a passive tracking device, so that avoidance maneuvers stop resting on guesswork. Pay last for tugs able to grab the heaviest hulks. The bill looks steep; it is trivial next to an access our networks take for granted.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a keeper of the nebula register worked from a desk
her colleagues observed directly under the dome
clouds often cut their sessions short
she examined photographic plates through a magnifier
she measured the spread and the tint of the pale patches
her colleagues delivered impressions, she delivered measurements
a single plate took up a whole sitting
one scratch was enough to spoil the examination
she told two categories of fuzzy objects apart
those who came after inherited her classification
text: The woman who kept the register of nebulae hardly ever left her desk, and from there she saw farther than the colleagues posted under the dome. They watched the sky one night out of two, and the clouds spoiled a good part of it. She bent over photographic plates instead, comparing pale patches, measuring how far they spread, noting their tint through a magnifier. Where her fellows wrote down an impression, she wrote down a number. Her patience matched an embroiderer's, since one plate filled an entire sitting and a single scratch was enough to ruin the work. In the end she told two families of fuzzy objects apart, some woven of gas, others made of stars beyond counting. Those who came after her inherited a classification that nights under the dome would never have built.

units: the instrument tested belongs to the cheapest range
the mirror keeps stars sharp out to the edge of the field
the mount lacks mass and shakes at the slightest touch
every focus adjustment sets off a wobble to wait out
the eyepiece supplied gives a cramped field and a soft image
the optical diagonal throws unwanted reflections
the finder adjusts without tools and keeps its alignment
the manual says nothing about adjusting the mirrors
the verdict advises replacing the mount first
text: The budget instrument we tried deserves a part-by-part look, with no favors done. Start with the optics: the primary mirror holds an honest figure, and stars stay as points right out to the edge of the field, which is a surprise at this price. The mount is another matter, far too light, shivering at the slightest touch, and every turn of the focuser sets off a wobble you have to wait out. The extras disappoint. The bundled eyepiece gives a cramped field and a soft image, while the diagonal throws stray reflections across bright stars. The finder, though, adjusts without tools and keeps its aim from one night to the next. Then the manual, rushed through translation, silent on collimating the mirrors, which the buyer will face in the first week. Verdict: a decent tube on a mount that cannot hold it.

text: You asked what dragged me out of bed before sunrise, so here is the whole story. The observing club had put out word about a close pass, and since the forecast promised a perfectly clean sky, I loaded the telescope into the back of the car. That meant a long stretch of dark driving and thoroughly frozen fingers, but what a sight it turned out to be. The planet slid right up against the edge of our own moon, then blinked out behind it, no fade and no warning. The air held perfectly still that night, so the view hardly wobbled at all and I picked out details I never manage from the balcony at home. The cold worked against me as well, since the tube took forever to settle, and I stood there breathing into my gloves while I waited. Come out with me tomorrow night and you will see the difference right away.

text: Should the crowding of the near orbits worry us? The engineer we spoke with does not hedge for a moment. Craft that stopped working long ago keep circling the globe well past the end of their missions, and every crash breeds a whole swarm of fragments. What does that mean for a satellite still in service? A nick no bigger than a grain can open a tank or strip an antenna clean off. So what does she want done about it? First, a planned descent, built into the design and paid for up front. Second, a sweep for the pieces already flying up there, snagged by net or harpoon and then steered down into a controlled fall at sea. Is any of that realistic? She thinks so, but only if the operators sign up to one shared rule and hold to it. Without that, each of them shoves the cost onto the next.

units: the keeper of the dome asks the narrator which he prefers between looking directly and recording

she concludes that taking a picture means handing over one's memory
text: The woman who keeps the dome asked me one evening which I liked better, the eye or the sensor. I told her honestly that I could never manage to choose. So she set the two of them side by side for me. The eye, she said, grabs a moment the way a hand grabs a stone from a riverbed, quick and leaving nothing behind. The sensor waits instead. It stacks moment upon moment until whatever is far too faint to see finally shows itself. I argued back that a drawing holds a warmth no machine ever gets anywhere near. She smiled and gave me that one without a fight. A sketch carries a whole evening inside it, she said, while a raw frame carries nothing at all. Then came the line I keep coming back to. Looking is remembering with your own eyes. Taking a picture is handing your memory over to a machine.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)

text: The story of sky watching breaks into families of instruments, each with its own habits. The earliest tools measured angles with the naked eye and leaned on tables copied out by hand, generation after generation. The lens telescope came next. It shut the view inside a closed barrel, yet it never shook off a stubborn colored fringe. The mirror cleared that fringe away, at the cost of far more weight to swing, and it opened the door to apertures ground glass could never reach. The sensitive plate followed, reaching bodies far too faint for any retina. Then came electronic sensors and linked antennas, which carried the work out past visible light altogether. No family ever drove out the one before it. Each inherited the older ways of measuring, the old catalogs, and often the old mistakes.

the most massive bodies end in an explosion

text: A star begins inside a cold cloud of gas that slowly gives way under its own weight. As the cloud draws inward, its core heats until fusion catches, and that fresh push outward halts the collapse for good. A long and even stretch follows, with the star working through its fuel at a thoroughly steady pace. Once the supply runs thin, the outer envelope swells enormously while the surface cools, and the whole body turns vast and reddish. Those outer layers eventually drift off into the surrounding space, seeding the medium around them with heavy elements. What stays behind is a dense, hot core that goes on cooling with no end in sight. The heaviest bodies take a rougher road and finish in an explosion whose blast squeezes the clouds nearby, where a fresh generation of stars begins to take shape.

text: A radio hobbyist made a habit of leaving his listening station running while he was away from home. A power cut knocked the clock out, so the recordings stacked up with nothing at all to date them by, and he came close to wiping the whole lot. On a whim he opened the last file anyway, and there it was, a short pulse returning at a perfectly steady beat. He had no idea what he was hearing, so he passed the trace along to a university observatory. A researcher there recognized the signature of an onboard transmitter that everyone had written off ages ago. Starved of power, the craft spoke up only when its panels caught the sunlight at one narrow angle. The broken clock had shifted his listening runs and dropped them straight into the one window where the thing had anything to say.

units: blurred images most often come from the setting of the mirrors and not from the sky

text: Fresh telescope out of the box, mushy images, and you are ready to quit? Nine times out of ten the mirrors are out of alignment and the sky is entirely innocent. Here is the routine. Set the instrument outside a good half hour before you plan to observe, or the heat trapped inside the tube will smear everything. Pull the eyepiece, drop a cap with a small hole in it into the focuser, and look through. You want circles nested neatly inside one another. If the middle sits off to one side, work the screws behind the rear mirror in tiny nudges, and never crank one down tight. Replace the eyepiece, aim at a bright star and throw it slightly out of focus until a ring appears. That ring should look even the whole way around. If it bunches up on one side, back the matching screw off by an eighth of a turn, no more.

text: Out on the dry plateau where the latest receiving array is going up, the engineers like to set their worksite against an observatory launched clear of the atmosphere. Both of them chase exactly the same bodies, and there the resemblance ends. The array on the ground can be stretched, patched and swapped out piece by piece. The orbiting craft has to work the first time, since no technician will ever climb up there to tighten a bolt. The array on the ground fights the air, which smears the very signals it wants. Its rival has nothing but vacuum in front of its shell. Power, on the other hand, runs freely into the plateau site, while the craft overhead counts every last scrap of energy it holds. The people running the project insist that the two answers fit together rather neatly.

units: the dome seen from the road looks like a pale pebble set on a ridge

text: From the road that climbs the hill, the dome looks like a pale pebble that someone set down on the ridge. Its slit stands open like a heavy lid and lets an icy draft slide inside. The floor within is bare gray concrete, and it throws back the sound of every single step you take. The great tube of the instrument leans toward the opening and swings slowly around with a low, steady growl. Along the wall run wooden drawers where colored filters sleep beside eyepieces wrapped in cloth. An electrical panel blinks above them, on and off, on and off, all night long. Outside there is not a shred of haze anywhere in sight. A milky trail spills across the vault overhead, a reddish body sits low over the horizon, and the thread of a satellite drifts silently from one edge of the field to the other.

text: The case makes the most sense told in the order it grew. At the start, a sky survey belonged to the team that had taken it, and nobody objected, since plates were scarce and instruments scarcer still. Then digital sensors began pouring out measurements in volumes that no single team could ever work through, and open archives took hold almost without argument. That brings us to now, when the hard part is no longer gathering the data but sifting through it. My position fits into one line. Funding an instrument and not funding the use of its data is digging a well and buying no bucket. Agencies ought to set aside a fixed share of every program for archiving, for calibration and for analysis tools that anyone can pick up. Otherwise we pile up measurements no one will ever look at.

text: You could pass her in a hallway and never guess she spends her nights minding a telescope. It sits high on a windy plateau, well away from the glow of any town, which was the whole point of putting it up there. Dust was her headache, she says. Within a week the mirror would go gray and the pictures lost their edge. Washing it often would have worn the reflecting coat right off, so she went looking for another way. Working with a mechanic, she rigged a soft cover that swings shut the moment the wind picks up. The mirror has stayed bright ever since, and the frames come out crisp. She laughs it off, as though anyone would have hit on the same trick. Her coworkers know better: that cover has saved whole nights of work. She is building a second one now for the instrument next door.

text: Two sky theaters have opened in the same region, and the comparison lands squarely in favor of the second. The first one banks everything on force. Its dome buries you under a torrent of stars so fierce that it dazzles far more than it teaches, and you come out dizzy with nothing held in your head. The second holds back. Its darker vault gives the eye room to breathe, and a spoken narration walks you through the workings of an orbit instead of decorating it. The gap shows plainly in the comet stretch: where one piles on effects, the other simply follows an icy core warming as it draws near its star. Admission runs to much the same either way. The second house also offers a showing with no narration at all, given over to silence. That choice, at any rate, is anything but silent.

units: the narrator writes from a terrace she used to visit with the woman she is writing to

text: I am writing from the terrace we used to climb to, and the sky above it is every bit as wide as you remember. Three sights stayed with me tonight. First the color of dusk, going violet before it drained away behind the ridge. Then a satellite, a patient point of light sliding across the vault without a sound. And last the silver dust of our galaxy, which I have never managed to describe without spoiling its softness. I brought along your old star chart, the one worn transparent at the folds. It still helps me pick out the figures you taught me. Warm wind carried the smell of dry grass, and I caught myself talking to you out loud. Nothing up there has changed, and that comforts me more than I had expected it would. Come back whenever you like. The terrace is waiting, and so am I.

units: liftoff starts once the thrust outweighs the whole assembly

the payload lets go and makes contact with a station on the ground
the phases are set off by physical thresholds and not by a clock
text: People often ask what goes on in the half hour after a launch, and the answer is a strict run of steps. The vehicle leaves the pad the instant its thrust outweighs the whole assembly, and those first seconds are spent punching up through the dense lower air in a blaze of flame. Next the bottom stage, its propellant spent, lets go. Where does it end up? In a stretch of open sea picked out well beforehand. Does the rocket turn at that point? It does. It tips its climb over to build sideways speed, because an orbit is held by speed rather than by height. The nose shroud splits open once air friction stops counting. The payload releases at last, and its antenna reaches for the station that will track it from the ground. Every step fires on a measured threshold, never on a clock set beforehand.

text: The operations manager informed the crew that the maneuver would have to be put off. A flare on the nearest star, he explained, had loaded the upper air with charged particles, and the radio links were suffering badly for it. The flight engineer asked whether the craft might dock all the same before the rotation ended. He answered that it could not, and he gave his grounds: with no steady link, the automatic pilot would stop receiving its corrections, and the approach would turn hazardous for everyone aboard. One member of the crew observed that the water reserves on board were ample. The manager closed the exchange by saying that waiting would therefore cost nothing beyond a measure of patience, and that the maneuver would start again as soon as the stream of particles had eased.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: angle measurements disagreed from one observer to another

metal took the place of wood for the sake of steadiness
adding a telescope to the moving arm cut the error to a tenth
people grasped that the date and the warmth of the air had to be written down
those notes served to allow afterward for swelling and shrinking
sky watching became in this way a strict craft of measurement
observing notebooks survive and bear out this practice
text: Early sky watchers ran into a stubborn trouble: the angles they measured never quite agreed from one observer to the next, and nobody could settle who was right. Wooden instruments warped as damp air soaked into them, and the unaided eye could fix a position only so finely and no further. The remedy came in stages. Metal took the place of wood, being far steadier under weather. A small telescope was then mounted on the moving arm, which cut the error to a tenth of what it had been. Last came the grasp that every sighting had to be written down with its date and the warmth of the air, so that swelling and shrinking could be allowed for afterward. That habit of writing changed the trade: sky watching stopped being a gift of keen eyesight and became a craft of measurement. The surviving notebooks show it, page after cramped page.

units: an asteroid is a dry heavy block

it mixes ice with rocky rubble
as it nears the star its ice turns straight into gas
that change draws out a long tail
both bodies bear witness to the same old beginning
the tail points away from the star whatever the direction of travel
text: Want to get the difference between an asteroid and a comet? Picture two stones. The first is dry, heavy and dusty, and it has been circling close to the star ever since the system took shape. Heat it, cool it, heat it again, and it hardly alters. The second one comes from much farther out, from the black cold at the edge. Ice is packed into it along with grit and rubble. Out there it looks much like the first. But let it swing in close and the ice turns straight to gas, drawing behind it a tail that stretches an enormous way. There is the whole difference: one is a leftover rock, the other a frozen lump that shows what it is by melting. One more thing worth knowing. That tail always points away from the star, whichever way the body happens to be traveling. Both carry the same old beginning, but only the second puts on a show.

units: a power cut left a neighborhood without lighting

her picture showed a blurred but recognizable streak
the power came back at sunrise
a good many of those there were sorry to see it return
the company running the grid blames a faulty transformer
text: The power cut that dropped a whole neighborhood into darkness turned out to have an odd upside. Three scenes tell it. In one courtyard, neighbors who had never so much as traded a word ended up sitting side by side, heads tipped back, counting the stars that had come out all at once. On a nearby roof, a retired teacher hauled out his telescope and put on a show on the spot, holding the rings of a pale planet steady for children who had never seen anything of the kind. Outside a darkened movie house, a cashier aimed her phone at the sky and got, to her own surprise, a blurred streak that anyone could still recognize. The power came back at sunrise. Plenty of those out that night owned up to being almost sorry it had. The company running the grid points to a fault in a transformer.

units: you have to pick a night with no moonlight in it

the star chart comes out only after that step

a falling star may show up toward the east late in the watch
the gear is packed away before the damp gets at it
it is worth writing down what you saw before going to sleep
text: Pick a night with no moon in it, and a rise of ground where your eye can run free. Give your eyes their long slow surrender to the dark, since faint stars will not show themselves to anybody in a hurry. Spread a blanket, lie back, and let your gaze wander the vault without trying yet to name a single thing. When some shape stands out, follow it until it settles into a figure you know. Only then bring out your chart, under a red filter that spares your night sight. Compare, doubt, begin again. Toward the end of your watch, turn to the east, where now and then a falling star cuts across and burns out in a short bright line. Write down what you saw before you sleep, or the next night will blur it. Pack your gear away before the damp works its way into it, and go back down slowly.

units: the count of satellites in low orbit is climbing steeply

the builders are darkening the surfaces that catch the light
the first trials halve the glare thrown back
text: The swelling crowd of satellites in low orbit now weighs on astronomical work, and the mechanism behind it is well understood. Each craft throws the light of the central star back down toward the ground, and when one crosses a sensor during a long exposure, it writes a bright streak across the frame. That streak floods the sensitive elements it touches, so that faint bodies sitting behind it drop out of reach altogether. Teams are left with two costly ways out: throw the frame away, or rebuild the ruined strip by computation. One observatory found that one exposure in ten was spoiled in the early part of the night. The builders have answered by darkening the surfaces that catch the light, and the first trials halve the glare thrown back. For wide field instruments the trouble is as sharp as ever.

units: a sky watched from a lit street looks almost bare
on a lonely plateau the same dome shows a swarm of stars
the whitish band then runs across the sky from one side to the other
the watcher also picks out different tints from one star to another
the gap between the two skies comes from the background, not the gear
the glow of the lamps wipes out the faintest objects
high up, dry air darkens the background of the sky
enthusiasts travel long distances to find darkness
text: Look up from a lit street and you would swear the sky is nearly bare. A dozen pale dots, a smear you can barely make out, and that is the whole show. Now carry those same eyes onto an empty plateau, far from any lamp post, and the dome fills with a swarm. The dots keep multiplying, the milky band runs clean across from one edge to the other, and your eye starts catching color, one star coppery here, another one bluish there. The gap between the two skies has nothing to do with your gear. It comes from the background. Down below, the glow of the lamps drowns the frailest stars and leaves a gray, hazy backdrop. Up high, dry air pushes that backdrop close to black, and the smallest spark stands out. That is why hobbyists drive for hours before they set up a tripod. They are not after a better telescope. They are after better dark.

units: the writer refuses to see near orbit treated as a dump
he lays out three sides of the problem
leftover launcher parts endanger working craft
highly reflective satellites spoil astronomical images
no operator carries the cost of cleaning up
the usual objection invokes the sheer size of the void
the writer answers that the lanes in use are narrow and overloaded
he concludes that a shared rulebook is missing
text: Low orbit should stop being treated as a dump with nobody watching it. Anyone willing to face the question squarely runs into three files. The first is debris: every rocket stage left behind turns into a projectile that threatens craft still doing their job. The second bears on watching from the ground, since bright strings of relay satellites streak across telescope plates and wreck whole measuring campaigns. The third gets discussed least. It is liability, because no operator picks up the cleanup bill it hands to whoever comes after. Someone will answer that space is vast, almost dizzying, and that the risk looks thin. The argument collapses the moment you look at the lanes actually in use, which are narrow and overloaded. A cluttered orbit is no engineering matter. It is a matter of shared rules, and those are missing.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: as a small child she watched the sky from the roof of her parents' farm

the image came out shaky and dim, which suited her
she was later hired as an assistant at a high altitude observatory
she recorded where the comets stood through whole nights
once she ran the survey work she spotted an unknown moving body
she refused to let that object carry her family name
late in her career she urged newcomers to draw the real rather than the expected
text: As a small girl she climbed onto the flat roof of the family farm to follow one far-off star, a notebook balanced on her knees. In her teens she put a telescope together from a cardboard tube and two lenses salvaged out of a glazier's workshop. The image shook, it never came out sharp, and that was enough for her. A mountain observatory later took her on as an assistant, and she spent whole nights on end under a freezing sky, noting down where the comets stood. Once she ran the survey work she picked out a body nobody had reported, a thin point that shifted from one night to the next. She would never let it carry her family name. At the end of her working life she was still teaching beginners the one rule she thought sufficed: draw what you see, not what you hope to see.

units: the reviewer finds the mechanical design of the instrument faulty

that heat stirs air currents which spoil the image at high power
the electronics box lets the damp of the night in
the damp eats away at the electrical contacts
the flaws pile up and drop the instrument to the rank of a beginner model
the remedies put forward cost little
text: The build of this telescope aimed at hobbyists deserves a hard look, since its mechanical choices set off one effect after another. The primary mirror rests on three pads and nothing more. Under its own weight it sags a little, so the test star spreads into an oval smudge instead of a clean disk. The tube, rolled from thin sheet metal, carries heat from the mount toward the optical axis, which feeds air currents inside and blurs the view at high power. The electronics box shuts badly and lets the night damp in, and the damp eats away at the contacts. Taken one at a time, each flaw would be bearable. Together they drag a scope sold as a performer down to the rank of a starter instrument. Putting it right costs almost nothing: a nine-point cell, insulation on the tube, a gasket on the box.

units: the request is made on behalf of an astronomy club
new lighting has gone up along the road bordering their site
observing sessions have become hard
part of the light output goes upward and creates a glare
faint objects turn invisible
members are losing heart and the workshops for newcomers are being dropped
the writers are not asking for the lighting to be taken away
they suggest hoods that aim the light at the ground and lower power at night
they invite the reader to come and see the nuisance after dark
text: I am writing on behalf of the observing society that meets on the plateau. Since fresh lighting went up along the road bordering our field, our sessions have turned into a trial. Part of the output from those lamps goes straight upward, and the glare it makes keeps us from picking out anything faint. Members are losing heart, and the workshops we run for newcomers are being dropped one after another. We are not asking for the stretch to go dark, nor for the work to be undone. A remedy already in use elsewhere would serve: fit each lamp with a hood that throws the light down onto the ground, then cut the power in the deep of the night. The outlay stays small, consumption falls, and the road loses none of its safety. We would gladly host a visit after dark, so that you can judge the nuisance yourself.

units: a rocky planet offers hard ground where a craft can land
a gas planet offers only a steady sinking toward denser layers
gas giants are far bulkier than solid planets
their heavy mass lets them keep a thick gas envelope
a rocky body would not hold that envelope
both categories form in the same starting disk
far from the star the cold binds ice and builds massive cores
those cores then draw in the surrounding gas
bare ground throws back a sharp glint while an atmosphere spreads a soft banded light
text: What sets a rocky planet apart from a gas planet? The first has a hard surface, rough underfoot, where a craft can actually set down. The second offers nothing but an endless fall through layers that keep thickening as you go. Are the two of them alike in size? Not in the least. The gas giants dwarf the solid globes, and their crushing mass holds on to a thick atmosphere that the pull of a rocky ball would simply let slip away. And where do the two come from? Both families grow out of one and the same disk, but far from the star the cold welds ice together, which builds cores heavy enough to trap the gas around them. Do we watch them the same way? Not quite. Barren ground throws back a hard glint, while a gas envelope spreads out a soft milky light in which you can make out bands.

units: the guide says right away that this session will differ from a usual screening
he begins by explaining that a star is a ball of burning gas

text: The guide warned us at the door that this would be no ordinary screening. He started with stars. Drop the idea of a fixed point, he said, and picture a ball of gas burning itself up. Then he took up distances. A woman beside us asked whether the nearest star could be seen at all. Yes, he said, though its light takes more than four years to reach us. After that he walked us through the instruments, from the wooden tubes of the early days to the mirrors of today. He paused on the dark patches on the face of the sun and told us never to aim at it without a filter, or we would burn our eyes. He ended with the probes, craft sent off toward something distant with no way home. The oldest of them, he added, is still rolling through the void, well past the planets on record. Nobody in the room stirred.

text: Long before anyone ground a lens, watchers were already mapping the sky with the naked eye, entering the places of the brightest stars in tables. Those records steered ships and carved up the year. Then came the age of glass instruments, and the dome filled with objects nobody had suspected: spots, rings, moons. The lists swelled, and the trade changed character, because measuring now counted as much as describing. The photographic plate tipped the discipline over. A long exposure brought out stars too frail for the eye, and charts stopped being drawn by hand. Later still, electronic detectors and automated surveys turned out inventories so huge that no single team could ever work through them. The dome overhead has not changed. What has changed is the way we set it down.

text: That shiver we hand to the stars is not theirs at all. It is born in the air we breathe, high above our heads. Warm and cold masses of air mix up there without pause, and each one bends the beam that crosses it, the way an uneven pane of glass would. The ray reaches us along a path that keeps moving, so the star seems to shudder, to flare and fade, to turn coppery and then blue. A planet shows a tiny disk instead of a single point. Its many rays cancel one another out, and its light holds steady. Hence the rule watchers keep: what twinkles is far off, what burns without a tremor is close. When the air settles, the dome sharpens, and the finest detail that all the churning had rubbed out comes through at last. Watchers wait for those lulls and trip the shutter right then.

text: The night promised to be a fine one when the drive motor quit, halfway through a run of exposures. With nothing driving it, the tube stopped offsetting the spin of our world, and every frame came out streaked instead of dotted. The man in charge of the dome suspected the power supply first, then measured the voltage, which read fine. The fault lay in a gear whose teeth had worn down until they slipped under load. Swapping the part meant a week of waiting, and the comet was not going to hold still that long. So the team cut each exposure to whatever the mount could carry without visible drift, then stacked the frames by computer. The outcome came out coarser than hoped, yet it served to measure how the nucleus moved. The lesson fit in one line: a mechanical failure can also be got around in processing.
